statement_of_purpose:
Investigating the metabolic dysregulation characteristic of Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) within TSC2-knockout models revealed to me that tumorigenesis is fundamentally a dismantling of cellular checks and balances. Witnessing rapid proliferation and specific lipid reprogramming in this context shifted my perspective from viewing disease as a static condition to understanding it as a dynamic failure of molecular signaling. This realization drives my current pursuit of biomedical sciences, specifically at the intersection of cancer metabolism and tumor immunology. A significant question in this field that particularly intrigues me is: How do metabolic byproducts of tumor cells actively remodel the tumor microenvironment to suppress immune surveillance? My long-term aspiration is to delve deeper into this crosstalk, aiming to identify metabolic vulnerabilities that can be targeted to reactivate the immune system against cancer.

My journey to explore this field began with rigorous undergraduate training at the ZJU-UoE Institute, where I maintained a 3.83 GPA and earned the Zhejiang University Second-Class Scholarship. Recognizing that modern oncology requires interdisciplinary skills, I independently developed proficiency in R and SnapGene to interpret complex molecular landscapes, ensuring I possess the necessary computational literacy alongside wet-lab skills.

To determine my specific research niche, I actively sought diverse research experiences. My research path commenced in biomaterials, where I synthesized SilMa/GelMa hydrogels and utilized directional freezing to fabricate aligned scaffolds. However, I encountered an intellectual obstacle early on: I realized that while material science was fascinating, my true passion lay not in the scaffold itself but in the intracellular machinery governing the cells within it. To address this, I made a decisive transition toward molecular mechanisms. I joined Prof. Dongli Pan’s Laboratory to build a comprehensive molecular toolkit, mastering techniques from sgRNA design and homologous recombination to viral transduction.

This culminated in my current work in Prof. Hengjia Liu’s laboratory, where I am now fully equipped to tackle complex questions in immuno-oncology. I am independently leading genetic ablation experiments utilizing Flow Cytometry and proliferation assays to dissect how a key lipid regulator impacts tumorigenicity in TSC2-knockout models. This progression—from materials to viral vectors to cancer metabolism—demonstrates my commitment and technical readiness to contribute immediately to a high-level research team at Purdue.

There are many summer programs, but the Purdue SURF program uniquely attracts me because of its reputation for fostering the convergence of engineering and life sciences. I am particularly drawn to Purdue’s collaborative research culture, which is essential for my interest in the intersection of metabolism and immunology. The resources offered by SURF, specifically the opportunity to work alongside distinguished faculty and utilize world-class experimental facilities, are exactly what I need to transition from an undergraduate researcher to an independent scientific thinker.

Participation in SURF will contribute significantly to my career goals by allowing me to immerse myself in an intensive research environment different from my home institution. I hope to gain advanced technical skills in experimental design and broaden my scientific perspective through mentorship from Purdue's experts. My long-term career aspiration is to pursue a Ph.D. in Translational Oncology and eventually lead a research group dedicated to developing metabolic immunotherapies. The rigorous training provided by the Purdue SURF program would be the pivotal next step in transforming this ambition into reality.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in engineering began during my first analog electronics laboratory. After years of learning circuit theory abstractly, observing a real waveform on an oscilloscope—produced by a circuit I had built—gave physical meaning to the equations I had studied. This experience led me to pursue Microelectronics Science and Engineering at Nankai University, where I developed a strong foundation in semiconductor devices, circuit theory, and system-level design.

As my studies progressed, I became increasingly interested in how physical constraints shape intelligent behavior in real systems. This interest was further clarified through hands-on research and project-based work that combined sensing, computation, and interaction with the environment.

Exploration of Research Interests and Preparation

I have explored my research interests through a combination of coursework, independent projects, team-based research, and competitive engineering activities. In a National Innovation Training Program project on backscatter communication, I built a MATLAB/Simulink simulation platform to study movable-antenna reception for low-power IoT systems. The project required addressing a non-convex optimization problem under realistic channel conditions, which strengthened my ability to formulate and solve open-ended research questions.

In parallel, I have been conducting research in Prof. Xudong Wang’s RF circuit group since April 2025, where I am involved in the design of a wideband Marchand balun operating from 2 to 18 GHz. This work has trained me to think carefully about tradeoffs between theory, simulation, and fabrication constraints, and has provided hands-on experience with professional RF design tools such as Keysight ADS.

Beyond circuit-focused research, I led a team project on autonomous driving perception, improving a YOLOP-based deep learning model for lane detection and object recognition. We achieved a 7% accuracy improvement over the baseline while maintaining real-time performance, and were encouraged by the course instructor to continue the work toward publication. This project gave me solid experience in machine vision and exposed me to the tight coupling between perception algorithms and system-level constraints.

I also completed a vibration analysis project using finite element methods, modeling an acoustic board as a Kirchhoff plate and validating analytical results with COMSOL simulations. This experience strengthened my understanding of physical structure and dynamics, which I later recognized as essential for embodied systems interacting with the real world.

More recently, my interest in Embodied AI was solidified through hands-on practice in multiple hackathon projects focused on embodied intelligence and autonomous systems. In these competitions, my teams consistently earned awards, which I attribute to our ability to rapidly integrate perception, planning, and physical interaction under tight constraints. These experiences made me realize that I am particularly well-suited to Embodied AI research, as my background in machine vision, physical modeling, and hardware-aware design naturally supports this interdisciplinary field.

Motivation for SURF and Career Goals

I am applying to the SURF program because of its strong emphasis on faculty mentorship, immersive research training, and access to advanced research resources. While many summer programs offer short-term research exposure, SURF stands out for its focus on independent inquiry, close collaboration with faculty, and preparation for graduate-level research. These features align closely with my goal of pursuing long-term research in Embodied AI.

Participation in SURF would directly support my career goals by allowing me to engage deeply with an open-ended research problem in an academically rigorous environment. Through SURF, I hope to strengthen my skills in experimental design, algorithm development, and system-level integration, while also learning how to clearly formulate research questions and communicate results. I also value the opportunity to build professional relationships with faculty mentors and peers, which I believe will be essential as I prepare for doctoral studies.

My long-term goal is to pursue PhD studies in Embodied AI and contribute to the development of intelligent agents capable of robust perception, adaptive planning, and effective interaction with the physical world. I am particularly interested in research that bridges learning-based methods with physical embodiment and real-world constraints. The research experience gained through SURF will be a critical step toward this goal, helping me refine my research direction, deepen my interdisciplinary expertise, and transition successfully into PhD-level research.

Challenges and Growth

Throughout my undergraduate research journey, one of the main challenges I faced was transitioning from well-defined coursework problems to open-ended research questions. Initially, I struggled with ambiguity and the lack of clear solution paths. I addressed this by actively seeking guidance from faculty mentors, studying research literature beyond required coursework, and learning to iteratively refine problem formulations through experimentation. These experiences have strengthened my resilience, independence, and confidence as a researcher, and prepared me to fully engage with the challenges and opportunities offered by the SURF program.

statement_of_purpose:
In Afghanistan, many girls grow up knowing that their ambitions will be questioned long before they are encouraged. Even when girls have wings, they are often taught by society not to use them. But I held onto a dream that felt larger than my surroundings. I wanted to become an astronaut, and when I realized that pursuing this goal would not be possible where I was, I began searching for a place where curiosity and persistence would be met with opportunity and not restriction just for being a woman. Attending an international high school and later enrolling at The College of Wooster gave me access to an academic path that once felt unreachable, and I chose to pursue it with full commitment.
At Wooster, I am majoring in mathematics on an engineering track to build a foundation that supports advanced work in aerospace systems. Besides, I have actively sought experiences that expose me to real-world space research and engineering design. One of the most formative experiences was my participation in L’SPACE Mission Concept Academy. With a team, we worked on a Mars exploration mission focused on detecting subsurface ice and brines. As a mission assurance specialist, I evaluated risks across mission phases, developed mitigation strategies using risk matrices, and collaborated with students from many engineering branches. This project introduced me to the reality that aerospace engineering is not only about optimizing performance, but also about designing for failure, uncertainty, and safety, these concepts that now shape how I think about engineering problems.
I was encouraged by this experience to pursue deeper exposure to research and technological innovation, and I attended a NASA proposal writing and evaluation program. There, I learned to identify NASA technology shortfalls, design feasible technical solutions, and communicate them through professional proposal formats such as quad charts and technical justifications. Our team’s proposal addressed windshield durability by combining removable tear-off layers with oxynitride-hardened thin glass, reducing replacement costs and improving operational safety. Working within the structure of NASA review rubrics taught me how research is evaluated based on feasibility, risk, and long-term impact. This process strengthened my interest in research that directly informs system-level safety and design decisions.
In parallel with structured programs, I have done independent academic projects that connect mathematical methods with aerospace applications. For instance, in a linear algebra project, I explored matrix-based modeling used in robotic control systems such as the Canadarm on the International Space Station, which deepened my understanding of how abstract mathematics governs real mechanical motion. The more I learned about math applications, the more I became interested in how these systems operate. I also began asking what their long-term consequences are as technology continues to scale. Through an independent project, I investigated space pollution and orbital sustainability and looked into how debris accumulation complicates mission planning, increases collision risk, and shortens satellite lifetimes. This led me to examine propulsion choices more closely, and I wrote an article on Medium to compare chemical, nuclear, and electric propulsion systems, focusing on how fuel efficiency, mission duration, and environmental impact shape the feasibility of future missions. Together, these projects shifted my perspective from viewing aerospace engineering as isolated technical problems to seeing it as an interconnected system where performance, safety, and sustainability must be considered simultaneously.
My experiences and projects in the engineering field, along with my background in mathematics, led me to an enduring interest in aerospace safety and reliability, especially in emerging technologies that will shape future flight systems. This is why I am especially drawn to the battery fire safety research conducted through SURF as my first choice. As aviation and spacecraft systems move toward electrification, batteries become not just power sources but critical safety components. High energy density cells introduce the risk of thermal runaway, where heat and flame can rapidly propagate and threaten entire vehicles, and SURF excites me because of its emphasis on mentored-intensive research, where I will be able to contribute to ongoing projects as an undergraduate rather than solely observing them. 
My academic path has not been without obstacles. I come from Afghanistan, where formal STEM pathways are limited for women, so I had to actively seek opportunities and programs that could substitute for what was not readily available to me. Although my circumstances now allow me to pursue an education, many girls in my home country remain denied that same opportunity, and this shapes how I define my mission. I see my work centered around aerospace engineering, with a focus on structures and systems for long-duration human spaceflight and planetary missions, and I carry these ambitions not only for myself but for those who are unable to study at all. Their absence from classrooms and laboratories reminds me that education is both a privilege and a responsibility, and it is not guaranteed for everyone.  This is why I am determined to contribute to engineering research and to pursue advanced education with seriousness and discipline, until one day I can make STEM accessible to people who do not have the opportunity to get an education.

Engineering was one such field where, from a young age, I always felt that it was intensely difficult, almost impossible. When I saw buildings being high, airplanes being assembled, or cars being produced, I could not help but wonder how, from where, human beings have been able to develop such technology as we are using in today's world. I have centered my interests in electrical engineering, particularly in hardware, such as microchips or electronic systems. I find it fascinating that breakthroughs in hardware make it possible to experience breakthroughs in artificial intelligence research, ranging from efficient calculation to intelligent sensing. I have also centered my interest in other areas, particularly in the design of combustion engines or rockets, and I am intrigued by the experience of designing large scale engines that will largely push the boundaries of human capabilities.

To investigate these interests, I have sought out coursework and laboratory involvement that highlights both theoretical concepts as well as experimental techniques. Specifically, my experience in microfabrication related projects such as photolithography and device processing has allowed me to learn laboratory equipment operation and understand the importance of laboratory cleanliness and accuracy in laboratory work. Additionally, my laboratory experience has allowed me to develop a range of techniques for device analysis and characterization utilizing high-end optical and measurement equipment. These laboratory experiences have allowed me to further develop my skills in systematically approaching an experimental procedure and interpreting results in order to document and articulate my findings effectively in clear and concise language.

Although many summer research experiences exist that provide a great opportunity for research engagement, what makes Purdue Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) interesting for me is its focus on intensive, faculty supervised research at a premier engineering environment. The culture of innovation at Purdue and its state of the art lab facilities make SURF a program that strongly resonates with my interests. The organized research environment at SURF together with its professional development and communication aspects make it a perfect place for gaining competence and experiencing research autonomy.

Being a part of SURF will be a very important component in the pursuit of my long term goal to acquire a PhD in Engineering. SURF will enable me to acquire extensive and full time research experience that will give me the opportunity to focus my research ideas and develop my analytical and experimental abilities and the skills to pose and analyze open questions in science. My personal goal in pursuing SURF will be to acquire extensive knowledge in experimental and analytical techniques in electrical engineering hardware and high-performance systems and to develop an understanding and familiarity with how faculty and graduate researchers conduct their work at the doctoral level.

One of the most challenging aspects of my pursuit of higher educational opportunities has been the transition from the initial stages of carrying out my university education in a foreign institution to furthering my educational pursuits in the United States higher educational system. I had begun my university academic program in the country of Algeria in an engineering-oriented academic program. My ambition to further my educational pursuits in the United States prompted me to practice tennis harder in order to obtain a scholarship to pursue my academic objectives in the United States.

However, once I arrived in the US, I was faced with an unexpected issue of being placed by the athletic department into a non-STEM major named Multiplatform Production, which was not aligned with either my previous or future academic objectives related to becoming an engineer. Moreover, a considerable number of the previously accumulated credits were not transferrable, and I had to fulfill proficiency requirements through either placement or competency tests of some of those subjects. To shift to a STEM major and adhere to NCAA regulations and keep my scholarship, I had to overload my credits heavily in school.

This adjustment required me to complete almost two years' worth of academic coursework in one year while I continued to meet the demands associated with collegiate athletics. I sought guidance through academic advisors and faculty, mapped out my course trajectory, and remained committed to disciplined time management. Demanding as it was, this experience hardened my resilience, adaptability, and ability to perform under sustained pressure, all qualities applicable to research environments.

Overcoming these challenges has made me even more committed to engineering and showed me my capability to handle intensive workloads while maintaining long term focus. It balanced academic rigor, research preparation, and my student-athlete responsibility that have prepared me to do well in challenging research settings such as SURF and to confidently and determinedly pursue advanced study in STEM.

statement_of_purpose:
If you had asked my fourteen year old self what I wanted to do, the answer would've been far from engineering. To my sixteen year old self, she would've answered straight away that she wanted to major in mechanical engineering and that she wanted to join one of the country's national higher schools of engineering, and I did. These universities offer 5 year programs culminating in a combined Bachelor's and master's program in whatever engineering discipline one chooses after 2 years of general engineering. I enrolled in the school closest to home, intending to transfer later to one that offered the discipline that I wanted. But due to circumstances, I had to stay in that school and major in the only specialty they offered : hydraulics engineering. 
Although I was disappointed at first, I've come to actually enjoy studying that major. I've come to think that after oil, water would become "the new gold". I learned about how water stress affects our world and realised how important my field is. Hydraulics engineering lies at the intersection of water resources, civil and environmental engineering, equipping me with quite a unique skill set. Moreover, since my interest in mechanical engineering is very much present, I found ways to merge my current major with it, through manufacturing of water treatment equipment, renewable energy systems, hydropower generation, desalination technologies, or marine robotics for underwater infrastructure and even computational fluid dynamics. Plus it can also be linked to a field that really excites me which is coastal/ocean engineering. Each new discovery deepens my commitment to this field. The breadth of possibilities is exactly what draws me in and drives me forward.

I've always wanted to experience the US research and university environment, not only because it is widely renowned, but also because of the mentorship and sharing culture. What stuck out to me is how teachers are present and willing to help students, always maintaining office hours and encouraging their curiosity beyond coursework. This mentorship culture doesn't exist in my home country, and it convinced me that conducting research in the US would accelerate my growth as an engineer and researcher. 
But the main challenge I faced is that most SURFs or similar programs are restricted to US citizens or PR. But Purdue welcomes international students. Beyond that, I was still worried about field mismatch, so when I saw that Fluid Modelling and Simulation was one of the project categories, which are just other words to describe hydraulics, it felt like this program was designed for me. The combination of cutting-edge facilities, expert mentorship, structured professional development, and the opportunity to present findings at the research symposium makes SURF a big stepping stone for me towards my future career goals.

The coursework I have taken has provided me with strong foundations in water and waste water treatment, fluid mechanics, structural engineering and hydrology. I've also completed core engineering coursework in calculus, chemistry, and computer science, ranking amongst the top 10% of my class with a course load of 30 credits (11 courses) per semester.  
I also interned at a desalination water plant in Algeria, where I got to learn about the entire process of desalination and its specifics and I monitored reverse osmosis units producing 200,000 m³/day and the instrumentation used. This experience taught me how large-scale water systems operate and gave me hands-on familiarity with membrane processes and hydraulic equipment. Currently, I am interning at a geotechnical engineering firm where I am learning softwares like QGIS and its appliances for geological mapping as well as conducting laboratory testing for soil analysis. 
During my fourth year at university, I had to take a gap year as I participated in the U.S. State Department's Global UGRAD program at the University of Mississippi in Spring 2025. I earned a 3.85 GPA and Chancellor's Honor Roll recognition across 18 credits, taking courses like wastewater treatment. It was also there that I got a research-adjacent experience through a project for my GIS course where I analyzed  the Chesapeake Bay watershed through processing HUC 12 catchments using ArcGIS Model Builder to quantify the correlation between agricultural land use, nitrogen loading and DO levels. This project showed me how computational tools can reveal patterns in complex environmental systems.
Additionally, I'm proficient in AutoCAD and SolidWorks for infrastructure design and currently serve as Head of IT for the Blue Gold Club at ENSH, our hydraulics engineering student association.

In my country, research opportunities are limited to graduate students, the curriculum is fixed for all students, and thesis work begins only in the final year at my university. To graduate I'll have to produce and defend two theses to earn my bachelors and masters.
Since I am eager to gain research experience before then and explore potential thesis directions, I sought international opportunities. Applying to the UGRAD program and securing a semester at the University of Mississippi was a first step, it required navigating an unfamiliar application process, adapting to a different academic system, and managing a rigorous course load in a second language. But it taught me that I thrive in multicultural environments, and demonstrated that I could succeed in a US research environment  and prepared me for independent research work.



My participation in this program would contribute to my career in three ways. 
First, I'm intending to pursue a master's degree abroad. I want to gain internationally recognised credentials as it will open more doors for me. Spending a summer doing research would significantly strengthen and boost my profile, making it stand out during selection. 
Second, I am still exploring what path to take, or what direction to head into in life. I am deciding whether I want to get into academia (pursuing a PhD and conducting research) or work as a practicing engineer. I believe that this SURF can give me a taste of what academia life can look like and real day to day laboratory experience, before committing to that choice. 
Third, I am also still trying to figure out what to specialise in and what to choose as my thesis research question. I am really interested in the fields of renewable energy integration with water systems, computational modeling and remote sensing for water resources, desalination and water treatment technologies, or even water infrastructure resilience... but I'm still unsure about which to pick, and labs like Warsinger's work on integrating renewable energy with desalination, or research on computational fluid dynamics for climate systems, directly align with these interests and could give me the insight needed to make that choice.

Through SURF, I hope to develop advanced computational skills, laboratory techniques, and technical writing abilities that will contribute to publications. These skills will be invaluable as I pursue graduate studies and build a career at the intersection of water resources, sustainability, and technology.

Statement of Purpose – Purdue SURF

I am applying to the Purdue SURF research program because I am deeply interested in understanding how we can build software that is not only efficient, but also provably trustworthy and reliable. Through years of programming and taking part in programming competitions, I have learned that many of the most dangerous bugs are not those that cause programs to “crash”, but those that silently break or violate the intended behavior and invariants of a system. The question of how we can reason about program correctness beyond testing has become one of my greatest interests.
This interest grew naturally from my background in competitive programming and algorithmic problem solving. I have participated in national and international competitions, including the International Olympiad in Informatics and ACM ICPC, where success depends not only on writing fast, but also reliable and correct code. In practice, however, even carefully designed solutions are usually validated only through testing against a finite set of cases. I have repeatedly seen apparently “correct” solutions that pass all tests yet fail for unseen inputs, highlighting the limitations of testing as a method for ensuring correctness of programs.
Purdue SURF represents a unique opportunity for me to move beyond this paradigm and engage in real research on how software correctness can be addressed more fundamentally. As a leading institution in engineering, Purdue's reputation for rigorous research and its history of pioneering work make it the ideal place to cultivate my skills. I am particularly attracted to SURF because it offers a structured research environment where undergraduate students can work closely with faculty on problems in computer science and software engineering, gaining hands-on research experience. I am especially interested in working with Professor DiVincenzo on the project “Gradual Verification: Assuring Programs Incrementally.” What makes gradual verification compelling to me is its pragmatic balance between theory and practice. Being able to specify properties incrementally and still receive meaningful feedback is something I see as essential for “real world” programming. This aligns closely with my experience: in real programming, invariants and guarantees are often discovered, refined, and corrected over time. The idea that verification can evolve alongside a program, rather than blocking development, strikes me as both powerful and necessary.
My technical background prepares me well for this type of work. Participating in Purdue SURF would be an important step toward these goals, giving me hands-on experience in research and helping me clarify my path toward graduate study or research-oriented industry work.
I am excited about the possibility of contributing to ongoing work at Purdue this summer, and I believe that the SURF program would be a remarkable and transforming experience in my development as a researcher and engineer.

I am interested in research at the intersection of human-computer interaction and applied machine learning. I believe that research should not exist purely in theory, but should serve a practical purpose of bringing social good. As AI becomes increasingly capable of performing complex tasks at scale, I want to design systems that translate technical advancements on benchmarks into real benefits in human-centered domains. My previous research experience has been dedicated to this intersection, specifically by applying computer vision (CV) and large language models (LLMs) to address challenges in education and accessibility.

After meeting Professor Max Fowler from UIUC's Computing Education department, I initiated a research project extending his prior work on automated grading of short-response programming exams. Motivated by growing concerns about student data privacy and over-reliance on proprietary architectures, my goal was to assess whether open-source models ranging from 8 to 70 billion parameters, small enough to be deployed on institution-owned hardware, could match the grading accuracy of flagship proprietary models for narrow-scope introductory programming exams. To test this, I built an evaluation pipeline that benchmarked these models on a test set of 620 student responses, labelled by the instructor for ground truth.

Challenges arose when early experimental results contradicted my expectations. Statistical testing showed that smaller open-source models significantly underperformed larger proprietary models, and even flagship LLMs frequently produced formatting errors that failed to follow my prompt, weakening their applicability for automated grading. In addition, limited compute resources restricted the range of models and hyperparameters I could evaluate. To address this, I reconsidered my experimental design to achieve more with less, such as using few-shot prompting instead of supervised fine-tuning. I also learned to reframe these unexpected outcomes as insights rather than failures, focusing my analysis on understanding why models broke under constraints. Throughout this process, I worked closely with faculty and graduate student reviewers to clarify my interpretations, refine my analyses, and improve how the results were communicated, ultimately leading to a peer-reviewed acceptance at ACM SIGCSE. This experience taught me how applied AI research operates under real-world constraints, such as cost and deployment feasibility, and shaped my approach to research as an iterative, collaborative process.

Complementing my academic research, I have also applied AI to real-world challenges through industry experience. In a research and development internship at AristAI, an education technology startup, I worked on improving the accessibility of course materials for students with disabilities. Many educational resources from client universities existed only as unstructured, image-only PDFs, making them largely inaccessible to users who rely on screen-reading technology. I was responsible for improving an existing prototype designed to convert scanned course materials into screen-reader-friendly formats. This solution frequently struggled with figure extraction: diagram crops often included surrounding text or were poorly scaled, producing cluttered outputs that rendered materials unusable in practice. Recognizing that the prior single-model approach was insufficient, I designed a multi-stage approach that integrated CV and transformer models to handle layout understanding, content extraction, and reconstruction. This pipeline used an agentic LLM-as-a-judge to determine processing steps, reconstructed PDF page layouts as structured HTML, and automatically generated descriptive image metadata. My solution is now used to transform hundreds of scanned documents across dozens of colleges, reinforcing for me how applied AI, when designed with users in mind, can bring genuine improvements in accessibility and educational equity.

I want to participate in the SURF program because it offers the opportunity to strengthen my foundation in empirical AI evaluation while gaining hands-on experience developing models and applied systems under the mentorship of experts. I am eager to test how my research intuition generalizes to cross-institutional, collaborative teams and to explore research experiences not available at my home institution. Through SURF, I hope to develop technical skills, identify potential advisors, and explore directions for graduate study, gaining experience directly aligned with the type of empirical AI research I aim to pursue in a PhD. In the long term, I plan to apply these skills in a nonprofit or industry lab, building systems that are technically robust and socially meaningful, eventually leading interdisciplinary teams to bridge the gap between AI capability and social equity. SURF represents a critical step toward these goals, providing mentorship, practical research experience, and exposure to innovative approaches that will prepare me to make impactful contributions to AI research and its applications.

Throughout my time exploring universities during the application process, Purdue has consistently stood out to me as a place that pushes boundaries and gives students the space to try something new. One thing I’ve learned from being here is that the most exciting opportunities aren’t always the ones that feel familiar, in fact they’re usually the ones that make you uncomfortable in a good way. That’s why I’m drawn to projects where I’m not just sitting behind a laptop, but actually building, testing, and working with real systems and real data and that’s also what drew me towards industrial engineering. 
While most programs focus on taking academic credits along with working on a research program, through Purdue’s SURF program I can focus solely on the research over the summer. This approach provides the ideal environment for applying my in-class knowledge to real-world scenarios where I would not be distracted by my academics. While there are many other summer research programs, I love how well SURF is structured. It doesn’t feel like you have to force yourself into one narrow lane and you can actually find research that fits what you’re curious about, and still learn something new.
A lot of people say constantly trying new things means you're unsure of what you want. But to me, it's the opposite. You won’t know what type of work truly inspires you until you’ve stepped into different spaces, picked up different tools, and stretched yourself beyond what’s comfortable. I’ve made it my goal to explore new areas of interest, and SURF gives me the chance to push that boundary, pushing me to a new environment.
Even though most of my past research has leaned more technical, I know it’ll help me here too. At Leibniz University, I had full control over a MATLAB-based plasma diagnostics project. Everything from decoding research papers to building physics-based models and writing an entire program was on me. At Purdue, working with Dr. Yih taught me the importance of explaining complex terms of Digital Twin (some even hard for me to pronounce) in clear, simple terms. When I didn’t understand something, I learned to sweat through it until I was confident that I could teach it to anyone (maybe even a seven-year-old). That mindset of knowing something so well you can explain it, is what I bring into every new project I take on.
On top of that, through DUIRI I’ve been working with a research professor on pilot stress and fatigue, and it completely changed how I think about data. We weren’t just looking at numbers but also how someone’s body reacts under pressure, and what those signals can reveal before a person even realizes they’re hitting their limit. I’ll be continuing this work during the semester, and we wrote a paper that’s currently in the publication process. The project also earned an award at the Fall Expo, which made the whole experience feel real, not just like practice.
That mindset is what I bring into every research environment: learn it deeply, understand the “why,” and communicate it clearly.
Through these multiple research experiences, one challenge I’ve faced is stepping into projects where I didn’t have a perfect background from the start. A lot of the topics I’ve worked on—like plasma diagnostics, digital twins, and physiological signal analysis—were things I hadn’t fully learned in class yet, so the learning curve was real. At first, it was overwhelming trying to understand the terminology, the research papers, and what I was actually supposed to be solving without feeling behind.
What I realized over time is that what I needed most was honestly just time—time to read, take notes, and work through a bunch of research papers, no matter how tedious it was. The most important thing I learned was giving myself room to become familiar with the work. In the beginning, I wasn’t allowing myself to be okay with not fully understanding something right away, and I kept thinking I should’ve known better. Once I stopped rushing the process and focused on getting a little better each day, I started learning faster, asking better questions, and actually contributing meaningfully.
I’ve learned that the best opportunities are usually the ones that feel unfamiliar at first. That’s why I’m excited about SURF, it’s a chance to step into a new space, learn what I don’t know yet, and grow through the process.

I examined how wall thickness, magnet orientation, and enclosure geometry of the magnetized iron casing influence field uniformity along the neutron beam path. Then I identified edge-induced field gradients that reduced polarization performance. After that I  performed a parameter tuning over casing geometry and magnet orientation to improve magnetic-field uniformity. Crawford’s Simulation group plans to use my simulation results to guide optimized design choices for the fabrication of the supermirror neutron polarizer. Through this work, I gained experience using numerical field modeling as a predictive tool to guide experimental design of a supermirror neutron polarizer.

The following winter break, while exploring the field of condensed matter physics, I read a review article on “X-ray and Neutron Diffraction in the Study of Organic Crystalline Hydrates” by Fucke and Steed. The article’s demonstration of using diffraction to probe atomic-scale order piqued my interest in crystallography and incentivized me to pursue hands-on experience with diffraction methods. As a result, the following semester I joined Professor Powers’s Solid-State Crystallography Research Group to conduct structural characterization of Galena. I prepared powdered crystalline samples and collected X-ray diffraction data using a laboratory X-ray diffractometer. By identifying Bragg peak positions, I calculated interplanar spacings and lattice parameters. To evaluate the sample's crystallinity, I analyzed the diffraction patterns by carefully examining peak sharpness and background noise. To deepen my interpretation of this data, I drew upon my concurrent coursework in Abstract Algebra. Viewing diffraction not just as data peaks but as manifestations of symmetry constraints and group actions allowed me to develop a rigorous, symmetry-based perspective on structural analysis. This combination of hands-on diffraction experience and theoretical group theory prepared me to conduct summer research at BYU.

In Summer 2025, I was selected as a Fletcher Research Summer Fellow at Brigham Young University to work with Professor Branton J. Campbell on the crystallographic analysis of perovskite-like materials. The goal of this project was to understand how structural dimensionality and lattice distortions in low-dimensional perovskites relate to physical properties such as optical and ferroelectric behavior. To address this problem, I developed a computational pipeline using Mathematica and Python to process crystal structures from the Cambridge Structural Database. I first cleaned and standardized CIF files and resolved crystallographic disorder using ISOCIF software. Then I used Mathematica to identify inorganic framework atoms and remove organic components. Next, I classified perovskite-like structures by dimensional connectivity from one to three dimensions. Through this process, I identified two-dimensional single-layered structures for further study. For selected single-layered structures, I applied ISODISTORT software to compare each structure to a high-symmetry reference structure for analyzing lattice distortions. Moreover, I used VESTA visualization software to inspect crystal structures and confirm bonding networks and layer connectivity. The Mathematica and Python code developed in this project will be used in Professor John Colton’s experimental research group to study optical properties of two-dimensional perovskite materials. I presented this work at the BYU Fletcher Research Poster Session and the Gettysburg College X-SIG Poster Session. This experience has taught me how developing computational code demands patience, systematic debugging, and collaboration to connect algorithms with physical insight. 

After my research at BYU, I wanted to further explore the field of  experimental condensed matter physics. During Winter 2025, I joined Professor Crawford’s Experimental Laboratory at Gettysburg College to gain hands-on experience in materials fabrication & characterization. In this work, I am currently fabricating ultra-thin gold films using high-vacuum thermal evaporation and studying their structural quality. I am characterizing film thickness, surface roughness, and material continuity using Atomic Force  Microscopy (AFM) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM). Through this project, I am learning how fabrication conditions influence nanoscale structure and experimental reliability. This experience allows me to connect my prior background in electromagnetic modeling and crystallographic analysis with direct materials characterization in a laboratory setting.

My research experiences have prepared me well for the Purdue SURF program. In particular, my experimental background in material characterization with AFM, SEM and strong computational experience in material characterization have qualified me for Professor Tiancong Zhu’s projects on “Epitaxial Growth of Wafer Scale Semiconductor Thin Films” and “Fabrication of Atomically Clean Two Dimensional Heterostructures”. I am also captivated by Professor Chen-Lung Hung's project on “Neutral Atom Array Trapping on Nanophotonic Circuits for Quantum Science and Applications”. Moreover, my earlier work with Professor Powers and my research experience with Professor Campbell  solidified my understanding of crystal structure defects & large scale data analysis. To further my electronic troubleshooting skills, I am taking an advanced electronics laboratory course in the Spring 2026 semester. All these skills are relevant for controlling and stabilizing electronic and optical components used in nanophotonic trapping experiments with Professor Hung and material synthesis & characterization experiments with Professor Zhu. 

Through the Purdue SURF program, I aim to learn MBE and atomic-scale characterization for thin films and heterostructures or to gain experience with optical and electronic control on neutral atom array trapping. I am cognizant that my time at Purdue will provide me with the technical depth to pursue further research at the intersection of low-dimensional quantum materials, quantum optics, quantum computing and prepare me for graduate level study in condensed matter physics and quantum computing.

It is not only fear of the disease itself, but fear of what follows when diagnosis and treatment depend on affordability. I remember a time when our domestic helper’s son fell ill with dengue. Reliable PCR tests were expensive. Waiting felt dangerous, yet acting quickly required resources many families simply did not have in a developing country like Bangladesh. My family helped financially where we could, and her son recovered. Relief came with discomfort, though. I could not stop thinking about how easily the outcome might have changed if circumstances had been slightly different. Survival depended not on the absence of scientific knowledge, but on whether that knowledge could be reached.

What unsettled me most was how widespread this situation was. Dengue was common. The chemistry behind detection and treatment already existed. Yet for many, that “last mile” of science, the actual access to it, remained distant. I felt a growing frustration that, over time, turned into curiosity. I slowly understood that a discovery in a lab meant nothing if it was too expensive to reach a village in Bangladesh. I began asking questions about why certain diagnostics were costly to manufacture. Soon, I learnt that molecular stability was a direct precursor to economic accessibility for most drugs that were difficult to synthesize. This realization led me toward biochemistry, where small changes in enzymatic stability at the molecular level can determine whether a solution is feasible beyond the laboratory. I became interested in how biological systems are regulated and how those systems can be studied and manipulated responsibly.

These experiences have helped me develop the interpersonal and analytical skills needed to contribute effectively to a structured research team while taking initiative in experimental tasks, thus preparing me to thrive in the mentorship-driven environment of the SURF program. My academic achievements, including the Outstanding Freshman Chemistry and Biochemistry Award and recognition on the Dean’s and President’s Lists, further reflect my sustained commitment and readiness for the rigor and responsibility that SURF demands.

My long term goal is to pursue advanced studies in biochemistry or drug design and contribute to research that considers both scientific rigor and accessibility. Similarly, the information-processing view: attention, encoding, storage, and retrieval, maps closely onto practical AI challenges: what to attend to in noisy inputs, how to form representations that generalize, and how to retrieve the right knowledge at the right time. As a high school senior already committed to studying physics, I did not fully understand what a qubit was or why dilution refrigerators were required. What I did understand, however, was the scale of what was being attempted. The idea that information could be encoded in quantum states, manipulated through fragile physical systems, and potentially redefine computation unsettled and fascinated me at the same time. That discomfort, recognizing both the promise of the technology and the depth of my own lack of knowledge, became a motivating question rather than a deterrent.

By that point, I had already decided to pursue physics in college with the intention of entering research. Physics, to me, represented the most direct way to contribute to humanity’s long-term progress: from the steam engine to semiconductor devices to satellite-based communication, foundational advances in physics and engineering have repeatedly reshaped society. Quantum technologies felt like the next such inflection point. Yet the questions lingered. What physical principles actually make quantum computation possible? How do theoretical ideas translate into working devices? I entered college determined not just to admire these technologies, but to understand them from the ground up, with graduate study and a research-focused career as my long-term goal.

I am an undergraduate Biotechnology student at BRAC University in Bangladesh. I grew up watching my parents manage diabetes every day. Helping with their care made me curious about disease, not only as a topic but also as something that changes real lives. Over time, that personal motivation became academic focus. I became especially interested in diagnostics and microbial health because in low-resource settings, many diseases become serious simply because detection is late or unavailable.

My current field is Biotechnology, and my interests sit at the intersection of microbiology, molecular biology, diagnostics, and computational work. I keep coming back to two problems. One is antimicrobial resistance (AMR), especially how resistance can spread through plasmids in the environment and affect human health. The second is early detection of disease. My main question is how we can design detection and monitoring systems that are sensitive enough for early diagnosis, but also practical for real settings like Bangladesh.

I have explored these interests through my ongoing wet-lab thesis and research roles. My undergraduate thesis is focused on plasmid presence and antibiotic resistance profiles in bacterial isolates from Dhaka city water bodies (Dhanmondi Lake and Hatirjheel Lake). I have chosen this topic to do a thesis on because these water bodies are used daily by people living nearby, which has direct relevance for public health in densely populated areas. The work is based in the Biotechnology, Microbiology, and Molecular Biology Laboratory and Microbial Genetics Lab at BRAC University. In this project, I learnt how to manage a full workflow from field sampling to lab results. I collected surface water samples in sterile bottles and transported them in cold conditions to keep the microbial population stable. I processed samples using filtration, then cultured them in LB and selective media (such as TCBS, EMB, and SS). I performed serial dilutions, spread plating, incubation, and CFU counting. I purified isolates using streak plating and prepared isolate stocks for later testing. So far, we have prepared around 390 isolate stocks, including E. coli, Salmonella, and Vibrio.

This project trained my discipline in lab work and data handling. I extracted bacterial DNA using the boiling method and used PCR and gel electrophoresis for confirmation. I also performed antibiotic susceptibility testing using the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method and interpreted results using CLSI guidelines. We used 13 antibiotics and classified results as resistant, intermediate, or susceptible based on measured zones. In addition, I worked on plasmid isolation using the PCI method and verified plasmids by gel electrophoresis. We prepared buffers and reagents ourselves, so I learnt careful solution preparation and troubleshooting, not only following a kit. This thesis work made me more patient, more accurate, and more realistic about research. It also taught me that AMR is already present in our environment.

Alongside my thesis, I have started working as a Research Assistant in drug discovery settings, where I supported research tasks and manuscript-related work. This has helped me see another side of biotechnology, where computation and biology meet. I have been learning Python, SPSS, and basic R, and I have used bioinformatics tools such as BLAST. I am also working on research papers in areas like in silico drug design and computational screening. These experiences made me more comfortable with learning new tools and working in structured research teams. They also made me interested in becoming a hybrid researcher who can work across wet lab and analysis. I have also taken part in research workshops and competitions, including winning an AMR-focused essay competition during World AMR Awareness Week.

I also hope to learn from Purdue mentors and research group culture so I can carry those standards back to my thesis work and future research in Bangladesh.

This project is also a strong fit for my background and my growth goals. Through SURF, I would like to learn more about DNA nanostructure assembly, functionalization strategies, and how delivery success is evaluated through imaging and quantitative analysis.

My courses built my base in molecular biology, diagnostics, microbiology, biotechnology lab work, statistics, and computer applications in biotechnology. I completed an academic internship at the Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (BCSIR), which introduced me to professional research culture, lab discipline, and structured reporting in a national research institute setting. I also started a physical internship at BRAC Healthcare with a tuberculosis focus, which is helping me understand how infectious diseases work and connect lab results, diagnostics, and real patient needs. Outside formal classes, I contributed to science communication by creating infographics for BRAC University Research for Development Club activities, which improved how I explain complex topics clearly to others.

In the short term, after SURF, I will return to BRAC University to complete my remaining coursework and defend my undergraduate thesis. After my BSc, I plan to pursue an MSc and continue building research experience. In the long term, I want to work in industry R&D in Bangladesh in areas related to diagnostics, AMR monitoring, and drug discovery. I want my work to help reduce disease burden through practical solutions, especially solutions that fit the realities of low-resource settings.

I am motivated to explore how we can architect hardware that inherently supports the safety and timing requirements of modern RTOS kernels, bridging the gap between high-performance architecture and reliable embedded execution.

statement_of_purpose:
Albert Einstein once said, “The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existing.” Curiosity has been the quiet force behind most of my choices. I always knew that I wanted to understand how things work beneath the surface. Small moments shaped this. Fixing something that others gave up on. Writing code that failed many times before it worked. Seeing patterns where at first there was only noise. Eventually, those moments pulled me toward Computer Science, specifically where math and real-world systems meet.

My name is Harsh Tayal and I’m currently a sophomore student with a GPA of 3.93/4 at BITS Pilani, one of India’s top universities. As an undergraduate Bachelor’s student of Computer Science, I have found university to be a space that actively encourages curiosity, giving me the freedom to explore ideas deeply, and engage with learning in a serious as well as thoughtful way. I started building projects to answer questions for myself. My favourite project was SkillSaga, a gamified learning platform with XP, challenges, live updates, and personal profiles. I built it using Django for backend logic like user management and XP tracking, and HTML, CSS, Bootstrap, and JavaScript for the frontend, with AJAX enabling live updates. From this project, I learned Django’s request-response flow, how models, views, and templates actually interact, and how backend decisions affect frontend flexibility. Later, I developed a Micro-Climate Stress Detector in Python using NumPy and Pandas, combining weather and satellite data with regression models to estimate felt heat and suggest cooler routes in real time. This project taught me how to preprocess real datasets, handle missing and inconsistent values, and use basic regression to turn numerical data into usable predictions. Most recently, I designed a Smart Plant Care Assistant that uses Python-based image analysis and environmental inputs to detect visible plant stress, compute a composite health score, and translate factors like watering, heat, humidity, and disease risk into clear care decisions. Here, I learned how to extract simple features from images, combine them with contextual data, and translate multiple signals into a single usable output. These projects taught me that real-world problems are rarely clean. They’re full of gaps, and you have to be okay with questioning your own assumptions. 

Broadly, I am interested in understanding and modeling complex systems under uncertainty, whether they arise from human behaviour, physical environments, or coordinated agents. What draws me to such problems is not just prediction, but the challenge of building models that remain interpretable, grounded, and honest about their limitations. At the core, the question that keeps pulling me back is simple: how do we make models that are useful when the data is messy, incomplete, and influenced by forces we cannot fully control? Whether it is people voting, weather evolving, or robots coordinating, I keep returning to the same problem of uncertainty, interpretation, and trust in models.

One area I’m particularly drawn to is the mathematical modeling of social systems, especially elections. The project that reflects this interest is “Mathematical modeling to forecast the 2026 US Elections” led by Prof. Alexandria Volkening. Elections are this strange mix of math, human behaviour, and massive uncertainty. I’m interested in how we take messy polling data, weigh it against economic signals, and come up with a forecast that actually means something. I’ve got a solid foundation in linear algebra, basic differential equations and data handling, and I’m comfortable in MATLAB, Python and R, but what excites me isn't just "predicting" a winner; it’s understanding why a forecast shifts and being transparent about where the uncertainty comes from. Through this project, I hope to deepen my understanding of uncertainty quantification, model calibration, and transparent forecasting.

A closely related extension of this interest appears in “Physics-Informed Machine Learning to Improve the Predictability of Extreme Weather Events”, led by Prof. Lei Wang, where uncertainty arises from physical complexity rather than human behaviour. Weather systems are messy, physical, and hard to predict, much like the social systems I’m interested in, but with very real consequences. This project appeals to me because it does not treat machine learning as a black box, but as something guided by physics. While building my Micro Climate Stress Detector, I worked with weather data and simple models, and I saw how noisy inputs and weak assumptions can easily mislead predictions. This project feels like a natural next step from that experience. The chance to work with large datasets by running simulations, and connecting predictions to real atmospheric dynamics fits closely with how I like to learn: slowly, carefully, and with an emphasis on understanding why something works.

This perspective also motivates my interest in “Multi-Robot Coordination for Maritime Environments” with Prof. Vishrant Tripathi, where uncertainty emerges from interaction, communication limits, and real-world constraints among multiple agents. I also have a deep interest in robotics and distributed systems; specifically, how multiple robots coordinate when things get difficult. I love the balance between the high-level theory and the actual implementation. Through my coursework and independent learning, I’ve spent time learning about feedback systems and optimization. Being able to help with everything from the initial theory to the final system development is exactly how I like to work. Think first. Test carefully. Then fix what didn't work. Working on this project would help me gain hands-on exposure to ROS, multi-agent control strategies, and real-world system validation.

Outside the classroom, my involvement in the university Coding Club and securing 2nd position in its poster competition helped me communicate technical ideas clearly and defend design choices. Even earlier experiences, such as scoring in a top percentile of IIT JEE-Main (a national-level competitive exam), and topping my class with a perfect 10 CGPA in Grade 10, shaped my discipline and work ethic.

The SURF program attracts me because it offers something I value deeply: immersion. Real research exposure and close mentorship. I want to see how research actually happens; not just the answers, but how the questions are asked in the first place. SURF would allow me to work closely with faculty, understand research culture in depth, and learn how collaboration shapes a project. I see this as a crucial step toward my long-term goal of pursuing graduate studies and a PhD in a STEM field where I work on complex systems that matter in the real world. SURF fits naturally into this goal because it offers my first chance to experience research in a rigorous, full-time setting.

Participating in the world-class research environment at SURF would help me refine my research skills, deepen my technical understanding, and gain clarity about my future path. I’m also eager to collaborate with people and build meaningful connections from different parts of the world through this program. I’m eager to bring my curiosity, energy, and commitment to the research teams at Purdue. I’m still driven by the same quiet curiosity that started years ago and this opportunity marks a turning point where that curiosity starts shaping into purpose and direction. SURF feels like the right place to follow it honestly, with dedication and heart.

My name is Facundo Aliaga, and through this Statement of Purpose I respectfully submit my application for consideration to the 2026 Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) Program at Purdue University. I am currently pursuing a degree in Electromechanical Engineering at Universidad Privada Boliviana, where I have developed a strong interest in research at the intersection of physics, engineering, and applied computation.
My interest in engineering began long before I understood the term itself. I grew up in an environment naturally inclined toward mechanical systems. I frequently accompanied my father, who, despite not being an engineer, has always been deeply interested in mechanics, to his mechanical projects and to the workshop where he restored his car. Through these experiences, as well as stories he shared about working as an aircraft mechanic in La Paz, I began to perceive machines as living systems: logical, functional, and aesthetically coherent. Combined with a natural aptitude for mathematics and physics, these early experiences shaped my desire to understand how complex systems operate. Although my initial goal was to study aeronautical engineering abroad, earning a full merit scholarship at Universidad Privada Boliviana redirected my academic path. Electromechanical Engineering proved to be a well-aligned choice, allowing me to build a rigorous foundation while remaining closely connected to the systems that had long fascinated me.
As I progressed through my degree, I came to realize that research is not merely an academic component, but a structured process through which curiosity becomes methodology. The arrival of a new department head played a key role in this realization by actively encouraging participation in conferences, engagement with scientific literature, and involvement in research groups. Over the past year and a half, I have participated in several research-oriented projects, including paper submissions in signal processing, renewable energy systems, and low-cost instrumentation. In one project, I was responsible for the data analysis of a national renewable energy matrix, which strengthened my skills in data validation, modeling, and interpretation. In parallel, I worked on hands-on engineering projects such as a biogas biodigester, a metal detector, and an Archimedes screw turbine, experiences that helped me bridge theoretical concepts with experimental implementation.
Through these academic and research experiences, three areas of interest clearly emerged: nanotechnology, automatic control, and fields and optics. Exposure to introductory materials in nanotechnology revealed the transformative potential of engineering at the nanoscale, particularly in how matter and energy can be manipulated. Automatic control naturally aligned with my electromechanical background, supported by my experience in signal processing, robotics, and system modeling. However, it is in fields and optics, specifically photonics, optoelectronics, and metamaterials, that I have found my strongest research motivation.
This interest has been reinforced through direct research experience. I became an active contributor to a project focused on assessing and correcting the quantitative performance of a low-cost spectrometer, where I analyzed spectra from specific LEDs and helped develop a Dynamic Wavelength Warping (DWW) algorithm to improve spectral accuracy. This work resulted in a technical poster and oral presentation at OPTILAS 2025, and a proceedings paper is currently in preparation. I am also co-leading a research team working with hyperspectral data to identify an appropriate Spectral Vegetation Index capable of discriminating among grape-leaf diseases, with the long-term objective of applying deep-learning techniques (autoencoders) for semantic segmentation. Additionally, I am a co-author of a national conference paper analyzing the impact of scientific paper replication as an innovative teaching strategy in higher education. These projects solidified my interest in optical modeling, spectral analysis, and light, matter interaction, particularly at small scales.
My research interests align strongly with the work of several Purdue faculty members. I am particularly interested in Professor Peter Bermel’s research in nanophotonics, optical materials, and device modeling, especially his work on photonic crystals, semiconductor optics, and solar-related materials. I also admire Professor Hadiseh Alaeian’s contributions to parity-time-symmetric plasmonic metamaterials, which closely match my interest in using numerical simulations and theoretical models to uncover novel optical phenomena. Additionally, my background in signals, robotics, and modeling aligns well with the work of Professors Shreyas Sundaram and Yaobin Chen in automatic control.
Given my current level of preparation, I believe the SURF program represents an ideal opportunity to further develop as a researcher. I have built a solid foundation in mathematics, physics, signal processing, and prototyping, and I am now seeking a structured research environment that will allow me to deepen these skills under expert mentorship. Purdue’s strong research culture, interdisciplinary approach, and emphasis on undergraduate research make it an exceptional setting. Through SURF, I hope to gain hands-on experience with optical modeling, photonic simulation tools, and exposure to micro/nanofabrication techniques, while contributing meaningfully to ongoing research efforts.
My academic preparation includes coursework in Signals and Systems, Thermodynamics, Physics II (electromagnetism), Circuits, Newtonian Physics, Chemistry, and specialized image-processing modules. I have developed electronic and embedded systems involving data acquisition and control. I am an author or co-author of works in low-cost spectroscopy, engineering education, and renewable energy modeling (the latter currently in its final development stage). I am proficient in Python for scientific computing, Excel and Power BI for data analysis, and engineering tools such as SolidWorks (CSWA-certified, preparing for CSWP), AutoCAD, LTspice, Simulink, and robotic platforms including Dobot Studio and Dobot Link.
During SURF, I aim to further develop skills in:
• Modeling light–matter interactions
• Numerical simulation of optical materials and devices
• Understanding metamaterials and plasmonic phenomena
• Applying computational methods such as FDTD and FEM
• Integrating optical modeling with control and signal-processing techniques
• Gaining hands-on experience in optical and micro/nanotechnology laboratories
My long-term objective is to pursue graduate studies, first an MSc and then a PhD, in photonics, optics, or micro/nanotechnology. I aspire to contribute to the development of technologies that integrate advanced materials, optical systems, and intelligent control strategies. Participation in the SURF program would be a decisive step toward this goal. Working with Purdue faculty would not only strengthen my technical expertise, but also help me develop the scientific discipline, perspective, and mindset required for a career in high-impact engineering research.

From an early age, I understood that studying would be my way of changing not only my own future, but also the story of my family.

Beyond transforming my family’s reality, I have always carried a deep desire to leave a legacy for society. I have never been motivated by recognition for who I am, but rather by the impact of what I can do to help others. For a long time, I believed that this purpose would be fulfilled through a career in law, and I dreamed of becoming a judge to promote justice. However, my understanding of how I could contribute to the world changed profoundly after I allowed myself to explore new possibilities.

I have always believed that while the answer can be no, the yes only exists for those who actively seek it. Guided by this mindset, I engaged in extracurricular activities during high school that reshaped my trajectory. The most decisive experience was a scientific immersion program in the summer of 2023, which I attended alongside other young women. At that time, I was still considering a career in the humanities, while many of the others had already chosen scientific paths. During those weeks, I was immersed in what I often describe as the pure essence of science. I visited laboratories, met scientists, and observed how curiosity is transformed into experiments, data, and discovery. That experience deeply fascinated me. Science became tangible, dynamic, and accessible. A seed was planted, and it continued to grow from that moment forward.

After an intense year of preparation, I was admitted to one of the top medical schools in Brazil. Entering medical school confirmed the direction I had begun to take. I vividly remember my first histology class. Observing tissues under the microscope, understanding cellular organization, and realizing how microscopic structures sustain vital functions was profoundly moving. I cried in a classroom not out of difficulty, but out of passion for knowledge. Since then, I have continuously deepened my interest in physiology, cellular biology, and human body systems through coursework, books, and scientific reading, becoming increasingly motivated by the questions that connect structure, function, and disease.

Although I chose Medicine, I never truly abandoned the humanities. On the contrary, I now understand that caring for someone’s health, investigating disease mechanisms, and contributing to healing may be one of the most human expressions of all. My technical background in systems development, along with participation in scientific immersion and leadership programs, strengthened my analytical thinking, autonomy, and sense of social responsibility. These are skills I am eager to bring into a research environment.

Within this context, the SURF program represents far more than a summer opportunity. It represents an intentional step of boldness and coherence with my journey. SURF’s emphasis on mentored research, practical laboratory experience, interdisciplinary collaboration, and academic development strongly resonates with my goals. I am particularly drawn to the program’s structured support for researchers at the beginning of their careers and its access to a research environment of international excellence. I see SURF as an opportunity to gain practical research experience, develop critical scientific thinking, and learn how to formulate and investigate meaningful scientific questions.

In the long term, I aspire to become a physician scientist, integrating clinical practice with research that advances medical knowledge and improves patient care. I am especially motivated to work with children, as education during my own childhood was transformative and shaped the person I am today. The experience gained through SURF will be essential in building a strong foundation in experimental research, scientific communication, and collaboration with mentors and peers. All of these are crucial for my future career in STEM.

Applying to SURF is, once again, my way of seeking the yes. It is an act of courage, a commitment to leaving a meaningful legacy, and a testament to how far education can transform lives. My family’s reality has already changed, and I am determined to continue that transformation by contributing to science and society. I believe that there is, indeed, a happily ever after. Not as a fairy tale, but as the result of perseverance, opportunity, and a genuine commitment to making a difference.
