This internship was my first contact with research, but I wanted to explore other areas of research. That was when I thought of genetics and its power to answer biological questions that can’t be seen by the eye.

My interest in genetics began in my first high school genetics class, where I learned how small genetic differences can lead to population-level effects. Biology shifted for me from a study of how organisms function to understanding the mechanisms shaping life. However, as a student at a primarily undergraduate institution, opportunities to pursue genetics research were limited.

Studying in West Virginia, we commonly see shrews in the parks. Due to natural or artificial causes, many specimens are killed, but we can’t identify if they are male or female because they do not have exposed genitalia. As I learned more about shrews, I began to ask: how can we discover shrews' sex without having to dissect them? This limitation stood out to me, particularly because knowing their sex could give further information if the death was sex-related. 

Working with a faculty mentor and a peer researcher, we decided to start a research project on it. We set up a small room as our PCR and electrophoresis lab. With minimal institutional resources, we transformed a small room into a makeshift PCR and electrophoresis lab. I was responsible for extracting DNA from various external body parts to determine the optimal PCR temperatures and which body part yields the most DNA. With a good amount of DNA from an outer part of its body, a genetic analysis could be performed on that tissue, and the sex could be determined without an invasive method. 

While the project is still ongoing, we had some challenges identifying the correct primer without the shrews’ genome being fully sequenced. We had to rethink how we would get the primer, as we couldn’t use traditional methods. Instead of using a pre-existing primer, we used the gene's codified region to create our own primer. 

I stopped assuming that research has to go as planned from the beginning, and that’s why we have to be flexible and open to starting again. Research depends heavily on not seeing mistakes as failures and refining questions and protocols in response to limited data or resources. I had never considered before the knowledge gaps we still have for some species and their genetics. This project made me realize how much biological data can come from limited genetic information. 

Through WV-INBRE and UC’s research, I learned the foundations. I learned how to work in a laboratory, communicate with mentors, and approach challenges without viewing setbacks as failures. These experiences taught me that research is rarely linear and that progress often depends on re-evaluating assumptions and adapting methods. Now, I have come to understand that becoming a researcher requires more than theoretical knowledge. It requires the ability to integrate concepts, ask meaningful questions, and design approaches that address them.

Now, I have become fascinated by how genetics allows us to draw conclusions when traditional methods are not possible. I am particularly motivated by questions where direct observation is impossible and genetic inference becomes essential. This motivates me to question how human genetics uses limited genetic information to reveal meaningful population characteristics. 

Looking ahead, I plan to pursue graduate studies and continue in academia, focusing on human genetics. I am particularly interested in understanding how genetic variation contributes to disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Through a career in scientific research, I aim to transform unanswered biological questions into meaningful advances in human health. My long-term goal is to contribute research that deepens our understanding of how genetic variation influences disease and informs improvements in human health. For this reason, I want my next step in research to involve greater intellectual ownership and independence.

Participating in Purdue would be a transformative next step. SURF’s emphasis on independent research with a well-supported mentorship aligns with my goal of developing more autonomy as a researcher. The opportunity to dive further into research questions, experimental approaches, and data interpretation while receiving guidance and professional workshops that support thoughtful decision-making will help me develop the confidence and judgment required for graduate-level research I aspire to do.

Additionally, exposure to different research environments across states will allow me to observe differences in mentoring styles, research cultures, and collaborative structures, helping me better understand where I thrive and how I can adapt as a researcher in different scientific environments. The opportunity to work alongside Purdue faculty and peers in a larger, more specialized scientific community will prepare me for the expectations and rigor of graduate-level research.

The SURF program bridges the gap between learning how research works and learning how to lead it. By participating in SURF, I aim to emerge not only as a more skilled researcher but also more confident and independent in the research process and prepared to transform unanswered biological questions into meaningful scientific contributions.

statement_of_purpose:
I am a double major in computer engineering and mathematics, which as far as I can tell is an unusual combination, so discussion how this came to be might be a good place to start. I met mathematics first, around 6th grade. Notice that by mathematics here I do not mean the boring algebra that you are exposed to way sooner than 6th grade. No, I would credit my first real encounter with mathematics to be 6th grade geometry. I still distinctly remember one of our first lectures where we were told the sum of the angles in a triangle was 180 every single time, and how I spent close to an hour drawing different triangles and measuring angles only to (predictably) find ~180 as their sum every single time. From this point on, my interest in math only grew. Not long after these events, my math teacher recommended that I participate in the OBMEP - Brazil's entry level math competition, which I did. 
This moment is when math went from just an interesting class I had in my grid to a central part of my life, a position it occupies to this day. The math competition just had a way of captivating my interest. Instead of bland formulaic problems I was used to from my homeworks, these problems were almost like logic puzzles, or riddles. While it is true math competitions are not research, I credit these as the first time I truly grasped, or at least glimpsed what mathematics was truly about: Reasoning about fun, novel problems. Starting from what you know, and connecting those pieces in a clever way to conclude something new. Nowadays, while I still participate in competition math, I know those days are nearly over (only 2 more years of Putnam ahead of me, and then as far as I know, no further competitions exist), and instead will venture into reading and playing with unsolved problems, purely for the fun of it. I know I am unlikely to crack them, but some have a special place in my heart (namely the sum of inverse cubes, or zeta(3)).
That explains how mathematics came into my life. But what about computer engineering? Well, for that, we have my father to thank. He is an Computer Science major, with a focus in Java. And when I was around 12, I was going through my Minecraft phase. It just so happens that Minecraft was made in Java, and had a hue modding scene, which I was aware off. Sensing an opportunity, dad offered to teach me how to make Minecraft mods, an offer I accepted. Now, this idea failed: I have yet to make a Minecraft mod in my life (despite successfully modding other games), but it put my foot in the door. It planted the very first seed of how computers worked in my brain, a seed that only grew: The more I learned, the more impossible the existence of computers seemed: Even if one accepts that making a rock (silicon) do math, it is not at all obvious how simply the ability to do arithmetic in binary really quickly lends itself to games, displays and videos being possible (we truly do stand in the shoulders of giants don't we?). This curiosity pushed me more and more towards computer engineering (and away from computer science), as a way of figuring out how the hardware of a computer truly works. 
My relationship with these two fields has shaped basically my entire life. Ever since the day I met mathematics (and later computer engineering), almost every life choice or academic choice was specifically made with the intention of maximizing my exposure to these topics, going as far as to switch schools in 7th grade for a school that was widely known to be more rigorous STEM wise (and offer more math olympiads). I would go on to participate in Brazil's OBI (informatics olympiad, but really it was just competitive programming), win the OBMEP (gold medalist, 7th grade) qualify for the OBM (a much, MUCH harder math competition. 2 days, 3 problems per day, 4 hour 30min to solve them. Invite only for the top 300 around the country), get obliterated by it, before eventually qualifying again in my senior year of HS, and becoming the only person in my state that year to achieve any prize in the OBM.
It also shaped my decision to study abroad: I understood that due to how brazillian education works, studying in the US was my only hope of continuing to walk the line between mathematics and computer engineering: There are no double majors in brazillian institutions, at least not the ones I was hoping to attend. Further, I also understood that for computer engineering specifically, most of the cutting edge research did not happen in my country, but instead was housed in the U.S or Taiwan.
Which, somehow, despite being from a relatively underdeveloped era of Brazil, where no APs or IBs (I flew 2 hours to take the SAT. Not drove, flew) are offered, I managed to do. I got into Purdue, cruised through my first semester, got destroyed by the Putnam (undergraduate math competition), but overall, had a lot of fun. Unfortunately for me, my smooth sailing was about to end. After cruising through the first half of my freshman spring semester, something happened over spring break: I woke up one day and couldn't feel my feet properly, a feeling I, unfortunately was familiar with and recognized almost instantly as the early symptoms of guillan barre syndrome, a condition I experienced in 2023. 
Sadly for me, I would turn out to be wrong: This was not GBS, but CIDP, a chronic relative of this disease, which I am now diagnosed with and receive monthly infusions for. This "little" episode lasted an entire 4 months, accross three hospitalizations (tow in the U.S and another back in brazil) and left me unable to walk until mid june. Not only that, but for the remainder of the semester after spring break, I had to live in a hotel room with my parents while the doctors figured out what the hell was wrong with me. I was not even strong enough to get my own laptop out of my backpack. My nerves so deteriorated that I could not handwrite (a very frightening realization as a mathematician. At least for me, handwriting "scribles" is a crucial and irreplaceable part of my process). 
At this point, I was offered the opportunity to take I's (incompletes) as my grades for this semester, and finish my coursework at a later time. Doing so, however, would leave me isolated, an ocean away from all my friends and without anything to do besides stressing over my condition. Not only that, but it would require starting over my diagnosis with a new doctor, instead of the one who was already seeing me from day 1 in the hospital. With this in mind, we made the decision to stay. Through a lot of work with my professors and the DRC, we found a way for me to continue making progress in my classes. I was pushed to class by friends and family, did my assignments on a computer (as I couldnt handwrite, but could type slowly), and perhaps, my personal "favorite" (in a twisted way), LaTeXed my MA 510 midterm 2, as it was open response. It took a lot of hard work and, quite frankly, sheer will, but completing this semester successfully, while balancing physical therapy and navigating a delicate medical investigation is one of my proudest achievements, and I can confidently say it was only possible because of the amazing support from my friends and family, and my (un)healthy obsession with two very special fields.

In addition, like many women,  I faced discrimination and was told physics was “only for boys with bright futures.” However, attending the Brown Pre-College Astronomy program changed my outlook. For the first time, I was valued for my curiosity and potential rather than being judged solely by my musical background.

Coming from a family of lawyers rather than STEM professors or engineers, I lacked the professional connections that many of my peers relied on. This motivated me to build and follow my own path. Therefore, I chose to pursue my degree in the U.S. specifically to find a learning and research environment where intelligence, skill, dedication, and hard work can outweigh prejudice.

This research experience was my first immersion into the field of astronomy and astrophysics beyond the classroom, and I loved every moment of it. I found that the inherent uncertainty of a research question, while frustrating, is also incredibly exciting, because it creates a space for both learning and discovering something entirely new.

While I deeply enjoyed the theoretical aspects of astrophysics, this experience sparked a desire to explore the practical side of the field, specifically aerospace engineering.  I want my future work and career to be directly impactful, and I feel a strong need to use my skills to help those who are not as fortunate as I have been, specifically those who lack consistent access to medicine, water, and food.

I was inspired by their commitment to reaching remote areas, and I saw firsthand how engineering can literally save lives. During my time there, I contributed to the design, mechanical structure, and code of an alternative navigation system to GPS, ensuring that small UAVs can reach isolated communities reliably. This internship was a turning point for me, as it provided the perfect intersection between my passion for physics and engineering and my desire to help those in need.

In Fall 2025, I had the opportunity to present my summer research as a poster at PhysCon in Denver, Colorado. I found joy in discussing my work with my peers and exploring niche areas of astrophysics I had never previously considered. A highlight of the conference was meeting Dr. Sarah Hörst, whose work on the Dragonfly mission was very inspiring to me. After her talk, we spoke about the scarcity of internships available to international students. Her advice was to keep fighting and to remember our worth in a field that can be particularly challenging for women, especially international women. That is why I am so drawn to SURF. As one of the few research programs open to international students, SURF demonstrates that it values applicants for their unique contributions and potential rather than where they come from. I am confident that I would flourish in such an inclusive environment and contribute to the research to the very best of my ability.

Beyond the research opportunity, the structural support SURF provides, specifically the grant and the housing subsidy, are particularly meaningful to me, because I am unable to return to my home country during breaks due to personal circumstances. In addition, the chance to network with like-minded individuals, an experience I greatly appreciated at PhysCon, represents another opportunity that neither my home country nor my family’s circumstances can provide. SURF is not just a research program to me, but an essential next step in my journey as an engineer and a global citizen.

It took me weeks of manual labor to carve a mathematically perfect paraboloid from a glass blank. Later, while calculating asteroid orbits at the Summer Science Program, I realized that traditional observation and simulation methods hit a similar ceiling. Monte Carlo simulations or the Method of Gauss often required thousands of iterations to achieve acceptable uncertainty bounds, consuming hours of computing time for a single orbit determination.

I view artificial intelligence not merely as a data processing technique, but as the next generation of scientific instrumentation. Just as the telescope extended our vision, AI allows us to model complex physical systems that are computationally intractable for classical techniques. My goal is to build these instruments: rigorous, scientifically grounded deep learning models that respect physical laws.

I currently serve as the Technical Lead on CaloQVAE at TRIUMF, Canada's particle accelerator centre, designing quantum-assisted deep generative surrogates for the ATLAS detector. As the Large Hadron Collider upgrades to High-Luminosity, simulation demands will outpace current CPU-based methods. My work combines a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) sampled on a D-Wave QPU to achieve high-fidelity generation with speed-ups of multiple orders of magnitude.

When I joined as a first-year researcher after receiving the FYSRE award, I immediately encountered a significant research obstacle: the CaloQVAE group faced a persistent gap in generative fidelity between our VAE's reconstruction and sampling performance. Standard techniques—data augmentation, hyperparameter grid searches, architectural tweaks—yielded only incremental gains. Rather than continuing to optimize at the surface level, I hypothesized that if common solutions were failing, the problem must be related to our unique hybrid architecture. I had the idea to evaluate our RBM at the level of the latent space rather than particle showers. I discovered the RBM was collapsing into a trivial distribution, performing worse than a simple factorizable Bernoulli prior. To resolve this, I engineered a two-stage training scheme and architected a fully connected, 2-partite RBM. I also designed a custom embedding to map this architecture onto the D-Wave QPU’s qubit topology, resulting in a 10x improvement in sampling quality. This experience taught me to diagnose failures at the level of underlying assumptions and to persistently pursue interpretability in scientific machine learning.

However, generative power alone is insufficient. Purely data-driven models can hallucinate violations of conservation laws. To address this limitation, I work on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), which embed physical laws directly into the learning process. In my independent research, I am demonstrating how PINNs can mitigate the curse of dimensionality by solving wave equations in four or more spatial dimensions—achieving solutions more than an order of magnitude faster than finite difference methods at equivalent error bounds. Implementing both approaches gave me a deeper appreciation for the elegance of classical simulations while revealing the specific computational bottlenecks where ML techniques offer genuine advantages. Through SURF, I'm eager to apply physics-informed methods to the high-dimensional, real-world problems that computational scientists currently struggle to solve with classical approaches alone.

I am eager to apply my generative modelling background to de novo drug design while mastering cutting-edge architectures like equivariant 3D-conditional diffusion and flow networks.

While social theories offer profound frameworks for understanding human behavior, I often find traditional qualitative methods insufficient for verifying dynamic mechanisms. Conversely, statistical tools are powerful, but without context, they can fail to capture the nuance of the human condition. This realization drove me to the intersection of Computational Social Science, motivated by a specific challenge: Causal Inference in high-dimensional observational data. In the age of Big Data, we excel at prediction, yet we often struggle to explain why complex social systems—like learning patterns or polarization—evolve the way they do.

I have actively explored this intersection through a combination of rigorous research and industry challenges. As a Research Assistant at Zhejiang University, I sought to decode the "black box" of Human-AI interaction. I engineered over 500 N-gram sequential features from interaction logs and built a Random Forest classifier to predict learning outcomes. However, this project presented a significant obstacle: the "Small N, High Dimensionality" dilemma. With only 24 participants but hundreds of features, standard models immediately overfitted. I addressed this by consulting statistical literature and implementing Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation instead of a simple train-test split. I also utilized aggressive Feature Importance analysis to prune noise. This experience taught me that research is not just about running code, but about making principled decisions under constraint.

To complement this research perspective with engineering rigor, I led a team in the Sandia National Laboratories Data Challenge. Tasked with minimizing scrap rates in additive manufacturing, I addressed severe class imbalance by implementing Probability Calibration and engineering spatial risk features. This project achieved a 63% Recall rate and reinforced my belief that rigorous data science can solve tangible, high-stakes engineering problems. Currently, as an AI Research Intern at ATLAS, I am bridging theory and practice by designing AI prototypes that integrate Large Language Models into educational workflows, a topic I further explored in my published paper, "Intelligence Amplification."

I am applying to Purdue SURF because it represents the ideal environment to elevate my research from "application" to "innovation." Unlike programs that focus solely on theoretical statistics, SURF emphasizes the integration of data science with engineering principles—a synergy I find essential for solving real-world problems. I am eager to collaborate with Purdue faculty who are pioneering methods in Human-Centered Computing and Data Mining. Specifically, I hope to gain deeper technical skills in Experimental Design and High-Performance Computing, moving beyond being a user of libraries to understanding the mathematical foundations of the algorithms I use.

Ultimately, my long-term aspiration is to pursue a Ph.D. in Computational Social Science. I aim to become a researcher who develops algorithmic frameworks that are not only mathematically robust but also socially responsible. I envision designing "Intelligence Amplification" systems—AI tools that understand and enhance human cognition rather than replacing it. Participation in SURF will be a transformative step in this journey, providing the mentorship, resources, and interdisciplinary exposure necessary to mature into a capable and innovative researcher.

statement_of_purpose:
My fascination with Computational Neuroscience and Machine Learning began with a simple curiosity: Can machines learn and adapt like the brain? This question led me to study the temporal and adaptive dynamics of neural systems. What motivates me most is understanding how the brain maintains stability and flexibility in constantly changing environments—a principle that could transform how artificial systems learn. I am particularly intrigued by how biologically inspired mechanisms, such as spiking communication and synaptic plasticity, can make AI more interpretable and robust.
To explore this field, I began my research journey at the Wuhan National Research Center for Optoelectronics, where I worked on Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks (RSNNs) for tactile signal decoding in rodents. My goal was to capture how biological neurons encode information through timing rather than amplitude. I trained RSNNs using unsupervised STDP pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, and implemented visualization tools to track membrane potentials and spike patterns. Early on, my models exhibited unstable firing and poor convergence. I overcame this by integrating adaptive thresholds and sparse connectivity, which significantly improved temporal stability. This experience taught me how computational models can reveal the principles behind biological efficiency—and how persistence and experimentation are key to solving open-ended problems in research.
Building on that foundation, I joined the Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, to study EEG-based Brain-to-Text decoding. Here, I explored Short-Term Plasticity (STP) as an adaptive mechanism for handling the cross-day distribution shift caused by electrode impedance changes. Instead of using standard normalization, I designed an STP-based encoding layer that mimicked Synaptic Depression (STD) to dynamically regulate signal gain. The model reduced cross-day feature deviation by more than 70%(measured by Wasserstain distance) and transformed continuous EEG into sparse, spike-like representations, making the data both cleaner and more energy-efficient. This work deepened my appreciation for the intersection of biology and computation, where theory and experiment reinforce one another.
I am drawn to Purdue University's SURF Program because of its emphasis on Deep Learning and Biological Modeling—precisely the intersection I wish to advance in. SURF offers the mentorship, interdisciplinary collaboration, and technical resources that would allow me to expand my expertise in large-scale model optimization and neuromorphic computing. I hope to work alongside faculty and peers who share a curiosity about how biological intelligence can inspire more efficient and resilient artificial systems.
In the long term, I plan to pursue a Ph.D in Computational Intelligence or Biomedical Engineering, developing adaptive, low-power Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) that can function reliably in real-world conditions. I believe the SURF experience will strengthen my foundation in both theoretical understanding and experimental design, helping me become a researcher capable of bridging neuroscience and machine learning.
The biggest obstacle I have faced so far was the steep learning curve at the start of my RSNN research. At first, I struggled with the mathematical formulation of spike dynamics and the instability of my models. To overcome this, I took a Python AI course, read key literature on spiking computation, and engaged in regular discussions with my mentor. This process not only  improved my technical skills but also shaped my mindset—to view every failures as an opportunity to refine my understanding.
For me, research in computational neuroscience is not only about building smarter machines; it is about learning from the most intelligent system we know—the brain itself.

Our research group has two primary goals: the first is investigating tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) and their emergence in high-grade serous Ovarian Cancer (HGSOC). We analyze immunofluorescence images from tumors taken from HGSOC patients using QuPath. We developed an automated script that combines a pixel classifier to identify the TLSs and a composite object classifier to successfully phenotype cells within the TLSs. With this script, batches of images could be analyzed in an automated fashion, allowing standardized, convenient analysis of immunofluorescent images. We then produced a web tool that uses this data to generate summary graphs for data analysis. With these two products, we aim to publish a standardized procedure to quantify and characterize TLS.

Even within this small project, I quickly learned that results do not appear overnight. Unexpected challenges are inevitable, but a successful researcher learns from them and transforms setbacks into meaningful progress through endurance, careful observation, and reflection.

statement_of_purpose:

This observation raised a critical question in my mind: How can intelligent systems remain reliable, adaptive, and interpretable when operating continuously in imperfect and human-centered environments? Guided by this thought, I focus on applied machine learning, system-level AI design, and human-aware intelligent systems that integrate continuous data streams, adaptive decision logic, and human-centered evaluation.
 
My rigorous coursework in computer science, data systems, and mathematics has provided a solid foundation for machine learning and data-driven research. Data Structures and Algorithms and The Hardware/Software Interface strengthened my understanding of computational efficiency, low-level system behavior, and how intelligent components operate within larger software architectures. Through Databases and Data Modeling, I developed experience in structured data management, data preprocessing, and analytical reasoning. In parallel, coursework in Research Methods and Intellectual Foundations of Informatics trained me to frame research questions, evaluate empirical evidence, and reason critically about technology in human and social contexts.
 
With this academic foundation, I joined the MIT Online Research Seminar to explore human-robot interaction (HRI) and emotion recognition. I systematically reviewed 58 papers and synthesized 21 core studies spanning perception-, EEG-, and multimodal-fusion approaches, which helped me identify recurring methodological limitations in real-world affective signals. Building on this survey, I evaluated representative CNN and Transformer methods across three datasets and observed a consistent challenge: model predictions exhibited high variance when contextual cues were ambiguous or labels were noisy. Even when validation performance appeared reasonable, failures concentrated in subtle expressions, occlusion, and cross-subject variation. This made it clear that the main source of error was often contextual uncertainty, not just model capacity. This experience shaped my interest in designing intelligent systems that incorporate adaptive reasoning, richer contextual signals, and feedback mechanisms beyond static prediction.
 
To further explore intelligent systems operating continuously in real-world environments, I developed Lexi-Jarvis, an AI-driven proactive notification system, under the guidance of Dr. Guy Laban from the University of Cambridge. The system continuously monitored real-time external data sources, including weather, AQI, UV index, and news APIs, to trigger context-aware notifications without explicit user prompts. A major technical obstacle was cross-platform reliability, particularly on iOS devices. Over a five-day evaluation period involving 120 triggered notification events, the system achieved a 95% delivery success rate on macOS, 92.5% on Android, but only 65% on iOS, largely due to token expiration and background process suspension. Average notification latency ranged from 2.8–3.1 seconds on desktop platforms and increased to 5.4 seconds on iOS under certain conditions. By systematically diagnosing these failures, I identified platform-level constraints rather than logic errors as the primary bottleneck. To address this, I implemented token re-registration and delivery logging, and adjusted notification frequency to reduce burst triggers that iOS tends to suppress. This process reframed my understanding of reliability as a system-level design problem constrained by OS policies, not an issue solvable through algorithmic tuning alone. The Lexi-Jarvis project strengthened my interest in robust intelligent monitoring systems, highlighted the importance of system-level evaluation beyond accuracy metrics, and reinforced my motivation to explore adaptive and human-aware AI designs.

We iteratively tested early prototypes through UW KidsTeam sessions, observing how children interacted with AI-generated stories and translated insights into system revisions. When faced with children’s pre-existing skepticism toward AI that caused hesitation before interaction, we leveraged this feedback to refine the design. We introduced the system as a “story spirit” and increased children’s agency through choices over characters, themes, and endings. Subsequent sessions showed higher engagement and reduced resistance. By combining market research, iterative prototyping, and participatory design, I deepened my interest in human-aware intelligent systems, particularly in contexts where trust, agency, and emotional response are critical evaluation criteria.

My prior experience in intelligent monitoring, deep learning-based pattern discovery, and system-level reasoning positions me to contribute effectively.

statement_of_purpose:
Introduction

I have always been a jack of all trades. For college, I chose computer science because it can be applied to almost anything in the physical world. After taking Discrete Mathematics and Calculus II, I fell in love with the rigor and structure of mathematics—how vastly different subjects relate via just axioms and definitions—and added the science of sciences as a second major. I was content, but not for long.

As graduation approaches, I needed to decide what comes next. CS or math? Which specific branch? The combination provided too many options. Hence I began the quest for my branch of passion, starting with everything my college offered. 

Research Experience and Journey

Between the Departments of Computer Science and Mathematics I was able to engage with a variety of branches in CS and/or math. 

My first try came during the summer of my freshman year in a one-month research program applying persistent homology to analyze fish locomotion. We crash-coursed through topology, read papers, learned numpy and a PH package. We asked questions, but this time the answers were for us to find. Some days brought more coding, some more discussion, some just brainstorming—or praying for inspiration. Yet the journey was strangely satisfying. You get to solve problems with people who love problem solving and care about the problem just as much as you do. At the start of the next year, we presented our findings at the undergraduate poster session at the Joint Mathematics Meetings. I want to become one of those mathematicians.

As I started taking more upper-level pure math classes and programming classes, it became increasingly apparent that my passion lies at the intersection of application and theory, with a subtle preference for the former. Thus, I started gearing my research topics towards that direction. I have dipped my toes into computer vision, machine learning, and graph theory, each topic being more intriguing than the former. This academic year, I am doing research in small language transliteration to practice NLP and continue growing my skills in elegant coding and collaboration.  

My favorite “research” experience—apart from my very first research experience, however, is the group project for my Theory of Algorithms course. Given the 2D nearest neighbor problem, we were to discuss and compare performances for two algorithms, namely, brute-force and divide-and-conquer. As the math and theory lead, I was tasked to explain the most critical part of the loop invariant for the divide-and-conquer algorithm-a proof by contradiction for why combining recursive calls results runs in O(n). The proof was dense. I read papers, watched tutorials, visited office hours. Eventually, the dots, lines, and letters on reference diagrams clicked. I presented the algorithm and the proof to the class, and that was my favorite presentation, because I know speak truth about the algorithm working as intended. 

Now, as a rising senior, I am certain my interests are in the intersection of applied mathematics and theoretical computer science, leaning more toward the latter. Although my background in programming languages is trivial, I believe my experiences with discrete mathematics, theory of algorithms, and this semester automata theory will prepare me well for software verification research. 

Why SURF

SURF stood out among other undergraduate research program because it is, first and foremost, one of the few programs that offers the opportunity to dive into cutting-edge software verification research. Awestruck by how beautifully mathematical proofs were incorporated into computer software via loop invariants in Theory of Algorithms, I hope to improve ease of access to the elegance and reliability of verification by working on gradual verification with Dr. DiVincenzo. 

Moreover, I hope to gain invaluable mentorship. A former undergraduate student in mathematics and CS navigating her way through in search for her true passion, Dr. DiVincenzo is now at the other side of the river. With students publishing and presenting their work at conferences, Dr. DiVincenzo demonstrates mentorship that pushes students to produce quality work; I hope to be so challenged as well.  

Finally, SURF welcomes international students. As an international student, I have limited access to NSF-funded REUs. While my college hosts summer research programs, the programs are at most 4-weeks long. SURF offers an extended research experience and opens doors that would otherwise be closed.

Career Goals and Skills

After my undergraduate studies, I plan to pursue a PhD in computer science or applied mathematics, focusing on software verification, discrete differential geometry, or graph algorithms. The immersive research experience SURF offers will inform me of whether software verification is my branch of passion while teaching me the foundations of programming language design, logic in computer science, and software verification techniques, which will be useful no matter which branch I focus on in the future. In addition, I will learn how to conduct independent research—formulating questions, reading literature, implementing solutions, and communicating results, which is essential for graduate school. 

SURF will be my first step into professional research. It is an invaluable chance to explore software verification, confirm that this is what I want to do, and to build the foundation I need to succeed.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in intelligence began in high school when I oscillated between the "magical power" of the artificial models I encountered in a machine learning elective and the biological complexity of the brain that I studied in my biology class. In spring 2023, Large Language Models (LLMs) surged in popularity in China, pulling my focus entirely toward artificial intelligence. Upon entering Tongji University, I embarked on an engineering project, developing a system to grade physics assignments using LLMs.

However, I found the experience to be intellectually limiting. I realized that I was merely mimicking human output with a "black box" tool without understanding the biological hardware that generates original intelligence. This realization reignited my high school curiosity about the biological brain. I decided that, to advance intelligence research, I needed to transition from software engineering to computational neuroscience. I now view machine learning not as a product to be deployed but as a tool to decipher the neural mechanisms underlying cognition.

My transition to neuroscience research was a deliberate, step-by-step process of developing the necessary technical skills. I began this journey in Professor Lianghua He’s laboratory at Tongji University. Initially, I focused on the fundamentals of cognitive experiments and EEG data collection. Once I was grounded in the basics, I advanced to developing EEG foundation models. I found that standard Transformers have difficulty with domain shifts in brain signals. To address this issue, I designed a Spectro-Spatial Aligner module that utilizes learnable channel mixing. I also validated a frequency-aware mechanism, Freq-LoRA, which targets brain rhythms.

To complement my signal processing expertise with a deeper understanding of biological pathology, I joined Professor Yujun Hou’s lab to study Alzheimer's disease. There, I was tasked with identifying biomarkers in high-dimensional scRNA-seq data. I discovered that traditional linear interpretations could not capture the complex gene interactions. In response, I used contrastive learning to design a "Latent Shift Importance" (LSI) metric that captured nonlinear gene shifts in the latent space. These experiences provided me with the theoretical frameworks to model neural signals and biological mechanisms.

Armed with these tools, I sought to test their limits with large-scale, real-world data at the University of Leeds under the guidance of Professor Faisal Mushtaq. There, I encountered the most significant obstacle of my research career: the "messy reality" of biological data.

In the "Citizen Neuroscience" project, I had to validate EEG data collected in classrooms rather than in controlled laboratories. This required me to apply rigorous statistical preprocessing to distinguish the true signal from environmental noise. Subsequently, in a "Brain Age Prediction" project using the Healthy Brain Network dataset, I encountered critical data imbalance and label ambiguity. My previous deep learning models failed to capture the developmental nuances in this imbalanced data. To overcome this challenge, I moved beyond standard regression. I developed a multi-band BrainNetCNN architecture and implemented label distribution learning (LDL) with custom KL divergence loss functions. Furthermore, I extracted effective connectivity features to interpret the direction of information flow. This experience taught me that success in AI for science comes not just from building complex architectures but also from tailoring the mathematics to the physical constraints of the data.

I am applying to the Purdue SURF program because it allows me to apply the rigorous "AI for Science" approach to experimental data. I have identified three relevant projects to which I can contribute and from which I can learn.

My primary interest is Professor Krishna Jayant’s project on probing transitions in motor learning. This project involves building a "physics-informed inference pipeline" that integrates "multimodal datasets." I can contribute to this project immediately by leveraging my experience designing custom architectures for time-series data. These skills will enable me to assist in implementing the "latent linear dynamical systems" and "switching dynamical systems" necessary for dissecting neural dynamics. While I have experience with offline data analysis, I plan to spend this summer mastering "closed-loop BCI strategies" and "state-space inference." Specifically, I wish to fill the theoretical gap in my training as a computational neuroscientist by gaining deep knowledge of how to link changes in connectivity to latent dynamics.

Secondly, I am interested in Prof. Linda Nie’s work on machine learning in human health. As the lab expands into a new research direction involving artificial intelligence, I can contribute the necessary deep learning expertise to detect metal deposition patterns. I am eager to expand my understanding of physical measurement tools. Specifically, I hope to learn about radiation-based instruments and neutron/X-ray technologies. Understanding how these "in vivo" measurements are collected will enable me to become a more effective interdisciplinary researcher at the intersection of physics and medicine.

Finally, Prof. Arielle Borovsky’s project on morphosyntactic networks offers a compelling intersection of linguistics and engineering. I can contribute to the project's goal of developing tools that parse child language samples. I aim to learn how developmental language disorder manifests in network topology.

Participation in SURF would be a pivotal step in my development as a computational neuroscientist. I look forward to the opportunity to gain mentorship from Purdue’s faculty and to utilize my skills in deep learning, signal processing, and neuroscience to contribute to the mechanistic understanding of the brain.

statement_of_purpose:
I am drawn to physics and applied mathematics because they provide a way to understand how complex, seemingly chaotic systems give rise to structure. Early in my undergraduate studies, I became fascinated by systems in which simple laws produce rich and unpredictable behavior—whether in quantum many-body dynamics, plasma turbulence, or atmospheric flows. This curiosity led me to pursue a double major in Physics and Applied Mathematics at UCLA, where I could develop both theoretical and computational tools for studying nonlinear dynamical systems. Over time, this interest naturally evolved toward the intersection of physics and machine learning, where data-driven models can uncover hidden physical patterns in systems that remain poorly understood.

What motivates me most is the challenge of extracting physical insight from high-dimensional, nonlinear data. Many of the most important scientific problems—from turbulent plasmas to climate extremes—are governed by partial differential equations that are too complex to solve analytically and too sensitive for long-term prediction. Yet within these chaotic systems, coherent structures and precursor patterns exist. A central question driving me is whether machine learning, when constrained by physics, can reveal these patterns and explain why extreme events occur. This perspective underlies my interest in ML as a tool for scientific discovery rather than a black-box predictor.

These ideas crystallized through my work on physics-informed machine learning for Thomson-scattering plasma diagnostics. Rather than training a neural network to directly map spectra to plasma parameters, I built a physics-based lookup-table forward model and embedded it in a learning framework with physically motivated loss functions. This allowed the network to learn systematic discrepancies while remaining grounded in plasma physics. Through this project, I began to ask a question that now drives my research: can machine learning uncover hidden physical structures and precursors in complex, nonlinear systems beyond the reach of existing models? This question has shaped my goal of earning a Ph.D. and developing ML-based tools to understand poorly explained natural phenomena.

The Purdue SURF program is especially appealing to me because it combines high-performance computing, large scientific datasets, and close mentorship in a research-focused environment. Many programs emphasize either theory or computation, but SURF integrates both in a way that is ideal for physics-informed machine learning. I am particularly drawn to Professor Lei Wang’s work on discovering atmospheric blocking precursor patterns using explainable CNNs in an idealized quasi-geostrophic model, which closely aligns with my interest in using ML to uncover hidden structure in nonlinear physical systems. Working with Purdue’s supercomputing infrastructure on this project would allow me to apply my background in numerical modeling and deep learning to large-scale, physics-driven climate simulations, while the collaborative mentorship structure would help me refine how I translate physical questions—such as the origins of extreme weather—into computational experiments, an essential skill for doctoral-level research. 

Participation in SURF would be a critical step toward my goal of becoming a researcher who uses machine learning to reveal physical patterns in complex systems. I hope to deepen my experience with convolutional networks for spatiotemporal data, learn how ML models are validated against physical theory, and gain exposure to interdisciplinary scientific workflows. I am especially interested in AI-for-science methods, where neural networks become part of the scientific reasoning process. The connections I would form with Purdue faculty and graduate students would also be invaluable as I prepare for Ph.D. study. 

I have pursued this field through rigorous coursework and research in both physical science and machine learning. In Professor Neuhauser’s group, I implemented Chebyshev polynomial expansions for high-accuracy special-function approximation, developed FFT-based spectral differentiation for Hamiltonian diagonalization, and wrote FORTRAN codes to parameterize screened-exchange Coulomb kernels for urea dimers and trimers under stochastic sampling. These projects required careful numerical analysis and large-scale computation on Linux-based HPC systems, giving me experience modeling strongly coupled, nonlinear systems from first principles.

On the computational side, I have applied deep learning to real-time perception and control. I built a YOLOv3-based vision system on an ESP-32 robotic platform to track and follow a moving person using only live camera input, and I reproduced the FastBEV model on the nuScenes dataset by configuring CUDA-based PyTorch/MMCV pipelines and tuning normalization and optimization for stable training. These projects involved full ML pipelines—from data processing to real-time deployment—and gave me practical experience translating deep-learning models into performance-critical systems. Together, they prepare me to integrate modern machine learning with rigorous physical modeling. 

One challenge I have faced is that opportunities truly integrate physics and machine learning are rare. Early on, I often encountered either theory without modern data tools or ML without physical grounding. To address this, I sought interdisciplinary mentorship. After reading Professor Schaeffer’s work on transfer learning for Thomson scattering, I contacted the first author, reproduced their model, and proposed my own physics-informed LUT approach. Through regular meetings, I refined how to frame ML questions in physically meaningful ways. I also filled gaps in my preparation through coursework in optimization and real analysis, online ML training, and close study of open-source codebases. These efforts turned a fragmented background into a coherent research direction. 

Through SURF, I hope to continue this trajectory by applying physics-informed machine learning to real scientific problems and move closer to uncovering the hidden patterns that govern our natural world.

The curiosity of understanding how complex systems work on the Earth, including pandemics, object motion, opinion dynamics, or extreme natural events, leads me to choose applied mathematics as my major. Throughout my coursework, I have worked on projects across multiple fields that allowed me to apply mathematical tools to real-world problems. Among these experiences, atmospheric science has resonated with me the most. When I began studying the motion of air and water on Earth, memories of watching a typhoon shatter my window repeatedly came back to me, connecting abstract equations to lived experience. 

My family lives on an island in southern China that is frequently affected by typhoons driven by interactions among temperature, pressure gradients, and Coriolis forces. I have witnessed both weak and severe storms making landfall, yet the damage I personally experienced was limited. My good fortune constrained my perception of the severity of extreme weather events. That perspective shifted when I learned about disasters in other regions, such as Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico in 2017, where communities lost access to clean water, electricity, and transportation for extended periods. Realizing how unevenly the impacts of extreme events are distributed, and how such systems continue to intensify under changing climatic conditions, motivated me to pursue a deeper understanding of atmospheric dynamics and the mathematical modeling of extreme natural events, to improve prediction and reduce societal vulnerability.

Looking ahead, I plan to pursue a PhD in atmospheric science or Earth science with the application of mathematical modeling. My goal is to conduct research that improves the understanding and predictability of atmospheric and Earth system processes, particularly those related to extreme weather events and climate variability.
Participation in the Purdue SURF program would be an essential step for my future career plan. Among all the summer research opportunity programs I reviewed, The program Purdue SURF program matches my interests the most. The project supervised by Professor Wang, applying physics-informed machine learning to idealized atmospheric models, strongly aligns with my interests. I am intrigued by the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze predictability and to forecast heat waves and atmospheric blocking with lead times of several weeks that are critical for preparedness, especially for places that are more vulnerable and unnoticed. In addition, I am interested in work that combines controlled experiments with numerical modeling to improve physical parameterizations, such as studies of ice mélange–ocean interactions in Greenland fjords, the project supervised by Professor Meng. Similarly, projects instructed by Professor Michalski that extend high-performance atmospheric models, incorporating stable isotope tracers into air quality simulations, appeal to me because they address fundamental limitations in model evaluation while requiring careful integration of physics, data analysis, and computational workflows.
I have pursued a combination of research experience and targeted coursework that emphasizes quantitative reasoning, physical intuition, and data-driven analysis. From November 2023 to May 2025, I worked on a research project supervised by Professor Sarah Marzen at the Keck Science Center. This project required me to analyze sperm whale vocalization data to investigate communication structure in a complex, noisy system. In this project, Professor Marzen and I first tried to employ CNNs on the sperm whale’s sound data, but the result turned out to be not informative and insignificant. Then we used hidden semi-Markov models to characterize temporal patterns in whale codas and examine how communication timing encodes predictive information about future vocalizations. This work has strengthened my ability to implement probabilistic models and interpret results using information-theoretic measures such as entropy and predictability, which are directly transferable to studying predictability and uncertainty in atmospheric systems. 
During my research experiences, I encountered challenges that were often difficult and time-consuming, particularly when translating mathematical or physical models into correct and consistent code. Many of these obstacles did not stem from simple programming errors but from mismatches between theoretical assumptions and their computational implementation. Resolving these issues required careful revision of model logic, close comparison between equations and code, and repeated testing to ensure conceptual consistency. In addressing these challenges, my research mentors played an important guiding role by encouraging independent problem-solving rather than providing direct solutions. They often pointed me toward relevant papers or textbooks, allowing me the time and space to work through the underlying theory on my own. I found this process especially rewarding: starting from first principles, reconstructing the reasoning step by step, and explaining the concepts in my own words to confirm my understanding. Through these experiences, I developed a more rigorous and reflective approach to research. When encountering difficulties in projects, assignments, or research, I now prioritize understanding the theoretical foundations behind a result rather than relying on surface-level answers.
Beyond my research experience, to better prepare for my research interest, I have deliberately prepare course work related to atmospheric science. At Columbia University, I have completed coursework in atmospheric science and physical oceanography, where I studied the dynamics governing large-scale circulation, air–sea interaction, and energy transport. I will soon begin to take geophysical fluid dynamics in the current Spring semester, which matches the research project SURF has offered, and my future career goal.
I am eagerly looking forward to participating in the Purdue SURF program and believe that I will strengthen my research training and take a meaningful step toward a PhD trajectory.

Across the materials systems I have worked with—battery electrodes, fastener assemblies, and functional wall-coating additives—the same theme keeps resurfacing: performance is rarely limited by a single “bulk” property, but by how processing shapes microstructure and how interfaces transmit force, mass, and charge. I am applying to Purdue Engineering’s Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowships (SURF) because I want a full-time, mentored research experience that trains me to investigate that processing–structure–properties linkage with rigor and to translate mechanistic insight into improved reliability.

My academic training in Materials Science and Engineering at the University of Washington, Seattle has given me the quantitative tools to reason about how materials behave under constraints. Courses in Mechanics, Engineering Statics, Differential Equations, and CAD have made me comfortable moving between physical intuition and mathematical description—whether that means interpreting load paths, anticipating failure modes, or designing fixtures and workflows that reduce experimental ambiguity. What I now seek is a research environment where these tools are exercised daily, and where careful measurement and analysis are treated as the pathway from curiosity to credible conclusions—precisely the pathway SURF is designed to support.

One place I learned that interfaces can dominate outcomes is structural joining, where friction and surface condition can outweigh the nominal strength of the material itself. In a collaboration with Boeing, I helped study the torque–tension relationship of BACB30LE4 aerospace bolts using a performance test machine to record real-time torque and preload. By comparing multiple lubrication conditions, I quantified how lubrication altered the torque required to reach target preload and how friction-driven scatter could shift fastening reliability. The work culminated in torque–preload curves, nut-factor calculations, and recommended torque windows tied to yield-strength targets. That project taught me to treat variability as a scientific signal—something to be explained and ultimately reduced—and it reinforced my interest in interface-governed performance.

A second setting where the same theme appears—now through electrochemical rather than mechanical performance—is lithium-ion battery fabrication. In my current laboratory role focused on batteries, I fabricate and test coin cells end-to-end: slurry preparation, electrode coating, cell assembly, cycling, and data tracking. I routinely work in controlled environments (glovebox, fume hood) and operate battery cyclers, and I have helped develop electrode formulations including NMP-based LFP cathode blends and both single-layer and bilayer coating architectures. What motivates me is that battery outcomes often hinge on processing details that determine particle dispersion, binder distribution, porosity, and interlayer adhesion—each of which is fundamentally an interface and microstructure problem. Seeing cycling curves change with subtle process choices has deepened my commitment to understanding how manufacturing decisions become performance metrics.

The same processing–structure logic also drives functional coatings, where microstructure and surface chemistry must be engineered to deliver a target function consistently. During an R&D internship developing a porous calcium-silicate-hydrate (CSH) additive for indoor dry-mix wall coatings, I assisted in CNT/NaOH–H₂O₂ oxidation and porogen-templated CSH calcination, prepared pilot blends, and helped standardize dispersion steps. Our modified CSH additive showed markedly improved ROS scavenging relative to controls, but just as important, the project underscored that “better chemistry” is not enough if dispersion and processing are not controlled. Standardizing protocols and documenting process parameters became essential for repeatability—again returning to the same question: how do we design processes that produce robust microstructures and predictable performance?

Taken together, these experiences have shaped the research questions I hope to pursue through SURF. How do interfaces—between layers in an electrode, between particles and binders in a slurry-derived film, or between contacting surfaces in a bolted joint—govern scatter, durability, and failure? What characterization strategies best separate competing mechanisms when multiple microstructural features evolve simultaneously? And how can processing routes be redesigned so that performance is less sensitive to small perturbations in handling, environment, or formulation? I am particularly interested in projects where reliability and manufacturability are central, because those constraints force research to be both mechanistic and practical.

Purdue is an exceptional environment to pursue these goals. The School of Materials Engineering’s breadth across structural materials, polymers and coatings, and energy materials matches the cross-cutting nature of the questions that motivate me. Equally important, SURF’s structure—full-time immersion, close mentorship, and an expectation of clear research communication—aligns with what I need to take the next step from “competent laboratory contributor” to “independent researcher-in-training.” I want to learn how Purdue researchers scope problems, design experiments that discriminate between mechanisms, and communicate results in a way that is useful to both scientific and engineering audiences.

My long-term objective is to pursue graduate study (Ph.D. or research-focused M.S.) in materials science and build a career developing materials and processes for demanding applications such as electrified transportation and aerospace. The common thread in those domains is that safety and reliability are non-negotiable, and progress depends on reducing variability through deeper understanding of interfaces and microstructure. SURF would accelerate my trajectory by strengthening my experimental design, sharpening my data analysis, and giving me sustained practice in translating observations into defensible, mechanism-based conclusions—skills that directly support my research ambitions.

Ultimately, my motivation for SURF returns to the theme that connects every project I have found most meaningful: processing creates structure, interfaces govern performance, and variability is both a challenge and an opportunity for discovery. I bring hands-on laboratory experience, quantitative training, and a commitment to careful, well-documented experimentation. I am eager to contribute to a Purdue research group this summer and to use SURF to deepen the interface- and microstructure-centered perspective that drives my interest in materials science.

statement_of_purpose:
Super Typhoon Usagi, forecasted to make landfall in my city in 2013, was the defining core memory in my childhood. With a mixture of dread and curiosity, I closely followed the forecasts of major meteorological agencies, tracking the dynamic evolution of its path and intensity for days.  The radar images of its eye were beautiful. Eventually, Usagi made landfall, bringing storm surge and high winds. I was mildly disappointed not to experience its calm, static eye. Nevertheless, I was mostly concerned for the populations displaced, injured, and killed in the vulnerable regions. The typhoon’s unpredictable nature held an eerie fascination for me. The interest quickly merged with my interest in natural sciences; I could see myself studying meteorology, flying freely on reconnaissance missions into the eyes of hurricanes.

Upon learning about Chaos Theory, it became the immovable source of despair hanging over my head. It prohibited precise predictions of dynamical systems, so I was under the impression that the study of atmospheric science would canonically lead to a dead end. It was not until I had this conversation with my high school physics teacher that my preconceptions were shattered. He showed me the advancement in weather models and how it improved 3-day forecasts from rarely correct to consistently accurate. I realized chaotic systems are not supposed to be spherical chickens in a vacuum. Atmospheric research is a field with endless potential to benefit humanity and save lives. Alongside my interest in PDEs and physics, I found that fluids, the chaotic yet ubiquitous entity that governs the atmosphere, coalesce all my academic interests.

This realization pivoted my interest toward geophysical fluid mechanics. In my Computational Physics course, I decided to explore fluid mechanics with PDE solvers as my class project. Fascinated by the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem but lacking the numerical tools to solve it at the time, I landed on the Burgers’ Equation as a simplified analog to address global existence and smoothness. Using Python, the Cole-Hopf transform, and the Crank-Nicolson method, I analyzed the equation and verified its global smoothness numerically for a 1D viscous fluid. This rewarding experience deepened my appreciation for the mathematical structure underlying fluid dynamics. It made the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem even more intriguing for me, as answering it could help bridge the gap between empirical modeling and rigorous mathematical understanding in fluid mechanics.

As a student at a small liberal arts college, I enjoy the close relationships with the faculty and student body, but I face limited access to research opportunities at my home institution. I reached out to faculty across the physics and environmental studies departments, but I found no projects that closely aligned with atmospheric science or fluid dynamics. Therefore, I sought external research opportunities during the summer and was offered a research assistantship at The Ohio State University for Professor Jana Houser, where I worked on tornado damage assessment. I committed 20 hours per week for three months, participating in training, data collection, and weekly supervision meetings. I was responsible for interpreting and wrangling radar data with GR2Analyst. A significant challenge in tornado imagery is distinguishing actual tornado motion from radar velocity folding, where the measured wind speed reverses sign when the target exceeds the radar’s maximum detectable velocity. This effect is often conflated with a tornado’s translational motion due to tornadoes’ rapid movements. To address this problem, I manually collected and analyzed over 1,500 data points from approximately 200 radar images. Using these data points, I helped reconstruct the paths, wind speeds, and sizes of eight tornadoes by the minute. This experience advanced my radar interpretation skills from qualitative to quantitative analysis and deepened my understanding of tornadogenesis.

Purdue SURF’s incredibly diverse research opportunities align closely with my interests in fluid mechanics and atmospheric sciences. I am particularly drawn to Professor Yue Meng's project “From fracture to flow: how calving ice sheets affect ocean dynamics," which strongly resonates with my background in geophysical fluids. Developing parameterizations of mélange-ocean drag for large-scale ocean models would allow me to strengthen my numerical modeling skills while addressing a physically and environmentally relevant problem. My long-standing fascination with polar regions and aspiration to work for the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station make this project personally compelling, as understanding ice-ocean interactions is increasingly critical in a warming climate. In addition, Professor Lei Wang’s “Physics-Informed Machine Learning to Improve the Predictability of Extreme Weather Events” interests me. Despite having limited prior exposure to machine learning, I am eager to explore how big data methods can be applied to address chaotic extreme weather systems. Professor Wang’s emphasis on atmospheric blocking and cyclonegenesis also resonates with my prior experience in tornadogenesis. Gaining exposure to physics-informed machine learning in this context would allow me to develop my computational skillset while maintaining a strong connection to extreme weather events. 

With the ambition of studying atmospheric fluid mechanics and dynamical systems, a PhD in atmospheric science became a reasonable next step in my academic journey. Like many modern sciences, most endeavors in atmospheric science require diverse perspectives from multiple contributors. Conducting research with students and faculty members from diverse backgrounds at SURF would offer me perspectives from scientists across disciplines, prompting me to go beyond my academic canon as a physics student at a small college and preparing me for a career in atmospheric science. Therefore, SURF offers many interdisciplinary research opportunities that I would otherwise not be able to participate in at my home institution or anywhere else. As a decent physicist, eager collaborator, and passionate meteorologist, SURF will significantly help me achieve my career goal of attending graduate school and becoming an atmospheric scientist.

With no equipment beyond paper cups and kitchen supplies, I began experimenting. I cut different hole shapes, varied the height of the water column, and changed viscosity using soap and oil. Even these improvised trials revealed how subtle geometric and material parameters influenced the jet’s spiral pitch and radius. Weeks later, I transitioned into a laboratory setting, where I designed and 3D-printed controlled hole geometries, built a measurement setup, and quantified how initial instabilities and geometric asymmetry governed jet deformation. As a result, I developed an analytical model to predict the jet’s shape and validated it using CFD simulations, which was later presented in a formal research paper.

The project was the first time I truly experienced what research meant. I saw how simple physical principles—energy, momentum, and geometry—could create unexpectedly elegant mechanical behavior, and I learned how much persistence it takes to uncover why. When I was dissecting the relationship between fluid viscosity and jet’s behaviors, I had no access to proper equipment. Therefore, I improvised: heating oil to vary viscosity, testing mixtures at different temperatures, and borrowing books from college students to understand the fluid mechanics behind the jet’s oscillations. Each obstacle pushed me to be more creative and patient. 
Years later at the University of Pennsylvania, that same fascination with geometry and mechanics resurfaced in a new context: kirigami mechanical metamaterials.

Last summer, working in Professor Igor Bargatin’s lab, I explored how kirigami—engineered cut patterns inspired by the Japanese art of paper cutting—can be used to create stretchable reflector materials for the next generation of lightweight space antennas. Space antennas today often rely on rigid metalized structures that are heavy, expensive to deploy, and constrained by launch vehicle size. To solve the problem, our research aimed to create an ultra-thin reflector made from aluminized polyimide film with carefully engineered cut patterns that allow it to compact smoothly and deploy reliably.

I researched how different unit-cell designs altered the mechanical response of the thin film. I tested several variations of rotating-square patterns, introducing subtle modifications such as additional slits or altered spacing. Using COMSOL, I studied how each design stretched, buckled, and rotated under tension. Through rapid prototyping, I fabricated samples to test their manufacturability. I kept iterating different geometries and concluded a few general principles for designing mechanical metamaterials for high stretchability. Finally, I conducted a comparative mechanical analysis of documented the proposed geometries and their related properties.

My initial trials revealed issues such as material burning, tearing, and poor release. I systematically analyzed the interaction between laser parameters, material handling, and thermal effects, and developed a layered support setup that stabilized the film, minimized combustion, and enabled clean cuts. In parallel, I proactively worked with another student and lab staff to recalibrate the laser cutter, including realigning the focus and replacing the cutting bed to improve precision.
