During a holiday, I helped care for my great-grandmother and noticed how a simple moment—standing up, taking a few steps, or reaching for a cup—could require both physical assistance and calm reassurance. That experience made me sensitive to how much people depend on stable support, and I later recognized a similar need in many adults who appear independent yet still carry loneliness and stress. I also noticed the limits of today’s technologies. Traditional service robots can perform pre-programmed tasks, yet they are often rigid and unreliable in changing environments. In contrast, AI systems can communicate and provide guidance, but they cannot offer physical assistance in the real world. These gaps motivated my interest in embodied intelligence at the intersection of robotics, machine learning, and human–robot interaction. I aim to develop assistive robots that can offer safe physical assistance while interacting in a manner that feels supportive and trustworthy. In particular, humanoid robots interest me because their form and behaviors can make assistance feel more natural—closer to a companion than a machine.
Building on this motivation, my long-term goal is to develop an assistive humanoid robot that can provide safe physical assistance while also offering emotionally supportive interaction for elderly care. To achieve this, I plan to pursue a Ph.D. in the United States and build a research-focused career in embodied intelligence and human-centered robotics, translating research into deployable systems for homes and healthcare settings. Guided by this career direction, I focus on two questions: (1) how can robots sense touch and interpret tactile data—pressure, deformation, and compliance—reliably in real time; and (2) how can we design safety-aware interaction policies that make users feel comfortable and appropriately trusting, so the robot is perceived as a dependable caregiver rather than a cold machine?
On the way to answering these questions, I realized that SURF is an ideal environment to turn my interests into testable research and real outcomes. First, SURF offers a research culture and perspective that I cannot easily access at my home university: full-time immersion in an English-speaking lab, close mentorship, and rigorous experimental practice. This experience is especially valuable for my career plan of pursuing a Ph.D. in the U.S., because it trains me to communicate research clearly, iterate with feedback, and meet international research standards.
More importantly, SURF offers projects that map directly to my two core questions. “Portable AI-Empowered Tactile Sensing for Real-Time Healthcare Palpation” addresses how robots sense touch and interpret tactile data in real time, giving me hands-on experience in device design/calibration, data pipeline development, and model training to infer stiffness and compliance for low-cost, portable screening. In parallel, “Learning for Humanoid Robot Whole-Body Control” addresses how to design safety-aware interaction policies that build comfort and appropriate trust; working with Digit would let me test how behaviors (speed, distance, gestures) affect users, analyze HRI data in Python/MATLAB, and learn how human-centered design can make assistive humanoids feel supportive rather than mechanical.
My preparation for this direction has followed a clear progression toward real-world, human-centered interaction. Humans outperform robots in complex real-world tasks not only because of “intelligence,” but also because of a highly capable physical system—structure, actuation, sensing, and coordination. With this belief, I first built my foundation from the mechanical side. I proposed a concept framework for elderly-care assistive manipulation that emphasizes safety and interpretability. I translated user needs into engineering requirements (safe contact, predictable behavior, stable manipulation), checked feasibility through kinematic and dynamic analysis, and modeled key components in SolidWorks and AutoCAD with manufacturability in mind. This stage trained me to think in the constraints that truly matter for assistive robots, especially safety during physical contact.
Over time, I realized that mechanical structure alone can make a robot precise, but it still behaves like a well-built puppet if it cannot perceive and respond to the world. To close the loop from sensing to action, I shifted toward multimodal perception and robot autonomy. I learned ROS and implemented pick-and-place experiments using a Dobot Magician with an Intel RealSense D435 depth camera. By working through calibration, coordinate transforms, latency, and failure cases in real scenes, I became more comfortable with end-to-end integration and systematic debugging. At the same time, I also recognized a limitation: vision-only pipelines often break under occlusion, viewpoint changes, and contact uncertainty—exactly the conditions that appear in real caregiving.
This led me to pursue more robust perception and manipulation in less controlled environments. I strengthened my modeling and debugging skills with the MATLAB Robotics Toolbox and worked on 6D pose estimation and manipulation experiments on a Unitree Z1 platform. These experiences helped me move closer to real-world conditions, but they also made a key lesson clear: even with better perception, hand-crafted rules and fixed scripts can remain brittle when the environment changes or when physical interaction introduces uncertainty.
To go beyond fixed pipelines, I began exploring robot learning. Rather than claiming robots can “think like humans,” I became interested in learning-based control because it offers a principled way to improve policies through data and feedback. In parallel, my study experience at UC Berkeley exposed me to cognitive science perspectives on how humans perceive the world and form comfort and trust—insights that naturally connect to human–robot interaction. This is why I am particularly excited about SURF projects that directly match my next research steps: the tactile palpation project can help me learn how robots sense touch and interpret tactile data under contact, while the Digit humanoid project can help me study how interaction policies and robot behaviors shape comfort and trust in humans.
As I started bridging these ideas to real systems, I faced my biggest obstacle: limited access to a mature research environment—stable hardware time, advanced equipment, and close mentorship for rapid iteration. To keep making progress, I shifted part of my work to simulation and learned Isaac Sim, where I could build repeatable pipelines, control variables, and debug systematically. However, when transferring the same workflow to real hardware, I encountered a clear sim-to-real gap. In simulation, trajectories and grasping behaviors were stable, but on the real system, I observed target pose offsets and failures caused by depth-sensing noise and perception-to-control delay (e.g., pose jitter under occlusion or reflective surfaces leading to misalignment). I addressed this by verifying coordinate frames and calibration, checking timing and control frequency, injecting sensor noise and varying key physical parameters in simulation, and tightening execution constraints such as velocity and acceleration limits. This process taught me to treat deployment failures as testable hypotheses and helped me refine my direction toward robustness and sim-to-real transfer for safe physical interaction.
Taken together, these experiences clarify why SURF is essential for my long-term plan. I am ready to contribute through hands-on system building and careful experimentation, but I also want the structured mentorship, rigorous experimental practices, and English-speaking research environment that SURF provides. With that support, I can iterate faster, evaluate ideas more scientifically, and develop deployable, human-centered embodied AI systems—especially for assistive and healthcare applications where tactile understanding, safety, and user trust are critical.

The technical work involves computer vision algorithms—optical flow, collision detection, temporal consistency—but the deeper question is about what it means for a model to "understand" causality. What keeps me motivated is that current AI systems succeed in weird ways and fail in weirder ways. LLMs generate coherent text but hallucinate facts. statement_of_purpose:
My academic interest sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, data science, and mechanism-based modeling. I am driven by a persistent question that first emerged during an applied analytics project and has since guided my research trajectory: how can computational models move beyond accurate prediction toward meaningful explanation, uncertainty awareness, and trustworthy decision support in complex systems?

This question surfaced during a telecom optimization project where I led a team to identify at-risk customers and design intervention strategies. Our models achieved over 85% prediction accuracy and reduced customer attrition by 10-15%. Yet when stakeholders requested explanations for individual decisions or asked how fairness could be justified, the model offered little transparency. I realized that strong predictive performance alone was insufficient when models are embedded in real organizational or societal decision pipelines. This experience motivated me to pursue a deeper understanding of how models represent mechanisms rather than merely correlations.

I began exploring this perspective through a Gillespie algorithm project in computational biology. I implemented stochastic simulations in Python and validated them against closed-form solutions for canonical systems. When extending the model to nonlinear protein dimerization, I observed that stochastic amplification fundamentally altered system behavior relative to deterministic predictions. Randomness was not noise to be eliminated but a structural component shaping dynamics. This shifted how I framed modeling problems, encouraging me to reason about generative processes and uncertainty rather than solely fitting outcomes.

My undergraduate research at Imperial College further strengthened this mindset. Working on space-time quasicrystal systems, I derived governing equations from Maxwell’s equations under Lorentz transformations and analyzed dispersion relations generated by Fibonacci tilings. Standard constructions produced bandgap misalignment and inconsistent scaling behavior. Rather than adjusting parameters heuristically, I redesigned the representation itself through a symmetrized Fibonacci construction and later developed a novel counting method that revealed consistent bandgap scaling across higher orders and generalized to Thue–Morse sequences. This experience taught me that uncovering structure often requires reconstructing models from first principles when conventional formulations obscure underlying patterns.

I then applied these ideas in a finance and data analysis internship at Zhejiang Tailong Commercial Bank. Working with a 120,000-record loan dataset, I built automated ETL pipelines in Python and SQL and re-engineered panel regression models by introducing interaction terms grounded in domain hypotheses, improving explanatory power from an R² of 0.62 to 0.73 with statistical validation. I translated the results into interactive dashboards supported by audit documentation so that non-technical stakeholders could interrogate assumptions and risk drivers. statement_of_purpose:
I am Shang Wang, an undergraduate student in Information and Computing Science at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University. With a strong academic foundation in mathematics, computer vision, and machine learning, and as a recipient of the China National Encouragement Scholarship 2025, awarded to the top 3% of university students nationwide, I am eager to join the the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship Program at Purdue University to pursue research in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science.

Research Interests
My primary research interests focus on the intersection of machine learning and structured representation, multi-modal intelligence, and graph machine learning, with an emphasis on the application of these technologies in areas such as visual understanding and predictive analysis within intelligent scenarios. The core of my research interests lies in exploring how to address these demands and challenges, including but not limited to effectively capturing data hierarchies and relational connections to improve modeling accuracy, solving the heterogeneity and uncertainty of multi-modal data, and transforming theoretical algorithms into practical systems that meet real-time and deployability requirements through technologies such as model quantization, knowledge distillation, and lightweight deployment. Simultaneously, I also follow other important areas to be breakthroughs in this field, such as enhancing model interpretability to improve credibility in practical applications, and exploring real-time modeling methods for structured data in dynamic scenarios.

Research Work
Started from my foundation, I joined Prof. Xiaobo Jin’s laboratory in the Department of Intelligent Engineering, where I began research projects in machine learning and structured representation. Under his guidance, I conducted two projects on Single Positive Multi-Label Learning and hyperbolic structured classification for visual scene understanding: for the first, I constructed a large-scale multi-label benchmark and developed a model to enhance verb classification in complex scenes, resulting in a full paper at ICDM 2025; for the second, I explored hyperbolic representations for structured label modeling and designed a framework to capture hierarchical and co-occurring relationships among labels, which was also published at ICDM 2025 Workshops.
Beyond laboratory research, I gained practical project experience through an internship, where I developed a multi-modal affective recognition model. Additionally, I contributed to the iGEM 2025 competition, in which our team was awarded a Silver Medal, by designing and implementing an online platform integrating a database of plastic-degrading enzymes and a predictive modeling system, and developing the platform’s full-stack architecture.
Project Experience
During my research on Single Positive Multi-Label Learning with Prof. Xiaobo Jin at XJTLU, I developed technical expertise tailored to the SPMLL research direction, and also led the implementation of two core projects. Focused on the practical application of SPMLL technology, these projects yielded substantial outcomes covering multi-label benchmarks, adversarially optimized models, and interpretable hyperbolic classification methods. I possess three core competencies: visual-language modeling, graph-based reasoning, and hyperbolic representation learning. My technical stack includes CLIP, BERT, Graph Convolutional Networks, as well as PyTorch-based optimization techniques such as the Fast Gradient Sign Method and Projected Gradient Descent. During this period, I led two key projects. First, for the SPMLL-based situation recognition project, I initially generated dual-prompt captions via VLMs and had LLMs score top labels; this was followed by manual verification from 8 annotators and 2 experts to construct a multi-label benchmark. Subsequently, I developed a Graph Enhanced Verb MLP, which integrates BERT embeddings with GCN-processed K-nearest neighbor label graphs, and used adversarial methods to optimize decision boundaries—improving multi-label mean average precision while maintaining Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy. Second, for the SPMLL hyperbolic classification project, I mapped CLIP features into the Poincaré ball via learnable Möbius transformations, and represented labels as hyperbolic balls that encode hierarchy, co-occurrence, and independence. I also designed a temperature-adaptive classifier with learnable scaling, combined it with double-well regularization and uniformity loss, and achieved competitive performance on NUS-WIDE and CUB-200-2011, while also realizing interpretable co-occurrence correlations on COCO.

Additionally, during my internship, I applied AI methods to real-world scenarios, developed a multi-modal affective recognition model based on the Qwen Omni framework, and ultimately built a deployable and optimized system that meets the real-time requirements of companion robots. In the development process, based on the adaptive modality weighting strategy guided by entropy-based uncertainty estimation, I integrated the fusion of multi-modal data including text, speech, visual, and physiological data into the hierarchical cross-attention module for enhancing cross-modal fusion, and achieved the industrial application of dynamic quantization and knowledge distillation techniques for efficiency improvement.In the specific project development process, I first built the model based on Qwen Omni and integrated multi-modal data such as text, speech, visual, and physiological data; then designed a hierarchical cross-attention module, matching temporal self-attention for speech features and spatio-temporal Transformers for visual and physiological streams to enhance cross-modal fusion effects; subsequently introduced adaptive modality weighting guided by entropy-based uncertainty estimation, enabling the model to focus on reliable signals in noisy environments; finally compressed the model through dynamic quantization and combined knowledge distillation to transfer capabilities from a large-scale teacher model, improving efficiency while ensuring accuracy. The finally optimized system not only improved emotion recognition accuracy, but also had inference latency that fully meets the real-time requirements of companion robots, demonstrating my ability to transform complex multi-modal AI algorithms into practical and deployable systems.

Building on the experience of developing multi-modal emotional AI models, I designed and implemented an online platform integrating a database of over 470 plastic-degrading enzymes and a cross-environment AI model system for predicting plastic-degrading enzymes in the iGEM 2025 competition, and helped the XJTLU-AI-CHINA team win the Silver Medal. The plastic-degrading enzyme database platform built on MySQL was developed using the React framework for the frontend and Flask for the backend, and integrated tools including rapid retrieval of biodegradable enzyme information, BLAST-based protein sequence similarity analysis, Mol*-supported protein 3D structure visualization, and iTOL-based dynamic visual phylogenetic tree analysis tools via the iframe framework. The Plaszyme model platform adopts a dual virtual environment isolation architecture; the lightweight deployment of two models—one based on protein sequence input for predicting the probability of biodegradable plastics and the other based on protein 3D structure data input for predicting the probability of plastic-degrading enzymes—is implemented on AWS EC2 g4dn.xlarge. Environment isolation is achieved via venv to resolve dependency conflicts, and cross-environment process calls are implemented through subprocess. Apache reverse proxy is integrated into the deployment to connect the access links between the HTML/JavaScript/CSS frontend and the RESTful-style Flask API, and systemd services are configured to ensure automatic application startup. Meanwhile, memory usage is optimized by configuring directory permissions, adjusting SELinux policy permissions, adding a swap partition, and limiting PyTorch thread count to ensure the best user experience. This project covers the entire process of the online platform from design to deployment; it not only demonstrates my technical proficiency in software engineering and full-stack development, but also enhances my practical capabilities in the lightweight industrial deployment of AI models.

Future work
My future research aims to advance graph-based and geometric machine learning methods for structured prediction, multi-modal data analysis, and intelligent system modeling. I plan to explore adaptive geometric embeddings for structured and relational data, as well as the integration of Graph Neural Networks for predictive maintenance and dynamic system monitoring. This line of research not only extends my prior work on SPMLL and multi-label classification but also complements ongoing research initiatives at Purdue in graph signal processing, image and video analysis, and networked systems.

Research Motivation
I am eager to apply for the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship Program at Purdue University. At the Davidson School of Chemical Engineering, I am particularly interested in Professor Can Li’s research on novel deep learning models that integrate physics and domain knowledge. Their approach of embedding optimization principles into network architectures to ensure predictive consistency strongly aligns with my previous work on structured representations and graph-based machine learning. Through my SPMLL project, where I developed a reasoning model based on graph convolutional networks and gained experience in lightweight deployment of multimodal systems, I have increasingly recognized the essential role of domain knowledge in enhancing AI trustworthiness. At the same time, Professor Yung-Hsiang Lu’s work at the intersection of audio signal processing and computer vision for AI-driven music applications also excites me. I hope to explore how multimodal intelligence can be integrated with real-world scenarios, advancing the transition from theoretical algorithms to practical systems. I am equally drawn to Professor Martin Jun’s AI-driven intelligent monitoring research. Their work combining IoT, data analytics, and robotics has inspired me to think about real-time modeling methods for structured data, such as hierarchical data capture in dynamic system monitoring, which closely relates to my interest in modeling structured data under dynamic conditions. I look forward to advancing the integration of graph machine learning with monitoring technologies to support the reliable deployment of intelligent systems. At Purdue University, I hope not only to continue building on my experience in multimodal fusion and lightweight deployment, but also to contribute to deeper integration of physical constraints with AI models. For these reasons, I sincerely hope to apply for the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship Program.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I am looking forward to the opportunity to contribute to the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship Program at Purdue University and further develop my research capacity within Purdue’s world-class academic environment.

Learning how fuels are produced, transformed, and utilized motivated me to pursue a field grounded in thermodynamics, transport phenomena, and reaction engineering, and led me to question how these systems can be made more sustainable without sacrificing performance. Recognizing that impactful solutions require more than technical design alone, I also chose to study Industrial Engineering, drawn by an interest in supply chains, optimization, and system-level decision-making. At the intersection of these fields, I aim to develop energy and fuel systems that are efficient, scalable, and economically viable.

I am writing to express my interest in a research internship at Purdue University, an institution renowned for excellence in engineering and innovation. As a Chemical and Industrial Engineering student, I seek to contribute to research that integrates thermodynamics, heat and mass transfer, and process optimization to advance sustainable energy solutions. Through this experience, I aim to learn from globally oriented, interdisciplinary research projects, collaborate with world-class faculty, and further develop my technical, research, and communication skills. Leveraging my Industrial Engineering training, I intend to study cost – energy trade-offs, develop decision tools for scale-up, and connect process metrics with operational performance indicators.

After completing my undergraduate degree, I plan to pursue a Master’s in Product and Process Design. My goal is to design and validate products and processes that rely on thermodynamics, transport phenomena, and advanced separations, applying model-based design, optimization, and PAT-enabled experimentation to ensure performance and manufacturability. In the long term, I aim to build a career in research and development within the energy or chemical industries, contributing to sustainable fuel technologies and efficient manufacturing systems.

To explore my field of interest so far, I have completed coursework in thermodynamic and transport phenomena, complemented by training in Industrial Engineering methods such as Design of Experiments and optimization. I am currently working on an independent self-heating meal project, where I compare exothermic reaction systems to evaluate heat generation and transfer performance. This project has allowed me to design experiments, analyze temperature profiles, and connect theoretical models with practical performance metrics, reinforcing my interest in research-driven problem solving.

Pursuing a double major has presented challenges, including a heavy academic workload and initial difficulties in structuring and justifying project-based work due to limited research experience. To address these challenges, I actively sought mentorship from departmental professors and peers, incorporated detailed feedback into my work, and developed structured plans with clear steps to manage complex tasks effectively. Dear Purdue University Research Internship Committee,

I am writing to express my sincere and enthusiastic interest in the research internship opportunity at Purdue University. Learning of this internship felt like discovering a perfect platform to apply my skills and passions toward meaningful research.

My central academic ambition is to pursue a PhD in Ecology or Conservation Biology, focusing on bridging empirical research with applied restoration strategies. I am particularly driven to understand how species morphologically and behaviorally respond to environmental shifts, a concern of critical importance in my home country of Colombia, where immense biodiversity faces growing threats. I believe that an internship at Purdue would be instrumental in providing me with the advanced analytical tools and mentorship necessary to address these complex challenges effectively.

My practical research experience is centered on using biological collections to investigate ecological and evolutionary questions. I am currently developing a project that applies geometric morphometrics to study potential adaptations in the gonopods of the endemic crab Neostrengeria macropa, investigating its response to historical geographic isolation on the Bogotá Savannah. Also, I am analyzing body shape variation in the damselfly Hetaerina caja across altitudinal gradients using linear morphometrics. These projects have allowed me to build substantial proficiency in data collection, curation, and analysis using tools like tpsDig2, MorphoJ, and R. Complementing this, my volunteer work in the Entomology and Aquatic Invertebrates collections at the C.J. Marinkelle Museum of Natural History has provided me with invaluable hands-on experience in specimen preparation, identification, and collection management, grounding my analytical work in practical museum science.

I have identified several research programs at Purdue where I believe I could both contribute and thrive. I am deeply impressed by Dr. Elizabeth A. Flaherty's work on wildlife responses to global change. Her focus on building predictive models to understand population and community dynamics aligns perfectly with my interest in forecasting ecological outcomes for conservation. I am also particularly drawn to the research of Dr. Patrick Zollner on animal movement ecology in human-modified landscapes. His approach directly addresses my curiosity about the tangible impacts of landscape change on fauna, and I am eager to learn how movement data can inform conservation strategies. Furthermore, I admire Dr. Songlin Fei's macroecological research. His use of large-scale data to tackle issues such as biological invasions and climate change effects on forests inspires me and represents the type of impactful, systems-level science I aim to conduct. Finally, given my hands-on experience curating crustacean collections and my current research on a freshwater crab, I am very interested in the work of Dr. Robert Gillespie in the Aquatic Ecology Lab. His research on crayfish and other aquatic organisms, particularly how they interact within their ecosystems, offers a direct and exciting opportunity to apply my skills and deepen my understanding of aquatic conservation.

My background has prepared me to be a diligent and contributing member of a research team. I am confident that my combination of morphological research skills, experience with biological collections, and deep commitment to conservation would allow me to add value to your research initiatives. 

Thank you for your time and consideration, let me know if I can provide any additional information or references.

Sincerely,
Valentina Bello Chivará

Since I was a child, I have been infatuated with understanding how the world around me worked. On long drives, my eyes would be glued outside trying to understand the magic behind wind turbines as we drove past. When the car would brake, my attention would shift to the gentle whirring noise the hybrid would make as it recharged its battery. Now, as a sophomore in Purdue’s mechanical engineering program, my curiosity of the unknown has transformed into a passion to engineer my own creations. 

My experience at Purdue has brought me a lot of insight into the mechanical engineering field. From learning about how engines work in thermodynamics to how engineers design and manufacture their products, the knowledge I have obtained has allowed me to understand mechanical systems I otherwise would not have. However, as I progressed through my coursework, I have realized that I don’t want to just analyze existing systems but rather create and improve them. For instance, last semester I had a final project for ME 164 where I was tasked with redesigning an air engine. The goal of the project was to redesign a given air engine to be at least 60% different along with designing an exterior for the engine. Working through the project, I felt captivated by it. I felt like I was gaining real experience as an engineer. I didn’t just change the sizes of the original design but rather modified it, removed components I didn’t need, engineered fits, and overall created something I was proud of. Furthermore, taking thermodynamics left me wondering and truly intrigued by how engines operated. Though we learned how gas and diesel engines worked on a small simplified scale, I began to wonder how complex engines such as jet engines operated. 

Outside of classwork at Purdue, my time with Purdue Solar Racing has been the biggest reason for my interest in research. When I first joined PSR, I was assigned to research and determine the feasibility of manufacturing a custom balance bar for the car’s braking system. I researched niche variants of balance bars and how different configurations of balance bars would impact the responsiveness and brake bias optimization of the braking system. Through my investigations, I compared and analyzed between manufacturing a balance bar in house and commercial balance bars. Ultimately, I decided that an already manufactured trusted balance bar would offer a much higher factor of safety and reliability for the driver than a custom balance bar. This experience of my research turning into real life results that would impact the car solidified my desire to pursue projects where answers were found through research.

Looking ahead, my plan is to pursue a Master’s degree in Mechanical Engineering at Purdue focusing on advanced design and energy systems. These  complex challenges in the engineering space need expertise and knowledge that go further than undergraduate study. I believe SURF is a necessary step for me to take in order to accomplish my plans since it will provide me with valuable foundations in researching and necessary lab experience to excel in graduate studies. Ultimately, I aspire to pursue a career in research and development where my foundations built from SURF will surely help me design energy efficient high performance mechanical systems.

I became interested in chemistry through moments when theory failed in practice, and when careful design and measurement were the only way forward.

That lesson first took shape during my work with Prakti, a nonprofit developing cleaner cookstove technologies for rural communities in India. Prakti’s approach differed from many failed cookstove interventions. Instead of replacing traditional stoves, the device integrates into existing ones, preserving generational cooking practices while improving airflow and combustion efficiency. Before deployment, I helped research villager cooking habits and refine the device design to fit different stove geometries. During the pilot, I measured emissions and evaluated how design changes affected airflow and smoke reduction under real cooking conditions. Comparing performance across iterations showed me how laboratory assumptions often collapse in real environments, and how material design, flow behavior, and communication determine whether a technology is actually used.

During the implementation pilot I led in Himachal Pradesh, I stepped into a villager’s home where the ceiling was completely black from only a month of soot accumulation. When the stove was lit, smoke filled the room within seconds and my eyes burned immediately. I had to step outside, but the woman cooking remained inside, and her children sat nearby as if this were normal. This felt personal. My ancestors likely lived under similar conditions, and I was standing in a place where a practical, chemistry-driven solution could matter.

I encountered the same theme in a different context through the YSP Scholars Program at UC Davis, where I investigated why irrigation sensors failed to measure water content in walnut sap. Our initial hypothesis that high-molecular-weight solutes were responsible was contradicted by vapor pressure osmometry and dimensional analysis showing an average solute molecular weight near 60 g/mol. Revising that assumption taught me how sensor interfaces, chemical composition, and physical properties interact in non-obvious ways. I now work in a computational atmospheric chemistry lab at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, validating air-quality sensors through colocation and correlation with reference monitors and analyzing large datasets in MATLAB. This work reinforced how early design and validation decisions propagate through entire analyses.

These three experiences have clarified my intention to pursue a master’s degree at the intersection of energy systems, chemical processes, and materials performance. I am interested in graduate training that allows me to work across areas such as environmental chemistry, catalysis, and materials. My long-term goal is to build a research career grounded in hands-on experimentation, where chemical and material systems are evaluated under real operating conditions and refined through iterative testing. Graduate study represents the next step in gaining the technical depth and independence needed for that kind of work.

What attracts me specifically to SURF at Purdue is the opportunity to participate in faculty-led research environments where undergraduates are expected to take ownership of experimental work. SURF offers access to catalysis and materials laboratories where questions of reaction performance, material structure, and environmental impact are investigated through hands-on experimentation and iterative refinement. I am especially interested in gaining experience with mass spectrometry, electrochemical instrumentation, and materials characterization tools used to study catalytic activity, emissions, and material durability in energy-related systems. This is the environment I want to learn in, one where I can move beyond executing procedures and instead develop the judgment needed to design experiments and understand how individual measurements support larger engineering and environmental conclusions.

In this course, my team and I synthesized PACS hydrogels and chitosan nanoparticles for wound-healing applications, gaining hands-on experience in sample preparation and in physicochemical and biological characterization. To further strengthen my research foundation, I completed the ACCBAL Formation Course for Animal Users in Research, which emphasized the ethical and responsible use of animals in science.

Following this experience, I joined the Microfluidics and Biomaterials Research Group, directed by Professor Juan C. Cruz and Professor Cristian Rodríguez, where I have been developing metal-organic framework (MOF) nanoparticles for stimuli-responsive, controlled drug delivery and bio-targeting applications. Working with Professor Lin’s team would be an ideal opportunity to expand my knowledge and contribute to advancing biomaterial-based therapies.

The SURF program will be deeply enriching for my professional growth, as I aim to become a researcher dedicated to creating solutions through biomaterials. I plan to pursue graduate and doctoral studies at a top university, most likely in the United States or Japan, focusing on biomaterials research and its applications. I am eager to contribute my ideas and effort, and I am deeply grateful for the chance to apply to a program that reflects my vision and values. I look forward to contributing to Purdue’s research community with dedication and passion.

I am Sergio Oliveros, an undergraduate student at Universidad de los Andes, Colombia, who is currently pursuing a double major in Mechanical and, Systems and Computing Engineering. While I've always been interested in Science, Technology, and Mathematics, it was Engineering that ultimately captured my heart, although not for the reason you might except. This realization came during the 2023 Mate ROV World championship in the U.S., a global competition showcasing student designed Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs). 

It was at the moment of our ROV's catastrophic failure. Despite months of rigorous designing, prototyping, securing funding, and traveling thousands of miles, our entry into the competition's product demonstration came to an abrupt halt. The moment we applied full power to the thrusters, our camera feed went dark, and device communication was lost. Amidst the ensuing panic, I should have been devastated. Instead, the failure sparked an intense wonderous curiosity, because at that moment it felt as if reality was stranger than fiction and only a groundbreaking revelation could make it all fit together. The subsequent analysis revealed the failure was a consequence of the competition's power supply being unable to handle our motors' current draw, causing a voltage drop that continuously reset our electrical systems. Nonetheless, I was left with an enduring fascination of reality’s unexpected behavior. This allowed me to understand that true engineering innovation begins when we move past conventional assumptions and embrace reality’s oddities and rarities as the tools to effectively shape our world.  

This mindset is precisely the spirit that defines research. There is no better setting to rigorously test assumptions and make transformative discoveries than in a research environment, where one’s knowledge is continually refined against the unpredictable, often counter-intuitive truth of the physical world. That’s why I could not be more excited when I was told there were research opportunities at Purdue University during the summer of 2026. However, I wanted to interact with materials directly by synthesizing, measuring, and refining them myself through experimental work. statement_of_purpose:
My research interests lie in the development of robust Artificial Intelligence for healthcare, specifically at the intersection of Physics-Informed Machine Learning and Multimodal Biomedical Data Analytics. These interests have drawn me toward two main research directions:

- Physics-Informed Modeling: How can we leverage known physical laws to constrain neural networks, enabling accurate inference from sparse medical data?
- AI for Multimodal Biomedical Data Analytics: How can we build resilient AI models that generalize across heterogeneous clinical data types, whether high-dimensional MRI scans or longitudinal physiological signals?

I have been pursuing these questions through my work as a research assistant at Cairo University and as a research intern at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). These experiences have shaped my technical approach and my desire to join the SURF program at Purdue.


My commitment to this field began during my first research assistant position, where I worked on seizure prediction using wearable technology. I vividly recall a conversation with an epilepsy patient who used a commercial detection bracelet. When I asked him about its greatest benefit, he replied, "Now my mom is a little bit more relieved as I can go out and if I had a seizure she would get a notification. Before, she was always overprotective and scared that if I had a seizure alone, no one would know to call for help."

This interaction showed me the real value of analyzing biomedical data, it translates signals into safety for patients and peace of mind for families. However, it also highlighted a critical engineering requirement. If we are going to rely on these algorithms for health monitoring, they must be robust and accurate.

This search for reliability and ways to address different problems when dealing with biomedical data as heterogeneity and scarcity led me to the paper “Hidden fluid mechanics: Learning velocity and pressure fields from flow visualizations” by Raissi et al. I was fascinated by how they managed to infer quantitative hemodynamics from limited observations by embedding physical laws into the loss function of a neural network, this was my first time encountering the concept of Physics-Informing a model. This approach significantly decreased the data dependency typical of standard deep learning models, which are often data-hungry. Motivated to delve deeper, I applied this concept to cardiac electrophysiology. As the first author of a paper recently presented at ICCTA 2025, I developed a pipeline using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to model electrical signal dynamics on the heart surface, accounting for anisotropic conduction. By embedding physical constraints, we achieved the robust activation mapping that reliability-critical medical applications demand.


The real challenge is applying AI to the messy reality of biomedical data. This challenge led me to my current role with Prof. Meena Makary, where I am developing an end-to-end deep learning pipeline for the longitudinal segmentation and tracking of multiple sclerosis brain lesions in FLAIR MRI images.

My path to research was not without significant obstacles, particularly regarding resources. In my sophomore year, I aimed to conduct research on Human-Computer Interaction for individuals with disabilities but lacked necessary resources such as computational power, devices, and sensors. Refusing to let this halt my progress, I directly approached the Chairman of the Academy to propose a research internship. My initiative succeeded, and I spent the summer developing a real-time multimodal cursor control system using spectral feature extraction from EMG signals and a computer vision-based eye tracker.

I faced a different type of challenge while conducting a scoping review on Algorithms and Modalities for seizure detection with Prof. Aliaa Rehan. We encountered a significant obstacle: the literature was saturated with ill-defined scopes regarding what constituted a 'modality' (e.g., EEG vs. non-EEG wearables) and 'algorithms' (classical vs. ML). We also faced ambiguity regarding inclusion criteria, such as how many patients we need in the study to include it, and whether we accept simulated data. Without a clear framework, our initial search yielded an unmanageable volume of irrelevant papers. Seeking guidance from Prof. Rehan, we engaged in rigorous discussions to refine our research questions, establishing answers for our questions at the beginning. My interest in computational approaches to human physiology stems from a fundamental gap: emotion recognition systems treat feelings as static categories, yet our bodies experience emotion as continuous processes of regulation, adaptation, and recovery. This disconnect has driven me to explore dynamical systems theory and computational modeling of physiological processes.

At SynHeart Research Lab, I work with multimodal physiological datasets including heart rate, HRV, skin conductance, and respiration. I preprocess and validate data, implement analysis pipelines, and build predictive models to capture regulation dynamics. These experiences revealed a key insight: the same physiological value can have entirely different meanings depending on recent history, trajectory, and system coupling. Static feature extraction fails to capture this temporal structure.
This insight shapes three research questions. First, can we identify stable configurations in physiological state space that correspond to emotional states, analogous to attractors in dynamical systems? Using time-delay embedding and recurrence analysis, I aim to test whether emotions emerge as stable regions rather than arbitrary labels. Second, can we distinguish behavioral phenotypes by transition dynamics rather than state occupancy? Modeling transitions captures resilience and adaptation that static summaries miss. Third, can stress be detected through sustained prediction error in personalized forward models? Predicting short-term signals from recent history and context allows residuals to encode individual baselines and temporal patterns. These questions lie at the intersection of computational neuroscience, machine learning, and psychophysiology, integrating neurovisceral integration theory, allostatic load models, and stress phenotyping with dynamical systems methods to reveal mechanisms classification approaches cannot capture.

The symposium provides essential presentation experience, and the program connects me with faculty who can guide me in translating theoretical frameworks into rigorous, interdisciplinary research.

statement_of_purpose:
Growing up in Gaza meant sharing 141 square miles with more than two million people, pressed shoulder to shoulder in one of the most crowded places on earth. Nights fell hard there as the power would flicker, hum, and then vanish, plunging apartment blocks and hospital corridors alike into sudden darkness. Every blackout and every dry faucet narrowed life until classes were cut short, surgeries delayed, and visits to friends quietly abandoned.

As a teenager, I often walked beside my aunt, a civil engineer, as she moved from one dusty work site to another to stitch together new water lines, electrical grids, and sewage networks for our battered neighborhoods. Her projects pulled together foreign governments, international aid groups, and local engineers around the same folding tables, where maps were spread out and arguments about pipes and pump stations blurred into conversations about dignity and survival. Watching her, I began to understand infrastructure not only as an engineering and technical challenge but as a public promise, a collective effort to make daily life more bearable through shared decisions and shared responsibility.

Since September 2025, I've worked in Dr. Ghanekar's Energy Photonics Lab characterizing materials for passive thermal management. I install and calibrate thermocouples, collect 24-hour temperature cycles using data-acquisition systems, and analyze material performance in MATLAB. One promising candidate is candle wax as it reflects sunlight and slowly absorbs and releases heat without electricity. This work directly addresses cooling in regions where power grids are unreliable or highly affected by climate change. I've learnt hands-on research methodology and how to translate raw experimental data into meaningful insights. I am actively working on strengthening my ability to communicate complex technical concepts clearly, especially in English as a second language. I also aim to develop greater independence in research by learning to troubleshoot problems and pursue solutions with minimal guidance, skills I expect an internship like SURF will help build.

I also modeled electrification pathways for Cairo and New York City using government energy datasets and thermodynamic equations in MATLAB, discovering that infrastructure optimization depends entirely on climate context. Cairo's heat load is 60% cooling; New York's seasons distribute across heating and cooling. Same renewable technology, opposite infrastructure needs. This research will be presented at the ASME Energy Sustainability Conference in Seattle during summer 2026.

For UMBC's Idea and Innovation Challenge, I designed a portable device integrating thermal storage, solar panels, water filtration, and solar cooking capability. We placed 4th. Now we are implementing this design and will compete in the CBIC competition, moving from concept to actual prototype that could serve communities without grid infrastructure.

Outside of academic pursuits, I have worked on developing my leadership and teamwork skills through engagement in student organizations. I joined Engineers Without Borders at UMBC and serve on the finance and research team designing composting sanitation systems for the Shiringamazu community in Peru. Using GIS mapping and field research to understand local soil and water conditions, I learned that successful infrastructure solutions must be deeply human-centric. As part of the future generation of engineers concerned about my region and developing countries globally, I recognize that energy and water infrastructure are the most important challenges that must be addressed in the coming decades. This spring, our team is traveling to Peru to collect field data and test designs.

SURF at Purdue directly empowers my career goals because it is interested in tackling similar issues. Professor Weibel's heat exchanger project fascinates me because it integrates additive manufacturing, the fabrication method my portable device requires, with topology optimization and thermal simulation. Learning OpenFOAM and advanced CFD will teach me how to design compact, high-performance thermal systems for AI data center cooling and electrified aviation. This directly enables the scalable manufacturing I need for resource-constrained contexts. Professor Mukherjee's energy storage analytics project addresses the missing piece in my research. My electrification modeling revealed that renewable integration depends on storage reliability, and I would like to deepen my knowledge of Li-ion degradation, thermal safety, and data-driven analysis. Understanding battery chemistry and thermal behavior will teach me the science underlying the energy systems I design computationally. Professor Raisul Islam's scanning thermal microscopy project teaches me how material properties at the nanoscale determine macroscale performance. Learning SThM to characterize thermal resistance at grain boundaries bridges my radiative cooling experiments and system-level design, understanding how to optimize materials from atoms upward. 

More importantly, I look forward to the mentorship relationships that faculty at Purdue can provide to the next generation of engineers. SURF provides the concentrated research experience, guidance on troubleshooting and independent problem-solving, and exposure to how thermal and energy research translates from lab to real-world implementation. This is exactly what I need to prepare for PhD-level research.

As a future engineer, I recognize that thermal management and energy infrastructure are among the most important challenges facing developing countries in the coming decades. Purdue SURF offers me the rigorous training, cutting-edge facilities, and mentorship I need to pursue PhD-level research that translates thermal science into solutions for vulnerable communities globally. Ultimately, I want to pursue a PhD in mechanical engineering and become an R&D engineer focused on thermal and energy systems for resource-constrained contexts.

That mindset guides all my projects. I start by identifying a real problem, then build the technology needed to solve it. That realization deepened during my software engineering internship at Google, where I worked on a performance critical desktop client for Google Play Games on PC. There, I saw how latency, efficiency, and reliability shape system design at scale, and how software decisions are inseparable from hardware realities. In parallel, my coursework in classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, electricity and magnetism, electronics, and scientific computing, along with laboratory experiments involving precision measurement and uncertainty analysis, strengthened my foundation in modeling physical systems. 

Limited access to advanced research infrastructure at a small liberal arts college pushed me to seek independent projects, external opportunities, and close mentorship. My long-term goal is to pursue a PhD in computer engineering with a focus on physical AI. I want to develop intelligent, resilient systems that operate reliably under uncertainty, whether in healthcare, agriculture, or scientific instrumentation. The gaps I encountered in my projects do not discourage me; they motivate me. They point directly to the training I seek and the researcher I aim to become: one who builds systems that work, not just in theory, but in the real world. 

Through SURF, I hope to build on this foundation by engaging in sustained, high-impact research within Purdue’s engineering ecosystem. The program represents a critical step toward my long-term goal of becoming a research-driven engineer and scientist who applies computation and engineering principles to advance scientific discovery and real-world innovation.

This journey began with my involvement in the Micromechanics of Extreme Materials Laboratory at the University of Miami, where I had the opportunity to lead a team of undergraduate students in the investigation and sample preparation of high entropy alloys (HEAs) composed of Titanium, Niobium, Zirconium, and Tantalum. I was tasked with developing a soft robotic sphincterotome used for bile and pancreatic duct cannulation in the duodenum. I was able to successfully design full CAD models for the robot, perform FEA simulations on Abaqus to quantify stiffness and evaluate mobility of pneumatic actuators, and test 7 iterations of resin printed prototypes. The final design achieved a 180° bending angle, significantly improving the operator’s maneuverability. A force-sensitive controller was integrated into the functional prototype for evaluation by endoscopist Dr. Akshintala. This system was used to measure the time taken for an operator to complete a targeting task, which determined that, on average, there was a 58% time decrease compared to the conventional sphincterotome. Seeing clinicians operating my device made me realize I want to devote my career to developing tools that will help surgeons save lives, so currently, I’m doing remote development for ex vivo testing of the soft robot.

Because of these two main challenges I have encountered in my experience, I have become highly interested in Dr. Blumenschein’s work in vine robots and activated permanent rigidity in soft robots, as these are clear solutions to current issues I have personally seen.

Overall, this program will strongly prepare me to pursue a Ph.D. in robotics while allowing me to use my dedication and perseverance to make great contributions to impactful work.

After many years, I revisited Axotlán in 2024, and I could hardly recognize the way back home. It was deeply disappointing to see that the place that shaped my interest in nature was mostly gone. Concrete slabs and industrial warehouses had replaced open land. During my visit to Axotlán, I reflected on how Santa Lucía, the town where I currently live, near the capital city of Tegucigalpa, Honduras, may be following a similar trajectory—one increasingly defined by urban sprawl. This visit prompted me to question prevailing urban development practices and to reflect on how sustainable, nature-integrated design could prevent such environmental loss. Although the process was challenging, I successfully implemented the pilot project independently, with mentorship from the nonprofit staff and faculty at my university, who guided me in designing an efficient RHS. I have also practiced field water and soil sampling techniques during site visits to a mining company, where we assessed compliance with environmental regulations and evaluated wastewater treatment processes prior to discharge into the river. Through chemistry-based courses, including general, organic, and environmental chemistry, I have developed a strong foundation in laboratory experimentation and water quality assessment. This approach ensures sustainable growth in my town and other rapidly urbanizing areas, while also preventing water resource challenges from becoming critical. I didn’t have the language for it then, but that feeling of wanting to understand something powerful and beautiful stayed with me. Over time it shifted from the sky itself to the machines we build to reach it. That curiosity is what pulled me toward aerospace, and it’s what keeps me here now.
Right now I’m especially drawn to propulsion and hypersonics, and more recently to the multiphase physics that sit underneath a lot of the engines we still haven’t fully figured out. I’m fascinated by the messy parts of propulsion that don’t have clean answers yet, like how to make new engine types such as rotating detonation engines work reliably in the real world, or how to model and measure flows that don’t behave nicely. Those questions feel wide open, and I want to be part of the generation that pushes them forward.
SURF stood out to me because it gives undergraduates a real chance to work directly with a PI, contribute to meaningful research, and build relationships that can continue into the fall and beyond. I’ve been trying to get involved with research at Zucrow since my first semester at Purdue, and SURF feels like the clearest path to finally doing that. I want to be in a lab where I can stay for multiple semesters, grow into more responsibility, and have a professor who can vouch for me when I apply for a thesis based master’s and eventually a PhD. My long term goal is to work in aerospace R&D, and I know that research experience is not just helpful but necessary for the kind of work I want to do.
I’ve tried to build toward that goal in every way I can. Through PSP Liquids I’ve been able to design and analyze regeneratively cooled hardware, rebuild film cooling models, run CFD and two phase flow analysis, and support cold flows and hotfires in the Zucrow courtyard. I’ve also been machining parts, building analysis tools in Python, and working with MATLAB, ANSYS, and CAD tools like NX and SolidWorks. Outside of PSP, I’ve been designing a low cost shock tunnel for schlieren imaging and worked on a soft robotics prosthetic that won a national competition. These projects taught me how to learn by building, how to debug my own ideas, and how to stay curious even when things don’t work the first time.
The biggest challenge I’ve faced so far has been adjusting to the pace and expectations at Purdue. I came in ambitious and excited, but it took time to figure out how to balance classes, projects, and the pressure I put on myself. I’ve had to learn resilience the hard way, especially when trying to get into Zucrow and hearing no more times than I expected. But each setback pushed me to refine my approach, build better habits, and keep moving toward the kind of engineer I want to become.
A SURF research position would give me the chance to take everything I’ve been building and apply it in a setting where I can grow for real. I want to deepen my understanding of propulsion and multiphase flows, learn new diagnostics and modeling techniques, and contribute to a project that challenges me. More than anything, I want to be part of a research group where I can stay for years, not months, and start shaping the direction I want to take in graduate school and beyond.

I am a third-year undergraduate student studying Mechanical Engineering at the Indian Institute
of Technology Gandhinagar. I have always been curious about how materials deform, how structures bear
loads, and why some designs fail under stress while others can withstand it. These questions found
direction when I was introduced to the subject of Mechanics of Materials, a course that quickly became
one of my favorites. This curiosity now drives my aspiration to pursue a doctoral degree in Mechanical
Engineering. I believe an internship at a reputable university will provide me with the exposure and
preparation I need for this journey. Most importantly, I look forward to learning from leading researchers
and making meaningful contributions to the field as I take this pivotal step in my academic and
professional growth.
Currently, I am working under Professor Ravi Sastri Ayyagari on a project based on foam stress–strain
analysis. We are using NEPER to design the tessellations and Abaqus to obtain the stress–strain
response. My task is to determine an optimum scaling factor for anisotropic foam samples and analyze
their mechanical behavior through simulations. This work has helped me connect theoretical stress–strain
relationships to actual deformation patterns and material anisotropy. Another project that strengthened my
understanding of solid mechanics was the finite element analysis of a truss structure, which I completed
as part of the Mechanics of Solids course. I developed a Python code to implement the stiffness matrix
method and determine stresses and displacements in each element. This first experience with the
Mechanics of Solids prompted me to explore it further.
Previously, in the summer after my second year, I interned at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay
under Professor Anjishnu Choudhury. My project involved developing a thin-film evolution solver using
numerical methods. I implemented finite difference schemes and tackled issues of numerical instability
and convergence. Although the project was based on fluid mechanics, it taught me how underlying
physical principles can be translated into discretized equations, a skill that directly applies to solid
mechanics and material modeling. I learned how careful mathematical formulation and stable numerical
implementation together produce realistic simulations, whether it involves stress propagation or flow
dynamics.
Beyond academics, I was a part of the founding team of Moksha Motorsports, IIT Gandhinagar’s
motorsport team. My work in the initial phase involved learning SolidWorks, designing and assembling
parts, and later assisting in the fabrication of the roll cage. The process of translating a 3D model into a
real structure deepened my appreciation for material selection, safety design, and load distribution in
practice.
Working alongside an international team of experts will expose me to diverse perspectives, fostering both
technical and personal growth. It will give me the chance to collaborate with like-minded researchers,
explore new areas within Mechanics of Materials, and access cutting-edge computational and
experimental facilities. I am eager to contribute my skills and enthusiasm to ongoing projects and to
continue learning through meaningful research experience.

statement_of_purpose:
I'm drawn to healthcare problems where we already know what matters biologically, we just can't measure it well enough or soon enough. My first encounter with this gap was personal. My mother spent years cycling through specialists as chronic pain, numbness, and cognitive fog worsened, even as she followed every treatment plan. She was forty-five before a severe B12 deficiency was finally identified.

Years later, I encountered research on whole-cell biosensors capable of detecting bioactive vitamin B12 in biofluids (Quispe Haro and Wegner, 2023). That work reframed the problem for me: my mother's delayed diagnosis wasn't a failure of medical knowledge, but of accessible measurement. I want to close that gap by building accessible diagnostic tools using biosensors and embedded systems that run ML to extract clinically actionable patterns from continuous monitoring data.

My current research in the Daniel Kim Lab, which builds non-invasive RNA biopsy technology for early cancer detection, is helping me build toward this goal. I develop a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty to generate synthetic RNA-seq data, addressing data scarcity challenges in cancer biomarker research. My hypothesis was that architectural modifications would improve the realism of generated samples. But standard training metrics couldn't test this since stable loss curves don't reveal whether outputs actually resemble real data. With guidance from my graduate mentor, I designed custom evaluations to measure what the loss function couldn't: PCA for cluster analysis by cancer type, distribution comparisons between synthetic and real samples, and statistical tests for specificity.

Initial results validated the approach: PCA revealed distinct clustering by cancer type in synthetic samples. Now I'm stress-testing the model, identifying failure conditions and mapping the boundaries of its reliability. This work has taught me that building ML for biomedical applications requires not just training models, but designing evaluation frameworks to know when to trust them.

My research has deepened my ML skills, but the biomedical devices I want to build require a hardware expertise I haven’t had an opportunity to explore yet. To build intuition for device development in a compact environment, I designed a Bluetooth Low Energy device from scratch (my first time going from schematic to custom PCB to working firmware). The challenges were immediate: 48+ hour battery life in a compact form factor, sourcing a small yet reliable power supply, and implementing efficient sleep modes. These are the same constraints that make wearable medical devices difficult to deploy outside the lab. That project showed me both the difficulty of low-power device design and the limits of self-teaching. 

My home institution has provided me with strong training in computation and embedded systems, but I have not yet had the opportunity to work in a research setting that integrates hardware design with biological data. SURF offers the opportunity to integrate both. Professor Yu She’s project on a low-cost, portable, AI driven sensing system for tissue abnormalities as an affordable alternative to imaging directly aligns with the accessible diagnostic tools I hope to build. A summer at Purdue would let me contribute my ML pipeline experience while gaining the exposure to sensor design, signal processing and biomedical development I currently lack.

I plan to pursue a Computer Engineering PhD starting Fall 2027, focused on low power biomedical devices that integrate embedded systems with machine learning. SURF is a critical step toward my future; it would give me the opportunity to explore medical applications in a context that complements my ML background, prepare me for my senior thesis and strengthen my PhD applications. The gap between what's possible in labs and what reaches patients remains wide. Devices are accurate but not deployable, algorithms work but drain batteries in hours, diagnostics exist but aren't accessible. I want to bridge this gap and spend my career ensuring a late diagnosis is not someone else’s story.

My YouTube channel peaked at double-digit views, but I spent my teenage weekends scripting biology explainers anyway, convinced I was the next Hank Green. That same kid went through a 9th-grade iGEM project on cancer diagnostics and came out realizing that biology without math felt like trying to read a book in the dark; I didn't want to "bridge" two disciplines- I simply couldn't see them apart. Now, I keep a photo of Rosalind Franklin on my desk. She smiles back at me like a cryptic Mona Lisa, and I ponder in response. I think discoveries are just refusals to look away until the pattern finally emerges. This obsession with "hidden logic" is why I pursue a dual degree in Mathematics & Computing and Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani. I am driven by a singular question: How do macroscopic patterns of order emerge from microscopic rules of chaos?

My research so far has been an attempt to answer that across scales. At the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), I worked at the systems level, modeling the stochastic coupling between circadian clocks and cell cycles using ODE-based networks. It was my first experience seeing how computational abstractions can reveal structure in noisy systems. At BITS Pilani, I moved to the molecular scale, running 600ns all-atom Molecular Dynamics simulations to explore how RNA riboswitches negotiate their way into stability. I build the code to capture that molecular "negotiation," using Markov State Models to map their conformational landscapes. In parallel, my internship at Lumos Labs has challenged me to apply machine learning to massive datasets, benchmarking sequential RNNs on over ten million user records. These experiences have equipped me with a "Swiss Army Knife" technical toolkit- from GROMACS and MSMs to PyTorch and manifold learning- ensuring I can contribute to a Purdue lab from day one.

I am coming to Purdue SURF to see exactly where my math hits a wall. I am drawn to Purdue because it is a global powerhouse for interdisciplinary engineering, providing the ideal sandbox for my "Bit-to-Atom" philosophy. I am particularly excited about projects that apply generative AI to drug discovery, where I can tackle the probabilistic challenges of GFlowNets and equivariant diffusion. Simultaneously, I am compelled by the prospect of building physics-informed state-space models to decode the latent logic of biological signals, or applying my MD experience to model the stability of designed nanomaterials. Through SURF, I hope to move past solving geometric puzzles in Foldit and start building them using Purdue's high-performance computing resources and rigorous experimental pipelines.

The greatest research obstacle I’ve encountered is the sheer high-dimensionality of biological noise. I addressed this by refusing to stay in a single box; I spent my first week on campus haunting a professor’s office just to talk about riboswitches and self-studying transition matrices before they were part of my curriculum. I learned that the noise isn't an obstacle to be avoided, but the very place where the logic is hidden. My long-term goal is a PhD in Computational Biology- so that I can ultimately lead a research group that doesn’t just analyze life as it is, but dares to design what it could become. I am ready to wrestle with real-world noise until it starts looking like logic.

My interest in engineering research emerged from a sustained engagement with dynamical systems rather than from a single defining moment. Early coursework in linear algebra, probability, control systems, and fluid mechanics revealed to me that many complex physical phenomena—turbulence, learning, biological motion, and climate dynamics—share a common structure: they evolve in high-dimensional spaces governed by constraints that are only partially observable or computationally tractable. This realisation motivated me to pursue a dual degree in Mechanical Engineering and Aerospace Engineering with a minor in Robotics, where I could work at the intersection of physics, computation, and learning.

Over time, my academic focus has shifted from solving individual instances of physical problems to understanding and approximating families of systems. Through my work on vortex particle methods and unsteady aerodynamics, I became particularly interested in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning—approaches that attempt to encode physical structure directly into data-driven models. Questions such as how physical invariances can be preserved under learning, how resolution-invariant representations can be constructed, and how data-driven surrogates can remain stable outside training distributions continue to motivate my research. These questions naturally place my interests at the intersection of applied mathematics, fluid dynamics, optimisation, and machine learning.

I am drawn to the Purdue SURF program because of its strong emphasis on faculty-mentored, problem-driven research and its culture of interdisciplinary collaboration. Unlike many short-term research programs, SURF emphasises ownership of a research question and access to institutional resources that support meaningful exploration rather than narrowly defined tasks. I see SURF as an opportunity to deepen my understanding of how physics-informed methods translate across disciplines, from climate systems to biological learning to thermal systems.

My long-term career goal is to pursue a PhD and contribute to research at the boundary between computational physics and learning-based methods, particularly for systems where traditional solvers are expensive or limited by scale. I am interested in academic research with strong connections to real-world systems, where theory, computation, and experimentation inform each other. Participation in SURF would allow me to refine my research direction, gain exposure to different modelling paradigms, and learn how large-scale, collaborative research is conducted in a leading research environment.

The research experience gained through SURF would be directly relevant to my goals. I hope to strengthen my ability to formulate research questions, work with imperfect or sparse data, and rigorously evaluate learned models against physical constraints. I am particularly interested in developing skills related to uncertainty-aware modelling, scalable optimisation, and interpretability in physics-informed learning. Just as importantly, I value the opportunity to work closely with faculty and graduate researchers, as these interactions often shape how one learns to think as an independent researcher.

I have actively explored my field of interest through coursework, independent projects, and research internships. At my home institution, I am part of the Dynamics and Control Lab, where I develop variable fidelity vortex particle simulations, study chaotic wake dynamics, and work on neural-operator-based surrogates for PDE-governed systems. I have also worked on sequential convex programming for drone docking, swarm robotics for search-and-rescue, and aeroelastic solvers, coupling FEM with meshless flow methods, with the global objective of making simulations computationally inexpensive.

Overall, I see the SURF program as a natural next step in my development as a researcher, one that will allow me to broaden my perspective, strengthen my foundations, and contribute meaningfully to challenging, interdisciplinary problems.
