statement_of_purpose:
My journey into Trustworthy AI began not in a classroom, but during a field study in Varanasi, India, where I investigated algorithmic pricing biases in ride-hailing applications. While interning at IIT-BHU, my team and I audited over 600 simultaneous ride requests to detect "dark patterns", specifically how algorithms targeted specific user cohorts with episodic surcharges. Presenting our findings to the Indian Ministry of Consumer Affairs was a pivotal moment. I realized that while AI can optimize systems, it can also amplify systemic failures if left unchecked. This experience shifted my focus from simply building models to investigating their vulnerabilities. I am now driven by a central question: As we transition from static models to autonomous agents, how do we mathematically guarantee their robustness against adversarial inputs and hallucination? This motivates my current independent research into "poisoning" attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs), where I am exploring how minute data corruptions can induce catastrophic model failure.

I am specifically applying to Purdue SURF to bridge the current gap between my independent experiments and the rigorous & scalable engineering Purdue is famous for. With my background in "Red Teaming", finding failure modes in AI systems, I am targeting Professor Alejandro Strachan’s work on AURA (Autonomous Universal Research Assistant). I understand that AURA is not just a chatbot, but is a complex multi-agent system that uses runtime metadata reasoning to orchestrate over 340 simulation tools on nanoHUB. This architecture fascinates me, but presents a unique security challenge: A scientific agent that autonomously plans research is only as trustworthy as its resilience to hallucination and data poisoning. I propose to apply my existing background to stress-test AURA, specifically, evaluating AURA's resilience against three threat vectors: (1) adversarial prompts designed to induce hallucinated scientific results, (2) data poisoning in the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data ecosystem that could corrupt scientific reasoning, and (3) workflow manipulation through malformed inputs. Drawing on my experience with mechanistic analysis of poisoned LLMs, I would develop automated testing frameworks to ensure AURA is not just efficient, but mathematically robust against manipulation.

My research foundation was established during my internship at IIT-BHU, which provided my first exposure to the intellectual rigor of a premier technical institution. This experience was transformative, instilling a methodological discipline I previously lacked. It taught me how to systematically navigate the research lifecycle: progressing from initial problem formulation and hypothesis testing to rigorous experimental validation and result synthesis. I subsequently applied this structured approach to my independent project on Adversarial ML, specifically replicating the "Constant-Number Poisoning" hypothesis on the Pythia-410m model. This project required not just implementing established methods, but troubleshooting novel failure modes under hardware constraints, eventually validating a stealthy DoS backdoor triggered by <0.01% of training data, via mechanistic loss analysis.

My research path has not been without significant technical hurdles. During my LLM poisoning project, I lacked access to high-performance GPUs and had to train the Pythia model on a standard Apple M1 laptop with only 8GB of RAM. I hit constant "Out of Memory" (OOM) errors that threatened to stall the project. Instead of giving up, I re-engineered the training pipeline. I implemented Adafactor optimization, utilized Gradient Accumulation to simulate larger batch sizes, and enforced FP32 precision to stabilize the training. This experience taught me that research is rarely about having perfect resources, but rather it is about finding engineering solutions to constraints, a mindset I am eager to bring to the Purdue engineering community.

The limitations of post-hoc auditing are becoming clear to me: by the time I detect algorithmic failures, systems are already deployed and causing harm. My long term goal is to develop mathematically rigorous verification methods for autonomous AI systems, essentially making "red teaming" a design principle rather than an afterthought. SURF would provide the foundation for this transition: learning to build robust scientific workflows on nanoHUB would teach me how to architect reliability into complex AI systems from the ground up, rather than testing for it after the fact.

This work required careful attention to filter stability, parameter smoothing, and nonlinear behavior to avoid artifacts during real-time modulation. In parallel, I developed a Python-based audio-to-MIDI system for monophonic signals using time–frequency analysis, onset detection, and pitch estimation. Debugging failure cases—particularly octave errors and false onsets—forced me to iteratively refine algorithmic assumptions rather than rely on library defaults. These projects gave me direct exposure to the research mindset of hypothesis, testing, and revision.

My interest in signal processing is strongly tied to hardware implementation. statement_of_purpose:
My interest in propulsion began with classical aerospace systems such as gas turbines and rockets, but it deepened when I was introduced to electric propulsion during my work on electrospray and Field Emission Electric Propulsion (FEEP) thrusters. While studying these micro-propulsion devices, I encountered Hall-effect thrusters as one of the earliest and most successful plasma propulsion technologies flown in space. What fascinated me was that despite their vastly different scales, both systems are governed by the same physics: plasma generation, charged-particle acceleration, and the challenge of maintaining stable, long-term neutralization. This intersection of plasma physics, electromagnetics, and propulsion engineering is what continues to motivate me to pursue this field.

In my current research project, I am developing an indium-based FEEP thruster from scratch, including electrode geometry, neutralizer concepts, and measurement probes, supported by numerical modeling in OpenFOAM. Through working with a laboratory electrospray system, I directly observed how increasing mass flow rate leads to droplet emission, while increasing voltage sharpens the Taylor cone and enables ion emission. Stable ion-mode operation was only achieved within a narrow operating window of flow rate and electric field. This experience gave me a first-hand appreciation of how emission stability, neutralization, and plume behavior are tightly coupled—issues that are equally central to Hall thruster cathodes and plume physics.

My exposure to chemical propulsion during my internship at ISRO’s Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) further strengthened my interest in experimental propulsion. I had the opportunity to observe hydrazine thruster firing tests, thermal-vacuum qualification, vibration testing, and sensor calibration facilities. My desk drawer holds a peculiar collection: printed papers with margins dense in pencil annotations. They're rejections, NeurIPS 2025 among others. I keep them because they taught me that research isn't about always being right.
I came to AI safety through a side door. During my college admission process in India, a health crisis disrupted everything. Months of treatment meant missed preparation, missed opportunities, and ultimately, a university that wasn't my first choice. That helplessness could have ended my story. Instead, it showed me that when traditional paths close, you build your own.
My nights became a rhythm of implementation and iteration. I taught myself through papers. I'd pull up Neel Nanda's glossary on one screen, a PyTorch implementation on another, and work through architectures line by line. GPT, then LoRA, then DPO[1]. Each one proved I could learn anything given enough time.
But learning alone has limits. My breakthrough came from explaining representation engineering badly to a junior researcher in the SPAR mentorship program. Their confusion forced me to strip away jargon and find the core idea. That's when I understood: mastery isn't perfect execution, it's rebuilding understanding from scratch.
This shaped my TopoReformer project[2]. Adversarial robustness fascinated me because it exposed something unsettling: these models we trust are fragile. One perturbed pixel could fool a system completely. It represented exactly what I'd been dealing with: systems that look robust but fail under pressure.
Standing at AAAI 2026 in Singapore, presenting to researchers whose papers I'd implemented late at night, something shifted. I wasn't an outsider anymore. I was part of this effort to make AI systems we can trust.
What draws me deeper isn't just technical elegance, though there's beauty in watching a sparse autoencoder reveal interpretable features or seeing representation engineering separate harmfulness detection from over-refusal[3]. It's the stakes. Every project exists in service of one question: how do we build systems powerful enough to transform the world but aligned enough to deserve that power?
We're building increasingly capable systems using methods we barely understand. My work on coherence-based deception detection[4] emerged from this problem. If we can't interpret what models are thinking, how can we trust them? The answer isn't some elegant proof. It's painstaking work: attention head analysis, activation patching, circuit tracing. Understanding these systems piece by piece.
After NeurIPS rejected my adaptive safety calibration work, my senior shared their own rejections. "Research is mostly being wrong in increasingly sophisticated ways," they said. The work that failed became the foundation for understanding why LLMs over-refuse benign requests while staying vulnerable to jailbreaks. Failure was just incomplete success.
The SURF program represents what I've been chasing since that difficult admission process: working directly with people who've spent their careers on these problems. The structured guidance I've been piecing together through Discord servers and programs like SPAR and Algoverse.
My vision is simple. Five years from now, I want to be deep in alignment research, contributing to making AI systems both powerful and safe. Maybe working on interpretability at a research lab, maybe building verification tools, maybe discovering problems we don't know exist yet. What matters is being part of the community working on the most important technical challenge of our generation.
The path here hasn't been traditional. No elite institution, no continuous access to professors, no clear roadmap. Just consistency: showing up every day to implement another paper, to push another commit, to make progress where I could find it. My portfolio[5] shows this: hundreds of commits, dozens of implementations, the quiet accumulation of understanding.
I keep those rejection letters as reminders. Not because research is easy or because I'm brilliant at it, but because the questions are too important to abandon when things get hard. How do we detect deception in systems smarter than us? How do we build robustness without sacrificing capability? How do we bridge the gap between what models do and what we understand?
These questions require persistence, collaboration, and deep technical work. The kind that happens when you're willing to be wrong, to iterate, to keep building even when the path isn't clear.
I've been doing this work alone. Now I want to do it together.

The system uses sound, facial cues, movement, and temperature to infer anxiety and respond appropriately. While working on it, I expected the main challenge to be technical. Instead, what stood out was how uncertain everything was. There were no clear labels, no definitive answers, only patterns that had to be interpreted carefully. That insight led me to build a sound-based machine condition monitoring system using unsupervised learning. In industrial environments, failures are rare and labeled data is scarce, so the system had to learn what “normal” sounds like before it could identify anything unusual. This project reinforced something I was beginning to understand: real-world intelligence often means learning structure where none is explicitly given.
I encountered the same idea again in a completely different setting while building a property-guided molecular generator. In many cases, the problem is not exposure, but fragility in how linguistic knowledge is structured and connected. Understanding and strengthening this structural is what draws me to "Professor Arielle Borovsky's work, on Parkinson's Disease", which helped me see that understanding can seem stable in familiar situations, but becomes less reliable when learners have to depend on it in new ways. Paying attention to this difference between managing tasks and truly understanding now shapes how I think about supporting early learners.

I kept noticing the same pattern across classes and datasets: students could complete work and earn reasonable scores, yet struggled to explain their reasoning or apply it in new and earn reasonable scores, yet struggled to explain their reasoning or apply it in new contexts. Working with learning data and classroom tools showed me how often confusion and reliance on support remain invisible in standard measures. I want to study these less visible parts of learning to help teachers better understand how students are actually learning, where AI tools increasingly shape student work and to design learning systems that genuinely support teachers, rather than masking gaps in understanding behind surface progress.

In my prior research at IIT Madras, I built end-to-end educational modelling pipelines  combining psychometric theory and machine learning, using Item Response Theory and Knowledge Space Theory to infer latent learner ability and concept dependencies, and neural embeddings to generalize to unseen questions. Designing teacher-facing dashboard at IIT Bombay taught me that effective learning analytics is not about showing more data, but about reducing cognitive effort for teachers. Our work focused on transforming latent student data into tools that enable quick, meaningful instructional insight, while analyzing teachers' clickstream behaviour to understand how such tools are actually used and how they can be improved. Building on this perspective, I want to better understand how children's language knowledge is organized through relationships between ideas, focusing on where those relationships start to falter, and what those points can teach us about supporting learning more thoughtfully.

One obstacle was finding where my curiosity fit. Although machine learning gave me strong technical grounding, its breadth made it hard to identify a meaningful interdisciplinary direction until teaching and time in learning environments, especially during a visit to a school where students were encouraged to ask questions and explain their thinking. Because educational technology remains underrepresented in India and lacked a clear pathway at my institution, I sought mentorship across departments at IIT Madras leading to work in learning analytics under Professor Andrew Thangaraj and engagement with faculty at IIT Bombay through attending conferences on education technology.  Working without predefined tracks, trying ideas, reaching out when stuck, and letting questions sharpen through exposure reshaped how I approach research, focusing less on labels and more on staying close to problems.

There are aspects of learning that only become visible when theory, data, and intervention are studied together, and the Purdue SURF program sits exactly at this intersection. What draws me to this environment is the chance to stay with a problem long enough to question my assumptions, refine my thinking, and see how ideas actually hold up when tested with real data and real learners. Across this work, I came to see that learning is modelled even during failure moments where performance appears weak and often reveals the most about underlying structure. Being part of a research community where questions are challenged, reframed, and sharpened through discussion would push me to think more carefully about both the structure of learning and how that structure can be acted upon.

This kind of sustained, reflective work matches how I want to grow as a researcher by staying close to real learning problems long enough to understand them and it motivates my goal of pursuing doctoral study in educational technology and learning sciences, where I hope to build systems that respond to how children actually learn, especially when learning paths are uneven and support matters most. This idea of impact-driven projects became the reason I decided to pursue computer science and has been the reason I have been at the intersection of computer science and biology. statement_of_purpose:
People often imagine curiosity as something that starts with clear questions. For me, it began out of not understanding much at all. I was that kid who asked questions long before he knew how answers were meant to be. Coming from a family where college was a distant idea, I became aware early on of how small gaps in technology limit access to even basic needs. I didn’t have any words for it then, but I noticed when things didn’t quite work. That habit stayed with me and over time, it led me toward engineering and eventually research. College didn’t change that habit; it simply gave the structure and direction. Computational Engineering felt natural, turning physical ideas into models I could test. Through labs and coursework, I began to see algorithms that were not just tools that succeed or fail, but as expressions of the assumptions behind them. A moment that stayed with me came from a numerical method that resisted every correction I tried. For days, I assumed I was missing something obvious, until I realized the limitation was built into the method itself and this reframed the questions I kept asking: why something works, why it fails, and what those failures reveal. This was the first time research began to feel less distant and more like the natural extension of questions that motivate me.
I ran into these questions again in a concrete way when I began working with Prof. Sai Sidhardh’s group on inverse modeling of viscoelastic materials. In practice, recovering hidden material properties meant replaying the full physics at every step. Some inferences stayed out of reach, shaped by how the model represented the behavior. Studying different formulations made this clearer: the model was not just slow, it was deciding which behaviors were even visible. That same concern reappeared during my work on semantic multimodal alignment, where combining visual context with text suggested that a representation can perform well while still failing to fully preserve the underlying structure it is meant to convey. It pushed my questioning from how a method was implemented to what it assumed. As simulations scaled, it became clear that increasing computation alone did not resolve these limits. My focus gradually moved from running bigger jobs to how a method’s structure shapes reliable inference when multiple physical effects interact.  It was the first time my curiosity felt like a deliberate research pursuit, and with this I realized knowledge gains value only when others can access and build upon it. That belief carried into my work with the AI-ML Club, where I led hands-on sessions breaking down model architectures and organised discussions on core papers to understand why approaches work and where they fail.
Research quietly began to reshape the path I once assumed for myself. As a first-generation student, I initially expected to complete my degree quickly, support my family, and learn the rest in industry. But as graduation approaches, I have realized that I still have much left to learn and I cannot leave with a gap. I kept returning to questions of representation learning through inverse modeling: how models encode structure and where those representations begin to break down. In inverse modeling, I often found that some parameters remained weakly identifiable under noise, as the available observations carried limited information about them, independent of how much computation I applied. Prof. Gómez’s work uses AI to take on parts of the modelling process governed by physical laws, so that simulations are not just solved but shaped by what the learning system notices. That approach treats computation as a way of discovering behaviour in a physics-based model, not only reproducing it. Work by Prof. Ruqi Zhang extends that idea using generative methods to build internal spaces that are shaped by what the model is allowed to consider, not just by where data happens to lie. Seeing how constraints form those spaces makes it clear that representation is an active choice about what a system can learn, not just a storage format. While my work has focused on analyzing representation choices after the fact, I have yet to develop a principled way to decide under uncertainty, which observations are worth refining for identifiability. I believe that Purdue SURF offers a setting where these questions can be examined through careful modeling, reproducibility, and sustained discussion. The program’s emphasis on independent work under close mentorship, provides space to test these assumptions early, before they harden into longer-term research commitments.

My fascination with electronics started not with the finished device, but with the unseen infrastructure behind it. I have always been intrigued by Electronics and Communication Engineering because even the most complicated real-world problems often have simple solutions hidden in the microscopic realm. As an ECE undergraduate at Jamia Millia Islamia, I explored many subjects that gave me various viewpoints; however, it was while studying VLSI Technology that everything began to click for me. I was fascinated by how billions of transistors are integrated onto a single chip, which led me to ponder over a critical question that fuels my academic pursuit: “How can we push the physical limits of materials to create defect-free devices?” This curiosity led me to the field of semiconductor fabrication, where the challenge is not just designing a circuit, but architecting the very materials that make it possible. This curiosity motivates me to bridge the gap between theoretically designing a device and the practical reality of fabricating it.

I am specifically attracted to the SURF program because it offers the one resource I need most: access to the cleanroom facilities. The most compelling resource SURF offers is access to the Scifres Nanofabrication Laboratory. The opportunity to work at the Birck Nanotechnology Center would allow me to gain hands-on experience in semiconductor fabrication. My long-term career aspiration is to pursue a PhD in semiconductor fabrication and contribute to research that impacts the scalability of electronic devices. Participation in SURF would be the most critical step toward this goal, transitioning me from a student who simulates fabrication to a researcher who performs it. I aim to gain proficiency in lithography and etching processes and to try these techniques myself. I also wish to learn about cleanroom safety protocols, metrology, and other essential skills needed for a career in this field. Additionally, I want to explore ways to optimize these processes while making efficient use of available resources. 

To explore this field, I have actively sought opportunities beyond my university curriculum. My most significant step was a summer internship at the Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL), DRDO, Ministry of Defence. Working under senior Scientists, I conducted a preliminary simulation study on fabricating deep cavities for a cesium T-cell using Deep Reactive Ion Etching (DRIE) Bosch process. I utilized IntelliSuite to model and validate microfabrication workflows, analyzing process parameters for MEMS based atomic clock. I analyzed critical process parameters such as gas flow rates, etch cycles and scalloping to optimize sidewall verticality and minimize scalloping virtually. This experience was pivotal, it taught me the rigorous patience required for research and the power of simulation in predicting experimental outcomes. 

A significant obstacle has defined my path to exploring this field: the lack of accessible cleanroom facilities. The primary obstacle I have faced is the simulation gap.  While my university provides a strong theoretical foundation, the on-campus cleanroom is non-functional due to operational constraints and access to cleanroom facilities in India is limited. To overcome this, I took the initiative to secure a research internship at SSPL, DRDO. However, even there, I faced a challenge. Due to strict security protocols at the Ministry of Defence, I was restricted from physically performing experiments in their functional cleanroom. Rather than being demotivated, I utilized the available resources to perform high-fidelity simulations. Yet, I recognize that simulation is only a proxy for reality. To advance as a researcher, I must bridge the gap between virtual modelling and physical fabrication. 

This simulation experience gave me a unique perspective that I can contribute to the Purdue research team. By analyzing process parameters, I learned to identify potential defects like scalloping and optimize process integration virtually. This background makes me a strong fit for the "Epitaxial growth of wafer scale semiconductor thin films" research project. The opportunity to use a Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) system to grow single-crystal films represents the missing piece of my education. I am eager to apply this understanding of wafer dynamics to the physical growth of semiconductors. 

In conclusion, I have explored the theoretical and simulated aspects of my field to the fullest extent available to me. I am now ready to face the rigors of experimental research. The opportunity to work in one of the most advanced academic cleanrooms in the world would allow me to finally translate my simulation experience into hands-on fabrication skills. I am eager to bring my resilience and my simulation-backed understanding of fabrication processes to the research teams at Purdue.

statement_of_purpose:
When two teammates left mid-semester, the project just became me and a graduate TA staring at an unfinished RISC-V core, part of Purdue’s System-on-Chip Extension Technologies development team. We had planned to split the job of embedding performance counters, the tiny sensors that show what a processor is actually doing, but now I was alone in the workroom tracing green waveforms across my laptop and asking the same question: why is this counter silent?

To someone outside computer engineering, a stalled counter is just a zero. To me it felt like trying to read a book with missing pages. I followed the trail through the memory stage, rewrote the chip’s 64-bit write logic for the counters, and checked every permission bit until the counts finally moved. When they did, the logic came into view. Presenting at Purdue’s Fall Expo and watching software read those signals showed me the value of making a hidden system visible.

That moment, turning a silent, opaque, system into something observable and useful captures why I study computer engineering. I am drawn to problems where failures hide behind complexities and where better instrumentation, clearer interfaces, or a small redesign can transform unusable behavior into actionable data. Two questions motivate me now: how can we design hardware that is inherently more observable and debuggable by software, and how can we apply the same clarity-first to emerging technologies? Both questions sit at the intersection of digital logic, computer architecture, and algorithmic tooling. Both reward the habits I’ve developed: moving closer, measuring carefully, and asking small, specific, questions until structure reveals itself. 

SURF appeals to me because its concentrated, summer-long converts that habit into true research. An uninterrupted block of time with dedicated mentorship and full access to lab resources lets me move faster than a fragmented semester allows: I can work in controlled experiments, iterate on instrumentation nightly, and follow up on unexpected results without losing momentum without being confined to other schoolwork obligations. Over the course of the summer I would take my RISC-V visibility work and push them into reproducible studies, defining clear metrics, building data collection, and validating fixes across. That focused cycle of rapid iteration and rigorous evaluation is exactly the bridge I need from classroom projects to a career in hardware-software co-design research. 

Concretely, I hope SURF will deepen my research methodology, give me hands-on experience with advanced measurement and test equipment, and expose me to state-of-the-art hardware toolchains and workflows. I also want mentorship that helps translate small, practical fixes into publishable experiments or follow-on projects. Long term, I plan to pursue a doctorate and a research career in industrial R&D building processors and improving hardware architecture.

My preparations so far have put me on a trajectory towards those goals. I’ve contributed to the VIP SoCET SoC and completed a summer research project building and training an 8-qubit hybrid quantum-classical neural network. I regularly draw and redraw block diagrams before coding so my debugging is reasoning rather than guesswork. I prioritize minimal, testable, experiments that preserve incremental wins. these projects demonstrate a readiness and eagerness to continue in hardware architecture and computer engineering research.

I have faced obstacles that tested and strengthened this approach. Losing teammates mid-semester forced me to shoulder unfamiliar responsibilities and to learn quickly under time pressure. Instead of deferring or scaling back, I partnered closely with the graduate TA, broke the problem into smaller verification steps, and iteratively validated changes with testbenches and waveforms. In the quantum project, an eight-qubit collapse into noise initially felt like a dead end; by sketching circuit diagrams, varying depth, and instrumenting the training loop, I traced the issue to a single entangling layer and restored reliable results. Those experiences taught me how to recover progress when systems become opaque. By forming a small, testable hypothesis, designing the minimal experiment to confirm it, and preserving incremental wins so research can move forward.

SURF would accelerate that cycle of hypothesis, experimentation, and iteration. With its concentrated mentorship and lab resources, I can convert the debugging techniques I developed into rigorous methods, broader tooling, and reproducible evaluations that address the visibility and reliability questions I care about. More than anything, SURF is an opportunity to learn how to ask better research questions, and how to answer them so other engineers can finally read the pages that were missing.

Studying aerospace engineering deepened that fascination: learning the physics behind an almost “unphysical” phenomenon made me realize how much planning, testing, and computational validation happens before a vehicle ever leaves the ground. This motivates the question I now want to pursue as a researcher: how can we build reliable simulation tools under these constraints? This is what led me to the intersection of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Scientific Machine Learning, especially Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).

This work shaped my research mindset: forming hypotheses, tracking failure modes, diagnosing instability in training, and iterating until results became robust. I learned that when something “doesn’t work,” it often signals deeper numerical behavior or physics that must be understood rather than bypassed. I learned to treat failure as a tool for understanding, and I also realized the value of seeking guidance from faculty and graduate researchers when stuck. Purdue’s strengths in CFD, HPC-driven simulation, and scientific computing make SURF an ideal next step toward this goal. statement_of_purpose:
No experience or instance led me to biomedical engineering; rather, it was my search for a logical framework based on the fundamental mathematical and physical laws to explain biological systems. I seek to explain every concept and system through a series of so-called ‘logic bricks’, consisting of the purest form of logical explanations I can find: the conservation laws, the fundamental forces, and the principle of minimum energy. With these, I can assemble an understanding of even broader laws, such as the laws of thermodynamics, and from there, construct an explanation for even broader phenomena, such as chemical reactions and, ultimately, biological systems.
The complexity of biology gives rise to a feeling of randomness, yet given the correct ‘logical bricks’, even the most seemingly random movement of particles can be described by the laws of diffusion. The phenomenon of diffusion presents a perfect example of how the biological phenomenon of particle movement can be described mathematically through both empirical observations (Fick’s first law) and through the fundamental principles of mass conservation (Fick’s second law). The biological phenomenon that was once a black box is now harnessed for use in drug delivery, drug dosing, and more. Flick’s laws exemplify what I admire most about quantitative biology: the process of using fundamental logic bricks to build a logical and predictive structure for biology.
While Flick’s foundational observations were established over a century ago, the drive to quantify biology continues. Professor Goergen’s project, predictive modeling of aortic root dilation, embodies the use of mathematics to construct a predictive model for a biological system. It seeks to establish how variables like echocardiographic features, hemodynamic forces, and genetic factors logically dictate the risk of aortic dilation. A satisfying case-and-effect relationship quantified by math. Similarly, Professor Qazi’s project on the cellular basis for fibrotic remodeling after injury in skeletal muscle appeals to my desire for mechanistic deconstruction. Through a reverse-engineering approach, this project aims to quantify the interactions between molecular constituents to create a rule-based understanding of tissue fate after injury. While methodologically distinct, these projects represent the different sides of my interests: using mathematics to model biological systems and disassembling biology to uncover the governing factors.
As a sophomore, I have prioritized developing my foundational skills and knowledge that will allow me to help contribute meaningfully to research. This focus culminated this past semester in my core major courses, where I applied these principles to biological systems. In Conservation Principles for Bioengineering, I learned how to deconstruct mass and energy transport into their governing equations. Applying mass and energy accounting equations to model blood flow or drug diffusion helped teach me how biology is constrained by universal physical laws. In Linear Algebra for Biomedical Data, I saw how math concepts, including differential equations and calculus, can serve as a framework for biological dynamics. Analyzing their solutions and end behavior introduced me to how math doesn’t just describe biology, but can also predict its stability or failure. These courses have prepared me with the analytical and logical framework to approach a SURF project as an apprentice who understands how integral fundamental principles are.
The SURF program offers the uninterrupted focus necessary to immerse oneself fully in a unique research project for eleven weeks, a depth that is unmatched by the pace of semester-based lab work. As someone who prioritizes depth in my learning, such immersion is essential to progress from learning techniques and concepts to helping contribute meaningfully to a research question. Furthermore, SURF integrates participants into active research groups, allowing them to observe the process of research, rather than just viewing polished outcomes, as is common in coursework. Aside from bench experience, I seek the more holistic development that Purdue’s SURF provides. The weekly seminars, along with the symposium and final report, are an essential investment in the skills required for a Ph.D. and a research career.
As someone driven to root my understanding of scientific phenomena in fundamental principles, a Ph.D. represents the ultimate opportunity to traverse such a path independently; to uncover a new black box and chart its constituents with my own logical framework. As a sophomore, I am still exploring research directions and developing my skills. Purdue’s SURF is the ideal apprenticeship to test my aptitude for full-time research, add invaluable bricks to my foundation, and help me take a definitive step towards my long-term goals.

My name is Praveen, and I am a 4th year dual-degree (Btech + Mtech integrated in 5 years) undergraduate student in Electrical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, pursuing minors in Computer Science Engineering and Artificial Intelligence & Data Science. I grew up in a small city where opportunities were limited, but curiosity was not. Moving to Mumbai (One of India’s largest metro cities) to study Electrical Engineering at IIT Bombay was a turning point, not just geographically, but intellectually. Being surrounded by one of India’s most intense academic environments exposed me to an extraordinary range of ideas, people, and problems.
I chose a dual-degree path in Electrical Engineering with minors in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence & Data Science because I did not want to view intelligence purely as an algorithmic abstraction. As modern machine learning models grow larger and more resource-intensive, their performance, efficiency, and feasibility are increasingly dictated by the underlying hardware, system architecture, and operating constraints. I wanted to understand how electrical systems, computation, operating systems, and learning-based models interact, and how intelligent algorithms can be designed, deployed, and optimized in tight coupling with real hardware and physical limits rather than in isolation.
My interest in research grew from repeatedly encountering the same question across domains: how can complex systems be explored and optimized efficiently without treating them as black boxes? This question has driven my work in diffusion models, transformers, program synthesis, and system-level optimization. From deepfake detection to financial time-series forecasting, I have been motivated by problems where structure matters as much as scale. I continue to pursue this field because the most impactful advances today happen at intersections, between machine learning and scientific reasoning, between algorithms and hardware, and between automation and human insight.
My first preference project, Generative AI for the Discovery of New Drugs, directly aligns with my strongest research interests. I have substantial experience with diffusion models, transformers, and generative modeling, including implementing DDPMs, classifier-free guidance, and advanced decoding strategies for LLMs. What excites me about this project is the shift from unconstrained generation to structured, physically meaningful generation. Designing molecules with desired properties is not just a machine learning challenge; it is a problem of embedding symmetry, geometry, and constraints into generative processes. This project represents exactly the kind of research I want to pursue: principled generative models applied to real scientific discovery.
My second and third preferences, Automated Characterization of CMOS+X AI Hardware and AI-Assisted Design Automation of ICs and Systems, connect strongly to my identity as an Electrical Engineering student with deep machine learning exposure. My coursework in processor design, IC and VLSI design process, signal processing, and formal verification, combined with hands-on experience in prototyping, and system testing, allows me to meaningfully contribute to hardware-centric research. At the same time, my internships and research in AI, program synthesis, and agentic systems position me well to develop intelligent automation frameworks for testing, modeling, and design.
In particular, the idea of building an automated characterization platform and extending it with an LLM-powered “digital twin” resonates with my past work on agentic AI systems. Similarly, AI-based methods for IC modeling and design automation align with my experience in optimization, numerical reasoning, and system-level learning. These projects reflect the direction I see the field moving toward: AI not as a replacement for engineering intuition, but as a force multiplier for it.
What attracted me to the SURF program at Purdue is not just the availability of summer research positions, but the depth of resources and mentorship it offers. Facilities like the Birck Nanotechnology Center, combined with Purdue’s strength in both AI and hardware research, make SURF uniquely suited to interdisciplinary exploration. Participation in SURF would help me refine my research taste, strengthen my experimental rigor, and learn how large-scale academic labs translate ideas into impact.
Through SURF, I hope to gain deeper exposure to collaborative research, advanced experimental workflows, and long-term problem formulation. These experiences are critical for my long-term goal of pursuing a PhD and contributing to research at the intersection of AI, hardware systems, and scientific discovery.
The path has not been without challenges. Transitioning from structured coursework to open-ended research initially felt overwhelming, defining the right questions was harder than solving them. I addressed this by actively seeking mentorship, taking advanced electives, and repeatedly iterating through failure in research projects and internships. These experiences taught me how to navigate uncertainty and learn independently.
In summary, my journey, from a small city to IIT Bombay, from circuits to generative models, has been driven by curiosity and a desire to build systems that think, adapt, and scale responsibly. I see the Purdue SURF program as a crucial step in this journey.

•	How can AI be corrected when it misunderstands context or intent without complete retraining in a way that enables smooth human-AI collaboration in sensitive domains such as healthcare, eldercare and education?

During the summer, I worked with Prof. Ravi Prakash at the Human Interactive Robotics Lab at the Indian Institute of Science to explore this problem better:

How can a robot plan motions that adapt to user requirements, provided freely through language or gestures? How can we satisfy collision, safety, and preference
constraints in high-dimensional spaces? 

I tested learning-based planners, which combine large vision-language models to understand ambiguous natural language instructions with diffusion models that learn strong priors and allow test-time guidance for zero-shot adaptation. Although these models planned well, their adaptation remained close to the prior which strongly limits flexibility. This insight drew my attention to the problem of generalization.

How do we achieve generalized autonomy? Humans can learn and adapt efficiently.
Robots cannot. 

Recent robot learning models like Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) show promise but need massive amounts of data to learn while humans do not. I found that introducing structured inductive biases, much like how the human brain learns from geometry and physics, is key.

As a self-project, I have been exploring this question by studying object-centric learning and in-context learning for few-shot adaptation to improve the capabilities of general-purpose robot models. I am also interested in Prof. Vishrant Tripathi’s work on multi-robot coordination for maritime environments. My experience participating in the Swarm Rescue Challenge by Institut Polytechnique de Paris exposed me to the significant challenges of multi-agent planning and coordination in complex, safety-critical tasks such as search and rescue, and I am eager to explore these challenges more deeply through his research. Additionally, I am interested in Prof. Yu She’s work on underwater robotic manipulation, particularly for inspection and assembly tasks, as it represents an exciting application domain for robust, general-purpose robotic systems.

Beyond these specific projects, I am enthusiastic about contributing to any lab whose work advances the development of general-purpose robots capable of solving real-world problems.

The Purdue SURF program would provide an ideal opportunity to contribute to frontier research while deepening my understanding of learning, control, and generalizable autonomy. At NTU’s VIDA Lab, I am working on combining large language models with diffusion architectures for infographic understanding and generation, focusing on semantic parsing, layout extraction, and code-based template synthesis.

Across these experiences, the technical theme that motivates me is the challenge of visual reasoning under imperfect conditions. Whether the problem involves noisy biological volumes, multimodal infographic data, or spatiotemporal scenes, the core difficulty is enabling models to infer structure that is not explicitly visible. I became interested in experimental quantum optics after encountering the limits of theoretical models in my early research. While working on projects in cavity quantum electrodynamics, I saw that many formally correct descriptions rely on assumptions difficult to maintain in real systems, such as negligible loss, ideal mode structure, or perfect alignment. This gap between theory and implementation shaped my research direction and motivated me to pursue hands-on experimental training. This motivates me to apply to the Purdue SURF program, as I want to develop the physical intuition required to build and work with real quantum optical setups.
My path toward experimental work began with a research project on optical control in molecular systems. To engage with the project, I independently taught myself quantum mechanics and quantum optics, later reinforcing this background through coursework. I worked with the Shin–Metiu model and ran numerical simulations of molecular dynamics both in free space and under cavity coupling. Although theoretical, this work forced me to think carefully about how light–matter interactions are modeled and where idealized assumptions fail.
A formative moment arose when I attempted to construct an effective model analogous to the Jaynes–Cummings Hamiltonian by treating the molecular system as an anharmonic two-level system. Although the analogy initially appeared plausible, I discovered a key relation required for the mapping does not hold. Rather than discarding the result, I traced precisely where the approximation broke down. This sharpened my understanding of light–matter models and the limitations of their approximations, which was further enhanced in my future work on polaritons.
Motivated by an interest in futuristic quantum hardware and driven, open quantum systems, I subsequently turned to exciton–polariton Bose–Einstein condensates as a concrete platform for non-equilibrium light–matter physics. While my long-term goal is to experimentally study such systems, I recognized meaningful experimental work requires careful, incremental preparation. As a foundational step, I began working toward the construction of optical cavities and characterization techniques, particularly angle-resolved spectroscopy for extracting dispersion relations.
I am currently designing and procuring components for an angle-resolved reflectivity spectrometer, including the optical layout, a 4F relay for the Fourier plane, wavelength-dependent components, and a 3D-printed housing for a Czerny–Turner design. The setup will be mounted on an optical cage system, emphasizing modular alignment and stability. Planning this has already shown me how choices such as pulsed versus continuous-wave excitation, detection geometry, and mechanical constraints shape an experiment long before data collection. This has been my first sustained exposure to experimental problem-solving and has taught me the patience and attention to detail required to refine optical designs.
I am particularly eager to learn about cold-atom platforms because they offer a clean, controllable environment for studying quantum many-body physics. While coursework introduced me to laser cooling and trapping, I am motivated to understand how this control is achieved and maintained in real experiments, especially when atoms are coupled to structured optical fields.
Professor Chen-Lung Hung’s research closely aligns with my interests in experimentally realizing and controlling engineered quantum many-body systems. His group’s work integrating cold atoms with nanophotonic structures, such as microring resonators, demonstrates how atomic ensembles can be trapped on photonic circuits and coherently coupled to guided optical modes. Reading Trapped atoms and superradiance on an integrated nanophotonic microring circuit clarified how experimental constraints such as optical loss, heating, and mode geometry influence trapping strategy and observable response. I am curious to learn about these intuitively and in greater depth than a review allows.
The Purdue SURF program appeals to me for its emphasis on close mentorship, focused timeline, and immersive experimental training. Working on a programmable optical tweezer array would allow me to develop core skills, including high-precision optical alignment, phase calibration for beam shaping, and applying Fourier optics to translate computed holograms into real trapping potentials. I am especially interested in learning how optical aberrations affect trap quality and how algorithmic wavefront optimization corrects non-idealities through experimental feedback.
I am well prepared through a combination of numerical modeling and early-stage experimental experience. My computational background includes Python-based simulations of quantum dynamics using methods such as split-operator Fourier transform, imaginary time evolution, and Fourier grid Hamiltonian among others, as well as reproducing results in driven-dissipative light–matter systems. Experimentally, I have worked on optical alignment and angle-resolved reflectivity measurements. While still early in my training, I am deliberately seeking extended experience iterating on a setup, diagnosing failures, refining alignment, and developing intuition that emerges only through hands-on work. Together with a strong background in quantum mechanics and laser physics, this preparation positions me as a strong technical fit.
I aim to pursue a PhD in experimental quantum optics, focusing on platforms where light controls quantum many-body systems. The Purdue SURF program represents a crucial step in building the experimental fluency, confidence, and physical intuition required for this path.

My interest in physics began as a cliché: watching cool science videos. This experience taught me grit and confirmed that research is not about knowing the answer beforehand, but about having the tenacity to find it.
My primary research focuses on the viscous evolution of protoplanetary disks. What began as a course project modeling a Shakura-Sunyaev thin disk using a standard explicit Finite Difference (FTCS) scheme evolved into a rigorous research endeavor when I encountered severe numerical artifacts: specifically, negative densities at disk boundaries. Rather than switching to pre-packaged software, I derived and implemented a Patankar-type consistent flux solver to guarantee positivity and benchmarked it against a Crank-Nicolson implicit solver I built using sparse matrix algebra. This taught me that computational research is not just about running code; it is about understanding stability constraints (CFL conditions) and conservation laws.
Prior to this, I developed numerical rigor in the Quantronics Lab on Spin Diffusion. My role was to validate stochastic models against continuum mechanics. I derived the weak form of the spin diffusion equation to build a Finite Element Method (FEM) solver from scratch and compared it against a Monte Carlo particle transport engine I developed. I performed rigorous convergence studies to quantify statistical error versus discretization error. 
This tenacity allowed me to serve as a core theory developer for the "Singing Flame" problem, where I persisted through weeks of failed hypotheses to derive a linearized model of the flame's electrical response, eventually validating it against experimental data and cleared rigorous national rounds to represent Team India at the International Physicists’ Tournament. I am particularly motivated by the project "From fracture to flow: how calving ice sheet affect ocean dynamics." The experience I gained handling numerical instabilities in viscous evolution is directly transferable to modeling the drag forces and flow dynamics of ice mélange. Because I understand how FEM solvers work "under the hood", having built them from the weak form up, combined with my formal training in Machine Learning I will receive, I am well-positioned to contribute to Prof. Hector Gomez’s work on automating these workflows.
Finally, I remain deeply interested in Astrophysics. The numerical methods I employ, such as CFD, Radiative Transfer, and Monte Carlo, are universal. I am eager to apply my computational expertise to any projects involving stellar dynamics or planetary formation, should they become available.
Participation in SURF would be a pivotal step in my career, allowing me to transition from developing solvers on my laptop to validating them in world-class experimental facilities and scaling them on institutional clusters. Motivation: From Sci-Fi to Civil Reality
My passion for engineering was not born in a classroom, but through the pages of science fiction novels and movies. I was fascinated by the evolution of energy—from fire to electricity harnessed from the air—and how civilization progressed from primitive discoveries to nanometers of semiconductor wafers. Initially, this fascination led me to believe my path lay in Electrical Engineering or high-tech robotics.

However, my perspective shifted to the civil and environmental domain when I looked at the tangible world around me. I realized that the greatest markers of human history are not just the technologies we invent, but the structures that house them. Witnessing the devastating aftermath of earthquakes in neighboring Nepal and India, seeing images of flattened neighborhoods, made me realize that in developing regions, the difference between life and death is often the structural integrity of a beam or a connection. It became clear to me that innovation is futile without safety.

Simultaneously, growing up in Begusarai—a city ranked among the most polluted globally—forced me to confront environmental degradation. I did not just study environmental science; I lived through the smog. The smoke patterns released by refineries and chemical fertilizer industries led me to dive deeper into the subject. I went beyond textbooks, avidly reading newspaper articles and monitoring global climate summits like COP summits. Witnessing the direct health impacts on my community transformed my technical curiosity into a moral imperative. I chose Civil and Environmental Engineering because I realized that the "tech fire" inside me could be best utilized to build resilient structures and heal the planet.

Academic Preparation and Exploration
To bridge the gap between my curriculum and my research interests, I have taken a proactive approach to learning.

Self-Study: Realizing the importance of flow dynamics in environmental engineering, I went beyond my class syllabus to study Fluid Mechanics through the lectures of Professor S.K. Som (IIT Kharagpur). This gave me a strong theoretical handle on how fluids interact with the environment.

Literature Review: To understand the failures I saw in the Nepal disasters, I reviewed academic literature regarding seismic behavior and the design of steel moment connections to understand how structural joints handle extreme dynamic stresses. Additionally, to better understand pollution control, I reviewed literature on advanced oxidation processes for modern environmental remediation.

Practical Application: I completed an industrial training program at the Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) Refinery. This was a crucial experience where I observed how large-scale industries manage waste. I studied their Effluent Treatment Plants (ETP) and Biological Treatment Plants (BTP), learning how they reuse or treat hazardous byproducts. This gave me a realistic view of the balance between industrial operation and environmental protection.

Why Purdue SURF and Future Goals
I am applying to the Purdue SURF program because its 2026 research projects perfectly align with my triple-focus on structural integrity, environmental recovery, and fluid dynamics.

Given my background in reading about steel connections and observing seismic devastation, I am eager to contribute to the project on the "Behavior and analysis of structural connections under earthquake." I want to understand how connection rigidities determine the survival of critical infrastructure. Simultaneously, my literature review on oxidation processes and my experience at IOCL drive my interest in "Solutions towards returning chemically contaminated infrastructure to safe use" under the guidance of Dr. Andrew Whelton. I am fascinated by his work on post-disaster decontamination and want to explore how we can detoxify water systems after the events likeoil/chemicial spills or wildfires. I aim to explore how we can not only build stronger structures but also detoxify the built environment after industrial disasters.

Finally, bridging my self-study in fluid mechanics with my interest in climate resilience, I am drawn to the project "From fracture to flow: how calving ice sheet affect ocean dynamics." This research on phase-field modeling aligns with my long-term goal of "Extreme Environment Engineering," providing the computational rigor I need for my future aspirations.

Long-Term Vision
In the future, I aim to pursue a Master’s and Ph.D., focusing on "Extreme Environment Engineering." My immediate goal is to design disaster-proof, pollution-free infrastructure models for India and the world. However, the sci-fi enthusiast in me still dreams big. Inspired by visionaries like Elon Musk, my aspiration is to apply these engineering principles to extraterrestrial environments—analyzing Moon and Martian soil or designing habitats that can survive the harshness of space.

Overcoming Challenges
The path to this point has not been easy. Living in a highly polluted city posed health challenges, and being in India’s most vulnerable earthquake zone was a constant threat. But rather than viewing this as a setback, I treated it as a research problem. I sought guidance from professors, studied official documents, and analyzed the environmental metrics of my city to find solutions. This ability to turn an environmental disadvantage into a source of academic motivation demonstrates my resilience and readiness for the rigors of the SURF program.

During the past summer, I completed a research internship under Prof. Thirupathi Gudi in the Department of Mathematics at IISc Bangalore, where I worked on finite element methods (FEM), variational formulations, and PDE/ODE-constrained optimization. A central project involved formulating an obstacle-type variational inequality as a constrained energy minimization problem, reformulating it as a complementarity system, and solving it using a primal–dual active set (PDAS) algorithm. This work required careful mathematical formulation as well as numerical stability considerations. In parallel, I developed FEM–PINN and variational PINN (VPINN) formulations for convection-dominated problems, carrying out systematic numerical comparisons to study stability and accuracy. These projects collectively motivated me to think beyond idealized deterministic systems. Real-world physical and biological systems are inherently noisy, heterogeneous, and stochastic, yet much of classical numerical modeling assumes smooth, well-posed dynamics. This gap has strongly influenced my current research interests. I am particularly interested in stochastic modeling and SPDEs, especially in settings where randomness at the microscopic scale gives rise to structured macroscopic behavior. Examples that intrigue me include yielding transitions in granular matter, pattern formation in biological tissues, and the onset of rainfall or transport phenomena, where stochastic effects play a central role and deterministic closures often fail.
Alongside mathematical modeling, I am deeply interested in how computational constraints and parallelization strategies influence the patterns inferred from large-scale simulations of such systems. Now I try to build in smaller pieces, test early, and avoid shipping changes that I have not really proven.

Overall, SURF fits what I care about most right now. I want to help make AI tutoring more reliable and genuinely useful for students, and I want to grow into someone who can do careful research and turn it into something real.

The question I used to dread getting asked the most is "So, what's next for your career?". I entered university as a physics undergrad, brimming with ideas and excitement, planning to change the world one equation at a time. The legends of Einstein in the patent clerk office, Newton under the apple tree, Galileo at the top of the tower - unravelling the universe's mysteries, was enough to hook me as a kid. 
At first, I was into everything, everywhere, all at once - trying my hand at quantum computing, astrophysics, AI, analytics - you name it. Unfortunately, I found everything interesting! That exploration phase was quite lovely, but once the time came to exploit and settle somewhere, I was simply too indecisive. I decided to let things take their natural course without worrying too much.

Finally, I believe I have carved out a niche for myself. It lies in the intersection (or union if you prefer) of physics, computer science, mathematics and robotics. "Modelling dynamical systems with inherent uncertainty and noise", using stochastic differential equations, reinforcement learning, controls and statistical physics. The importance of solving this problem for deep space exploration, understanding the brain, safety for autonomous vehicles - impactful applications for everyday life - really motivates me and has given me a path to follow now!
I'm particularly intrigued by "stabilization by noise" (beautifully counterintuitive!) and the "exact simulation of multivariate diffusions", which turns up in weather prediction and financial markets.

So, how did I end up here? I first encountered these problems during a second year course on dynamics, where we were taught chaos theory. It didn't take much to lure me into this field. I was onboard the moment I saw the Lorenz Butterfly! 
My coursework covers a lot of breadth within physics, including a lot of topics unrelated to this domain but ones every (self-respecting) physicist should know. So, I took on multiple elective courses (from Math and CS) and even extra credits (additional courses) to develop a solid mathematical and conceptual foundation to tackle such problems. Courses : Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Convex Optimization, Stochastic Calculus, Fundamentals of AI Reasoning.

As far as academic achievements go, I am currently ranked third out of sixty in my class (based on CGPA).

My most fruitful research experience so far has been a summer+winter internship (still ongoing) at IISc Bangalore. I worked on an interdisciplinary project at the Departments of Nano Science and Computational Data Sciences, developing an anomaly detection algorithm for extremely noisy environments - with applications to quantum sensing systems. I studied the limitations of Kalman filters in low SNR regimes due to information theoretic bounds, alternative signal processing techniques and formulated a stochastic algorithm (advection diffusion network) using Kolmogorov Forward Equations, which was successfully able to detect anomalies upto -20dB SNR.
I have also worked on related projects - simulating RL algorithms on partially observable systems (position only pendulum), improving robustness of GW classifiers using adversarial training and built a hangman playing bot using machine learning and statistical approaches.
I do have limited hands-on experience with robotics - other than building a simple pathfinder robot using Arduino and PID controllers. But I'm eager to learn and get my hands dirty!  

The reason I have a strong preference for the Purdue SURF program is because it clearly listed the projects and supervisors, allowing me to choose which labs to apply to (which is missing in some other summer programs). Knowing what I am signing up for means a huge deal. Along with that, being able to present my work to an audience at the final symposium would be really gratifying, and is something I really want to experience since I haven't been to a research conference yet!
If I am accepted into the program, I am hoping it will serve as a bridge to graduate school (for applied physics and mathematics) and help me circumvent the looming terror of further admissions applications.

Which brings me back to that (previously) dreaded question. "What's next for my career?" I now have clarity. It has become clear to me that I am not cut out for the corporate world. I simply must work on something challenging, stimulating, constantly evolving and with the potential to impact people's lives, or else I'd probably die of boredom. The answer therefore, lies in research. SURF would help me accomplish this, give me new avenues to explore and develop a taste for a career in academia. In the long term, I hope to be able to become a research scientist focused on stochastic dynamical systems, and develop robust control systems that are able to operate safely within the chaotic real world, and maybe someday, even lead a research group of my own! I aim to be at the forefront of a movement in STEM that shifts our engineering paradigms from rigid, deterministic models to resilient, probabilistic frameworks capable of thriving in an increasingly unpredictable world. Till then, dreaming is free, and working hard is the way!

Thank you for your time and consideration.

This curiosity led me to pursue Electronics and Communication Engineering, where I became particularly drawn to problems at the intersection of device physics, circuit design, and computation. My first formal research experience was in computational materials and device physics during my summer internship at Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, where I worked on transport properties of spintronic devices. Using NEGF+DFT simulations in QuantumATK, I analyzed tunnel magnetoresistance in LiCrSi/MgO/LiCrSi magnetic tunnel junctions. I implemented transport calculations, varied barrier thicknesses, tuned material parameters, and ensured numerical stability across simulation environments. Many results required recalibration across parameter settings and repeated validation, reinforcing that simulation-based research is driven by iteration and hypothesis testing rather than single-run outcomes. This shaped the way I view research problems not as isolated experiments, but as structured processes for testing physical assumptions and understanding why certain trends arise, or sometimes do not. 

That internship laid a strong groundwork for me in atomistic modeling, but it also pushed me toward broader questions of scale and reproducibility. Next, my later academic coursework and project work, in electronics and VLSI, broadened my interests to CMOS characterization and hybrid CMOS–spintronic modeling, as improvements must hold across parameter ranges rather than isolated simulations. To support this, I designed Python-based workflows to automate parameter sweeps, Monte Carlo analysis, and post-processing, enabling consistent comparison of device and circuit behavior across operating conditions. This shift toward automation and reproducibility has become central to how I now frame research questions.

In later projects, I characterized Sky130 CMOS blocks across process, voltage, and temperature corners and fitted compact MTJ models derived from first-principles data to study hybrid CMOS–spintronic behavior at the circuit level. The focus was on building repeatable characterization pipelines to evaluate delay, power, and noise margins, rather than proposing new device concepts. Through this work, I developed a strong interest in benchmarking, validation, and research infrastructure areas where rigorous characterization is essential for meaningful comparison of emerging hardware technologies.

Beyond individual characterization tasks, I am increasingly interested in how research processes are designed to support reuse, accessibility, and validation at a community scale. While building scripted simulation pipelines, I encountered how difficult it can be to reproduce results when workflows depend on local environments or undocumented assumptions. Platforms such as nanoHUB, with their emphasis on standardized tools and community-driven research, align closely with how I hope to contribute as a researcher by treating workflow design itself as a scientific problem.

In parallel, I have maintained a strong interest in problems requiring careful physical interpretation at the atomistic scale. First-principles transport simulations highlighted how defects, interfaces, and modeling assumptions at the nanometer scale can propagate to device- and system-level behavior. This perspective naturally connects to challenges such as radiation damage and defect formation in semiconductors, where physical understanding is a prerequisite for assessing reliability and mitigation strategies. I aim to contribute to atomistic modeling efforts that combine simulation with systematic analysis to inform device reliability and system-level design.

I am drawn to the Purdue SURF program because of its focus on immersive, full-time research under close faculty mentorship. Unlike many short-term programs, SURF provides the structure, depth, and intellectual environment necessary for students to dive deeply into a single research problem while learning how rigorous academic research is conducted. Purdue’s emphasis on device physics, materials modeling, and computing systems provides a perfect backdrop for the kind of practice I want to use to translate physical intuition into engineering choices. I am particularly drawn to SURF’s emphasis on independent research, technical communication, and professional development, which closely mirrors the expectations placed on graduate researchers. 

It is my hope that SURF will further cultivate my skills of creating clear research questions, validating my assumptions through a systematic process of analysis, and communicating my results effectively within a research group. I also aim to gain exposure to how the organization of large-scale academic research, as well as the cooperation among students, faculty, and shared research infrastructure, supports such research and contributes to meaningful projects. These skills and experiences will be critical as I prepare for graduate studies and pursue a long-term research career. 

In the long term, my research will be at the interface of device physics, computing, and system design, focusing on physically grounded approaches for designing reliable and scalable technologies. I do not wish to specialize prematurely; instead, I aim to refine how I translate low-level physical phenomena into higher-level engineering decisions. I see SURF as a critical step toward this goal, allowing me to test my readiness for graduate research and to develop the methodological rigor required for a career in STEM research.

statement_of_purpose:
Ever since I was introduced to science, I have had an affinity for chemistry. A childlike fascination of colour changing reactions metamorphosed into a driven passion for the subject which encouraged me to pursue a Bachelor’s degree in Chemistry at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Mumbai, India. 

As a part of my coursework in the first year, I had a class on Introduction to Biology. The course content  made me interested in biomolecules and the biochemical pathways which govern all facets of life. Through my second year I took courses in biosciences to develop a better understanding of life and the role molecules play in them. My electives taught me about the rise of Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in pathogens. An article titled “Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019: a systematic analysis” published in the Lancet estimates up to 10 million deaths can occur annually by the year 2050 if proper action is not taken to deal with AMR. Such concerning statistics is why I decided to work in AMR. There are several routes to tackle this issue, such as trying to study the cause of the resistance and finding ways to neutralise it, or come up with new drugs and/or therapies which could overpower resistant microbes. I have been fortunate that I have been able to see both these paths hands-on.

My first project at IIT Bombay dealt with understanding how erythromycin resistance develops in certain bacteria. Here, I used polymerase chain reactions to perform site-directed mutagenesis on the genes coding for a certain ‘riboswitch’ which governs a mechanism erythromycin resistance. I also learnt plasmid transformation and extraction.

In my second project in the Gerdt Lab at Indiana University Bloomington, I was tasked with screening compound libraries to check if any of them inhibited a bacteriophage defence system based on a Serine/Threonine Kinase called Stk2 observed in some strains of S. aureus. Screening against 1000+ compounds, I was able to obtain one compound that appeared to promote phage infection of resistant bacteria. In order to determine whether this compound was inhibiting the kinase in question or affecting some other part of the defence mechanism, I extracted the plasmid forming Stk2 in the lab S. aureus strain and ligated the gene of interest into an expression vector as the first step of the protein production pipeline.

My third project, which I am currently working on, deals with exploring Indian origin microbes as a source for antibiotic discovery at the Medicinal Chemistry and Drug Discovery Lab (MCDD) at IIT Bombay. For this, I have been working with soil samples from different parts of India to isolate actinomycetes from them and analyse their secondary metabolites. Since I was working with soil samples, there was the risk of unwanted microbes swarming the selection and isolation plates and stalling progress. This indeed happened, and to be honest it was disheartening. Isolation of bacteria is a time consuming process and every time I got contamination I had to restart the process. But I did not yield and by trial and error as well as the help of my colleagues working on this project, we came up with a combination of antimicrobials which was able to arrest contamination growth while still allowing bacteria of interest to grow in the first screen.

Although varied in scope, all my work till now has given me a lot of insight into the different ways in which the scientific community is trying to tackle AMR. The different biochemical techniques I have learnt from my experiences form a strong foundation for me to acquire  more sophisticated and advanced techniques that will be beneficial for my growth as a biochemist working in AMR and Natural Product Discovery (NPD). This is why the Parkinson Lab at Purdue has particularly piqued my interest. Their research on NPD will allow me to learn more biochemical and synthetic biology assays. Their project “Small molecule inducers of Streptomyces Natural Products” will allow me to explore a different facet of NPD and interacting with other lab members working on the various projects in the lab will all provide me with insights that would help my current ongoing project at the MCDD lab and any future work I will undertake.

My interest in biochemistry is the base of my motivation, my courses and projects, the catalyst. There is a dire need for new antibiotics driven by overuse and overexposure. Due to a lull in natural antibiotic discovery after the 70s and 80s, a smaller proportion of resources have been dedicated to this field which was regarded as a dead end. But there has been a resurgence since the 2000s with many groups reporting potential molecules. There is light at the end of this antibiotic void tunnel, but the path is laborious and I am willing to tread it with the dedicated professionals already on this road. Participation in the SURF program, especially if given the chance to work in the Parkinson Laboratory, will help me gain more skills and knowledge that will aid me in my scientific journey.
