The first time I realised that machine learning problems are often constrained more by data than by models was during my summer 2025 work on soil organic carbon (SOC) prediction. Initially, my task was to build a predictive model, but within the first few weeks I realised that no reliable, India-specific dataset of bare agricultural land existed to support meaningful modelling. The limitation was not due to oversight, but rather to the challenge of identifying bare soil across India's diverse cropping patterns and agroecological regions at scale. Tuning hyperparameters or changing architectures could not solve the problem. Stepping back to rethink what data was required and whether it could even be collected was necessary.

That realisation fundamentally changed how I approached research. Instead of treating data limitations as secondary constraints, I began to see data construction and problem formulation as central research challenges. I pivoted the project towards designing an algorithmic pipeline to identify bare soil pixels across India using multispectral Sentinel-2 imagery integrated with Dynamic World land-cover classifications. In my work with soil-type-aware and state-specific detection criteria, I encountered scale, heterogeneity, and uncertainty, and I realised that progress in machine learning often depends on understanding real systems rather than refining models independently. This experience is what led me to pursue data science and machine learning more deliberately, and it continues to motivate my interest in research.

Looking back, this way of thinking felt familiar. Long before I encountered research formally, I was drawn to problems that required patience and structural reasoning. Mathematics, puzzles, and riddles never felt like tasks to complete; they felt like situations to solve. I was comfortable revisiting assumptions and trying again until the structure of a problem became clear. Having studied programming, probability, and algorithmic coursework in colege, I realised that this mindset naturally aligned with data science and machine learning, especially in settings where data is imperfect and assumptions are uncertain.

This perspective was reinforced during my work forecasting power outages caused by extreme weather events. The one-size-fits-all approach consistently underperformed when I built generalised predictive models based on high-resolution weather forecasts and outage data. Different weather phenomena disrupt power systems through distinct physical mechanisms, and ignoring those differences leads to unrealistic models. Designing event-specific models required understanding of domain processes, temporal alignment, and data reliability. Together with my SOC work, this project shaped a central question that continues to drive me: how can machine learning systems be designed to remain reliable and interpretable when real-world data violate the assumptions we often take for granted?

It is this research-oriented mindset that draws me to the Purdue Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF). Among the many summer research opportunities available, SURF stands out because it is structured around sustained inquiry rather than short-term execution. The emphasis on close faculty mentorship, iterative exploration, and reflection aligns with how I want to grow as a researcher. Rather than optimizing for deliverables, SURF prioritizes learning how to ask better questions, exactly the skill I want to develop at this stage. Purdue’s strength in applied, interdisciplinary research, particularly where data science intersects with engineering, environmental systems, and infrastructure, makes it an environment well-suited to the kinds of problems I want to work on.

In the long term, I aim to build a career in applied research involving artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data science, focused on solving real-world problems rather than optimizing abstract benchmarks. I am interested in research-driven roles in industry labs, mission-oriented organizations, or interdisciplinary teams where uncertainty, data limitations, and deployment constraints are central considerations. My goal is to contribute machine learning systems that are robust, interpretable, and genuinely useful to domain experts and decision-makers.

The research experience gained through SURF would be a critical step toward this goal. I want to learn how experienced researchers evaluate whether a research direction is worth pursuing, how they decide when to pivot versus persist, and how they measure progress when results are ambiguous. Working closely with a faculty mentor over an extended period would help me develop this judgment, which I see as essential for effective work in applied research setings.

Through rigorous coursework, research projects, and independent learning, I prepared for this career path. Though my academic training is interdisciplinary and not a traditional computer science major, I have taken advanced courses in machine learning, deep learning, algorithms, statistics, and econometrics. Complementing this, my research projects in geospatial analysis, semantic segmentation, power-system forecasting, and dataset creation have required me to engage deeply with data quality, modeling assumptions, and domain constraints. I have also invested significant effort in learning geospatial tools and reading applied research literature to understand how machine learning is used beyond academic benchmarks.

One of the main challenges I have encountered is adapting to the uncertainty inherent in my research. Unlike coursework, research problems rarely have clearly defined objectives or endpoints. Through feedback from faculty mentors, deeper engagement with literature, and deliberate reflection on assumptions, I have learned to distinguish between technical difficulties and conceptual misalignments. This experience has made me more patient, deliberate, and honest in how I approach complex problems.

statement_of_purpose:
I chose Computer Engineering without a clear long term plan, but as I progressed through my coursework, I became increasingly interested in how simple assembly code compounded into the impressive machines we see today. Once I saw how changes in a program affected memory and data movement in hardware in one of my early systems computing classes, I was drawn in by computing systems and how system level decisions affect correctness and efficiency. Eventually , this curiosity evolved into a genuine interest in understanding and improving computing systems under real constraints.

My interest in research developed through  experiences that exposed me to computational work in unfamiliar domains. In a remote sensing and ionospheric physics project, I worked with large collections of night sky airglow images and helped cluster data points to identify distinct wave structures in the upper atmosphere. What excited me most was seeing how raw images could be transformed into meaningful statistics through a Python based analysis pipeline. I was particularly struck by how sensitive the final results were to small changes in preprocessing and clustering choices. Exploring how these decisions affected extracted physical features introduced me to experimental rigor and made me curious about how computational pipelines can be made both reliable and meaningful when working with noisy real world data. I will also continue this work as an independent researcher under ECE 396 during Spring 2026.

In parallel, I contributed to a bioengineering focused project aimed at developing a handheld biosensor. My work involved building a reliable backend for a Raspberry Pi based device and performing image cropping and preprocessing in Python to support downstream CNN machine learning models. After building the backend and connecting it to the device, the task of cropping images initially did not feel like a big deal. However, that notion disappeared rather quickly when I realized even small inaccuracies could propagate through the pipeline and affect everything downstream. This experience forced me to slow down, try different approaches, and apply a high level of scrutiny to my own work to ensure it was compatible with the rest of the system and the team.

Outside of these projects, one of the most formative moments for me was working independently on modifying a pix2pix GAN to better suit a dataset used in a machine learning project. This was the first time I experienced the excitement of building something on my own that had a direct and measurable impact on model performance. I spent long nights running the model for several hundred epochs and repeatedly modifying the dataset to observe even small improvements in the balance between the discriminator and generator. That experience made it clear to me that machine learning was something I wanted to pursue seriously in my career.

As a result, I am now interested in exploratory research questions such as how computational pipelines for image based data can be made more robust to preprocessing choices, and how system constraints such as memory hierarchy or limited compute shape the performance and reliability of machine learning models in practice. While I do not yet have definitive answers, I am extremely eager to find out more through more research.

I am particularly drawn to the Purdue SURF program because of its emphasis on immersive, mentored research within active research groups. SURF offers access to research environments such as the Purdue AI Institute, the ECE system architecture groups, and the Purdue Quantum Science and Engineering Institute, which together span machine learning, computing systems, and emerging computational paradigms. Looking at all these problems from a combined perspective of my interested areas of study would be crucial for me to find out how different approaches to systems and architecture influence the design and deployment of learning models.

One of the biggest challenges I have faced in my degree was my introductory course in systems level programming in C and C++, ECE 220. After repeatedly struggling on exams, I became convinced that programming was not for me. At the time, I attributed much of this difficulty to my living situation( my dorm room housed four students) and moved on. However, after taking more programming intensive courses such as CS 225, I realized that my earlier struggles were also due to the unstructured nature of the course and the degree of independence given to the student in ECE 220. Additionally, seeking guidance from my assigned mentor, Dr. Rakesh Kumar, helped me better understand how my interests in machine learning and computer architecture intersect in both academia and industry. Working with my academic advisor to plan my coursework and graduate early also helped reduce financial and mental stress. 

In the long term, I aspire to pursue graduate study and a research oriented career in STEM, potentially in academia or an industry research lab. I view the Purdue SURF program as an important step toward clarifying my research direction, gaining deeper exposure to the research process, and preparing for a future career in computing research. I am eager to contribute to a SURF research group while continuing to grow as a motivated and thoughtful researcher.

What particularly drew me in was the challenge of understanding how different modalities interact and how models can be trained to learn these relationships with minimal supervision.

I continue to pursue this field because several questions deeply intrigue me: How can we reliably distinguish human-created content from synthetic media? How can multimodal systems learn robust representations when individual modalities may be noisy or incomplete? And how can self-supervised learning reduce dependence on large labeled datasets while still achieving strong generalization? These questions sit at the intersection of multimodal AI, computer vision, and audio processing—an intersection that has consistently motivated me to explore research-driven approaches rather than purely application-level development.

Research Experience and Current Work 

As a computer science student at Manipal University Jaipur, I am writing to convey my keen interest in a research position within Artificial Intelligence. My aspiration is to secure a role where I can apply my proficiency in Deep Learning, Computer Vision, and audio processing. I am passionate about using AI to solve meaningful, real-world problems.

I am a co-author of the paper titled "CLAM: Safeguarding Authenticity and Addressing Implications for the Music Industry," which received acceptance for publication at the NeurIPS 2025 AI for Music Workshop. Expanding on this work, I additionally contributed to "Melody or Machine: Benchmarking and Detecting Synthetic Music via Cross-Modal Contrastive Alignment," which was published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR). These experiences have equipped me with practical expertise in crafting and evaluating novel models designed to confront emerging challenges in synthetic media.

Aside from my published research, I am applying my capabilities to a range of diverse and demanding projects. I am presently engaged in the development of "Music Bind," a deep learning model designed for classifying songs by leveraging multimodal inputs, such as tags, images, and text. My primary research interests are in multimodal AI, applying computer vision to other domains, and self-supervised learning. I am confident that I can make a positive contribution and am eager to learn from new challenges. I thrive in situations where there are challenges, and I love to work under pressure. I want to develop AI solutions that people actually use and it motivates me to work hard.

I aim to contribute to the development of robust, interpretable, and socially responsible AI systems, particularly in areas related to media authenticity, multimodal understanding, and self-supervised learning. In the long run, I want my work to bridge academic research and real-world deployment, ensuring that advanced AI systems are both useful and trustworthy.

How SURF Will Contribute to My Career Development

The research experience gained through SURF will help me sharpen critical skills such as hypothesis formulation, experimental rigor, and collaborative problem-solving. I hope to deepen my understanding of advanced machine learning techniques, improve my ability to communicate research findings effectively, and gain exposure to diverse research methodologies. Additionally, the mentorship and professional connections formed during SURF would be invaluable as I prepare for graduate studies and future research collaborations.

Preparation and Exploration of My Field

I have actively explored my field through a combination of coursework, independent research projects, and peer-reviewed publications. My work on synthetic music detection and multimodal contrastive learning reflects my commitment to tackling emerging challenges in AI. Developing Music Bind has further strengthened my hands-on experience with multimodal architectures and large-scale data handling, preparing me well for research-intensive environments.

Challenges and Growth

Balancing rigorous coursework with research commitments has been challenging, particularly while working on publication deadlines and experimental iterations. I addressed these challenges by actively seeking guidance from mentors, improving my time management strategies, and independently studying advanced topics beyond the curriculum when needed. These experiences have strengthened my resilience, adaptability, and confidence in navigating research-driven environments.

My academic path has increasingly reflected this focus. Through coursework in fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, turbulence, and numerical methods, I developed a strong theoretical foundation in transport phenomena. Building on this, I sought research experiences that required translating theory into predictive models. I am currently developing a Volume-of-Fluid framework in Basilisk to study droplet coalescence with thermal effects, including air-film drainage, surface tension driven flows, and temperature-dependent interfacial dynamics. This experience exposed me to the challenges of coupling heat transfer, phase change, and inference, and it reinforced my interest in hybrid modeling approaches that combine first-principles physics with modern computational tools. Earlier work on droplet collision dynamics and combustion simulations further strengthened my interest in flows where nonlinear coupling between momentum, heat, and material response governs system behavior.

These experiences have led me to pursue deeper questions in my field. I am particularly interested in how multiphase and thermal transport models can be constructed so that they remain predictive across regimes, and how experimental data can be used not merely for validation but to inform reduced models and parameterizations. The microfluidics project also appeals to me for similar reasons, especially the opportunity to study fluid behavior at small scales using imaging, data analysis, and modeling.

statement_of_purpose:
Growing up in India’s competitive exam environment, I often found myself buried in differential equations with little room for curiosity. My refuge was the afternoons spent in my high school biology lab- ten of us crowded around a table, formalin-preserved frogs in the background, debating genetics with my teacher. Among those conversations, the one that stayed with me most was the idea that from a “metabolic soup,” given enough time and interaction, remarkably complex systems can emerge. Millenia old systems whose precision and efficiency challenge the most advanced machines of today. 

After high school, I carried those biology lab discussions forward into the dry lab team of iGEM IIT Madras, part of the International Genetically Engineered Machine (iGEM) competition in synthetic biology. Working in the modeling subgroup without a background in computer science, I taught myself computational biology through extensive problem solving on Rosalind, a bioinformatics platform. Through this, I developed a strong foundation in string algorithms, graph theory, and dynamic programming, and at one point ranking among the top 60 solvers in India.

During iGEM 2024, I applied these skills to model a diatom–bacteria coculture using community metabolic modeling frameworks. The model showed that silica-solubilizing bacteria enhance diatom growth by improving silica availability for frustule formation. This work supported a broader project on in-situ resource utilization on Mars, where bacterial processing of Martian silica could enable diatom-based production of useful compounds. In parallel, I worked at Numberz.ai, a startup, where I trained LSTM sequence models on velocity-derived time-series data to predict successive two-dimensional positions in ant trajectories. This was my first formal exposure to AI and deep learning, tools that have since become central to much of the computational work I do.

The following summer, I worked at the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre, modeling the development of cortical folding in fetal brains across the first two trimesters. My work involved automating MRI segmentation pipelines, extracting cortical surfaces, and visualizing the emergence of gyri and sulci. This research made use of data from what is now the world’s largest fetal brain atlas, developed in-house, with a cell-level resolution. I have continued working in neuroscience since, most recently at the Indian Institute of Science, where I design neurofeedback games aimed at modulating pain perception through self-regulation of brain rhythms.

Across both my neuroscience and metabolic modeling work, I’ve realized that I’m consistently drawn to understanding and modeling how complex systems develop and function. At iGEM 2025, this continued in the form of designing a precise epigenetic editor using a deactivated Cas9 fused to a methyltransferase, enabling locus-specific DNA methylation. Here, I led the development of a modeling pipeline to estimate how these epigenetic modifications affect cellular metabolism. While genome-scale metabolic models can incorporate transcriptional regulation, they do not directly account for epigenetic state. To bridge this gap, I developed gene-specific convolutional neural networks to predict gene expression from methylation profiles and integrated these predictions into existing transcriptome-informed metabolic modeling frameworks. Using this pipeline, we were able to simulate cancer-associated metabolic phenotypes, including the Warburg effect, by selectively altering methylation patterns in oncogenes in silico.

While these experiences were formative, they offered different limitations. At iGEM, the work was entirely student-run, which encouraged exploration but came with limited scientific guidance, while my roles in academic labs involved contributing to projects defined by senior researchers. This changed with the Young Research Fellowship (YRF) program at IIT Madras, where a cohort of 25 undergraduates is selected and funded to pursue independent research. Through YRF, I continued working on metabolic modeling, studying metabolic robustness across microorganisms under varying nutrient conditions, temperature stresses, and community interactions. Under the fellowship, for the first time, I am now tasked with devising problem statements and taking ownership of the direction of my projects. At this stage, I am seeking a reference point for how strong research labs approach early-stage questions, structure feedback, and how principal investigators think through and guide work on a topic. Beyond the strength of Purdue's research itself, the SURF program’s emphasis on close interaction with faculty offers this exposure in a way that many research programs do not. I believe this experience would directly inform my ongoing YRF work, my role leading the iGEM 2026 team, and help me carry back concrete research practices to the labs that have trained me in India.

In the long run, I want to do research, and experiences like presenting my work at the iGEM Grand Jamboree in Paris or talking to teams from universities across the world genuinely excite me about going down that path. Beyond my own work, I would also like to mentor other student teams and help build research communities outside the usual classroom setting. At the core of what I want to work on moving forward is the same question that first drew me to biology: how do complex biological systems emerge and function, and how can we model them in a way that meaningfully captures that complexity? The Purdue SURF program feels like the continuation of my high school lab, where the questions are the same, but the tools and conversations are far richer

statement_of_purpose:
My first tryst with robotics came in the spring of 2025, when I joined the Machine Intelligence Lab (MIL) at the University of Florida as a robotics software developer. I worked on SubjuGator 9, the lab’s autonomous submarine, where I implemented a Doppler Velocity Log to help the vehicle measure its velocity and position underwater during long missions. In simulations, the submarine moved smoothly and predictably, with clean sensor data and no surprises. But that’s when the trouble began, as real-world conditions rarely matched the clean assumptions made in code. How can a robot know where it is when its sensors are imperfect? What happens if those small errors build up over time? Questions like these kept plaguing me. While a robot can be programmed to perform flawlessly, I realized that it must be able to react to unexpected changes in the environment. Through my time at MIL, I kept encountering this same problem in different forms: robots are expected to make decisions in the real world, yet the real world is significantly more unpredictable. This is exactly what motivates me to apply for Purdue University’s Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) program, as I seek to explore robotic perception, control, and coordination for robust autonomy in complex, real-world environments.

As I continued, I was particularly fascinated by how robots physically interact with the world. For the next two semesters, I further worked on SubjuGator 9’s gripper arms to enable more precise underwater manipulation. I programmed a system that allowed the gripper to open and close smoothly to pick up and drop objects at the correct location and tested these movements in simulation before deploying them on the real robot. Through this work, I realized how critical careful control design and calibration are for reliable robotic manipulation, especially in environments where sensing and feedback are limited. Looking ahead, I hope to build on this experience through Purdue’s SURF program by contributing to research on underwater robotic manipulation, where autonomy, perception, and hardware reliability must come together to enable robust operation in challenging environments.

As an undergraduate researcher at the Virtual Experiences Research Group (VERG) Lab at the University of Florida, I am working on developing an AI video generation system for the U.S. Air Force, aimed at producing training videos for military cadets on sexual assault prevention. One major challenge was ensuring that the AI-generated scenarios remained realistic while being sensitive to the subject matter, as early outputs sometimes produced scenes that were unintentionally stereotypical or could be misinterpreted. To address this, I implemented a set of content filters and human-in-the-loop review checkpoints that guided the AI’s generation process, allowing the system to produce videos that were both accurate and respectful and aligned with educational goals. I built the pipeline to process inputs, generate animated scenes, and combine them into coherent videos, which also dramatically reduced both the time and cost required for content creation.

While working on the sensing system for SubjuGator 9, I observed that performance limitations often stemmed from communication bottlenecks and delays in information sharing between system components rather than from a lack of data. I seek to further investigate these challenges through the Multi-Robot Coordination for Maritime Environments project under Professor Vishrant Tripathi in the Multi-Agents Network Group, where I aim to study how control and communication frameworks can enable reliable coordination among heterogeneous robotic teams operating under limited bandwidth and high latency conditions.

In addition, my experience developing AI pipelines that integrate data filtering, inference, and evaluation aligns well with the AI-driven smart monitoring and data analytics project led by Professor Martin Jun. I am particularly interested in understanding how machine learning and sensing can be jointly leveraged to monitor complex systems more effectively. I have also worked on underwater gripper control in Gazebo-based submarine simulations, where I observed how uncertainty and feedback delays adversely affect manipulation performance. This experience has motivated my interest in the Underwater Robotic Manipulation project under Professor Yu She, where I hope to contribute to the Robot Operating System (ROS) stack for autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs). At Purdue, I hope to benefit from the mentorship and rigorous research environment fostered by the SURF program to build upon my prior experiences beyond my home institution.

While I have explored diverse topics as a researcher, I have been able to contribute effectively across them. Each experience has deepened my understanding of the research process and clarified my motivation to pursue graduate studies focused on rigorous, impactful research in the future. My discussions and collaborations with my mentors have significantly influenced my perspective on research and enhanced my ability to recognize and connect the gaps between theory and practice. Persevering through dead-ends has taught me the vital skill of recognizing shortcomings in my ideas and using them as seeds for stronger, more refined approaches, while remaining cognizant of potential breakthroughs. Through the SURF program, I seek to further develop as a researcher by learning from the esteemed Purdue faculty. With its strong emphasis on engineering research and collaborative innovation, the Purdue SURF program would be an outstanding environment to prepare me for further graduate studies.

statement_of_purpose:
I am an undergraduate in Aerospace Engineering at IIT Kharagpur, driven by a fundamental scientific challenge that spans all modern propulsion systems: how instabilities emerge in high-energy flows and how they can be controlled to enable efficient, reliable propulsion. From thermoacoustic oscillations in combustors to plasma breathing modes in Hall thrusters, propulsion devices are ultimately governed by the same physics of feedback, density gradients, and energy-release coupling. My long-term goal is to become a researcher who develops propulsion systems that are not only high-performance but also inherently stable, by understanding and manipulating these instability mechanisms at their physical root.
My first exposure to this problem came not through textbooks, but through hands-on experimental work. During my first-year summer, I joined the Advanced Propulsion Systems (APSYS) Laboratory at IIT Kharagpur, where I worked on thermoacoustic instability in a vertical dump combustor under the supervision of Prof. Amardip Ghosh. I was involved in both operation and diagnostics of the facility, using LabVIEW to control mass flow rates and equivalence ratio, and employing high-frequency pressure transducers and photomultiplier tubes to measure pressure and heat-release oscillations. By performing FFT and spectrogram analysis in MATLAB and Origin, I identified the dominant instability modes and directly observed Rayleigh’s criterion in action, where phase-locked heat release drives self-sustained acoustic oscillations. Using high-speed imaging and CH chemiluminescence, I visualized the formation of hot and cold spots in the flame and the role of vortex shedding and shear-layer dynamics in modulating combustion.
What made this experience transformative was not simply observing instability, but realizing that it is governed by feedback between flow, energy release, and field variables. This insight led me to study a wider class of instability mechanisms, including Kelvin–Helmholtz vortices, flame liftoff and reattachment, triple-flame structures, and classical hydrodynamic instabilities such as Rayleigh–Taylor and Richtmyer–Meshkov. I later extended this to density-stratified flows and baroclinic vorticity by working on a cold-flow model of a shear-coaxial rocket injector, where I fabricated an acrylic rig and performed mass-flow and choking calculations in MathCAD to study pressure–density coupling relevant to transverse combustion instability in liquid rocket engines.
Through this work, I began to see a deep analogy between combustion instability and plasma instability. In both cases, instability emerges from the interaction of strong gradients, an energy release or ionization process, and a feedback field that sustain oscillations. This realization motivated me to expand my understanding of propulsion beyond chemically reacting systems and toward advanced electric propulsion devices. In an SPT-100 thruster, electrons trapped in an ExB drift ionize neutral propellant, and the resulting plasma is accelerated by an axial electric field. Yet this process has instabilities, producing breathing modes, spoke instabilities, and cathode–plume coupling. In these phenomena, plasma oscillations become mechanistically analogous to thermoacoustic oscillations in combustors. Just as unsteady heat release destabilizes a flame, unsteady ionization and electron transport destabilize a Hall discharge.
I am therefore particularly excited by the opportunity to work with the SPT-100 Hall thruster in Prof. Shashurin’s laboratory, where both thruster operation and plasma diagnostics are central to the project. I am deeply impressed by the laboratory’s diagnostic methods and the advanced lab equipment. I am more eager to learn the diagnostic methods and experiments that will take place in the lab.  Purdue’s Electric Propulsion and Plasma Laboratory provides a rare environment in which a full-scale Hall thruster, a neutralizer system based on cathodic vacuum arcs, and detailed plume diagnostics are all available. This allows direct measurement of plasma parameters and oscillations, which is exactly the experimental setting required to study instability physics in ExB discharges. My background in high-bandwidth diagnostics, FFT-based spectral analysis, and coupled-field instability interpretation directly prepares me to contribute meaningfully to the characterization of Hall thruster plasma dynamics.
SURF is uniquely aligned with my career goals because it offers immersion in a real research laboratory, not a classroom simulation. I intend to pursue a PhD focused on instability and control in advanced propulsion systems, spanning both reacting flows and electric propulsion. Working with the SPT-100 will allow me to extend my expertise from combustion-driven instabilities to plasma-driven instabilities, giving me a unified physical framework that few students develop at the undergraduate level. The opportunity to collaborate with researchers in electric propulsion and to learn modern plasma diagnostic techniques will be foundational for this trajectory.
My path to this point has not been straightforward. I entered APSYS as a first-year undergraduate without formal coursework in combustion, plasma physics, or instability theory. To contribute meaningfully, I had to independently study graduate-level fluid mechanics, thermoacoustics, and instability literature while simultaneously learning experimental operation and data analysis. This process taught me how to bridge theory and experiment under real constraints — a skill that is essential in high-energy propulsion research. It also confirmed that I thrive in research environments where complex physical systems must be understood through careful measurement and modeling.
Ultimately, I seek to build propulsion systems that are not limited by destructive oscillations, whether in rocket combustors or Hall thrusters. The SPT-100 project at Purdue represents the electric-propulsion frontier of the same instability problem that has guided my development so far. Through SURF, I hope to deepen my understanding of plasma-field coupling, acquire advanced diagnostic skills, and contribute to the scientific understanding of Hall thruster stability, taking a decisive step toward a career in next-generation propulsion research.

I am pursuing a field of study in the intersection between chemical engineering, data science, and material science because I want to contribute to the theoretical understanding and modeling of electrochemical energy systems, particularly batteries and fuel cells, and further impact the society and environment that all of us are living in. My passion for this began in high school when I built and raced hydrogen cell-powered RC cars. At the time, I was fascinated by the applications of electrochemical energy systems like fuel cells, and I was determined to pursue a field that would provide me with an opportunity to advance technologies such as this.
My pathway to pursue research began with an independent chemistry course project, in which I needed to design an experiment that relates to analytical chemistry. My topic was to detect and quantify lead concentrations in soil samples along Strawberry Creek. This experience was particularly memorable, as it marked my first exposure to the process of independent scientific inquiry as a freshman, which is formulating a research question, designing an experimental methodology, and interpreting real data with uncertainty. It was both exciting and rewarding for me to tackle an open-ended problem like this, and it motivated me on a path of research to pursue my own curiosity. 
After high school, my passion still lies in electrochemical applications. By the end of my freshman year, I pursued a research project investigating lithium stripping on lithium electrodes and its relationship to the charging speed and surface irregularities. This project was very exciting for me to work on because stripping of the lithium electrode can affect the lithiation of graphite, which can further limit battery performance. To analyze this phenomenon, I developed a Python algorithm utilizing various libraries, such as OpenCV, to distinguish lithium and separator from tomography scans of the interface, and then I quantified the stripping and related the stripping to various factors. I verified that there is a linear relationship between charging speed and the depth of lithium stripping in the tomography scans, and lithium stripping tends to even out some surface irregularities, such as hills, but not so much on irregularities such as pits. 
While further advancing my coursework, I grew a strong interest in data science as I realized how important statistics and machine learning are to the field of modeling in electrochemical systems. During the summer of 2025, I pursued another project utilizing data-driven machine learning models to classify different chemicals and predict their concentrations from a sensor array as part of a REU program hosted by the University of Missouri. To do so, I reviewed a lot of literature to learn and build my own machine learning framework from chronoamperometry data from a sensor array to the desired outcomes, such as the type of chemical and their concentrations. 
The data, unlike working with course projects, where the dataset is already cleaned and everything is set up, is affected by many factors, such as gas pumps that change environment and delays due to surface reactions on the sensor.  Thus, the very early steps involved a lot of interpretation of what is going on with the data and how to clean it. 
Additionally, another common problem is dealing with the bias-variance tradeoff. Dealing with overfitting involves a lot of effort in feature engineering and feature selection. My first approach to this is to use tsfel, a library for automatic feature extraction on a time series, and do a feature selection to alleviate overfitting, and then compare the performance of three algorithms: MLP, SVM, and RF, for which I present the results at the 2025 Summer Forum at the University of Missouri. Later, I incorporated signal transformation tools such as DWT to improve performance, while only using features that have been proven to be very predictive based on RF feature selection results.
Those research experiences allowed me to discover my passion for research. I would love the opportunity to contribute to more projects that relate to modeling in electrochemical systems. The SURF program was particularly attractive to me due to how exciting the projects are and the opportunity they provide to develop new skills while working closely with mentors on open-ended problems. It is my passion to work on research, and I plan to pursue graduate school after my undergraduate years. Having such opportunities can be very valuable in gaining insights into thesis-leading projects. I hope to continue to strengthen my preparation for graduate school and take an important step toward a long-term goal of advancing understanding by modeling with electrochemical systems.

When those structures were removed, I found myself far more engaged. Coursework had trained me to reach correct answers; research taught me to ask whether the question itself was well posed. Research offered a different rhythm: open-ended questions, uncertainty about whether an approach would work, and the responsibility of deciding what to try next. I came to enjoy the tension of waiting for results, debugging failures, and watching an idea behave outside carefully designed assignments and coming to life. The freedom to move beyond definite scopes and work toward problems that felt meaningful rather than graded is what ultimately pulled me toward research.
This interest crystallized during my undergraduate studies after completing the JEE Advanced examination. While the preparation gave me a strong analytical foundation, it was a course in machine learning that showed me how mathematical ideas could be translated into working systems. Implementing models, testing them on real data, and observing how sensitive they were to modeling assumptions pushed me from passive learning toward active experimentation. From that point on, I actively sought research settings where iteration, failure, and reformulation were unavoidable parts of progress.
My first research experience was in the laboratory of Prof. Rajesh M. Hegde, where I worked on AI-based air pollution source attribution using large-scale environmental and climate datasets. The project aimed to model emission sources by integrating emission inventories with climate reanalysis data. Early in the work, I identified and resolved a spatial inconsistency between datasets that nominally shared the same resolution, implementing careful grid alignment and interpolation to ensure meaningful correspondence. With this foundation in place, I developed supervised neural network models that achieved strong predictive performance and then extended the work toward unsupervised methods to explore latent source structure without explicit labels. This direction remains ongoing, with progressively improved results as modelling choices and training procedures are refined. Through this experience, I learned how resolving fundamental technical issues often enables deeper methodological innovation rather than limiting it.
My second research experience was conducted in the laboratory of Prof. Tushar Sandhan, where I worked on visual localization with the specific objective of projecting the trajectory of a moving camera onto a global reference image. I began by evaluating visual odometry and feature-matching methods on standard open-source benchmarks, where many approaches appeared reliable. However, when tested on real-world data captured under low illumination, weak texture, and motion blur, these methods degraded significantly. To understand this gap, I studied camera projection, calibration, triangulation, epipolar geometry, essential and fundamental matrices, and bundle adjustment from first principles. Rather than adopting any single method, I iteratively modified and integrated existing codebases, handling numerous edge cases through repeated experimentation and debugging. This process led to a fused localization pipeline that produced preliminary results more stable than any individual odometry or feature-matching method I had evaluated earlier. This work taught me how much of real progress comes from system-level iteration and careful engineering rather than algorithm selection alone.

The Multi-Robot Coordination for Maritime Environments project strongly matches my interests in distributed decision-making under communication constraints. My background in trajectory reasoning, sensor fusion, and failure analysis positions me well to contribute to simulation-driven evaluation of coordination strategies and to reason about how partial observability and delayed information affect collective behavior. I am particularly interested in how theoretical coordination frameworks translate into system-level performance when assumptions about communication reliability are relaxed.

The Real-Time FPGA Acceleration of Attention-Based Bidirectional LSTM Networks project appeals to my desire to ground machine learning in physical constraints. My experience with sequential models and attention mechanisms, combined with my electrical engineering training, makes this an ideal opportunity to study how algorithmic choices manifest as latency, power, and determinism on hardware. I am keen to learn how learned models behave when deployed under strict real-time constraints and how hardware-aware design influences model structure.

Finally, the Pattern Analysis of Player Movement for Space Creation in Soccer project interests me as a problem in spatio-temporal decision modeling rather than sports analytics. Player motion provides a clean, data-rich setting to study latent structure, coordination, and emergent behavior in multi-agent systems. The use of clustering, dimensionality reduction, and sequence models closely parallels the analytical tools required for broader applications in robotics and autonomous systems.

Beyond these projects, I have been independently studying attention mechanisms and transformer-based models, preparing for future work in multimodal and language-driven systems. I am also actively building the foundation required to extend my current work toward reinforcement learning for autonomous navigation, where perception, control, and learning intersect.

In addition to the specific projects, Purdue’s engineering research culture is a strong draw for me. The integration of theory, simulation, and deployment within the Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with facilities that support robotics, embedded systems, and high-performance computing, makes Purdue an environment where my interests in sequential decision-making, real-time systems, and robust learning can be developed in a grounded and practical way. During my research internship, I designed Monte Carlo simulations of the Laser Directed Energy Deposition (L-DED) process, which predicted stray grain formation and subsequent remelting into a single crystal. This sparked my interest in using computational tools to bridge the gap between process conditions and microstructural evolution. 

I am an undergraduate student at National Institute of Technology Karnataka (NITK), Surathkal, India, pursuing a major in Metallurgical and Materials Engineering with a minor in Computer Science.

When I began my major three and a half years ago, I started exploring different areas within this field, and I was fascinated by materials engineering's bottom-up approach–from atomic and crystallographic levels to macroscopic phenomena. In my second semester, I began learning about machine learning and developed an automated license plate recognition system using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs); however, I found the work unfulfilling without a clear connection to materials engineering. This realisation highlighted the importance of integrating computer science with domain knowledge, prompting me to pursue a minor in Computer Science.

To structure my learning, I felt starting by understanding the various length-scales would be good, and thus I undertook a project, ‘Multiscale Materials Analysis’, learning electronic properties, energy bands, and atomic-scale simulations using VESTA, abTEM, LAMMPS, and ASE. To gain some theoretical knowledge, I attended workshops on Molecular Dynamics and Density Functional Theory. 

As a metallurgist, I was eager to explore the experimental side of things first to better understand how shortcomings can be addressed using computational techniques. I worked with two professors as part of a consultancy team investigating a cooling fan failure at a nearby oil refinery, analysing operational history, maintenance logs, and fracture signatures present on the failed component. We determined that over-torquing the bolts in the coupling clamps led to local stress corrosion, accelerated by the moist and corrosive operating environment, ultimately causing failure. After co-authoring the investigation report, I recognised that failures often follow predictable patterns—fatigue, overloading, creep, and corrosion—which inspired my capstone project, AI-Assisted Failure Analysis. In this project, I curated a dataset, built a custom CNN model (37% accuracy), and developed an image preprocessing workflow and methodology for fracture signature identification, and I am currently exploring methodologies to improve model accuracy.

I strongly believe that experimental research is necessary, and computational efforts could at best supplement, rather than replace, experimental research in my field. In the summer of 2025, I joined Prof. Abhik Choudhury's research group at the Department of Materials Engineering, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, as a research intern. Under his guidance, I developed a Python-based workflow for thermal data analysis from infrared imaging during L-DED 3D printing. This workflow was used to analyse thermal gradients and melt-pool solidus contours, which were then correlated with experimentally observed microstructural features. Insights derived from thermal history, process parameters, and custom Monte Carlo simulations were used to predict optimal scan speeds and laser powers, which were implemented through a closed feedback loop to achieve single-crystal epitaxial growth. My coursework in cyber-physical systems has provided hands-on experience in IoT development. I have prior experience in MD, data analysis and scientific programming, which makes me competent for ‘Atomistic modelling of radiation damage in semiconductors’  offered by Prof. Alejandro Strachan.  I am open to contributing to any project matching my expertise and research interests.

After completing the program, I intend to pursue higher studies, and I strongly believe that SURF will provide me with direction in my career, a chance to hone my skills, and networking opportunities that will help me pursue a PhD in the field of Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME). 

With my strong dual background in Materials Engineering and Computer Science, and experience in prior organised research, I believe I am uniquely qualified and look forward to an opportunity to contribute to research at Purdue University.

statement_of_purpose:
I was drawn to civil engineering through a growing curiosity about how engineers make high-stakes decisions when perfect information is impossible. Long before I became interested in formal design methods, I was intrigued by how large, safety-critical structures continue to perform reliably despite uncertainty in loads, materials, construction, and long-term use. Rather than viewing engineering as the mechanical application of fixed procedures, I became interested in the reasoning processes that allow engineers to predict structural behavior when direct verification is impractical or insufficient. This curiosity became focused during my involvement in high-rise building projects under the supervision of Dr. Loizos Pelecanos, where I worked directly with the analysis and evaluation of tall structural systems.
In this work, I examined global load paths and lateral force–resisting behavior using both simplified analytical formulations and commercial finite element models. Rather than treating software outputs as definitive, I interrogated how modeling assumptions—particularly boundary condition idealization, stiffness distribution, and load combination strategies—governed predicted drift, force redistribution, and demand-to-capacity ratios. By comparing analytical predictions with expected construction-stage and serviceability behavior, I observed how small modeling choices could produce materially different interpretations of structural safety. This experience made clear that numerical precision does not equate to physical accuracy, and that models are tools for reasoning rather than substitutes for it.
As a result, my understanding of civil engineering shifted from procedural compliance toward first-principles interpretation. I began to see global structural response as an emergent outcome of mechanics, material behavior, and load transfer, rather than as a direct consequence of codified equations. Equally important, I recognized that uncertainty is not an error to be eliminated, but an intrinsic feature of structural engineering that must be explicitly understood and managed. This realization now shapes how I approach both analysis and design.
My academic projects further reinforced this perspective through technically rigorous inquiry. In a study on mass concrete incorporating bio-admixtures, I analyzed hydration-induced temperature rise and thermal gradient development in large pours, evaluating how material properties, boundary conditions, and scale influence cracking risk and long-term durability. This work demonstrated how material-level behavior, when amplified by structural dimensions, can dominate system performance. In a separate project on soil liquefaction, I investigated how variations in soil stratigraphy, relative density, and cyclic loading affect pore pressure accumulation and stiffness degradation, and assessed mitigation strategies using simplified analytical correlations. Additionally, a case study on construction and demolition waste management expanded my perspective to lifecycle-level decision-making, reinforcing the responsibility of engineers to integrate sustainability with structural performance.
My practical training with the Central Public Works Department on the Central Vista Project (Vice President Enclave) further grounded these insights. Observing the execution of large-scale infrastructure under stringent quality control, safety requirements, and logistical constraints highlighted the persistent gap between analytical idealization and field reality. Massive concrete placements, tight construction sequencing, and complex steel coordination underscored the necessity of engineering judgment in reconciling simplified design models with construction tolerances, material variability, and execution-stage uncertainty.
Across these experiences, I have developed a set of research-driven questions that continue to guide my intellectual trajectory: How effectively do simplified analytical and numerical models capture the governing behavior of complex structural systems? Where do their assumptions become critical limitations? How do engineers make rational, defensible decisions when uncertainty cannot be removed but must be accommodated? I am particularly interested in the interaction between theoretical formulations, computational modeling, and observed structural response, and in how sound engineering judgment develops through this interaction rather than through reliance on equations alone.
I have also learned to engage productively with discrepancy. Early in my analytical work, mismatches between predicted and expected structural behavior were sources of frustration. In one instance, inconsistencies in stiffness response compelled me to reassess boundary conditions and material idealizations, revealing how subtle modeling choices can fundamentally alter structural interpretation. Through faculty mentorship, targeted literature review, and focused simulation studies, I learned to treat uncertainty as a source of insight rather than failure. This process strengthened my independence, analytical discipline, and capacity to reason critically under ambiguity.
I am drawn to the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) because its immersive, mentorship-intensive structure aligns precisely with how I have developed as an engineer—through iterative engagement with theory, computation, and observation. SURF would provide the ideal environment to formulate focused research questions, develop simplified analytical or numerical models, rigorously interrogate their assumptions, and refine them through comparison with experimental data or high-fidelity simulations. I am particularly motivated to contribute to research involving structural modeling, experimental validation, and uncertainty-aware analysis, where even narrowly scoped investigations can yield fundamental insight into model reliability.
My long-term goal is to become a structural engineer-researcher who bridges theoretical mechanics, computational methods, and construction-stage realities to advance resilient, efficient, and sustainable infrastructure systems. Participation in SURF would be a critical step toward this goal, allowing me to gain hands-on experience in experimental structural testing, advanced computational modeling, and uncertainty quantification, while refining my ability to pose meaningful research questions and interpret discrepancies between prediction and observation.
Through sustained engagement with structural analysis, material behavior, geotechnical response, and large-scale construction practice, I have confirmed both my readiness and my commitment to research-driven civil engineering. My experiences have taught me that the most important engineering insights arise not from perfect models, but from understanding why imperfect models succeed or fail. SURF represents a decisive opportunity to transform this perspective into rigorous research capability and to prepare for advanced study and impactful contributions to the field of civil engineering.

statement_of_purpose:
The first time I encountered a blockchain bridge exploit report, I was struck by a paradox: systems designed to eliminate trust were failing precisely because they required trust in validators, in cryptographic assumptions, in the absence of future technological disruption. Bridge exploits have now exceeded $2.8 billion in losses, yet the underlying vulnerability remains: classical cryptographic protocols are not designed to survive the quantum computing era, and current architectures offer no migration path. This is not merely a technical problem but a design philosophy problem. How do we build systems that anticipate disruption rather than react to it?
This question drives my research across two domains that initially seem distinct but share a common thread. In quantum-safe blockchain protocols, I investigate how emerging technologies threaten existing infrastructure and how we can deploy countermeasures before attacks become feasible. In LLM evaluation, I studied how we establish the boundaries of AI capabilities before deploying systems in high-stakes domains. Both are fundamentally about building trust through rigorous anticipation rather than reactive patching.
My work on the first problem began in the Blockchain Data Intelligence Lab at Penn State under Professor Madhusudan Singh, where I developed QLink, a Layer-3 quantum-safe interoperability protocol. The core insight motivating QLink is that securing bridges requires addressing three simultaneous vulnerabilities: validator key theft, proof forgery, and the looming threat of quantum decryption. Existing solutions address these piecemeal; QLink integrates post-quantum cryptography, quantum key distribution, and hardware security modules into a unified architecture. I developed the security threat model analyzing five attack categories, from classical validator compromise to quantum-capable signature forgery using Shor's algorithm and conducted experimental evaluation using the OpenQKD simulator. My results demonstrated that QKD throughput exceeds validator consumption by 62–707× across fiber distances up to 50 km, confirming that quantum-safe bridging introduces less than one second of cryptographic overhead. This work, available as an arXiv preprint, represents the first interoperability framework combining these mechanisms for cross-chain security.
The second problem of understanding AI system boundaries before deployment emerged from my work in the RAISE Lab under Professor Amulya Yadav. I designed and executed a complete research project evaluating LLM diagnostic reasoning capabilities: can state-of-the-art language models perform the complex, multi-step reasoning required for rare disease diagnosis? I constructed a novel dataset of 176 symptom-diagnosis pairs extracted from House M.D., a medical television series validated in peer-reviewed literature for teaching rare disease recognition. I built the complete evaluation pipeline which involved web scraping, structured prompt generation, and fuzzy string matching and systematically evaluated four LLMs. The results were striking: accuracy ranged from 16.48% to 38.64%, with even the best model failing on nearly two-thirds of cases. Deploying these systems in clinical settings without understanding these limitations could lead to misdiagnosis and patient harm. This work has been accepted at the AAAI 2026 Workshop on Responsible Synthetic Data.
The connection between these projects is not incidental. Both quantum computing and large language models create new capabilities and new risks simultaneously. My research work centers on understanding those risks before they manifest as catastrophic failures, whether a drained bridge contract or a misdiagnosed patient.
I learned more from my failures than from any successful project. My first research, a fairness-in-ML study, took an entire semester without yielding results. It was frustrating, and I probably stuck with it longer than I should have. That experience taught me to recognize broken approaches earlier, communicate setbacks instead of hiding them, and set clearer milestones. I applied all of these skills to the LLM evaluation project. I also started talking to my advisor sooner when things stalled instead of trying to solve everything alone. Research takes as much resilience as technical skills.
Purdue SURF is appealing because it prioritizes intensive, mentored research that leads to real scholarly output, which matches how I work best. Three projects connect directly to my current work. Professor Chen-Lung Hung works on neutral atom array trapping. My QKD simulations gave me a sense of how physical constraints shape information transfer, but that work was purely computational. I want to see how these ideas play out in experimental quantum systems. Professor Jenna DiVincenzo's gradual verification research connects to my interest in trustworthy systems: her work on using machine learning to generate specifications sits right at the intersection of security and AI evaluation, where I have been working. Following that, Professor Ilias Bilionis's cardiac flow MRI reconstruction project would extend my medical AI work into imaging, letting me apply my evaluation background while learning physics-informed machine learning.
My long-term goal is a PhD focused on secure computational systems where quantum computing and AI meet. I want to lead research that influences both the theory and the deployment of systems protecting critical infrastructure. SURF offers preparation I cannot get at my home institution: new methodologies, mentorship from faculty at these frontiers, and a research community that will challenge how I think.
Beyond my publications, I interned at Jubilant Pharmova, where I built a LangChain-based AI agent that is currently being used across 46 radiopharmacies in the United States. That experience taught me what it takes to move research into deployment. Coursework in systems programming, quantum computing, and blockchain development supports this direction, and I have experience carrying projects from problem formulation through publication.
I bring demonstrated productivity, resilience, and intellectual engagement with problems at the intersection of quantum computing and AI. The opportunity to work with Purdue faculty on these questions offer an ideal next step toward building systems that anticipate, rather than merely react to, technological change.

My journey with research began as I was taking Professor Parasuraman Swaminathan’s course on Electronic Materials and Devices. As part of this course I was introduced to band diagrams, pn junctions and the charge transport mechanisms that made these devices work. The course connected atomic scale phenomena to electronic properties. This pushed me to want to explore how these ideas manifest in real devices. I was also keen to learn about the tools used to characterize their performance, and through this to understand their limitations imposed by defects and interfaces, and how to engineer them to optimize their performance. Transitioning from my coursework to the Electronic Materials and Thin Films Laboratory,  I applied these concepts to the domain of charge storage. I began to appreciate how charge flow can be manipulated through materials engineering to make smaller, faster, more sustainable devices- especially in a time where sustainable energy is a global concern. This is something that continues to motivate me. These experiences have clarified my central research interest - the effect of atomic scale interfaces and defects on the macroscopic performance of energy and electronic devices. 

Under the guidance of Professor Parasuraman, I began developing core shell MoS2-Ag nanowires. Coating MoS2 on Ag would form a heterojunction aimed at enhancing the charge storage capacity, exploiting the conductive nature of silver as well as the pseudocapacitive nature of MoS2. The interface quality between the Ag nanowires and MoS2 layer was critical to the capacitor’s functioning and a lot of time was spent improving this. I learned a lot about energy storage mechanisms used in supercapacitors and what distinguishes them from batteries. We used Direct Ink Writing (DIW) to deposit prepared composite inks on flexible substrates. To this extent, I read about various forms of printing to achieve thin film layers. Such microsupercapacitors are now being  integrated into flexible and low-power electronics. They are being used where conventional batteries cannot operate - in sensors and health monitoring devices. Through this project, I learned about hydrothermal synthesis of MoS2 on Ag, formulation of composite inks, and tuning printing parameters to create uniform interdigitated electrodes.  I realized that while DIW is scalable, it is difficult to control surface contamination and precision, which affects the intrinsic performance of the device. I also became familiar with electrochemical characterization techniques like CV and GCD. 

Building on this, I designed and fabricated MoS2-ZnO-Ag photodetectors, once again printed using DIW on flexible PET substrates. During this project, I focused on understanding how transport layers affect charge transport and overall device performance. I performed electrical I-V and I-t characterizations to test stability and optical responsivity. This strengthened my skills in device fabrication and data interpretation. It also deepened my understanding of how band alignments and defect states and vacancy traps influence optoelectronic behavior. 

Throughout these processes, I overcame several challenges - finalizing the ink compositions for the supercapacitor was a rigorous process of balancing MoS2, which promoted charge storage and Ag, which improved conductivity. There were several problems that came up during the printing process - merging of electrodes, insufficient wettability of the ink onto the substrate and so on. I addressed these by systematically tuning the rheology of the ink and optimizing the print speed and substrate temperature. These highlight the importance of precise process control in this field. 


In my fifth semester, while doing coursework, I was able to draw connections between redox reactions that occur in corrosion engineering and the pseudocapacitive nature of MoS2. My course in Physics of Materials dealt with the opening of bandgaps at the edges of Brellouin Zones. These connections between something new that I learn to something I already know always excite me. These strengthen my understanding that meaningful work in this domain lies in drawing these cross connections: not just showing that a device works, but showing its working mechanism and drawing comparisons to other similar devices. This reinforces my belief that macroscopic performance in a variety of applications depends on microscopic factors like interfaces and defects. 

Through the Purdue SURF program, I hope to integrate synthesis, advanced characterization tools and device physics. I look forward to moving from inks to the fabrication of clean van der Waals heterostructures using a mechanical exfoliation process in Professor Tiancong Zhu’s group. This would allow me to explore the quantum limits of the materials I will be working with. Simultaneously, my interest in the effect of defects on performance draws me to Professor Raisul Islam’s work in Scanning Thermal Microscopy. Here, I hope to understand and visualize thermal scattering mechanisms in nanomaterials, and how these would affect device efficiency. Finally, Professor Babak Anosari’s group presents an ideal research trajectory for me. It allows me to leverage my experience with 2D materials like MoS2 supercapacitors to the MXenes, making use of my background in solution processing to tackle advanced challenges in high energy density storage. 

The SURF program offers the rigorous experimental mentorship I require to pursue graduate programs in Materials Science or Applied Physics, connecting low dimensional physics and scalable device technology. 

Beyond these technical aspects, I am eager to step into the global research community fostered by the SURF program. Purdue boasts a highly international environment and this presents a unique chance to interact with and learn from peers and mentors from diverse geographical and academic backgrounds. I believe that this will give me exposure to multiple scientific approaches and problem solving strategies, which are essential to a collaborative career in research.

I eventually noticed that I was most fascinated with systems like financial systems, collective behavior, and learning algorithms, and perhaps not coincidentally, that they were also inherently unpredictable. Not just the coding, not just the AI, but the whole puzzle of getting intelligent systems to work in the real, physical world. That night planted a question in my head that I have been chasing ever since: what does it take to make AI run in real time, on actual hardware, without a data center backing it up?

That question led me here, to Professor Kildishev's FPGA acceleration project. When I read about implementing attention-based bidirectional LSTM networks on edge computing platforms, everything clicked. This is exactly the intersection I have been circling around for the past two years, the place where algorithm design meets hardware constraints, where theoretical machine learning becomes something you can actually deploy on a device that fits in your hand. I want to understand how attention mechanisms translate into timing determinism and bandwidth limitations. I want to get my hands dirty with Vivado, build something that processes analog signals faster than the alternatives, and contribute to research that actually matters.

My path to computer engineering was not straightforward. I came to Purdue fascinated by AI but treating it as purely a software problem. Suddenly I was staring at digital logic gates, timing diagrams, and signal processing fundamentals, and I started to see something I had completely missed: the hardware underneath all the software I had been building. For the first time, I understood that the neural networks I was training in Python were not just abstract math. They were operations that had to execute on physical systems with real constraints. That realization reframed everything. I stopped asking "how do I build smarter AI?" and started asking "how do I build AI that can actually run fast enough to matter?"

My primary research interest is understanding how large language models reason, particularly in domains that require logical consistency, constraint handling, and step-wise problem solving. 

My interest in deep learning began when I realised that, unlike traditional machine-learning methods, neural networks could represent layered, hierarchical computations that resemble simplified cognitive processes. Wanting to understand how models like GPT achieve this, I enrolled in an intensive course on large language models to study their internal mechanisms more seriously. Concepts such as instruction tuning, model distillation, and the limits of current models in mathematics and code generation made me think critically about what “general intelligence” in these systems actually means, and how improved model reasoning can lead to more reliable real-world applications of language models, including lightweight SLMs (“small-sized” language models) that are efficient enough to run locally. Hence, in the summer after my second year, I started projects at research labs at my university, wanting to explore more in this area.

Recognizing that large language models (LLMs) still struggle with tasks requiring strict logical structure, such as competitive programming, I initiated a code-generation project within the Cognition Lab with two core objectives: improving model performance under tight time/space constraints, and investigating if these capabilities can be effectively distilled into smaller, efficient models (SLMs) for privacy-preserving deployment. I took the clear initiative to deeply understand the theoretical foundations of the problem and evaluation strategies. A significant early contribution involved independently setting up and operationalizing the evaluation framework LiveCodeBench (LCB) on our cluster, which required implementing specific metrics, resolving complex dependency conflicts, and optimizing the workflow to function within limited compute resources. Critically, my analysis of preliminary SLM outputs revealed a key failure pattern: the generated code lacked the algorithmic complexity required to pass imposed time limits. Guided by this data-driven insight, and my proactive review of both foundational and recent literature, I formulated our current research direction: fine-tuning using a newly released, algorithmically complex 2025 competitive programming dataset to directly address this algorithmic weakness. 

Further, during my second year, I completed a Data Mining course project that focused on analyzing challenges in text data, such as ambiguity, context dependence, negation, and the need to convert language into numerical representations for machine processing. Our chosen application was emotion detection, where sentences were mapped to one of five emotion-based emojis, motivated by the importance of conveying emotional tone in digital communication. We implemented and compared two rule-based approaches: a lexicon-driven sliding window model with beam search, which was simple and efficient but limited in contextual understanding, and an improved model using POS tagging, parse trees, and weighted lexicon matching to better capture grammatical structure, word importance, and scoped negation. Using NLTK for preprocessing and parsing, we evaluated the system qualitatively on a small, manually constructed dataset. The parse-tree-based approach demonstrated superior emotional sensitivity and interpretability, and the project concluded with directions for future work such as improved sarcasm handling, multilingual support, and scaling to supervised, data-driven models.

Alongside these structured research projects, I independently developed a conceptual proposal for a Multimodal Fake News Detection System tailored for Tamil and other low-resource Indian languages under my project mentor. The system integrates: a text encoder like IndicBERT; an image encoder such as CLIP; a BLIP-based captioning mechanism to extract text representations from images; a retrieval-augmented verification component (RAG) to validate claims against factual sources.
The proposal addresses challenges such as figurative language, inconsistent orthography, and cross-modal alignment. This work helped me develop the ability to construct full-stack research architectures, reason about multi-component systems, and analyze how multimodal models integrate and fail.
