statement_of_purpose:
Motivation & Career Goals 
My interest in research sits at the intersection of Electrical Engineering and Physics—specifically, the realization that the future of technology requires us to engineer materials at the atomic limit and harness quantum mechanics. While my coursework introduces me to device logic, I am driven by the physical constraints we are rapidly approaching. I am particularly intrigued by the potential of 2D materials for advanced nanoelectronics and nanophotonics. My long-term aspiration is to pursue a PhD in EE, Materials Engineering, Applied Physics, or Quantum Engineering, eventually leading a research & development group dedicated to transitioning quantum materials from theoretical novelties to practical components. My goal is to engineer the hardware that solves our greatest challenges in energy, medicine, and computation.

Why SURF? 
I am drawn to Purdue SURF because it offers the opportunity to continue & delve into the research I do during the school year with the incredible people and facilities that Purdue offers. Unlike external summer programs that often require restarting in a new lab, SURF will allow me to maintain momentum on my current work at the Birck Nanotechnology Center. The summer provides the immersive, uninterrupted time necessary to take my project from its current synthesis phase to full device characterization—a transition that is difficult to achieve during the fragmented academic year.

Research Plan & Preparation 
This summer, I aim to master the "second half" of the research loop: nanofabrication and optical characterization. Having recently achieved a milestone by synthesizing single-crystal MoOCl₂ via chemical vapor transport (CVT) under Prof. Shalaev, I plan to use the SURF period to explore phonon interactions with hyperbolic plasmon polaritons (HPPs). I hypothesize that by pumping phonons for the metal oxide chain channeling the HPPs, we can achieve optical switching, which I will test with a pump probe s-SNOM experiment. I also hope to fabricate hyperbolic plasmonic Field-Effect Transistors (FETs) on these crystals, using an architecture similar to graphene FETs. Gaining proficiency in cleanroom fabrication and pump-probe experiments is the critical next step in my development as a researcher. Also, there are so many great people working in those fields to connect with. I’d love to have the unbroken time to have meals and deeper conversations with people.
This work builds on my strong foundation of hands-on experience. As a SULI intern at Oak Ridge National Laboratory last summer, I developed a room-temperature quantum sensing microscope, giving me the instrumentation skills necessary for this proposal. I worked on relaxometry measurements of boron vacancies in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). Last year at Purdue, I worked with Prof. Yong P. Chen on 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs), learning the 2D device characterization and building process. Before that, I had the honor to do crystal synthesis research at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, which has truly been a great basis that my interests have built from. Materials make up everything. Beyond the lab, I am dedicated to building the quantum community. As Vice President of Purdue's Quantum Student Organization (QSO), I teach quantum topics in our quantum crash courses and lead projects on Qiskit quantum computing and bloch sphere visualization. I also helped organize/host Spring into Quantum, Quantum Open House, QSTEP, and more. As an Executive Board Member for the international Quantum Coalition non-profit, I work to manage global university partnerships and create educational resources for the next generation of innovators. I oversaw, organized, & judged the international quantum hackathon Future Leaders in Quantum (FLiQ) challenge with the United Nation’s International Telecommunication Union and Princeton’s quantum club.

Overcoming Obstacles 
Not having obstacles in research is like winning the lottery in my experience. Thankfully, I can come up with a solution or pivot. I encountered this recently with my MoOCl2 crystals. Initial X-ray diffraction data revealed complex pseudo-merohedral twinning—a common defect in monoclinic van der Waals materials that threatened to complicate our optical data. Rather than viewing this as a failure of synthesis, I delved into the crystallographic literature to understand the energetics of the stacking faults. I realized that by using a thin-flake exfoliation strategy and inspecting flakes with a cross-polarized microscopy, we could isolate single-domain regions and proceed with device fabrication. That problem hit me in the face and took some exploration. Sometimes it’s more subtle (and stupider). My optical microscope data at ORNL had a weird oscillation in its relaxation curves. After isolating different possible issues and measuring with SPAD & oscilloscope as recommended by the scientist I worked under, I ended up discovering that the issue was just that the wire connecting the laser to the pulse sequencer was too long and slightly bent.

SURF would give me the invaluable opportunity to continue to build on my personal relationships, research experience, ambitious ideas, and dreams.

This pushed me to question the intelligence behind these systems—how ChatGPT adapts to user sentiment, how email predicts my next phrase, or how Instagram surfaces content based on the shows I watch. As I experimented further, a central question began to guide my work: how can AI systems understand human sentiment, emotion, and intent beyond surface-level pattern recognition, and how can such systems be made robust to real-world noise and variability when models are typically trained on idealised datasets? This question continues to shape my academic and research choices.

In my second year, I shifted toward multimodal learning and began building a Smart OCR-based semantic video retrieval system under the guidance of mentors. What began as a vision-based assignment gradually drew me toward speech modelling and broader questions about how systems interpret human audio.

In my third year, I mentored a team of three while leading the multilingual speech-to-speech module for UniComm, a multimodal assistive communication system for individuals with hearing, speech, or language limitations. I am Om Awadhoot, currently pursuing B.Tech in Information Technology at G H Raisoni College of Engineering, Nagpur. Alongside my academics, I build XR-based STEM experiences for Aviation students for both flight training and maintenance training, as a Junior Unity Developer at Vighnesh Inc. After nearly 2 years in this role, I wanted to research how XR affected the learning process both in academia and industry. That's why I chose Augmented Reality as the focus of my diploma capstone project at Thakur Polytechnic, Mumbai, which resulted in my first peer-reviewed publication "AR Application: Homewise Vision," published in the International Research Journal of Engineering and Technology (IRJET) in February 2024. The application allows users to view 2D architectural blueprints as interactive 3D models on their mobile devices, with additional features such as cost estimation and interior customization. The project secured 2nd place at the 24-hour National Level Hackathon at VNR VJIET, Hyderabad and 3rd place at the capstone project competition at Thakur Polytechnic.

While this project demonstrated the value XR brings to visualizing static architectural data, I am also drawn to the potential of immersive technology in more dynamic engineering fields, especially where hands-on training is not easily accessible. A prime example is bioprocess engineering, where traditional bioreactor training is often limited by steep financial and time requirements. Large 30-liter stainless-steel bioreactors can cost between $30,000 and $200,000, and each fermentation run uses significant media, utilities, and staff resources over 24 to 72 hours. As a result, universities may maintain only two or three units for upwards of thirty students, giving most students just three to five practical sessions through their degree. This is often too few to build real proficiency. In addition, key aspects like mixing dynamics, oxygen transfer, and biomass growth remain hidden, making it difficult for students to connect theoretical knowledge with real system behavior.

To address these limitations, Dr. Xinyu Zhang at Purdue University and her virtual bioreactor project, originally developed at NC State's Biomanufacturing Training and Education Center, offer a compelling solution. Funded by the DELTA grant and published at EDULEARN19 (Fisher, Polyak, & Zhang, 2019), the initial system used virtual reality to introduce students to bioreactor orientation and SIP (Sterilization in Place) tasks. The project has now advanced to mixed reality on the Meta Quest 3, allowing learners to adjust fermentation parameters like pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen, and nutrient levels, and see how these changes influence microbial growth or pollutant removal. By removing cost, risk, and time barriers, this platform empowers students to repeat experiments until they gain genuine problem-solving skills.

However, bridging the gap from a working prototype to a classroom-ready tool presents distinct challenges I aim to help address. Optimizing the application for the standalone Meta Quest 3 headset so that it performs reliably in extended sessions is one such challenge. Equally important is validating the underlying fermentation simulation against established kinetic models and experimental data, ensuring students encounter authentic biological responses and not oversimplified behaviors.

These needs define the heart of what I can contribute. My research would focus on preparing the virtual bioreactor for successful classroom deployment. I plan to do this by carefully testing and optimizing its performance, then systematically validating its biological accuracy. I faced similar performance challenges early in my tenure at Vighnesh Inc., where our XR aviation modules initially dropped frames during complex interactions of training instructions, resulting in user motion sickness. By leveraging Unity Profiler and optimizing texture compression, I traced bottlenecks and stabilized frame rates, greatly improving feedback from aviation instructors and students. I plan to apply these same optimization methods to the bioreactor project and develop solutions to new challenges as they arise.

I am equally focused on ensuring the simulation behaves realistically. While developing the A320 MCDU Trainer at Vighnesh Inc., I worked well outside my core background, learning from aviation instructors how real systems validate flight plans, generate errors, and respond to diverse inputs. I asked questions, iterated on behaviors, and adjusted the simulation based on direct feedback until it matched real-world expectations. This process taught me that in training applications, authenticity of system response matters even more than visual accuracy.

I am eager to extend this same careful approach to the fermentation simulation, learning from Dr. Zhang as well as from kinetic literature what genuine microbial responses should look like, such as how growth and metabolism shift with changes in pH and temperature. My aim is to validate the simulation using real datasets and to supplement this technical work with a comprehensive literature review on XR effectiveness in STEM settings. Through Dr. Zhang’s mentorship, I hope to both contribute my Unity and usability testing skills and deepen my understanding of bioprocess modeling and academic research practices.

This intersection of technical innovation and learning validation is what makes the Purdue SURF program, and the chance to work with Dr. Zhang, especially meaningful for me. The program represents the ideal setting to transition from industry XR development towards academic research. I am excited for the chance to learn academic research techniques I haven’t touched upon in industry yet, such as experimental design, scholarly writing, and synthesizing literature for publication and presentation.

Participating in SURF will provide the vital bridge between my current industry experience and my eventual goal of contributing to graduate-level research. The program will help me build the interdisciplinary approach needed for making learning tools that are both practically robust and educationally effective. Ultimately, I aspire to pursue a master’s degree in Human-Computer Interaction with a focus on XR applications to help make STEM education more accessible through validated immersive technologies. I am fully committed to advancing and optimizing the virtual bioreactor toward classroom deployment and look forward to the opportunity to collaborate and learn with Dr. Zhang and the Purdue SURF community.

statement_of_purpose:
As a young girl, I aspired to become a physician. I wanted to be on the front lines to treat diseases and give patients a second chance at life. As I explored medicine more deeply, I was drawn to the fundamental biological pathways and chemical interactions that build the foundation of drug discovery. I became interested in questions such as: What are the key biological targets that drive cancer, and how can we improve the selectivity and potency of existing therapies? These curiosities steered me away from clinical practice and towards research, where I hope to contribute to revolutionizing medicine by advancing safer, more precise, and more accessible treatments.   
  
My journey through chemical research began in my freshman year of high school with the Aspiring Scholars Directed Research Program. Here, I conducted organic chemistry research focused on cancer-therapeutic development and delivery. One of my most impactful projects focused on investigating the biological relevance of andrographolide, a natural product derived from the plant Andrographis Paniculata. Through reactivity-informed pharmacophore editing of andrographolide, I synthesized a library of andrographolide analogs. I examined how structural modifications of andrographolide influenced its metabolic stability and interactions with biological targets.   
  
Through my research at ASDRP, I have faced numerous obstacles. Before joining ASDRP, I had no organic chemistry research experience. I was faced with a steep learning curve in organic reaction mechanisms and biological interactions. However, my inexperience did not stop me; I studied online chemistry and biological resources and scheduled meetings with my advisor to discuss topics I was struggling with. I reached out to my more experienced peers by spending additional time in the laboratory to shadow and develop stronger laboratory techniques.   
  
In my most recent project with ASDRP, I applied these skills to spearhead a 10+ step synthesis of a self-regulating molecule tailored to target cancer cells. This process involved rigorous experimental design, never-ending troubleshooting, and the use of numerous analytical instruments to assess compound purity. My efforts resulted in my team filing our provisional patent for “Auto-Tuning Drug Regulator Constructs.”   
  
My research experience with ASDRP built the foundation of my interest in drug discovery related research, prompting me to pursue a major in biochemistry and involve myself in ongoing cancer research. This led to me working in the Yang laboratory, where I explored the significance of G-quadruplex DNA secondary structures in cancer development and examined how targeting this structure can affect cancer proliferation. The primary cancer target in the Yang Lab is the MYC oncogene, which is overexpressed in more than 80% of human cancers. The MYC promoter region contains a highly guanine-rich sequence that can form G-quadruplex (MYC-G4). The MYC-G4 acts as a transcription silencer and downregulates MYC expression. Our lab has previously discovered that a class of compounds, indenoisoquinolines, can bind and stabilize MYC-G4, thus downregulating MYC expression.   
  
In my project, I studied how different sidechains on indenoisoquinolines can affect the compound's binding affinity to MYC-G4 using fluorescence spectroscopy. Working with a fluorophore-labeled MYC-G4 DNA probe, I monitored binding affinity through fluorescence quenching upon binding. I discovered that different characteristics including steric hindrance, intermolecular forces, and charge greatly affected the compound’s binding affinity to MYC-G4. Through my experience in the Yang lab, I learned of the importance of repeatability and reproducibility in science experimentation. I refined my laboratory technique to produce reliable results.   
  
Through my experiences, I developed a love for research. My long-term career goal is to become an independent researcher in the field of cancer drug discovery. To achieve this goal, I plan to apply to graduate research programs after I complete my undergraduate degree. Full-time research through SURF will be a great opportunity for me to further refine my laboratory research skills. Continuing in Dr. Yang’s lab, I hope to explore different methodologies in studying drug interactions with G-quadruplex DNA for anti-cancer drug discovery. I look forward to continuing to work with the Yang lab researchers, learning how to attack scientific questions, strengthen laboratory techniques, and familiarize myself with complex analytical machinery. The Yang lab is notable for its research with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, which I hope to learn how to apply to my research. These skills will be essential for my pursuit of graduate research on cancer-specific molecular targets.   
  
Beyond research, the SURF professional development programs will be a great opportunity for me to learn how to navigate graduate and industrial research environments. Additionally, I believe science is most impactful when shared, and I am deeply interested in cross-disciplinary research. The SURF symposium offers a great opportunity to present my work to a diverse audience while learning from researchers across a wide range of fields. Overall, SURF offers an invaluable experience for me to work towards my research goals.

statement_of_purpose:
I committed to pursuing a career in the future of aerospace manufacturing, driven by a lifelong passion for aviation and a growing interest in computational analysis and modeling that began during my freshman year at Purdue. This interest led me to pursue a minor in information technology alongside my degree in aeronautical technology. While my background differs from traditional aerospace engineering, my academic foundation and research experiences have prepared me to contribute meaningfully to SURF.

My journey into computational analysis began in my freshman year of college. I attended a CAD course taught by Dr. Garam Kim, where I was introduced to CATIA. I later applied these skills in an advanced manufacturing class, participating in labs where I fabricated components I had designed. With Dr. Kim’s guidance, I collaborated on a research project with senior undergraduate student Stan Melkumian and fellow sophomore Edward Kim, designing and constructing composite bridge elements for the Society for the Advancement of Material and Process Engineering (SAMPE). During the project, Stan further introduced me to analysis and simulation tools within CATIA. Using these tools, we created a generative structural analysis for different beam designs. Starting with an initial load of 2000 Newtons (N), we found that the square beam with a middle insert to be the most effective of the designs at withstanding and distributing the most concentrated loads, as it could withstand a maximum von Mises stress of 6.23 x 106 N/m2. Meanwhile, I-beams were often weaker in regards to withstanding concentrated loads. This was expected due to the structural behavior of the respective designs, as I-beams were designed to handle loads spread out over a larger area. Using this knowledge, I also performed a double undulating I-beam analysis, which showed a maximum stress tensor of 5.88 x 105 N/m2 with a maximum von Mises stress of 2.12 x 106 N/m2. After these simulations, the three of us performed a three-point bend test and compared these results to that of the simulations. The ultimate load proved to be 2552 N with a specific strength of 1.725 N/kg. Overall, the tests and simulations demonstrated the effectiveness of the prototype I-beam bridge. Video analysis pinpointed torsional deformation under load, which aligned with generative structural simulations. The project highlighted the crucial role of composites in manufacturing aircraft components and their potential as lighter, environmentally friendly alternatives to aluminum. It reinforced the idea that if composites can be manufactured cheaply, thus becoming more widespread to the industry, the aviation industry and the manufacturing industry overall can truly experience a long-awaited revival. My group presented this project at the Purdue Spring 2025 Undergraduate Research Conference, finishing in 2nd place.

Beyond coursework and research, I have gained practical experience through SAE Aero at Purdue, which designs competition aircraft and is run by associate professor Thiago Guimaraes. As part of the club’s aerodynamics team, I used the software xflr5 to analyze wing and tail configurations and became proficient in concepts such as Reynolds number and fluid mechanics, many of which I had not yet encountered in class. My team eventually decided on a monoplane minimal fuselage configuration, with an FX 63-137 airfoil for both the main wing and the high boom tail. Initially, I initially had no experience with xflr5 and stumbled out of the gates. However, I committed to learning the software and the concepts. After acquiring the basic understanding, I also started teaching other members of my team about the software and the concepts surrounding them. I’m still seen by them as a mentor, and at the same time, teaching them made me feel like an actual contributing member, giving me confidence that I could learn on the fly and expand on skillsets not explicitly learned in the classroom. 
I have also participated in Purdue’s Autonomous Robotics Club, working on a project called DogCopter, which combined a robotic dog with a drone. My role focused on integrating a Pixhawk with a Raspberry Pi to communicate via MAVLink, enabling transitions between terrestrial and aerial modes. The servos for the propellers also served as joints for the legs, creating a hybrid structure capable of multiple modes of operation. The system as a whole would be connected with a custom made remote control that enabled transition between dog and drone mode. Although I was forced to back out of the project for a year due to scheduling conflicts, I plan on returning to it for this upcoming year and finish what I had started.

Through these experiences, I have built a foundation in computational analysis, design, aerodynamics, and systems integration. They have also taught me how to persist through challenges, adapt quickly to new tools, and work collaboratively in team environments. I believe these qualities, combined with my technical preparation, make me well suited for SURF.

I took the opportunity to explore these ideas through the URSA program, conducting undergraduate research with the Singh Lab on succinic acid process intensification. The experience solidified my interest in process optimization and gave me a comprehensive introduction to laboratory scale chemical process analysis. 
My research, along with my avid interest in computation, led me to consider multiscale process modelling and simulation as a field I would like to pursue. I have continued my pursuit through joining the Peters Lab, where I work on developing their new analytical microkinetic model for a heterogeneous catalytic system, allowing me to get experience in the design of simulation models.
Over the past year, I have come to appreciate the interplay between in silico modelling and ex silico results. I’ve had the opportunity to work in both wet lab and computational settings, and I’ve realized the significance of having both approaches contribute to each other; computational models acting as predictors for physical behavior, and in vitro or in vivo experimentation informing model design. This is why I’d like to focus my research on a hybrid of experimental and computational methodologies, exploring multiscale modelling of chemical processes towards the objective of process intensification. Having explored current approaches in the field, I am interested in investigating top-down modelling approaches, using macroscopic targets and data to design models informed by microscale first principles. Through this approach, I hope to optimize industrial processes, especially in the energy sector.

SURF provides a structured environment for impactful research opportunities that can allow me to explore my hybrid systems modelling research interest over a substantial amount of time. The currently listed projects showcase a myriad of avenues for research in a diverse set of industrially relevant areas where I can gain firsthand experience in hybrid research methods, including batteries, heat exchangers etc. This has convinced me that I will be able to gain a unique research experience here, not only through the faculty and graduate student I am assigned to, but also through networking with faculty and peers in related areas.

statement_of_purpose:
What led me to my field and the questions that drive me:

My interest in machine learning research began with a project involving Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) imaging. These sensors can detect individual photons, yet their outputs are binary, noisy, and extremely low-resolution. I wanted to know whether we could recover the information that appears to be lost. This led me to a deeper question that continues to motivate me: can physics-informed approaches outperform purely data-driven methods when the underlying physics is well-understood?
To explore this, I built a SPAD image enhancement pipeline from scratch. The hardest part was not the neural network itself. It was learning to simulate realistic SPAD physics. I studied how Poisson statistics govern photon arrival, how dark counts and crosstalk corrupt measurements, and how these noise sources interact. I implemented these physical models as a data generation pipeline and trained residual CNN architectures to perform 16x super-resolution.
The results were instructive but incomplete. On synthetic data with known noise characteristics, my physics-informed pipeline achieved a 30 dB improvement in PSNR. But when I varied the simulated sensor parameters, performance degraded unpredictably. I could not determine whether the problem was my architecture, my data generation assumptions, or my evaluation methodology. This experience taught me something important: I had reached the limits of what I could learn without guidance. The questions that emerged from this project (how do physics-informed loss functions compare to standard losses when sensor characteristics vary? what happens when simulated data diverges from real sensor behavior?) are questions I want to investigate with proper mentorship.

What I have done to explore my field:

Beyond the SPAD project, I have applied machine learning and software development to various practical problems. I developed HydroSense, a platform designed to help users understand how much rainwater they can save. When the user enters their location, the system uses GIS techniques to identify the roof area automatically. HydroSense integrates weather data and groundwater level information using different APIs, estimates installation costs, and calculates how many years it would take to recover the investment. Building this end-to-end system taught me that research insights matter only if they can be deployed in tools people actually use.
I also developed a behavioral fraud detection system for Android banking that uses statistical analysis and Z-scores to profile user touch patterns. This project started as a hackathon prototype with rule-based checks, but I continued refining it afterward, adding an ML model that learns user behavior over time. This habit of continuing to improve projects beyond formal deadlines has become central to how I work.

Why SURF and the projects that interest me:

Two SURF projects align with my research interests, and I see a connection between them.
Prof. Lei Wang's work on Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Extreme Weather Prediction addresses the exact question I have been exploring: how do we combine domain knowledge with neural networks effectively? My experience with CNNs, PyTorch, and physics-based data pipelines directly applies to this work. I want to use Purdue's Bell supercomputer to run idealized atmospheric simulations and develop prediction algorithms for atmospheric blocking events. The goal of providing weeks of lead time for heat wave preparedness connects this research to real societal impact.
Prof. Jenna DiVincenzo's work on Gradual Verification interests me because it addresses a related problem from a different angle. My SPAD project isn’t useful in part because I had no way to formally specify what "correct" behavior meant as my system evolved. Her research direction on using machine learning to generate formal specifications speaks to this gap. I want to explore whether gradual verification can help developers incrementally verify ML systems without demanding complete specifications upfront.
The common thread is this: both projects ask how we build trust in complex systems incrementally, whether by incorporating physical constraints into neural networks or by adding formal specifications to code. I find this question compelling across both domains.
What attracts me to SURF specifically is the structure it provides. I have done independent research, but I have not yet worked under mentorship from experienced researchers. SURF offers weekly tutorials, access to computational resources like Bell and Data Depot, and the opportunity to present or publish findings. This combination of guidance and real research responsibility is what I need at this stage.

How SURF contributes to my career goals:

My long-term goal is to pursue a PhD in computer science, focusing on the intersection of machine learning and formal methods or physical modeling. I want to become a researcher who can bridge theoretical foundations with practical systems.
SURF would contribute to this goal in specific ways. I hope to learn how experienced researchers frame problems and design experiments. I want to gain skills in running large-scale simulations on supercomputing infrastructure. I also want to develop the ability to interpret negative results productively, something I have struggled with in independent work. The connections I build with faculty and other SURF participants would help me understand what a PhD commitment actually requires before I make that decision.

Challenges I have faced:

As a female undergraduate student pursuing an engineering degree in India, I have found that structured research opportunities are not always easy to access. My biggest challenge has been the lack of formal research mentorship. Most of what I have learned about machine learning and research methodology has come from online resources, papers, and trial and error. When my SPAD project produced results I did not fully understand, I had no advisor to consult. I spent weeks debugging whether the issue was my architecture, my data generation, or my evaluation metrics.
I have addressed this by being systematic about self-education. I read papers from EPFL's AQUA Lab on SPAD imaging. I studied from PyTorch tutorials and experimented with different architectures. I learned to document my failures so I could revisit them later with a fresh perspective. SURF represents an opportunity to complement this self-directed learning with structured mentorship while I still have time to shape my research direction.

As I spent more time with these subjects, however, a pattern began to emerge. Many of the ideas I was engaging with, whether that be efficiency, equity, incentives, or decision-making, were no longer confined to theory or policy documents. They were increasingly being embedded into algorithms, platforms, and automated systems that shape markets, governance, and everyday life. It became difficult to meaningfully study social systems without confronting the technological infrastructures that now mediate them. Gradually, I realized that if I wanted to engage seriously with these questions, I could not do so from outside the technical domain. I would have to enter it.

That realization led me to pursue a B.Tech in Data Science, Economics, and Business at Plaksha University. What drew me to Plaksha was not only its technical orientation, but the fact that it explicitly positioned computation alongside economic and societal thinking. Studying programming, statistics, machine learning, and economics in parallel has changed how I think about problems. I began to see computational tools not merely as instruments for prediction, but as frameworks that encode assumptions about the world. I am especially drawn to the idea that data-driven methods can reveal structure in complex systems, but only when their limitations and implications are actively interrogated rather than taken for granted.

Over time, what has kept me engaged in this field is the tension between abstraction and reality. In coursework and project work, I have repeatedly encountered models that are mathematically sound yet struggle to account for real-world behaviour, particularly in economic and social contexts. These moments have been formative. They have pushed me toward questions of robustness, interpretability, and how qualitative phenomena like values, constraints and institutional frictions can be meaningfully translated into quantitative frameworks. Whether working with clinical data, sustainability metrics, behavioural datasets, or operational systems, I find myself motivated by the challenge of designing methods that remain technically rigorous while staying grounded in context.

I have explored these ideas through a range of research-oriented and applied projects. In a supervised research project on multi-view learning for glioblastoma patients, I worked with incomplete clinical data to develop ensemble models for survival prediction. Beyond improving predictive performance, I focused on interpretability through explainable AI techniques, learning firsthand the importance of preprocessing choices, hypothesis-driven feature selection, and evaluation beyond headline metrics. Alongside this, I have worked on several applied data projects, including the development of a sector-agnostic ESG index for India’s top companies using large-scale sustainability disclosure data. Here, the central challenge was not simply handling high-dimensional data, but deciding how qualitative notions of environmental and social impact could be translated into defensible quantitative measures. These experiences collectively deepened my interest in research that sits at the intersection of data, decision-making, and real-world consequences.

This orientation is what draws me to the SURF program at Purdue. What appeals to me is not only the technical depth of the work being done, but the emphasis on mentored research in settings where models must operate under uncertainty, time constraints, and competing objectives. I am particularly interested in working with real or realistically simulated data to understand how decisions are made when resources are limited and trade-offs are unavoidable. Through SURF, I hope to strengthen my experience with data-driven modelling, optimization, and computational experimentation, while developing a deeper intuition for how modelling assumptions shape outcomes in practice.

Several SURF projects reflect the kinds of questions I find compelling, especially those focused on applied decision-making and resource allocation in complex systems. Reframing the problem through these insights led my team to propose a more targeted solution involving near-infrared (NIR) spectrometer-based technology for plastic differentiation at waste hubs. This experience reinforced a lesson that has stayed with me: meaningful research often begins with asking better questions, and technical solutions are most effective when they emerge from a deep understanding of context.

Entering a technically intensive program without a conventional science background has been challenging. Many concepts were unfamiliar at first, and I often found myself building foundational understanding alongside advanced coursework. Rather than discouraging me, this process taught me persistence, adaptability, and how to learn deliberately. Over time, it sharpened my ability to approach complex problems methodically and to engage with unfamiliar material without losing sight of the larger question at hand.

statement_of_purpose:
I fell in love with nonlinear dynamics in Summer ‘24. Those days were spent pouring over Strogatz’s textbook, and exploring the vast zoo of complexity science. It was a happy coincidence then that our college’s Mathematics club released applications for “Dynamix”, a year-long group project where I had lots of fun studying dynamical systems through the lens of category theory. The programming language Julia natively supports category theoretic formulations like Petri nets to solve high dimensional ODEs. Since building Petri nets is relatively easy, we were able to extend the usual SEIR model of infection to account for more complications, like vaccinations and location-based infections simply by drawing a larger Petri net and feeding it to Julia, which solved the resulting ODEs—a much simpler way of modelling complicated systems (such as voting prediction models!), as opposed to painstakingly writing down every one of the 20-30 differential equations.

Fast forward to the last day of my Nonlinear Dynamics course, Prof. Mahesh Panchagnula made an observation that really stuck with me: throughout history, mathematics has transformed one major domain at a time, first beginning with physics, then creeping into biology, and perhaps now the time has come for a revolution in the social sciences. Does there exist a mathematical formulation of society, one that is as solid as any equation of physics? Do we expect a simplistic answer, and would such an answer need a new kind of mathematics? Ignited by the possibilities, I approached him for a summer research project, and he promptly agreed to mentor me.

The project centered on a simple but powerful question: how can we effectively model the evolution of opinions in society? Though we noticed several compartmental models in the literature, we decided instead to represent society as a network of individuals, each holding a binary opinion, and studied how the dynamics changes as a function of topology, or how sensitive the system is to the addition of influencers to swing the majority, etc. This work pushed me beyond the traditional physics curriculum into areas like network science and computational social modeling. The professor often brought in many people such as social scientists, economists, and even physicists who had given this problem a fair deal of thought, and the conversations I had with them were genuinely exhilarating. We are now considering taking an experimental approach to the problem, and are very excited to see how that goes!
To complement my summer project, I wanted to explore agent-based modeling (ABMs) as a model of opinion evolution so I promptly completed Santa Fe Institute’s summer course on the same. Here we dived deep into NetLogo and its various features, and the final project was a variant of my actual summer project, where I earned a grade of 97%. Then when my semester began, I took up Complex Networks as part of my coursework due to its relevance to my project. But the summer project wasn’t my only experience in research.

Every year, as a prequel to the International Physicists’ Tournament, we have a national pre-selection round. The premise of this competition is as follows: work on an open physics problem for a month, detail your findings in a 5 page report, and fight your way through by fiercely debating with other teams. All those late nights spent staying up and coming up with original ideas through intense discussion and study brought us first place this year, and we are very excited to represent India at the international stage!

Despite these wins, my academic journey has not been without difficulty. During my first year, I faced serious setbacks such as unsuccessful club applications, periods of academic burnout, and uncertainty about my long-term career goals. While discouraging, these experiences forced me to reflect seriously on what I wanted from my education. With invaluable support from my family and friends, I came to realize that getting my hands dirty with real research could provide the focus and sense of purpose I had been missing. Taking the initiative to approach a professor for a research collaboration was hence a very decisive step forward. More importantly, I began to gain confidence in my ability to engage deeply with open-ended research problems. Prof. Panchagnula has since offered me a teaching assistantship for Nonlinear Dynamics, and I am quite looking forward to it!

The professor is an alumnus of Purdue University, which prompted me to explore the university’s programs and imagine myself following a similar path. I was delighted to learn that SURF 2026 offers a project I am genuinely enthusiastic about. Additionally, the close mentorship, opportunities to interact with a highly motivated peer group, and the structured financial support enables focused research, which is exactly what I need at this stage of my career. 

If selected, I look forward to enjoying many hours with my peers hypothesizing, analyzing and verifying our ideas. Not only will this be a fabulous opportunity to learn from them, it would also be a great way of building friendships and connections that could possibly last a lifetime. The experience strengthened my foundation in coupled heat transfer, fluid flow, and material response, and it made me excited about engineering problems where thermal behavior and reliability are critical. statement_of_purpose:
Growing up in India in a household of physicians, I knew the consequences of uncertainty in clinical decision-making. In ninth grade, the death of a close colleague of my mother due to postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) made this reality tangible. I was surprised by the fact that blood loss after delivery is still often estimated visually, despite the high stakes of delayed intervention. Motivated by this gap, I designed the PPH Cup, a modified menstrual cup with an integrated calibrated collection system to to measure postpartum blood loss in real-time. While working with a government medical college to develop and evaluate the device, I got to know about study design, safety testing, and data analysis. This experience shaped my interest in research-driven solutions to real life problems and motivated me to seek more scalable computational approaches.

At the University of Texas at Austin, I am pursuing a triple major in Computer Science (Turing Scholars Honors), Mathematics, and Computational Biology, and joined Professor David Soloveichik’s laboratory to work on problems in molecular programming. My research focuses on understanding how collections of simple molecular components can reliably assemble into stable structures, a question that is central both to natural biochemical systems and to the design of synthetic molecular programs.

In particular, I studied Thermodynamic Binding Networks (TBNs), a model in which the molecular building blocks (“monomers”) have complementary binding sites and form polymers through local interactions. A fundamental challenge in this setting is to characterize all the unsplittable polymers—stable assemblies that cannot be decomposed into smaller, independent substructures. Enumerating these polymers is necessary for predicting which molecular configurations are fundamentally stable and therefore likely to arise in practice.

This problem can be analogously presented in a mathematical form: monomers can be replaced by integer vectors encoding their binding sites, polymers as nonnegative combinations of these vectors, and irreducible polymers correspond to a well-studied algebraic object known as a Hilbert basis. While this correspondence gives a method to find the set of unsplittable polymers, it also has a computational bottleneck.The size of a Hilbert basis can grow unboundedly, and direct computation using existing tools such as Normaliz becomes infeasible even for moderately sized networks.

I tried to fix this bottleneck by exploiting a practical observation: in real systems, most unsplittable polymers involve only a subset of monomer types or binding sites. I developed algorithms that compute Hilbert bases over small subsets of monomers of size 'k'(or subsets of binding site types) and then aggregate the results. Each subset enumeration captures polymers containing at most k monomer types (or binding site types), drastically reducing computation time while still recovering the majority of relevant stable polymers. This approach introduces explicit trade-offs between completeness and efficiency and provides a practical way to explore large combinatorial spaces that would otherwise be prove difficult.

Through this project, I gained experience of working on open-ended theoretical problems, formalizing them, validating assumptions against practical behavior and utilizing heuristic approaches. I'm currently working on benchmarking these methods, understanding which classes of polymers are reliably recovered, and developing a more robust stopping criteria based on combinatorial constraints.

During the summer of 2025, I worked as an undergraduate researcher at the Icahn School of Medicine, studying the problem of detecting rare diseases from large collections of clinical notes using transformer-based language models. Rare diseases present a particularly difficult challenge: patient populations are extremely small, clinical text is noisy, and diagnostically relevant information is often distributed across long patient histories rather than concentrated in a single encounter.

I designed a data preparation pipeline to convert clinical notes into structured representations for training the model. Using the MIMIC-IV database, I identified patients diagnosed with rare diseases and aggregated all notes written prior to each patient’s first recorded diagnosis into a single longitudinal record. To address class imbalance and ensure well-matched controls, I paired each positive patient with control patients of similar age, gender, and race, and truncated their records to the same observation window. This setup encouraged the models to learn subtle pre-diagnostic patterns rather than relying on unrelated cues such as record length or post-diagnosis documentation.

I trained multiple transformer architectures, including various BERT-based models and sparse-attention models, using stratified k-fold cross-validation. To capture both local and global patterns in patient histories, I implemented a sliding-window approach that incrementally exposed the model to longer segments of each patient’s record. This strategy was effective even in data-scarce settings: across 31 rare diseases, with as few as 30–150 positive cases per disease, the models achieved an average AUC of approximately 0.85.

Beyond predictive performance, I also worked on the interpretability aspect. In medical applications, model predictions must be backed by clinical evidence. I developed an interpretation pipeline using attention analysis and feature attribution methods to identify which words or phrases most strongly influenced predictions, and tested these signals against known clinical characteristics. This analysis helped validate the model's predictions.

Through these experiences, I have come to view computer science not as an isolated discipline, but as a set of tools for solving complex problems across domains. This perspective is what motivates me to continue doing research..

I am particularly drawn to the SURF program because of its emphasis on close faculty mentorship, sustained engagement with open-ended research problems, and integration into an active research community. SURF’s structure aligns with the way I have learned best—by iterating on ideas over time, receiving critical feedback, and doing technical work within a broader context. Access to research seminars, peer cohorts, and dedicated mentorship would help improve my ability to frame research questions, evaluate assumptions, and communicate results effectively.

In the long term, I plan to pursue a PhD and a research career in STEM, where I can continue developing computational methods and apply them across scientifically demanding domains. The world is full of opportunities but you need to look for the opportunity that best suits you. Since my childhood, I harbored a deep fascination for rocket launches. I spend most of my leisure time watching YouTube videos on space-shuttles and rocket launches. Repetitively watching videos on launches, I noticed that space-shuttles rotated 180 degrees after take-off. This piqued my curiosity and upon delving deeper I found that it was meticulously choreographed to increase vehicle performance and save fuel. This realization sparked a question in my mind which soon became my research topic: how a rocket’s rotational velocity affects its maximum altitude. This research was not a walk in the park as I had faced a lot of challenges like lack of necessary materials, and many more. Overcoming these challenges, I marched towards completing the research. This research unraveled a new aspect of me to myself. I realized that various aspects of aerospace engineering are under-researched and await exploration. Therefore, I want to dive into this vastness of unexplored realm and explore various fascinating yet obscure concepts.

Eagle can pinpoint a moving snake on the ground from thousands of feet from the air. Similarly, I can pinpoint the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship program among all summer research opportunities. It is because the program’s goal aligns with my educational and career goal, which is to dive deeper into the unexplored realm of aerospace engineering to gain advanced knowledge of the field. Additionally, through SURF I would be able to work with advanced tools to conduct the research in aerospace engineering under the mentorship of experts. This would not only help me foster new connections, but will also help me explore the field from different perspectives and hone important skills like project and budget management, critical thinking and problem solving skills and many more. Also, unique opportunities of weekly professional development will help me grow professionally. Moreover, the opportunity to pitch my research at the student research symposium and produce the final report documenting my research outcomes would also help me grow personally and it will boost my confidence level and make me an independent learner. Upon completion of my undergraduate education, I intend to pursue graduate education and the above mentioned factors would make it easier for me to transition from my undergraduate to graduate education. Also, the research experience provided by SURF will help me succeed in both my undergraduate and graduate education.

Sri Ravi Shankar once said “Motivation is external and short lived. Inspiration is internal and lifelong.” Following this, I embarked on a journey to determine for myself whether research in the aerospace engineering field is my inspiration or motivation. My curious mind led me on my research journey where I set out to explore how a rocket's rotational velocity impacts its performance. Initiating my exploration, I had trouble finding information because the topic was under researched. I spent the whole night scavenging  scholastic journals, textbooks, YouTube videos and many more resources to extract information. I just kept gathering information in bits and pieces regarding the topic. I started to feel that I was not moving ahead in my research until a day arrived when an idea hit my mind which cleared all my confusion: I should find the relationship between rolling moment and drag. 

As I moved on to the experimentation phase, I ran into a big problem. Potassium Nitrate was not available in the chemistry lab, forcing us to use an alternative: sodium nitrate. I hammered the powdered fuel in the rocket motor, made an outlet and placed it on the stand, ready to be launched. I ignited the motor with the fuse along with my supervisor. My hopes shattered as I watched the stationary motor not propel. Returning back, my supervisor advised me to buy potassium nitrate. Upon chemical’s arrival, we commenced making the fuel and rocket motor once again. Postschool hours, we tried to launch the rocket but what we witnessed was just an ejection of gas and a fiery roar. Disheartened, we analyzed the cause behind the rocket's failure. One factor we hypothesized was the use of inadequate material. So we started investigating and found that it indeed was the reason. I progressed slowly as the trials and failures continued. Soon a day arrived when we were well prepared to launch a rocket using all the learning from setbacks and using critical elements like nozzle, perfect fuel ratio, fuel quantity, etc. Anxious, I held my breath as I ignited the fuel. Tears ran down my cheek as I saw my first success. However, due to factors like lack of control over rotational velocity, and lack of instrument to measure the rotational velocity, I had to refine my research question to how the number of fins affect the rocket’s maximum height. 

This experience made me realize that research is not merely a source of motivation for me, but a true inspiration that drives my willingness to contribute meaningfully to this fascinating domain. It sparked my curiosity about fuel chemistry and strengthened my desire to learn more about fuels, sustainability, and their broader impact. Through the SURF program, I hope to engage in interdisciplinary research that allows me to explore areas such as aerodynamics, design, and emerging technologies while applying them to real-world challenges. Working under the mentorship of faculty researchers, I aim to deepen my understanding of topics ranging from aerodynamic principles to hands-on skills such as computational analysis, prototyping, and 3D printing. This experience would also help me broaden my perspective on fuels, energy systems, and sustainability. Additionally, exposure to advanced research tools and collaborative environments would enable me to foster meaningful connections, refine my problem-solving approach, and develop essential research skills. My strong determination and eagerness to explore new ideas will prepare me to make the most of this opportunity and contribute effectively to ongoing research efforts.

It would be a great honor to be accepted into the highly prestigious SURF program. I am eager to build on my current skills and knowledge and explore the unexplored realm to achieve my career goal.

My interest in fluid mechanics began during the Fluid and Particle Mechanics course taught by Prof. Anki Reddy Katha. I still remember how Prof. Anki would show videos of simple yet fascinating experiments, one that particularly stood out demonstrated the no-slip condition at fluid-fluid interface, where dyes of different colors moved together at the same speed at the interface through the two immiscible liquids. Seeing such a simple concept appear so clearly in an experiment immediately drew me into the subject. Over time, I developed a deeper appreciation for the beauty of fluid mechanics problems and experiments, especially those involving complex fluids, porous media, and diffusive transport.
As part of the Fluid and Heat Transfer Laboratory course we demonstrated experiments to study the rheological behavior of fluids, including yield stress in clay suspensions, viscoelasticity in silly putty, and memory effects in elastic PVA polymer solutions. These experiments started my obsession with understanding the properties of non-Newtonian fluids.
I was selected for the highly competitive SRFP program as a summer research intern at Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) under the guidance of Prof. Ganesh Subramanian. My project involved deriving the governing equations for velocity fields inside and outside a neutrally buoyant drop in a second-order fluid, and I successfully obtained the particular solution. I formulated the leading-order Stokes flow using vector spherical harmonics and incorporated interfacial conditions and viscoelastic stress contributions through a perturbation expansion in the Deborah number. This amazing experience further fueled my interest in complex fluids.
I started working under Prof. Anki on modeling nanofiltration processes using the DSPM Reduced Order Model. I implemented the DSPM ROM algorithm in MATLAB, reproduced reported single-salt NaCl transport results, and extended the formulation and code to model multicomponent salt systems of NaCl and Na2SO4 mixtures. This work enhanced my understanding of coupled transport phenomena and numerical modeling.
Currently, I am working on an undergraduate research project involving COMSOL Multiphysics-based simulations of species transport between immiscible fluids in a wavy microchannel, with a comparative analysis against a rectangular channel. I am also investigating interfacial dynamics using the level-set method to better understand the role of interface deformation on mass transfer. This work familiarized me with microscale transport phenomena. 
Motivated by these experiences, I became interested in how fluid elasticity and microscale geometry influence flow and transport in biologically relevant systems. I seek to understand how viscoelastic stresses alter classical Stokes flows in complex biological fluids, and how interfacial deformation affects mass transfer in microfluidic environments that mimic physiological conditions. These questions lie at the intersection of fluid mechanics, transport phenomena, microfluidics, and biological systems, and form the foundation of the research direction I seek to pursue.
Thus, I am very interested in the opportunity to work on the research project “Microfluidic system for studying the transport of therapeutics.” To better understand this project, I reviewed literature on microfluidic drug screening platforms, including “Microfluidic Devices for Drug Delivery Systems and Drug Screening” and “Tumor-On-A-Chip Models for Predicting In Vivo Nanoparticle Behavior”. These studies showed how microfluidic systems enable controlled studies of transport processes and how results connect to real biological systems, further strengthening my interest in microfluidic approaches to biological transport.
Since my internship at JNCASR, I have closely followed the work of Prof. Arezoo Ardekani and studied several of her publications, including “Dynamics of Particle Migration in Channels of Viscoelastic Fluids” and “Perspectives on Viscoelastic Flow Instabilities and Elastic Turbulence”. In my ongoing semester, I am pursuing advanced coursework in Biological Fluid Mechanics and Bioprocess Engineering to further deepen my understanding of transport phenomena in biological systems.

The program’s emphasis on expert mentorship, professional development seminars, and research presentation at the SURF Symposium strongly attracts me, as these opportunities are not commonly available through other summer research programs. I am confident that the mentorship, skills, and research exposure gained through the SURF program will play a pivotal role in shaping my future career in complex fluid mechanics research.

As my work grew into AI and larger software systems, I started to feel the limits of staying purely at the abstraction layer – I could build models and the surrounding software infrastructure, but I lacked an intuitive sense of what the machine was actually doing underneath, and how low-level realities can quietly dominate system behavior. That curiosity pushed me toward the deeper question that still motivates me today: how do we design intelligent systems across layers, from learning algorithms down to architectures and physical devices?

Adding Electrical Engineering gave me the vocabulary to connect those layers. Through coursework and projects, I began to understand how digital signals become instructions, how microprocessors move and store data, and how integrated circuits and semiconductor devices ultimately shape performance and energy efficiency. What keeps me pursuing this intersection is the belief that the next leap in AI will come from co-design – better learning methods paired with better systems. I’m especially motivated by work that treats performance and reliability as system-level properties – linking modeling choices, evaluation discipline, and implementation constraints into one coherent stack.

SURF attracts me because it turns research into a practiced discipline rather than an aspiration. The 11-week, full-time structure – supported by the stipend and anchored by a final report and symposium presentation – creates focused time, clear milestones, and accountability to outcomes. Just as importantly, SURF pairs that structure with close mentorship from faculty, graduate students, and postdocs. This is exactly what I am looking for as I learn how strong R&D is conducted: scoping a question precisely, choosing a defensible methodology, validating results, and iterating when early attempts fall short. Purdue’s research ecosystem makes this especially compelling for my interests in AI and microelectronics: facilities like the Birck Nanotechnology Center for device and fabrication-related work, strong groups spanning design automation and systems, and campus-scale computation through RCAC for simulation and ML workloads.

Career-wise, I want to build a research-driven path at the intersection of AI and computing systems, while staying flexible in how I apply that lens – hardware-aware ML and efficient inference, reliable and reproducible ML workflows, and tools that accelerate engineering design, testing, and verification. In the near term, SURF would equip me with research readiness by giving me a scoped problem to own end-to-end and feedback from mentors who can shape how I frame questions and evaluate claims. After SURF, I want to carry that mindset into R&D-focused industry roles – ideally in teams at places like NVIDIA, Intel, or leading AI and semiconductor organizations – where research directly shapes real systems. Over time, my goal is to use those research and industry lessons to build a research-driven startup that develops practical tools or platforms at the AI-hardware boundary, advancing both the models and the machines that run them.

To explore this intersection so far, I have deliberately built experience across modeling, hands-on engineering, and applied ML systems. On the device side, I completed a FinFET simulation project using Synopsys TCAD (Sentaurus) on nanoHUB, running process and device simulations, extracting key metrics (threshold voltage, subthreshold swing, on/off current, DIBL), and using controlled parameter sweeps – such as metal work function and interface-trap density – to explain observed behavior with device-physics reasoning. I documented assumptions, ran systematic experiments, and verified that extracted trends matched expected mechanisms rather than treating the simulator as a black box.

Complementing modeling, I have circuit and system-building experience that strengthened my experimental instincts. In an optical heart-rate sensor project, I built the sensor using an IR LED and phototransistor, designed active filter stages to isolate the physiological band, and added a comparator with hysteresis to produce stable digital pulses from a noisy analog signal. In industry at Limitorque India, I commissioned and debugged an electric-actuator test bench by tracing circuits, resolving wiring and logic faults, calibrating sensors, and validating performance across repeated runs. Outside the classroom, I also pushed deeper into modern ML by implementing real-time vision (MobileSAM-based segmentation for track boundary detection in Autonomous Motorsports Purdue) and studying transformer internals. Following Andrej Karpathy’s Zero-to-Hero series, I implemented a small GPT-style transformer from scratch to understand the full training pipeline – tokenization, attention and feedforward blocks, causal masking, training dynamics, and sampling for text generation – which helped me reason about models as systems rather than only as API calls.

A formative challenge early in my time at Purdue also shaped how I approach complex technical work. In CS 180, my first programming course, the final team project was a large Java marketplace system with a shared codebase and tight deadlines. Late in the project, I mishandled a Git merge/conflict and accidentally overwrote my cart-system work close to the deadline. I rebuilt the feature by breaking it into testable pieces, spending the next two days in focused iterations, using office hours to debug blockers quickly, and learning to integrate cleanly with an existing architecture. Together, these experiences demonstrate my commitment and readiness for SURF: I can translate open-ended questions into testable experiments, build and evaluate prototypes across software and hardware, analyze results quantitatively, and communicate findings with rigor.

I am Suraj Dayma, a 3rd year Robotics and Autonomous Systems major at Plaksha University. Through this SOP I want to take you through my background, career aspirations, and why I am interested in the Purdue SURF program.

I come from an agrarian family belonging from a rural village, in Rajasthan, India where necessities like education, healthcare, telecomm, are all limited. My dad was fortunate enough to start working in Abu Dhabi, where I completed most of my schooling in a more diverse and inclusive environment. When I would visit my hometown, I would notice a lot of societal differences. The community there is very conservative. Education is seen as a fancy and not a necessity, and aspirations are limited. Women are seen as house makers, married off early, and denied education.

Seeing the women of my family go through this really disheartens me, and I personally believe that the only way to change societal beliefs is through education, and the development of technology.

Due to this strong belief, I knew I wanted to get into academia where I can teach and conduct research. I was attracted towards Plaksha University, which is a research based university with interdisciplinary programs. After multiple discussions with my professors, I felt that robotics has the most potential for impact, especially in fields like agriculture, where I have seen my family’s problems.

Growing crops in Rajasthan is very prone to erratic weather and crop diseases, and that is exactly the problem Prof Sunita’s research in precision agriculture aims to solve. I interned with her in the Low Altitude Remote Sensing (LARS) project which deploys a UAV-UGV ecosystem for early distress detection, forecasting, and intervention. I was responsible for the development of a UGV testbed. I built a ROS 2 and Gazebo digital twin, tuned ROS controllers, and deployed a full navigation stack including SLAM, localization, and path planning on a physical robot. The project has been taken over since and my work is being put on an All Terrain Vehicle (ATV) for field trials. 

In Northern India, practices such as stubble burning, industrial emissions, and traffic have resulted in extremely poor air quality. To study this phenomena and advocate for sustainable and smarter cities, I proposed to develop low-cost air quality monitoring nodes with the Dixon IoT Lab at my University. We have developed an end to end pipeline - from hardware design and firmware to backend databases, and have begun the geospatial data analysis from the nodes we have deployed. This project caught the eyes of the Chandigarh Citizens Foundation, for whom we created Tricity Watch - a platform for residents to view in depth air quality metrics beyond AQI, and understand the effects of gases and pollutants which we all inhale. 

Through these projects, I gained enough experience and skills to serve as a Student Tutor for the Mechatronics course with a class of 180+ students. I learnt a lot of patience and resilience in the process of taking labs and tutorials. Prof. Andy Runia, the instructor of the course also taught me how to gauge students’ abilities and navigate the teaching side of academia.

After thoroughly enjoying the System Dynamics and Control course - in which I was the first person to earn an A+ grade in the course history - my interests began shifting toward the theoretical foundations of control and system stability. Motivated by this, I undertook a research project with Mr. Suraj Kumar at UR Rao Satellite Centre, Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO), focusing on optimal control using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). In this project, I worked on solving infinite-horizon optimal control problems, trying different neural network architectures, and conducting a hyperparameter study. The controllers we designed for systems like the inverted pendulum were able to converge from the entire state space, including states the controller was not trained on. We are currently preparing a manuscript for the European Control Conference, and Conference on Decision and Control.

This project involved a lot of control theory, system dynamics, optimization, and knowledge of neural networks. I found it challenging to even understand the project initially, but through reading papers, I gained context. Through reading textbooks and talking to peers and mentors, I understood topics like trajectory optimization, MPC, HJB PDE defined value functions, and was able to formulate the research problem. I also found that going back to the basics and building up to a concept helped, not only in understanding it, but also in proposing new hypotheses. This experience gave me confidence in myself and the ability to “figure it out”.

Purdue University strongly appeals to me due to its longstanding excellence in robotics and engineering, as well as its culture of undergraduate research. In particular, research groups such as the Terrain Robotics Advanced Control and Experimentation (TRACE) Lab whose work in modeling, estimation, control, and locomotion are areas I have been introduced to in coursework and would like to pursue in my research. 

The research at the Mechanisms And Robotic Systems (MARS) Lab experiments with mechanism designs and robot types for all applications from maritime to agriculture. This gives them great insights in robot design and learning. Being involved in a project at MARS would be extremely valuable to me. 

The Multi-Agent Intelligent Networks (MAIN) lab works at the intersection of the two, experimenting with networks, optimization, learning and control. It provides an opportunity to integrate theory with actual robotic systems and also explore networks and computing in the context of robotics.

I have reviewed these labs’ works in venues like ACC, CDC, TRO, and INFOCOM and through my undergraduate training in robotics and research experience believe I can contribute meaningfully to their research by designing parts, modelling systems, calibrating sensors, implementing controllers, writing software, collecting data, training models, validating policies, and anything in between. The Purdue SURF program provides me the opportunity to do so.

Through SURF, I hope to contribute to cutting-edge research while developing as an independent researcher and take meaningful steps toward my long-term goal of pursuing a PhD and contributing to academia through impactful research and teaching. I would be honored to be part of the program.

Sincerely,
Suraj Dayma

I have been drawn to robotics by a curiosity about how complex autonomous behavior emerges from relatively simple ideas in control, perception, and decision-making. When I joined my university, this curiosity deepened as I moved across different subdomains of robotics and began to see that reliable autonomy is rarely the product of a single component working in isolation. Instead, it depends on how control algorithms, planning strategies, and learning-based perception interact with one another. My own work on the problems of safe navigation, planning by optimization and generalization by learning has exposed me to this interplay and has fueled my interest across autonomy. What excites me today is the problem of how to make robotic systems robust in the presence of uncertainty—limited communication, sensing or environments—and how control, optimization and learning can all come together for this.

A significant part of my research experience was gained during my internship at CINT Lab, Department of Aerospace Engineering, IISc Bengaluru, under the supervision of Dr. S. N. Omkar.  I worked on control and safe navigation for a transmitter-controlled UAV, where the central challenge was ensuring reliable behavior when the system was operated by untrained users. Designing an artificial potential field–based obstacle avoidance framework required me to think carefully about how control actions should adapt as proximity constraints changed, rather than relying on fixed responses. I implemented and validated the controller in a ROS-based simulation environment, which helped me build a practical understanding of concepts such as gain tuning, stability, and PID-based velocity regulation before moving to hardware. This simulation-based approach allowed a systematic study of behaviors and failure modes. Porting the algorithm to a hardware platform with an off-the-shelf flight-control software stack later expanded my horizons to practical issues like sensor noise, sampling delays, and real-time requirements. This taught me to think less about controllers in isolation and more about controller behavior in the context of autonomous systems, and it solidified my interest in these areas of work in fields exhibiting multi-agent coordinated behaviors.

After my UAV work, I faced a setback when my application to a summer research program that aligned with my areas of interest was rejected. After speaking to Dr. Omkar, I opted to work on a planning problem based on optimization to acquire the required analytical and computational skills for autonomous decision making. I proposed a new approach to the combinatorial routing problem by constructing a discrete adaptation of a metaheuristic for continuous optimization. The problem entailed reasoning about resource constraints and instance-specific variations. By incorporating spatial clustering and local search, I overcame scalability and convergence challenges to obtain stable results across standard benchmark datasets. This resulted in a first-author IEEE conference paper. Beyond the explicit outcome of this project, it also allowed me to become proficient at formulating constrained optimization problems, knowing how to balance efficiency and feasibility, and handling research decisions independently—all skills that can be applied to temporal planning and resource allocation challenges.

While continuing to pursue robotics-related research, I became increasingly aware of a limitation at my home institution: the absence of a sustained robotics research culture and limited access to long-term mentorship in autonomous systems. To address this gap in my training, I began to pursue the additional skills that are now regarded as a staple in the field of learning-based perception in robotics research. I have also completed the Modern Robotics specialization from Northwestern University, including a capstone project focused on mobile manipulation, and I want to further investigate manipulation in extreme environments where kinematic reasoning, grasp stability, and contact interactions take precedence over sensing and calibration. In sum, this program will enable me to best hone my ability to apply concepts to practice.

I see SURF as an opportunity to frame my work and interests in a world-class robotics research environment and to understand what it means to do research in a setting like Purdue. Exposure to a vibrant robotics research community shaped by faculty, laboratories, and a strong collaborative culture would allow me to directly observe how high-quality research is conducted, refined, and shared.
