statement_of_purpose:
The evolution of my research interests has been driven not by a single moment of inspiration, but by a recurring pattern of technical dissatisfaction. I was initially captivated by the elegance of classical Control Theory. It promised safety, stability and optimality, a mathematical guarantee that if we modeled the world correctly, our systems would behave perfectly. My first significant research endeavor at the Walmart Center of Tech Excellence was an exercise in this belief. I built complex optimization algorithms for hybrid energy grids, generating solutions that were theoretically “Pareto-optimal”. Yet, I watched these perfect solutions crumble the moment real-world stochasticity, fluctuating demand and extreme weather unpredictability, entered the equation. This was my first realization that optimality without robustness is fundamentally brittle.

This pushed me away from deterministic engineering and toward probabilistic modeling. I began to see uncertainty not as an error term to be minimized, but as a fundamental property of the world that must be modeled explicitly. I implemented Gaussian Mixture Models to quantify risk in energy grids, shifting my focus to identifying latent structure in noisy data as a prerequisite for reliable decision-making. However, even this felt incomplete. While I could model uncertainty in data, I lacked the tools to enable an autonomous agent to perceive and react to it in real-time. This intellectual gap drove me to the intersection of Robotics and Machine Learning, a convergence that felt necessary rather than optional. I realized that to build truly autonomous systems, we cannot just control them; we must enable them to learn.

Today, the question that drives my work is the tension between the flexibility of modern AI and the safety guarantees of classical control. We have data-driven models that can reason semantically about the world but have no concept of physics, and we have control systems that execute motion perfectly but struggle with unstructured environments. I am deeply troubled by the “black-box” nature of current learning-based approaches. How can we deploy a system in safety-critical environments, whether a robot in a crowd or a climate model informing policy, if we cannot interpret its internal states? This problem shapes my research trajectory: I want to develop algorithms that fuse the adaptability of data-driven methods with the physical inductive biases of control theory. I am not interested in building models that work most of the time; I am interested in autonomy whose behavior can be bounded, interpreted and trusted.

It is this specific focus on rigorous, fundamental research that draws me to the Purdue SURF program. I am not looking for a generic internship where I simply implement existing code. I am drawn to Purdue because its engineering culture is famously grounded in the collision of theory and reality. The opportunity to work in labs that possess both world-class theoretical expertise in dynamical systems and heavy experimental testbeds is critical for my growth. SURF’s structure, which emphasizes direct mentorship and the communication of scientific results, offers the environment I need to transition from a student who completes projects to a researcher who contributes new knowledge. I view SURF not as a credential, but as a proving ground where my ideas will be challenged, tested and refined through close mentorship.

My preparation for this research has been an aggressive pursuit of the full stack of intelligent systems. When I founded the Aerial Robotics team (SUAS) at IIT Madras to compete internationally, I confronted the harsh reality of hardware constraints. We needed to detect small payload markers from 65 feet in the air, but we had absolutely no training data. The easy path would have been to pivot to a simpler problem. Instead, I treated this as a research constraint. I taught myself to use physics engines like Blender and AirSim to procedurally generate photorealistic synthetic data, solving a real-world perception problem by embedding physical constraints directly into the data-generation process. This experience taught me that valid research often requires building your own tools to bridge the sim-to-real gap.

Simultaneously, I have sought to deepen my theoretical understanding through independent study. I have developed Risk-Aware Model Predictive Control (MPC) for UAVs extending from a journal paper, forcing myself to derive state-space constraints and cost functions from scratch rather than using off-the-shelf solvers. My recent internship at the National University of Singapore further expanded my horizon, where I developed high-level planners for Embodied AI agents. Working there, I learned that even the most advanced AI can fail if it isn't grounded in the physical reality of the robot, a failure mode I addressed by engineering a “Dynamic Overlay” system to estimate the robot’s world state in real-time.

My path has not been without failure. Leading the SUAS team, I initially underestimated the difficulty of integrating vision with control in a distributed system. Our early flight tests failed spectacularly because our vision latency was too high for the control loop. This failure forced me to stop coding and start analyzing system dynamics. I had to learn about latency compensation and interface design, moving beyond my silo of computer vision to understand the entire robotic system. This obstacle fundamentally changed how I approach research: I no longer view subsystems in isolation. I learned that in complex systems, whether swarms of robots or coupled climate models, the most consequential failures and insights emerge at the interfaces between components.

Looking forward, my long-term vision is to pursue a PhD and eventually lead a research lab dedicated to the Physics-informed learning of Adaptive Systems. I want to spend my career working on the hard problems of safety, reliability, and explainability in AI. I envision a future where systems are verifiable, where we can trust a robot not because we trained it on a trillion images, but because its behavior is bounded by provable constraints.

From SURF, I seek the rigorous mentorship and experimental exposure that will sharpen this trajectory. I want to learn the disciplined habits of high-level research: how to ask the right questions, how to design experiments that isolate variables, and how to persist when real-world data contradicts the hypothesis. I am ready to engage in the iterative, failure-driven process of research and contribute meaningfully to the frontier of knowledge, and I believe Purdue is the right place to begin that work.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in Machine Learning developed through exposure to the mathematical analysis of learning algorithms, particularly stochastic approximation and reinforcement learning. While taking advanced courses in reinforcement learning and optimization, I became interested in how convergence, stability, and performance guarantees are established for iterative learning algorithms operating under noise and approximation.

A concrete research question that has motivated my recent work is: can policy optimization and alignment algorithms be designed to explicitly account for uncertainty in feedback and provide guarantees on robustness or performance degradation? While studying LLM alignment pipelines, I observed that even small misspecifications or noise in reward or preference models can cause significant policy degradation. Existing uncertainty-aware methods often rely on heuristic reward shaping and offer limited theoretical control. This motivated my work on uncertainty-aware alignment, where we developed a policy optimization framework that provably reduces the probability of policy degradation and empirically validates the predicted robustness improvements.

More broadly, I am interested in understanding how noise, optimization, and sampling interact in learning algorithms. Perspectives such as the Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto variational formulation of Langevin dynamics have strongly influenced my thinking, as they reveal that algorithms often treated heuristically are approximating well-defined gradient flows on spaces of probability measures. This viewpoint motivates my interest in studying learning algorithms as stochastic dynamical systems with underlying geometric and variational structure, rather than as black-box optimization routines. This question continues to shape my research direction toward developing learning algorithms with explicit robustness and stability guarantees.

I am drawn to the Purdue SURF program because of its emphasis on mentored, project-driven research embedded within engineering and scientific applications. SURF offers a structured environment where theoretical modeling, algorithmic design, and empirical validation are tightly integrated. This aligns well with my goal of developing learning methods that are both theoretically grounded and applicable to structurally constrained systems. Participation in SURF would allow me to refine my ability to formulate research questions, develop principled models, and collaborate closely with faculty on focused research problems.

My long-term goal is to pursue a PhD and an academic research career in Machine Learning, with an emphasis on reliable learning for decision-making and control. I am particularly interested in reinforcement learning, stochastic optimization, and generative models, studied through their stochastic dynamics and stability properties. SURF would serve as a critical step toward this goal by strengthening my research foundations, exposing me to new application domains, and sharpening my ability to translate theory into practice. In particular, SURF’s close faculty mentorship and structured research setting provide strong support for engaging in focused, theory-driven research with applications.

To explore my field of interest, I have pursued both rigorous coursework and sustained research collaborations. I have completed advanced courses in measure-theoretic probability, stochastic calculus, concentration inequalities, stochastic approximation, bandits, optimization, reinforcement learning, nonlinear systems and generative models. In my sophomore year, I worked with Prof. Aditya Gopalan on provable uncertainty-aware alignment for reinforcement learning from human feedback, motivated by the observation that learned policies can be highly sensitive to noise and misspecification in reward or preference models. We developed a policy optimization framework (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.15906) that explicitly incorporates uncertainty into the learning objective and provides formal guarantees on robustness, provably reducing the probability of policy degradation relative to standard alignment methods. I subsequently worked with Prof. Gugan Thoppe and Prof. Aditya Gopalan on policy iteration under function approximation. We studied the Reliable Policy Iteration (RPI) framework, designed to restore the monotonic improvement guarantees of classical policy iteration in settings with function approximation. My contributions focused on implementing and benchmarking RPI in modern deep reinforcement learning agents and empirically validating its monotonic value improvement and critic lower-bound guarantees; this work has been accepted at ICC 2025 (https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12088v1). In parallel, I explored learning problems in computer vision, including feed-forward deblurring for 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the limitation that existing approaches are largely per-scene and unsuitable for real-time, scene-agnostic deployment. I am also currently working on the finite-time analysis of multi-timescale stochastic approximation, aimed at understanding convergence and stability in hierarchical learning systems, as well as on gradient-flow analysis on the space of graphons, motivated by studying optimization and sampling algorithms in infinite-dimensional settings.

One challenge I faced was that many of the problems I became interested in required mathematical tools beyond the standard undergraduate curriculum. Questions involving non-asymptotic guarantees, stability of learning dynamics, and robustness under uncertainty required deeper exposure to probability theory, stochastic calculus, and dynamical systems. I addressed this by independently studying these topics, taking advanced electives, participating in reading groups, and seeking regular guidance from faculty mentors. While the learning curve was steep, this process significantly strengthened my mathematical maturity and research readiness, and it is reflected both in my academic performance and in my ability to engage with technically demanding research problems.

I am interested in the project Probing Transitions in Motor Learning via Physics-Informed State-Space Models, as it aligns with my interest in generative models and control theory, and with my coursework in nonlinear systems and control and generative modeling. In particular, the project’s emphasis on Bayesian inference, switching latent dynamical systems, and structured state-space models for identifying regime transitions closely matches my interest in modeling learning as an evolving dynamical system under explicit constraints. I am also interested in the project on physics-informed machine learning for extreme weather predictability, which focuses on integrating physical structure into data-driven models for climate dynamics. I am particularly interested in understanding the nonlinear structure learned by convolutional neural networks in this setting, and in evaluating how these learned representations compare with sophisticated climate models in detecting and anticipating extreme weather events in idealized atmospheric systems. Finally, I am particularly interested in the project Generative AI for the Discovery of New Drugs, which investigates equivariant 3D conditional diffusion models and generative flow networks for structured molecular design. The focus on guided generative modeling under geometric and physical constraints aligns closely with my interest in diffusion-based generative models and in understanding sampling and optimization through stochastic and variational perspectives.

Through SURF, I aim to further develop my ability to conduct theory-driven research while engaging with applied problem settings. The program’s structure and mentorship would help me consolidate my research direction and prepare for doctoral training in Machine Learning, potentially at institutions such as Purdue.

statement_of_purpose:
MOTIVATION AND FIELD OF STUDY

Looking at the power-law distributions and scaling patterns in my coral fluorescence data, I started thinking about how similar patterns appear in completely different physical systems. In Professor Dahmen's group, I'm using statistical physics frameworks—power spectrum analysis, mean-field avalanche models, and critical exponents—to analyze collective behavior in coral ecosystems. What fascinates me is how these same mathematical tools can describe phase transitions in materials, earthquake dynamics, or biological systems. This universality of statistical physics across different scales and systems is what draws me to computational materials science.

My quantum physics course introduced me to superposition, entanglement, and the Schrödinger equation, but it also raised bigger questions: how do we actually use quantum mechanics to predict real material properties? When I learned that computational methods exist to calculate material behavior from first principles—without needing to synthesize anything in a lab first—I was genuinely excited. Professor Zeng's project on modeling catalyst-support interactions represents exactly this approach: using quantum calculations to understand how electrons behave at metal-support interfaces, which determines catalyst efficiency. Since catalysts are crucial for clean energy and industrial chemistry, being able to predict their properties computationally could accelerate their development.

I'm also drawn to Professor Zhu's epitaxial growth project because it connects to my statistical physics background. Growth processes are inherently non-equilibrium—local atomic interactions produce larger-scale structural patterns. Understanding how microscopic deposition processes determine final material properties is the kind of connection between scales I find fascinating.

WHY SURF AND CAREER GOALS

I'm attracted to SURF because it offers hands-on experience with computational materials science methods I haven't accessed yet at UIUC. While I have strong foundations in statistical physics and Python programming, I want to learn quantum chemistry software and density functional theory approaches. Many summer programs offer general lab work, but SURF's focus on substantive computational projects means I'd actually learn these tools while contributing to real research.

The professional development aspects also appeal to me—learning to present research effectively and network with other computational scientists would prepare me for graduate school. The connections with Purdue faculty and other students could lead to future collaborations.

Long-term, I want to get a PhD and then become a professor with my own research group working on computational physics. I'm interested in using computational methods to understand materials—especially problems where you need both quantum mechanics and statistical physics. SURF would help me learn the computational quantum methods I'll need for graduate school.

CONTRIBUTION TO CAREER GOALS

SURF would provide specific skills I need. First, I'd learn quantum chemistry computational tools like DFT software. I'm experienced with Python, NumPy, and SciPy for statistical analysis, but I haven't used quantum chemistry packages. Learning how to set up these calculations, choose appropriate parameters, and extract meaningful results requires mentorship from experienced researchers—it's not something I can easily learn from textbooks alone.

Second, I'd gain experience modeling actual material systems. Understanding how to analyze electronic structure, interpret quantum mechanical calculations, and connect results to physical behavior would be directly applicable to graduate research. These practical skills—knowing what works, what fails, and why—come from hands-on experience.

Third, I'd build connections in the computational materials science community. Meeting other students doing quantum modeling, discussing computational challenges, and learning from Purdue faculty would integrate me into this field before graduate school. Many research collaborations start from relationships built during summer programs.

PREPARATION AND EXPLORATION

I've built relevant foundations through coursework and research. My physics courses—Quantum Physics, Thermal Physics, Electromagnetism, and Relativity & Math Applications—provide theoretical background. Abstract Linear Algebra (MATH 416) taught me eigenvalue problems and linear operators fundamental to quantum mechanics. Differential Equations and Statistics & Probability give me mathematical tools for quantum problems and stochastic processes.

My current research in the Dahmen Group has taught me computational modeling skills. I implement mean-field avalanche models and analyze critical exponents using Python with NumPy and SciPy. I've learned to debug numerical code, validate results, and extract physical insights from data. While I'm working on biological systems, the computational approach transfers—both require implementing physical models, processing noisy data, and finding meaningful patterns.

In Data Structures (CS 225), I learned algorithmic complexity and efficient design. Understanding algorithm scaling shapes my scientific computing approach. As a CS 124 Course Assistant, I regularly debug code and explain algorithms, reinforcing computational thinking.

As Project Manager of Atlas Conversational AI, I built a real estate voice assistant achieving sub-200ms response latency using Pipecat, OpenAI, Deepgram for speech-to-text, and ElevenLabs for text-to-speech. I implemented a 4-path routing engine that handles automated answers, escalations, and Fair Housing-compliant declines, with full transcript logging in MongoDB. Building this required understanding how data structures scale, implementing efficient real-time processing, and managing WebSocket connections—skills that translate directly to scientific computing where you need to process large datasets efficiently.

Earlier research gave me experimental perspective. At Allegheny College, I used electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy to study superconductors. At Karma TMS, I analyzed electromagnetic induction in medical devices. These experiences taught me experimental techniques and scientific communication (both published).

CHALLENGES AND GROWTH

My main challenge is that I don't really know quantum chemistry yet. I understand quantum mechanics from my PHYS 214 course, but that's very different from actually using it to calculate material properties. I'm very enthusiastic to learn about DFT by reading papers and asking questions and I am extremely excited to attain hands-on experience with actual software and guidance from someone who does this regularly. That's why SURF would be really valuable.

Another challenge is that I'm interested in a lot of different things—statistical physics, quantum mechanics, computer science—and sometimes it's hard to know what to focus on. I've been trying to think about how they all connect rather than treating them as separate fields, but I'm still figuring out exactly what direction I want to go.

CONCLUSION

SURF represents the ideal opportunity to learn quantum chemistry methods essential for my goals. Professor Zeng's catalyst project would let me apply my quantum mechanics knowledge and programming skills to technologically important problems while learning DFT approaches I'll need in graduate school. Professor Zhu's epitaxial growth project would connect my statistical physics background to materials science questions about non-equilibrium processes. Either project would provide the mentorship, technical skills, and research connections I need to pursue computational physics at the intersection of quantum mechanics, statistical physics, and materials science.

statement_of_purpose:
My academic journey has been shaped by a recurring question: how can intelligent systems infer reliable structure from noisy, incomplete, and constrained data when deployed in real world settings? I have encountered this question across domains including robotic perception, biomedical signal processing, and AI hardware design. Over time, I came to recognize these efforts not as disconnected interests, but as different instances of a shared challenge. Learning systems must operate under physical, statistical, and computational constraints, and meaningful inference depends on how well these constraints are understood and incorporated into models.
This perspective has both personal and academic roots. Growing up, I was exposed to two complementary views of computing. My mother works on the algorithmic side of machine learning, developing data driven models, while my father works closer to the hardware layer on FPGA based systems. Observing both perspectives shaped my understanding that progress in AI does not arise from models alone. Instead, it emerges from the interaction between algorithms, numerical representations, and the systems that execute them. This realization motivated my decision to pursue Electrical and Electronics Engineering and to focus my research at the intersection of machine learning, systems, and physical modeling.
When choosing my undergraduate path at IIT Indore, I did not view Electrical Engineering as an alternative to Computer Science. I saw it as a way to approach machine learning from first principles. The curriculum provided rigorous training in linear algebra, probability theory, optimization, and signal processing, which form the mathematical backbone of modern learning algorithms. Courses in signals and systems and stochastic processes trained me to reason carefully about noise, uncertainty, and stability before I encountered neural networks. I came to view learning models not merely as software abstractions, but as mathematical systems operating under numerical and statistical constraints. I also realized early that components such as loss functions cannot simply be implemented; they must be understood, analyzed, and validated in terms of optimization dynamics.
My first concrete exposure to constrained inference came through ZEUS 6D, an independent research project in robotic perception. I aimed to design a training free, zero shot 6D object pose estimation pipeline. A significant obstacle I encountered was that standard geometric descriptors failed in the presence of object symmetries, leading to pose ambiguity. To overcome this, I developed a Symmetry Aware Refinement stage that fused semantic features with geometric descriptors. Implementing the full pipeline in Rust and optimizing it using INT8 quantization required careful reasoning about numerical stability and efficiency. While the application focused on robotic manipulation, the deeper lesson was about extracting geometric structure from uncertainty using principled constraints rather than relying on brute force learning.
As my coursework and research progressed at the NanoScale Devices, VLSI Circuits and Systems Lab at IIT Indore, this interest expanded into hardware algorithm co design. Under the guidance of Prof. Santosh Kumar Vishwakarma, I contributed to XR NPE, a mixed precision SIMD neural processing engine accepted at IEEE VLSID 2026. My primary contribution was the design of Reconfigurable Mantissa Multiplication and Exponent Circuitry, which enabled efficient support for low precision formats such as FP4 and Posit while significantly reducing area and power. This experience taught me that numerical precision is not a secondary implementation detail, but a modeling choice that directly influences learning behavior and error propagation.
Building on this experience, I am currently working on SPHURTI, a Posit 8 RISC V spatial AI accelerator designed for deterministic, ultra low latency inference. I designed a 32 by 32 coarse grained reconfigurable array and contributed to the full stack workflow, including quantization aware execution, widened accumulators, compile time scheduling, and RISC V controller integration. With a 28 nm ASIC tape out ongoing and an IEEE ISSCC 2027 submission in preparation, this project has provided my most complete exposure to end to end hardware software co design.
Alongside hardware research, I pursued theoretical robustness under Prof. M. Tanveer through the development of Copula Calibrated Cross Entropy (C3E), a noise robust loss function targeted for ICML 2026. Standard cross entropy assumes independent noise, which became a limitation when dealing with datasets containing structured, collective noise patterns. To address this limitation, I modeled batch level collective hardness using a copula inspired statistic to modulate gradient influence. My work focused on the mathematical formulation and optimization dynamics of the loss, strengthening my grounding in robust risk minimization and statistical learning.
I applied these robustness principles to a safety critical setting through my work on a machine learning enabled implantable pacemaker system on chip, with a manuscript in preparation for IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Circuits and Systems. Collaborating with PhD researchers, I designed a signal aware arrhythmia detection pipeline operating under strict power, latency, and reliability constraints. This experience reinforced my belief that statistical stability and interpretability are essential in life critical systems.
I was encouraged to apply to Purdue SURF by my graduate advisor, Mr. Mukul Vishnu Lokhande, who recognized that my research trajectory would benefit from an environment centered on inquiry. While IIT Indore has provided me with a strong theoretical foundation, Purdue SURF offers a unique ecosystem for translational research. The opportunity to work within Purdue’s world-class engineering infrastructure, alongside mentors who bridge the gap between theory and physical implementation, is the ideal environment to refine my research methodology.
I have identified three SURF projects that strongly align with my background. Prof. Krishna Jayant’s project on physics informed state space modeling resonates with my work on sequential robustness and constrained dynamical systems. Prof. Qi Guo’s research on next generation imaging closely parallels my experience in geometric perception and uncertainty aware reconstruction. In addition, the generative AI for drug discovery project under Prof. Arezoo Ardekani offers an opportunity to extend my understanding of probabilistic generative models to domains governed by strict physical constraints.
Looking ahead, I intend to pursue a PhD focused on the intersection of machine learning and hardware systems. I seek to broaden and deepen my understanding of statistical learning, particularly in areas connected to computer vision and reinforcement learning. I am motivated by mathematically grounded approaches to perception and decision making, including robustness, geometry aware learning, and optimization dynamics. I see SURF as an essential step in this process, allowing me to internalize research practice and grow through close mentorship and collaborative inquiry.

From the moment I first watched rockets and spacecraft streak across a screen, I knew I wanted to be part of that kind of work. Growing up in India, seeing the achievements of ISRO and later the revolutionary progress of organizations like SpaceX and NASA shaped a childhood dream into a purposeful career choice: I chose Aerospace Engineering at India’s top university, IITB, to become an aeronautical scientist. That early spark — part childhood idolization (yes, Iron Man played a role), part curiosity about our place in the universe — has matured into a committed, methodical interest in how vehicles move, sense, decide, and safely operate in challenging environments.

My core intellectual curiosity sits at the intersection of control theory, experimental engineering, machine learning, and computational fluid dynamics. Two research questions drive me today. First: how far can modern machine learning — especially reinforcement learning — be pushed to design reliable, certifiable control algorithms for autonomous aircraft? Second: how do we design experiments and diagnostics that reliably translate simulation improvements into measurable, repeatable, real-world gains (whether for thrusters, biorobotics, or multi-robot systems)? These questions motivate my ongoing pursuit of rigorous, experimentally grounded research rather than incremental implementation.

Purdue’s SURF program excites me because it explicitly supports the three research phases I value: formal analysis, reproducible simulation validation, and laboratory/hardware demonstration. The program’s mentorship model, collaborative environment, and access to specialized labs map directly to the way I want to learn and contribute. Facilities such as the Autonomous & Intelligent Multi-agent Systems (AIMS) Lab, the Autonomy and Control groups, Zucrow Propulsion Laboratory, and the Hypersonics and Applied Research Facility (HARF) are experiences that are difficult to access elsewhere. Working around/in those labs would let me learn domain-specific tools and safe experimental procedures — for example, OpenFOAM and topology-optimization workflows for aerodynamics, plasma diagnostics and high-voltage safety for thruster work, and ROS-based multi-robot testbeds for coordination research — and would accelerate my transition from competent systems engineer to independent researcher.

My near-term goal with SURF is to sharpen the fundamentals of good research: defining rigorous problem statements, producing reproducible simulation studies, instrumenting experiments to collect meaningful data, and learning to present reproducible results. In the long term I aim to pursue a Ph.D. focused on autonomous aerospace and robotic systems, followed by a career in academic or industrial R&D working on robust autonomy, controls, and deployable multi-robot solutions for challenging domains (maritime, planetary, and contested environments). I believe the mentorship and the network I would gain through SURF — working alongside faculty, graduate students, and dedicated technical staff — will be instrumental in reaching those goals.

To prepare for this path I have combined coursework, independent projects, and laboratory experiences. Relevant course work I have completed or am pursuing includes Statistical Machine Learning and Data Mining; Computational Fluid Dynamics; Robotics; Adaptive Control Theory; Optimization; Intelligent Feedback and Control; Aerospace Propulsion and Thermodynamics; Propulsion Laboratory; and Control of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems. Practically, I have built and validated simulation stacks (ROS/Gazebo), implemented Pixhawk-based flight-control integrations, performed SLAM and autonomous navigation experiments, and used tools such as OpenVSP to design aircraft geometries and Python & MATLAB/SIMULINK for analysis and prototyping. I am actively learning robotics-toolbox-python and expanding my numerical skills through project-focused practice.

My hands-on projects reflect both breadth and depth. At CSIR–National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL), within the Flight Mechanics and Controls division, I contributed to building an industry-standard helicopter simulator under Sr. Scientist Dr. Omkar Halbe. That work resulted in a research paper at the Vertical Flight Society’s Asian Rotocraft Forum 2025; our submission emphasized a modular Python architecture, variable-fidelity aerodynamic models, and code optimization using Cython for real-time helicopter simulation (SILS). At DRDO-DRDL’s hypersonic missile division (HCMD), I modeled and simulated 6-DoF trajectories for a hypersonic glide vehicle and experimented with trajectory control and guidance laws under practical constraints. I have also worked on a CubeSat propulsion prototype that used water electrolysis to generate the propellant (HHO gas); the project required careful experiment design, instrumentation, parametric testing, and many iterations to manage issues such as fuel slosh, valve systems and gas production rate. More recently, a team and I developed an amphibious quadcopter prototype, where building the Gazebo simulation demanded understanding hydrodynamics reported in the literature; for that project we tuned the PID controllers in Ardupilot and learned valuable lessons about bridging simulation and hardware.

Beyond technical work, I have taken leadership roles that improved my communication, documentation, and project-management abilities. I have led technical teams (The Humanoid Project team at IIT Bombay), represented student cohorts, and helped translate complex technical work into clear progress updates and reproducible reports — skills that matter immensely in collaborative, experimental research. I am also one of the founding members of a venture, Atmospheric Flight Technologies Pvt. Ltd., which grew out of continued development on simulator work started at NAL; I remain engaged part-time with the GNC team while continuing my undergraduate studies.

My path has not been free of obstacles. Limited access to specialized labs early on meant validating ideas in simulation and building low-cost but well-instrumented rigs before proposing higher-risk experiments. The CubeSat propulsion project involved many failed configurations and tedious parametric studies (e.g., testing various electrolysis arrangements and methods to reduce slosh), and overcoming those required systematic experimentation, careful mentorship, and persistence. When I face steep learning curves I seek guidance from professors and graduate students who are working in those domains and attack the problem by clarifying the problem statement until I can explain it simply and precisely, even when half asleep. These habits — methodical validation, a safety-first experimental mindset, and the willingness to iterate after failure — have strengthened my research readiness.

I am confident that SURF’s emphasis on mentorship, reproducible experiments, and multi-phase research projects is an ideal match for my experience and goals. If given the opportunity, I will contribute my background in controls, simulation, fluid dynamics, experiment design, and team leadership while learning advanced experimental and computational techniques available at Purdue. I am eager to collaborate with faculty and graduate students, to learn the lab workflows and safety protocols essential to high-quality experimental research, and to turn simulation ideas into measured, reproducible advances.
Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the possibility of contributing to and learning from Purdue’s research community.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in working at the intersection of machine learning, evaluation, and software engineering grew from a mix of curiosity and frustration while working with AI chatbots. Models like Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.2 fail at several requests while producing generic impersonal responses despite impressive benchmark scores. That got me into how these systems reason, fail, and generalize.
The continued surface-level insights we gather from existing evaluations motivate me to pursue this field. It sits at the intersection of theory, systems, and societal impact, which further interests me from the approachability perspective. Lately, I have become interested in questions surrounding multimodal social AI and LLMs for coding, especially as they feel practically important.

In these sub-fields, I am exploring how human factors interact with language models to better understand and model the latter’s capabilities. A course on Software Engineering got me into this line of work over the last autumn semester, where I secured the best grade. In my latest research, I modeled real-world heterogeneous workloads like computer-based test taking (where LLMs must log in and navigate a web interface, besides solving questions) to simulate how humans take exams. This is a new kind of evaluation, unlike the static reasoning-only or web search-only tests like MMMU, MathVista, and WebArena, and cutting-edge models like GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 failed poorly, often getting 0% results. Interestingly, Claude Sonnet did better at text-only exams but failed when the same images were served as images.

Through this work, I asked several questions: Why do LLMs fail when we chain multiple unrelated skills in the same task, despite the model excelling at each one individually? Why does multimodality break the model’s exploration skills? Why does GPT-5.1 Codex Max write 300 lines of code while Claude writes 1600? These problems are at the core of LLM behavior and software engineering, and revealed several gaps in real-world use cases that weren’t previously measured.

Building on these directions, I find Purdue’s SURF to be the next step in shaping my research questions and skills. Prof. Jenna DiVincenzo’s project on gradual verification particularly interests me, specifically in the direction of exploring LLM usage to generate specifications supported by the paradigm. Through my previous work, I have gained insights into how models behave when given an open-ended coding task like web navigation. However, how these models perform in a more constrained and verifiable scenario is what I am curious about.

I am also interested in SURF as it offers access to network with academics and peer researchers the summer after my junior year, which will directly help me prepare for graduate school applications. The summer opportunity will be crucial to my career goal of pursuing doctoral research after my Bachelor’s degree. Besides access to mentorship, the program also offers an opportunity to pursue research full-time and early exposure to the expectations of graduate-level research, which will help me make an informed decision come this Fall.

Through the SURF program, I hope to improve my ability to frame and refine research questions that contribute to crucial interdisciplinary machine learning research. Most importantly, I aim to hone my skills in crafting the novelty of a research project by interacting with senior researchers and peers. Finally, the programs also offer a unique opportunity to build mentorship relationships that will help guide my long-term career trajectory, especially as I prepare for graduate school.

To prepare myself for this opportunity, I have undertaken a few research projects to explore my field of study. My first project was at the intersection of cultural competence and multimodal vision-language models, where I performed a large-scale study on how models utilize their existing cultural competence knowledge in downstream tasks like story writing. Existing benchmarks like CVQA mostly studied for presence of cultural knowledge, which I argued is a myopic probe.
Through my analysis, I uncovered several problematic patterns in real-life usage of cultural competence data: models resorted to “safe” stories that didn’t contain enough nuance for most readers or misidentified key cultural icons like the Berlin TV Tower.

My work was accepted for an oral presentation at the Artificial Social Intelligence (ASI) workshop at ICCV 2025 in Hawaii, where I had deep meaningful conversations about evaluations and theories of social AI with senior researchers.

Building on insights from this project, I delved into multimodal STEM reasoning, with an angle of diagnostic evaluation that reveals the exact breaking point. I prepared a benchmark, mmJEE-Eval, comprising difficult JEE Advanced question and four specific probes (cross-lingual consistency, diagram dependence, OCR perturbations, and self-correction). 

By testing 17 cutting-edge VLMs on the test, I observed twice the discrimination between frontier open and closed models as compared to MMMU, the standard for multimodal STEM reasoning tests.
Moreover, my probes also revealed problematic English bias in models like Llama 4 Maverick and Scout. Most importantly, while VLMs detected about 53% of their errors, they only fixed about 3.5% on average.

mmJEE-Eval was accepted to the Findings track of IJCNLP-AACL 2025, a highly-ranked *CL conference, and was also invited for an oral presentation at the SciProdLLM workshop. 

I also built a scalable data collection framework for multimodal reasoning, which automatically collects high-quality synthetic data across coding, math problems, and geospatial reasoning to fine-tune models. Through a dataset of 10,000 instances, my method improved over Walton Multimodal Cold Start and MM MathInstruct by 2.1% on VMCBench and LiveXiv VQA. I submitted my results to the DCVLR challenge at NeurIPS 2025, where it won the 6th position, ranking in the top 10 percentile.

Throughout the development of the scalable framework, I faced several difficulties in the technicalities of a reliable data source. Performance behavior differs from model to model, which had me worried about generalization. I sought support from my mentor, Dr. Shreya Ghosh, who helped me refine a specific direction for data collection.

Reading literature also helped me overcome a few obstacles. For instance, I took the insight that fine-tuning on coding problems before STEM results in better reasoning performance from the DeepSeekMath paper. Through these projects, I have realized that research is often about forging a path where none seems to exist. By spending more time delving into these questions at SURF, I aim to sharpen my research skills and deepen my ability to formulate and investigate open-ended problems at the intersection of LLMs, software engineering, and evaluation.

statement_of_purpose:
The rapid evolution of the space sector, with discussions surrounding human settlement in outer space and space travel, captured the interest of a 15-year-old, who became motivated to pursue a career as an aerospace engineer. As I grew older, the expansion and privatisation of the space economy further strengthened my aspiration, presenting opportunities for innovation, entrepreneurship and applied research. Furthermore, the allure of aerospace also has its appeal; it sounds exciting, ambitious, and cool. However, what began as a fascination has since matured into a sustained, academically driven pursuit.

I continue to pursue the field due to its interdisciplinary nature and the scope of discovery. Advances such as intercity travel using STOL aircraft, VTOL-based delivery ecosystems, aerial robotics for agriculture and construction, and the long-term vision of space habitats and research facilities demonstrate how aerospace engineering integrates mechanical design, controls, robotics, computer vision, and electrical systems. This convergence allows me to engage with multiple engineering disciplines simultaneously.

Through my undergraduate journey, I have been intrigued by the potential of drawing inspiration from natural systems to improve efficiency and adaptability, such as flapping-wing mechanisms, morphing wings for different Mach regimes, and bio-inspired aerodynamic concepts.
Another area that strongly motivates me is the development of strong, lightweight structural materials. As weight reduction remains a persistent challenge in aerospace systems, the use of origami-inspired structural patterns to enhance stress distribution while maintaining structural integrity and reducing mass is particularly exciting to me. 

Among the many summer research programs available, SURF stands out to me primarily because of Purdue University’s strong legacy in aerospace engineering and its culture of research excellence. Purdue has consistently produced influential engineers and researchers, making it an ideal environment for someone aspiring to contribute meaningfully to the aerospace and space technology sectors. 

Purdue’s emphasis on nurturing interdisciplinary researchers strongly aligns with my academic interests. Participating in SURF would allow me to engage in hands-on research within a globally competitive academic setting, providing exposure to advanced methodologies, collaborative research practices, and real-world problem-solving. This experience is particularly valuable to me as I seek to understand how impactful research is conducted at leading international institutions.

In the long term, I aim to pursue graduate studies, where I can contribute to cutting-edge research. SURF would play a crucial role in helping me refine my research interests, identify specific focus areas, and gain clarity on the problems I wish to pursue.  

Technically, I would like to gain proficiency in industry-specific software and interfaces, as well as develop a workflow for research activities. I want to develop intuition to cause rather than textbook remembrance. These skills should help me in my graduate level research and thrive in R&D environments. Further, I would like to be exposed to all problem statements in the Purdue research facilities and develop meaningful connections with faculty such as Professor Collicot, Professor Heister, to name a few and their network. These relationships would play a crucial role in accelerating my development as a researcher and guiding my future academic decisions.

At the beginning of my sophomore year, I got the opportunity to work on a real-life space engineering problem when I joined Team Abhyuday, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras’ rocketry team. As a new team, we lacked the technical knowledge and the hands-on skills to manufacture the rocket systems. The absence of a mentor further pushed us to gather the knowledge required to build a rocket on our own. Driven by a strong desire to tackle a problem that resonated with me and aligned with my envisioned future, I dedicated countless hours to searching for online resources and learning about rocket design and manufacturing. The gruelling search for resources helped me develop a skill for critically reviewing and analysing literature. I also learned how to use commercial packages, such as Ansys, Fusion, Simulink, and OpenRocket, for design and analysis. These skills enabled me to design novel and critical components for our rocket, including an active control system, as well as transition and manufacture the structural parts in-house. Our team’s consistent efforts led to the development of Asia’s Best Rocketry Team in Spaceport America Cup 2024, with the only team to develop an active control system. Further developing a control system, is trying to research a blackbox, with guided mentorship from faculty and alot of youtube hours, we were able to create a theoretically working model, which was then tested to fine tune and develop insights. For our constant effort to reinvent and experiment, we were recognized by the judges of the competition two years in a row. This experience further solidified my desire to work in this field and industry.
 
During my 5th semester, I took a course on Finite Element Methods (FEM). For its project, I decided to develop a novel FEM implementation to simulate Flow over a canard, to characterise flow instabilities at high angles of attack. Under the guidance of Prof. Sundararajan Natrajan, I formulated the research problem independently and developed subroutines to compute the fluid flow and track the interface. I have developed a keen interest in numerical methods and scientific computing through this project. I am currently working on validating the overall model. The outcome of this project will be a comparison of the FEM solution with results from the finite difference and finite volume methods.
 
To gain practical experience in structural research, I joined a team led by Professor Prashant Rawat, dedicated to developing novel composite structures. My project involved developing an origami-designed composite for ballistic applications. The patterned, fold-inspired architecture embedded in a fibre-matrix composite is intended to improve the diffusibility of impact stress. The work was deeply interdisciplinary, drawing on materials science to select constituent fibres and matrices, mechanics to model how folding patterns redistribute loads, and manufacturing processes to translate designs into testable prototypes. That process taught me the importance of connecting simulations to experiments. I understood that results without validation aren’t conclusive. The ongoing experience has taught me patience and the ability to perceive help, as well as feed my curiosity about the unknown. 

I have tried to diversify areas of research to narrow down on things I like and seek more appropriate guidance then. First step to any success story is knowing what you want, and I am figuring out just that.

I am a second-year Electrical Engineering student at IIT Delhi interested in computing systems where hardware,
signals and architecture meet. My motivation lies in understanding how we take noisy, imperfect physical be-
haviour and turn it into computation - whether in classical or quantum systems. I want to work on problems
where the theory is known, but the engineering is still being invented.
 began my undergraduate studies in Engineering Physics because physics was the subject I enjoyed most, and
I wanted a foundation that involved mathematics, electronics and theory together. Early on, I encountered
quantum computing as a system that forces you to rethink everything about computing. What fascinated me
wasn’t the abstract side of quantum mechanics, but the engineering challenge behind making qubits operate
reliably, controlling analog signals with precision, and imagining architectures fundamentally different from the
ones we use today.
As I progressed, I realised I wanted to be on the building side of that problem, not only the analytic one.
That led to my department change to Electrical Engineering, where I could work closer to devices, circuits and
systems. It felt like moving from understanding the laws to engineering something within them.
Signal processing entered naturally into this picture. Through Signals & Systems and research seminars, I
began to see signals not as equations, but as the language of hardware - especially quantum or experimental
hardware, where information must be extracted from noise rather than delivered perfectly. That connection :
physics, devices,system architecture and signal processing - is now the space I want to work in.
Courses like Physical Electronics and Quantum Mechanics showed me the physics that sits underneath every
transistor and device, and how much of engineering is about bending those laws in useful ways. Right now
Digital Systems and Verilog are showing me how all of this becomes the electronics we use every day, while
Data Structures Algorithms, Probability and Stochastic Processes, and Electromagnetics are helping me think
better about computation, uncertainty, and signal flow across systems. This mix of physics, devices, circuits, and
systems is where I want to stay.
When I looked at summer programs, Purdue SURF stood out not just for the research itself, but for the
environment in which that research happens. The scale of experimental facilities at Purdue, particularly around
the Birck Nanotechnology Center and the close integration between fabrication, characterization, and system-level
research, is exactly what I am looking for. The ability for undergraduates to work with cleanroom processes,
advanced measurement tools, and interdisciplinary research groups makes SURF meaningfully different from
programs that remain mostly conceptual or simulation-based. Combined with SURF’s emphasis on mentorship
and professional development, this provides the setting I need to learn how serious experimental research is
actually done.
The three projects I selected: Advanced Packaging with Prof. Haitong Li, Nanotechnology with Prof. Chen-
Lung Hung, and Microelectronics with Prof. Dimitrios Peroulis form a coherent technical path across materials,
devices, circuits, and system integration. Prof. Li’s work in advanced packaging addresses fundamental con-
straints in modern hardware, including interconnect density, thermal management, and signal integrity, and I am
particularly interested in how packaging-level decisions propagate into architectural limits on power, performance,
and scalability for AI accelerators. Prof. Hung’s work in nanotechnology extends this stack downward into the
material and fabrication limits that define future device behavior, where emerging materials and nanoscale effects
introduce new sources of variability and noise beyond conventional CMOS assumptions. Prof. Peroulis’s work
in microelectronics then grounds these ideas in the design, characterization, and high-frequency operation of real
circuits and systems. Together, these projects provide an integrated view of computing systems across scales,
from materials and devices through circuits, packaging, and architecture.

In current era of exponential technological growth, most of the systems are trusted for making decisions that have direct impact on day to day events of humans and their choices. Due to the expected accuracy these results are even accepted in area dealing with human safety e.g., aviation, healthcare, industrial automation, military operations etc. Besides being advantageous, this comes with some fatal results, whether it is the incorrect cancer treatment by IBM’s Watson AI, Boeing 737 MCAS malfunction, failure of auto pilot vehicles, robotic arm etc. However, we continue to trust these techniques and models. Mathematical models work well under fixed assumptions but tend to fail in real world scenarios with too many variables in play. In contrast, data-driven methods like machine learning perform well on real data but struggle with limited data and changing environments. Connecting this gap between mathematical algorithms and data driven adaptability remains one of the challenges in intelligent system design. 
With this aforementioned problem, I, Udit Mittal, an Aerospace Engineering student at IIT Bombay presenting my Statement of Purpose, in order to secure my candidature for research internship through the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) at your esteemed institution under expert mentorship & guidance.
I have always been a curious and inquisitive person, searching for scientific explanations to every phenomenon that caught my eye. My mind could never settle for a surface level explanation, a mindset that was supported and developed by my parents and teachers. My first ever participation in a scientific event was in my 8th grade School Annual Science Fair. My team won 3rd place and this experience sparked a lifelong interest in science that motivated me to attempt India’s largest engineering entrance examination and eventually led me to pursue aviation and space engineering at IIT Bombay.   
During my high school years, I came across the book Tao of Physics, written by Fritjof Capra, that covered the randomness and probabilistic nature of sub–atomic particles, yet the world & nature shows repetitive patterns, and a behaviour in which historical trends can help us predict the future. This contradiction of being random at the very core and still show historic patterns according to old data got me very fascinated. 
Coming to college shattered the bubble I had been living in. I got to become part and learn things which I only read in news headlines and television. I got to explore many other fields apart from aerospace. Before coming here, I heard about growing developments in field of Data Science and Al/ML but here I got to learn it and also work on it. To learn about Data science and AI/ML, I attended the sessions to learn the basics and know how did it work. 
Then in my 1st year summers to get hands on experience I decided to do a project which was on House Price Prediction. In that project we had a dataset of houses in King Country, USA where we had to predict price of Houses, by which I learnt about Simple linear and Ridge Regression. After, completing this project I had decided to pursue Data Science & AI minor, and walk on an interdisciplinary path to integrate my aerospace knowledge with AI and Data Science. Despite intense competition, I secured admission to two minors which are Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning, driven by the belief that future problem solutions require multiple subject knowledge lying at their intersection. 
In my second year, I worked on customer churn prediction project, and based on customer’s app usage and personal data I made a prediction model using logistic regression whether the customer will stop using the platform or not(churn). Based on the insights derived, I developed techniques and policies to reduce customer churn overtime. This project helped me learn how to work on large datasets, how to derive insights from the data, and how to make changes in present model parameters based on the data. 
During this time, I also really liked the controls course which motivated me to join Student Satellite Program at IIT Bombay in GNC subsystem (Guidance, Navigation & Controls). I kicked off my journey by building an orbital propagator using physics based perturbation models in MATLAB, validated against GMAT simulations. In this project I compared two perturbation models which show how the final state vector is different on applying two different force models and propagating them using Runge Kutta 4 method. Currently in the team we are working on our mission NAVIKA, in which we aim at launching two 3U Cubesats and perform their docking in space. 
Side by side, I was also learning about Deep Learning, where I learned about CNNs & ANNs architectures, covering the mathematics and backpropagation, which I used in my Wildlife Grid Classifier Project where, we used Logistic Regression, Random Forest, MLP(20), XGBoost to identify presence of a wildlife on 8*8 grid level, where MLP(20) neural network gave the best results. In this project I had a noisy dataset which intrigued me about how I can make more accurate results even in a noisy environment without overfitting the data, which is a very big problem in the present world scenario as autonomous models tend to fail and resulting in catastrophic results due to presence of noise. 
To learn more about how to handle noise in large and dynamic datasets, I took a project on Kalman-filter-based reinforcement learning trading agent which helped me learn how to handle dynamic and noisy data like stocks price also teaching theory and technique of multivariable Kalman-filters & application of Reinforcement learning. This project was at an intersection of finance & reinforcement learning.
My long term ambition is to participate in the research of developing models which are highly reliable even in presence of noise by combining mathematical models with data driven approaches so that no living being has to face problems caused by failure of these models. Also, aiming to integrate my interdisciplinary knowledge to develop solutions for the field of aerospace.
Since I am motivated, hard-working and dedicated towards my work with the vision to work for the welfare of society. Hopefully you will consider me as a good candidate for the research fellowship. If got selected I will put my maximum efforts in my work.
Hope to hear from you soon. 
Sincerely, 
Udit Mittal

statement_of_purpose:
I didn't start college planning to work on drug delivery systems. Honestly, I barely knew what microfluidics was. But somewhere between building a neural network builder for my own learning and watching actual researchers use it, something clicked: the most impactful AI work happens when you deeply understand the problem you're solving, not when you're just throwing models at data.

That realization has shaped every research decision I've made since. At the Advanced Learning Technologies Lab, I built multi-agent pipelines to analyze wearable learning devices, not because I was chasing "AI for education" as a buzzword, but because I sat with the researchers and understood they were drowning in CSV files, manually trying to find patterns in how kids learn through embodied games. Automating that with Hugging Face APIs cut their parsing time by 60%, but more importantly, it freed them to actually think about the pedagogy instead of data wrangling. That's what hooked me: using ML to accelerate real scientific discovery.

My current work at ASAPP takes a similar approach. Extractify, the agentic NLP system I built with LangGraph and Gemini 2.5 Flash, achieves 95-100% accuracy on extracting structured information from customer conversations. But the interesting part wasn't the accuracy. It was learning why a hybrid regex + LLM approach worked better than pure deep learning: sometimes you need rule-based constraints because language in enterprise contexts has patterns that matter. That insight only came from actually talking to the domain experts about what they needed, not from reading papers.

What draws me to Prof. Ardekani's microfluidics project isn't that I want to "apply AI to biology." That phrase is so overused it's meaningless. What excites me is the specific problem: understanding how therapeutics move through biological barriers. Traditional computational fluid dynamics simulations are slow and can't explore the massive parameter space of different drug formulations, flow rates, barrier properties. But generative AI (specifically equivariant diffusion models and flow networks) can learn representations of these physical systems that generalize across conditions. The challenge is making sure these models respect physical constraints, which is exactly where my experience with hybrid approaches and evaluation frameworks matters.

I'm particularly interested in how we validate these models. In my current work at the Machine Learning for Education Lab, I'm co-authoring a study comparing LLMs against nutrition experts for dietary recommendations in cancer prevention. We're not just checking accuracy: we're building evaluation frameworks that assess bias, adherence to medical guidelines, and reliability across different demographics. This same rigor will be essential for any ML system predicting therapeutic transport: the model needs to be physically plausible, not just statistically accurate on held-out data.

SURF at Purdue is the right environment for this work for a few specific reasons. First, the Eli Lilly partnership means access to real pharmaceutical contexts, not toy datasets, but actual drug delivery problems that matter. Second, Prof. Ardekani's expertise in microfluidics means I'll actually learn the domain deeply enough to build meaningful computational tools, not just black-box ML. Third, the ten-week immersive structure gives me time to fail, iterate, and properly validate approaches, something you can't do in a three-month industry internship where shipping code is the priority.

I'm planning to pursue a master's degree after graduation, focusing on machine learning for computational health. I'm still figuring out whether a PhD makes sense. I want to see if I'm actually good at research that requires years of sustained focus on one problem, not just semester-long projects. SURF will help me answer that question honestly.

The skills I need from this experience are specific. First, I need to learn physics-informed machine learning: how to encode conservation laws, boundary conditions, and physical constraints into generative models. My background in TensorFlow, PyTorch, and production ML (from building Modelic, my deployment platform with drift detection) gives me the implementation skills, but I need to learn the physics. Second, I need experience with interdisciplinary validation: how do you know your ML predictions are meaningful in a wet-lab context? What experiments would confirm or refute the model's predictions? Third, I want to understand how pharmaceutical research actually works. What constraints matter, what tradeoffs exist between computational speed and accuracy, what kinds of predictions are actionable versus just interesting.

My preparation has been deliberate. At the Advanced Learning Technologies Lab, I built multi-agent pipelines and automated data processing, which taught me how to structure ML systems that researchers can actually use. At ASAPP, I learned how to combine rule-based approaches with learned models and how to present results to technical leadership (I presented our extraction benchmarks to ASAPP's ML team). At the Machine Learning for Education Lab, I'm learning rigorous evaluation methodologies for ML in sensitive domains. I've taken Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics, and Calculus through III, which gives me the math foundation for understanding diffusion models. My projects (the neural network builder, Modelic's drift detection system) show I can build end-to-end ML systems, not just run Jupyter notebooks.

The honest challenge I've faced is learning to slow down. In my first research position at Khwarizmi Lab, I tried to implement a complete transaction tracking system in two weeks and ended up with fragile code and half-validated results. My mentor sat me down and explained that research isn't about speed. It's about understanding. That conversation changed how I work. Now, when I hit unexpected results (like the bias patterns we found in LLM nutritional recommendations), my first instinct isn't to patch them quickly but to dig deeper: why is this happening? What does it tell us about the model or the problem?

I'm applying to SURF with the understanding that good research often means spending weeks on things that don't work. I'm okay with that. What I'm not okay with is building ML systems that look impressive but don't actually advance scientific understanding. Prof. Ardekani's microfluidics project, combined with the computational approaches I can bring, has the potential to meaningfully accelerate therapeutic development. But only if we do it rigorously, with proper validation and domain understanding.

That's what I want to learn at SURF: how to do applied ML research that actually matters, in a domain I'll need to deeply understand, with mentors who care about rigor over hype. The LPRC's industry connection means working on problems that have real stakes, not just academic exercises. And honestly, after a year of working on education tech and customer service AI, I'm ready to work on something where the impact is more direct: helping design better drug delivery systems is pretty damn motivating.

As I matured and began considering my future, it seemed obvious that I should select the career that is built on curiosity and what allowed me to study machines and systems. By becoming a mechanical engineer, I can apply myself to many different areas of engineering that other engineers cannot, like renewable energy, and discover advancements that make it a viable alternative to gas and coal. Ultimately, my love for mechanical engineering stems from my passion for questions, whose answers will hopefully be the key to a brighter future. 

Some of the main qualities about SURF that I found appealing  was the opportunities to join a new productive community, to receive guidance from experienced mentors, and to gain experience in my  field of interest. While participating in SURF, I can collaborate with fellow students, which can enhance my communication and teamworking skills while I receive advice from experienced mentors that can further my learning. Moreover, the opportunity to present my findings in a Symposium with other faculty, students and mentors is a great way to expose myself to a more professional environment that I will encounter more frequently in the future. One of my long term career aspirations within STEM is research in renewable energy technologies, in which I wish to discover cleaner and more effective ways to transport and harness renewable energy. Through SURF I kickstart my research experience and give me the tools necessary to pursue my lifelong dream.

Research experience, whether it relates to renewable energy or not, would be help me achieve my career goals of advancing renewable energy technology and implementing new clean technology because I can gain skills in collaboration with my peers, receive guidance from mentors and foster connections with them, and develop enhanced communication skills by presenting my ideas to my peers and faculty. Building a strong foundation of communication through collaboration with my peers and through presenting my research will help me express my ideas better, become more confident, and provide me feedback from experienced faculty and fellow peers, which will allow me to build the foundation necessary to make groundbreaking advancements in renewable energy technologies. Moreover, creating connections with mentors and receiving guidance from them will enhance my learning and aid me in my future career, because I can receive advice from them and can always have those people in my network. This will help me reach my career goals of implementing new environmentally clean technology because I will always have these connections, and so anytime I need to look for an opportunity, for a new job, or for a favor, I will have these people to rely on. 

So far I have participated in clubs like American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) and I have explored career fairs and spoken to various companies, like Constellation Energy, about their renewable energy practices and of their internship opportunities. In ASME, I explored their energy section to find what was most interesting to me. My interest in those classes, as well as my performance, highlight my dedication and passion for engineering. 

One major obstacle that I have encountered is struggling to decide exactly what I am passionate about. However, seeking guidance from Purdue students, Purdue alumni and from my relatives, I managed to create a plan for the future. By majoring in mechanical engineering, I have created a platform for myself to grow and learn in a very adaptable way. In the future, if I ever feel that one discipline of engineering is more attractive than other, I can always pivot to that side without having to switch majors and restart my progress.
