statement_of_purpose:
My academic path in Biological Engineering at IIT Madras has been shaped by a persistent question: how can computational models move beyond pattern recognition to become reliable scientific instruments-models that not only predict, but also explain and generalise across messy biological and real-world data, which could help in curing cancer and reverse ageing. This motivation has steadily pushed me toward research at the intersection of machine learning, representation learning, and computational biology, where I have found that the most exciting progress often comes from combining strong mathematical structure with careful empirical validation.
​
A defining influence on my research direction has been working on problems where standard Euclidean assumptions break down, whether due to hierarchical structures, graphs, trajectories, or multimodal contexts. In my ongoing work as a Student Researcher at SENAI IITM, I have explored geometric representation learning, focusing on sparse hyperbolic convolutional networks and interpretability via Hyperbolic Grad-CAM to surface hierarchical part–whole structure in images. This project taught me that interpretability is not just a post-hoc visualization step; it can be treated as a design constraint that shapes representations, sparsity, and even the geometry of the latent space. It also culminated in a workshop publication on “Sparse Hyperbolic Convolutional Networks with Enhanced Object Localization via GradCAM” at the ICCV Beyond Euclidean Workshop, reinforcing my desire to build methods that are both principled and measurable.
​
My interest in the biological applications of machine learning deepened during my research internship at Kansas State University, where I developed a Position-Aware Inductive Graph Transformer for single-cell RNA-seq to model cell-cell relationships on sparse-label, non-synthetic datasets. I also worked on trajectory inference and benchmarking. In that setting, I became especially interested in how inductive bias and data geometry interact: single-cell data is not merely high-dimensional, it is structured by developmental trajectories, batch effects, and neighbourhood relationships that demand models capable of reasoning over graphs and manifolds. This experience strengthened my conviction that progress in computational biology depends on methods that can integrate structure (graphs, hierarchies, trajectories) while remaining robust under weak supervision and distribution shift.
​
Across these experiences, several research questions continue to intrigue me. First, how can representation geometry be used as a controllable lever for generalisation, especially when data is sparse, noisy, or weakly labelled, as in many biological and scientific settings? Second, how can interpretability be made quantitative and falsifiable, rather than anecdotal, particularly for deep models used in high-stakes scientific workflows? Third, as foundation models and multimodal systems become ubiquitous, how can we ensure that “tool-using” or agentic pipelines remain faithful to evidence, provide transparent reasoning traces, and resist shortcut learning-especially in domains where the cost of hallucination is high? These questions motivate my longer-term goal of building learning systems that are trustworthy enough to accelerate discovery, not just automation.

My work has also repeatedly placed me at the intersection of multiple disciplines like biology, machine learning, and multimodal/agentic AI systems. At RBCDSAI, I modeled gene-protein relationships for reaction prediction by building a seq2seq pipeline using ESM-encoded proteins and a BART-style cross-attention decoder to generate SMILES sequences, while experimenting with tokenization and data partitioning to improve chemical validity. Beyond purely biological tasks, I have explored agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for technical documents, including an EMNLP FinNLP publication on “Enhancing Financial RAG with Agentic AI and Multi-HyDE,” and a related patent titled “SECure RAG.” While these applications differ, the underlying research theme is consistent: designing systems that can integrate structured signals, retrieve and ground evidence, and provide explanations that can be audited.

I am particularly drawn to Purdue SURF because it formalizes the elements that most accelerate undergraduate researchers: full-time immersion, close mentorship, and structured professional development. SURF’s model of matching undergraduates with a faculty advisor and graduate mentor aligns strongly with how I learn best-through rapid iteration, rigorous feedback, and frequent research discussions that connect implementation details to research principles. I am also excited about the prospect of communicating outcomes through a final report and a symposium presentation, as my prior research and Inter-IIT experiences have shown me that writing and presentation are not endpoints, but rather tools for sharpening the research question itself.
​
Participation in SURF fits directly into my long-term goal of pursuing a research-driven career in STEM, with graduate study as the next step. I want to contribute to research that combines geometric deep learning and computational biology-building methods, which could aid in curing diseases like cancer and reversing ageing. SURF would help me transition from strong project execution to deeper ownership of a research direction by providing me with the time and mentorship to frame a question precisely, test baselines carefully, and produce outcomes that withstand external scrutiny.
​
I have taken deliberate steps to prepare for research, both through coursework and by building end-to-end systems. On the engineering side, coursework in statistics, linear algebra, signals, and AI has supported my ability to reason about modelling assumptions, optimisation, and evaluation. On the execution side, I have repeatedly built research pipelines under real constraints: during Inter IIT Tech Meet, I led a six-member team to develop an on-prem remote-sensing vision-language system (GeoNLI), curating datasets, fine-tuning large models with LoRA, and integrating grounding and segmentation modules into a functional tool-based stack within a short timeline. These experiences strengthened my ability to manage ambiguity, debug at multiple levels of the stack, and still deliver measurable outcomes-skills that translate directly to SURF’s full-time research environment.
​
One challenge I have repeatedly faced is navigating steep learning curves while balancing rigorous academics with high-intensity research timelines. Moving from core biological engineering to advanced machine learning research required self-driven upskilling, including reading papers, implementing methods from scratch, and learning to evaluate methods with the discipline expected in research settings, rather than coursework. Short, competition-style research cycles (such as Inter IIT) further taught me to prioritise fundamentals like clean data pipelines, strong baselines, and careful ablations so that speed does not compromise scientific clarity.
​
Ultimately, I am applying to Purdue SURF because I want to spend this summer doing what I find most meaningful: working closely with mentors on a well-defined research problem, producing results that can be communicated clearly, and growing into the kind of researcher who can bridge methods and impact. With my background in geometric deep learning and computational biology projects, I am prepared to contribute from day one while remaining eager to learn new tools and perspectives through SURF’s mentorship and research community. I hope to use SURF as a stepping stone toward graduate study and a career developing trustworthy machine learning methods that aid in curing diseases and reversing ageing.

I grew interested in technology at a young age through curiosity and not through a formal education at any school. When I was younger I loved websites and online services, I would look at sites and think to myself, "How do people create things that are so visually appealing, interactive, and rich in content?" Initially, I thought these types of sites could be created using simple drawing software or document programs. But when I was about 14 I came to realize these web pages were created through programming, that was a very big moment for me and it sparked my interest in coding. I began to teach myself the fundamentals of front-end web development languages along with building web pages. I read blogs and technical articles to keep learning while I was doing this.
As a child, I was very fortunate to be exposed to both software and hardware. I grew up witnessing my older friends and their friends (hackers) working on computer parts such as CPUs and monitors and laptops by taking apart the different components of each item and putting them back together again. Taking apart these parts and reassembling them from memory helped me understand how the individual components (RAM, ROM, hard drive, processor, etc.) work together, which is similar to how one would build a LEGO set.

My parents always encouraged me to learn about computers, which I think had a big impact on my early interest in electronics. The laptop that I received when I was 12 years old was my first computer. I had the opportunity to take the laptop apart and see what was inside with my parents' help. I documented everything I learned about computer architecture and system design in a notebook and continued to add to this as I gained more knowledge about computers and electronics.
Although the increasing academic pressure during my senior year of high school created constraints that prohibited me from learning about coding on a regular basis, my original curiosity remained. When I began college, I made a deliberate decision to jump back into my technical studies from previous experiences but with a newly focused interest in computer science and artificial intelligence. The rapid advancement of AI systems as well as the availability of large-scale AGIs have also fueled the desire within me to learn more about machine-learning models. I found the most interesting aspect of machine-learning technology is the way algorithms can mimic how humans process information, including identifying objects, detecting abnormalities, creating future probabilities from the past, modelling probabilities from current inputs, and even predicting tomorrow’s weather based on trends. The combination between the computational and intelligent aspects of machine-learning and the direct impact on the real world is what keeps me driven to learn more in this field.
I am currently enrolled in an Integrated Dual Degree - Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering and Master of Technology in Artificial Intelligence - and I am completing a Winter Research Internship at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad focused on the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the field of mining. My particular research in the area of AI relates to the areas of Predictive Maintenance, Anomaly Detection, and Mineral Resource Estimation using traditional Machine Learning and Deep Learning techniques. To this end, I have developed and trained convolutional neural network models (CNNs), Autoencoders and Variational Autoencoders to detect cracks and anomalies in mining images. Additionally, I have created several ensemble models for conducting tabular ore classification and estimating mineral resources, including Random Forests, Extra Trees, XGBoost, and Histogram Based Gradient Boosting. This experience has only strengthened my desire to apply AI to solving complex, domain-specific issues at the intersection of data, physics, and uncertainty.
The biggest challenge I face every time is the absence of structured and complete end-to-end learning materials for advanced AI topics among freely available learning platforms. Therefore, most of my learning has been self-guided through research papers, technical blogs, YouTube videos, hackathons, and practical experimentation. I develop small end-to-end projects to reinforce concepts learned and document my findings on GitHub. Though arduous, this method has enhanced my capacity to explore unfamiliar fields through independent research, troubleshoot models, and apply theory to practice; this skill will be crucial for my research career.

Aside from my coursework and research, I have been involved with technical activities outside my area of expertise. One of the highlights was my participation in a Hot Air Balloon Workshop where I finished in second place. The goal was to improve payload capacity, make sure it flew well, and add IoT parts. The workshop was directed by Professor R. K. Pant from IIT Bombay and has further developed my understanding of systems engineering and experimentation, as well as helping me learn to work collaboratively to solve complex problems.
The SURF Program at Purdue University appeals to me strongly for several reasons: 1) Purdue University's emphasis on MENTORSHIP-FACULTY RESEARCH FOR UNDERGRADUATES, which is unique among the university’s programs; 2) Encouragement of INTERDISCIPLINARY EXPLOREATION; and 3) The broad range of SURF Projects, including many areas of interest to me, fall between AI/ML/Robotics, Data Analytics, Imaging, and Applied Sciences. Examples of SURF projects including AI Driven Smart Monitoring, Physics Based ML, Agent Based AI in Simulations, Medical Imaging Reconstruction, and Generative AI for Drug Discovery align very closely with my graduate research experience and Long Term Goals. The SURF Program's emphasis on structured research with structured mentor support, as well as direct access to best-in-class computing systems, and Purdue's affiliates, create an ideal environment for my transition from applied experimentation into more theoretical, rigorous, and methodologically research.
SURF will be instrumental in moving me closer to my professional objective of conducting more advanced-level research pertaining to AI, primarily how to develop robust, intelligible, and domain-specific ML systems in diverse real-life applications. Upon completion of SURF, I plan to pursue graduate studies, where I intend to be involved in AI-centered research with respect to engineering, healthcare, environmental issues, and industrial systems.

Through SURF, I will develop a better understanding of complex research design and methodologies; develop better, more precise, and relevant research questions; obtain additional experience in conducting large-scale empirical research projects; and establish mentoring relationships with faculty and peers lasting into the future.

In conclusion, my research experience has been shaped by an ongoing interest and a commitment to self-directed learning, and information gained through participation in the SURF program at Purdue will better equip me for further technical expertise development and interdisciplinary approaches to pursuing my goal of producing quality research contributions to the STEM fields.

statement_of_purpose:
When I began university three years ago, I never would have imagined that I would end up doing biological sciences research. I entered as a Computer Science engineering major, largely because it felt like the safe option as most people around me were choosing it, and it seemed to guarantee a stable future. But deep down, I was never truly happy with that choice. I have always wanted to do something different, something that stands out, something that could make a real and lasting impact on people’s lives. The idea of settling into a conventional corporate career never sat right with me, and I knew I was searching for more than that. In search of direction, I explored widely across disciplines, including a robotics program at Seoul National University’s summer school. While intellectually stimulating, the experience still lacked the deeper sense of purpose I was searching for. It became increasingly clear that technical complexity alone was not enough. I wanted my work to matter in a more fundamental, human way.
That clarity arrived unexpectedly during my sophomore year in a biology course called Nature’s Machines, which I initially enrolled in as a requirement, despite having no background beyond high school biology. There, I was struck by the elegance of DNA: how its simple, universal structure encodes astonishing biological complexity. I was fascinated by its dual nature: its ability to preserve cellular order with remarkable precision, yet its vulnerability, where even a single mutation can destabilize systems and lead to diseases such as cancer or neurodegenerative disorders. This balance between robustness and fragility deeply resonated with me.
Motivated by this shift in perspective, I switched my major to Biological Systems Engineering and dedicate myself to understanding molecular biology, genome stability, genetic engineering, and their far-reaching implications for health and disease. I subsequently undertook the demanding task of building a novel dataset and fabricating fluorescent, pH-responsive theragnostic hydrogels to develop a machine learning model for point-of-care diagnostics in patients with diabetic foot ulcers. Working under the guidance of Prof. Siddarth S and Prof. Rucha Joshi at Plaksha University, this project demonstrated how materials science and machine learning can converge to deliver interdisciplinary solutions to pressing healthcare challenges. Recognizing that modern biological research is increasingly data driven, I also committed to a minor in Artificial Intelligence, where I am developing proficiency in deep learning techniques to approach biological questions with more integrative analytical tools.

To further deepen my research experience, I interned last summer with Prof. Swagata Halder at Plaksha University, where I studied DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs), highly toxic genotoxic lesions that obstruct DNA replication and transcription. My project synthesized over two decades of research on DPC repair mechanisms, with a focus on the SPRTN/DVC1-mediated proteolysis pathway. I was particularly intrigued by how mutations in SPRTN give rise to Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome, a rare disorder characterized by both premature aging and cancer, once again reflecting the biological duality that initially drew me to the field. As an outcome of this work, I am currently drafting a review article under the mentorship of Prof. Kristijan Ramadan, Director of the Cancer Discovery & Regenerative Medicine Programme at LKCMedicine, Nanyang Technological University. Engaging directly with researchers shaping the field further solidified my commitment to fundamental biological research.

Starting this semester, I have been involved in an ongoing research project under Prof. Swagata Halder that examines the regulation of the human recombinase RAD51, a key protein in homologous recombination mediated DNA double-strand break repair. While RAD51’s role in accurate DNA repair is well established, how post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation influence its activity remains poorly understood. Using prior in-silico modeling that identified candidate phosphorylation sites, my project aims to experimentally assess how these modifications affect RAD51 function. I am working toward expressing and purifying wild-type and phosphorylation-variant (phospho-deficient and phospho-mimetic) RAD51 proteins using a baculovirus-based Sf9 insect cell system, followed by homologous recombination assays to evaluate DNA binding, ATP hydrolysis, and strand exchange activity. In parallel, I will be exploring cancer-associated mutation databases to assess the biological relevance of these regulatory sites. This project helped me realize how much remains unknown even in well-studied systems, and how careful experimental design is required to translate computational predictions into biological insight.
In parallel, I completed a course in research communication, which strengthened my ability to clearly and effectively convey scientific ideas. Following this training, I co-authored and published my first research paper with Prof. Brainerd Prince through the American Society for Engineering Education. To strengthen both my wet-lab and bioinformatics foundations, I have gained hands-on experience in recombinant DNA technologies, including molecular cloning and protein purification. I have also developed computational skills in genome assembly and functional annotation through a project focused on elucidating the biocontrol mechanisms of Trichoderma, with the aim of advancing it as a sustainable alternative to environmentally harmful chemical pesticides.
What draws me to SURF is the opportunity to spend an entire summer immersed in a research environment where asking the right questions matters as much as obtaining results I am particularly excited by projects that examine how cells respond to disease and stress, and how these responses can be engineered or redirected toward therapeutic outcomes. Project on stem cell-derived immune engineering for targeted cancer therapy strongly aligns with my interest in how molecular mechanisms can be harnessed to generate robust, functional cellular responses at both the single-cell and system levels. The ability to engineer human pluripotent stem cells into scalable, genetically enhanced immune effector cells represents a powerful convergence of fundamental cell biology and translational medicine. At the same time, I remain enthusiastic about contributing to any SURF project that bridges mechanistic biological insight with meaningful clinical impact. Through this experience, I hope to gain hands-on expertise in advanced experimental techniques, some of which are beyond what is currently available at home university, enhance my ability to design and troubleshoot experiments, and develop a more rigorous approach to scientific reasoning with a global work perspective, all while building connections with people who love the field.

In the long term, I hope to pursue a PhD and build a career in biological research that sits at the intersection of molecular mechanisms and translational impact. I do not yet know exactly which system or disease I will focus on, but I am certain that I want to ask questions that connect fundamental biology to human health. SURF represents a critical step toward this path, offering intensive research training, close mentorship, and global academic exposure at a pivotal stage, as this will be my final summer to fully immerse myself in research before graduation.

statement_of_purpose:
As a first-generation student from a low-income background, I never imagined I’d be applying to an opportunity like Purdue’s SURF Program. Yet, it’s precisely that background that led me to pursue biomedical engineering at the intersection of nanotechnology, tissue engineering, and translational medicine. It’s precisely that background that shapes the identity I will leverage to enrich my research environment with a necessary perspective and close the gap between innovation and equitable clinical impact.

Growing up, I saw firsthand what can happen when diverse experiences like mine aren’t integrated into medical development and healthcare. My sister has a genetic disorder, and without access to adequate treatment, she was placed in foster care and raised by a system that didn’t know how to support her. I, on the other hand, was raised in custody courthouses watching families fight for stability without the resources to do so, including my own.

My upbringing ultimately shaped my interest in nanotherapeutics as systems that must be designed not only for biological efficacy, but for clinical feasibility and accessibility. It emphasized to me that someone needed to innovate the “how” of translational medicine just as much as the “what.” So, I bet on myself. I started working at 14 to save for the education I knew I could not afford. I enrolled full-time at community college while still in high school and graduated with my associate's degree, and I made family history by attending university. I didn’t have the same support systems my peers relied on to achieve this; instead, I threw myself into every opportunity for learning and growth that arose. I persevered with the adaptability that embodies precisely what I plan to become: a researcher pursuing a PhD in biomedical engineering, specifically focused on nanotherapeutics.

Today, I continue to seek out every opportunity to turn my drive into action. I'm a biomedical engineering student at FSU on an accelerated track to graduate my five-year program in three. I get involved in every way I can: I'm a chairperson at my school's chapter of the Biomedical Engineering Society, where I design solutions for health institutions, such as a post-mastectomy bra prototype for Tallahassee Memorial Hospital to improve patient comfort and recovery. I’m also the Assembly & Integration Lead for the Generational Relief in Prosthetics group, where I use SolidWorks to make custom prosthetic elements tailored to community needs and then scale, assemble, and validate them with CAD to fabricate and donate patient-specific 3D-printed prostheses.

Academically, I’m a research assistant at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, where I balance multiple projects. I’m collaborating with the Mayo Clinic Thoracic Surgery Department to develop a confidential medical device prototype that streamlines and enhances the success of intraoperative procedures, and I work with the Computing Research Association’s UR2PhD program to study cell proliferation under microgravity while establishing a reproducible workflow for machine-learning-assisted image analysis. I also assist with developing and determining the efficacy of tissue models for the lab’s Nanobio Materials and Robotics group, all while maintaining a part-time job through FSU manufacturing and testing magnetic and cellular nanoswimmers.

Having worked on quantifying cell behavior, biological modelling, and developing nanoswimmers and translational medical devices, my experience can seem scattered. How does it all intersect? That’s the question SURF answers. Thus far, my research has addressed standalone considerations like therapeutic carriers, treatment receptor characteristics, and external device components, but it has neglected how they all interact with each other for specific biomedical therapies. I am motivated by questions of how nanoscale delivery systems, cellular responses, and engineered tissue environments can be co-designed rather than optimized in isolation. SURF stands out to me for its interdisciplinary flexibility on projects between departments and research areas. Topics like stem cell immunoengineering for targeted cancer therapy, neutrophil engagers to treat tumors, and the development of DNA nanomaterials for miRNA delivery across the blood-brain barrier address the bigger picture of how each of the foundational concepts I already have experience in can be wielded in conjunction to offer complete treatment proposals. Without a program like SURF that explicitly supports cross-departmental collaboration, these components will remain siloed rather than integrated into cohesive therapeutic strategies.

Through SURF, I hope to emerge not only as a more technically capable researcher, but as one better prepared to ask questions that consider feasibility, ethics, accessibility, and long-term patient impact simultaneously. The specific pliability of SURF will allow me to strategically place the program as a stepping stone to completing my PhD and making space for others from similarly underprivileged upbringings to follow. It will further my development as a role model who shows kids our backgrounds don’t limit us—they forge us, an advocate to disadvantaged families who understands their reality and can tailor care accordingly, and a researcher who once doubted she’d make it this far and will now work fervently to go even farther. I would welcome the opportunity to contribute my perspective to SURF while developing the technical and intellectual foundation necessary to pursue doctoral research in biomedical engineering.

Statement of Purpose, SURF Purdue

Bhumika Adhya

My interest in machine learning, deep learning and computational research developed gradually. I realized that I am most intellectually engaged when I try to understand how systems work and how to improve them when they fail. As an undergraduate studying computer science, I was initially attracted to artificial intelligence for its power and elegance. Over time, my curiosity shifted from building functioning models to asking deeper questions about how and why they generalize, where they fail, and how to make them more reliable in real-world situations where data may be limited or noisy.

What drives me now is a recurring question in my academic and research experiences: how can we design learning-based systems to remain robust, interpretable, and meaningful beyond controlled environments? This question has guided my academic path and research choices, particularly my interest in image analysis, computer vision, and learning informed by optimization. I am especially fascinated by issues at the intersection of data-driven models and formal constraints, such as geometry and physics. Incorporating structure can significantly enhance both performance and trustworthiness. My work on these problems has shown me that strong models rely not just on data but also on thoughtful use of domain knowledge and theory.

My research interests span machine learning, computer vision, biomedical imaging, and optimization theory. I view this diversity not as a lack of focus but as a natural response to the complexity of today's scientific challenges. Many important research questions do not fit neatly into a single discipline. My experiences across these fields have improved my ability to address problems from various perspectives while maintaining a rigorous approach. This interdisciplinary exposure has also taught me to learn quickly, work independently, and communicate effectively across technical boundaries.

I am particularly drawn to the SURF program at Purdue because it emphasizes mentored, inquiry-driven research in an environment that values depth over speed. While many summer programs focus on quick results, SURF encourages students to engage thoughtfully with research questions, learn from failures, and become independent scholars. This philosophy aligns closely with my view of research as an ongoing process of questioning, refining, and learning. I look forward to working closely with faculty mentors, collaborating with peers who share my passion for discovery, and immersing myself in a culture that prioritizes intellectual growth.

I wanted to build an AI that would in turn help solve humanity's other great challenges. I reverse-engineered a plan. During this time, I was fascinated by the unreal demos by Atlas, Optimus, Figure, Digit. I made it my singular ambition to solve Physical/Embodied Intelligence. Moravec's paradox, and the fact that we are far from the Physical turing test for robotics, pushes me everyday in this direction. I jokingly call it the last nail in my coffin (of course, I have a utopian view of our future with AI). At the moment, I usually spend time thinking, and researching on, "An architecture that can learn continually in a data-efficient manner, performing non-trivial actions and planning on long horizons". Consequently, through my personal and research projects, I have roughly traced the journey that robot learning has had in recent years -- 
1. Control policies such as MPC (controlling an exoskeleton for the terrain simulator project)
2. Sample-efficient offline-to-online RL algorithms with automated Domain Randomization and Reward Classifiers such as HiL-SERL (locomotion for a 6DoF biped project)
3. ACT, Diffusion policieis for Behavioral Cloning and VLAs for generalizability (object manipulation and toy sorting on 41DoF biped in ICRA REAL-I competition)
4. World models such as JEPA, Dreamer (Cross Modal Image Retrieval using Self-supervised Learning project).


Learning for humanoid WBC, and a foundational model for satellite imagery (my first 2 preferences) are exactly the projects I have been working on. Also, I took a course on Equivariant Systems, where I watched a few talks by Prof. Yan Gu. Secondly, Purdue offers a well-funded SURF, which is essential for people like me, from developing countries. 
I am very sure, that I want to pursue a PhD in Embodied Intelligence in the US, following which I would love to work at research startups such as Physical Intelligence, Agility Robotics, Figure, Boston Dynamics etc. Getting to work at a physical AI lab there, is a dream-come-true. Working under such exceptional and talented professors and students, will definitely be rewarding. India does not have much discourse on Embodied AI. I have struggled to find peers to talk to, and work with. This SURF finally gives me a way to connect with fellow pioneers in this nascent field. 


I am pursuing a dual minor degree in Artificial Intelligence and Systems and Control, along with major in Mechanical Engineering. I have taken courses on design of mechanical systems, Machine Learning, Estimation on Lie Groups and Computer Graphics. Following are some relevant projects.
Learning for humanoid robot whole-body-control (Preference 1)
1. Participated in REAL-I competition at ICRA. I implemented Decoupled Q-chunking and a custom architecture inspired by DreamerV4. I also read other papers on Robotic World Models, 1000 layer RL, DINO-WM etc. We achieved >70% success rate on picking soft parcels from a conveyor, weighing them and placing them in simulation. We also achieved 60% success in toy sorting. We are working on a paper at ICRA, and also awaiting physical testing on 41DoF LeJU robot (organizers). Results will be announced in May.

“Third time’s a charm, right?” I thought, climbing up the staircase as I clutched the egg. I had spent over a week on a project that should have been completed in two days. When my teacher first introduced the egg drop project, I was eager to start. A week later, after countless trials and four do-overs, I stood at the top of the staircase, still optimistic. The goal was simple: create a device that protected an egg when dropped off the roof. The process, however, was nowhere near “simple". My partner pointed out that our models looked nothing like everyone else’s. While others had constructed basic straw pyramids, our trial models were an assortment of dodecahedrons made of a plethora of materials. The models might have seemed arbitrary, but to me, they were meticulously executed. If only they succeeded. 

Now, at the top of the staircase, I prayed my hard work would pay off and grimaced as I let go of the egg encased in a uniquely shaped polyhedron. I watched as it fell, seemingly in slow motion. Countless doubtful thoughts ran through my mind, and the two seconds that the creation took to fall seemed painstakingly long. When it touched the ground, my partner ran to examine the egg, carefully taking it out of its case. I waited anxiously, wondering if I should just run down and check for myself. Just as I was about to, my partner looked up and, with a huge smile, screamed “TRUSHA, WE DID IT!” 

That project was where I first fell in love with engineering as a process of iteration rather than an act of intuition. It sparked a long-term curiosity that I carried into science fairs, where I explored ideas ranging from mycofiltration to biodegradable super-absorbent polymers, textile engineering, and even the biology of Parkinson’s disease. Through these projects, I discovered how exciting it was to take a question, translate it into an experiment, and produce tangible results. The recognition I received, including the Sir John Gurdon Award for perseverance for my work on mycofiltration, 2nd place at the North Carolina Regional Intel Science and Engineering Fair, the Elizabeth Blackwell Award for antimicrobial studies on Azadirachta Indica, and the Broadcom MASTERS Award for superabsorbent polymer design, was secondary to the rush of discovery itself. These experiences made me realize that the fields I was drawn to most were the ones where biology and engineering intersected.
If the egg drop project taught me the thrill of innovation, then my R&D internship at Axiva Sichem Biochem taught me the discipline behind it. The problems here were no longer classroom constructions but recombinant protein assays with implications for HIV diagnostics. Instead of improvisation, the work demanded precision, reproducibility, and meticulous documentation. A minor oversight could lead to lost reagents, unusable bands, or contamination. It was during those weeks that I began to appreciate science as a system, a sequence of assumptions, controls, parameters, and optimizations. When my gels finally produced clean, reproducible bands, I felt the same exhilaration as watching the egg survive its fall, but now the result mattered beyond the classroom. It was the first time I felt that research was not just interesting, but consequential.

When I entered my first machine learning course in college, I found myself drawn to a different form of biological data: behavioral and physiological signals. I led a project for Early Parkinson’s Detection On-the-fly using a dual-branch architecture that fused motor sensor data with patient questionnaires. I implemented statistical, wavelet, and cross-channel feature extraction, followed by Random Forest-based feature selection and convolutional networks tuned for time-series inputs. Working on this project showed me that behavioral signals can encode disease in ways that are imperceptible to both patients and clinicians but detectable through computational modeling. It also raised scientific questions that continue to motivate me: How early can disease be detected? How can computation help us interpret biological systems that do not reveal themselves easily?

These questions explain why I am drawn to the SURF program. Unlike many summer opportunities that offer exposure, SURF offers participation in active research environments where experimental design, modeling, and scientific communication are embedded into daily work. It also aligns with my goal of pursuing graduate research in biomedical engineering, particularly at the intersection of computation, physiology, and diagnostics.

The project that aligns most directly with my experience and interests is the behavioral characterization of Fmr1 knockout rats. My Parkinson’s work made me appreciate movement as a window into neurological dysfunction, and I am eager to study such phenomena earlier in development and closer to biological ground truth. The Fmr1 project’s use of video-based behavioral tracking, sleep and wake cycle analysis, and pose estimation tools resonates with my interest in extracting biomarkers from subtle behavioral signatures. Only after recognizing this alignment did I learn that the project also involves Fragile X syndrome, a neurodevelopmental condition I had previously encountered in literature on synaptic plasticity. I am excited by the possibility of contributing to a project that connects biological mechanisms, behavior, and computational modeling.

I am also strongly interested in the predictive modeling of aortic root dilation in pediatric patients, which would allow me to expand from behavioral signals to imaging-based physiological biomarkers. Ultrasound imaging poses challenges involving segmentation, noise reduction, and feature representation, and contributing to the development of ML models that support cardiology decisions would broaden my understanding of biomedical data pipelines and clinical contexts.

Finally, the generative AI for drug discovery project appeals to me as a way to explore the therapeutic side of the biomedical pipeline using computational tools. While my work has focused more on detection and modeling of disease states, learning how generative models accelerate molecular exploration would give me a more complete view of how computational methods contribute to healthcare research.

My coursework in biological systems engineering, molecular biology, physiology, and machine learning has given me a formal foundation, but my most meaningful preparation has come from learning how to read literature, debug experiments, and handle the ambiguity inherent in research. These challenges ultimately clarified that academic research is not just something I enjoy, but something I want to pursue seriously.

In the long term, I hope to pursue graduate research in biomedical engineering with a focus on computational modeling for diagnostics and physiological signals. I am drawn to problems where algorithms and biology meet, where data helps make sense of complex living systems and improves human health. SURF represents an essential step toward that trajectory by providing mentorship, research immersion, and scientific communication experience within a rigorous academic environment. I am excited by the possibility of contributing to Purdue’s research community and deepening my understanding of how biological systems can be measured and interpreted.

I thought: this is exactly the kind of repetitive, high-stakes visual analysis that computer vision should be able to help with. I found a Kaggle competition on the exact same problem and spent the next three months building MSCAN, a three-stage detection and grading pipeline. When it got accepted to CVPR 2025 Demo Track with 0.971 AUROC, I realized I wasn't just excited about making models work. I was excited about solving real problems where getting it right actually matters.
That realization has shaped everything since. I've worked on deepfake detection (PhaseFormer, submitted to CVPR 2026, combining frequency-domain analysis with semantic features), dental scan classification (DentalNet at NeurIPS 2025, fusing 2D images with 3D point clouds via cross-attention), and satellite imagery search (Grand AI Challenge, securing Rs. 8 lakhs in government funding with a Siamese ViT retrieval system). I co-founded StarkVision, a 20-member research collective at IIIT Delhi, leading to publications at CVPR and ICMR. Each project taught me that interesting research happens at the intersection of technical challenge and practical constraint.
The natural next step is a PhD in computer vision and multi-modal learning. I've been doing research seriously for over a year with first-author publications spanning object detection, medical imaging, and deepfake detection. I've built complete ML pipelines from data preprocessing to deployment. But I also know what I'm missing. My work has been driven by experimentation more than theory. I can make architectures work, but I want to understand the mathematical foundations behind them. A PhD is where I can build that depth while continuing to work on real problems.

The program provides access to cutting-edge facilities, mentorship from faculty working at the frontier of computer vision and machine learning, and a collaborative research environment with graduate students. I'm drawn to projects that push me into new technical territory while building on my existing experience. Three areas particularly align with my background and research interests:

Video analytics and real-time computer vision systems. I'm interested in projects involving robust computer vision under challenging real-world conditions: variable lighting, occlusions, temporal dynamics, and real-time processing constraints. My tiny object detection work (TOAM-YOLO, under review at CVPR 2026) developed a 4M-parameter architecture with a TOA-MoE module and BiFPN+CARAFE fusion for handling small, low-resolution targets in cluttered scenes. My experience with temporal modeling in MSCAN (Bi-GRU and LSTM layers for fusing sequential MRI data) applies to video-based tracking and sequence analysis. I haven't worked extensively on real-time deployment constraints or annotation pipeline design, which makes projects in this space valuable for broadening my practical skills. Agricultural computer vision, human action recognition, or precision monitoring systems all present similar technical challenges: maintaining accuracy across different camera angles, handling occlusion and environmental variation, and building systems that work without constant retuning. The combination of algorithm development and ground truth generation would teach me about domain-specific data challenges I haven't encountered in medical imaging or satellite analysis.

Optical systems and computational imaging. Projects that combine deep learning with hardware co-design represent new territory for me. I've built image processing pipelines for medical scans and satellite imagery, but those systems take the camera hardware as given. I'm interested in problems where computational methods overcome physical limitations in the imaging system itself. My work on multi-modal fusion provides a foundation: DentalNet integrated 2D intraoral images with 3D point cloud representations through cross-attention, and MSCAN required handling MRI artifacts and slice registration. But working on the full stack from sensor design to reconstruction algorithms would push me to think differently about the imaging problem. Prototype system assembly and experimental validation would give me hands-on hardware integration experience. The academic communication aspect is also valuable. Problems involving audio signal processing combined with computer vision are particularly interesting because they require temporal alignment across modalities with different sampling rates and feature representations. Mobile deployment adds constraints I haven't worked with: power efficiency, on-device inference, user interface design, and latency requirements. The user experience evaluation component would teach me about human-centered design and validation beyond purely technical metrics.

These areas share a focus on building systems that work under real-world constraints rather than optimizing benchmark metrics. That's where I want to grow as a researcher. Third, connections with graduate students who can guide me through PhD applications and show me what it takes to succeed in a top-tier program.

Perhaps a little childishly, I was also inspired by the anime Dr. Stone, where a young scientist rebuilds civilisation from scratch through sheer understanding(In fact, this was the final straw that made me pick my classes in high school). My choice was an act of conviction as much as passion and perhaps sprinkled a little bit with wonder.

What continues to drive me now is the thrill of discovering deep structure beneath complexity. A recent example that left a strong impact on me is Prof. Chen-Lung Hung’s paper on Sakharov oscillations in quenched atomic superfluids. The idea that density power spectra in a two-dimensional Bose gas can mirror the angular power spectrum of the early universe is profoundly beautiful. It is not merely a demonstration of experimental finesse, but of conceptual elegance: a simple, universal mapping between cosmology and cold-atom hydrodynamics, folding together two vastly different physical regimes into one coherent mathematical picture. That ability to extract universality, to recognise that seemingly unrelated systems whisper the same equations, is a skill I aspire to cultivate. It is this very mindset of abstraction and modelling that inspires my interest in computational physics, simulations, and theoretical frameworks that span scales from the microscopic to the cosmic.

I am drawn to SURF precisely because it nurtures this spirit of interdisciplinary curiosity. Many summer programs exist, but Purdue felt uniquely welcoming. As an international student, I was struck by how responsive and warm the staff were: an inquiry I sent about the application was answered on the very same day. That small gesture revealed a culture of hospitality and support. SURF itself stands out because it brings together fields I am excited about, quantum optics, mathematical modelling, environmental physics, and fluid dynamics! The opportunity to potentially work with professors such as Chen-Lung Hung, Alexandria Volkening, or Yue Meng excites me, because each of them embodies a different direction that I may take as the scientist I hope to become.

Equally important is the chance to build connections, an international network of researchers from whom I can learn, ask questions, and shape my future research direction. 
My preparation for such work has been steady and purposeful.
 
At the Centre for Quantum Technologies(CQT), I helped assemble and test a stray magnetic field correction system for qubit trapping. I analysed correlations between applied currents and measured magnetic field values and learned how to transform raw bit-level sensor outputs into physical units. It was my first exposure to calibrating real data against theoretical expectations, and it taught me the importance of careful, critical modelling. I have completed simulations such as a two-body planetary system for my own muse, strengthening my comfort with numerical solvers and dynamical modelling. To prepare myself further, I am taking graduate-level modules, such as: Advanced Numerical Methods, Graduate Quantum Mechanics, an Introduction to General Relativity, and Statistical Mechanics, because I want to understand how to model systems at every scale, from single particles to the curvature of spacetime, and from few-body interactions to thermodynamic ensembles.

Outside the laboratory, my life has always been defined by a duality of interests: the high-speed strategic coordination of football and the meticulous, silent precision of sketching and painting. These are not mere hobbies; they are the foundations of my engineering philosophy. Sketching taught me to observe the world with spatial granularity understanding how joints move and how light hits a surface while football taught me the importance of real-time multi-agent coordination and rapid decision-making under pressure.
As I progressed into my undergraduate studies at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Dharwad, I carried these lessons with me. While many of my peers had been coding since childhood, my major contribution to robotics began relatively later, during my college years. This "late start" proved to be an advantage rather than a setback; I approached the field with a mature curiosity and a hunger to bridge the gap between abstract computer science and the physical reality of machines.
The turning point in my career was the development of a 4-DOF robotic arm. This project was my first deep dive into the "ocean" of robotics. I found myself navigating the complexities of forward and inverse kinematics, the nuances of servo motor control, and the intricacies of microcontroller architecture. It was a mind-boggling experience where every solved equation resulted in a tangible, physical movement. Our team’s dedication culminated in winning the competition, where we were honoured with the Best Design and Optimization Award.
This recognition was the catalyst I needed. Instead of seeking the immediate comfort of a conventional corporate job, I realized that building things transforming lines of code into kinetic energy, made me genuinely happy. I decided to dedicate my career to the pursuit of advanced robotics. To build better robots, I knew I had to understand the "brain" and "nervous system" of the machine. Consequently, I immersed myself in rigorous coursework, including Computational Geometry, Algorithms for Robotics, Mechatronics & Robotics, Operating Systems, and Computer Architecture.
My research and project work evolved rapidly. At the InterIIT Tech Meet 13.0, I tackled the challenge of Drone Motor Failure Handling. This required a sophisticated integration of Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for real-time failure detection and Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) control for stabilization. Working within the PX4 and QGroundControl ecosystems, I faced the daunting task of tuning PIDs and managing sensor fusion under partial thrust loss.
I also explored the intersection of robotics and consumer electronics. I designed custom PCBs for projects ranging from an iPod-style resistive scroll pad to modular robotics kits for children. Furthermore, I contributed to the development of a Prosthetic Arm, utilizing a machine learning model to detect hand motion through vision and sensor data. This project solidified my interest in Embodied AI the idea that intelligence must be deeply integrated with the physical form it inhabits. One of the most intriguing questions that motivates me is: How can we enable robots to possess a "sense of touch" and "proprioceptive intuition" that matches biological systems? Investigating the gap between high-level reasoning (VLAs) and low-level tactile execution remains the core problem I wish to solve.
To explore this field, I have pursued a mix of industry-standard internships and high-stakes competitions. My research seeks to develop a Deep RL architecture that enables coordinated motion for tasks requiring high levels of dexterity. I am working with Interbotix Viper300 (6-DOF) and VectorX 150 (5-DOF) arms, developing a pipeline that translates 5-DOF control logic into 6-DOF space.
In the simulation phase, I have conducted extensive analyses across MuJoCo, Isaac Sim, and Newton, focusing specifically on the Sim2Real bridge. I have tested various functions defining friction coefficients to optimize policy transfer. For RL training, I have utilized Isaac Lab to implement Diffusion Models, Graph-based RL, and YOTO (You Only Teach Once). My work focuses on deep RL architectures to make arms capable of the bi-dexterous tasks that human hands perform naturally.

This obstacle ultimately became a strength, instilling in me a rigorous work ethic and a unique perspective that combines CSE logic with mechanical intuition.

Participation in SURF would allow me to refine my Sim2Real methodologies under the guidance of world-class faculty, gaining the specialized knowledge in probabilistic policy networks and domain randomization that is vital for my future research.
My long-term career goal is to become a Research Scientist in the field of Embodied AI, leading a laboratory that focuses on "Human-Level Dexterity in Autonomous Systems." I aspire to develop robotic systems that can assist in complex surgeries or hazardous environment recoveries tasks where machine precision must be wedded to human-like adaptability. Participation in SURF at Purdue is a critical stepping stone, providing me with the global connections and rigorous research experience necessary to pursue a Ph.D. and contribute to the next generation of STEM innovation.
Purdue University stands as a global leader in engineering and robotics innovation. The interdisciplinary research culture at Purdue aligns perfectly with my research trajectory in bimanual manipulation and deep reinforcement learning. Vasudha Kannan | Personal Statement
I have learned that meaningful scientific insights often emerge when curiosity is paired with careful attention to unexpected results, as exemplified by discoveries such as penicillin, RNA interference, and CRISPR. I experienced this firsthand while standardising a novel chemical dye as a total protein stain for western blotting. I questioned whether the dye’s chemical properties could be applied beyond protein detection and independently tested its ability to stain DNA during electrophoresis. To my surprise, it worked. By potentially replacing ethidium bromide, this approach could offer a safer and more affordable alternative for routine DNA visualisation, particularly in laboratories operating under resource constraints. This is why I love the process of research: the adrenaline rush that follows persistence through wearisome, mundane work and failed ideas, and the possibility that, someday, this work might make a difference in someone’s life.
Motivated by a fascination with biological systems developed during my high school years, I enrolled in the BS–MS program in Biological Sciences at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras), admission to which required ranking within the top 1% nationally across 1.5 million aspirants. I was also awarded the INSPIRE Scholarship from the Government of India in recognition of my performance in the Class 12 standardised examinations. IIT Madras’s interdisciplinary curriculum, spanning programming, biostatistics, biochemistry, molecular and cellular biology, epigenetics, and human physiology, provided broad foundational training while allowing flexibility to pursue coursework aligned with my primary interest in molecular biology. Alongside coursework, I actively pursued research projects both within and beyond formal laboratory settings. The skills and insights gained from these projects gave me the confidence to contribute to a book chapter on proteins, DNAs, yeasts, and peptide-based biotemplates for catalyst synthesis. Through these experiences, I developed a strong interest in molecular biology across physiological, disease, therapeutic, and developmental contexts.
My research journey began in Professor Baskar’s laboratory at IIT Madras, where I worked on an exploratory project examining the response of Mimosa pudica to neurotransmitters and their inhibitors. I treated hydroponically grown plants with compounds including dopamine, serotonin, and alcohol, quantified changes in leaf-closure kinetics, and designed an experimental setup that delivered consistent mechanical stimulation while enabling measurements of action potentials. Although I entered the project with no prior background in electronics, I learned to integrate principles from multiple disciplines to build and refine the system. In the same laboratory, I also conducted biochemical assays to study enzyme production in Dictyostelium and presented my findings as a poster at the Vivekananda Institute of Mycology conference.
Coursework in molecular biology further ignited my curiosity about what research in this domain would entail, prompting me to apply for and receive the Young Research Fellowship (5% acceptance rate out of 300 competitive applicants) to support my work in Professor Nitish Mahapatra’s cardiovascular genetics laboratory. There, I investigated the role of protein cysteine sulfhydration in ischemia–reperfusion injury and hypertension. My work focused on understanding why only specific cysteine residues exhibit susceptibility to post-translational modification. To address this question, I analysed proteomics datasets to identify consensus motifs and physicochemical features associated with modification-prone residues. This experience provided me with a strong foundation in proteomics data analysis and experimental cardiovascular biology. I presented my findings at the International Society for Heart Research conference (2025) and incorporated the feedback received into subsequent analyses. In parallel, I am preparing a first-author manuscript on the novel dye-based total protein staining approach for western blotting developed during this period.
Building on my work in the cardiovascular genetics laboratory, I became interested in nitric oxide biology and its role in vascular regulation, which led me to independently formulate a hypothesis linking microRNA-33 to hypertension through endothelial signalling pathways. This hypothesis formed the basis of my selection for the highly competitive Amgen Scholars Program at Kyoto University, where I worked under the guidance of Professor Koh Ono. My journey into engineering began when I organized my first campaign against the bursting of firecrackers on an Indian festival called Diwali in 2016. I lived in a beautiful hill station in India, called Shillong — the Scotland of the East — and I didn’t want our actions to make Shillong like Delhi, the capital of India. Ironically, Delhi experiences significant deterioration in air quality after Diwali due to excessive use of firecrackers. In 2025, the Delhi AQI increased from 148 to approximately 500 just after this festival. While there were a few people who supported this cause, I faced considerable criticism. They argued, “You are against pollution-causing firecrackers, why don’t you stop plying vehicles that release harmful pollutants into the atmosphere daily?” That made me curious about how engines work and what causes them to release such harmful pollutants into the air. The curiosity, combined with my interest in physics and mathematics, prompted me to pursue a bachelor's degree in Mechanical Engineering at Iowa State University. 

My long-standing interest in energy efficiency in automobiles was sharpened and redefined by exposure to undergraduate research, which transformed my fascination into a focused research interest. After contacting several research groups during my first year of college, Prof. Jonathan Claussen, from the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Iowa State University (ISU), who specializes in biosensors, invited me to work in his laboratory. Although the research group’s research focus didn’t perfectly align with my initial interest, I joined the group to develop transferable skills in sensing, materials, and experimental research that underpin a wide range of sustainable engineering technologies. Firstly, I worked on a project focused on testing a scalable biomimetic “collect-and-sense” system that can efficiently harvest pesticide spray and accurately quantify glyphosate in farm fields in real-time. In this project, I conducted an experiment by placing laser-induced graphene (LIG) fern leaf-like pesticide collection patches in farm fields to collect pesticide spray, and monitored the quantity of pesticide actually deposited in different areas of a field. The work was subsequently published in the RSC Journal, Nanoscale Horizon [2024, 9: 1543-1556], where I was a co-author. In the following summer, I worked on fabricating LIG sensors to measure their capacitive response to pesticides sprayed in agricultural fields. The experience provided hands-on experience with the operation of a gantry-based CO2 laser, enabling the precise etching of a polyimide film to fabricate an LIG sensor whose surface properties could be varied by modulating the system settings on the laser. As a researcher in this laboratory, I gained experience in calibration, data collection, and data analysis. While I enjoyed using the laser to fabricate sensors, my modern physics class deepened my interest in laser technology and its importance in material characterization. In my sophomore year, I had the opportunity to learn more about laser technology under the guidance of Prof. Dr. Jiang Wang, from the Department of Physics at ISU, in his ultrafast imaging lab. Through my engagement with laboratory personnel and active participation in laboratory group meetings, I gained a foundational understanding of laser alignment and operation, as well as non-linear optical techniques, including Raman spectroscopy and fluorescence spectroscopy. Initially, I undertook a project to modify an Igor Pro macro program and enhance the performance of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on data collected in the lab. Subsequently, during the summer of 2025, I interned with the same research group at Ames National Laboratory to investigate the lifetime decay of ruby utilizing fluorescence spectroscopy.

While working in the ultrafast imaging laboratory, I was taking coursework in thermodynamics and fluid mechanics, which emphasized the importance of non-intrusive, high-resolution measurements of velocity, temperature, density, and species concentration in complex flows. Since these parameters can help optimize designs to improve fuel economy and reduce emissions, I wondered whether optical diagnostics could be used for high-power-density fluid analysis. Motivated by this question, I joined Dr. Todd Kingston’s lab to learn about thermal-fluid transport and energy storage research, while continuing my training in the use of high-class lasers at Ames National Laboratory. In Dr. Kingston’s lab, I am currently leading a project to build a thermal management system for lithium-ion batteries. It may be noted that during operation, batteries generate heat which, if not effectively dissipated, can result in localized temperature rise that accelerates side reactions, causes uneven cell aging, and, in extreme cases, lead to thermal runaway — a major safety hazard. To address this challenge, I have built a flowline to perform forced-immersion cooling on a commercial cylindrical battery. The battery is immersed in a high-velocity dielectric fluid that affects the convective heat transfer coefficient, which in turn influences the temperature gradient within the battery. Using a data acquisition system interfaced with a LabVIEW program, I systematically monitor the flow rate and temperature of the dielectric fluid, enabling heat transfer analysis of the cooling process’s impact on the battery’s internal temperature gradient during charging and discharging. This information will finally be used to gain insight into the battery’s lifetime, performance, and efficiency. 

In conducting heat transfer analysis to estimate physical quantities that determine the battery's internal temperature gradients, I realized that the geometric complexity of the flowline and modeling assumptions limit the accuracy of these estimates. Through the SURF program, I want to develop the physical intuition for advanced diagnostics, modeling, and fluid transport analysis, which will help me address these limitations and apply them broadly across several engineering applications. I am highly interested in Dr. Mukherjee’s group due to its strong alignment with my research focus and the opportunity to develop new skills in energy storage research. He has made significant contributions to understanding thermal behavior and the evolution of internal cell temperatures. His group’s work on measuring the internal temperature of lithium-ion pouch cells piques my curiosity about how these techniques can be extended to commercial cylindrical cells and how the results would be affected when the battery temperature is regulated by a battery management system. Working in his group will help me gain a deeper understanding of the experimental techniques, simulation, and data-driven analytics used to characterize the thermo-electrochemical behavior, which I can apply to my current battery cooling research and future work. Dr. Weibel’s work also highly attracts me because of his research focus on cooling technologies. I am eager to develop skills in simulation modeling and believe that my background in conductive and convective heat transfer analysis will allow me to contribute meaningfully to simulation-driven design and optimization efforts. In Dr. Ardekani’s group, I am eager to explore the potential of microfluidic transport and apply my experience with optical instruments to determine how fluorescence microscopy can be used to measure therapeutic solutions within the hydrogel. 

Purdue’s excellent engineering program, along with the SURF program’s close alignment with my research interests, made SURF my top choice. Additionally, I view the SURF program as an ideal environment to deepen my understanding and evaluate my aptitude for long-term graduate study at Purdue University, particularly within laboratories that emphasize fundamental measurement science applied to real-world energy systems.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in materials engineering began with a techno-economic analysis of Solid Alkaline Fuel Cells (SAFCs) for off-grid communities. I realized that the main challenge in sustainable energy is not a lack of engineering concepts, but rather the absence of materials that combine efficiency, durability, and cost-effectiveness. This insight drew me to the intersection of 
Materials Science and Artificial Intelligence. I am particularly interested in the "inverse design" problem: instead of relying on trial-and-error, can we computationally generate material structures that meet specific property targets? During my research internship at IIT Madras, I used a hybrid inverse design and high-throughput screening approach to discover novel perovskite materials with targeted green optical emission. This work aims to address the "Green Gap" in optoelectronics, which refers to the efficiency drop in LEDs in the green spectral range. Addressing these challenges requires moving beyond traditional methods to approaches that can scan large chemical spaces and rapidly calculate material properties.

To explore this field, I have actively sought research opportunities. During my time as an Indian Academy of Sciences Summer Fellow at the SaiMat Group, IISc Bengaluru, I focused on the fidelity of Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs). I benchmarked Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) such as MACE-MP0, SevenNet-MF-OMPA, and OrbNet-v3 against Density Functional Theory (DFT) baselines to assess their accuracy in high-throughput screening of Transition Metal Oxide (TMO) surfaces based on surface energy and oxygen vacancy defect formation energy to accelerate the discovery of 
novel and functional materials for catalysis applications and 2D semiconductors. Along withthe benchmarking exercise, I also gained valuable insights into frameworks such as Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and Symmetry Adapted Atomic Orbitals (SAAO) for representing crystal structures as graphs, and I was introduced to concepts like Message-Passing-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks and understood the architectures of various MLIPs. This experience reinforced the idea that AI-accelerated computational methods can dramatically expand the search space for functional materials, while also teaching me 
the critical importance of validating model accuracy to ensure reliable predictions in materials discovery.

Building on this, I joined the Low-Dimensional Semiconductors Laboratory at IIT Madras for my winter internship, where I developed a hybrid generative screening pipeline to discover novel Perovskite structures with target optical emission properties in the green region using a generative diffusion model, an MLIP, and DFT calculations. During this internship, I automated DFT calculations in Quantum Espresso and integrated them into a Python workflow using the Quantum Espresso binary and the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE) wrapper. I successfully deployed this pipeline on the PARAMSHAKTI supercomputer at IIT Madras and discovered novel crystal structures with interesting and useful properties (e.g., magnetic semiconductors). I am currently writing a manuscript on my work. In this pipeline, I used a novel approach to screen the diffusion model-generated structures based on their structural and thermodynamic stability, as determined by phonon calculations using Machine-Learned 
Interatomic Potentials. As part of my second project in this internship, I discovered several double-halide perovskite structures and chalcogenide-based perovskites using the generative-screening pipeline and computationally evaluated the synthesizability of chalcogenide-based perovskites from double-halide perovskites via a novel synthesis route. A manuscript is currently being written on this work as well. During this internship, I also gained hands-on experience in synthesizing perovskite thin films by spin coating and powders by solid-state synthesis. To characterize the structures generated by the pipeline, I computed their Raman Spectra and photoluminescence using DFT and validated the computational results by measuring photoluminescence, X-ray diffraction patterns, and Raman spectra of the 
structures after synthesizing them in the laboratory. This experience demonstrated the power of closing the computational-experimental loop: by bridging AI-driven generation, computational validation, and experimental synthesis and characterization, I could both accelerate materials discovery and ensure that computationally predicted structures translate 
into real, synthesizable materials with verifiable properties.

In addition to these experiences, I am working on a project with Dr.-Ing Prince Gideon Kubendran Amos at the Department of Metallurgical and Materials Engineering at NIT Trichy, contributing to developing a symbolic regression model to generate interpretable and accurate empirical relationships between processing parameters and material properties using genetic programming. I am preparing and preprocessing the dataset for model training. This project complements my previous work by emphasizing interpretability alongside prediction accuracy, while generative models and MLIPs excel at exploring vast 
chemical spaces, symbolic regression provides human-readable equations that reveal underlying physical relationships. Together, these experiences have equipped me with a comprehensive toolkit spanning generative AI, physics-based simulation, experimental validation, and interpretable machine learning for materials discovery.

I am excited about the Purdue SURF program as an exceptional opportunity to improve my expertise in both computational materials engineering and laboratory procedures (synthesis and characterization of materials) to solve real-world problems in electronics, semiconductors, and energy storage technologies. I find myself particularly drawn to Prof. Alejandro Strachan’s work on expanding the AURA platform. I believe that my experience wrapping DFT codes with ASE and integrating MLIPs into Python workflows has prepared me to contribute to the design of modular, reproducible simulation tasks required for agentic 
AI. I would be thrilled to apply my background in handling multi-fidelity data to help develop robust workflows that enable AURA to autonomously execute complex reasoning tasks. Similarly, Prof. Thomas Beechem’s objective to optimize ferroelectric endurance strongly resonates with my research on material reliability. Having computationally quantified oxygen vacancy formation energies for TMO surfaces and, both computationally and experimentally determined photoluminescence and Raman spectra in perovskites, I would be eager to apply these spectroscopic techniques to isolate life-limiting defects in Hafnia-based memory. Whether contributing to the architecture of software for autonomous workflows for computation on nanoHUB or characterizing process-induced defects at the Birck Nanotechnology Center, I am enthusiastic about the opportunity to contribute to Purdue’s innovative research ecosystem.

Beyond research internship experiences, my role as the head of the Payload and Research sub-team of the first-ever student team representing NIT Trichy in the IREC Spaceport America Cup 2026 has given me a systems-level perspective on the vulnerabilities of electronics in space environments. In designing payloads, I have seen firsthand how standard commercial components are insufficient for extreme operating conditions. This drives my specific interest in Prof. Alejandro Strachan’s work on atomistic modeling of radiation damage. I believe I am well-positioned to contribute to this research; I am currently using LAMMPS to develop and parameterize interatomic potentials for Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations of TRIP steels. I would be excited to apply this computational expertise to investigate the fundamental physics of radiation damage, specifically how interfaces and microstructural features influence defect evolution during collision cascades. This combination of hands-on 
Experience in designing payloads with the constraint of damage of electronic components due to radiation and foundational experience in MD simulations would allow me to approach radiation damage modeling with both technical rigor and a clear understanding of the end-use application.

Ultimately, I view the Purdue SURF program as a pivotal step toward my long-term goal of pursuing graduate research. I am eager to immerse myself in Purdue’s collaborative ecosystem, learn from world-class mentors, and translate my passion into tangible scientific contributions. I look forward to the opportunity to bring my curiosity, dedication, and technical drive to your campus this summer.

Working on estimating the world’s first OTEC potential through Machine Learning and Data Analysis was the first time that I was able to put my skills and tools to the test on a project of that scale – contributing to something meaningful. Over the course of two semesters, I was able to create an interactive global map of OTEC (that could visualize thermoclines) potential in the world using NumPy, Pandas, Plotly, Seaborn, and matplotlib in Python, built on an ML-based database.
