how_found_surf_other: As a prospective PhD student in Music-ML, I have been looking for research opportunities. I have been proactively emailing labs and startups to inquire about such opportunities. The graduate mentor for AIM (Benjamin Chou) responded to my email and recommended I apply via SURF.
statement_of_purpose:
Before starting college, I was a full-time independent artist with 15+ years of musical experience. My debut single premiered with over 12,000 YouTube views, yet hundreds of songs remained unreleased in my Google Drive due to one frustration: mixing. This recurring problem across the musician community drives my interest in music information retrieval (MIR).

While MIR open-sources valuable tools, they remain confined to GitHub repositories requiring terminal and programming fluency that limit artist access. This gap motivates my pursuit of data science and music as a unified research direction: building applied machine learning systems that support musicians through interactive and deployable musician-centered tools.

Research Experience
During my sophomore summer, I received Knox College's highest independent research grant to address a gap in music discovery systems. Musicians possess the vocabulary to describe what they enjoy in a song, but streaming platforms don’t allow content-specific queries like "recommend psychedelic rock songs by The Beatles with sitar, but no piano." Prompting large language models with such queries led them to search through written media, not the audio tracks. I built such a prompt-based music recommendation platform via metadata web scraping, source separation for instrument detection, and librosa heuristics for audio feature extraction. 

Following the research program, I wished to get external feedback and further deepen my understanding of neural architectures underlying modern MIR systems. The week after the program, I attended Stanford's Deep Learning for Music Information Retrieval summer workshop at CCRMA led by Professor Iran Roman and Dr. Zhengshan Shi. There, I learned of transformers, variational autoencoders, and foundational audio-ML works like CLAP and MusicLM [1, 2]. Upon deployment, I presented my work to my instructors who strongly encouraged me to apply to ISMIR. I was accepted at ISMIR 2025 as a Late-Breaking Demo and later, the AI4Music workshop at NeurIPS 2025 as one of the few single-author undergraduate works at either venue [3, 4].

Ongoing Works
Currently, I am pursuing an honors thesis on automatic mixing systems with Yen-Tung Yeh (Arthur), who developed FX-encoder++, a contrastive learning framework for extracting instrument-level audio effect embeddings from mixtures [5]. We considered several ideas for a novel mixing system: implementing inference-time steerability along principal component axes for exploring new mixes [6], integrating iterative sound-matching for a style-transfer system [7], or accounting for parametric automation in mixing effects, something SOTA models frequently miss [8, 9]. 

Ultimately, guided by the lack of feedback during our formative years as music producers, we decided to develop a multi-turn conversational mixing agent employing a joint embedding space between audio effects parameters, audio, and textual descriptors. This would allow novice producers to provide reference tracks and natural-language prompts to iteratively improve their mix. To further explore this field, I will also study abroad in London next year to conduct research with Professor Joshua Reiss, a pioneer in Intelligent Music Production systems.

Additionally, I am working with cultural MIR researchers and classical musicians to develop a text-to-music generative model for melodies rooted in classical structure. Unlike stacked harmonic structures, Hindustani classical music routinely employs gliding melodies, making efficient representations like MIDI inadequate. We are currently collecting multi-track training recordings to train a model that learns from and generates lightweight pitch contours, creating baseline compositions for improvisation.

Why SURF and the Artificial Intelligence for Musicians Project
SURF's Artificial Intelligence for Musicians project provides collaborative experience with a music technology research group, something my liberal arts college lacks. I would gain essential skills in UX design, user evaluation, and mobile application development for building accessible musician-centered tools, plus hands-on experience with MIR-specific concepts like Polytune's learnable alignment mechanism using MT3 and dynamic time-warping [10]. 

My work on joint embedding spaces in the mixing agent would transfer to Polytune's shared latent space between score and performance audio. My Hindustani classical and DAW background could help expand Evaluator's timbral and non-Western musical vocabularies, limitations identified in the 2025 paper.

Professor Yung-Hsiang Lu's expertise in deploying low-latency, memory-efficient vision transformers and commercializing research through startups like Alethia and Perceive demonstrates the real-world impact I aspire toward. Mentorship from Dr. Kristen Yeon-Ji Yun, a practicing musician-researcher, would provide invaluable perspective on designing tools that genuinely serve performers' needs.

Overcoming Obstacles:
Pursuing MIR from a small liberal arts college without signal processing courses or an active research group has required initiative. Since Knox does not offer digital signal processing coursework, I worked through Dr. Youngmoo Kim's Applied DSP course independently and studied Dr. Müller's Fundamentals of Music Processing—a seminal MIR book my research supervisor personally purchased for me after seeing my commitment to the field [11].

Lack of domain-specific mentorship led me to join WIMIR’s (Widening Inclusion in Music Information Retrieval) mentorship program, where I was paired with Arthur based on my interest in automatic mixing. To overcome the lack of research funding on my campus, I work three on-campus jobs - research ambassador, mathematics tutor, and peer career advisor. All of these positions allow me to fund my conference trips and assist students in navigating the same obstacles I faced: accessing mentorship, identifying funding, and building technical skills outside formal coursework. 

At conferences, I push myself to engage deeply. At ISMIR, I performed six songs during the jam session, one in a language I had never spoken. These performances became conversation starters as I sought meaningful connections. Dr. Xavier Riley offered to proofread papers, Dr. Simon Dixon and Dr. Paris Smaragdis shared what they look for in PhD applicants, and several graduate students and professors continue to mentor me virtually.

Music information retrieval sits at the intersection of my identities: a former producer frustrated with technical growth, a practicing musician who understands the creative process, and a researcher committed to building tools that expand access. I want to build systems that assist creative workflows - a mixing agent, melody generator, error detector or posture recommender. SURF would provide the collaborative environment, technical mentorship, and deployment-focused training necessary to continue this work, transforming my passion for helping musicians into rigorous, impactful research that serves communities beyond academia.

statement_of_purpose:
Q1.
My interest in AI and Robotics began in 9th grade, when I saw a robotic hand for the first time at an inter-school science exhibition, which I had participated in. Watching a machine move automatically, almost like a human being, made me ponder how such systems sense, decide, and function. Later, when I got my own smartphone, I used to search through random science and technology-related videos, where I came across the hydraulic-powered Atlas robot from Boston Dynamics and the Sophia humanoid robot, which responded like a human being. These instances deepened my curiosity about the thinking mechanism of robots, and I began to ponder how they are able to perform complex tasks. From there, I came across Artificial Intelligence, which was used to train robots to handle complex tasks. Moreover, after joining IIT Madras, I joined the AI Club, where I could explore AI and also learn how it could be used to solve complex problems that once seemed extremely infeasible, apart from building a robot's brain. This early fascination has grown into a commitment to study AI and robotics, using models to solve real-world problems ranging from seismic hazard prediction to path predictions for autonomous vehicles.

While being interested in the intersection of Robotics, AI, and physical sciences, as well as with a background in Civil Engineering, I am driven to solve several fundamental and application-based questions. I get motivated by the following questions:
1. How do the current AI architectures, like Attention, Diffusion, and Flow models, and Reinforcement Learning algorithms work?
2. How could I build a better algorithm than the above architectures that could not only reduce cost and training time, but also could generalize, reason, and be intuitive in nature?
3. How could I use AI in interdisciplinary fields to foster innovations that would be beneficial to humans?
4. How could I make a framework to properly solve the 'sim-to-real' problem?
5. How could I foster the use of Generative models and 3D Reconstruction methods like Gaussian Splatting to improve the imagination of Robots, which could easily help them think of their next steps in a particular task?
6. How to help the robot understand and function perfectly in an unstructured environment?

Q2.
Purdue is one of the most prestigious institutions in the world, with a reputation as a global leader in AI and Robotics. The SURF program at Purdue will provide me with an ideal platform to transition from theoretical and small-scale research to large-scale system implementation, which excites me a lot. I am particularly drawn to the program's unique synergy between high-performance computing and specialized testing facilities at Purdue. These resources would allow me to gain invaluable hands-on experience and significantly expand my repertoire of practical research skills.

This environment also perfectly supports my academic trajectory. Prof. Arezoo Ardekani’s project on Generative AI for the discovery of new drugs directly aligns with my specialized coursework in Advanced AI and my research experience with 3D Gaussian Splatting. I am eager to apply my knowledge of Diffusion Models, Flow Models, and 3D structural representations to her investigation of equivariant 3D-conditional diffusion, accelerating molecular design through guided search spaces. Similarly, my pursuit of advanced coursework in Reinforcement Learning and Marine Autonomous Vehicles has built a theoretical foundation for Prof. Vishrant Tripathi’s project on Multi-Robot Coordination in the Maritime Environment. My experience developing attention-based fusion transformers for autonomous vehicles would allow me to contribute immediately to his goal of creating communication-efficient control frameworks for heterogeneous maritime swarms.​Finally, my research background in Seismic Data Analytics, where I used VQ-VAEs to enforce physical constraints in the Latent-Faults project, resonates with Prof. Lei Wang’s Physics-Informed ML project. I am excited to apply this "physics-aware" deep learning expertise to his challenge of predicting extreme weather events using idealized atmospheric models.

Q3.
Participation in SURF will be a transformative step towards my long-term goal of pursuing a PhD in AI and Robotics with a focus on reasoning-based learning as well as algorithmic and sensor-based autonomy for complex, real-world scenarios. Beyond technical skills, the program offers a unique opportunity to build global research and entrepreneurial connections and learn the rigorous methodologies of a world-class institution. In the long term, I aspire to translate these research innovations into entrepreneurial ventures, building intelligent models and robots that serve as fundamental drivers of discovery across interdisciplinary fields such as climate resilience and would also enable manufacturing and labor efficiency, undertaking dangerous tasks like mining and disaster response, which are currently done manually.


Q4.
My journey into the field of AI and Robotics has been defined by a continuous loop of exploration, competition, and rigorous research application. It began with my selection for the IIT Madras AI Contingent, where I explored AI through national-level hackathons. I took part in diverse hackathons, from enhancing OCR quality and entity normalization for
multilingual e-commerce text extraction (Amazon ML Hackathon) and building a video-based
interview assessment tool with speech and posture analysis (Plugin Hackathon) to build a credit default prediction system, which placed us in the Top 3 in India, at Convolve 3.0 (IDFC First Bank). I also tackled complex NLP tasks, designing a probabilistic solver for Trexquant that blended heuristics with human-like reasoning to solve word games. My competitive streak culminated at the Inter-IIT Tech Meet 13.0, where I contributed to our team's 5th-place finish by designing a novel adversarial purification framework to detect deepfake images, integrating Explainable AI tools like GradCAM and MOLMO to understand generation artifacts.

The hackathon background deepened my interest in the field of AI and Robotics, with an added advantage of thinking creatively and intuitively in a faster-paced environment. I started by exploring AI research by first collaborating with ImmersoAI and Prof. Pravin Nair to engineer personalized visual generation frameworks using Dreambooth and textual inversion, ensuring character consistency across 2D scenes. Eager to apply these generative skills to scientific problems, I worked with Prof. S.T.G. Raghukanth on Latent-Faults, where we successfully modeled earthquake fault planes using VQ-VAEs despite extreme data scarcity, a work currently under review at the Discover Hazard Journal.

Currently, I am pushing the boundaries of what AI can do in dynamic, physical environments. Under Prof. Kaushik Mitra, I am developing a novel watermarking technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that is resilient to style transfer, with our method currently outperforming State-of-the-Art (SOTA) baselines and being prepared for submission to ECCV. Simultaneously, I am working with Prof. Lelitha Devi Vanajakshi to develop the first-ever attention-based CNN framework specifically designed to predict vehicle trajectories in the chaotic, unstructured traffic of India. To ensure my theoretical knowledge keeps pace with my practical work, I am actively pursuing advanced coursework in Reinforcement Learning, Automated Planning, and Marine Autonomous Vehicles, preparing myself to tackle the complex, system-level challenges that are perfectly central to the SURF program.

Q5.
One significant challenge I faced in my research was during the Latent-Faults project, where I aimed to model earthquake fault planes using deep learning. The primary obstacle was the extreme scarcity of reliable seismic data, which was insufficient for training any kind of Deep Learning models. Standard regression approaches were not able to capture the complex, non-linear physics of fault ruptures, leading to poor generalization. To address this, I refined the research question by fundamentally reframing the problem. Instead of treating it as a standard parameter-to-slip prediction task, I converted it into an image generation task to leverage the latent space-based semantic learning, which aided in understanding physics patterns.

Another significant challenge I faced in research was the Watermarking 3D scenes against style transfer, which was a very complicated task since we had to maintain two important things: one, the watermark needs to flow through the 2D rasterization pipeline and get sustained in the images extracted from the 3D scene, and at the same time, it should not get erased by style transfer. For this problem statement, I started to talk not only to my guide but to other professors working in this field, whose invaluable guidance helped me to come up with the current approach of using a content-driven watermarking method, that would both handle style transfer (since the content of the image/scene doesn't change during style transfer) as well as use a decode plus trainable watermark to overcome this problem of watermark getting lost during 2D image conversion from the 3D scene.

We can develop vaccines, design perfect screening tests and publish groundbreaking data, yet patients still suffer because life does not comply with our protocols. This disconnect drives me. I now realize that if I want to strengthen the intersection of what we can do and what we actually do, I cannot just study the sociology of health. I must master the biological fundamentals first. My application to SURF is a step to understand the cellular mechanisms of disease before I move to effectively scale those solutions to “good health” as a molecular epidemiologist.
 
I first experienced real-world science during high school internships at Biogenomics Pvt. Ltd. and Dorf Ketal. At Biogenomics I learned the fundamentals of molecular work: running PCRs, conducting gel electrophoresis and performing gram staining. The real lesson, however, was learning the techniques that make results reliable like clean controls, careful pipetting and detailed notetaking. It trained me to approach protocol like a chain of methodical steps. At Dorf Ketal I worked with nanoparticles. I assisted with optimizing titanium glycolate (Ti-84) synthesis conditions using TnBT and MEG, aiming to produce high aspect ratio Ti-84 nanoparticles. I tested three temperatures and dilutions, confirming that the literature-standard condition (175°C, 1:500 ratio) produced the optimal high-aspect-ratio nanoparticles. These internships exposed me to research in industrial operations under real-world settings. It widened my view on how research works under pressures and constraints of safety, time, costs and the need for process discipline and traceability.
 
Reproducibility at the bench and discipline under pressures are the two guiding principles that have shaped how I study biology and chemistry. I’ve learnt to think experimentally and move beyond rote memorizing of facts. My coursework at Emory, along with their lab components, have given me a solid foundation in experimental thinking. When I read about disease processes, I build a hypothetical mechanism beginning at the cellular level, an experiment to test it and then a plausible intervention-testing approach. This habit extends to my reading too where I move from concept to hypothesis to clean testing method. Recently when I read a paper on ciliary ARL13B playing a role in regulating the body weight of mice, I began by unpacking the abstract and looking up unfamiliar genes and terms. Next  I worked through the figures to understand what the data showed. Finally, I drafted my own mechanistic model for how the absence/presence of ARL13B in the cilia would alter downstream signalling. I focused on it triggering hormone release and other cues such as hydrophilic signals, that eventually impacted the mice body weight.
 
Recently my research in Prof. Gerardo’s Lab at Emory University has shaped me the most. As the Undergraduate Research Assistant, I work on an ant-fungus system and what changes when a parasite fungus shows up. I culture fungus-garden samples from multiple ant species (higher attines, lower attines and apterostigma), challenge them with parasitic fungi and measure the attraction/inhibition zones created over time. I also manage the day-to-day mechanics of my project work including conducting bioassays, making stock solutions, plate inoculations and monitoring, maintaining colonies and proper documentation. The lesson is constant: outcomes hinge on conditions, and good biology demands controls, consistency, and humility. The mindset of treating every result as something to defend has shaped how I pursue every question.
 
My high school independent project obstacles taught me many valuable lessons. My experiment aimed to analyze the allelopathic effects of sunflower seeds on four crops (flax, fenugreek, moong, hemp and chia). Ambitiously, I planned on setting up a hydroponic system to separate five dependent variables, assuming that a sterile, water-based environment would aid in replicating the advancements in the world of agriculture.
 
My challenges started immediately. First, I realized my design was fundamentally flawed. While staring at the struggling plants, it struck me. The farmers in India that I hoped to help with the outcomes of my project were not growing plants in hydroponic settings. The majority of them grew plants in soil. My expected setup was “clean” but irrelevant to the real-world scenario I was trying to model. Secondly, the hemp component of my setup failed to thrive in the soil conditions, threatening to invalidate the entire dataset. 
 
I tried salvaging a weak dataset but was soon forced to start over. This time I scrapped the hydroponic system and redesigned the experiment using a soil-based method. This approach was far more tedious, requiring manual measurement of results and careful control of variables without automation. However, it mimicked the actual environmental conditions of the crops.
 
This changed strategy allowed me to generate a robust dataset, with statistical significance being established by one-way ANOVA tests. This experience was my first lesson in scientific resilience. I learned the hard way that when a plan breaks, the solution isn't always to force the original method to work. Rather as my teacher put it succinctly “the solution is to refine the question to ensure the answer actually matters.”
 
I’m ready for a research experience where my determination and consistency is channeled into one direction of full-time research with real ownership. What draws me to SURF is the way it turns a summer project into a full research cycle with structured scientific communication. I’m not just entering a lab to “help out” when I can. I would work to produce original data and results where the work can be explained, challenged and understood outside the bench. The workshops and program milestones would keep my work from becoming mere lab tasks and the symposium and final report would enforce clarity. Knowing I will have to defend my reasoning and incorporate feedback that exposes gaps and inspires the next iteration is exactly what I want from a research program.
 
I’m studying Biology and Chemistry on the pre-health track and I plan on pursuing my PhD in molecular epidemiology. My long-term goals in STEM sit between two worlds of mechanistic lab science and real-world health outcomes. If I want to work on strengthening the intersection of what we can do and what we actually do in health sciences, I need to do more than just generate data. I need to strengthen my ability to turn biological questions into testable designs and learn to communicate these uncertainties responsibly. Purdue’s SURF program would be a great step towards this for me. 
 
SURF places undergraduates inside working labs where the faculty would teach you how a research team thinks, argues, revises and communicates. That structure appeals greatly to me because it emphasizes training by real mentorship, not just plain lab hours. Dr. Nicholas Noinaj’s work with gram-negative bacterial surface proteins that help infect hosts and evade immunity fits with the kind of research I want to work on. One result that intrigues me from his work is when they locked BamA in place with engineered crosslinks, the machine stopped working. The function reverted back to normal only when the lock was chemically released. Such concrete results help you see exactly what step the cells depend on. It also points to a practical idea as if you can jam a process the bacterium cannot survive without, you may have a way to fight infection.
 
Dr. Catherine Searle widens the lens further. Her work on how biodiversity shapes infectious disease risk echoes what I study in Dr. Gerardo’s lab: disease depends on the community, not just the pathogen. She addresses questions like who are the best hosts? What changes when the community changes? In a study on the amphibian pathogen Bd, she manipulated host diversity and found a clear dilution effect: as species richness increased, disease risk in larval amphibians fell. This approach appeals to me greatly because it treats the environment as part of biology, not just the backdrop. Thai underscores that impact can come from understanding the conditions that raise disease risk, not only from inventing new tools.
 
SURF gives me the one thing I can’t get from scattered hours in a lab: sustained time to run a project from developing a sharp question to answering a defensible conclusion. Over eleven weeks, I can learn the system, test ideas, troubleshoot what fails, and repeat until the signal is real. I also want the discipline of turning that work into a clear claim of what the data supports, what it doesn’t, and what should come next. That kind of rigor and accountability is exactly what I’m looking for as I train to link mechanistic science to better health outcomes.

The path so far has already given me glimpses of this role: implementing FPGA‑based accelerators to cut the compute cycles of a vision transformer from seven to three, or benchmarking different machine‑learning models for predicting SpaceX Falcon 9 landing outcomes with around 90 percent accuracy.Through SURF, I hope to deepen three things that are essential for that future: first, a more mature understanding of experimental design and statistical rigor in AI research; second, the habit of writing for and collaborating with an interdisciplinary team; and third, the humility to debug not just code, but my own assumptions.

At IIT Jodhpur, where I am pursuing Data Science and AI with a 9.0/10 CGPA, I chose courses that forced me to engage with both the mathematical and systems sides of computing: pattern recognition, optimization in machine learning, operating systems, computer networks, databases, and data structures and algorithms.  Outside the classroom, I built projects that let me connect theory with messy data: network analyses of the Indian stock market using graph‑theoretic tools like Louvain community detection, crisis‑time behavior studies using pre‑ and mid‑COVID data, and geospatial codebases that had to run reliably for external clients.Each project taught me something different: how to design pipelines that do not crumble on edge cases, how to quantify uncertainty, and how to say “I was wrong” when the data disagreed with an elegant idea.

My journey into entrepreneurship and leadership has come from the same restless curiosity. NeuralSky began as a small effort to use satellite data for better decision‑making, and over time it grew into a B2B product stack that serviced more than sixty startups, mostly in urban planning and agriculture. Along the way, I learned how to talk to customers, translate vague problem statements into tractable ML tasks, and pitch at events like the Inter‑IIT E‑summit, the Hult Prize, and IIT Madras’s entrepreneurial bootcamp, where our team placed as national first runner‑up.These experiences grounded my research ambitions: a model is not useful simply because it has a high F1‑score; it must plug into a workflow, respect constraints, and still be understandable to non‑experts.

The obstacles behind these lines on my CV are harder to quantify. Growing up, money for school was never guaranteed. When I was 13, I realized that no one was going to magically fix this for me, so I stopped treating YouTube as just an escape and started treating it like work. I scripted, filmed, edited, learned basic thumbnails and analytics, and slowly grew a channel that eventually crossed eight million total views and fifty thousand subscribers. The revenue from that channel, plus early freelance video‑editing and programming work, paid my school fees as well as helped at home. Balancing this with preparation for the JEE and later SAT and IELTS meant waking up earlier than my classmates and quietly saying no to things that normal teenagers do without thinking. There were months when my grades slipped, when a sponsorship fell through, or when an algorithm update wiped out earnings overnight. Each time, I went back to first principles: what am I trying to optimize for, and what can I control today?

This mindset carried me through later setbacks. When early attempts at Olympiads did not translate into the ranks I wanted, I had to confront the gap between effort and outcome and adjust how I studied rather than just how long I studied. When I first encountered real research at ISI and ETH Zurich, I realized how often experiments fail and how much patience is needed to get a clean result; that was humbling but also strangely comforting because it echoed my own path. [1] Whenever I felt out of place – as a student from a modest background sitting in high‑end labs, or presenting at national competitions – I reminded myself that I had already navigated steeper gradients. Instead of trying to appear flawless, I leaned into honesty: asking naïve questions, admitting confusion, and seeking mentorship wherever possible.

SURF, to me, is not just a line on a resume but a chance to stand in a community where curiosity, discipline, and humility are the norm. I want to bring to Purdue the same energy that helped me pay my school fees at 13 and later build systems that serve real users: a willingness to do unglamorous work, to take responsibility when something breaks, and to stay up late not because of a deadline but because a question has lodged itself in my mind. In return, I hope to leave SURF with sharper research instincts, deeper technical skills in machine learning and data‑driven science, and mentors and peers who will challenge me long after the summer ends. That is the next step in a journey that started with a borrowed physics book and a second‑hand smartphone, and that I now hope will pass through Purdue on its way to a life in research and impact‑driven engineering.

statement_of_purpose:
Since high-school, I had been determined to pursue higher studies where I could do research on fundamental problems in mathematics — not because I had already found my topic of research, but simply because I had always enjoyed solving mathematical problems. Unfortunately, in my country, it is not very common to pursue higher education in mathematics due to limited opportunities. In contrast, computer science, and other engineering courses are in high demand and only a few highly-ranked students get the opportunity to enrol themselves in top colleges. This is because CS courses are designed in such a way that they generate the possibility of pursuing research either in theoretical computer science or in mathematics, along with the possibility of pursuing a corporate career.
I decided to pursue computer science, focussing on theoretical computer science, as it was the most mathematics-adjacent engineering subject I could find. It gave me the opportunity to explore the kind of mathematics that I enjoyed, i.e. algorithmic mathematics.

I believe that the SURF programme would cater well to my aspirations and provide me with an excellent opportunity, because of the academic strength of the faculty of Purdue University.
In the long term, I am determined to pursue an academic research career in algorithmic and computational mathematics and algorithm design for various purposes, including the former. This exceptional opportunity would immerse me in an academically rigorous environment, where the exchange of high-quality ideas and work would provide unparalleled experiential learning, which, in turn, would enable me to contribute to the STEM ecosystem with greater efficacy. Working under the guidance of the faculty would provide me with a strong environment for pursuing my interests and advancing my research. Another major benefit would be that I could bring the perspective and experience I have accrued, allowing me to explore further.

During the course of this programme, I’d be excited to work with Prof. Alexandria Volkening, Prof. Jenna DiVincenzo, or Prof. Qi Guo, on their respective projects — ‘Mathematical Modelling to Forecast the 2026 US Elections’, ‘Gradual Verification: Assuring Programs Incrementally’, and ‘Next-Generation Compact and Robust 2D and 3D Imaging System Development’.
Professor Volkening has done very interesting work on pattern recognition in mathematical epidemiology. I particularly enjoyed reading about the inspired usage of compartmental models — typically used for biological contagions — to model social contagions such as political behaviour, in her paper ‘Forecasting elections using compartmental models of infection’ (2020).
Professor DiVincenzo has done significant work on gradual verifiers. I’ve been going through her papers, such as ‘Gradual C0: Symbolic Execution for Gradual Verification’ (2024), and I’d be interesting in exploring how the verifier could be expanded to the wider C language. I’d also be interested in exploring and working on solutions that evaluate gradual verifiers’ soundness and their adherence to gradual properties.
I’ve worked on a few projects in image processing, including quantum image processing and image processing based deep learning, during my undergraduate research career. Continuing in that field under the guidance of Professor Guo would provide me with an opportunity to deepen my understanding of the subject and its variations. Another benefit would be that I could bring the perspective and experience I have accrued, allowing me to make connections and comparisons to the work I’ve done before.

My past research experience has allowed me to explore different domains so that I may discover my specific interests, and in doing so has given me an eclectic research background.
Since the beginning of my 4th semester, I have been a core member of a research team under the supervision of one of our university professors, Prof. S. K. Saha. Our problem involves designing deep learning algorithms for the classification of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC) from clinical white-light images. Most of the existing literature on the topic uses histopathological images - often manually pre-annotated. Our problem was compounded by the scarcity of well-documented and extensive clinical white-light OSCC image datasets.
My main contribution was designing a lightweight classifier, based on a vision foundation model as a feature embedding extractor. The results of our model are comparable to, or better than, those of any of the benchmark results of heavyweight pipelines. To our knowledge, this is the first work that clearly demonstrates the direct transferability of dermatology vision foundation models to the oral cancer scenario, especially in low-resource environments, where OSCC is most prevalent. A first-author paper based on this work has been submitted for the IEEE ISBI 2026 conference in London. 
We have also tested a similar pipeline for histopathological images, with comparably good results. A paper based on this portion of our work led to a publication in the MICAD 2025 conference in London. 
Additionally, I did a project at the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI), Kolkata (as part of a summer school) in June-July 2025, which was an offshoot of the above work, where I designed a different classification model using a convolutional autoencoder and a SVM.
I have also been working on an “AI for Social Good” research project, under the supervision of another of our professors, Prof. Sarbani Roy, since the beginning of my 5th semester. The research problem involves using a variety of deep learning models to develop a pipeline for landslide severity detection from multimodal data, mainly images. My work so far has involved designing classifiers (and its corresponding feature embedding generator) to separate the landslide and non-landslide data, and exploring pretrained vision foundation models for feature generation and image segmentation.
In June 2025, I did an internship on Quantum Image Processing (QImP) at the Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee. I was tasked with designing and implementing a Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection (QHED) algorithm, as described in Yao et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031041 (2017). I was able to finish this work well before the deadline and was also able to identify gaps in the existing literature.
Some of my main research interests lie in the fields of algorithm design and mathematics (specifically in computational and convex geometry, number theory, combinatorics, etc.). I enjoy designing and have designed several algorithms for a wide variety of purposes. For example, once we were asked — given two polygons, say pentagons, find out whether they intersect or not. My lab partner and I decided to extend the problem to cover any two convex polygons. To that effect, we designed a convex hull selection algorithm from scratch, which formed the base of a C code to generate a convex polygon from any given set of points. At this point, our endeavour for a robust, generalised solution to the problem had turned into a full-fledged mini-project, and we further implemented a series of checks to decide, not only if the polygons were intersecting, but also whether one polygon was inside the other, if they were inside and touching, or if they were outside each other but still touching, or even whether they were the same polygon.
I have also designed a Qt Creator based C++ implementation of the classic ‘Snake Game’, with several unique features, as well as built FTP, CSMA/CD, and other network servers from scratch in C++.

It is inevitable that one will face obstacles, big or small, in their lives. I’ve been fortunate enough to encounter ones on the smaller side, or atleast ones I could overcome smoothly. In the pursuit of research, one will invariably face numerous challenges. If such problems may be considered obstacles, I’ve experienced a few, one of which is mentioned below.
During my internship on quantum computing at IIT Roorkee, which was hosted by the physics department, I encountered several distinct challenges, despite the relatively short duration of the experience. I had a limited timeframe — about a week — to familiarize myself with the required material, largely drawn from Nielsen & Chuang’s Quantum Computing textbook, before the internship. While I managed to have a solid grasp of quantum computing by the start of the internship, my lack of understanding of quantum mechanics became a minor hurdle. To overcome this, I engaged in discussions with the graduate students, who were very helpful in guiding me through the basics, to establish a foundational understanding of quantum mechanics, which in turn enhanced my understanding of quantum computing. As my project focused on quantum image processing, specifically QHED — a task rooted firmly in computer science — I found myself without much specialized support in the physics department. To tackle this, I turned to academic papers and extensive literature surveys, online resources like Wikipedia, pushing through the information gap on my own. In the end, I was able to design and successfully run the required algorithm well ahead of schedule.

Finally, for the committee and faculty: Thank you very much for your time and consideration. I look forward to hearing from you soon.

statement_of_purpose:
What Led Me to Neuroscience
Curiosity! Curiosity is what makes us the most beautiful part of the universe; yes, black holes, neutron stars and all are brilliant and complex, but they all fail to shine in front of the part of the universe that tries to understand itself, the brain. My journey into understanding how our brain works began in ninth grade when I took an artificial intelligence course, initially just because it was "the new thing." However, as I learned more about AI, I began to appreciate our human brain in ways I hadn't before. How does it take sensory inputs and, using billions of neurons and trillions of synapses, magically make sense of everything? How does it maintain an unbroken stream of consciousness and memory that makes us feel alive? The realisation that spontaneous chemical reactions can give rise to beings who think they have free will and emotions genuinely excited me.
When I entered IIT Bombay for my bachelor's degree, I dove deeper by taking a psychology course in my first year. I was exhilarated when I could draw parallels between how the eye processes visual information and how computer vision models work. This fascination led me to reach out to professors and explore opportunities in neuroscience research.
But it was during my computational neuroscience internship at the Donders Institute that this curiosity crystallised into a concrete research direction. Working with Prof. Marius Peelen, I developed RSA and MDS-based neural decoding pipelines to analyse primate electrophysiology data, comparing IT cortex responses with human fMRI and AlexNet features. It wasn't just that my model achieved 74% accuracy; it was when it happened. Pinpointing that information processing spike at exactly 100ms post-stimulus shifted my focus from simple classification to the underlying mechanics: how do entire populations of neurons actually encode and transform what we learn?
This question has since defined my research trajectory across three complementary domains. At the University of Tokyo, under the guidance of Prof. Takashi Kohno, I'm designing FPGA-optimised neuromorphic circuits and implementing attention-based spiking transformers. I am learning to balance biological plausibility with computational efficiency through the BluePyOpt-based fitting of Piecewise Quadratic Neuron models. My aerospace work at Missouri S&T involved architecting meta-MARL control systems for satellite guidance, which provided me with hands-on experience with state-space representations and detecting transitions between operational regimes. Even my role as a Teaching Assistant for the Analog Electronics Lab at IIT Bombay, under Prof. Pradeep Sarin, supervising labs on op-amp circuits, feedback systems, and instrumentation amplifiers, reinforced the understanding that understanding neural circuits requires both computational analysis skills and circuit-level hardware intuition.
I find myself at the intersection of multiple fields: astronomy, neuroscience, and electronics, all tied together by large-scale population optimisation problems and my innate curiosity. Each experience has contributed to building a piece of what I need. Still, the critical frontier isn't just better recording technology or faster circuits; it's developing physics-informed inference frameworks that can interpret multimodal neural data and extract interpretable dynamics. This is precisely why Professor Jayant's project on "Probing transitions in motor learning via physics-informed state-space models" represents where I need to be next.
Why SURF at Purdue
I've admired the Nano Neurotechnology Lab's work since learning about their custom NeuroGrids, which allow simultaneous electrical and optical imaging of the brain. Prof. Jayant's lab is pushing the frontier of understanding neural dynamics, and I would be honoured to contribute.
After discussing the project with Prof. Jayant and receiving his support for my application, I committed to this opportunity. There are other great summer programs out there, but I don't believe in backing out of commitments once they're made. This feels like one of those meaningful leaps of faith, when you find a project that aligns with your path and a mentor willing to guide you, you go for it.
SURF offers something unique: ten focused weeks to build a complete, validated modelling framework from the ground up. The goal of creating an open-source toolkit that can predict learning transitions and guide adaptive brain-computer interfaces for rehabilitation mirrors my own long-term vision. I hope to develop real-time, adaptive neuroprosthetics eventually, and this project touches every part of that pipeline: extracting latent states, detecting transitions, and closing the loop with control.
My Envisioned Contribution
Drawing from the project description and our conversations, I would aim to contribute through a Bayesian switching dynamical system framework that incorporates circuit-level biophysical priors. Specifically, I'd hope to:
Integrate multimodal data, using methods I developed at Donders to align surface potentials with cellular recordings.
Apply biophysical constraints from my neuromorphic work to maintain the model's interpretability and biological grounding.
Implement transition detection, leveraging my background in control systems to identify shifts between learning phases.
Work toward closed-loop validation, leveraging my experience with real-time embedded systems from satellite projects.
I know ten weeks is short, but it's one of the longest summer programmes (which are usually 8 weeks) I have come across, a plus point for choosing SURF. I'm prepared to focus on whichever component Prof. Jayant believes is most valuable. My goal isn't to do everything at once; it's to learn a rigorous, physics-informed approach to inference that I can apply in graduate school and beyond.
Long-Term Goals & How SURF Fits
Ultimately, I aim to pursue a PhD in neural engineering or computational neuroscience and work as a research scientist developing adaptive, closed-loop neuroprosthetics. This requires mastering three interconnected areas: neural recording technology, dynamical systems theory, and adaptive control. Prof. Jayant's project beautifully spans all three.
SURF would provide not only technical training but also mentorship, hands-on experience with cutting-edge tools, and clarity on the research questions I want to pursue in a PhD. It's a chance to learn how translational neuroscience labs operate and to start building the connections and vision that will shape my career.
What I've Done to Prepare
I've deliberately built my path to be ready for this kind of work:
Coursework: Beyond my Engineering Physics core, I've taken psychology, neuromorphic engineering, and minors in AI & Aerospace to build a cross-disciplinary foundation.
Research: My internships at Donders, Tokyo, and Missouri S&T were chosen to fill specific gaps: neural decoding, biophysical modelling, and control systems.
Teaching: As a TA across three departments (analog electronics, biosciences, and physics) taught me to explain complex concepts and deepened my own understanding.
Large-scale projects: Working with the Zwicky Transient Facility at Caltech, I helped build a pipeline that sifted through hundreds of thousands of images, teaching me end-to-end data analysis and resilience.
Independent learning: When I couldn't find a suitable course, I taught myself, whether it was Python for neuroscience or spiking neural networks through papers and online resources.
Challenges & Support
My path hasn't always been straightforward. Preparing for the intensely competitive JEE Advanced exam taught me discipline. When I started at IIT Bombay, I was underweight, and I committed to improving my health by building a routine that included going to the gym, running 10K, and enhancing my nutrition, which I continue to maintain today.
Not having a neuroscience department at IIT pushed me to be proactive; I cold-emailed over 30 professors before landing my Donders internship. Through it all, mentors like Prof. Varun Bhalerao have been invaluable, guiding me both personally and professionally and encouraging me to pursue interdisciplinary research with bold confidence.
Why Now
I'm at a turning point. I've gathered tools from various fields, neural decoding, circuit design, and control theory, and now I'm eager to integrate them into a unified approach to real-world neuroscience problems. Prof. Jayant's project is the perfect training ground. His willingness to mentor someone with my interdisciplinary background is an opportunity I don't take lightly.
In Closing
For me, science has always been driven by curiosity, the kind that makes you wonder how chemical reactions can give rise to a thinking, feeling self. My grandmother once told me that a good life isn't measured by time, but by the depth of one's experiences. This pursuit of understanding feels less like a career choice and more like a calling. The ancient verse from the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam (1.2.10) captures this essence: "kāmasya nendriya-prītir lābho jīveta yāvatā jīvasya tattva-jijñāsā nārtho yaś ceha karmabhiḥ." ("A human being is meant for inquiry about the absolute truth.”) This deep-seated need for inquiry first drew my gaze to the brilliant, energetic phenomena of the cosmos, and it now compels me to look inward, to the profound mysteries of the brain. The brain's ability to learn and remember is more than a fascinating engineering puzzle; it is a fundamental truth about existence that awaits discovery.
This project represents precisely the convergence I've been searching for: multimodal neural data, biophysical constraints, and closed-loop control. It aligns with my skills, my curiosity, and my goals. I'm not just looking for a summer position; I'm seeking the mentorship and foundation that will shape my career in translational bioelectronics. I would be honoured to contribute to this inquiry at Purdue, and I am ready to dive in with focused dedication.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Over time, I became especially interested in understanding how computation is realized in hardware and how architectural decisions affect performance, efficiency, and reliability.
I first explored this field through a course project on designing a RISC-V processor in Verilog, where I implemented both sequential and pipelined architectures with hazard detection, forwarding, and control logic. Debugging pipeline behavior at the register-transfer level taught me the importance of reasoning about system state, understanding the value of each register and flip-flop at every clock cycle. This project motivated me to join the Centre for VLSI Design and Embedded System Technologies (CVEST) at IIIT Hyderabad as an undergraduate researcher.
At CVEST, I am currently working under Prof. Zia Abbas on a custom FPGA IP for 7th-order polynomial regression to digitally assist a current reference circuit under PVT variations. The system predicts output current based on frequency-based process monitors, supply voltage, and temperature, and computes trim bits in real time. I implemented the regression engine in Verilog using fixed-point arithmetic, interfaced via AXI-Lite, and controlled through bare-metal C in Vitis on a Zynq-7000 platform. A key challenge involved precision instability, which I resolved by redesigning the datapath and normalization strategy after careful analysis of numerical behavior at the hardware level. This project strengthened my ability to bridge algorithmic modeling and hardware constraints.
In parallel, I explored accelerator architectures through a course project on accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation workloads on the Versal VCK5000 platform. Using roofline analysis, I identified memory bandwidth as the primary bottleneck in the baseline design. By restructuring the computation, improving data reuse, and optimizing tiling and precision(broadcasting and packet-streaming), I transitioned the kernel from a memory-bound to a compute-bound regime.This experience deepened my understanding of dataflow and architectural trade-offs in modern accelerators.
Beyond design, the SPARC Nano X program conducted across IIT Hyderabad and Purdue University—provided invaluable exposure to semiconductor fabrication. Designing and fabricating a MIM capacitor in a cleanroom environment gave me an end-to-end perspective of the hardware stack, from devices to systems. Combined with my mentorship at Texas Instruments through the BYTE program, these experiences have prepared me for rigorous, hands-on research.
I enjoy using AI as a tool to make hardware processes more efficient across metrics such as performance, energy, and reliability, while also understanding how these systems function at a fundamental level. Although modern AI-based coding tools can accelerate development, they often introduce layers of abstraction that hide what is happening inside the system.What motivates me is going beyond that abstraction by reasoning about system state and register-level behavior at each clock cycle to understand and fix problems when they arise.

My field of interest lies at the intersection of hardware and artificial intelligence, focusing both on making AI models run efficiently on hardware and on using AI techniques to improve the efficiency, reliability, and performance of electronic circuits.

What attracted me to the Purdue SURF program is how closely the available projects match my current coursework and research. I am particularly interested in the projects on FPGA-based acceleration of attention models and automated characterization of emerging AI hardware, as they directly relate to my work in fixed-point design, hardware–software co-design, and system-level debugging at CVEST.
Because I am already working on similar problems—such as implementing polynomial regression models on FPGA and optimizing dataflow for accelerator platforms—I feel I can adapt quickly to the research pace and contribute meaningfully during the internship. Seeing the close connection between fabrication, materials, and electrical engineering at facilities like the Birck Nanotechnology Center showed me how interdisciplinary work enables practical innovation from devices to systems. This combination of strong project alignment and a collaborative research environment is why I chose the SURF program.
In addition to technical development, I am eager to strengthen my research communication and collaboration skills through SURF. I hope to work closely with graduate students and faculty in designing experiments, documenting methodologies, and presenting results through posters or technical reports. Developing a reproducible characterization or acceleration framework as a tangible research outcome will be an important goal for me, as it will help me learn how to translate engineering work into clear, shareable research contributions.
My long-term career goal is to build strong expertise in VLSI and embedded hardware design, with a focus on accelerator architectures and hardware–AI co-design. I eventually plan to work in the semiconductor or computing industry, contributing to the design of next-generation accelerators and efficient hardware platforms.
I see this internship as a critical step in bridging my current undergraduate training with advanced research, allowing me to clarify my research interests, build meaningful mentorships, and prepare for a research-driven career in STEM.
Through my first-choice project, Automated Characterization Platform for Beyond-Silicon “CMOS+X” AI Hardware Prototypes, I hope to gain hands-on experience in hardware validation and system-level testing for emerging semiconductor technologies. Working with the NI-PXIe characterization platform and participating in PCB design and test development will strengthen my understanding of how advanced devices and 3D-integrated systems are evaluated in practice. This will complement my background in circuit design and FPGA-based modeling by exposing me to the often-overlooked but critical stage of translating prototypes into reliable, measurable systems. 
In my second-choice project, Real-Time FPGA Acceleration of Attention-Based Bidirectional LSTM Networks, I aim to deepen my skills in hardware–software co-design and real-time AI deployment. Implementing quantized and fixed-point models on FPGA and embedded GPU platforms will allow me to build on my current experience in precision-aware design and accelerator optimization. This project will help me better understand how algorithmic choices in sequence models translate into hardware trade-offs involving latency, bandwidth, and resource utilization, which directly aligns with my interest in efficient accelerator architectures.
My third-choice project, Machine Learning for Semiconductor Packaging Automation, will expose me to the application of machine learning in a manufacturing and robotics context. Learning how vision-based models are used to automate packaging processes will broaden my perspective beyond chip design to system-level automation and validation. This experience will be valuable for developing a holistic view of the semiconductor pipeline, from fabrication and packaging to deployment.
Across all three projects, I hope to build strong mentorship relationships, improve my ability to design and communicate experiments, and develop confidence in tackling open-ended research problems. 
One of the most significant challenges in my academic journey occurred during my preparation for the JEE Main and JEE Advanced examinations, among the most competitive entrance exams in India. The breadth and depth of the syllabus required strong conceptual clarity under intense time pressure. To address this, I made it a habit to approach professors immediately after class to clarify doubts, and before subsequent lectures to resolve questions from previous topics. When instructors were unavailable, I revisited textbooks, re-derived concepts from first principles, and attempted problems again independently. This approach helped me develop discipline, persistence, and confidence in self-learning.
As I transitioned into research, I encountered open-ended problems with no predefined solutions. I learned to combine multiple resources, including research papers, technical documentation, online forums, and AI-assisted tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot. I treat these tools as aids for exploration rather than answers, validating all conclusions through reasoning and experimentation. When needed, I also seek direct guidance from professors after initial investigation to confirm understanding or refine my approach.

The goal was to predict the output current of an analog current reference using polynomial regression based on digitally measurable parameters: two frequency-based process monitors (f₁ and f₂), supply voltage (V), and temperature (T). The regression model was implemented fully in hardware using fixed-point arithmetic. During validation, I observed unstable fractional outputs despite stable integer values, initially suspecting issues in the AXI data path or control logic. After systematic debugging, including isolating and printing fractional components, I identified insufficient precision in the 32.32 fixed-point representation used for polynomial evaluation. By redesigning the datapath using a 16.48 format and restructuring normalization stages, the prediction stabilized and matched expected behavior.
This experience reinforced the value of methodical debugging.

statement_of_purpose:
My area of research is in robotics and machine learning, as I am interested in developing autonomous systems that can operate reliably in complex and uncertain environments. Robotics combines sensing, perception, control, and decision-making, while machine learning provides tools that extend beyond classical control and perception, enabling systems to adapt, generalise, and learn from data. The combination of these two fields excites me because it allows robots to move beyond predetermined rules and make their own decisions. My interest in this area has been shaped by hands-on experience in designing, building, and working with real robotic systems. I was part of a student team that designed and built an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV), and I was also part of a student team that built sounding rockets. Apart from these technical projects, I have undertaken various research projects in the field of controls and robotics. Through these projects, I saw firsthand the practical challenges of reliability, uncertainty, and decision-making in physical systems.

One issue that stood out to me is the large gap between simulations and real-world experiments. While working with physical systems, I saw that simulations often fail to capture uncertainty, noise, and unexpected behaviours that appear in real environments. A separate but equally important challenge is that learning-based methods offer robust and often optimal algorithms, but testing and validating them on real systems is expensive, time-consuming, and risky. As a result, many promising approaches remain difficult to deploy on real hardware. These challenges motivated me to continue pursuing robotics and learning-based research, to make algorithms that are reliable in real-world conditions and practical to implement and test on physical systems.

As part of the Marine Autonomous Vehicles Lab, under Prof. Abhilash Somayajula, we were a student team working on the design, simulation, and deployment of an AUV. My work combined sensing, estimation, control, and system-level integration in both theory and a strong focus on practical implementation. My contributions focused on sensor integration and state estimation using an IMU, Doppler Velocity Logger (DVL), depth sensor, and acoustic modem, on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano. To minimise the cost and logistical burden of underwater testing, we developed a physics-based simulation framework for the AUV. I modelled the vehicle dynamics and implemented classical control and guidance strategies, including PID and LQR controllers, along with Line-of-Sight (LOS) and fully actuated guidance laws. The theoretical foundations for this work were derived from coursework, including "Control of Automotive Systems" and "Principles of Guidance and Control of Autonomous Systems," which informed the design of controllers, stability analysis, and performance evaluation. I also conducted energy consumption analysis across different control strategies to estimate battery requirements for real-world missions. Our work culminated in participation at the Singapore AUV Challenge, where we placed 9th in the qualifiers. I also presented our results at the OMAE Conference 2024 in Singapore.

Building on these model-based approaches, we later transitioned to data-driven system identification methods to improve computational efficiency and model fidelity. Drawing on concepts learned in the Data-Driven Modelling of Complex Systems course, I identified both linear and quadratic dynamical models of the AUV using Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy). The Dynamic Mode Decomposition with Control (DMDc) was also used to obtain a best-fit linear model of the system on the trajectory and control input data collected from simulations. Comparative analysis revealed that the linear SINDy-based model, when combined with LQR control, yielded superior path-following performance compared to an LQR controller directly designed on the complete nonlinear model, while facilitating faster computation of control inputs.

I also worked with Team Abhyuday on the development of sounding rockets. My primary role was designing and implementing the flight computer for accurate altitude estimation and parachute deployment at apogee. I implemented a Kalman filter to fuse data from an IMU, GPS, and pressure sensor, improving estimation accuracy under dynamic flight conditions. I wrote the embedded software for the flight computer and participated extensively in ground testing and system integration, including brainstorming and validating the parachute ejection mechanism. During our launch at the Spaceport America Cup in New Mexico, the system successfully predicted altitude with 97% accuracy, contributing to our team's placement as 1st in Asia and 20th globally.

As a recipient of the Young Research Fellowship awarded to 17 students out of over 300 applicants at IIT Madras, I worked with Prof. Satadal Ghosh on vision-based navigation and control for autonomous systems. I implemented LiDAR odometry using the open-source KISS-ICP framework and developed stereo visual odometry pipelines using ORB feature detection, brute-force feature matching, and PnP with RANSAC for pose estimation and outlier rejection. To improve robustness, I integrated inertial data and utilised the OpenVINS-Mono framework to achieve monocular visual–inertial odometry. I also explored perception-driven autonomy by implementing YOLOv11 for object detection and ByteTrack for multi-object tracking and localisation on the KITTI dataset.

In the summer of 2025, I completed a 12-week, fully funded international research internship at Aalto University, Finland, working under the guidance of Prof. Ville Kyrki on system identification for an F1TENTH autonomous vehicle. I developed a multi-node ROS2 communication pipeline to interface an OptiTrack motion capture system with the onboard Jetson Xavier, using a middleware laptop to ensure synchronised transmission of state estimates and control commands. Using experimental data, I performed system identification by fitting parameters of a nonlinear bicycle model. I also conducted a detailed latency analysis to decouple actuator dynamics from motion capture delays. To validate my findings, I incorporated wheel encoder data from an Arduino, allowing me to precisely identify the source of system delays. This experience enhanced my skills in experimental robotics, modelling, and real-time systems, while also exposing me to collaborative international research.

I am currently working with Prof. Rachel K.K on developing control algorithms for multi-robot formation control and obstacle avoidance using Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs) and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs). We have extended this approach to multi-robot formations using a virtual centre-based formulation. The formation is modelled as a virtual circle whose centre and radius are optimised online, allowing the team to move and adapt its size in response to obstacles, enabling navigation in cluttered environments. The formation motion and radius are obtained by solving an optimization problem subject to CLF and CBF constraints. The initial formulation was non-convex, so I introduced suitable relaxations and derived an error bound to reformulate it as a convex problem. We have validated this framework in both simulation and experiments on TurtleBot4 robots, demonstrating safe and stable navigation. I aim to publish these results in the near future.

My interest in machine learning has grown in tandem with my research in robotics. I have completed coursework in Foundations of Machine Learning and Data Analytics, and applied these concepts in a project on LLM-as-a-Judge score prediction, where the goal was to predict evaluation scores for language model outputs without using an external judge model. I worked with a multilingual dataset consisting of metric names and prompt–response pairs with human-assigned scores that were heavily skewed toward high values. To address the imbalance, I introduced a negative sampling strategy by mismatching metric embeddings with prompt–response pairs and assigning a score of zero to these pairs. For metrics with both high and low scores, I generated synthetic samples by interpolating between the embeddings, biasing them toward lower-quality responses. This helped the model learn to distinguish clearly between good and poor outputs. I then trained an ensemble regression model combining XGBoost, Random Forest, and Support Vector Regression, which generalised well across the full score range.

While many programs offer summer research opportunities, I am particularly drawn to SURF because of its strong emphasis on mentorship, structured research training, and access to world-class research facilities. The program's focus on close interaction with faculty and graduate students, combined with professional development activities, makes it well-suited for students who are serious about pursuing research careers. In particular, SURF's interdisciplinary and collaborative environment aligns well with my interests in robotics and machine learning, where meaningful progress often happens at the intersection of multiple fields. The opportunity to work on real research problems using advanced experimental platforms is especially attractive, as it allows ideas to be tested beyond theory or small-scale simulations.

Participation in SURF would directly support my long-term goal of pursuing a PhD in robotics and building a career in research, either in an industry research lab or in academia. Through SURF, I hope to gain deeper research experience, improve my ability to formulate and communicate research ideas, and learn how to identify impactful and feasible research directions. Exposure to rigorous research practices and mentorship from experienced researchers will help me understand what it takes to succeed in a PhD program. In the long term, I aim to develop autonomous systems that are reliable, practical, and beneficial to society, and SURF would be an essential step toward building the foundation needed to achieve these goals.

Research itself has been one of the main challenges in my academic journey, as it rarely yields immediate results. In hardware-based projects and field testing, I often encountered unexpected bugs, failures, and inconsistencies that required patience and repeated iteration. These experiences taught me to stay persistent, debug systematically, and accept setbacks as part of the research process. Another challenge I faced is that research problems are rarely well-defined at the start. To address this, I regularly met with professors and mentors to clarify the problem and refine my research direction. We went back and forth on various ideas, some of which were successful, while others were not. These discussions helped me better understand the problem space and identify feasible approaches. When certain directions required additional technical knowledge, I attended seminars and research talks hosted by faculty members and took extra courses recommended by my mentors. Through this process, I learned how to refine research questions, build the required background, and steadily make progress. Together, these experiences have prepared me well for rigorous research and the next stage of my academic journey.

But what lingered wasn't the optimization itself; it was the dataset: nested medical records revealing an 83-fold price variation for identical obstetric procedures across California facilities. The technical challenge was solved, but the fundamental question remained: how do we build intelligent systems that don't just process data efficiently, but extract meaningful patterns that drive decisions that matter? This tension—between computational power and genuine insight, between algorithmic sophistication and real-world impact—is what draws me to AI research.

My journey into machine learning and data science began not with textbook algorithms but with messy, real-world problems that demanded both statistical rigor and engineering discipline. At IIT Kanpur, my double major in Statistics & Data Science and Economic Sciences taught me that the most compelling research questions emerge at intersections—where mathematical theory meets economic behavior, where machine learning intersects with domain expertise, where computational methods encounter human decision-making. Whether developing hybrid SARIMAX-LSTM models for agricultural commodity price forecasting (achieving R² of 0.84 over 22 years of volatile data) or engineering 15+ microstructure features from 930,000 high-frequency order book records for cryptocurrency market regime detection, I've learned that different data modalities demand fundamentally different analytical approaches. This realization shapes how I think about artificial intelligence: not as a monolithic field of generic algorithms, but as a diverse ecosystem where understanding the underlying data structure, the domain constraints, and the human context is as crucial as the computational methods themselves.

What particularly fascinates me are the emerging challenges in building AI systems that are not just accurate but also robust, interpretable, and trustworthy when deployed in complex, real-world environments. During my work on fraud detection systems analyzing 284,000+ financial transactions, I encountered the classic challenge of severe class imbalance (0.17% fraud rate). The naive approach—throwing standard algorithms at imbalanced data—achieved 76% recall. But through careful undersampling, feature engineering, and threshold optimization with Random Forest classifiers, we pushed fraud detection to 94.5% recall while maintaining 96.4% overall accuracy. The deeper lesson wasn't about any single technique; it was about understanding when and why algorithms fail, and how to systematically address those failures. This habit of rigorous validation, of understanding model limitations, and of questioning assumptions is what I believe distinguishes impactful AI research from mere technical exercises.

The challenge of processing streaming sensor data, extracting meaningful features in real-time, and building predictive maintenance systems represents a natural extension of my work on time-series analysis and anomaly detection.

statement_of_purpose:
In my 2nd year of university I enrolled in an Introduction to Machine Learning course, because I was genuinely intrigued to know the inner structure of machine learning models. That experience sparked a deeper interest in more advanced models, which led me to pursue a Deep Learning course focused on neural networks. But even after those courses, I still had one question stuck in my mind: we see the input and we see the output of the model, but we have no idea how the model formed that decision in between. This black-box problem especially stayed with me, because without understanding the reasoning behind model outcomes, we become powerless to correct or question them. In high-stakes domains like healthcare, hiring, education, or banking, this lack of transparency can lead to unreliable, unfair or even harmful outcomes. This realization pushed me toward the field of interpretable and transparent machine learning, where the goal is to understand model reasoning, identify which inputs drive predictions, and ensure decisions stay ethical and human-centered. And as AI becomes deeply integrated across sectors, including systems in my home country, the black-box problem feels even more urgent and critical to solve. 

My goal is to make machine learning models interpretable so we can build systems that are not only powerful, but controllable, safe, and genuinely human-centered. At Purdue, I see a direct path to developing these skills. In Prof. Arielle Borovsky’s lab, I would contribute to early language learning tools where transparency and ethical decision support are essential for young learners. With Prof. Martin Jun, I could explore how AI-driven monitoring systems can provide clear, understandable diagnostics which is a key challenge in interpretable ML. In Prof. Yung-Hsiang Lu’s group, the posture recommender project offers an opportunity to turn computer-vision decisions into feedback users can act on, but to do so we need first leverage the explainability of the model. Working with world-class mentors who design AI that communicates its reasoning to the people who rely on it would help me gain experience and shape the key aspects and factors in interpretable machine learning. 

I took the first steps towards my goal by initiating several projects in AI and machine learning. During the summer startup incubator program I developed the SalesGym.app which was tried by more than 180 real users. It is a full-stack platform where users practice sales conversations with an LLM-powered client and receive detailed performance feedback. Beyond applications, I have experience building full machine learning pipelines end-to-end starting from raw data to producing personalized report with workout and nutrition plans. In the “Personalized Workout and Nutrition plans generation” project, I developed a system that creates a personalized workout and nutrition plan according to the user's goal (lose weight, neutral, gain weight). The pipeline combines user clustering (K-Means), domain-informed feature engineering, and supervised learning (XGBoost). To transform predictions into daily sets of meals and workouts, I applied content-based recommendation methods (TF-IDF, cosine similarity, MMR).  When I was beginning my path I also completed more traditional analytics and modeling projects as well. In the “Regression Model for Insurance Pricing" project, I engineered and evaluated a complete machine learning pipeline using 10,000+ real insurance records from Kazakhstan, tested multiple models, and optimized a Random Forest model to R² = 0.80. In the Quantium retail analytics case, I analyzed 246,000 customer transactions to segment users, identified dominant purchasing patterns, and generated actionable recommendations for product strategy. Together, these experiences convinced me that the next step I must take is to move beyond building models to understanding how to explain, challenge, and improve their decisions.

To do that I aim to shift my focus from implementation to inquiry, meaning to move beyond building systems to rigorously examining how and why they behave the way they do. Through the SURF program, I want to strengthen the research skills essential for this transition: designing controlled experiments, auditing models for bias and fairness, and interpreting results with scientific rigor. I believe the SURF is the strongest environment for graduate studies preparation. Unlike most summer initiatives it lets students be responsible for producing real results and communicating them through a formal poster presentation. It is especially meaningful to me, because summarising findings, explaining methods, and standing behind your work publicly brings a sense of rigor and ownership that makes the work feel real like I am taking my first true steps into research. I am also drawn to SURF’s 1-to-1 mentorship and track record of sending students into top graduate programs. Through this immersive training I am willing to gain the competencies required to pursue graduate-level work in interpretable machine learning and ultimately contribute to systems where transparency, trust, and human judgment remain central. In the long run, my mission is to bring power back to people by making models answerable, understandable and equitable to users, institutions, and societies.
