I have always been drawn to hands-on problem solving and computing, which led me to electrical engineering. I discovered that the semiconductor field lies at the intersection of these interests, combining physical device fabrication with CAD and analysis. What excites me most about semiconductors is the manufacturing process itself, experimenting with materials, structures, and process parameters to optimize device performance. This interest has only deepened as the field approaches physical scaling limits. As transistor dimensions approach physical and economic barriers, the long-standing trend of performance improvements driven by increased transistor density is becoming difficult to sustain. This challenge primarily motivates my desire to contribute to research focused on next-generation devices and materials that can enable continued progress.

In addition to majoring in Electrical Engineering, I am pursuing a minor in Materials Science and Engineering, which has shaped my interest in emerging semiconductor materials such as carbon nanotubes and two-dimensional materials like graphene. These materials offer promising paths toward reduced power consumption and improved performance, both of which are critical as computational demands continue to rise. In particular, the rapid growth of large-scale machine learning and AGI models has made the environmental cost of computation, energy, cooling, and water usage, a pressing concern. I am deeply motivated by the challenge of how novel device architectures and materials can reduce the carbon and water footprint of modern data centers while improving computational capabilities.

SURF is particularly appealing to me because it provides an immersive, research-centered experience that is difficult to replicate during the academic year. By allowing students to focus primarily on research, SURF offers an environment similar to that of a research internship, where skills are developed through sustained engagement rather than fragmented coursework. 
I see SURF as an opportunity to synthesize and apply the knowledge I have gained over three years at Purdue while developing new experimental, analytical, and collaborative skills. I plan to pursue at least a master’s degree in Electrical Engineering and intend to remain involved in research whether I enter industry or academia. SURF would be a critical step in preparing me for that path by strengthening my ability to conduct independent, rigorous research.

I am particularly interested in continuing work at the Birck Nanotechnology Center, where I currently conduct research through the Semiconductors@Birck VIP program. That program has played a major role in solidifying my interest in semiconductor manufacturing and process development. Through hands on cleanroom work, I have gained experience fabricating and characterizing devices such as metal–insulator–metal capacitors. Even for relatively simple structures, the precision and process control required at the micro and nanoscale present a compelling technical challenge. This experience taught me how small variations in processing can significantly impact device performance, yield, and reliability.

My commitment to semiconductor research was further strengthened during my summer internship at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 2025. There, I worked on developing a short loop raised source drain (RSD) process flow to support sub-90 nm technology development. This project required reviewing academic literature, collaborating with process engineers, and adapting theoretical process flows to fit within their existing CMOS integration framework. In addition, I developed a wafer scratch identification algorithm by validating classified defect data and creating a curated wafer library. By tuning a defect detection recipe in Discover Pattern software, I achieved an 87.5% reduction in false fail rates compared to the initial algorithm. This work directly contributed to improved defect localization and yield optimization. These projects exposed me to a structured research environment that blends academic rigor with industry-driven constraints, including the need to account for downstream integration and stakeholder requirements.

Additionally, I am actively involved in building the semiconductor community at Purdue. I am the Outreach Chair of the Semiconductor Student Alliance, where I work to connect students with the broader semiconductor ecosystem. This semester, I hope to help establish an academic book club that facilitates discussions between undergraduate students, graduate students, and faculty around research papers in the semiconductor field. I am also involved in the early stages of developing a HackerFab at Purdue, a DIY nanofabrication space intended to increase accessibility to semiconductor fabrication and enable rapid prototyping and experimental process development. 

One of the most significant challenges I encountered in research occurred during my first semester with the Semiconductors@Birck VIP team. The steep learning curve of cleanroom processes, fabrication tools, and semiconductor theory initially felt overwhelming. To address this, I sought guidance from senior team members, reviewed process documentation independently, and spent additional time with my group to cover the gaps in my knowledge. This experience taught me how to approach complex, unfamiliar problems systematically and reinforced the importance of asking questions and learning from failure.

Through SURF, I hope to further develop my experimental design skills, deepen my understanding of semiconductor device physics and fabrication, and build stronger connections within the ECE department and Purdue’s research community. The opportunity to conduct focused and mentored research during SURF aligns directly with my long-term goal of contributing to the development of next generation of semiconductor technologies. I am confident that the skills, knowledge, and professional relationships gained through SURF will play a pivotal role in shaping my future career in STEM.

statement_of_purpose:
Many of today’s health problems are not limited by a lack of ideas, but by a lack of scalable, reliable measurement. How should we detect disease early, quantify progression, and evaluate whether an intervention is working? I became drawn to this challenge through lab experience, where I saw that strong research depends as much on how we measure as on what we study: two microscope images can look similar at first, but careful quantification can reveal meaningful differences or show that an apparent effect is only noise. This is why I chose Life Science and Biotechnology and why I continue to pursue work at the intersection of wet-lab biology and quantitative analysis, so that biological conclusions become reproducible and actionable.
Several questions motivate me to delve deeper. First, how can we quantify biological state such as cell identity, stress, activation, or degeneration from imaging and molecular readouts in a way that generalizes across batches and experimental conditions? Second, how can we detect disease signals at extremely low concentrations using assays that remain feasible outside highly resourced laboratories, including from non-invasive samples? Third, how can engineered cell therapies be made more scalable and standardized so they are not limited to small-batch, patient-specific manufacturing? These questions connect directly to my longer-term goal of contributing to translational biotechnology and medical technology, where strong biology must be paired with rigorous measurement and data-driven validation.
I have explored these interests through both research and structured skill-building. In my current research internship in a neural stem cell biology lab, I am training in core wet-lab and imaging workflows (immunostaining and microscopy procedures, RNA-to-cDNA preparation and qPCR-related concepts, and responsible mouse handling) while also contributing to an image-analysis direction: developing a patch-based CNN pipeline (PyTorch with MATLAB) to identify dopaminergic neurons from microscopy image patches for Parkinson’s disease. This experience has made the measurement challenge concrete. Experimental design, image quality, and labeling strategy all affect downstream quantification and model performance. In parallel, through a summer research program at the Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence, I built reproducible research tooling by developing a secure CLI workflow with testing and deployment practices.
Purdue Engineering SURF would directly support my long-term goal of pursuing US graduate research and, ultimately, contributing to biotech/medtech solutions for major health challenges. I am especially interested in three groups because each addresses a distinct health problem – infectious disease, tissue repair, and cancer –while matching my interest in rigorous measurement and quantitative analysis.
In the Kinzer-Ursem Lab, I am drawn to the biosensing and particle-diffusometry approach because it transforms microscopy data into quantitative diagnostic signals. The project’s emphasis on assay optimization, microscopy data acquisition, and ImageJ/algorithmic quantification aligns with the way I would like to work: careful controls, systematic troubleshooting, and measurable performance metrics. I would be excited to contribute reproducible analysis habits from my prior experience (clean data organization, validation checks, and clear documentation) while strengthening the algorithmic side of the workflow. For example, building robust quality control, calibration steps, and cross-condition validation so that detection performance is interpretable and comparable across experiments.
Qazi Lab’s work on granular hydrogels in volumetric muscle loss shows that microporosity enables Pax7+ satellite cell invasion and eMHC+ regeneration myofiber invasion, unlike bulk hydrogels that largely exclude cells. Building on my current training in mouse handling, tissue sectioning, immunostaining, and confocal microscopy, I would contribute immediately to the immunofluorescence and imaging workflow, while also strengthening the quantitative side by developing consistent analysis pipelines and objective remodeling metrics. I am especially excited to connect cellular readouts to structural outcomes by quantifying features such as myofiber morphology and scar formation.
I am excited by the Bao Lab’s approach to scalable immunotherapy that starts with CRISPR-engineered hPSCs and produces functional immune cells using defined differentiation workflows. In their recent work, the lab used CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in in hPSCs to generate CAR-neutrophils and then applied them as a delivery platform that crosses the blood–brain barrier to target glioblastoma. I can contribute skills including microscopy workflows, RNA-to-cDNA and qPCR concepts, and disciplined documentation from my current internship in addition to the computational analysis skills from building pipelines. My current CNN experience on microscopy images would also translate well to building consistent image-based readouts for cell purity, phenotype, and assay QC so that differentiation outcomes and variability are tracked systematically.
Beyond technical training, SURF’s structure would help me build research maturity. I want to improve how I frame research questions, design plans with appropriate controls, troubleshoot systematically, manage data reproducibly, and communicate results clearly through a report and presentation. As someone preparing for graduate school in the United States, the relationships formed through SURF are also crucial. I want to learn directly from faculty and graduate mentors and to work alongside peers with similar interests. statement_of_purpose:
I work at the intersection of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), machine learning (ML), optimization, and renewable energy — four fields that, for me, naturally grew into one another.
My interest in CFD started with aerospace. At the end of my first engineering year, I joined the, the Lebanese Automotive and Aerospace club (LAAS) at AUB, specifically the Vertical Takeoff and Landing (VTOL) medical-delivery drone project. I was clearly behind; people were discussing aerodynamic shapes and drag simulations while I barely understood what CFD meant. But I have always been curious. I did my own digging, took Cornell's Engineering Simulation course online to learn ANSYS fundamentals, and applied that knowledge to analyze airfoil performance and structural loads on the fuselage. That simple curiosity has culminated in me now leading the entire team, and we're on track to have a working prototype by early summer. I wanted to go deeper, though, so I reached out to Dr. Lakkis, the most prominent fluids professor on campus. Under his mentorship, I learned ANSYS Fluent properly (meshing strategies, turbulence models, solver selection) and spent six months modeling airflow through human lungs.
My interest in machine learning, I'll admit, started pragmatically. I noticed it appearing in nearly every recent publication, so I enrolled in Stanford's Machine Learning Specialization. Once I understood the fundamentals, I approached Dr. Bilal Kaddouh, an aerial robotics and applied ML expert. Under his supervision, I developed a YOLOv11 pipeline for orange tree detection from drone imagery, evaluated several CNN options for health classification, and built a projection-based GPS tagging system. Together, we submitted this work to the IEEE IGARSS 2026 conference.
Then it hit me: why not combine CFD and ML? CFD is powerful but slow — running hundreds of simulations to optimize a single design takes days. This led me to the first question that now drives my research: can ML surrogates replace expensive CFD simulations while preserving physical accuracy? That's why I'm developing a physics-informed MeshGraphNet for indoor airflow. It's a graph neural network trained on ANSYS simulation data, with node connections built directly from Fluent's mesh, that predicts thermal comfort. But faster simulation is only half the problem. The real value comes when you close the loop: if we can predict flow in seconds, can we use that speed to optimize decision-making in real-time? This second question drives two of my current projects. With Dr. Elsa Maalouf, I built a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) that takes six months of injection flow rates as input and predicts production well temperatures. I then formulated an SLSQP optimization that uses the TCN as a surrogate to find the injection allocation that maximizes energy output. We are now working on validating these predictions against CFD simulations. With Dr. Naseem Daher, I'm developing a two-phase system for off-grid microgrid energy management. The first phase focused on solar forecasting, where I built a physics-informed TCN incorporating solar elevation angle and clear-sky index, achieving 27.6 W/m² MAE at 1-hour horizons. The second phase uses these forecasts to train a TD3 reinforcement learning agent that learns when to store energy and when to discharge, all based on a hierarchical structure of loads. I'm currently enrolled in an undergraduate research course to push this work further.
Renewable energy is where I want to apply all of this. I already took a technical elective in wind turbine design, and I helped found the Association of Energy Engineers student chapter at AUB, where I now serve as Vice President. I am working to transform the chapter from event-focused to research- and project-driven, so I can give back to the community where I discovered who I really am. I want students to experience the fascination I felt when I first saw a converged simulation validated in real life. My first major initiative was building a small wind turbine demonstrator and presenting the prototype, as well as ANSYS-produced graphics to over 1,300 students during a STEM outreach event.
Beyond clubs, I led my team to first place in a clean energy competition organized by Innovating Green Technology at AUB, a company specializing in renewable energy integration across Lebanon and Cyprus. We designed an off-grid humanitarian shelter, where I sized the PV array, selected inverters, and chose LiFePO₄ batteries. I also built a Python simulator that processed three years of hourly weather data, ran DC power calculations with temperature derating, managed battery dispatch within SOC limits, and tracked when the system couldn't meet the load. The model validated our design at 98.6% reliability, meaning the shelter could run almost entirely on solar, with diesel only needed for a handful of winter days. 
SURF offers the environment to take these experiences and transform them into something career building. Prof. Weibel's CTRC heat exchanger project is my top choice because it sits at the intersection of CFD, optimization, and real-world impact. I have spent the past year developing CFD skills in ANSYS Fluent, and this project would let me expand to OpenFOAM while learning topology optimization and additive manufacturing, which I have not yet explored but see as essential for designing efficient thermal systems. The physics-informed ML project aligns directly with my research interests: I've been embedding physics into every model I build, whether it's simulation-derived values in a graph neural network for airflow, spatial well relationships in a TCN for geothermal prediction, or solar elevation and atmospheric transmittance in a TCN for irradiance forecasting. Working with Prof. Wang on atmospheric modeling would show me how to scale these ideas to larger, more complex systems. His weekly tutorials and access to Purdue's supercomputer would fill gaps I cannot address on my own. Prof. Mukherjee's energy storage analytics project connects to my work on solar microgrid optimization, where I am training RL agents to manage battery charge/discharge under load uncertainty. This requires an intuitive understanding of battery behavior under normal and anomalous conditions, which I am sure this project would help me develop.  Beyond the individual projects, SURF represents a critical step in my career. I plan to pursue a PhD in mechanical engineering focused on renewable energy, and ultimately a career designing sustainable energy systems. SURF would be invaluable preparation, both for the skills and for the relationships that could open doors for PhD opportunities and collaborations.
Getting here was not straightforward, though. My biggest obstacle was simply not knowing. No one told me undergraduates could do research or that professors would welcome students into their labs. By my second year, I wanted research experience but had nothing to show. So, I joined a Vertically Integrated Project as a volunteer — no credit, no recognition — just to gain experience. Finally, I had something to show when approaching faculty. Since then, I reached out to Dr. Lakkis for CFD, Dr. Maalouf for geothermal energy, Dr. Daher for solar and RL, Dr. Kaddouh for precision agriculture. Each time, the answer was yes. What felt like a closed door was never locked. I just had not tried to open it.
Another challenge was that my combination of CFD, ML, and optimization for renewable energy was not widely pursued on campus, so I learned to meet professors where they were. Dr. Maalouf had interest in ML but no project combining it with geothermal energy, so I proposed one. Dr. Daher's specialty was controls, and he had recently started exploring RL, so I pitched solar microgrid optimization. It was always me coming up with the idea, then finding the right professor to advise it. However, this drive came at a cost. I put all my time into research and coursework, leaving nothing for myself, and ended up in the ER for exhaustion. Since then, I have committed to at least one hour a day for my well-being and started counseling. The result? I submitted my first paper to IEEE as a third-year student, with three more in progress. I have learned how to sustain this work, and now I am ready for an environment that can push me further, which is what SURF offers.

statement_of_purpose:
Engineering problems are rarely solved by a single discipline. As a mechatronics engineering student, I have learned that meaningful solutions often emerge at the intersection of software, hardware, control logic, and iterative testing. I am applying to this summer experience to further develop an integrated engineering approach within a research environment.

I am currently pursuing a degree in Mechatronics Engineering, where I have come to value the close relationship between mechanical design, electronics, and digital control. While coursework has provided a strong theoretical foundation, most of my practical learning has taken place through practical projects involving microcontrollers, FPGA development, and electronic design, along with a solid grounding in mechatronics and system dynamics.

Much of my interest in engineering has grown from working on projects where systems must function as a whole rather than only on paper. One such experience was developing a water rocket with a real time telemetry system. Despite having no prior experience in rocketry, my team and I designed the entire system from scratch, including the rocket structure, onboard electronics, and a launch platform with a ground station for real time data visualization. Using microcontrollers, sensors, and wireless communication, we measured variables such as position, velocity, pressure, and time. The process involved extensive research, discussions with professors, and constant trial and error. Often, individual components worked correctly in isolation but failed once integrated, requiring us to step back, analyze the issue, and iterate until the system functioned reliably.

A similar learning process occurred during the development of an FPGA automated conveyor system. The system allowed users to define a batch size, detect incoming parts, measure them using sensors, reject parts exceeding a defined threshold, and reset once the batch was completed, while simultaneously sending real time data to a Python program that generated a log file. Debugging finite state machines and timing issues taught me the importance of patience, organization, and thorough documentation when working with digital systems.

In parallel, my experience as an intern through the ICATEY program at LEONI, a German company and one of the world’s largest suppliers of automotive wiring systems, allowed me to observe engineering within a real production environment. I saw firsthand how a small assembly error could halt an entire production line and affect many people, reinforcing my understanding that engineering extends beyond technical design to include processes, constraints, and teamwork.

Another experience that shaped my interest in problem solving was participating in UChallenge, a university competition focused on addressing a real logistics issue for Camino Real Hotel in Mérida. This project represented a different form of research for me, as it required understanding how an organization operates rather than approaching the problem from a purely technical perspective. Our team spoke directly with hotel staff, managers, and even the owner to identify communication and coordination gaps. After evaluating several possible solutions, we designed and implemented a Python chatbot to improve interaction between personnel and guests. The project combined observation, discussion, iteration, and technical development, and our proposal was awarded first place.

I am particularly motivated to apply to SURF because of its strong emphasis on applied engineering research that aligns closely with my background in mechatronics. After reviewing the 2026 SURF research proposals, I was especially drawn to the projects “Learning for Humanoid Robot Whole Body Control” and “Underwater Robotic Manipulation.” Both projects reflect the type of engineering work that interests me most, where mechanical systems, sensing, control, and experimentation must be integrated to perform reliably in real world conditions. The humanoid robotics project resonates with my interest in system behavior and control, while the underwater robotics project closely matches my experience building, testing, and debugging hardware systems that require careful calibration and iteration.

In addition to current research topics, I have been inspired by past SURF projects and by the trajectories of students who have participated in the program. Projects from earlier years that focused on robotics, sensing, and human centered systems reflect the interdisciplinary and applied research environment I hope to be part of. In particular, the path followed by Natalia Sanchez Tamayo after her participation in SURF in 2018, continuing into advanced research in robotics and human–robot interaction, is an example I find especially motivating. Seeing how early undergraduate research through SURF contributed to her development reinforces my interest in the program as a meaningful step toward building a long term career in applied engineering and research.

I recognize that it is unrealistic to have a fully defined career path at this stage, and I view this uncertainty as a natural part of engineering and research. For me, SURF would represent a first genuine step into a research environment and an opportunity to determine whether pursuing a long term path as a researcher is right for me, which is one of my goals.

I am particularly interested in robotics and electronic systems that aim to improve how technology serves society, rather than research conducted for its own sake. My interest lies in developing new technology and designing functional systems through prototyping and practical work.

At this point in my training, I feel I have established a solid technical foundation, but I am ready to continue learning through larger and more demanding projects. I am motivated to work within a diverse research team, learn from experienced mentors, and understand how collaborative research is conducted in practice. I believe SURF would help me clarify my future plans for graduate studies while allowing me to contribute meaningfully to an important research project.

While I am still building experience, I am highly motivated by challenging problems and committed to learning through practical work. When I am genuinely interested in a project, I am persistent, proactive, and willing to put in the effort needed to move ideas forward. I see SURF as an opportunity where this motivation can translate into meaningful growth and contribution.

How do we design systems for users who cannot articulate their needs, or even understand the technology affecting them? Where do we draw the line on surveillance in a world where we are often unaware of being watched? These questions guided my research as I began exploring how privacy-enhancing technologies can be designed for children, who cannot give informed consent to being photographed.
Last summer, I was awarded the student faculty grant at Skidmore College to design a wearable embedded in a child’s jacket that detects nearby cameras and disrupts image capture using infrared light, activating only when a camera is detected. I used Arduino to process sensor input and control infrared LEDs, integrated electronics into clothing, and tested the system across varied lighting conditions and camera types, systematically logging results and analyzing false positives and missed detections to improve accuracy. Early prototypes produced false positives. I conducted multiple tests under varied lighting conditions and with different camera types, logging every result in a detailed datasheet. Through trial and error, I refined my code until the detection became consistent enough for practical use. Throughout this process, I learned to fully make use of resources. I reached out to professors for guidance on hardware improvements and peers in diverse disciplines. I relied on extensive research, data collection, and testing to make decisions. I saw every mistake as a data point I can learn from to improve my decision making. 
Since the system was designed for infants, wearability and comfort were very important. I ensured the system was lightweight, secure, and unobtrusive. I presented my work as a research poster and continue to develop a user study with parents and children to assess usability and comfort. 
I also bring experience with qualitative research methods through the New York Academy of Science’s Junior Academy program, where I conducted interviews with farmers on environmental challenges, specifically eutrophication. Through coursework in anthropology, I practiced ethnography, interviewing, and behavioral analysis, understanding how culture, context, and environment shape people’s behaviors.
This research project solidified my interest in human-centered computing research with societal impact. Taking an idea from concept to a working prototype taught me that I enjoyed the messy process of designing, testing, and refining systems while balancing ethics and usability. I learned to approach problems from multiple perspectives and teach myself unfamiliar concepts quickly. My summer research exposed me to computer vision and image processing.
At DivHacks, a hackathon hosted by Columbia University, I led a team to develop a health app that minimizes the risk of medication errors while conserving patients’ privacy, alerting healthcare professionals to potentially harmful interactions using AI, earning first place in the Patient Safety Challenge.  I further improved my data analysis skills through Girls Who Code’s “Data for Good” course, where I worked with messy, real-world datasets to extract meaningful insights and patterns, while considering ethical implications, bias mitigation, and responsible handling of sensitive information.  I continued to develop skills in pandas, Scikit-learn, NumPy, and MatPlotLib to clean, visualize, and model data.  
Other than applying computer science academically, I am committed to using it to empower others. Growing up in Morocco, I saw firsthand how early exposure influences who enters the tech field. Coming from a background with limited access to these fields, experiences like TechGirls and Kode With Klossy inspired me to major in CS. I organized two-week computer literacy and Python workshops in schools in Morocco, teaching approximately forty middle school girls. I adapted the curriculum in real-time based on students’ prior knowledge. Several participants have since started coding clubs in their schools, which I continue to mentor remotely, helping make tech more accessible.
Through my liberal arts education, I have developed a multidisciplinary, human-centered approach to computer science, with interests in human factors, cybersecurity, data science, machine learning, and embedded systems. SURF offers a unique opportunity to gain hands-on experience in user-centered research and study design while collaborating in an interdisciplinary environment. Through faculty mentorship, I hope to deepen my research skills and better prepare for my goal of pursuing graduate study in computer science and contribute to meaningful research at the intersection of technology and society. I look forward to finding my community and engaging with people from diverse backgrounds, learning from their research and sharing my own. The weekly professional development workshops and faculty mentorship will allow me to strengthen my research skills, explore cutting-edge topics, and contribute to projects with real-world impact.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in engineering has always been closely tied to environmental impact. Growing up, I was motivated by the challenge of addressing climate change through tangible, technical solutions, which naturally led me toward mechanical engineering and energy systems. I enjoy building and analyzing systems, particularly when engineering decisions have large-scale societal consequences. This interest solidified during my internship with the Northern California Power Agency, where I observed firsthand how California generates an abundance of renewable energy, especially solar, yet struggles to store that energy efficiently for times of peak demand and low production. That disconnect between energy generation and usability highlighted energy storage as a critical bottleneck in the clean energy transition and motivated me to explore the field more deeply. Since then, I have become particularly interested in questions surrounding battery degradation and efficiency in both grid-scale and electric vehicle applications. This past semester, my focus has expanded to sodium-ion batteries, whose potential for improved sustainability compared to lithium-ion systems led me to conduct research on their commercialization under Professor Partha Mukherjee. Our research has motivated me to investigate how data-driven approaches can be used to understand and mitigate cathode degradation in sodium-ion batteries, a key barrier to their long-term performance and commercialization.

I was initially drawn to the SURF program because of its emphasis on immersive, one-on-one research mentorship and professional development. Having worked with Prof. Partha Mukherjee this past semester, I have seen how his mentorship style encourages both technical rigor and independent thinking. I am eager to continue our work this summer through the support of SURF, where we will make more progress on our research by discovering more robust material configurations for the sodium-ion batteries we manufactured this past semester. Additionally, the SURF program’s structure (combining full-time research with seminars, networking opportunities, and presentation training) will allow me to further my development of such academic soft skills. SURF’s focus on communication and professional growth is particularly appealing, as it prepares students not just to conduct research but to articulate its impact within academic settings. In the long term, I would like to pursue a career as a professor of energy science, designing more robust and efficient systems for large-scale energy storage. By participating in SURF, I hope to take a key step on my path to this goal, deepening my engagement with the energy science community at Purdue. 

The research experience gained through SURF will play a pivotal role in preparing me for graduate school and a future career as a professor of energy science. Through this SURF, I hope to further strengthen my skills in data-driven modeling, machine learning-based analysis, and experimental interpretation within the context of lithium-ion battery systems. Equally important, I aim to improve my ability to communicate complex technical findings through presentations and written work, skills that are essential for success in research-focused careers. The professional development seminars offered by SURF will also provide insight into different pathways within academia and research, helping me make informed decisions about my future. Finally, expanding my professional network through SURF is especially valuable, as mentorship and collaboration are central to long-term success in research.

I have actively explored the field of energy and engineering research through a combination of coursework, hands-on projects, and research experiences. I am pursuing a minor in Nuclear Engineering, which has strengthened my understanding of energy systems, safety considerations, and large-scale power generation. As the Design Lead for Purdue ASME’s Hydrogen Fuel Cell Energy Team, I have worked on the design and analysis of fuel cell components, gaining experience in CAD, materials evaluation, and system-level optimization. My internship with the Northern California Power Agency exposed me to real-world challenges in energy generation and infrastructure, further motivating my interest in energy storage solutions. Most importantly, my work in Dr. Mukherjee’s Energy and Travel Sciences Laboratory, where I have conducted data-driven analyses of sodium-ion battery performance (and specifically the degradation mechanisms within) and presented my work at the Purdue Undergraduate Research Symposium, has prepared me for independent research. These experiences collectively demonstrate my commitment to energy research and my readiness to fully engage in the SURF program.

One challenge I have encountered in my pursuit of research has been narrowing my focus within a broad and rapidly evolving field. While I have long been committed to renewable energy and energy storage, I initially struggled with defining a highly specific research direction within energy science early in my academic career. Through conversations with faculty mentors, particularly Dr. Mukherjee, and through hands-on research experiences, I have learned that breadth is not a weakness, but an opportunity to gather diverse technical perspectives and refine my interests through experience. For example, when I began working with Dr. Mukherjee, he helped me refine my interests by encouraging me to pursue a project with significant experimental components, while also including some computational and simulation-based work. 
In addition, by engaging in multiple energy-related projects, taking advanced coursework, and remaining open to interdisciplinary approaches, I have developed a more grounded understanding of where my interests and strengths lie. These shifts in mindset have allowed me to move forward with greater confidence and intentionality, and they continue to shape how I approach research questions and my long-term academic goals.

As a first gen student, I didn't have an elite orientation to my career. choosing AI was a coincidence, the best coincidence in my whole life. It all started when this young girl was watching her favorite show "Ehsan from the Future" and in one of these episodes, everything clicked, she felt like a bulb switched on in her head. Ahmad Al Shugairi nailed this episode so well that he made me fall for robotics and AI.From that moment, the internet and my brother's laptop were my absolute friends. I started following YouTube robotics projects, and once I felt confident, I began integrating AI into my builds. I spent nights watching Nicholas Renotte videos  and It's when I start developing these models and agentic systems that I felt like a goddess who's able to address real world problems and implement almost anything she can imagine. It was then that I knew AI was my calling. 
My passion was ignited further by Aurélien Géron's Hands-On Machine Learning book , but what keeps me here is the field's limitless versatility. I love that AI bridges the gap between disparate worlds, one day I'm exploring medical diagnostics and cybersecurity, and the next I'm delving into different cultures and traditions. It's the only field that keeps fuelling my insatiable desire for learning. 

As I was working on my research project aiming to generate optimized medication with reduced adverse side effects, I encountered many challenges and I had many lingering questions in my mind as I was systematically analyzing the chemical composition and bioactive compounds of existing pharmaceutical drugs and trying to create new compositions that are safer or plant based... 
 How could I actually optemize what the model was producing? can I use generative models that could learn valid chemical and physical constraints instead of producing unrealistic outputs? And How can reinforcement learning and generative models be combined to optimize drugs efficacy and safety? These questions and others pushed me to continue the exploration and apply to SURF. 

Indeed, a lot of summer programs feel like a sprint, you do the project, make the poster, and you’re out. SURF hits differently. It feels heavier, maybe?, but in the way I need. It seems built for people who are actually trying to survive a PhD later, and not just a summer activity. That focus on the long game and the rigor of it is exactly what I’m looking for. Also when I came across the "Generative AI for the Discovery of New Drugs" project it grabbed me, and I knew then that surf is the right research program that would help me answer the questions I still have.
  
Pursuing engineering and research for me is not about certainty. It’s about staying curious despite confusion, and stubborn enough to keep asking questions. SURF for me represents this environment where that mindset can grow into something rigorous and lasting. Although my knowledge regarding Equivariant 3D conditional diffusion models and Generative Flow Networks is limited, I am highly motivated to learn along with the research program and get valuable insights from my mentor. I am particularly interested in AI driven scientific discovery, where machine learning accelerates innovation in medicine and other fields. But l’m also studying cybersecurity alongside AI as I believe It’s not enough for the model to just work. We’re integrating these massive AI systems into research in pharma, agriculture and other sensitive fields, if we can’t trust the pipeline, the output is useless. That’s actually why I’m holding onto the cybersecurity side of my degree so tight. It’s one thing to generate a molecule, it’s another to guarantee the data behind it hasn’t been tampered with. I want to build systems that are smart, sure, but also bulletproof because in this field, secure and ethical are the difference between a breakthrough and a liability.
  
I’m especially drawn to the research workflow itself. The constant loop of experimenting, breaking things, reevaluating assumptions, and refining ideas is something I’ve already tasted in my current research, and SURF would let me deepen that process under strong mentorship.

Working hands on with advanced generative models like diffusion models and GFlowNets that deal with messy high dimensional molecular data, and that challenge of learning how to reason in spaces where intuition doesn’t come easily is exactly what excites me. I see SURF as a space to grow as a researcher, framing meaningful scientific questions, explaining results clearly, and learning how to communicate ideas to people outside my immediate field. Also having access to Purdue faculty and researchers, learning how they think, how they ask questions, and how they guide research decisions would be incredibly valuable as I prepare for a PhD path.

In the future, I see myself pursuing a research driven career in AI, working at the boundary between AI systems and real world societal needs. My goal is to create technologies that don’t stay trapped in papers or labs but actually reach communities, whether that’s through medical AI, sustainable robotics or intelligent systems designed for low resource settings. SURF would be a critical step in that trajectory. Just being around other people who are obsessed over the same niche problems is a blessing. I want to meet people who challenge my assumptions about how these models should be built.  

My journey into AI has been defined by resilience. As a woman in a community that often views STEM as a male domain, I had to fight against gender bias while navigating limited resources and a lack of mentorship. Fueled by a deep passion for AI, I studied rigorously to secure a spot in my country’s top engineering school. And earn admission to my selective major, while supplementing my curriculum with curated courses from leading researchers and self directed projects. 
However, I wanted to explore the world of research and although my university restricts research programs to final year students, I refused to let that timeline define me. I proactively approached my AI professor to mentor me in  an independent research project focused on AI driven drug discovery and optimization, effectively creating my own research track where none existed.
Beyond the coursework, I pushed myself to apply AI in tangible ways, from building robotic systems to competing in national hackathons, eventually taking 1st place at the Google Developers Group OpportunAI Hackathon and earning a nomination as a Galactic Problem Solver in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. But some of my proudest moments weren't on a podium, they were in workshops and events, leading robotics and AI workshops for middle schoolers. These experiences taught me lessons that code never could, that if knowledge isn't shared clearly, it doesn't travel far, and that's why I want to be the kind of researcher who doesn't just make discoveries but makes them accessible.

My path hasn’t been smooth. Access to resources hasn’t always been guaranteed, and 
 Being an orphan added layers of responsibility and uncertainty early on. There were moments where I had to self teach entire concepts because formal instruction wasn’t available. But instead of seeing that as a limitation, I’ve taken online courses to fill gaps and learned to ask for guidance strategically, reaching out to professors, mentors, and peers, and refining my questions until they made sense. Juggling these heavy technical projects while prepping for exams has been a lesson in time management. There were days where nothing worked, but my motivation kept me trying again and again,and I learned that stuck is just part of the process.


If anything, these challenges strengthened my commitment to research. They taught me resilience, independence, and the importance of community. They also shaped my belief that talent exists everywhere, but opportunity does not, and that research programs like SURF play a critical role in closing that gap. 
I continue to pursue my field because I genuinely enjoy working in it, I have never felt the heaviness of the long nights spent on my projects because this field constantly unsettles me in the best way possible. There is always another assumption to question, another system to improve, another problem to fix... and SURF represents a space where that kind of curiosity is taken seriously, a place where I can grow not just as a student, but as a future researcher committed to meaningful impact.

Regarding data analysis, I have only used Excel so I would like to learn how advanced computer programming software can be used to analyze the experimental data. I would like to observe how the experienced scientists train students so that I can do the same when I become a chemist and professor.

Through my work as a student researcher in the Department of Chemistry at Ball State, I have developed a strong foundation in laboratory research and data analysis. My research focuses on synthesizing and characterizing platinum nanoparticles supported on semiconductor materials and using them in photocatalytic reactions. I am exploring how nanoparticles can be used to reduce organic compounds in a sustainable manner following the principles of green chemistry.  This work has allowed me to gain hands-on experience with a wide range of analytical techniques including HPLC, NMR, GC-MS, TEM, SEM, UV-Vis, IR, and TGA. I also review scientific literature to support experimental design and interpret results. I have presented my findings through oral and poster presentations at Indiana Academy of Science Annual Meeting, ACS-Indiana “Think Like A Molecule” poster session, Ball State Student Symposium, and Ball State Summer Research Program. This experience has helped me become comfortable working carefully, documenting procedures accurately, analyzing data independently and communicate scientific findings to scientists as well as general public confidently.

One of the main challenges I encountered in my pursuit of research was transitioning from structured coursework to the open-ended nature of independent research. I have been working on the photocatalytic reduction of benzonitrile to benzylamine with platinum-titanium dioxide nanocomposite catalysts for nearly two years. The first obstacle was controlling the shapes of the nanoparticles. My goal was to get cubic and octahedral nanoparticles in uniform sizes but due to the sensitive nature of reaction conditions in nanoparticle preparation, there were times I got particles with irregular shapes and sizes. After the synthesis of particles, the next step was to carry out the photocatalytic reaction which is reducing benzonitrile to benzylamine. From qualitative analysis with HPLC, we concluded that we got a new product, but we had to confirm if the new product is benzylamine. On the HPLC chromatogram, the peak for residual benzonitrile is very close to benzylamine in retention time which is impossible since benzylamine is more polar than benzonitrile. After comparing it with standard compounds, we figured out that the product is not benzylamine, but the dimer which is N-benzylidenebenzylamine. For quantitative analysis, we had to figure out the best solvent composition and running system to separate the two peaks and measure the conversion percentage accurately. Currently, we are trying to figure out why we got only N-benzylidenebenzylamine. At first, it was so hard for me to accept the fact that experiments do not always produce expected results. Moreover, I served as a laboratory teaching assistant for General Chemistry 1, where I guide students through laboratory experiments, data collection, and analysis while emphasizing safety and clear scientific communication. Recently, in August 2025, I founded the organization called Organic Chemistry Initiative (OCI), with three other colleagues, in collaboration with OCI at the Johns Hopkins University. The organization offers free weekly content review sessions, lecture and lab exam review sessions, 24/7 support through GroupMe, study materials on OCI website, videos on YouTube, and daily multiple-choice questions on Instagram. In addition to general chemistry and organic chemistry, I organized one-on-one and group tutoring sessions for analytical and instrumental chemistry, calculus 1 and 2, as a tutor at the Ball State learning center. Whenever I teach, I make sure that, at the end of each session, students become more confident in problem solving and appreciate interest in the subject beyond the requirements of their majors by connecting the relevance of science to their everyday life. These roles have strengthened my ability to communicate complex ideas clearly, collaborate with others, and take responsibility in both independent and team-based settings. 

I also maintained a 4.0 GPA and earned placement on the Dean’s list every semester which reflects my strong work ethic, discipline, and commitment to academic excellence. After my freshman year, I was recognized with an Excellence in General Chemistry Award, which is given to the top thirteen students who displayed an exceptional scholastic ability in general chemistry sequence. Balancing a demanding course load with research, teaching, and work responsibilities has strengthened my time-management skills. As I progress academically, I plan to enroll in graduate-level chemistry courses such as Advanced Organic Chemistry and Advanced Analytical Chemistry during my senior year to further challenge myself and build a strong foundation for graduate school.

In short, I hope the skills I will gain from the Purdue SURF program will prepare me for contributing meaningfully to the sustainable chemistry research and mentoring the next generation of chemists as well as strengthen my readiness for graduate school.

I often joke that I 'steal' ideas. I quote writers, scientists, and thinkers not because I lack my own thoughts, but because their words help me express things I haven’t yet found the language for. For most of my life, I’ve been a consumer: of ideas, of education, and of the care others have given me. But as I grow into my own identity, I feel a shift in responsibility. I want to give something back. Science, after all, is built collectively, through centuries of curiosity, failure, persistence, and imagination. What excites me most is the possibility of contributing something original to that shared body of knowledge, even if it is small.
The brain absolutely amazes me. Not just the human brain, but brains across species. I believe they are among the most powerful systems in the universe, more powerful than forces that can destroy us, because they can also heal, adapt, and imagine. Despite decades of research, we are only beginning to understand neurological and psychiatric disorders, neural plasticity, and the molecular mechanisms that shape cognition and behavior. Emerging fields such as cancer neuroscience and the study of neuronal primary cilia have shown me how much remains undiscovered, and how transformative new perspectives can be.
What draws me to Neurobiology/Neuroscience is not only its complexity, but its impact. Understanding the brain means understanding suffering, identity, and possibility. It means asking how pain can be reduced, how quality of life can be improved, and how this work can be done responsibly, with careful attention to ethics. I am currently a biology major with strong interests in neuroscience and neurobiology. Because my university does not offer a neuroscience major, I chose to minor in both Neuroscience and Chemistry to gain as broad and rigorous a foundation as possible. I also work as a student researcher in the Social Minds Lab at Caldwell University, where I use EEG and ERP techniques to study neural activity. While I am not yet certain about the exact path I will pursue, I am certain that I want a career rooted in research, discovery, and contribution to the scientific community.
I am particularly drawn to Purdue’s SURF Program because it emphasizes not only conducting research, but also communicating it through poster presentations, seminars, and the process of compiling research into a final document. Since I plan to become a researcher, these skills will allow others to learn from my work and enable meaningful collaboration. Additionally, as one of the few programs that accepts international students, SURF offers the opportunity to work alongside individuals from diverse backgrounds and perspectives, which I see as a major strength of scientific research.
Several projects at Purdue have really caught my interest, especially the Development of DNA Nanomaterials for miRNA Delivery across the Blood–Brain Barrier with Professor Tamara Kinzer-Ursem, Controlled Drug Delivery for Tissue Repair with Professor Taimoor Qazi, and Identifying Drug Treatments for Functional Recovery after Spinal Cord Injury with Professor Daniel Suter. I’m especially drawn to the blood–brain barrier project because it tackles the challenge of delivering therapeutics to the brain. Using DNA nanostructures to deliver miRNA for diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s feels meaningful not only intellectually, but ethically, because it has the potential to directly improve patients’ lives. All of these projects excite me because they connect neuroscience, biology, chemistry, and biomedical engineering while translating research into real-world outcomes. Learning techniques like hydrogel fabrication, drug encapsulation, DNA nanomaterials assembly, cell culture, and imaging will help me think critically about new ways to deliver drugs to the nervous system and grow into a skilled neurobiologist.
My interest in research has also been shaped by challenges. During my first research project, the cell line I was working with became contaminated with bacteria, making it difficult to obtain reliable results. I had already registered to present at undergraduate research symposiums, including the ICUNJ Undergraduate Research Symposium. Instead of hiding the issue, I presented what I observed and explained the contamination honestly. That experience taught me an important lesson: research does not always go as planned, and integrity matters more than polished outcomes. Admitting uncertainty or failure can feel uncomfortable, but it is essential to meaningful science.
Ultimately, through both failures and successes, I am driven by the desire to create something that others can build upon. If one day someone learns from my work, questions it, or even “steals” an idea from it, I would consider that a success. That is how science moves forward and how I hope to find my place within it.

I didn't know what computer science was until I was sixteen. Growing up in Nepal without internet access, I thought computers were just tools for word processing. Education was our pathway forward, but by grade 10, even that seemed uncertain. We didn't have funds for high school.

I spent four months visiting 70 colleges on foot. One administrator told me bluntly, "You are not entitled to anything. You should earn it." That conversation shifted how I thought about my future. When Xavier College finally awarded me their patron scholarship, I'd learned something crucial about persistence. More importantly, during those visits, I discovered that people built careers writing code. That revelation changed everything.

The research questions that drive me now sit at the intersection of sensing, autonomy, and computation under constraint. How can intelligent systems remain robust when data is noisy, communication is limited, and computational resources are unevenly distributed? These challenges appear everywhere, from wearable health monitoring to underwater robotics to access to high-performance computing itself. I'm particularly interested in multimodal perception and autonomous decision-making in environments where assumptions of constant connectivity or clean data break down. These aren't just technical problems. They're questions about who gets to benefit from technological advancement.

SURF offers exactly what I need at this stage. I've completed several research projects, but I haven't learned how to formulate original research questions or refine ideas through sustained collaboration. SURF's emphasis on full-time immersion, close faculty mentorship, and structured research communication is particularly attractive because I need an environment where I can iterate on ideas, receive critical feedback, and present my work in a rigorous academic setting. Purdue's interdisciplinary engineering culture, combined with strong research groups in autonomous systems, robotics, and high-performance computing, creates the exact ecosystem where my interests in sensing and accessible computation can develop. I'm not just looking for another summer project. I'm looking for mentorship that teaches me how to think like a researcher preparing for doctoral work.

Through SURF, I hope to develop three specific capabilities. First, the ability to formulate research questions that connect technical problems to real-world impact. Second, deeper experience with sensor integration and autonomous systems operating under constraints. Third, connections with researchers working at the intersection of theory and application, which would be invaluable as I prepare PhD applications this fall. These skills represent the gap between executing projects and shaping original research.

My research journey started during my first year at Texas State. While working 20 hours weekly in the campus dining hall to cover rent and expenses, I joined Dr. Heping Chen's robotics lab, working on gait analysis using wearable IMU sensors. I handled data preprocessing in Python and learned that reliable results come from disciplined methodology. Seeing our work published at an IEEE conference taught me how research actually works.

Last summer at Lehigh University's NSF Research Translation Accelerator program expanded my perspective significantly. I co-designed a six-degree-of-freedom underwater ROV, working on the mechanical framework and thruster configuration for environments where communication is slow and sensors behave unpredictably. That experience taught me that good research requires understanding not just technical problems but also who needs solutions and why. When our ROV placed second among 103 projects, I realized how much I still needed to learn.

Currently, I work as an HPC intern at Texas State, managing the LEAP2 computing cluster. This role taught me something unexpected. Making computational power accessible matters as much as the algorithms themselves. Who has access? Who knows how to use it? This connects back to why I'm drawn to computer science. Innovation only matters when it reaches people beyond well-resourced settings.

Being a first-generation college student from a single-parent household shaped how I approach everything. When I proposed creating the first Director of International Affairs position in student government and we won by 18 votes, I learned that sustainable impact comes from building systems, not just individual effort. That same principle applies to research.

Long term, I aim to pursue a PhD and become a researcher developing intelligent systems that operate reliably in resource-constrained environments, either in academia or applied research labs focused on robotics, sensing, and human-centered computing. SURF represents my final summer as an undergraduate and a critical bridge to that journey. I want to spend my career in research because building something new, testing it in unpredictable conditions, and knowing it might help others is what drives me. But I need the mentorship SURF offers to get there.

However, it was through hands-on research that I discovered the central problem that now motivates my work: modern AI systems can achieve high performance while remaining opaque, fragile, or misleading to the humans who rely on them.

My interest in explainable AI was shaped not only by practice but also by theory. Reading The Book of Why by Judea Pearl challenged my early assumption that predictive accuracy alone implies understanding, emphasizing instead the role of causal structure and counterfactual reasoning. Similarly, Cynthia Rudin’s work on interpretable models reframed interpretability not as a visualization problem, but as a question of whether models should be transparent by design. These perspectives sharpened my research focus: explanation should not be an afterthought added to complex models, but a constraint that shapes model architecture, evaluation, and deployment from the outset.

This realization became concrete during my work on explainable AI for medical imaging. I developed multimodal diagnostic models using convolutional architectures and achieved high predictive accuracy across multiple imaging modalities. Yet, when integrating explanation methods such as Grad-CAM and concept-based summaries, I observed that explanation format significantly influenced clinical interpretation. Highly detailed heatmaps often encouraged overconfidence, while simpler, concept-level explanations led to more cautious and calibrated decision-making—even when the underlying model was unchanged. This experience transformed my understanding of explainability: the challenge is not merely what a model attends to, but how humans reason with the information they are given.

These observations raised questions that continue to drive my research interests: How should explanations balance fidelity and usability? When does additional information improve decision-making, and when does it amplify cognitive bias? How can uncertainty be communicated in a way that meaningfully constrains human judgment rather than overwhelming it? These questions place my interests at the intersection of machine learning, mathematical modeling, and human-computer interaction.

I have explored this intersection through diverse research experiences, including integrating SHAP and permutation-based explanations into large-scale sensor analytics at the Ubicomp Lab at NUS, conducting multimodal behavioral analysis in an NSF-funded learning sciences lab, and combining numerical solvers with neural networks in computational modeling. Across these settings, a consistent pattern emerged: explanation, robustness, and human alignment are not peripheral concerns—they fundamentally determine whether AI systems succeed outside controlled benchmarks.

As a Research Assistant at the Institute for Advanced Analytics and Security (IAAS) — a research department located at the University of Southern Mississippi (USM) — I have been deeply involved for over six months in several aspects of the Aquaview project, which is funded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). This experience has not only provided me with real-world exposure to Data Science and Software Development, but also taught me how technology is an integral part of ocean science.

A major part of my work revolved around the World Ocean Database (WOD) project. It contained datasets of worldwide oceans and seas stored in an S3 bucket in NetCDF (.nc) format from the year 1800 to 2024. The tasks involved processing all of them, indexing in Google Cloud, creating metadata in MongoDB, and copying to Elasticsearch so that results are visible in the User Interface (UI) when queried based on spatial and temporal filters. It is available for users at aquaview.org/map. This project was finalized in three phases. The first step involved storing more than 17 million metadata records in a centralized collection called globalindex on MongoDB. However, due to the overwhelming number of data points, the processing speed was significantly reduced, which caused the team to design a new layout. Thereafter, a separate collection was assigned to each data source on MongoDB so that each could function independently. It solved the speed issue to a great extent. Thirdly, a new UI was designed in which WOD was reindexed to better reflect over 17 million data points in the result bucket. Due to the significance of this project in ocean science and the extensive amount of work involved, we are aiming to present it at the OCEANS 2026 Monterey conference.

Next, I also led the development of the “aquaview” Python library in early June 2025, which has been downloaded over 1,000 times by IAAS and NOAA researchers so far. It provides streamlined access to oceanographic datasets through the AQUAVIEW API. Likewise, I also played a key role in classifying platforms for data points in the result bucket for more than 20 million data points across 10+ sources in real time, using the Gemini API key. It aided the NOAA executives in better understanding which platform was used to collect each data point. At the moment, I am working on the National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) datasets. It has two kinds of data: historical (stored as raw data in the form of NetCDF files) and real-time active stations (accessible via the NDBC API). I am following the same process as the WOD — indexing in Google Cloud, storing metadata in MongoDB, and copying to Elasticsearch — to provide users with easy access to NDBC data.

From all of these experiences, I have developed a genuine interest in the integration of technology and ocean science. Notably, it was the reason why my talk at TEDx Southern Miss 2025 was based on “AI for Ocean Health”, where I mentioned how Artificial Intelligence can be used to solve several problems and create opportunities for the Mississippi Gulf Coast. Throughout my time at IAAS, I have faced numerous setbacks and hurdles in the form of back-to-back code errors and uncertainty about how to proceed. Every time, I resolved them by conducting independent research, reporting the issues to the director, seeking guidance from the student team leader, and collaborating with colleagues.

In addition to my work at IAAS, I am volunteering as an Undergraduate Research Assistant at the Cyber Innovation Lab located in the USM School of Computing Sciences and Computer Engineering, under the guidance of Dr. Nick Rahimi, an Associate Professor. My research is focused on cybersecurity and how AI/ML can solve evolving cyber threats. 
Notably, my first paper was based on using machine learning to classify adversarial passwords into strong, medium, and weak categories. Although several studies on password classification exist in Google Scholar, almost none focused on adversarial passwords, making our work one of the few in the field. My teammate and I presented it at the 2025 Undergraduate Symposium on Research and Creative Activity (UGS) at my university and secured first place under the Computational Approaches category. We also presented it at the 2025 Software and Data Engineering (SEDE) conference held in New Orleans. It was published by Springer, with me as the first author. At the moment, we are working on detecting social engineering attacks in corporate communications using deep learning. We are dealing with several aspects of the corporate world, including phishing simulation and psychological manipulation. It is expected to be completed in the coming months.

Although focused on a different industry, this volunteering experience — like my work at IAAS — leverages the broad applications of Data Science, a field intriguing to me. statement_of_purpose:
My name is Trillyon Earl, and I am a third-year undergraduate at Saint Louis University studying Mathematics, Computer Science, and Data Science. I plan to pursue a PhD in machine learning, focusing on topology-informed memory and world models for partially observable decision-making (POMDP) agents. In many real-world settings, such as robotics, navigation, and scientific forecasting, an agent rarely has access to the full state of its environment. Instead, it receives limited observations and must use its history to infer hidden variables, maintain a belief about what is happening, and predict how the world will evolve. My research interest is in designing deep learning architectures where memory is not just a black box but a structured state that remains stable and useful over long periods. I am drawn to topology because it offers a clear way to describe what a memory representation should preserve: connectivity, invariances, cycles, and other persistent structures. This helps ensure that an agent’s internal model stays reliable even when observations are noisy, incomplete, or change over time.

When I was about 12, I became interested in game development because I wanted to create realistic worlds with interesting mechanics. I soon realized that realism depends more on intelligence than on graphics. In many games, the main limitation is how non-player characters interact with players. They often follow scripts, repeat actions, and do not adapt to changes. This made me want to learn programming so I could experiment with character behavior, not just game mechanics. Teaching myself to code at that age was my biggest challenge, but it taught me to break down problems, work step by step, and learn independently. Later, I saw that making NPCs truly responsive takes more than smart code; it needs structure and a way to handle uncertainty, memory, and interaction, which are all mathematical ideas. That is why I decided to study mathematics along with computer science: I want to understand and build systems that act in believable, adaptive, and reliable ways, not just follow scripts.

I am applying to Purdue’s Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) because it offers the immersive, mentored research environment I need to turn this interest into real progress. SURF’s structure of full-time research, close faculty guidance, and professional development matches my goal of becoming a researcher who can connect theory, implementation, and evaluation. I am especially interested in Purdue’s focus on research that links mathematical modeling, computation, and real-world systems. This fits how I want to approach POMDP agents: by combining dynamical modeling, representation learning, and practical evaluation in complex environments.

The three SURF projects I selected align closely with my goal of building structured world models. The project on probing transitions in motor learning with physics-informed state-space models interests me because it treats learning as a dynamical inference problem. I am especially interested in whether the hidden paths in these models exhibit persistent structure, such as recurring modes or phase-like transitions, that can be described using topological summaries and serve as a stable base for memory. The project on novel deep learning models informed by physics matches my interest in building world models whose hidden states remain grounded in reality. In POMDP settings, if a memory state ignores physical or structural constraints, errors can accumulate quickly; therefore, constraint-aware designs are essential to keep internal representations realistic. Finally, the project on physics-informed machine learning for extreme weather events connects directly to sequential prediction under changing conditions. I am interested in whether topology-informed representations can capture stable global structures in these dynamics, making models more robust and interpretable. While these applications vary, the underlying methodology of extracting structure from sequences is directly applicable to the development of world models for embodied agents.

My preparation comes from both coursework and hands-on experience. Proof-based mathematics has taught me to reason carefully from assumptions and to value invariance and structure, which shapes how I think about designing architectures. My background in probability and statistics supports my interest in uncertainty, evaluation, and model selection, which are central in partially observable settings. On the computing side, I am comfortable building and testing models in Python and R, using C or C++ for performance-focused work, and working in Linux environments with version control.

This spring, I will start research with Dr. Cody Gilbert at Saint Louis University on how neural networks interact with quiver representations. I am excited about this because it helps connect abstract structure with learning systems, supporting the research identity I want to build: using mathematical frameworks to guide representation and architecture design. I have also developed strong communication skills by tutoring in both the SLU Mathematics & Statistics Department and the Computer Science Department. Teaching has taught me to explain complex ideas step by step and to work patiently with others. I value these skills because research relies on clarity, organization, and teamwork.

In the long run, I want a research career focused on building agents that work reliably when information is incomplete and conditions change. I want to create agents that can form world models, retain memory, and maintain essential structure, rather than having to relearn everything from scratch. Purdue SURF is a clear next step for me because it would place me in a strong research community, let me contribute to projects based on dynamical modeling and physics-informed learning, and help me develop the research skills and habits I need for a PhD program.

This question has become my motivating principle and now anchors my interest in artificial intelligence research. While much of modern AI news and research seems to emphasize minimizing the loss function or to achieve marginal improvements in performance metrics, I am increasingly motivated by what these systems ultimately offer to humans, communities, and the living systems they interact with. Only after grappling with this issue was I able to design datasets and evaluate models that produced meaningful results. failure, casually said, "It would be nice if there were a robotic kidney like that," as he was
watching a YouTube video about robotic arms. A few weeks later, he sadly passed away. That
sentence stayed with me though, not because I understood how to build such technology, but
because it made clear how distant advanced medical systems remain from the people who need them the most. When I started my undergraduate studies, I knew I wanted my work to eventually matter in settings like that.

That is why, as soon as I arrived at Carnegie Mellon University in Qatar, I searched for ways to
work at the intersection of Computer Science and medicine. Artificial intelligence research was
the closest path I could find. Knowing that I lacked formal training early on, I independently
audited Andrew Ng's Machine Learning and Deep Learning Specialization to build a strong
theoretical foundation from my very first semester. That preparation led to my first project under the mentorship of Dr. Eduardo Feo Flushing. By my freshman summer, I was working on kidney ultrasound segmentation research, developing a lightweight U-Net based architecture with attention mechanisms. The work felt personal given my uncle's condition, and it taught me how to translate clinical problems into technical solutions. However, it also revealed a gap in my understanding. I could build models that performed well on benchmarks, but I had no real sense of what it meant to deploy them in practice.

That realization motivated me to spend my sophomore summer working at Omma, an agri-tech
startup in London, specifically to understand real-world constraints. I built computer vision
pipelines for deployment on Raspberry Pis across farms in England and Portugal, often in
environments with limited connectivity. Through this experience, I learned to optimize the models for edge devices and even though the work had nothing to do with medicine or healthcare, it taught me a crucial lesson. Making AI useful in the real world is not just about accuracy. It is about building systems that continue to function when the environment shifts, when the data changes, and even when unexpected failures occur.

That perspective now shapes my current research with Dr. Hasan Demirkoparan. I am currently working on failure-aware solvers, integrating Bayesian neural networks with traditional numerical approaches for modeling renal structures. The core idea is to build systems that recognize when they do not know the answer - systems that can quantify their own uncertainty and flag potential failures before they propagate downstream. Through this work, I am learning to design AI systems that are transparent about their limitations and are trustworthy not because they are always right, but because they are honest about when they might be wrong.

This progression, from building accurate models, to understanding deployment, to quantifying
reliability, all of which began with my uncle's words, has clarified what I want to pursue in my
doctoral research: building scalable and trustworthy AI systems for healthcare applications.
