statement_of_purpose:
When I left Nepal on an F-1 visa to study in the United States, I carried with me two years of uncertainty. The gap I took after high school had been terrifying, a decision that could either clarify my direction or leave me more lost than before. A friend recommended the University of Southern Mississippi, noting that it offered substantial scholarships for international students. I applied, received full tuition coverage, and suddenly found myself in Mississippi, still unsure of what I actually wanted to study.

My high school science classes always drew me to their laboratory portions. Dissecting a mouse, playing with electric circuits, performing acid-base titrations and salt analyses: these experiences taught me far more than any textbook ever could. There was something about working with my hands and watching reactions happen in real time that made abstract concepts suddenly make sense. I knew I wanted to pursue something hands-on and applied, where theory and practice would meet. Engineering or applied sciences seemed like the right direction, though I didn’t yet know which specific field.

During my first semester at USM, I came across a program called polymer science and engineering. I had never heard of it before. Out of curiosity, I enrolled in an introductory polymers class, and it changed everything for me. Here was a field that combined chemistry, engineering, and constant laboratory work, precisely what I had been looking for without knowing it existed. The class covered everything from polymer synthesis to why plastic bottles behave differently than rubber bands, and every concept connected to something tangible I could touch and test.

After that semester, I conducted extensive research on careers in polymer science. I met with career services, took aptitude assessments, and tried to make sure this wasn’t just excitement that would fade after a few months. Everything kept pointing in the same direction. I declared polymer science and engineering as my major, with a minor in chemistry, and immediately began looking for research opportunities. I wanted to understand not just what we learned in class, but what we still don’t know and what questions remain unanswered.

I joined a research lab studying the physics of polymer blends, specifically polyethylene and polypropylene. It seemed pretty straightforward at first, but the more I learned, the more complex it became. PE and PP are immiscible, meaning they don’t like to mix, which creates real problems when trying to recycle mixed plastic waste. Also, mechanical recycling causes chain scission during high-temperature, high-shear processing, resulting in lower-molecular-weight fragments with fewer tie chains between crystalline lamellae. This phenomenon significantly reduces mechanical performance. With government policies now mandating recycled content at increasing levels, the question became: how do we use recycled PP and PE when they perform so poorly together? Previous approaches have relied on chemical crosslinking or additives, which can be time-consuming and expensive at scale and further complicate waste streams.

My first project examined solvent immersion annealing as a potential solution. We explored whether swelling PP blends containing high- and low-molecular-weight fractions could promote their co-crystallization and improve mechanical performance without additives. Our results showed over a six-fold increase in extensibility, effectively transforming blends that would have been considered waste into reusable materials. We published this work in ACS Macro Letters this past January, which still feels surreal to me. We’re continuing the research with a focus on optimizing the same system’s processes. But working on this project has raised questions I’m still trying to answer. How exactly does molecular weight disparity control chain diffusion and entanglement at the interface? Why does co-crystallization work so effectively here? Could this approach be applied to other immiscible blends, particularly PE-PP mixtures from mixed recycling streams? What are the fundamental limitations? I’m still working to fully understand what governs these interfacial interactions at the molecular level.

Through this research, I’ve learned various characterization techniques, including DSC, TGA, microcompounding, melt pressing, 3D printing, and tensile testing. Each method has taught me something different about material behavior, though I know I’m only beginning to understand what these techniques can really tell us about polymer physics.
Beyond my research lab, I also work at the Mississippi Polymer Institute in a compostable materials certification lab, where I support ASTM and ISO testing for biodegradation, disintegration, and environmental impact assessment of sustainable polymers. This work is quite different from research. It’s more standardized and protocol-driven, but it’s shown me how laboratory findings eventually become industry standards and regulations.

I’ve tried to explore polymer science from different angles. I’m active in Women in Science and Engineering and the Polymer Science Association, where workshops and seminars have introduced me to research areas I wouldn’t have encountered otherwise. I also joined a robotics team working on autonomous underwater vehicles, which had nothing to do with polymers but taught me valuable lessons about troubleshooting experimental designs when nothing worked as expected. Last year, I won a hackathon for an AI-based database management tool, which surprised me since I’d never thought of myself as particularly strong in computer science. Apparently, the problem-solving skills I developed in the lab transferred better than I expected.

Adjusting to the American university system was challenging at first. The pace was different, the teaching style was unfamiliar, and I wasn’t always sure what professors expected from me. I spent a lot of time in office hours, asked for help whenever I needed it, and worked through tutoring sessions to make sure I understood foundational concepts well enough to build on them. Being an international student added another layer of complexity, navigating visa requirements and simply figuring out how academic culture works here. But I learned that asking for help early, rather than waiting until I was utterly lost, made all the difference.

The hardest part of my journey wasn’t the academics themselves, but instead figuring out where I actually belonged in this field. Polymer science intersects with biomedical engineering, materials science, sustainability, and manufacturing, so many different directions. I spent months talking to professors and attending seminars across various departments, trying to understand what kind of work would sustain my interest over an entire career. Eventually, things became clearer. I’m most interested in the intersection of biomaterials and sustainability, particularly in developing polymers that address either human health challenges or environmental concerns. I want to work on materials such as injectable hydrogels for tissue engineering or bioinspired adhesives derived from sustainable sources, problems where the material itself becomes the solution.

This is what drew me to the SURF program. SURF offers precisely the kind of experience I need right now: intensive, hands-on research in areas I haven’t explored yet, under the mentorship of experts in those fields. The three projects I ranked, hydrogel microparticle fabrication, bioinspired sustainable materials, and MXene nanomaterial synthesis, each push me into new technical territory while still connecting to my core interests. The hydrogel project would teach me microfluidics and soft lithography, techniques I’ve read about extensively but have never actually performed. The bioinspired materials project would deepen my understanding of how nature solves complex materials problems, which seems increasingly relevant as we try to move away from petroleum-based polymers. The MXene project would introduce me to two-dimensional nanomaterials, a completely different class of materials from the bulk polymers I’ve been working with.

I’ll be taking more advanced courses in the upcoming semesters, and I’m genuinely excited to deepen my understanding through that coursework. But what I need most right now is the opportunity to work independently on a research problem at an institution like Purdue. I need to make mistakes, figure out why experiments fail, and learn from researchers who have been working in this field far longer than I have. I want to develop the kind of intuition for material behavior that only comes from spending extensive hours in the laboratory. I need to learn techniques that aren’t part of my undergraduate curriculum but are essential for the kind of research I want to pursue. Working at a top-tier research institution like Purdue would expose me to advanced equipment, sophisticated experimental approaches, and ways of thinking about problems that I haven’t encountered yet. I’m planning to pursue a PhD in polymer science, biomaterials, or materials engineering, and I know that SURF will help me understand what that commitment truly means before I make it.

The technical skills I hope to gain from SURF are clear: microfluidics, rheological characterization, nanomaterial synthesis, and biomimetic fabrication. But beyond these techniques, I want to learn how to design experiments from the ground up, troubleshoot at a more sophisticated level, and communicate my findings effectively to people outside my immediate subfield. I want to build connections with faculty whose research I’ve only encountered through publications, and with fellow students who share my passion for materials science. I believe those relationships will be just as valuable as the technical skills.

Two years ago, I was in Nepal, genuinely unsure whether I would even be able to continue my education. The progress I’ve made since then feels almost unbelievable. But I also know how much further I still need to go. Working at Purdue would give me access to state-of-the-art equipment, sophisticated experimental approaches, and mentorship from researchers who have dedicated their careers to materials science. That level of training and exposure is precisely what I need to advance my understanding and contribute meaningfully to this field.

SURF isn’t just another line on a resume for me. It’s the bridge between where I am now and where I need to be. It’s an opportunity to prove to myself that I can handle the intensity of focused research, that I can learn quickly and contribute something meaningful in just ten weeks, and that this career path I’ve chosen is truly the right one. I’m ready to learn. The uncertainty I felt two years ago has disappeared. I know what I want to do with my life now. I want to understand how materials work at the most fundamental level and use that understanding to solve real problems. I need the right opportunity and mentorship to take that next step, and I genuinely believe that SURF is precisely what I need.

statement_of_purpose:
I come from a small village in Nepal. I'm the eldest son, and I grew up mostly with my mother and grandparents because my father worked abroad in Gulf countries and later Israel to support us. We'd only see him for about a month every few years. Both my parents finished high school but couldn't go further, so they worked relentlessly to give me opportunities they never had. That made me feel responsible for making the most of what their sacrifices provided.
A lot of my foundation came from my mother. She was decent at math, and when I had homework, she'd sit with me and we'd work through problems together. Those quiet moments made math my strongest subject and gave me confidence when I felt lost elsewhere. When I was in grade 5, my mother actually left home to go to Kathmandu to apply to work abroad, and during that time, me and my sister basically stopped studying because there was no one strict enough to make us. My grandparents would ask us to study, but we just didn't listen. So my mother decided to come back and hired a village teacher to help us, and that's when my skills really improved.
In grade 9, I watched this movie my cousin showed me called "The Theory of Everything" about Stephen Hawking, and I got completely hooked on physics. I searched for email addresses of theoretical physicists at Stanford and sent messages to six or seven professors saying I wanted to become a theoretical physicist and asking what I should do. One of them actually replied and pointed me toward resources that helped me teach myself calculus in grade 10, which is usually taught in grade 11 in Nepal.
But things changed during my A levels. In grade 11, I had an internal chemistry exam and didn't do great. I think I got a 67 or something like that. My English teacher, in front of other students, told me I should drop chemistry because my grade was so low. That comment really got to me because I'd always been a decent student, especially in math. I'm naturally a shy person, so I wasn't comfortable asking teachers for help in class. Instead, I went home and started watching YouTube videos to teach myself chemistry. At first, I was just stubborn and wanted to prove that teacher wrong, but as I kept studying, something shifted. I actually started to understand the material, and more than that, I started to like it.
Organic chemistry became my favorite part. I had this teacher who explained things using real life examples, and it made everything click. Like when we were studying alkanes, he explained that farts aren't just carbon dioxide, they actually contain methane. Those kinds of examples stuck with me. What really got me about organic synthesis was that it felt like solving a multi-step math problem. You start with something simple and build it into something complex, step by step, and I think my love for math kind of transferred over to synthesis. By the time I graduated, I was one of the top students, especially in math and chemistry, and I'd gone from almost dropping chemistry to making it my focus.
When I started college, I still wasn't completely sure which area of chemistry I wanted to pursue. I searched online about different branches and thought organic, polymer, nuclear, and analytical all seemed interesting. But over time, my focus narrowed to medicinal chemistry. The idea that I could research new ways of making drugs that could eventually treat real people felt like meaningful work. And then last year, my father was diagnosed with Acute Myeloid Leukemia, and suddenly it wasn't abstract anymore. Chemistry became personal. I wasn't just thinking about it as a subject; I was thinking about it as a tool that could help people like my dad.
When my father got diagnosed with AML, everything shifted for me. He'd spent his whole life working abroad so we could have opportunities, and now he was the one who needed help. I actually went to India where he was being treated, and I donated my stem cells for his transplant. Being part of his treatment process made me realize that chemistry isn't just about understanding reactions on paper. It's about building the tools that actually save people's lives.
What really fascinates me now is the question of efficiency in drug discovery. Making complex molecules is expensive, slow, and wastes resources. I'm interested in how we can use catalysis and reactive intermediates to make that process better. Reactive intermediates are these unstable species that form during reactions, and if you can understand and control them, you can discover entirely new reactions or make existing ones way more efficient. That's the kind of fundamental chemistry I want to learn, because if you can design better synthetic routes, you can make drugs more accessible and affordable. That matters when you've watched your family struggle with the cost of treatment.
I'm also interested in scaffold synthesis, which is basically the core structures that drugs are built around. A lot of anticancer drugs have really complex scaffolds, and figuring out how to make them efficiently is a huge challenge. I want to understand how chemists design the roadmap from simple starting materials to those complex targets. It's not just about following a recipe; it's about being creative and strategic, knowing when to take risks on new methods, and understanding the mechanisms well enough to troubleshoot when things go wrong.
I go to Knox College, a small liberal arts school, and I've learned a lot here. The professors know me personally, and I've built a strong theoretical foundation. But I also know that if I want to go to graduate school and eventually work in drug discovery, I need to experience what research looks like at a bigger scale. I need to be in a lab where there's a whole group of graduate students working on related problems, where there's advanced equipment and the infrastructure to do synthesis seriously.
I've been looking at faculty at Purdue, and Professor Gabriel Lovinger's research on reactive intermediate analysis is exactly what I want to learn. His group works on designing catalysts and discovering new reactions by understanding those unstable intermediates I mentioned earlier. That's the kind of fundamental skill set that underlies all of drug discovery. If you can't design efficient reactions, you can't make drugs.
I'm also actively preparing for this kind of work. Next spring, I'm taking a research course that focuses on Schlenk line techniques and air sensitive manipulations. Reactive intermediates are often really unstable in the presence of air or moisture, so being able to handle them properly is essential. I want to come into SURF with that training already underway so I can hit the ground running and actually contribute to the research instead of spending the whole summer just learning basic techniques.
Coming from a small school, I don't have access to the same resources or research community that Purdue has. SURF would give me that immersion. I'd be working full time in a lab, surrounded by graduate students who are doing this every day, and I'd get to see what a Ph.D. really looks like. That's what I need to figure out if I'm ready for graduate school and to understand what I need to work on before I apply.
My long term goal is to get a Ph.D. in organic chemistry and then go into the pharmaceutical industry as a medicinal chemist working specifically on anticancer therapeutics. I don't want to stay in academia; I want to be in the industry where the actual drug discovery is happening, where what you make in the lab eventually goes into clinical trials and becomes something that patients use.
But I also know that before I can design drugs, I need to master synthesis. Drug discovery isn't just about having good ideas; it's about having the technical skills to execute those ideas, and that takes years of training. SURF would be a critical step in that training. It would give me a summer of full time synthesis experience in a rigorous environment, and that's exactly what I need to be competitive for Ph.D. programs.
I've also been thinking ahead about my senior year. I'm planning to do an honors project where I'll spend the whole year doing research with my organic chemistry professor, who's also my academic advisor. Between SURF this summer and the honors project during my senior year, I'd have a strong research background by the time I apply to graduate schools, and I'd have a much clearer sense of what kind of chemistry I want to focus on in a Ph.D. program.
I've always been the kind of person who goes looking for answers when I don't know something. Like I mentioned earlier, when I got interested in theoretical physics in grade 9, I didn't just read a textbook. I looked up email addresses for professors at Stanford and sent them emails asking for guidance. One of them actually responded, which was huge for me at that age, and pointed me toward resources that let me teach myself calculus a year ahead of when it was normally taught.
That same mindset has continued in college. Last summer, I did an independent research project with one of my professors on water quality in Galesburg. We were looking at fluoride concentration in household tap water and how it changed based on distance from the water treatment plant. It was analytical work, not synthesis, but it taught me a lot about patience and consistency. Research isn't always exciting. A lot of it is just collecting data carefully, checking your work, and being methodical. That project gave me a real sense of what research feels like when it's not just a class assignment.
I've also tried to challenge myself in other ways. In grades 11 and 12, I participated in a National Math Quiz and my team placed sixth. I also prepared for the National Linguistics Olympiad, and my team got an honorable mention. I did those competitions partly because I wanted to see how I'd do, but also because I wanted to push myself in areas beyond just chemistry. Here in college, I even took a class on Middle Eastern politics because my father worked in that region for years, and I wanted to understand the place where he'd been living.
I'm also on the cross country team at Knox College, and honestly, running has taught me as much about perseverance as anything academic. When you're deep into a long run and your body is telling you to stop, you have to find a way to keep going. Research is the same way. Experiments fail, data doesn't make sense, and you have to have the mental endurance to push through and figure it out. I even did the David Goggins Challenge, which is this intense test where you push your body to its absolute limit over 48 hours. It sounds extreme, but it taught me that I'm capable of more than I think I am, and that translates directly to how I approach difficult problems in the lab.
The biggest obstacle I've faced was when my father was diagnosed with AML. It happened last summer, and everything changed. He was being treated in India because we couldn't get the treatment in Nepal, and because he was considered an international patient and didn't have insurance there, the costs were enormous. My family was suddenly under massive financial stress, and I was here in the U.S., thousands of miles away, feeling completely helpless.
Being a first generation college student, I didn't really know how to navigate the financial aid system or who to talk to. I tried appealing to my college for help, and at first, I was basically just told to look for outside scholarships. That didn't feel like enough, so I decided to reach out to someone I knew personally. I'd worked as an orientation leader, and during that time, I'd been trained by the Assistant Vice President for Student Development. I reached out to her directly and explained what was happening. Because I had that relationship with her, I felt like I could be honest about how serious the situation was. We're still working through possible solutions, but at least I have someone advocating for me instead of just being told there's nothing the school can do.
During all of this, I also flew to India to donate stem cells for my father's transplant. That was one of the hardest things I've ever done, not physically, but emotionally. I was stressed about money, I was worried about whether the transplant would work. But being there and being part of his treatment made me feel like I was doing something that mattered. My father spent his whole life working abroad so I could have opportunities, and now I was able to give something back.
He's recovering now, and seeing him get better has only made me more certain about what I want to do with my career. I'm not studying chemistry because it's interesting in the abstract. I'm studying it because I've seen firsthand what it means when treatment works and what it means when families can't afford it. That's why I want to work on anticancer drugs, and that's why I'm applying to programs like SURF. I want to build the skills that will let me contribute to solutions, not just understand the problems.

Businesses closed, buildings were red-stickered and deemed unsafe, and conversations in schools revolved around how “lucky” we were to have been spared the fate of Christchurch in 2011. These experiences sparked a lasting fascination with seismic events and with how the built environment responds to them. Health outcomes were not determined by biology alone, but by circumstance. When I later moved to the United States, I expected to leave those disparities behind. Instead, I encountered a different version of the same problem, one where chronic illnesses like cardiovascular disease and stroke disproportionately affected marginalized communities, again shaped by systemic barriers rather than scientific limitations. These parallel realities play a pivotal role in anchoring my commitment to biology and medicine.
That commitment became deeply personal when my father suffered a stroke. As an immigrant family navigating insurance restrictions and financial strain, I attended every appointment, helped interpret medical information, and watched as care was delayed, not because of medical uncertainty, but because of cost. I witnessed how clinical urgency was often secondary to administrative and financial considerations. Losing my father was devastating, but it also clarified my purpose. It transformed biology from an academic interest into a responsibility: to understand disease rigorously, to question why inequities persist despite available knowledge, and to contribute to solutions rooted in evidence rather than access alone.
Academically, my interests lie at the intersection of biology, physiology, and public health. I am particularly intrigued by questions surrounding cardiovascular physiology, nutrition, and environmental influences on chronic disease, areas where molecular mechanisms and population-level outcomes can be used to improve health. I am motivated by the challenge of translating biological insight into prevention, policy, and equitable care. This intersectional perspective is why I continue to pursue biology despite all the obstacles I’ve faced. It gives me the opportunity to ask not only how disease occurs, but why its burden falls unevenly on certain populations, as I have seen repeatedly.
The SURF program stands out to me because it emphasizes immersive, mentored research rather than passive exposure. I am drawn to the opportunity to work closely with faculty, contribute meaningfully to ongoing projects, and experience firsthand how research questions evolve from real-world health challenges. SURF’s structure would provide the environment, I believe, that brings the best out of me; one where my inquisitive nature is rewarded with the same level of passion I plan to bring to this program. Participation in SURF would be a critical step toward my long-term goal of becoming a physician-scientist. I plan to pursue a medical degree, with strong consideration for an MD or MD/PhD pathway, and to build a career that integrates clinical practice with research. I aspire to work as a surgeon or physician-researcher who not only treats disease but also contributes to the scientific understanding that informs prevention and equitable healthcare delivery. Additionally, I worked with a nutritional dataset examining dietary fiber intake in children, where I analyzed trends and considered implications for long-term health outcomes. This experience reinforced my interest in data-driven health research and motivated me to pursue more hands-on, hypothesis-driven investigation.
My path has not been without obstacles. Navigating higher education as an international student while coping with personal loss has tested my resilience. These experiences have not deterred me from research; they have strengthened my resolve to pursue it with purpose. statement_of_purpose:
Science is, I would say, the inquisition into how life works. Growing up in urban Nigeria, I found myself constantly asking questions, not only of our immediate surroundings, but of mother nature. Why was the sky blue, why did I have this black being following me in the Sun that looked like me, and what was this ‘cancer’ that every character in movies always succumbed to. I began to garner answers as I got older, and particularly in high school, due to my introduction into the three main fields of science. What stood out to me though was I seemed to perform better in Biology, Chemistry and Physics in comparison to my other courses. That was primarily what steered me in that direction. As for my motivation to stay on that path? Diseases. In my family, we have a history of hypertension and obesity, so I spent my teenage years wondering if our lifestyle choices were the total cause. I eventually found myself seeking alternatives such as embarking on a keto diet and replacing sugar with artificial sweeteners. This didn’t last long, however, as I discovered studies linking the sweeteners to increased risks of cancer and gut microbiome issues. It just seemed like every dietary decision we made always had one adverse effect to come along with it and so we just reverted to our usual diets. Hence one of my main goals in research is to further explore the impacts of certain dietary components on disease risk. I was therefore particularly interested when I saw the project being proposed by Dr. Julia Laskin’s lab. The use of the principle of mass spectrometry to locate biomolecules in tissue could help provide insights into some diseases. I was not aware of mass spectrometry use beyond differentiating organic compounds, as I did in my organic chemistry labs, and proteins, so I am looking forward to joining her lab to work on this project and really interested in finding out more about this technique.
When it comes to research, my initial experiences come in the field of bioinformatics, as I was involved in creating a novel documentation of marine bacteria present in our college oceanarium. As part of a two-man research team, my partner and I approached this question initially by filtering liters of water from the tanks in the oceanarium and trying to isolate the DNA from bacteria caught in the filter. This was however unsuccessful, and we pivoted to use the water directly to culture bacteria on plates, using a rich marine broth food source. We had a variety of growth and proceeded to isolate, amplify using PCR, and performed nanopore sequencing. This experience helped foster my teamworking abilities, as well as my adaptability when faced with problems in a research project. 
More recently, I participated in the summer research experience program at North Dakota State University, where I was assigned on a project involving predicting Ice Adhesion Strength in polymers. One might wonder how this would be important scientifically, but Ice Adhesion is actually a really common obstacle when it comes to energy generation and aviation. So on this project I worked on collecting datasets from primary literature on different polymers involved in horizontal, vertical, tensile and centrifugal ice stress tests. I was required to take note of all polymer structures in the datasets, accounting for additives, so as to calculate chemical descriptors for the polymers and possibly relate those to the ice adhesion strength values from our multiple datasets. I did end up using a random forest model, created using python, to establish a relationship, as it seemed that there were just layers of complexity that a linear model would not work. I was able to identify about 15 descriptors that appeared pivotal to the Ice Adhesion process. Future works would involve creating polymers that vary the chemical properties described by these descriptors to assess the effect on ice adhesion.
On an independent level, my previous research involved analyzing the carbon uptake of mutants of a marine bacterium, R.pomeroyi. I was provided with an array of mutants and a wild type bacterium through a collaboration with the University of Georgia, and was tasked with identifying possible substrates for annotated transporter genes. This project entailed a combination of wet and dry lab aspects, as I was not only carrying out growth screens of the bacterium using different organic carbon sources, but also performed fundamental bioinformatic analysis using BLAST on the sequenced genes in order to narrow down possible functional groups associated with them. This experience helped lay the foundation for me regarding working in multiple parts of a lab, on the same project. I am hoping to extend and build on this learning process and gain an advantage in my pursuit of knowledge in the field of science.

There, I worked on large-scale manufacturing and infrastructure systems alongside PLC technicians, mechanical designers, and controls engineers. Across these projects, I observed that electrical systems—shaped by computation—formed the backbone enabling manufacturing, automation, and power management. This experience redirected my focus to Electrical Engineering, specifically to how computation and engineering systems interact.

I viewed software not as the backbone of engineered systems, but as an amplifier whose effectiveness is fundamentally constrained by hardware. While algorithmic improvements can enhance performance, power limitations and physical deployment often define what is practically achievable. This realization motivated my interest in understanding how hardware design choices shape computational performance and vice versa, and how hardware–software co-design can unlock capabilities neither layer achieves independently. I am particularly drawn to questions surrounding how computationally intensive methods, including machine learning, can be made practical under real-world resource constraints. These questions require principled investigation into how software and models map onto hardware, how efficiency tradeoffs emerge, and how non-ideal system behavior influences performance—motivating my pursuit of research training.

During an NSF-funded REU at the University of Utah, I worked on the design and validation of a miniature electrocutaneous stimulation system intended to evoke tactile sensation through a wrist-worn interface. I designed and simulated a constant-current, high-voltage stimulation circuit using MATLAB and PSpice, modeling the human body as a simplified RC network to guide initial parameter selection. In practice, electrode placement, skin condition, and inter-subject variability introduced non-deterministic behavior that diverged from simulation. Addressing this required iterative testing and curated experimental thresholds, reinforcing for me the importance of robustness when working with physical systems.

I continued this work at my home institution in the bioelectronics laboratory, where I am developing and testing single-channel electrical stimulation protocols across varying current amplitudes and frequencies. My role spans algorithm development in MATLAB and Arduino, hardware interfacing, and preparation for human-subject testing. This continuation emphasized experimental repeatability and parameter sensitivity, as well as the need to design systems that tolerate variability without compromising safety or performance.

As the systems I worked on became more complex and less deterministic, I struggled to translate conceptual understanding into sustained research progress. Although I could follow theory and contribute in meetings, I often returned to the lab stuck and without a clear, executable plan. I resolved this challenge in two parts. Firstly, by formalizing my workflow: documenting meetings in detailed technical notes, sketching schematics, logging design decisions, and writing down concrete next steps and open questions. And secondly, by creating tighter feedback loops with my research mentors, moving from once a week to twice or three times a week, to ensure I stay on track. These shifts allowed me to iterate more efficiently, ask more precise questions, and produce consistent experimental results.

Complementing my academic research, I interned with Hallam-ICS Engineering, where I supported industrial electrical and control systems projects. I produced build-ready electrical and process drawings, assisted with PLC troubleshooting and Ignition SCADA tasks, and helped assemble control panels for automation upgrades. This experience grounded my research interests in real deployment constraints, emphasizing reliability and cross-disciplinary coordination in engineered systems—constraints I had already encountered in research, now at industrial scale.

Building on these experiences, I am particularly interested in how emerging computational approaches—including machine learning—interact with hardware architectures in practice. Rather than viewing software or learning models as standalone solutions, I aim to understand how they are constrained or reformulated to operate within the limits of implementation and reliability imposed by physical systems.

I aim to deepen expertise in hardware–software co-design, circuit and control theory, and translating computational methods into deployable hardware, especially for resource-constrained or safety-critical environments.

The solution - switching to LangChain's create\_agent with API enforced structured outputs - eliminated the silent failures. This debugging experience revealed a principle directly applicable to nanoHUB’s AURA platform - reliable workflow automation depends on enforced contracts between tools, not just requested compliance.

CSALT at LUMS gave me an opportunity to extend the PakBBQ: A Culturally Adapted Bias Benchmark for QA (accepted for EMNLP 2025) to Sindhi, Pashto, Punjabi, and Balochi. PakBBQ benchmark revealed a 12 percent accuracy gain from explicit disambiguation in Urdu and even though Urdu shows stronger counter-bias than English overall, it still suffers a 7–17 pp accuracy gap and higher variance, quantifying the low-resource challenge and how most multilingual models fail on culturally specific constructs like Pakistani regional bias, sectarian nuance, and language formality (pronoun registers, honorifics, and morphology. We had been systematically adapting templates, confronting scarce data, and evaluating however my recent read about MBZUAI’s ArabCulture provided a transformative direction to address scalability crisis. The finding that just a dozen culturally grounded demonstrations could improve cross-cultural understanding by an average of 10 percent- and up to 34 percent in a specific case- was a highly efficient revelation encouraging me to explore and integrate it into our research extension. My proposal to leverage the culturally adapted templates from PakBBQ extension as demonstration sets to teach a base model via DITTO to generalize its understanding across Pakistani languages and regional cultures was highly appreciated by my supervisor.

These experiences give me a methodological toolkit for creating structured, reproducible evaluations and an instinct for connecting techniques across fields to solve challenges, positioning me to contribute meaningfully to the AURA project’s goal of designing workflows that AI systems can use reliably and efficiently. What excites me most about this opportunity is the chance to learn by contributing.

Inspired by the RAG approaches in SciToolAgent (2025), it would function as a suggestion system with human readable justifications, allowing researchers to verify logic before execution. Crucially, it would use API level structured output enforcement to guarantee that proposed workflows conform to AURA’s interface specifications.

A workflow profiling module could instrument AURA executions to collect detailed runtime metrics such as CPU/GPU utilization, memory patterns, I/O bottlenecks - similar to OS performance monitoring tools. This profiling data would create the foundation for future optimization efforts while delivering immediate visibility into resource usage patterns.

A complementary error aware validation and provenance framework can systematically compare AI executed workflows against baseline results. This directly addresses the project’s requirement to ``compare AI-driven execution with manual execution to evaluate accuracy, speed, and reliability.'' Building on the self checking paradigm of AG2 (2024) and the guardrail system I implemented at NETSOL (with versioned rules and audit trails) this framework would log each execution step, validate intermediate outputs, and flag discrepancies. It would provide the metrics and traces needed to debug workflow failures and quantify AURA’s efficiency gains.

Inspired by PRISM's reusable experimental protocols (2024), a version controlled library of well documented workflow modules could further promote reproducibility and reuse. By creating Git tracked nanoHUB components with explicit input/output schemas, validation rules, and test fixtures, this library would make existing tools more discoverable and composable while maintaining the contract enforcement needed for reliable automation.

I am comfortable with Python, Git, and modular system design, and I am eager to dive into nanoHUB’s toolchain and learn from Prof. Strachan’s team. I may not have prior experience with materials simulation, but I am a quick and curious learner, and I believe my experience with agent orchestration, structured evaluation, and system debugging positions me to contribute meaningfully to AURA’s mission of making scientific computing more accessible through reliable automation within the Strachan Lab.

This motivation first came from my wish to protect my identity. I saw that my native language, Brahui, was slowly disappearing from the digital world. Because of this, I worked with my mentor to digitize it. We developed a system that can recognize handwritten and printed Brahui text using deep learning and sentiment analysis. When I saw a computer read my mother tongue, it confirmed my belief that technology can protect what truly matters.
After this, I focused on our land. My region depends on agriculture, but we lack modern systems to handle harsh conditions. I could not change the weather, but I could improve our response. Therefore, I worked on an AI-powered, IoT-based soil testing system to help farmers use fertilizers better and increase crop yields.

While working in rural areas, I saw the serious health crisis in Balochistan. Communities faced malaria, respiratory infections, and severe maternal and child health problems like malnutrition. I also saw many non-communicable diseases, made worse by poverty, cultural barriers, and the lack of health facilities.
I stood in areas where there were no hospitals, and doctors were very far away. I realized how helpless the situation was. I could not build many hospitals or bring thousands of doctors. The gap in infrastructure was too large to fix with buildings alone.
However, I realized that I could help bridge this gap with code. Physical resources are limited, but software can be scaled and shared. An AI diagnostic tool can reach places where a doctor cannot. This understanding turned my curiosity into a clear mission: to use artificial intelligence to expand access to modern healthcare in resource-limited communities.

Medical AI must be safe, stable, and trustworthy in real hospital conditions.

I would value the chance to apply my computer vision skills to his work in pediatric cardiovascular health, moving from theoretical accuracy to clinical utility.
My long-term goal is to pursue graduate studies in computer science, with a focus on trustworthy AI. I want to bring this knowledge back to underserved regions and build systems that are safe, accessible, and based on real human needs. SURF is the key bridge between where I am now and the future I want to build.

statement_of_purpose:
My name is Abdullah Ejaz Janjua and I am a 3rd year Computer Science undergraduate at the Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute of Engineering Sciences and Technology (GIKI), Pakistan. I am writing to express my interest in Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowships (SURF) at Purdue University.

My broader research question is "What is required to make machines perceive the world with human-like intuition?". To this end, I built my ML foundations by taking Machine Learning Specialization by Prof. Andrew Ng, CS231n: Deep Learning for Visual Recognition by Prof. Fei-Fei Li, and Computer Vision by Prof. Andreas Geiger.

In addition to my coursework, I have practical research experience. I cold-emailed Dr. Waqas Sultani at the Information Technology University (ITU) because his research group’s direction aligned more closely with my interests than the opportunities at my home university. Under his guidance at the Intelligent Machines Lab, I contributed to two separate projects. On my first project, I worked on Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA), where the model was trained on the labeled domain (source) and adapted to an unlabeled domain (target). Our method proposed a novel across the batch image-mixing technique along with psuedo-labeling to ensure smooth model adaption, which achieved 51.7 mAP@50 on Malaria M5 Dataset (HCM_100x -> LCM_100x), where ’HCM’ stands for High-Cost Microscope, ’LCM’ for Low-Cost Microscope, and ’100x’ is magnification level [1].

However, high inter-class and foreground-background similarity led to high model uncertainty in the psuedo-labeling and image-mixing process, resulting in sub-optimal feature representations and negatively affecting performance. In order to explore potential improvements on their existing approach, I extensively reviewed relevant literature. Through my review, I identified the potential of Monte Carlo Dropout (MCD) method as a way of capturing epistemic uncertainty. I selected MCD as it offers an optimal trade-off between robustness and computational efficiency compared to Bayesian networks and model ensembles, which increased performance upto 53.1 mAP@50. I also considered contrastive loss, but ruled it out because it assumes the availability of one-to-one correspondences between the source and target domains which is often not the case in the real-world. Additionally, I also contributed by setting up and running experiments, as well as assisting with the write-up. This work is currently under review.

In my second project, I worked on Domain Generalization (DG), where the model was only trained on source domain and tested on a target domain. To begin the project, the professor assigned me the task of presenting MR-PLIP [4]. I thoroughly read and analyzed the paper, breaking down its intricate design into key steps. Inspired by their use of text as a "helper" to guide image features, we aimed to apply a similar approach to learn domain-invariant features for hematology microscopy images.

At first, I explored using text generated by a Vision Language Model (VLM) without human supervision as the "helper". However, I quickly realized that this was an ill-posed problem. In addition to the lack of a known target domain, there were no VLMs trained on hematology images, which resulted in textual descriptions that were heavily noisy and, in most cases, inaccurate. As the best alternative, I instead used VLMs trained on histopathology images, but the issue of noisy descriptions remained. This added constraint limited my options; for instance, I couldn’t use contrastive loss, as relying on noisy descriptions would have negatively impacted the model’s performance. Instead, I explored using prompting techniques in combination with the noisy textual descriptions to mitigate the noise. Specifically, I provided a text model (trained via histopathology image-text pairs) with the descriptions as prior knowledge and used prompting techniques to extract prompts following TCP [3]. This approach resulted in an improvement, achieving 31.1 mAP@50 on LuekemiaAttri (H_100x_C2 -> L_100x_C2), where ’L’ stands for Low-cost and ’C2’ refers to a higher quality camera, up from the baseline performance of 23.6 mAP@50 [2].

After recognizing the challenges posed by noisy texts, I explored alternative approaches and chose the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) as a potential solution. My controlled experiments on images revealed that DFT could effectively extract both textural and spatial information. However, I noticed that when images were blurry, many details were lost. To address this, I divided the image into windows and applied DFT to each window independently. This variation of DFT captured the previously missed details. Inspired by research highlighting the importance of feature fusion, I incorporated DFT into the intermediate layers of the model. I hypothesized that repeatedly applying DFT to intermediate features and fusing them would improve model generalization. Empirical analysis confirmed this hypothesis, resulting in a further improvement and achieving 38.7 mAP@50. This work is currently under review at Computer Vision Conference.

Through these experiences, I have learned how to communicate information effectively, modify codebases to suit my needs, conduct experiments, and draw meaningful insights from them. Furthermore, this work has reinforced my belief that enabling models to adapt to unseen domains is a critical milestone in answering my research question. I am particularly attracted to Purdue’s SURF program for the chance to apply these skills to interdisciplinary challenges, such as Prof. Craig Goergen’s predictive modeling in biomedical imaging or Prof. Lei Wang’s use of CNNs for extreme weather forecasting. 

These skills, along with my interest in addressing fundamental challenges in computer vision, have motivated me to pursue this program. It offers both the research opportunities and the mentorship necessary to build on my expertise and will support my aspirations to become a researcher in the field of computer vision.

I am a junior-year undergraduate student studying bioinformatics at SINES, NUST in Pakistan. My curriculum is a combination of biological sciences and computer science courses, of which, 43% belongs to computer science. Never would I had though that this 43% changed my views, ideas, and interests over the past year or so, making me realize that my real interest lies in mathematics and theoretical computer science (TCS) -- specifically formal verification (FV) and interactive theorem proving (ITP).

My path here started when I encountered discrete mathematics (DM) in spring 2024. I was really attracted by the logic and the proof side of it. Most students, I noticed, found the formal proofs meaningless (what's the point?), tedious as well as redundant (too much work for something such as this?!) and challenging (what did I just read?). On the other hand, I was drawn to them, because of how precise, rigorous, and clear they were. I also found them to be amazing mental exercises. However, because of some unfortunate circumstances, I couldn't do well in the course initially; and instead of moving on, I kept exploring the material after the semester ended. Digging deeper and deeper, I discovered that TCS, particularly FV, exists as its own field -- that CS isn't just about building applications or handling data, but its more about mathematical foundations and formal reasoning.

Ever since that, I've been hooked into this field and have been trying my hardest to learn and pursue it, while fighting the limited interest shown by peers and professors. That resulted in me looking for and eventually finding and then working with a very nice FV professor, Dr. Adnan Rashid, and a teammate on learning ITP; and then eventually pursuing our degree's final year project (FYP) in this area; this was in summer 2025. We started with HOL4, moved to Lean4, and worked through some books a bit (FPIL and TPIL). We did basic formalizations like calculators and Fibonacci series, and practiced with the games from the lean game server. We really enjoyed Lean4 and spent significant time with it.

This past semester (fall 2025), I took two courses which I found very intriguing; operating systems (OS) and design and analysis of algorithms (DAA). In OS, I learned that systems in general are very cool and in them, scheduling, virtual memory, and so on feels magical: providing, between processes, time sharing, isolation, protection, an illusion of infinite memory, and so on. But we were just given the intuition that this stuff "just works," but I kept wondering how we actually know that these systems and their components work the way we're told. It made sense that there needs to be certainty on correctness due to their critical nature because bugs in them would even break the actual correct software written while assuming system correctness. To the rescue came the things I learned from DM and DAA -- loop invariants, logic, induction -- which we can use in proving that these system components works correctly. This is exactly what FV techniques like ITP do, to mathematically reason about the system, and hence was born another area of my interest: systems verification.

Recently, me and my FYP teammate started brainstorming the topic for our final year project and realized systems verification would be very nice and intellectually interesting -- verifying OS modules starting with schedulers -- inspired by seL4, world's first fully-verified microkernel written in C and verified in Isabelle/HOL (to my knowledge). Ultimately, we have decided that Rocq/Coq is better suited for this work than Lean4, so we've been learning it. My end-semester exams ended recently, so now I'm spending time on going through software foundations series for learning Rocq as much as I can. During exams, I was also working through the introduction to logic in the lean game server whenever I got free time because I genuinely enjoy it and don't want to lose what I've learned.

I also did an internship at NCAI deep learning Lab (also known as TUKL DL Lab) in summer 2025, working on medical image analysis with active learning strategies. There were no local research opportunities in TCS or FV, so I thought gaining any research experience would help my profile for the long run. To improve my profile so that I get into this super amazing field was the motivation. It turned out that the work I did there, I found it sort of interesting -- I reproduced results from a research paper on dental X-ray disease detection using multimodal systems -- but the experience made it clear to me that I prefer the formal methods side over more empirical ML. When there's work bridging both areas, I'd be more engaged with (and thus would enjoy) the theorem proving and verification aspects.

Finding research opportunities in FV has been difficult locally. There's limited interest in this specialized area here in Pakistan, which is unfortunate because it's exactly what I want to pursue. I'm aiming for a PhD in TCS right after my bachelor's, focusing on formal methods and program verification. This is where SURF programs become really important for me. But why specifically Purdue's SURF? There are two main reasons. First, it has a project related to formal verification: "Gradual Verification: Assuring Programs Incrementally" by Professor Jenna DiVincenzo. Second, this program is ideal for international students like me who need full funding including housing allowance to participate in programs outside their country. Not all SURF programs or undergraduate research opportunities offer this level of funding support. Additionally, it offers a structure research experience including the chance to present and/or publish the work at conferences and to meet the diverse community of people working on interesting problems. The opportunity to work on verification projects under expert supervision would be very valuable for me. It would also complement my FYP work and give me the guided research exposure needed for my future progress as a researcher. I want to learn more advanced verification techniques, work with tools and frameworks I haven't been exposed to yet, and develop the research skills I'll need for doctoral studies and beyond.

Coming from a bioinformatics background to theoretical CS isn't typical. Most CS students don't explore the formal, mathematical side of the field the way I have. The intersection of rigorous mathematics with computing and the idea of proving mathematically appeals me a lot. I've realized that being in an interdisciplinary program actually helped me see what I really wanted to pursue, even if it meant diverging from the biology side entirely. The obstacles have been the lack of local resources and community in FV. I've had to be self-directed -- teaching myself through online resources, finding remote supervision, working through textbooks independently. But these challenges have also made me more determined and shown me how much I value this field.

I grew up seeing two ways of solving problems, one built on systems, logic, and iteration, the other empathy and understanding. For a long time I respected both paths without being sure where I belonged. However, that started to change during the COVID quarantine and I began to code consistently. What began as small scripts quickly became something I genuinely enjoyed, not only because it was creative, but because progress was visible. You write, test, break, fix, and improve, and that loop suited me. By the time I entered university, computer science felt like a decision I was making for myself.

I saw them as the point where software becomes adaptive, where a program learns from data instead of relying solely on hard-coded rules. Coming into university without a strong computing background from high school made that shift feel steep at first: concepts like backpropagation and optimization weren’t intuitive, and early experiments failed in ways I couldn’t easily explain. I responded by changing how I learned. I started leaning on professors, seniors, and peers, using office hours more intentionally, and following structured resources to close gaps step by step. Over time, I grew comfortable with iteration and debugging as a normal part of progress, and that mindset shaped how I approached more complex work.
Computer vision especially interested me, and my earliest curiosity was around common applications like facial recognition. Over time, what kept pulling me deeper were the harder questions behind working demos: how models behave when data changes, how to tell whether a result will generalize, and how to interpret a decision when the output matters. Those questions became even more real as I started working on projects that sit closer to real-world deployment.
I have explored these interests through coursework, an internship, and ongoing research work. At NUST, I have been working alongside Dr. Rabia on content extraction and filtering from video streams. I contributed to building a real-time Video Monitoring System (VMS) that continuously captures live YouTube streams in 5-second chunks, converts video to audio, synthesizes user-defined trigger words using a pre-trained HiFiGAN, and uses correlation-based matching (>70%) to save the surrounding context while discarding irrelevant segments. Building on this, I am now working on Siamese-network–based audio similarity models to learn discriminative embeddings and improve robustness of audio matching, moving beyond purely correlation-based detection. That work has pushed me to think in terms of pipelines, not isolated models, especially around selecting relevant segments from continuous input and reducing redundancy while staying efficient.
Last summer, I interned at PureLogics, where I worked on Retrieval Augmented Generation pipelines and also contributed to computer vision tasks. In RAG, I learned that output quality often depends on retrieval, filtering, and grounding choices, not only the language model. On the computer vision side, I evaluated and tested OCR models, where noisy images, layout variation, and edge cases quickly exposed the gap between a promising model and a dependable system. That experience made me more careful about evaluation and made me want to pursue work that is not only accurate, but reliable.
Alongside this, I have been working with professors on an ongoing medical computer vision direction centered on fracture and abnormality detection in X-ray images, using the MURA dataset and recent literature as a foundation. I have been particularly drawn to elbow-related cases because they are clinically important and often subtle, which pushes us to be careful about preprocessing choices, dataset splits, and understanding failure modes rather than only chasing performance. In the same space, I have also been exploring explainable AI methods with faculty guidance, mainly to understand when interpretability tools are genuinely informative and how model evidence can be presented in a way that supports clinical decision-making without overclaiming what explanations can guarantee. This direction feels personally meaningful to me because it naturally connects the two worlds I grew up around—computing and medicine—into one research focus.

Through the prototyping and build process of my team’s radio transmission payload experiment, I realized how necessary electrical engineering is to any astronautical engineering application. It very quickly became apparent to me that a wonderfully designed mechanical system cannot perform any function autonomously without at least some component of an electrical or computer system. Because it is necessary for many space instruments to carry out their functions autonomously, electrical and computer engineering are extremely important to the payload missions that are designed to explore and collect information about space. I found that I thoroughly enjoy the design process of what could be referred to as the “brains” of a system. Consequently, controls and autonomous systems is one specific area of electrical engineering that I find attractive. 

The SURF program is of particular interest to me because, as a current Purdue student, I value the fact that SURF is embedded into the university itself. Whereas other summer research programs would be a standalone experience for me, SURF has the opportunity to provide me with connections that I can continue to build even after the program is complete. I also value how SURF welcomes new STEM researchers, specifically how the program provides information about available research projects as well as creates many opportunities for mentorship experiences for students new to research. As someone who intends to pursue a graduate degree in a STEM field before entering the workforce in the space industry, it would be deeply valuable to me to start understanding now what practices and ways of thinking will set me up for future success in academia.

My exploration of aerospace and electrical engineering goes beyond just the coursework for both my major and minor, and these experiences have prepared me to be successful in the SURF program. Through my experience on this competitive technical rocketry team, I have discovered and explored my passion for electrical engineering and how it can be applied to astronautics. 1- Why I chose Computer Science and why I keep pursuing it

I came into Computer Science through a pretty practical route. Before starting my BS in CS, I completed a diploma in Software Engineering at Aptech Computer Education. Most of what I learned there came from building things, breaking them, and fixing them again, so CS didn’t feel like a purely theoretical subject. It felt more like a set of tools I could actually use.

The moment CS started to feel personally meaningful (not just “useful”) was in my second year, when I joined The Bridge of Hopes (TBoH) as a developer. TBoH is working on an R&D project to develop AI-based software that supports children with intellectual disabilities in learning and development. My contributions were mainly on the web and product-facing side: building the project’s web presence and designing UI for the early version of the software.

What surprised me was that the hard part wasn’t only the code. We had to earn trust from special schools, explain the idea to educators who had every reason to be skeptical, and communicate what we were building in a way that was clear and responsible. A working website and an MVP helped us show that this wasn’t just a concept slide deck. It made outreach conversations easier, helped with credibility, and supported collaboration with schools and the broader push for funding and support.

A separate but related moment was building FORKED NUCES. Watching the system grow made a simple point feel very real: complexity shows up quietly. A codebase that starts out clean can become hard to change faster than you expect, and small feature requests can trigger uncomfortable redesign decisions. That experience made me take software engineering more seriously, and it made me curious about why systems become difficult to evolve, especially once ML components enter the picture.

Right now, the questions that keep circling in my head are things like:

How do we build AI/ML systems that remain trustworthy in high-impact settings like education and assistive technology, especially when the data is noisy, limited, or sensitive?

What does “usable and interpretable” look like for real users, not just for engineers reading metrics? Accuracy may matter, but it rarely tells the whole story.

How do we engineer ML systems so they stay maintainable over time, instead of slowly degrading under scale, feature creep, shifting requirements, or changes in data?

Those questions are a big reason I’m leaning toward formal research training, not only product development experience.

2- Why SURF at Purdue, and how it supports my career goals

What draws me to SURF is the structure. It appears to be designed as a real research experience with mentorship, professional development, and concrete research outputs.

I want to get better at research methodology in a rigorous setting: defining a problem precisely, doing a serious literature review, forming hypotheses, designing experiments, evaluating results, and communicating what I found in a way that holds up to scrutiny. I can build prototypes, but turning curiosity into a research plan with measurable outcomes is a different skill set, and I want to develop it properly.

Another piece that matters to me is Purdue’s broader ecosystem around translation and entrepreneurship. My long-term plan includes building in industry and eventually launching a startup, so I value being in a place where research and real-world impact are both treated as serious goals. Purdue Innovates points to support for founders through resources, mentorship networks, and early-stage funding pathways. And the Purdue Foundry (managed by the Purdue Research Foundation) is described as a business accelerator for Purdue faculty, staff, and students interested in creating startups. That combination fits how I think about my future: research discipline first, then building something real with it.

3- Long-term STEM career goals, and how SURF contributes to them

Long-term, I see my career sitting at the intersection of:

Industry AI/ML (applied research plus product work)

Startup building, ideally in an area where AI can create measurable social value (assistive learning technologies, education, or other human-centered AI products)

In the near to mid term, I want to work in industry environments where ML is built for real users and real constraints. That means learning how strong teams deploy models responsibly, validate them beyond offline accuracy, monitor performance over time, and iterate without causing harm or confusion. Over the long term, my goal is to combine research discipline with product execution and build a startup that solves a focused, high-impact problem using AI.

Working closely with faculty and graduate mentors, plus presenting at the symposium, is likely to create relationships that can shape future research direction, collaborations, and references. Even one strong mentoring relationship can change how you think about research.

4) What I have done so far to explore AI/ML and prepare for research

So far, my preparation has been a mix of practical development, mission-driven R&D exposure, and leadership roles where I had to be accountable for delivery.

R&D and mission-driven development (TBoH)

Joined The Bridge of Hopes (TBoH) as a developer in my second year.
Contributed to an R&D initiative focused on AI-based learning support software for children with intellectual disabilities.
Built the organization’s website and designed UI for the early software, which helped the team communicate direction, connect with special schools, and strengthen the MVP’s credibility.

Engineering execution and systems thinking (ACM NUCES, tech operations)

Currently serve as Co-Head of the Tech Operations team at ACM NUCES.
Automate workflows that support large-scale events like Coders’ Cup and Developers’ Day.
This work has pushed me toward reliability and operational thinking: reducing error-prone manual steps, designing processes that don’t break under event pressure, and building systems that other people can actually use without needing me to babysit them.

Industry exposure (internship)

Interned at Devcir PK, a service-based company.
Learned what “real delivery constraints” feel like: timelines, shifting requirements, and the expectation that your work has to be readable and maintainable for the next person.

Leadership in development teams (Procom)

Served as Co-Head of the Web Development team for Procom (a flagship annual event at FAST NUCES).
Strengthened project ownership, coordination, and delivery under deadlines, especially when multiple people are touching the same codebase.

Growing interest in research-level engineering questions (FORKED NUCES)

Building FORKED NUCES made scalability and maintainability feel non-negotiable, not optional “nice-to-haves.”
It directly shaped my interest in research-oriented software engineering and ML system design, particularly the long-term costs of complexity.

Taken together, I’ve had enough experience to know I can deliver production-facing work and lead teams. At the same time, I’m motivated to move from only building systems to also studying how and why they break, and how we can design them better, especially in AI/ML contexts.

Obstacles and challenges, and how I addressed them

Two challenges have been especially formative for me.

Bridging stakeholder needs with technical work (TBoH)
Working on a project aimed at children with intellectual disabilities made it obvious that technical success is only part of success. If educators and institutions don’t trust the work, or can’t understand what it does, the project stalls. We dealt with that by prioritizing deliverables that were concrete and easy to demonstrate (a website plus early UI and MVP work). That made discussions with schools more practical, helped build credibility, and supported the team’s broader outreach and support efforts.

Limited access to formal research training
Compared to major research universities, it can be harder to find structured research mentorship and methodology training at the undergraduate level in some environments. I tried to respond by seeking R&D exposure through TBoH, building systems that raised deeper engineering questions (like FORKED NUCES), and taking leadership roles (like ACM Tech Ops) that forced disciplined problem-solving. Still, I feel the gap. SURF seems like the next step because it offers the formal research structure I’m intentionally looking for: mentorship, professional development, and research outputs that force you to think and communicate like a researcher.
