My pursuit of mathematics has been shaped not by accident, but by a sustained curiosity about structure, abstraction, and the hidden order that governs both natural and artificial systems around us and inside us. This curiosity first took shape during my years at Cadet College Kohat (from where I did my Matriculation), a multicultural boys only residential institution where intellectual exploration had to coexist with a demanding military routine and adjustment to boarding environment at such a tender age. Even within that rigid environment, mathematics offered a sense of freedom, a way to fly into the pleasures of imagination. In eighth grade, after having studied his (S. Thompson's) book on the history of electricity, I taught myself calculus from Silvanus P. Thompson’s Calculus Made Easy. That experience proved formative not only because of the material itself (though I cannot forget the pleasure of knowing how euler's number was related to compund interest to this day...), but because it gave me the sense that serious intellectual engagement could be self directed, rigorous, and deeply fulfilling at the same time. It gave me the confidence to move with belief in my unique academic path.
While my early interests leaned toward theoretical computer science (problems like computataional complexity, convergence rates etc.), I soon recognized that mathematics was the common language underlying everything that drew my attention. Whether in algorithms, physical systems, or computation, mathematical structure consistently emerged as the organizing principle. Over time, I came to view mathematics not merely as a tool for application, but as a discipline worthy of study in its own right. I became increasingly intrigued by questions of structure, symmetry, and abstraction, as well as by the strange unexpected connections between pure theory and its often unexpected relevance. Mathematics: Form and Function by Saunders Maclane and an essay of Nobel Laureate Dr. Egene Wigner titled, "The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences" became favourite readings of mine.
This perspective guided my decision to study mathematics at Quaid i Azam University Islamabad, one of Pakistan’s strongest academic centers for the discipline. The transition, however, was not without difficulty. Due to limited university housing, I spent my first year living in a private and unsafe area near campus. Administrative rigidity restricted my ability to formally enroll in several core computer science courses which I intended to take with my mathematics degree concurrently. Undergraduate research opportunities were scarce, in short non existent simply. Requests for mentorship were frequently declined on the basis that research was reserved for graduate students. At times, inconsistencies in teaching quality and grading further complicated the learning environment; despite our formal protests no attention was paid to these matters. This affected our grades and morale.
Rather than allowing these constraints to define my education, I became deliberately self reliant. I immersed myself in independent study, engaging deeply with mathematical texts beyond the syllabus and making extensive use of the university’s central library. I became one of its most frequent users because my of sustained intellectual curioisty. When formal pathways were limited, I maintained momentum through self study, discussion with like minded friends, and exploration.
Alongside this independent work, I sought spaces that encouraged intellectual exchange. I joined the Quaid i Azam University Science Society and served as its Editor in Chief, overseeing the publication of the annual science magazine and contributing articles aimed at communicating complex ideas with clarity and depth. I also became involved in the library society, where we founded Pakistan’s first open library on a university campus, based on "Take a book give a book" model. These initiatives were guided by my belief that knowledge gains value when it is shared freely.
Within my formal coursework, I consistently pursued opportunities to engage mathematics at a deeper level. Under the guidance of my Numerical Methods instructor, I participated in a poster competition presenting work on Penrose tilings. The project appealed to me because it lay at the intersection of geometry, symmetry, and abstraction, demonstrating how pure mathematical ideas can possess both aesthetic elegance and conceptual depth and surprising utility for science and technology (in this case surgical instruments made using quasi-crystals which are modelled partly with the help of penrose tilings). Our work was recognized among the best posters in a competition involving four universities from the federal capital region.
In a separate end of semester project inspired by recent flooding in Pakistan, I along with my team developed a mathematical framework motivated by Lagrange interpolation to model continuously varying water levels for an early warning system. While applied in nature, this work strengthened my appreciation for how theoretical tools can be adapted to socially relevant problems that demand a great amount of urgency. Together, these experiences deepened my interest in both pure and applied directions within mathematics.
More recently, I have become increasingly drawn to mathematically grounded approaches to machine learning and deep learning. Rather than viewing these fields as purely computational, I am interested in the underlying questions of optimization, generalization, and structure. I am particularly motivated to understand how ideas from linear algebra, probability, geometry, and analysis inform modern learning algorithms, and how theoretical insight can lead to models that are not only powerful, but also well understood and interpretable.
Teaching has been an important part of my intellectual development. As a volunteer tutor with the Quaidian Mathematical Society, I spent have spent over two years teaching discrete mathematics and logic to freshmen students. The process of explaining abstract concepts refined my own understanding and reinforced my desire to remain engaged with mathematics at a foundational level. In fact to teach is to learn twice! I agree.
I am drawn to the Purdue University Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship because it offers precisely what has been largely absent from my academic journey so far: sustained mentorship, early immersion in active research, and the freedom to engage seriously with open questions. Purdue’s strength in mathematics, theoretical computer science, and data driven research makes it a particularly compelling environment for someone with my interests. I am especially motivated by the possibility of learning within a research culture shaped by scholars such as Professor Saugata Basu, whose work in computational and real algebraic geometry exemplifies deep structural thinking, and Professor Zachary Kingston, whose research connects geometry, algorithms, and computation. Exposure to such perspectives would help me better understand how abstract mathematical theory informs algorithmic design and mathematically principled approaches to machine learning and deep learning.
Beyond technical training, SURF offers the opportunity to build meaningful academic relationships and to observe closely how research is conducted at a leading global institution. These connections would be invaluable as I consider long term pathways toward doctoral study, whether at Purdue or elsewhere. More importantly, they would allow me to experience science as a living research discipline shaped by collaboration, curiosity, and sustained inquiry.
My long term goal is to pursue graduate study and a research career in mathematics or a mathematically intensive area of computational science such as deep learning and mathematical modelling. I am open to paths in pure mathematics, applied analysis, and theoretically informed machine learning, and I view these directions as complementary rather than exclusive. The mentorship, research exposure, and intellectual rigor offered through SURF would play a decisive role in helping me refine this trajectory and prepare for future doctoral work and beyond.
The challenges I have encountered have shaped my academic identity in meaningful ways. When systems were restrictive, I learned to think independently. When opportunities were limited, I learned to create intellectual space for myself. These experiences have prepared me to contribute thoughtfully and utilize to the best of my abilities a research intensive program like SURF.
For me, mathematics is not merely a discipline, but a way of thinking, a language through which reality becomes obvious and understanding solidifies. My aim is to learn this language with rigor and imagination, and to use it responsibly in both theory and practice. SURF represents a natural and necessary step in that journey, and I am eager to bring my curiosity, discipline, and commitment to the program.

I am a second-year undergraduate pursuing a double major in Electrical Engineering and Physics, with interests in plasma engineering and optics. My interest in optics began after attending the Inertial Fusion Energy(IFE)–STARFIRE virtual course in Spring 2025 (listed at UCLA as Physics 296), where I gained foundational exposure to inertial fusion energy research and learned about recent advances at the National Ignition Facility (NIF). I developed an interest in high-repetition-rate laser systems for driving inertial fusion and was drawn to optical imaging systems used in fusion research, such as the Crystal Backlighter Imager at NIF.

My interest in plasma engineering developed through undergraduate research at UCLA’s Basic Plasma Science Facility (BaPSF). During onboarding, I observed plasma etching experiment setups and learned about their role in semiconductor fabrication, which sparked my interest in industrial applications of plasma physics. Through further independent study, I developed interests in plasma engineering, particularly plasma thrusters and plasma deposition. My interests in optics and plasma engineering are closely connected, as optical diagnostics, imaging systems, and laser technologies are commonly used to monitor, drive, and control plasma systems. I plan to explore both areas to determine my future graduate-school specialization.

I further explored my interests through coursework and research. As a undergraduate researcher at UCLA’s Basic Plasma Science Facility (BaPSF), I built a foundational understanding of experimental instrumentation by developing a program to control and monitor the Large Plasma Device’s 45-degree Langmuir probe system, gaining experience with plasma diagnostics and Ethernet-based motor control with encoder feedback. In my Physics 296 research seminar, I explored laser–plasma interaction in inertial fusion energy by completing a final presentation on laser-driven ignition schemes for inertial fusion, comparing predicted neutron yields, hotspot pressures, and associated challenges. I further deepened my understanding of plasma physics and optical system development by attending the IFE Winter School in 2025, where lectures and laboratory tours highlighted recent research in laser system development, optical diagnostics for inertial fusion energy, and applications of optical devices across fusion research areas.

Motivated by my interest in optics, I pursued research in Thomson scattering, a non-invasive plasma diagnostic technique whose signal strength depends critically on precise optical alignment. Under the mentorship of Professor Christoph Niemann, I am currently developing a program that runs concurrently with data acquisition to analyze signal amplitudes across spatial positions and actively adjust a motorized fiber array relative to the laser beam, maintaining optimal alignment and maximizing signal throughput. I developed a numerical simulation to model the expected Thomson scattering signal collected by the fiber-array system, accounting for alignment drift caused by experimental instabilities. Building on this simulation, I am designing a control algorithm that uses continuous Gaussian fitting to regulate motor motion and align the fiber array to the position of maximum integrated scattering intensity through real-time image analysis. I also implemented EPICS-based instrumentation control as part of this project. This work has been accepted into the UCLA Undergraduate Research Fellowship Program (URFP). My current coursework in Signals and Systems and Engineering Electromagnetics would provide essential preparation for working with optical and hardware systems.

statement_of_purpose:
My father has always told me that if the sky is the limit, I must build a ladder to reach it. I think about that a lot when I reflect on how I ended up falling in love with chemical engineering and materials research. For me, science has never been about getting the right answer on paper. It has been about taking something invisible, like molecules and heat flow, and turning it into something real, something that works in the world.

One of my earliest memories of that feeling happened when I was fourteen, at a workshop at UTEC (Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología) in Peru about platinum nanoparticles and their applications. I did not understand every detail, but I remember being amazed that something as small as a nanoparticle could change how a material behaves. It was one of the first moments when I realized that chemistry could become technology, and that there was an entire world behind the word “materials.” That experience stayed in the back of my mind as I chose my degree.

I later began my chemical engineering studies at UTEC, and that is where I had my first direct research experience under Dr. Alejandro Ríos Cuadros, a faculty member specializing in nanomaterials and semiconductors. Through a beginner project focused on thermal analysis, I was introduced to Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA). Preparing an exposition on DSC and TGA forced me to understand what the curves actually meant, not just what the instruments did. It taught me something simple but important: research is not only curiosity. It is discipline. It is learning a tool deeply, asking a question it can truly answer, and then having the responsibility to communicate results clearly.

After two years studying chemical engineering at UTEC, I transferred to the United States to pursue a better education and broader research opportunities. That transition asked me, once again, to step out of my comfort zone and take risks, the same kind of risks I have taken again and again to reach my goals. In the U.S., I chose a dual foundation in Chemistry and Chemical Engineering because I wanted both molecular understanding and quantitative engineering reasoning. Courses like Analytical Chemistry and Physical Chemistry strengthened how I think about measurement and interpretation. In Physical Chemistry II, learning the foundations of quantum mechanics changed how I see modern research. It made me realize that modeling and simulation are not “extra,” they are part of how we ask better questions and understand what experiments cannot show directly.

I have always liked the feeling of building things, and programming has become one of the ways I do that. At UTEC, I completed two semesters of programming coursework and built projects in Python and C++, including a small Python game and an object-oriented C++ project. I still use Python as a working tool today. For example, I wrote a small searchable dataset of chemical elements and components from Felder because I noticed I was wasting time flipping pages for the same information. It sounds small, but it reflects how I think: I like systems, I like efficiency, and I like turning learning into something practical.

Right now, my strongest research interest is how materials behave where it actually matters, at the boundaries. I keep coming back to a question that keeps pulling me in: where does heat get stuck? Materials can look great in bulk, but the real limitations often live at interfaces, grain boundaries, voids, and defects, and in demanding thermal environments those local resistances can decide whether something lasts or fails. Since reviewing the projects, I have arrived at a parallel question about wet adhesion: what actually makes something stick so strongly underwater, and why can slight changes in surface chemistry or hydration shift durability so much? I want to learn how to measure these effects at the right scale and connect what I observe to better design decisions, not simply better explanations.

That is why Prof. Raisul Islam’s project on Scanning Thermal Microscopy for Studying Defects in Solids stands out to me as a direct match. The idea of studying nanoscale heat flow where defects and interfaces dominate is exactly the kind of work I want to grow into, especially in contexts relevant to thermal interface materials and advanced packaging or integration. I am prepared to contribute through careful experimental work and strong lab habits developed through lab support roles, and I am eager to apply coding-based organization and analysis to connect measured behavior to material features in a clear, defensible way.

Sustainability matters deeply to me. That is why I am drawn to Prof. Jonathan Wilker’s Development of Sustainably Sourced, High-Performance Materials project. It stood out to me not because it mirrors my current work, but because I felt an immediate connection to the questions and ideas his group is developing. As a child, I spent years scuba diving along the Peruvian coast and saw how strongly mollusks, including mussels, adhere to rocks even under constant waves. Prof. Wilker’s research brought that observation into a scientific context, and the topic captivated me from the first moment I encountered it. I am especially interested in mussel-inspired catechol (DOPA-type) interactions and in understanding how molecular-scale chemistry translates into measurable adhesion, durability, and interfacial performance in wet environments.

I am also interested in Prof. David Warsinger’s Efficient and Sustainable Water Technology project because it connects sustainability to core chemical engineering principles: transport phenomena, thermodynamics, and materials performance. Membrane-based systems and approaches that improve efficiency through optimization, control, and data-driven methods align with both my technical interests and my desire to work on scalable impact. With my programming foundation and continued use of Python, I would be excited to contribute to analysis and optimization tasks while learning more about membrane performance characterization and system-level design.

Purdue’s Chemical Engineering SURF program appeals to me because it offers the structured mentorship and high-intensity research environment I am seeking. In particular, I want stronger instrumentation training and uncertainty analysis skills. I want to be able to design more rigorous experiments, interpret measurements with greater confidence, and communicate results with the precision research requires. For thermal and materials measurements, small errors can change conclusions, especially when the goal is to understand interfaces and defects.

To prepare for SURF, I have built both academic strength and laboratory readiness. I hold a 3.91 Chemistry GPA (after three years) and a 4.0 GPA in Chemical Engineering at my current university. I am developing an undergraduate research direction involving phase change material (PCM) packaging inserts for thermal stability, which has reinforced my interest in performance-driven design under constraints such as durability, leakage resistance, and thermal cycling. In parallel, my roles as a Laboratory Assistant, Teaching Assistant, and Laboratory Preparation Assistant strengthened habits that translate directly to research productivity: careful documentation, organized workflow, safety, preparation discipline, and methodical troubleshooting.

We have hosted workshops on research opportunities, and I am creating a simple resource hub that helps students take concrete steps, from finding mentors to reaching out to labs with confidence. This work is ongoing, but it has strengthened my leadership and reflects what I bring to research environments: community-building alongside high standards.

I responded by actively seeking mentorship, strengthening my technical communication through repetition and feedback, and consistently pursuing scholarships and opportunities that support my long-term trajectory. Through SURF, I hope to deepen my skills in materials characterization, experimental design, and data analysis while strengthening modeling and research communication habits. Long-term, I plan to pursue graduate study and build a career in research and development focused on advanced materials and packaging-relevant technologies, including thermal management materials, polymer systems, and sustainable high-performance materials that can scale.

If the sky is the limit, I am still building my ladder and I am confident Purdue SURF is the right step to build it with stronger tools, better training, and the kind of research discipline that turns curiosity into real impact.

When I think about why I keep choosing engineering—and why I keep choosing research inside engineering—I always return to the same image: coming back to my community after being abroad and finding riverbeds that had once been alive now cracked and dry. I did not have the vocabulary then for hydrology, land-use patterns, or human-water systems, but I felt the stakes immediately. Water was not—and is still not—an abstract resource. It decides whether people can stay, farm, live, and plan a future. That shock did not make me want to “do something” in a vague way; it made me want to understand mechanisms—what changed, why it changed, and what interventions are actually ethical and effective for the benefit of life. Research became the only honest path forward, because I did not want to bring solutions to my community that were based on intuition, trends, or good intentions alone. 

However, I did not come to college with this pathway in mind. While I had entertained the idea of a career in the sciences while growing up, and had been admitted to the best high school in Peru with a full-ride scholarship, responsibilities, economic stakes, family, and even culture made it hard for me to continue clinging onto that dream. I became furious and desired to change things as I went forward with my life. I started delving into the humanities, social work, civics, history, and politics, and with that mindset I hopped on a new trajectory abroad. 

I became the recipient of a full-ride scholarship to study two years in The Netherlands, at the United World College Maastricht. Not only did my day-to-day life change, but my whole path was now set on a newfound track: anthropology and ecology. I became so involved with social and environmental projects, and discovered immense joy in them. I received awards and grants in these areas, and became devoted to this life. Nevertheless, without realizing it, I also encountered my first “research” experience when I went back home to employ one of the grants I had won on a summer break project. I decided to go to my grandmother’s village, not in the capital city where I lived, but up in the highlands, in Cajamarca. As I walked up the mountains, and reached my destination, my eyes laid upon a dry river—the one I had dear memories of having played and swam in as a child. My grandmother was also heartbroken, as it was not only dear for us but to all the people whose livelihoods depended on its flow. 

My first instinct was to find out what happened. And after some time of gathering information, I decided to make this my paper for one of my classes’s final assessments. I ended up investigating how Eucalyptus globulus plantations related to changes in the Jequetepeque River’s flow in Cajamarca. I pushed for data access from the Peruvian Ministry of Agriculture, traveled between Lima and Cajamarca, and used tools and perspectives I had learned across Peru and the Netherlands to build an argument grounded in evidence. What mattered most to me, though, was not the final “product” of the paper—it was what the process taught me about responsibility. I translated my findings back to my relatives and neighboring villages in a way that was accurate but also humane, because research that cannot be communicated ethically becomes useless or even harmful. I shared evidence that the expansion of Eucalyptus plantations was a major contributing factor in the river’s decline, and then worked towards finding other means of income for their families so they slowly stopped relying on an activity that was diminishing their water resources. 

While not an experience in a state-of-the-art laboratory, this showed me something that has shaped my academic direction ever since: the world’s problems are never only technical. They sit inside culture, governance, power, and trust. That is why my field of study became an intersection by necessity. I study Human Ecology, but I am building my path intentionally around civil, environmental, and hydraulic engineering. I want the freedom to hold different “ANDs” at once: theory AND fieldwork, modeling AND community realities, quantitative rigor AND human consequences. I have founded and led MenstruAction, and even there, I created a specific area for “Research, Development, and Sustainability” because I learned early that programs cannot be sustainable if they are not continually updated by evidence and continuous research. Whether the question is the safety of menstrual health products or the safety of drinking water systems, I am drawn to the same core problems: how do we detect risk before it becomes crisis? How do we design interventions that are technically sound and socially adoptable? And how do we communicate results so that knowledge is not trapped in institutions, but actually becomes usable?

In college, those questions narrowed into a long-term research commitment to water: demand, quality, and resilience. While in my first semester at College of the Atlantic (COA), I decided to take a Physics and Mathematics course. It became the spark that reignited my love for science, and ever since, with the combination of all my experiences in a diverse array of areas, I decided engineering was my path. 

Engineering was the stream my mind settled into because it is the one space where my urgency can become structure. Growing up in Lima, water was never guaranteed; it arrived on a tanker, and each family’s bucket had to become a week of survival. Scarcity is often disconnection:  aging centralized systems and shrinking Andean reserves. Yet the Pacific mist still blankets our coast every day, a paradox of abundance that remains unusable without design. I want more than awareness or advocacy: I want the technical tools to redesign water systems so they are resilient, decentralized, and real. Engineering offers that: a disciplined creativity grounded in physics, data, and materials, where you can test ideas, quantify tradeoffs, and build solutions that scale. I am especially eager to explore how ancestral hydraulic practices can be integrated with contemporary water technologies; for instance, combining atmospheric water capture with gravity-fed canal/terrace concepts to support decentralized supply in Lima.

Therefore, I have sought out engineering training beyond what a small, rural, non-engineering institution can typically offer, not because I am dissatisfied with my college, but because I know exactly what I need to grow. COA operates on a three-term calendar, and with a small science faculty, many science courses are offered only every other term. I have consistently enrolled in the most rigorous science coursework available to me. I have pursued independent learning (including structured technical coursework beyond my curriculum), and I worked hard to place myself in research environments where I could learn the daily rhythm of scientific work. Across my research roles at other institutions, such as University of Miami and Florida International University, I have learned to balance field and computation: installing and calibrating sensors in green stormwater infrastructure contexts; cleaning and harmonizing messy datasets; running analyses that reveal patterns rather than just producing plots; and contributing to manuscripts where precision and clarity matter. I have co-authored a paper in my first year, authored and completed a second manuscript during my sophomore year, and I am leading a third project that I have submitted to present at the Maine Sustainability & Water Conference. Each time I step deeper into research, I feel more convinced that I do not want research to be something I “try” for a summer—I want it to be my life’s work.

I also want to be a vessel of support for students who, like me, had to learn to navigate opportunities without a clear institutional pathway, and who carry the quiet pressure of being the first in their family to pursue advanced education.

This is exactly why Purdue’s SURF program stands out to me among summer research opportunities. One aspect of SURF that especially excites me is the symposium, where I will get to both present my work and hear from that of my peers. I believe this, paired with all the weekly professional seminars and support from a real research community, is what will round up the experience. I began to see hybridization not as a compromise, but as a challenge: how do you preserve the thrill of motorsports while meeting the realities of efficiency, emissions, and sustainability? That question is what led me to pursue Motorsports Engineering, and it’s why I continue to pursue it, because motorsports is one of the few fields where engineering decisions are immediate, measurable, and unforgiving.

Over time, my interests have settled at the intersection of propulsion, sustainability, and intelligent systems. I am motivated by problems where performance and responsibility are not opposites, but variables that can be optimized together. In motorsports, sustainability is not just about changing fuels. It includes combustion efficiency, thermal losses, lubricant cycles, component durability, and even the logistics footprint of moving teams and equipment. What excites me about research is the chance to quantify where energy and resources are being lost, understand the physics behind those losses, and then design systems that turn “waste” into performance.

A specific experience that made this personal happened during my summer internship at Go Auto Performance, where one of my main tasks was draining oil during routine oil changes. I still remember disconnecting a hose fitting and watching the dark, viscous oil pour into the catch can. The smell, the heat, and the sheer volume coming from a single line made me realize how much lubricant is treated as disposable in performance settings. That led me to ask a simple question: where does all of this go, and why? When I learned our used oil was being sent to a waste facility, it did not sit right with me. I looked for credible numbers and found a fact that reshaped my thinking: one gallon of used oil can yield the same 2.5 quarts of lubricating oil as about 42 gallons of crude oil, when it is properly re-refined. That ratio made the opportunity obvious. The future does not hinge only on producing more petroleum, it also hinges on recovering and recirculating what we already extract. I brought the data to my boss and, after persistent discussions, convinced the shop to send waste oil to a recycling plant instead. That experience taught me a grounded definition of leadership, one based on evidence, communication, and follow through, and it clarified the kind of engineer I want to become: someone who sees inefficiency, quantifies it, and builds a better system.

The questions that motivate me now are research questions with direct consequences on track. I am especially interested in combustion and propulsion phenomena that limit efficiency and reliability, including how spray quality affects ignition stability, how atomization and mixing influence power consistency and emissions, how thermal management governs durability, and how particle erosion or debris ingestion degrades performance over time. Motorsports is full of small losses that accumulate into big lap-time differences, and research is how those losses get identified, measured, and reduced. I am also drawn to the future facing side of the field: AI and automation in motorsports. My experience building autonomous systems has shown me how sensing, controls, and data-driven decision-making can transform how teams test, diagnose, and iterate. Across these teams, I am not just participating, I am helping lead and execute: aligning people around requirements, coordinating timelines, documenting decisions, building and validating hardware, and turning test results into design changes. I have also pursued research driven team experiences through VIP projects connected to Formula E and my current work in the Aerodynamic Design of a Pikes Peak vehicle. These roles have pushed me beyond doing tasks and into building systems, both technical systems and team systems.

That is why I am applying for SURF. I want to take the hands-on momentum I have built at Purdue and deepen it with research rigor. I am excited by the opportunity to learn research grade methods like experimental planning, uncertainty analysis, instrument calibration, and technical communication, and then apply those methods to propulsion and vehicle system problems that matter. Long term, I want a career in propulsion and advanced vehicle systems, in roles that bridge test engineering and design, where I can run experiments with discipline, interpret complex data honestly, and translate findings into actionable decisions.

Ultimately, I pursue Motorsports Engineering because I am motivated by the hardest version of engineering: making systems that perform at the limit, under real constraints, with real consequences. I am currently a third-year Computer Science and Engineering student at the National University of Science and Technology MISIS, where I maintain a GPA of 5.0. While my formal training is in computer science, my pursuit of this field has been shaped by sustained hands-on work with wireless systems, instrumentation, and data-driven analysis of real-world signals.
My interest in RF systems began in high school with a Wi-Fi based indoor localization project, where I inferred spatial position from noisy RSSI measurements collected across multiple access points. I designed both the data collection and inference components, and this experience introduced me to the challenges of multipath propagation, measurement uncertainty, and repeatability. These challenges motivated me to continue exploring communication systems from an experimental and systems-oriented perspective. Over time, this interest expanded into building antennas, working with software-defined radio (SDR) platforms, and decoding real satellite transmissions from satellites such as the ISS, MetOp, Proba-2, and Elektro-L. statement_of_purpose:
What does research mean to me? It is trying an idea, failing, and understanding why. In classes, progress is often linear and clearly measurable, while in research you can spend a lot of time going in the wrong direction. At first, I was disappointed in myself thinking about how much time I had wasted, but I talked about this with my supervisor and they helped me build a framework for thinking: we should treat failed attempts as very helpful data. They often reveal which intuitions are wrong and where the interesting difficulty actually lies. Doing research has turned out to be exactly the kind of work I enjoy.

My name is Arslan Iamaletdinov, and I am a sophomore in the Applied Mathematics and Information Sciences program at the Faculty of Computer Science at the Higher School of Economics. There are many summer research programs, but I am applying to SURF because I want to spend this summer doing something I genuinely love and to grow as both a researcher and a person. I imagine a lab where I can contribute, learn, and also be part of its everyday life: mentorship, feedback, and a community where I learn how to do research by doing it. 

I was introduced to graphs in high school, and I liked how simple the definition looked. They are as simple as just two sets, yet they come up everywhere and can represent anything from U.S. rail networks to molecular compounds. But when are two graphs the same (or, more precisely, isomorphic)? It sounds simple; however, for graphs with unlabeled vertices, this is no easy problem. In fact, this is an important question in graph mining.

We can try answering it using graph kernels for “inexact” graph matching. Currently, I am working on this problem at the International Laboratory of Stochastic Algorithms and High-Dimensional Inference. We are interested in kernels based on random walks, since they can be computed very effectively by exploiting the structure of the Kronecker product of normalized adjacency matrices of graphs. Guided by the intuition that, for sparse graphs common in the real world, such matrices should be relatively low-rank, we believe we can approximate them by tensor decompositions into smaller matrices and compute kernels even more efficiently. For me, it is really beautiful how linear algebra, probability, graph theory, and computation all meet in one problem. I also find it motivating that something I do now might one day help someone solve a completely different problem. This feels much more honest and motivating than grades alone.

So far, I have explored my interests both through research and through building things. I like building complex systems and implementing theoretical ideas using code. I developed a ROS-based computer vision pipeline for robot pose estimation and worked with simulation and visualization tools (Gazebo and RViz). I implemented high-efficiency public-key algorithms Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal for encryption and decryption in E(F_q), Z_p*, F_q∗ algebraic structures in C++. These experiences made me comfortable moving between math and code, and taught me to respect details: even one wrong line or letter can destroy the rigorous theory behind it.

More generally, I enjoy applying clean and rigorous mathematical ideas to messy reality. I like turning a theory into something you can actually compute, test, and trust. This interaction of mathematical rigor, algorithms, and real-world problems is what I am looking for.

You can’t do research alone, so I want to learn how research teams work. After the official weekly meeting is over, our research group usually goes to a university cafe to grab lunch (I have to admit, I love those chocolate croissants there), and we end up discussing everything from research ideas to random topics far from math. All this may seem obvious, but these small rituals are important to me. They remind me that behind the very, very abstract objects we work with, there are always humans who get excited, tired, confused (and hungry) together. When I imagine myself at Purdue, I do not just imagine a project description; I imagine the people I will work with.

I like working with others and trying to help them. As a teaching assistant in a linear algebra course, I have learned to listen carefully and pay attention to where other people are in their understanding. The word “obviously” has almost disappeared from my vocabulary. Something that feels obvious to me after taking a course is not obvious to students taking it for the first time. This experience has helped me understand how important it is to ask questions early, to be honest when you do not understand something, and to create an atmosphere where others feel comfortable doing the same. This is also how I try to approach research: asking early, clarifying early, and not pretending I understand what I don’t.

In the long term, I want to pursue a Master’s degree and then a PhD (maybe even at Purdue) in order to build a strong foundation for my career in research. I am still early enough in my studies that a single research experience can shift my trajectory a lot. This Summer Research Fellowship would help me check a simple but important hypothesis: am I ready for full-time research in this kind of environment, and where can I contribute the most? I want to leave the summer with stronger research instincts: better experimental design, clearer scientific writing and presentation, and a wider view of where I can contribute. I imagine spending weekdays in the lab and then on weekends going to Indianapolis to see places like the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum or the Indiana State Museum with my fellow researchers and new friends.

Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely,
Arslan Iamaletdinov

Dear SURF Admission Committee,
My name is Mikhail Pesotskii. I am a 5th year student at the Chemistry Department of Lomonosov Moscow State University, and would like to do a research internship at Purdue University during SURF.
I was introduced to ESG principles from my early childhood thanks to my family as my mother works for a charity that collects, sorts, and recycles unwanted clothing, donating it to the most vulnerable people in Russia thus promoting conscious consumption and recycling principles. At home, we always sorted trash, collected used batteries, and used reusable bags (shoppers) for shopping. At school, I participated in paper collection events, tree plantings, and attended various lectures on environmental issues.

I really enjoyed school and had several favourite subjects: I equally liked both tracks: sciences and humanities. However, on my last years at school, I became very much interested in chemistry. I still find the structure and logic of the periodic table of chemical elements amazing, and I consider electronic orbitals and the mechanisms of organic reactions incredibly beautiful. There were several students in my class who were passionate about chemistry, and after regular school hours we often stayed to work in the chemistry lab with our teacher and curator who was a postgraduate student at Moscow State University that time. He influenced me a lot and became my role model advising me to enter MSU. I love chemistry as science and the chemistry department because you are not limited to just one area: it is important for a chemist to know not only chemistry itself but also physics, math, biology, and ecology.

At the beginning of my first year (October 2021) of study, we were assigned to laboratories to complete a course work project in inorganic chemistry. I asked my lecturer to recommend a laboratory and supervisor that focused on environmental issues. That's how I met the Catalysis and Gas Electrochemistry Laboratory and my supervisor, mentor, and truly exceptional person— Prof. Ekaterina Sergeevna Lokteva. I am very grateful to her for truly opening up the world of catalysis to me – a very complex but interesting field of chemistry. I ended up diving into this research area and my research group so deeply that decided to stay with them.
At the end of my third year, we had to choose a department for distribution, and I chose the Department of Physical Chemistry to deepen my knowledge in catalysis. During this time, I am not only completed a number of courses that allowed me to expand my expertise in various physicochemical research methods and catalysis, but also consolidated my skills in classical quantum mechanics calculations, and mastered molecular dynamics methods. Although I believe that computational methods are the future of chemistry and provide an important theoretical basis for predicting reaction mechanisms and calculating thermodynamic parameters, I think that, as a chemist, experimental experience would be important for my future work.
I'm now on my fifth year at the laboratory and have already begun preparing my thesis. All my work, including my upcoming thesis, is dedicated to the synthesis and investigation of hydrodechlorination catalysts. The hydrodechlorination reaction is important from an environmental point of view, as treatment facilities are unable to remove chlorinated microecotoxicants from water. We synthesize catalysts, study them using various physicochemical methods, and test them in the catalytic diclofenac hydrodechlorination reaction. 

To gain insight into the wide range of applications of sorbents and catalysts for solving environmental problems, I completed internships at various scientific organizations.
At ITMO University's SCAMT Center, I worked on the project "Polymer membrane for lithium extraction from brines." The technology is based on the use of sorbents that can selectively absorb lithium ions. This method is environmentally friendly, which gives it a significant advantage over other methods. At AlmetTech, PISH ITMO, I worked on the "Cleanest Biodiesel" project under the supervision of Artem Poryvaev, Ph.D. We synthesized sorbents based on bentonite clay and tested them in the purification of mustard and sunflower oils. I also had the opportunity to work in the Laboratory of Metal Hydride Energy Technologies at the Federal Research Center of Problems of Chemical Physics and Medicinal Chemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences (FRC PCP MC RAS) under the guidance of Artem Arbuzov, Ph.D. We worked to improve the hydrogen sorption properties of a hydrogen storage material based on the intermetallic compound LaNi4.45Al0.55.

The SURF program attracted me because of the opportunity to participate in projects related to catalysis and sustainable development, which are the fields that interest me the most. In the past, I took part in summer schools that were quite short—no longer than three weeks—and sometimes this is not enough time to truly immerse yourself in a research topic. The SURF program offers the chance to study and work in a laboratory for 11 weeks, so I expect to learn a great deal.
To become a truly good scientist, it is essential to gain research experience in as many areas as possible. In my current work at the laboratory at Lomonosov Moscow State University, I focus on a rather narrow field and use a limited set of research methods. Therefore, I hope to learn something new in each of the projects I have selected.
If I am fortunate enough to work on the project “High-throughput Electrocatalysis with Metal Oxides,” I hope to become familiar with electrocatalysis as well as with quantum chemical calculations, which are actively used by the research group. It is possible that I will be able to apply these methods in my own research in the future.
If I am accepted into the group working on the project “Mass Spectrometry of Biomolecules and Nanoclusters,” I expect to become acquainted with and thoroughly study mass spectrometry. During my studies and research so far, I have had almost no experience with this method, yet it is extremely important, and I am confident that this knowledge will be useful to me in the future.
Within the framework of the project “Sustainable Recovery of Lithium-Ion Battery Cathode Materials,” I hope to gain practical skills and strengthen my knowledge of electrochemistry. The knowledge and skills I acquire will also help me look at the water purification problem that I currently work on from a different perspective, since water can also be treated using electrochemical methods such as electrooxidation, electrocoagulation, and electrocatalysis.
I am planning to go to graduate school, and during my postgraduate studies, I would like not only to continue developing my knowledge of catalysis. In my scientific work, I want to develop effective and low-stage methods for the synthesis of catalysts, which can subsequently be used in industry and bring benefits, rather than remaining only on paper.  

Sincerely yours,

P. Mikhail

I am drawn to problems where fundamental mechanisms become design rules for translational therapies. That is why my interests sit at the intersection of molecular engineering and patient impact, and why I am seeking a summer experience that pushes beyond proof-of-concept toward platforms that could realistically change clinical practice.
I first learned scientific rigor early. In high school, I earned the Moscow Golden Medal for outstanding academic success and achieved national recognition through federal-level STEM competitions, including the All-Russia School Olympiad in Physics and the All-Russia Science Research Olympiad in Engineering. In the engineering competition, I designed and presented an independent research project on  Characterization of Volatile Compounds Using Ion Mobility Spectrometry and Magnetic Moment and drafted a paper from my findings. Those experiences trained me to enjoy science and they established a foundation of discipline that I later carried into research and teaching.
My path then became shaped by interrupted opportunity and an obstacle that transformed into long-term motivation. Following high school, I took a gap year during the outbreak of the war in Ukraine under circumstances that disrupted nearly every conventional academic trajectory. Half of my immediate family, including my mother, became trapped in Mariupol under wartime restrictions and severe humanitarian conditions, and I remained with them because my presence was essential for safety and for securing basic resources during prolonged siege conditions. At the same time, my fiancé - my classmate for seven years and my partner for five years prior to the war - was unlawfully deployed to the war zone in the initial days of the conflict despite being a medical student cadet, and he was reported missing shortly thereafter. These circumstances compelled me to remain in the region and contribute directly to humanitarian and medical relief efforts.
During that period, I worked as a nurse and shelter volunteer with the Russian Red Cross in Donetsk and Mariupol, primarily at 9 Misʹka Likarnya. In a resource-limited, high-acuity environment, I provided basic nursing care, supported triage and wound care, monitored patients, and coordinated emergency medical supplies. I also supported emergency shelter operations by assisting displaced civilians with medical screening, hygiene support, and access to essential care. Working amid elevated public-health risks associated with armed conflict - disrupted vaccination programs, increased prevalence of respiratory infections, COVID-19 transmission, tuberculosis, and other communicable diseases exacerbated by overcrowding and limited healthcare access - strengthened my understanding of emergency medicine, epidemiological risk in humanitarian crises, and ethical decision-making under extreme constraints. Even during this unstable year marked by caregiving and volunteering responsibilities, I kept studying for multiple high-stakes exams and later scored 100% on Russia’s national biology exam, an honor earned by 73 out of approximately 105,000 students that year.
Arriving in the U.S. as a first-generation international student, I brought strong drive but limited networks for research. I responded by building the support structures I wished I had while pursuing research experiences that consistently bridged mechanism and translation. I first developed bench discipline as a lab technician in the University of Minnesota Department of Ophthalmology, supporting a project on neural development and signaling. Working with mouse lines taught me reproducible workflows - mouse handling and tissue collection, confocal imaging, and quantitative image analysis - and I helped refine a key genotyping protocol for PdgfRβ lines by optimizing gel conditions and timing. For months, I managed end-to-end genotyping and colony-support tasks, an experience that solidified my appreciation for careful experimental design, documentation, and quality control.
That foundation motivated me to pursue therapeutic delivery platforms more directly. In the Reineke Lab, I engineer polymeric micelleplex platforms for efficient mRNA delivery with a long-term goal of enabling targeted immunotherapy applications and extending delivery into clinically relevant cancer models. A major goal of my first project, which I led throughout my sophomore year, was to build a standardized framework for evaluating micelleplex stability and performance. In this storage-optimization study, I designed and implemented an experimental workflow to identify optimal buffer and temperature conditions for A7- mRNA micelleplexes across 1–6+ week timelines using complementary readouts including DLS, gel-based assays, cell-based transfection, and flow cytometry. I am currently extending the storage-duration studies and incorporating RiboGreen fluorescence assays to quantify mRNA release, with the goal of producing a generalizable storage-testing pipeline that can be applied to additional formulations, including mixed micelleplex systems. This work resulted in a first-author poster presentation at UMN, and I am continuing to drive the project forward with graduate-student collaborators toward a planned first-author publication.
In parallel, my second first-author project focuses on improving mRNA delivery to Jurkat T cells. I synthesized and evaluated a library of polymeric nanoparticles while controlling key formulation variables to refine a robust in vitro T-cell transfection workflow. The broader goal is to establish design rules—polymer composition and formulation parameters—that maximize transfection efficiency and mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) while maintaining cell compatibility. This work also culminated in a first-author poster presentation and now serves as the foundation for my Honors Thesis (planned first-author publication), where I am engineering an antibody-targeted nanoparticle platform for mRNA delivery to T cells. Specifically, I will evaluate and implement multiple established conjugation strategies to functionalize our polymer platform with a CD63 antibody (Bio-Techne) and report performance outcomes. Beyond my first-author work, I contribute to lab-wide efforts to translate these systems in vivo and clarify structure–function relationships. For a collaborative manuscript led by S. Panda, I contributed to mouse biodistribution and safety studies through animal handling and organ harvests to evaluate organ-specific delivery profiles. For a second project led by M. Leyden, where I am a second author, I led key experiments quantifying transfection and cytotoxicity across formulations and introduced a new dye-exclusion assay workflow to assess micelle stability and cellular compatibility under serum versus serum-free conditions. I am also contributing as a co-author to a related manuscript led by Plinio Rosales Lopez that extends targeted delivery into primary ovarian cancer cell models in collaboration with the Moriarity Lab, including work using a CD71 antibody.
To complement synthetic delivery systems, I sought exposure to biologically derived nanoparticles as therapeutic scaffolds. As a summer intern at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, I designed and executed two complementary projects in exosome engineering using exosomal tetraspanins CD63 and TSPAN3. I identified TSPAN3 as an effective anchor for surface display and validated KRasG12D–CD63 constructs as a candidate cancer vaccine platform. This experience taught me how to move from a mechanistic hypothesis to a testable engineering strategy, culminating in a poster award and multiple national presentations. This work led to one local and three national poster presentations and abstract acceptances to ASBMB 2026, NCUR 2026, and NCRC 2026 (Harvard University). I received the CARES Symposium Poster Award (one of five recipients across Johns Hopkins summer programs) and was selected for an ABRCMS 2025 Travel Award, though I could not accept it due to a change in residency status.
Most recently, in the Kirtane Lab (UMN Pharmaceutics), I have been integrating computation with wet-lab translation by leading a project to engineer mRNA sequences encoding extremotolerance proteins and computationally evaluate 5′UTR variants for improved translation using the RiboNN neural network and related machine-learning workflows, paired with experimental assays of nanoparticle–cell interactions. The goal is to integrate formulation optimization with mRNA sequence engineering to create delivery systems that not only enter target cells efficiently, but also drive reliable, high-level protein expression, enabling scalable design of next-generation mRNA therapeutics and synthetic biology tools. This work has resulted in a university poster presentation featuring three mock 5′UTR constructs, and my abstract reporting the full dataset across 70+ constructs was accepted to SRC 2026 (Stanford University). I also received the CBS Undergraduate Research Travel Award to support dissemination of this work.
These experiences are the reason Purdue SURF - and specifically Prof. Xiaoping Bao’s project, “Stem cell immunoengineering for targeted cancer therapy” - is the most aligned next step for my development. Cancer remains a major threat worldwide, with over 18 million new cases and 9.6 million cancer-related deaths in 2019. While CAR-engineered T and natural killer (NK) cell therapies have shown impressive clinical responses, current practice is limited by the need for large numbers of healthy immune cells, resistance to gene editing, lack of in vivo persistence, and a burdensome manufacturing strategy requiring donor cell extraction, modulation, expansion, and re-introduction for each patient. The ability to generate universally histocompatible and genetically enhanced immune cells from continuously renewable human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) lines offers the potential for a true off-the-shelf cellular immunotherapy. Yet a critical gap remains in scalability, the long timeline of differentiation (five or more weeks), and the purity and robustness of existing methods due to reliance on serum and/or feeder cells, which increase contamination risk and batch dependency. Prof. Bao’s goal of developing a novel, chemically defined platform for robust production of CAR-T and CAR-NK cells from hPSCs directly targets this translational bottleneck, and it matches my core motivation: creating therapies that are not only powerful in principle, but practical in reality.
Participation in SURF would advance my long-term goal of becoming a scientist-engineer who builds scalable immunotherapies by strengthening three capabilities that my prior work has prepared me to apply but that this project uniquely integrates. First, I would deepen hands-on experience with gene editing in hPSCs, extending my background in molecular workflows and quantitative assay design into a renewable cell source with direct clinical relevance. Second, I would learn how to differentiate stem cells into immune cells with a manufacturing mindset, focusing on chemically defined, serum-/feeder-free strategies that enable reproducibility and scale—an emphasis that parallels my work on stability, serum effects, and compatibility in mRNA delivery platforms. Third, I would expand my toolkit for molecular and cellular characterization of engineered immune cells, connecting phenotype to function and using those readouts to guide iterative engineering.
My commitment to this field is inseparable from my commitment to access. As an international, first-generation student, I began TAing because I remember how intimidating it felt to ask questions when I was new to U.S. classrooms, and I wanted students to have at least one person who felt approachable from day one. In Spring 2025, I TA’d Biology Foundations and C++ for Engineers: I graded weekly work for 100+ students, ran exam and content review sessions for each midterm, and held 7 -8 hours per week of office hours for each course. I also designed and led scientific poster workshops for the biology class group project with guided practice talks and real-time feedback so students could learn by doing. The biggest challenge was supporting students with very different starting points while I was still building confidence myself; I learned that consistent follow-ups matter and that empathy is the main lead. By junior year, strong faculty recommendations helped me become Head TA for a high-level Genetics class and lead a general chemistry lab section of 24 students. Next semester I will grade for Physical Biochemistry, the highest and hardest class in my major so far. These experiences taught me that I thrive when I pair rigor with warmth - and that I can help students feel capable and seen.
I have applied that same approach to building health equity and research communities. I co-founded the Prometheus Cancer Literacy Initiative (PCLI) from personal experience: my parents do not speak English, and I have always worried about how they - or anyone new to the U.S. - could navigate a complex medical system during something as frightening as a cancer diagnosis. After seven years with the Red Cross and working in Hennepin Healthcare Welcome Services translating for Ukrainian and Russian refugees, I saw how language barriers can turn “available care” into inaccessible care. I co-founded PCLI to close that gap by creating medically accurate, culturally accessible cancer treatment education and translating it into multiple languages. Before our public launch, I built our website for volunteer recruitment, recruited 32 volunteers across 11 languages (UMN and Johns Hopkins graduate and undergraduate students), and partnered with the UMN Red Cross, MN Cancer Clinical Trials Network, MICaB, and the Masonic Cancer Center to support outreach. As President and Founder of CatalystPlus, I built a community for undergraduates pursuing PhDs, especially first-gen and international students navigating research pathways. In one semester, we ran seven professional development workshops, a faculty talk, four undergraduate research presentations, and a 3MT collaboration event; we advised 24 students one-on-one, connected seven to research positions, supported five international students with CPT registration, and secured funding for a March grad-school application workshop series with six faculty presenters plus an undergraduate 3MT competition. I also serve as Grant and Finance Editor for MURAJ, directing the Biological Sciences Publishing Section and mentoring 15 undergraduate reviewers across eight UMN publications while helping secure annual undergraduate research grant funding, leading an In-Focus series on UMN faculty startup founders, and launching a biweekly MURAJ podcast. These efforts contributed to my selection to represent UMN in the CUR STR program, where I will visit Capitol Hill in March to advocate for undergraduate research in the House of Representatives policymakers meeting and interview Rep. Kelly Morrison on healthcare policy, women’s rights, and Minnesota’s research impact.
Ultimately, I am applying to Purdue SURF because it offers an immersive research environment where I can contribute to a project that matches the problem I am most motivated to solve next: making advanced immunotherapies scalable, robust, and broadly accessible. Prof. Bao’s chemically defined hPSC-to-CAR immune cell platform aligns with my trajectory across polymeric mRNA delivery to T cells, exosome engineering, and translation-focused assay development, and it would expand my capabilities in gene editing, stem cell differentiation, and immune-cell characterization. SURF would be a decisive step toward my long-term aim: to engineer targeted cancer therapies that are not only scientifically elegant, but manufacturable, deployable, and equitable for the communities who need them most.

I am driven by the "verification gap", the reality that as chip complexity grows exponentially, our ability to validate that complexity is struggling to keep pace. I want to delve into the rigorous reasoning and systematic debugging required to ensure that the next generation of hardware is not just fast, but trustworthy.
Several hands-on experiences have shaped this direction. These experiences highlighted a fundamental truth: a system is only as good as its verification suite.
My transition into low-level correctness was cemented by building a MicroC-to-RISC-V compiler. Ensuring that high-level constructs translated into valid, efficient assembly felt remarkably similar to the logic required in RTL verification. It was here that I realized I enjoy the "adversarial" nature of engineering, anticipating edge cases, handling architectural constraints, and finding the flaws before they become permanent.

While I am still early in my formal verification training, my background in compilers and embedded systems has prepared me to reason across layers of abstraction. statement_of_purpose:
A turning point in my academic journey came when I saw my father, whom I had always considered strong, quietly crying because of the bankruptcy that followed the death of his brother. He kept his struggles hidden to support my education, but the stress took a toll on his health and led to thyroid cancer. That night, I realized that waiting for someone to share their difficulties is often insufficient, especially for those who view vulnerability as a weakness. I faced something similar during my service in the Republic of Korea Marine Corps, when my capable successor struggled with depression in an environment where openness was discouraged. I started a weekly peer-support program, but I learned that support often depends on people being willing to speak up. This experience motivated me to look for ways to help even when someone cannot or does not want to ask for support. I became interested in how computational systems can identify psychological distress before it is spoken about.

My motivation to address these hidden challenges is grounded in my own experience overcoming obstacles. As a first-generation, low-income student in South Korea, I did not have access to the expensive private tutoring that many of my peers relied on. While others attended private academies, I took responsibility for my own learning early. I remember asking my parents to use our limited money for extra math workbooks instead of toys. I spent many evenings working through these books and teaching myself new concepts before they were taught at school. Rather than seeing this as a burden, I enjoyed tackling difficult problems independently, which gave me confidence I would not have developed otherwise.

This resilience became important when I arrived at Dartmouth and realized I had been learning the “hidden curriculum” on my own. I saw that some friends had parents with PhDs who could guide them, which made me appreciate that my progress came from my own efforts. I started building my support system by seeking mentors such as Professor Andrew Campbell. I viewed our meetings as opportunities to learn about research and to explore how to pursue a Ph.D. Because of my background, I am not discouraged when instructions are unclear. Instead, I look for resources and teach myself what I need.

Motivated by this question about detecting unspoken distress, I applied my resourcefulness at the AIM HIGH Lab while developing a therapeutic intervention. I thought that people who hesitate to share their struggles might feel more comfortable talking to an anonymous AI. My primary role was to build a generative AI system using LLaMA-3.1 to generate synthetic therapeutic dialogues for training Therabot, a therapeutic AI chatbot. I soon faced a challenge: we needed to fine-tune a very large model, but we lacked access to powerful GPU clusters. Instead of giving up, I relied on my experience working with limited resources. I evaluated solutions and used 4-bit quantization (QLoRA), which reduced our training costs by 35% without sacrificing performance.

Even though my work at AIM HIGH produced a model that outperformed the baseline, I saw a key limitation: support still depended on people reaching out first. This made me wonder if distress could be detected when evidence is incomplete or unreliable before someone asks for help. This question led me to focus on passive sensing at Dartmouth’s HealthX Lab, where I now lead a study targeting Interspeech 2026. I approach multimodal stress detection as a conditional inference problem, modeling the available evidence and its reliability as sensors fail or degrade in real-world settings. My current work examines modality dropout by studying how different fusion methods behave when data are missing or degraded. To support this, I built a multimodal pipeline using Wav2Vec 2.0 for audio, EMO-AffectNet for video, and MOMENT for physiological data. In standard tests, my approach reached 75% accuracy in audio stress classification, a 9% improvement over the original StressID baseline.

Looking ahead, I plan to pursue a Ph.D. in Computer Science or Biomedical Informatics, focusing on AI for Healthcare. My goal is to research how computational methods can support clinical decision-making, thereby enabling AI systems work reliably in healthcare settings. Right now, I am considering which healthcare areas, such as mental health, physiological monitoring, or clinical prediction, best fit my interests and skills. My studies have provided me with a strong background in computer science, but I am drawn to Purdue SURF because it focuses on faculty-led, engineering-based research that addresses real-world problems. As a computer science major, I often work with abstract data, but Purdue’s College of Engineering would allow me to work more closely with how algorithms interface with sensing hardware, clinical needs, and system design. This would enable me to adopt a more hands-on, interdisciplinary approach to research.

I have selected three projects that together create a focused training plan in computational modeling for health. My first choice, Probing transitions in motor learning via physics-informed state-space models, would strengthen my skills in time-series modeling and latent state inference for neural data. My second choice, Predictive modeling of aortic root dilation, would let me apply statistical and machine-learning methods to real clinical data, deepening my experience with diagnostic challenges. My third choice, AI-guided Drug Development, would expand my background in generative modeling to structured chemical data, giving me broader exposure to biomedical discovery pipelines.

Through Purdue SURF, I aim to further develop as a biomedical researcher while deepening my training in computational modeling for health. By the end of the summer, I aim to improve my skills in latent variable analysis and better understand the rules and challenges of working with clinical data. I aim to contribute my experience in multimodal fusion and generative AI to the Purdue community while developing research methods that support early, reliable intervention in real clinical settings.

statement_of_purpose:
I entered college as a biology major because I've always been fascinated by how living systems function. From my 5th-grade science project to my AP biology course in high school, I was drawn to everything from human physiology to microbial growth. During my first semester of college, after taking general chemistry, I realized I loved the "why" behind biological functions from the intramolecular cyclization of sugars to the formations of peptide bonds in amino acids, which is why that realization led me to switch my major to biochemistry. One significant problem that I find compelling is antibiotic resistance and the need for new therapeutics. Many of our antibiotics are naturally product-derived, and one large contributor to natural products has been the Streptomyces bacteria. Yet a significant barrier is that the biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) that encode these metabolites are silent and/or cryptic within standard lab settings. Given the rise of antibiotic resistance, if new techniques and routes can be determined to activate and upregulate the production of metabolites, then hopefully new novel antibiotics can be discovered to combat this growing crisis.  

SURF stood out to me because this program not only focuses on placing students in a lab, but also actively trains them to problem solve, write, and present as professional researchers. It would be an immersive experience of 11 weeks of full-time research paired with expert mentorship and opportunities to enhance my communication skills through seminars, which will overall equip me with the support and guidance I need to achieve my academic goals, such as presenting my research at a professional conference. Long term, I plan to pursue a PhD in chemistry and to work in organic chemistry, focusing on drug discovery/drug design. After obtaining my doctorate, I aim to enter the industry, focusing on medicinal chemistry. I am especially fascinated by research that investigates actinobacteria's natural product regulation and pathways of induction, as these cyclic peptides often possess antimicrobial, antibacterial, and other therapeutic properties. SURF would accelerate this path by giving me sustained research momentum and a better understanding of what a research career looks like, which would help me confirm and refine my long-term trajectory in STEM.  

As a first-generation American and college student, I would be the first in my family to pursue and obtain a PhD. I have not always had the same access to research networks or guidance about graduate school, which is why SURF would be valuable in helping me understand what the PhD pathway realistically looks like and guide how I shape my future. The full-time structure would let me experience research hands-on through planning experiments, troubleshooting, and interpreting results. Writing a final report and presenting at the SURF symposium would strengthen my communication skills, research analysis, and scientific writing. Additionally, professional development seminars, networking opportunities, and overall engagement are a major benefit because they provide structured guidance and opportunities which would help me build a professional network and gain insight into research careers that align with my goals. 

I've explored biochemistry hands-on through coursework and undergraduate research. In Biology 145 with Dr. Olson, I worked within a small team to design an experiment investigating cytokine production, specifically IL-10 and TNF, in Raw 246.7 macrophages. These macrophages were stimulated with LPS in the presence or absence of the microbial metabolite HPPA. The goal of the project was to explore the role of HPPA in regulating the production of cytokines and whether it increased anti-inflammatory or inflammatory cytokine production in Raw 246.7 macrophages. This project strengthened my experimental design and data interpretation skills, and I presented our findings in a poster presentation at the end of the semester. This past semester, I joined Dr. Parkinson's research lab, where I was paired with a PhD student mentor and assigned an adjacent side project focused on XAD-16 in situ resin catch on Streptomyces hygroscopicus LL-AC98. This strain has been shown to produce natural products, specifically cyclic glycopeptides called mannopeptimycins, with reported antimicrobial bioactivity against some gram-positive bacteria. This past semester, I have mainly been investigating the ideal media growing conditions and testing XAD-16 resin capture approaches to upregulate the production of the mannopeptimycins. Ultimately, I hope to combine the XAD-16 resin approach with the use of chemical elicitors, specifically antibiotics, to further upregulate the production of the mannopeptimycins, as my PhD student mentor has had success with this approach in different strains of Streptomyces. Together, these experiences have demonstrated my commitment to research and helped me develop core laboratory skills like designing experiments, maintaining detailed data records, analyzing data, troubleshooting methods, and collaborating with other lab members.  

One challenge in my path early on was navigating a shift in academic direction. I entered college focused on biology but quickly learned through coursework that I was most interested in the chemical mechanisms that are the foundation of biological systems. Therefore, I changed my major to chemical biology and biochemistry, which meant reorganizing my course plan, taking new required classes, and catching up on prerequisites. I addressed this by meeting with my advisor and mapping out a few semesters' plan. A second challenge has been within my research project and learning to handle setbacks. During my initial media screening, where I was trying to find the ideal growing conditions for the Streptomyces hygroscopicus LL-AC98, I expected certain conditions to upregulate production of peptides. However, my results did not match my hypothesis. After over a month of experiments that did not lead to answers, my mentor guided me and helped me reassess what variables might be limiting production and what new media I should try. I revised and created new media protocols, as well as tried other media protocols, and my last round of experiments based on UPLC analysis seems to have promising leads and increased peptide production. This setback taught me that research is rarely a straight, predictable path. Experiments fail, unexpected results happen, and outcomes aren't always expected or support one's hypothesis. But I have realized that setbacks don't inherently mean failure but are a part of the process and still contribute to overall progress.
