In real-world deployments, small perception errors can escalate into safety or operational failures. That reality drew me to AI/ML and keeps me committed to Computer Science: I want to build robust video understanding systems that work under challenging conditions, can justify their outputs through vision-language grounding, and can be adapted efficiently to new environments without costly retraining. I am broadly interested in computer vision, with a focus on video understanding, vision-language models (VLMs), and efficient fine-tuning, because these capabilities are increasingly required for reliable AI in the wild.

My research direction has been shaped by applied work across robotics, security, healthcare, and education. At Vitasoft (Sep 2022 - Oct 2023), I led R&D on an autonomous cart system that performed real-time detection/segmentation and user tracking, integrating vision outputs with motor control. I learned to design for real-time performance and robustness upfront, since deployment failures are costly. At CNAI (Oct 2023 - Dec 2024), I led end-to-end R&D of NexLook, an AI-powered security camera system, from scratch through PoC to prototype, showcased at CES 2024 and demonstrated in a subway station. I customized a real-time DeepStream pipeline with RTSP input/output, multi-object tracking, and per-stream output handling, and I worked end-to-end from data collection/annotation to prototype demos. I implemented cross-camera tracking by storing ReID embeddings into a vector database and using similarity search to associate identities across streams. This work highlighted the need for robustness to illumination changes, occlusion, and domain shift in real-world settings.

At Nuvilab (Jan 2025 - Jun 2025), I led AI R&D of an AI Food Scanner with Morrison Healthcare (Compass Group) and deployed it across U.S. hospitals to prevent meal-ticket mismatches via instance segmentation and fine-grained classification. I refined noisy hospital data into a standardized dataset (12,088 images / 215 categories), then fine-tuned DINOv2-Large as a teacher and applied task-oriented distillation using a 1.22M-image unlabeled transfer set retrieved from open datasets using similarity search. The resulting FastViT student replaced a ResNet-101 baseline (+49.22% macro-F1, ~2-3x lower Android latency). I migrated the system from Jetson to Android and supported the first deployment in a new hospital site, focusing on generalization under unseen facility conditions without site-specific data.

Finally, since Aug 2025, I have been a Research Assistant in Prof. Qiang Qiu’s lab, where I developed and integrated a multi-stage LLM tutoring pipeline (rewrite → retrieve → plan → answer). I implemented conversation-aware query rewriting to improve RAG retrieval and added a structured hint-ladder planner to generate step-by-step, hint-based guidance rather than direct answers. The system has been deployed for Purdue ECE 20875 (Python for Data Science).  This work made me appreciate structured pipelines with explicit reasoning steps in system design. I’m excited by many recent video/VLM systems that select evidence frames, reason over time, and support their conclusions with visual evidence.

These experiences motivate the research questions I want to pursue through SURF. First, in video understanding, how do we move beyond frame-level predictions to sequence-level reasoning that remains robust under changing lighting, shadows, motion blur, and partial occlusions? In many real applications, performance depends on consistent reasoning over time, not on a single-frame prediction. Second, in VLMs, how can we ground outputs in evidence by linking predictions to specific frames or clips and generating concise explanations that users can understand and trust? Third, in efficient fine-tuning, how can we adapt models to new cameras, sites, or conditions using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, distillation, or lightweight domain adaptation instead of full retraining? More broadly, I want to build video and multimodal systems that are robust in real-world settings, can point to the visual evidence behind their decisions, and can be adapted efficiently as cameras and environments change.

To pursue these questions more systematically, I am applying to Purdue SURF. I want an immersive, mentored research environment where I can turn my hands-on deployment experience into clear research questions, well-designed experiments, and reliable evaluation. SURF’s full-time structure, close faculty and graduate mentorship, and emphasis on research communication (a written report and presentation) will help me strengthen my research habits and communicate results clearly. Long term, I aim to pursue a PhD and contribute to trustworthy and efficient AI systems that work reliably in real-world settings.

Estimating individual cattle feed intake and assessing feed texture consistency during mixing require combining information across multiple frames, while remaining reliable under changing illumination and shadows. I hope to build a strong baseline that combines detection/segmentation with temporal modeling, using tracking and simple sequence methods to integrate information over time. I also plan to evaluate robustness across lighting conditions using unseen test videos and targeted augmentations, and to diagnose failures under domain shift. If feasible, I would explore a lightweight VLM-based component that points to key frames or time windows behind each estimate and provides short, clear explanations for practitioners. This project fits my background in real-time video pipelines and evaluation, and I’m excited to contribute through implementation, labeling where needed, and clear communication of results.

My second choice, Next-generation compact and robust 2D and 3D imaging system development, strongly matches my interest in building perception systems that are both accurate and practical under tight hardware constraints. This project combines optics and machine learning to build camera systems that are compact, accurate, and energy-efficient, which aligns with how I think about deployable AI. I would be excited to collaborate closely with a graduate mentor to help advance the prototype by contributing to deep learning-based image processing, analyzing real measurement data, and running careful experiments to understand accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs. Given my background deploying edge models, I am particularly interested in using distillation and parameter-efficient adaptation to preserve imaging quality while meeting strict compute and energy budgets, and to study how reliability changes under tighter resource limits.

My third choice, Automated Characterization Platform for Beyond-Silicon “CMOS+X” AI Hardware Prototypes, appeals to me because it connects automation with data-driven analysis. My experience building multi-stage LLM pipelines makes me interested in a reliable tool-using assistant that can summarize measurement results, suggest next tests, and speed up debugging while remaining grounded in the underlying data. This aligns with my interest in building systems that are not only accurate, but also verifiable.

One challenge I have faced across projects is adapting quickly to new environments and imperfect data while maintaining momentum. I address this by building reproducible pipelines early, defining clear evaluation metrics, and iterating through focused experiments with frequent feedback from mentors and teammates. I’m eager to apply this approach in SURF and contribute meaningfully to one of the listed projects.

In summary, I am applying to Purdue SURF to deepen my research training in video understanding, vision-language grounding, and efficient fine-tuning, and to produce a focused research contribution this summer. I believe SURF is an ideal next step toward my goal of developing trustworthy, efficient AI systems and ultimately pursuing a PhD.

However, my academic path took a turn when I had the chance to work in my current controls lab. I realized that the mathematical tools used to stabilize an aircraft are not limited to aerospace; they are universal. This realization led me to dive into multiple disciplines, and that is what fascinates me the most, specifically, how methods from one field can be applied to others. I continue to pursue this path because I want to be an engineer who is not limited by the boundaries of a single department. I am motivated by the challenge of taking rigorous mathematical frameworks and applying them to solve dynamic problems in new contexts, whether that is in robotics, biological systems, or eventually, next-generation aircraft.

I am attracted to SURF because it offers a unique environment where engineering disciplines converge. Purdue is a powerhouse in STEM, and since my goal is to eventually work in the Aerospace industry, potentially in Research & Development, I believe it is crucial to step outside my comfort zone and see how other fields approach complex problems. Long-term, I plan to pursue graduate studies to deepen my technical expertise before entering the aerospace sector. I am still exploring which specific niche of engineering I want to specialize in, and I view SURF as the perfect testing ground. It will allow me to apply my skills to a real-world research problem, helping me determine if a research-focused career path is the right fit for me.

My career goal is to design control systems for safety-critical environments. To do this, I need to move beyond theoretical derivations and gain experience with computational modeling and validation. Through SURF, I specifically hope to gain proficiency in data-driven modeling tools. In my current work, I focus on the theory of constraints; at SURF, I want to learn the application of those constraints in high-fidelity simulations. Gaining these computational skills will make me a more versatile engineer. Equally important to me are the connections SURF offers. I want to leverage Purdue’s strong ties to industry. Engaging with professors who collaborate directly with corporate partners will give me insight into how research is translated into real-world technology, helping me shape my path toward an R&D career.

My most significant exploration of the field is my current role as a Research Assistant. Despite being an Aerospace major, I sought out this role in the Electrical Engineering Department to deepen my understanding of Constraint Control. Currently, I am leading the development of a MATLAB simulation for an 'Inverted Pendulum on a Cart'. This project requires me to translate theoretical control barrier functions into a working physics-based model. This experience has taught me how to read academic papers, formulate research questions, and debug complex code. In terms of coursework, I have excelled in Aircraft Dynamics and Linear Systems, Thermodynamics, and Heat Transfer. My ability to cross departmental lines (Aero to Electrical) demonstrates my adaptability and my commitment to learning the necessary tools to solve the problem at hand, regardless of the discipline.

This experience taught me that I am capable of 'learning how to learn' quickly, a skill that I know is essential for the fast-paced environment of the SURF program.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in aerospace engineering and physics emerged from a desire to understand how fundamental physical laws translate into complex, real world systems. I was initially drawn to aerospace through flight and propulsion, but as my coursework progressed, my motivation deepened toward understanding why these systems behave the way they do. This includes how electromagnetic fields accelerate plasma, how structures adapt to changing aerodynamic loads, and how energy transport at small scales can dictate macroscopic performance. This curiosity has led me to pursue Aerospace Engineering alongside Engineering Physics at the University of Michigan, placing my academic interests at the intersection of applied engineering, electromagnetism, and fundamental physics.

Through coursework in fluid mechanics, gas dynamics, structures, and electromagnetism, I have become particularly interested in how energy and momentum are exchanged through coupled physical processes. Topics such as plasma field interactions in electric propulsion, flow stability and thermal transport in compressible regimes, and the coupling between materials, structures, and external forcing have become central to my academic focus. Studying electromagnetism alongside propulsion has reshaped how I think about thrust generation, not only as a fluid dynamic problem, but as one governed by charged particle motion, magnetic confinement, and energy efficiency, as seen in Hall thrusters such as the SPT 100.

These interests strongly align with the SURF projects I am applying to. The operation and characterization of Hall thrusters directly reflects my desire to study how electromagnetic fields, plasma dynamics, and energy efficiency interact in space propulsion systems. The micro morphing aircraft project resonates with my interest in flow structure interaction and adaptive systems, where small structural changes can lead to significant aerodynamic and performance benefits. The neutral atom trapping project also appeals to me conceptually, as it explores precise control of energy, fields, and matter at the nanoscale, reinforcing my interest in physics driven systems where electromagnetic theory underpins real technological applications.

I am especially drawn to the SURF program because it offers a structured, immersive research environment centered on fundamental mechanisms rather than purely end use design. Unlike industry internships, SURF enables sustained engagement with a focused research question, whether that involves characterizing plasma behavior, modeling morphing structures, or understanding atom field interactions. The opportunity to work closely with a faculty mentor, iterate on a well defined research problem, and communicate results in an academic setting directly supports my goal of pursuing graduate study and ultimately a PhD. Through SURF, I aim to develop core research skills essential for a long term career in physics driven aerospace research, including formulating hypothesis based research questions, designing experiments or simulations to isolate fundamental mechanisms, and validating theoretical models against experimental data. Working closely with a faculty mentor will help me develop research judgment by learning how to refine assumptions, interpret ambiguous results, and iterate on methodology, which is critical preparation for graduate level research. Presenting findings in a formal academic setting will further strengthen my ability to communicate complex physical ideas clearly, an essential skill for research leadership and interdisciplinary collaboration.

In the long term, I aspire to pursue a career in STEM that bridges advanced physics research with aerospace system development. I am particularly interested in electric propulsion, energy efficient flight, and space systems that rely on electromagnetic or plasma based technologies. I am motivated by the idea that deep physical understanding of fields, transport phenomena, and scaling laws can meaningfully improve aerospace performance and sustainability. SURF represents a critical stepping stone toward this career path by allowing me to build the research independence, technical depth, and faculty mentorship experience required for success in a PhD program and research oriented aerospace roles.

To explore these interests, I have pursued both hands-on engineering design and research oriented experiences. As a member of the MACH Design Build Fly team, I work across propulsion, aerodynamics, and systems subteams, applying theoretical models to real aircraft constraints. My work includes airfoil analysis using AVL, propulsion and propeller efficiency evaluation using APC data, and interpreting multidisciplinary design tradeoffs. Participating in composite wing layups and fuselage construction reinforced how structural assumptions and material behavior directly affect aerodynamic performance.

As a complementary design focused experience, I led a personal High Lift RC Aircraft Design project aimed at developing a research relevant airframe suitable for future Design Build Fly cycles. I independently designed the wing and tail geometry to prioritize high lift, stability, and durability, incorporating dihedral, taper, and flaps to manage lift distribution and control authority. I analyzed airfoil behavior, aerodynamic coefficients, and stability characteristics using AVL, XFOIL, XFLR5, and Star CCM +CFD, allowing me to evaluate performance tradeoffs and validate design assumptions across multiple fidelity levels. In parallel, I iterated APC propeller data in MATLAB to match propeller performance with motor selection and overall aircraft requirements. The project culminated in a technical design presentation used to communicate subsystem decisions and receive critical feedback, reinforcing how physics based analysis directly informs practical aerospace design.

In parallel, I worked as a Research Assistant at Geminus Technology and Development under Dr. John Hinkey, where I conducted research on high temperature processes including carbon black pyrolysis, membrane separation, and energetic materials. This role strengthened my ability to analyze energy transport, thermal effects, and system level constraints while maintaining scientific rigor. Presenting results to both technical and non technical stakeholders taught me how to translate complex physical phenomena into actionable engineering insight, an essential skill for research in propulsion, morphing systems, or nanophotonic technologies.

Overall, SURF represents a pivotal opportunity for me to transition from applied coursework and industry adjacent research into deeper physics driven inquiry aligned with propulsion, adaptive aerospace systems, and electromagnetic control of matter. By strengthening my ability to conduct physics based research, evaluate experimental and computational results, and communicate findings within an academic research environment, SURF will directly prepare me for advanced graduate study and a research focused career in aerospace and applied physics. I am eager to use this program to refine my research interests, prepare for graduate study, and contribute meaningfully to aerospace and physics based research. I am confident that SURF will play a defining role in my development as a researcher and future leader in STEM.

For my sixth birthday, I received my very first Lego set: a 500-piece by-the-book Batmobile. Watching it storm the streets of Gotham on a TV screen couldn't compare to being able to feel the real thing. Six-year-old me quickly realized that following the instructions to a tee was both intimidating and a drag. So I tossed it aside and built something of my own: the “Scuba-Bat-Haque”, an all-terrain super vehicle that sparked a lifelong drive to make things that could be seen and felt on my own terms.

As I grew older, my love for creation took new forms. From making master grade Gundam plastic model kits to drafting houses in CAD, I knew that I wanted the freedom to make something impactful; the question was what. 

Starting college as a Computer Science major, I switched tracks when I saw the freedom and physical impact that designing and creating structures provided through civil engineering. Studying Civil Engineering at Stony Brook University (SBU) helped me to narrow my vision towards a future of constructing the next Flatiron Building or SpaceX launch pad. Using the resources provided to me at school, I pursued my new major by exploring the built environment with intention. I took courses in drafting software, AutoCAD, and Revit, and became certified. Learning these new tools allowed me to make meaningful contributions within the ACE Mentor Program and the American Society of Civil Engineers Steel Bridge Competition. Through ACE, I was a part of a team aimed at designing a mock exhibition for the Museum of Modern Art. I outlined the public and private sectors and consulted structural engineers regarding column placement for each floor of our library exhibition. In the Steel Bridge Competition, I assisted my team in drafting designs for the competition bridge under size, measurement, and weight constraints. With each experience, I felt more resolute in pursuing a career where I could see and feel the impact of my work through built structures.

Through clubs such as Solar Racing and the National Society of Black Engineers, I began to explore the different specializations and sub-branches within Civil Engineering, which introduced me to renewable energy. Through exploring the intersection between renewable energy, sustainability, and civil engineering, I started interning at the Renewable Community Initiative, a not-for-profit hydrogen energy start-up. In assisting the CEO with key operations such as site analysis and energy research, I learned about the emerging capabilities of hydrogen. It offers a clean, high-density alternative to fossil fuels, enabling zero-emission power generation and energy storage solutions that can strengthen resilient, sustainable urban infrastructure.

Looking into ongoing research among the civil engineering faculty at SBU, I came across one notable professor, Paolo Celli. Professor Celli’s research delved into shape-morphing meta-materials, specifically the unique properties these materials exhibited, potential implementations, and programming them. While touring his laboratory, I became captivated by his ongoing projects, including programmable bistable structures that could change shape and snap into place based on deliberate geometric perturbations. Through further conversations, Professor Celli showed me the potential that programmable meta materials had on the environment through applications such as temperature-dependent ventilation components, impact-resistant building materials, soft automated robotics, and so much more.

	Through my passion for designing structures in the built environment, ive been exposed to renewable energy, green infrastructure, and shape-morphing materials. At the intersection of all these research areas lies innovative sustainable building practices through employing emerging energy resources and materials. I seek to advance my passion for design through research in resilient and sustainable structural design. SURF would be an amazing opportunity to explore and contribute to ongoing research within these fields, as well as provide me with a strong foothold towards a career in innovative structural engineering.

What appeals to me particularly in SURF is its emphasis on interdisciplinary research and its support system in place for undergraduate students conducting research. Being able to participate in faculty-led research at the forefront of innovation, while receiving guidance through workshops, talks, and a group setting for conducting research, sets SURF apart from other summer research opportunities. Being a part of SURF would allow me to learn not only technical skills pertinent to conducting research, but also the ability to communicate ideas and work effectively in teams within interdisciplinary studies.

The experience SURF provides would also be an invaluable stepping stone in my pursuit of a long-term career within structural engineering. As the populations grow and resources naturally diminish, it is essential that research and development of cutting-edge materials and technologies be done to make infrastructure more resilient and efficient in its use and production of energy. By participating in the SURF program, I hope to better assess not just the theoretical applications of new materials and structures but also how they might be applied in the real world. Long term, I envision myself as a part of a global design firm at the forefront of making tomorrow's infrastructure.

Through collaboration with faculty mentors, I am looking to cultivate practical experience in experimental design, modeling, and analysis, all of which are crucial skills in innovative structural engineering. The aspect of SURF, focusing on the presentation and preparation of reports such as posters, will also allow me to communicate complex ideas in a group setting, an essential aspect of working with clients in the contracting field. Moreover, the network achieved through SURF will help me land future research roles during graduate school and mentors to guide me while pursuing my professional engineer license. For example, Professor Akanshu Sharma’s work in designing earthquake-resistant structural connections focuses on analyzing structural components using experimental setups, fabrication, and numerical modeling, followed by poster presentations and publications, which offer a holistic research experience with a strong foundation in technical ability, research etiquette, and public speaking.

I envision a future where I can actively leave my legacy on the world through physical contributions in the form of structures. Whether that’s helping design the next World Trade Center or a high school basketball court, I hope to change lives sustainably and for the long term. SURF would be an immeasurable opportunity to start that journey through building the necessary skills, network, and drive for my ambitions.

statement_of_purpose:
At two in the morning, helicopter lights flooded our house in the woods. My father and I had just finished watching Terminator. At just eight years old, huddled beneath blankets, my dad, holding a coconut machete and calling the police, told me to hide. In my mind, I was certain that the movie had come to life—a giant, AI-driven killer robot was about to crash through our door. It turns out our neighbors had been robbed. As a kid, everything about that night deterred me from pursuing a career in tech.
Although it took a bit for my eight-year-old brain to stop wondering if the toaster could turn deviant, I came to understand that fear comes from the unknown. The day I begged for my first Arduino Developer Kit, I began tackle the fear that came along with the unknown and through curious agency, I decided to make a change in the rising concerns about technology. Ever since joining Mercer a year ago, I have pursued this passion.
I study autonomous humanoid and soft robotics—the intersection between biologically modeled hardware and computer-vision-driven software. This field allows for the analysis of the polished mechanisms of nature and adds a layer of computational intelligence achievable only through machine learning and artificial intelligence. This multidisciplinary engineering approach is what I believe to be the future of life-saving specialized technologies designed to explore dangerous environments.
The biggest platform for this pursuit has been my leadership in the Machine Intelligence and Robotics Laboratory (MIRL) under the guidance of Dr. Anthony Choi. As the largest student-led laboratory in the School of Engineering, we oversee eleven innovative projects all dedicated to biomodeled autonomous robotics, three of which I lead. Starting in January 2025, my biggest passion project has been MerBot, a humanoid semi-autonomous robot designed to use vision-language-action machine learning models to interact with its environment. Trained with emerging software such as Isaac Sim Laboratory, it serves as a platform to train current undergraduates in industry-critical skills. At its prime, it will be one of the first open-source, AI-driven humanoid robotics projects, allowing us to validate our work as hundreds of users scrutinize and build upon it, breaking technical barriers in an industry expected to reach 38 billion dollars by 2035.
Alongside MerBot, I have worked with Dr. Lianjun Wu, an expert in soft robotics, researching alternative low-cost actuation methods. Specifically, we investigate thermo-reactive actuators for bionics using agonist–antagonist muscle dynamics, manufactured with conductive wire coils wrapped around nylon filaments. When exposed to voltage-induced heat, these actuators contract, and when stacked, they can produce immense strength. Both Dr. Wu and Dr. Choi have been active guides and supporting backbones in my career, connecting me with funding, contacts, and fully committing to the process of student-led research.
Despite the success we’ve found, including plans to release our first working MerBot demo by the end of 2026, with no PhD programs at Mercer professors do not have graduate students to rely on. As a result, undergraduates are forced produce graduate-level work as undergraduates, but when you are developing technology while still learning its fundamentals, gaps in knowledge become evident. Navigating this has been the biggest challenge of research. 
As I navigate the world of autonomous robotics, SURF feels like a natural progression. I am driven by consumer-forward technology, believing that only when we frame technology around the user can we create something truly impactful. In my time there, I programmed nine FANUC robots for an automated manufacturing machine. The precision of the robots was the first thing that stood out to me; the second was their inflexibility. While these machines have and will continue to revolutionize manufacturing, their lack of awareness remains a frustrating limitation to their efficiency. In debugging, I realized that if a part was a centimeter out of its designated location in a robot’s pick-and-place script, the robot could not adjust, requiring operations to stop. Because of this, extremely precise, and therefore extremely expensive, control systems were necessary to ensure manufacturing viability. I’m fascinated by how machine learning could be implemented to provide robots with more flexibility to adjust to volatile environments. However, for this integration to become feasible, the computational costs of the neural networks involved must be reduced. I believe non-classical architectures will play an essential role in making machine learning more computationally efficient, in particular neuromorphic computing. By using hardware that mimics neuronal dynamics, the bottlenecks associated with traditional Von Neumann computing can be overcome. This will lead to hardware far better suited for machine learning. As I pursue graduate studies, I hope to examine the interplay between these novel architectures and robotics.

SURF will help me realize this aim due to Purdue’s status as a leading institution for robotics innovation. Conducting research in an environment with such a wide array of perspectives on robotics will provide me with a deeper understanding of both the obstacles and opportunities of the technology. Through the SURF program, I have the chance to pursue my interests in automation and neuromorphic computing from several angles. 

For example, Dr. Haitong Li's lab on automating the testing of AI hardware prototypes would provide the unique opportunity to work with cutting-edge hardware architectures. By taking part in this research, I can familiarize myself with the issues facing these novel designs. My programming and controls experience would be used in a setting which expands my knowledge of non-classical architectures. Dr. Yan Gu’s research on the interactions between humans and humanoid robots also aligns with my research interests. There are few things less predictable than a human being, and I believe machine learning could allow robots to navigate this volatility. The chance to add to my industrial automation experience in Dr. Martin Jun’s lab on the use of digital twins to optimize manufacturing processing appeals to me as well. Dr. Jun’s previous work on using machine learning for object recognition is exactly the type of functionality I would like to implement in automation systems, and I want to contribute to research like this. As an assistant in Dr. Susana Cerqueira’s lab on neural inflammation, I examine neuronal connections under the microscope. My study of neurons has given me biological inspiration for novel computing architectures. While the lab techniques do not apply directly to the research I would like to pursue, the challenges I encountered involving attention to detail will stick with me in all my research projects. My design of an experiment examining how inhibitory neurons affect axonal regeneration exemplifies this. I narrowed my original, overly complex design into a simple and precise setup, with a detailed procedure and data collection methodology, utilizing feedback from my PI. Last summer, I participated in an REU with the Alabama Water Institute and CIROH, where I worked with Dr. Jonathan Frame on developing a surrogate model for the National Water Model. I trained a single-layer LSTM using WRF-forced NWM v2.1 simulation data and, as part of this work, helped pioneer a method for detecting extrapolation using convex hull analysis in the model’s internal state space. Prior to this experience, my research interests were primarily focused on theoretical physics, and I had been working on galaxy formation simulation analysis, which provided a strong foundation in physical modeling and computational methods.

This REU experience significantly reshaped how I approach scientific research. I became interested in machine learning not simply as a predictive tool, but as a framework for understanding model behavior and failure modes in scientific applications. I continued developing this project beyond the REU, which resulted in my first preprint and a presentation at the AGU Fall Meeting. These experiences reinforced my desire to develop machine learning methods through their application to challenging, real-world scientific problems.

A central question that now motivates my work emerged directly from this hydrological research: How can we improve model performance under extreme events? In hydrology, such events have disproportionate societal impact, yet they are often poorly represented in training data, and standard neural architectures are not designed to handle extrapolative regimes. This limitation led me toward physics-informed machine learning and neural operators, which integrate physical constraints and governing equations into learning architectures. I find this direction particularly compelling because it moves beyond interpolation and toward models that encode physical structure and enable more reliable generalization.

I see myself as a problem solver at the intersection of physics, mathematics, and machine learning. I am motivated by the challenge of designing models that remain faithful to physical laws while leveraging the expressive power of modern AI. My goal is to contribute to Scientific Machine Learning by developing approaches that are both accurate and physically consistent, with an emphasis on interpretability and robustness.

I learned about the Purdue SURF program through the graduate school booth at AGU, where I also spoke with several Purdue faculty working in AI-driven scientific research. What attracted me to SURF is its strong emphasis on artificial intelligence in science and its integration within a rigorous research environment. The program’s structure, mentorship, and project-based focus align well with my academic interests and my goal of pursuing a PhD in computational mathematics.

Participation in SURF would be an important step toward my long-term career goals. I hope to deepen my technical expertise in scientific machine learning, mathematical modeling, and large-scale computation, while gaining experience working within interdisciplinary research teams. Equally important, I aim to build mentorship and professional connections that will inform my graduate school preparation and future research direction. Ultimately, I aspire to pursue a research career in Scientific Machine Learning, whether in academia, national laboratories, or industry, focused on developing principled, physically grounded models for complex systems. I believe the SURF program would provide the training and perspective necessary to advance toward these goals.

n terms of preparation, one challenge I encountered early in my REU was recognizing that my programming skills did not yet fully match my mathematical background. Addressing this gap became a priority. Throughout the summer and subsequent semesters, I deliberately worked to strengthen my computational skills by completing machine learning courses through Coursera, supplementing them with technical lectures and tutorials, and gaining hands-on experience with Python and PyTorch. In the upcoming spring semester, I will further formalize this training by taking a physics-oriented machine learning course (PH 451) at my home institution.

I have also intentionally selected code-intensive final projects in my astronomy courses to develop programming skills in a research setting, allowing me to learn computational techniques while working with real scientific data. By the time of the SURF program, I will have completed coursework in ordinary and partial differential equations, which I have applied extensively in intermediate classical mechanics, electrodynamics, and magnetodynamics. I have also completed courses in probability theory and applied probability, which have been particularly valuable for understanding uncertainty and generalization in machine learning models.

Beyond coursework, I actively engage with the research literature on machine learning applications in hydrology and astrophysics, as well as both foundational and recent work on neural operators. At the AGU Fall Meeting, I attended a wide range of oral sessions focused on artificial intelligence in the geosciences and spoke with multiple faculty members to learn about the techniques, modeling approaches, and computational tools they use in their research. These efforts reflect my commitment to research at the intersection of physical science and machine learning and have prepared me to contribute meaningfully to a rigorous summer research program such as SURF.

statement_of_purpose:
Back in junior year of high school, I joined a summer program geared towards getting high school students interested in the emerging quantum technology sector. We went on trips to a lot of different places during that program, such as the Eisenhower Building, Georgetown University, and the University of Maryland, but the only one I wasn’t falling asleep for was the trip to the NASA Langley Research Center. I lived in Hawaii for seven years and still I felt that I had never seen anything so beautiful. We saw all sorts of things at the research center, but what I fell in love with was the robotics. Pristine, robust, suspended in complex electromechanical rigs, enshrouded in cabling with streams of data and diagnostics sprinting across nearby screens. I distinctly remember my first question after seeing the engineers working on the James Webb telescope in the cleanroom being “How do I get in there?” Before all this I had been seriously considering a career in art and animation, but after a two hour long exposure to robotics I was smitten. I didn’t even care about drawing anymore - the only thing on my mind was getting enough money to buy my own components and materials to assemble my own robots. I have found engineering to be so much more fulfilling and exciting of a pastime and career than drawing ever was for me. My high school didn’t have much in the way of STEM, so I worked on lots of personal projects to compensate for the gap in experience and knowledge. AI was super popular at the time, so I taught myself to understand research papers and made ASRs, GANs, DQNs, facial recognition systems, transformers, mixture of experts models, and a hexapod robot. In college I chose to major in Computer Engineering so I could later do a concentration in Controls, Robotics, and Autonomy. In my first year I became a research assistant for a PhD student working on applications of robotics in construction, and I was also promoted to Chief Engineer at VT CRO, the largest robotics design team on campus. Before the start of my second year, I acquired an undergraduate research internship with the MAOP program, with my project focusing on investigating real world applications of multi agent systems. These experiences have reinforced what I knew instantly when I walked into the NASA Langley Research Center - I want to spend my life researching and building robots and AI.
Throughout my life, vocational experiences and otherwise, I’ve found that my primary motivator above everything else is curiosity. I care about the pursuit of knowledge more than fame or money. If something doesn’t pique my interest, I could not care less what other incentives or benefits are offered to me to do it. I want to get a PhD for research in robotics because I want to know all I can know, and then discover new things nobody knew previously, contributing to an ever expanding body of knowledge. While I’m still narrowing down which subfield intrigues me the most, via reading papers and watching videos I have taken an interest in soft robotics, microrobotics, multi-agent systems, and robotic manipulation. After obtaining a PhD, I’d like to work on directly applying my skills and research experience to other fields that interest me, such as space habitation and asteroid mining via work at NASA, since that’s where all this started. It would be a dream come true to one day become an astronaut and travel to the Gateway, the lunar space station NASA plans on building, conducting novel experiments on the applications of space robotics. Of course, I wouldn’t stop there. Why not make robotic avatars that can be controlled through virtual reality, or investigate consciousness through applying mechanistic interpretability techniques to ever more advanced AI systems, or make microscopic organic robots that target and kill cancer cells? I plan to go into my grave making new discoveries.
Acceptance into Purdue SURF is an essential component of making all that happen. To do top tier research, I have to get into a top tier PhD program, and to do that I need to have sufficient experience and expertise to prove to PhD programs that I’m a top tier candidate. This is why I want to work under professional researchers at Purdue such as David Cappelleri, whose work in deep learning and precision agriculture would be instrumental in my development as a researcher. I was excited to see such an application-focused project from him on the list of research being conducted during the program, and would be overjoyed to collaborate with him on his outstandingly innovative ways of creating and organizing robots, as can be seen in his recent work on a magnetic micro-robot assembly system. Given my interest in pushing the boundaries of the state of robotics, Vishrant Tripathi’s project on Multi-Robot Coordination for Maritime Environments is also an obvious choice. Having the opportunity to work alongside Tripathi on a project that could have significant implications for so many fields would be an incredible opportunity. Given that underwater communication is far more challenging compared to typical air-based communication, success in making a multi-agent network that operates underwater would imply potentially even greater success recreating the network above water, paving the way for future projects that will allow these robots to help us in a variety of scenarios, ranging from disaster relief to reconnaissance. Still, other researchers like Dimitrios Peroulis and his project on the “Automated Radio Evaluation Suite: Modular Testing Architecture” catch my attention too, as advances in microelectronics and RF will be increasingly crucial to successful and safe robotic systems. Even disregarding future advances in robotics, the project has a lot of promise to facilitate research in its field, and is something I’d be honored to contribute to. Given the lineup of outstanding mentors and projects on the Purdue SURF research projects page, it was such a struggle to limit this part of the essay to just a couple of my favorites. However, that’s exactly why I’m certain that SURF would be one of the most instrumental opportunities in my professional development, and why I’d be honored to be accepted into the cohort for Summer 2026.

My path into computer hardware and applied mathematics was shaped by a singular realization during my freshman year: the most impactful engineering happens at the intersection of physics, mathematics, and practical implementation. When I learned that computational bottlenecks in AI weren't primarily algorithmic but rather architectural, rooted in how data moves through chips, I knew my career had to focus on hardware innovation.

What initially attracted me to mathematics was its universality, but what captivated me was its application to unsolved physical problems. Specifically, I became fascinated by neuromorphic computing, photonic interconnects, and probabilistic logic, three fields where mathematical elegance directly translates to energy efficiency gains that matter for edge AI on constrained devices.

The significant problem that motivates me most deeply is this: How can we build AI hardware that operates powerfully but sustainably? Current GPU-based accelerators consume kilowatts; drone inference should consume milliwatts. This gap isn't just an engineering inconvenience; it's a bottleneck preventing AI from reaching billions of resource-constrained devices globally. Through my OmniAI Chip v1.2 project, I've been modeling solutions using stochastic computing, neuromorphic principles, and silicon photonics. These are the domains where I want to develop genuine expertise.

1. Embedded Research Culture at Scale: Purdue Engineering's research infrastructure (EURO, ECE research groups, fabrication facilities) gives me access to mentorship and resources that most undergraduate programs simply cannot offer. Your emphasis on "research in both West Lafayette and Indianapolis" suggests deep institutional support.

2. Faculty Alignment with My Exact Interests, Specifically, Prof. Supriyo Datta's work on probabilistic computing (p-bits) and Prof. Kaushik Roy's neuromorphic group are directly adjacent to OmniAI v1.2's core architecture. A summer under their guidance wouldn't just be an experience; it would validate or refine the theoretical foundations of my chip concept.

3. Clear Path to Transfer & Graduate Studies, As someone planning to transfer to MIT, Stanford, or Georgia Tech in Fall 2026 for my final two years, a SURF internship completion serves as a proof point of research readiness that strengthens my transfer applications immensely. It also signals to PhD programs that I've successfully operated in a research environment.

My long-term career goal is to become a hardware innovator at the intersection of neuromorphic and photonic computing, eventually founding or leading a team at a company like Lightmatter, Extropic, or within a major semiconductor firm (Intel, NVIDIA, TSMC advanced R&D). The trajectory is SURF (summer 2026) → Transfer + continued research (Fall 2026, Spring 2028) → DOE SULI or lab internship (summer 2027) → PhD at top school → Industry innovation leader.

SURF is a critical stepping stone because it establishes research credibility and technical depth that PhD programs and industry labs scrutinize heavily.

Current Research Activities (as of January 2026):

OmniAI Chip v1.2 Architecture Design (Self-directed, 6+ months): Architecting a heterogeneous edge-AI processor integrating neuromorphic cores, probabilistic computing units, photonic interconnects, and 2D materials integration. Currently in the behavioral simulation and literature synthesis phase. (GitHub: public repository with technical documentation)

Radio Telescope Control System (Hands-on hardware, mentored): Designed and deployed motor control electronics for a tracking system, integrating Raspberry Pi, relay circuits, and signal processing. This project taught me embedded systems rigor, and debugging hardware requires precision that software often forgives.

IoT Low-Power Monitoring (Independent project): Built power-optimized sensor nodes using Arduino, implemented sleep scheduling, and profiled energy consumption. Directly relevant to the edge AI constraints I want to solve.

Academic Coursework Demonstrating Research Readiness:

Calculus I-III, Linear Algebra (Spring 2026), Physics I-II with labs

Undergraduate Research Project (STEC 4500, Spring 2026): Currently active, self-directed research component

Dean's List: Fall 2024, Spring 2025, Fall 2025 | GPA: 3.87 (trending to 3.90+)

What This Shows: I don't treat research as an abstract exercise. I've initiated multi-month projects, debugged real hardware failures, and integrated mathematics with engineering practice. SURF would accelerate this trajectory by placing me under expert mentorship in a resource-rich environment.
Obstacle 1: Limited Institutional Resources at GGC
My college doesn't have a fabrication lab, advanced semiconductor equipment, or faculty specializing in neuromorphic computing. How I addressed it: I leveraged open-source tools (PyTorch for simulation and SKiDL for circuit design), engaged with online research communities, and designed OmniAI in software first, a strategy that forced deeper theoretical understanding. This resourcefulness will serve me well in demanding research environments.

Obstacle 2: Bridging Theory Gaps (Self-Taught Physics)
I came to physics late and needed to rapidly acquire solid-state physics fundamentals for semiconductor work. How I addressed it: I systematically completed Physics I & II coursework, supplemented with MIT OpenCourseWare, and focused on physical intuition before mathematical formalism. This self-directed learning has made me comfortable teaching myself new domains, essential for research.

Obstacle 3: Keeping OmniAI Grounded in Feasibility
Early versions of my chip concept were overly ambitious. How I addressed it: I read fabrication papers, studied published p-bit designs, and constrained v1.2 to integrate only technologies at TRL 6-7 (lab-proven, not purely speculative). This taught me that innovation requires both vision and realism, exactly the mindset strong researchers cultivate.

Gain hands-on facility experience using Purdue's CAD tools (Cadence, Synopsys), cleanroom access (if available), or measurement equipment that I cannot access elsewhere.

Strengthen my transfer and graduate applications; SURF completion and publication proof demonstrate I can operate independently in a research environment, a threshold many T20 PhD programs now expect from undergraduates.

I'm applying to SURF not to check a box on a resume, but because the research environment you provide directly enables the innovation I want to pursue. The intersection of neuromorphic computing, photonics, and stochastic systems is where the next decade of hardware breakthroughs will happen. I want to be part of that work, and SURF is the exact catalyst my trajectory needs right now.

I am fully committed to making meaningful contributions to whatever research group I join. My track record shows I work independently, think rigorously, and persist through challenges. I'm ready to bring that energy and intellectual honesty to Purdue this summer.

statement_of_purpose:
Every single cell in your body once looked the same. They were totipotent stem cells. They eventually received differentiation signals, and many went off to become uniquely adapted for specific functions. Learning about cells always seemed incredible because they begin unpredictably. You won’t know what will happen to them until you can see it with your own eyes. That is why learning about cell health always fascinated me – the mystery.
Near the beginning of this school year, I started research in Dr. Kim’s lab. At first, every cell looked like a random blob, and I couldn’t tell how much longer they needed to grow or when to change the type of media. Then, I got used to them. I learned what they looked like as they grew up and when it was time to start differentiation. I knew when they’d turned immature from too little water in the incubator versus grown and healthy. Eventually, I became more comfortable knowing my cells, and research put me in a nice flow state. Perhaps it is because I feel relaxed with the cells, and I am improving in deciding what they need and when in order to grow. 
Aside from just growing them, seeing results has been my favorite part. After treatment and measuring, the difference between the control and treatment was so strong. It showed that all our work truly meant something and might be contributing something meaningful to the scientific world. I enjoyed creating my presentation because I got to look into what might have caused the difference between the control and the treatment groups, and while we won’t know whether my theories were accurate yet, the results helped lead us to deeper questions and new experiment ideas.
Research has also made what I learn in the classroom more interesting. When my biology professor mentioned PFAs, I began to wonder how they would affect my research cells and what would happen if we used PFAs as a treatment. I read previous research on PFA effects on cells, where I saw the images of how it increases the cross-links between them. Thinking about my own research cells made the classroom information more real and visual. 
Aside from being pre-med, I’m also studying food science. Food science is about creating what our cells will consume in order to improve their health. We eat about a credit card’s worth of plastic every year, and trying to minimize the plastics and other harmful chemicals in our food such as PFAs seems like a difficult, important, and exciting challenge.
Environmental exposure, nutrition, and improving cell health make me want to keep learning and understanding how we are affected by specific chemicals and what could be done to improve the quality of life.
One thing I’ve learned about research is that it isn’t all fun. It requires a ton of patience. Once, we found a result that we were not sure how to explain. Our treatment had increased the diameter of the muscle cells, but why? What caused this? In order to get closer to understanding this, we had to come up with a new question: what part of the treatment causes the growth? To start, we fractioned the treatment into different parts and have been working on treating the cells with each part. The problem with that is that there are so many different compounds in the treatment, and we have only started making about six of them at a time. Though it will take a long time, we must still keep going and doing a little more every day, taking it one step at a time. We may not test every single compound from the treatment, but we aim to find which ones generally cause the growth. This would be able to help us make a new research question to further determine why it has that effect on the cells. While research can be tedious and frustrating sometimes, especially when you have to discard an entire 12 well-plate after making a mistake, the challenge makes the results all the more satisfying, which makes me want to continue doing research this summer.
	When I was looking for summer research, the SURF program stood out to me because it was more than just a regular research program. It has workshops to help with communication skills, which is a skill I’m specifically trying to improve. When I was interviewing for a job a few summers ago, the interviewer told me one important skill is learning to communicate with different people. When deciding to hire someone with better skills but worse communication, he told me he had chosen the person with better communication skills. I think it’s important to be able to effectively present scientific research, and having weekly workshops and a graduate student mentor to talk to would really help me. 
The graduate student I currently work with at Purdue has helped me learn so much and has helped make me more comfortable in the lab. If the SURF program graduate mentor is anything like him, I know it will make the experience really fun and useful.
He has told me a lot about graduate school and what it is like, and one thing I’m strongly considering is going to graduate school to continue studying cells and how certain foods can be used to improve muscle growth. While the specific topic I would like to study is not set in stone, I want to go to graduate school because of him. He gets to spend the majority of his time working in the lab with mice conducting research. I would like to study something related to cell biology or food science.
With the strong mentorship and help in improving presentation skills, SURF could really help me strengthen my abilities for the future going into graduate school. It also provides connections with research professors, graduate students, and other fellow students you get to work alongside. Maybe the research professor would look to me to work for them as a graduate student in the future, as well.
SURF will also help me learn what other types of research I may enjoy and build critical thinking skills in relation to cells and the lab, as well as more independence and confidence when conducting experiments.

statement_of_purpose:
My interest in artificial intelligence developed through working with systems that appeared to function correctly but behaved unpredictably in practice. Early projects I worked on produced outputs that looked plausible, yet failed when context shifted slightly, inputs were noisy, or tasks required consistency over time. Debugging these failures made me more interested in understanding how AI systems behave once they are embedded into real workflows, rather than improving isolated performance metrics. That focus has guided my academic and research direction since.

I am a final-year undergraduate majoring in Computer Science (Big Data and Artificial Intelligence) at the University of Wollongong. My coursework provided training in machine learning, algorithms, data systems, and software engineering, but my research interests developed primarily through applied projects and independent study. I became increasingly interested in how AI systems operate autonomously, process language over time, and interact with human decision-making. This places my work at the intersection of AI systems and natural language processing which aligns closely with the projects I am applying to through Purdue SURF.

My main research experience comes from an IEEE-accepted project on livestream transcript highlight detection. I built and evaluated NLP pipelines on real-time, multi-speaker conversational data, where interruptions, topic shifts, and fragmented context were common. Instead of relying on a single performance score, I analyzed how speaker changes, timing differences, and topic transitions affected model outputs. I found that models with similar aggregate metrics often behaved differently under minor distribution shifts. This project clarified my interest in studying reliability and failure behavior rather than peak accuracy alone. Presenting this work at an international IEEE conference reinforced my intention to pursue research training focused on evaluation and system behavior.

I extended this approach during my internship at InspAIre (Amsterdam), where I worked on agentic AI workflows designed to autonomously complete multi-step tasks using retrieval-augmented generation, structured prompting, and tool calling. While these systems frequently completed tasks quickly, they also exhibited repeatable failure patterns, including hallucinated intermediate steps and error propagation across workflow stages. I developed Python-based evaluation scripts to compare AI-driven task execution against expected outcomes and manual baselines. This experience gave me practical exposure to the challenges of designing autonomous workflows that must remain stable across repeated use.

These experiences directly motivate my interest in the project “Expanding and Evaluating Autonomous Scientific Workflows on nanoHUB.” While many summer programs focus on short-term experimentation, SURF emphasizes sustained research within established platforms such as nanoHUB, where design decisions have long-term consequences. I am particularly interested in examining how workflow structure influences robustness and reproducibility in AURA-powered systems. My background in defining structured inputs, evaluating autonomous execution, and comparing AI-driven workflows with human baselines would allow me to contribute productively to this work.

In parallel with systems-focused research, I have developed a strong interest in language and cognition. During my undergraduate research internship at Sabancı University Istanbil, where I was selected among the top 2% of applicants for the Turkish government’s YTB AI scholarship, I worked with instructional language datasets and examined how AI systems interpret pedagogical content. The STEMI alert pierced through the hallway, and I sprinted to the ER Room 8. Nine clinicians surrounded the patient, with a surgeon on standby in case things collapsed. As an EMT, I stepped in to perform CPR multiple times while the room pulsated with urgency. I was scared not because it was my first time, but because, for a moment, I found myself caught up in a trance, reminiscing about how my grandmother's situation would have changed if she had access to a room like this, providers like these, and a chance like this.

They say the heartbeat is the most common miracle, but not until this miracle no longer holds for your beloved. My journey to cardiovascular science began with the demise of my grandmother due to a treatable cardiac arrest. The only clinic in such a health desert was not equipped with cardiac and respiratory devices or services to treat such emergencies. The silence following her demise was more than grief; it was a realization of a harsh truth: where you live determines the chances of survival. From that moment, my thoughts constantly drifted to the same question that guides me to this day: why do some lives slip away not because medicine cannot help, but because it never arrives?

I grew up in a Ghanaian community where hypertension, stroke, and heart failure were very rampant, claiming several lives, often without diagnosis. But I refused to accept this situation as inevitable, as I sought to understand these threats at their roots. Through my role as a health assistant with the non-profit Starlight Foundation, I helped organize health education programs, sanitation exercises, and health interventions through mobile clinics. These initiatives impacted over 1000 lives. Each encounter reinforced my conviction, which I now carry into research: healthcare must be both scientifically precise and accessible to areas that need it most.

Today, I am an undergraduate, studying biochemistry and data science at a private liberal arts institution in northwest Pennsylvania—Allegheny College. My interest in science is driven by the same question that haunted me as I stood beside my grandmother years ago: How can we build cardiovascular interventions that are safe, effective, and equitably delivered to every patient—no matter where they live?  My academic curiosity and community-driven approach have been recognized through a nomination from Mario Capecchi, Nobel Prize Laureate in Medicine, for the 2025 Congress of Future Medical Leaders Award of Excellence. This award reflects my outstanding academic performance, leadership potential, and sustained commitment to serving humanity in the field of medicine. Doing scientific research that can have a positive human impact gives me purpose! This commitment to impact-driven science is why I am interested in the Purdue SURF program, as it provides me with the ideal opportunity for this kind of service through its exposure to cutting-edge research, hands-on laboratory experience, and built-in mentorship.  

I want to be a part of the Purdue SURF program because it will give me the opportunity to learn how to predict, prevent, and respond to cardiac failures long before they become fatal through innovative experimental techniques and built-in mentorship. Purdue’s strengths in cardiovascular physiology, biomedical imaging, and data-driven analysis align closely with how I approach science. Particularly, I am drawn to research avenues that investigate how heat-based therapeutic strategies influence microvascular blood flow and tissue oxygenation in conditions such as diabetes and peripheral artery disease. Also, I am intrigued by works that apply imaging and computational modeling to predict cardiac dysfunction before irreversible decline occurs. These approaches reflect the kind of translational cardiovascular research I hope to pursue, where physiological measurement, data analysis, and clinical relevance are interrelated.  SURF offers the opportunity to move beyond executing predefined protocols toward defining questions, troubleshooting experiments, and learning how research evolves through iteration.

In my inquiry-based laboratory class under my biology professor, Dr. Bradley Hersh, I used zebrafish to investigate how ethanol exposure affects embryonic development, particularly the formation of pericardial edema. Experimenting with this model has taught me how micro-molecular disruptions can lead to dramatic cardiac defects during early development. This work has drawn me toward questions of how early anatomical variation predicts long-term cardiac risk. Professor Goergen’s research on predictive modeling of aortic root dilation directly reflects this interest, combining cardiovascular physiology with computational analysis. I am more excited to build skills in echocardiographic data preprocessing, feature extraction, and predictive modeling using Python, translating biological insight into clinically actionable forecasts. 

Revolutionizing the healthcare landscape in underserved communities requires systemic change, which requires complex and specialized knowledge. This is what has motivated me to pursue higher education to train as a cardiothoracic surgeon and researcher. I’m not just seeking a degree; I’m acquiring tools to rewrite the narrative of healthcare access in vulnerable communities. Within the first 5 to 7 years after completing my graduate studies and residency, I plan to return to Ghana and collaborate with the Ministry of Health and various NGOs to develop and provide life-saving technologies, including artificial hearts, utilizing AI and machine learning. Such devices of the future would provide hope to countless heart failure patients who might otherwise wait indefinitely for suitable donors. By bridging this technological gap, especially in the Global South, we can improve survival and patient outcomes.

My long-term plan is to establish sustainable heart and lung transplant programs in underserved areas of the world through partnership with colleagues in the medical field. This initiative would involve fixing gaps in the medical services infrastructure in impoverished regions, training and adequately supplying local medical teams to handle prevalent health challenges, and using accessible digital interfaces, such as telemedicine and fully equipped surgical medical vans, to make complex cardiac care accessible and affordable. I want to establish a network of cardiac care centers in rural communities that are equipped with modern technology and staffed by highly trained medical volunteers. This approach will save lives and enhance healthcare capacity in the regions that need it most. Every academic pursuit and every volunteer assignment I undertake brings me one step closer to reinventing the healthcare landscape for communities in need.  

A single heartbeat can determine the future of a family, a community, or even a nation. I hope that the Purdue SURF internship will provide me with more tools and resources to help protect those heartbeats, especially in places where medical miracles are needed the most but seen the least. This program is more than simply a research opportunity; it’s an investment in bridging healthcare disparities in marginalized regions. I hope you will see me as a human investment that will yield great returns that can transform and heal communities in need. With your support, we can be the difference, quite literally, between life and death.

Currently, these reactions require expensive catalysts and waste a significant amount of the light energy. By the time doctors identified her condition, which could have been caught through proper diagnostic imaging years earlier, we faced months of fear, uncertainty, and desperate struggle for her survival. Millions of families endure similar preventable tragedies. Witnessing this crisis convinced me to dedicate my career to developing interpretable biomedical AI systems that clinicians can trust for early disease detection, combining computer vision with mathematical optimization and medical domain knowledge to build solutions grounded in anatomical reality rather than black-box pattern recognition relying on blind statistical correlation.
Recognizing that biomedical computer vision's most challenging problems demand both rigorous optimization theory and architectural innovation, I structured my academic path around Mathematics and Applied Mathematics with an intensive machine learning focus. My preparation began with building mathematical foundations through graduate-level Partial Differential Equations and Advanced Linear Algebra courses, which taught me to formulate vision problems as rigorous optimization objectives. Introduction to Biomedical Imaging provided hands-on experience with histogram equalization, image reconstruction, artifact suppression, Laplacian and Sobel filtering, X-Ray/CT/MRI analysis, and frequency-domain denoising—classical techniques essential when neural networks alone cannot compensate for fundamental data quality limitations. Machine Learning and Survey of Probability and Statistics strengthened my understanding of statistical inference and model architectures, complemented by a top 13.5% national performance in the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition demonstrating my ability to solve unconventional mathematical problems under pressure. This combination of theoretical rigor and practical image processing prepared me to approach computer vision as principled mathematical modeling of physical imaging systems rather than pure pattern recognition.
Applying this foundation to scientific imaging, I worked with Senior Scientist Tom J. Greenwald at UW-Madison's Space Science and Engineering Center on 8× thermal satellite super-resolution without ground truth data—a constraint structurally identical to medical imaging, where high-resolution labels are often unavailable. Working autonomously, I formulated a semi-supervised learning approach: generating 300,000+ synthetic degraded-to-original pairs through maxpool downsampling with self-designed thermal-specific noise patterns modeling AMSR2 radiometer physics, then implementing Zero-Shot Super-Resolution with spatial attention to create 10,000+ pseudo-enhanced targets for transfer learning. I designed domain-adapted loss functions balancing pixel accuracy, edge-preserving gradients through Laplacian filtering, and high-frequency detail preservation via unsharp masking, while incorporating penalty terms that rejected physically implausible temperature gradients and enforced mean conservation. To preserve high-level details not only in 2× enhancement, on which models were trained due to lack of training data, but throughout the cascaded 8× approach, I developed a hybrid architecture combining SwinIR's transformer capabilities for fine detail retention with a pretrained Real-ESRGAN discriminator, achieving realistic, high-contrast outputs. This work demonstrated that integrating physical laws directly into both degradation modeling and loss function design, rather than relying solely on architectural modifications, produces physically consistent image reconstructions while preserving computational efficiency. I plan to carry this principle into medical imaging by incorporating anatomical constraints throughout the reconstruction pipeline.
Beyond computer vision, I applied mathematical optimization to algorithm development in algebraic topology through work on knot unification at the Bard Summer Research Institute. Rather than optimizing the existing unification algorithm through incremental computational improvements, I approached the problem by simplifying its underlying mathematical representation. By proving four combinatorial theorems that established structure-based solvability criteria, I incorporated these insights directly into the algorithm, allowing it to identify and exploit problem structure automatically. This reduced the undefined solution space and achieved a 30%+ runtime improvement through mathematical pattern recognition embedded in the algorithm itself. This methodology—optimizing computational systems by encoding domain-specific mathematical knowledge into their design—translates directly to biomedical imaging, where embedding anatomical and physiological constraints into model architectures improves both efficiency and clinical interpretability.
Currently at Stony Brook’s Computer Vision Lab, I am gaining hands-on experience with medical imaging data while developing U-Net architectures for subcellular organelle segmentation in volumetric ZEISS microscopy. I am exploring different architectural components, including ResNet skip connections and CBAM modules, to better understand which configurations capture fine morphological details most effectively. Similarly, when engineering data augmentation pipelines to expand the training set, I am learning to design transformations that preserve biological realism, such as volumetric rotations and flips that maintain membrane continuity and geometric consistency, rather than applying generic computer vision augmentations indiscriminately. Through this work, I am developing an understanding of how domain-aware model design leads to more accurate and interpretable results in biomedical applications.

The emphasis on extracting quantitative features from cine loops and diameter tracings directly leverages my experience with histogram equalization, edge-preserving filters, and domain-specific preprocessing for cleaning complex imaging datasets. My work designing physics-constrained approaches translates naturally to developing feature extraction pipelines that respect cardiovascular physiology, while my Python experience developing supervised learning models and analyzing sequential imaging data positions me to contribute to baseline model development and performance evaluation. Beyond the technical alignment, the project's clinical focus on improving diagnostic decisions for children with connective tissue disorders resonates deeply with my motivation to build systems that prevent delayed diagnoses. Working with Professor Bilionis would provide invaluable mentorship, as his research on physics-informed neural networks, Bayesian reconstruction methods, and information field theory directly addresses theoretical challenges I encountered when generating synthetic training data for satellite enhancement. His publications on scalable Bayesian cardiovascular hemodynamics reconstruction and neural information field filters offer sophisticated mathematical frameworks for uncertainty quantification that I am eager to master. My experience developing hybrid transformer-GAN architectures and designing domain-adapted loss functions that enforce physical constraints positions me to contribute immediately to the deep learning reconstruction pipeline, particularly in formulating physics-informed loss terms that reject physiologically implausible flow patterns and incorporating GAN components that produce more realistic, visually plausible reconstructions.
