My interest in computers began early. In 2nd grade, I was introduced to code.org during our computer labs. The platform used games themed around Star Wars and Frozen to teach coding through block-based programming. It may seem insignificant, but it was enough to get a 7-year-old hooked on the logic and creativity behind coding. 

My father played a crucial role in fuelling this interest. Most of our dinner table conversations revolved around his work using IBM Watson, an AI platform that analyses large datasets and processes human language to cater to client requests. He was working on implementing a medical use case where Watson would speed up the process of analyzing neuro scans and incorporate a wide spectrum of brain parameters to improve the prediction of neurological disorders. I didn’t fully understand it at that time, but I was in awe of what AI could do. 

A few years later, my younger brother was born prematurely and had to stay in NICU. It was a stressful time for my family. My parents would leave at 6 in the morning and would return after 12 at night. 

Being the tiniest baby in the NICU, his chances of survival were slim. Every time we saw a baby die due to undetected brain swelling, untimely treated infection, our family became even more anxious. Early detection of infections and complications were entirely dependent on the doctor’s knowledge base: limited and prone to delays. 

Years later, while researching my review paper on AI, I came across an article my father wrote about that experience, where he suggested using AI to refine the analysis of medical scans and improve diagnosis. This made me wonder; what if AI could catch subtle signs of complications earlier? Could machine learning models trained on more extensive datasets improve survival rates and treatment outcomes? These questions made me curious to explore AI’s role in healthcare, particularly in improving medical diagnostics and drug discovery. 

In college, I started exploring AI and machine learning through both coursework and independent projects. I began with basic Python and built a picture description app that converts images to text. Later, I learned about computer vision libraries like face recognition and encoding, which led me to build a face recognition-based attendance recorder as a personal project.  

My experience with research began during a summer school in India, where I published a review Journal paper covering different challenges, types, definitions of AI in an UGC-approved journal. For that paper, I reviewed over 20 academic papers, learned citation styles, worked with Google Scholar, and became proficient in LaTeX for writing and formatting.  

In Fall 2025, I had my first formal research experience under vertically Integrated Projects at Purdue. I was part of the “AI use for disaster response” research team. Our team was responsible for building a two-stage classification pipeline trained over 100K+ tweets that could categories tweets over social media into different humanitarian categories such as infrastructure damage, casualties, etc, which could be used for resource allocation.  

I was responsible for building and training the first stage (a neural network) using Keras and different training and data augmentation methods (SMOTE) which isolated the informative tweets from non-informative ones. This ensured a decreased and more accurate input load for the stage two model. The stage two model (a softmax regression model) was responsible for classifying the informative tweets into different human categories. This research experience taught me about the math behind machine learning models, the architecture of neural networks, and team collaboration. We were able to present our work at the Fall 2025 Undergraduate research expo, which was indeed a surreal experience. 

In Spring 2026, I will be involved in another VIP project named AI for Education that is currently investigating the broad potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Ollama in education, ranging from AI chatbot tutor to adaptive learning systems, intelligent content creation, and automated assessment. Most of my coursework taken to this date revolves around data engineering, Data Science Statistics, Data Structures and Algorithms. 

Apart from my research experience, I also work on personal projects and certifications in my free time to explore more about RAG, LLMs, Agentic AI, and automation tools like n8n. Some projects include a Memory augmented knowledge Agent that uses a RAG pipeline to read PDFs and answer questions contextually. 

Adapting college life at Purdue was challenging. Coming from a competitive environment, I was used to performing at my best. However, the fast pace of coursework, constant deadlines, and midterms left me overwhelmed. I remember blacking out once due to exhaustion and stress. It took time to adjust, but talking to my professors and advisors helped me. Dr. Jeffrey Turkstra, my CS 240 professor, compared learning programming to learning to play the piano, frustrating at first, but eventually rewarding with enough practice. This advice helped shift my perspective. I started managing my workload better by setting realistic to-do lists and balancing my technical courses with gen-eds to avoid burnout. 

My long-term goal is to combine AI with healthcare to develop innovative solutions in medical diagnostics and drug discovery.  

After completing my BS in computer science, I plan to pursue an MS in Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence. I want to devote my time building a healthcare startup that focuses on AI driven solutions for analysing large amounts of patient data, early diagnosis and prevention, and drug discovery. There are several companies that are already doing this for example companies like Atomwise uses AI to screen billions of molecules to develop potential drugs for Parkinson's and Multiple sclerosis. 

As a Purdue student, Purdue's Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) is exactly the best option for this. No hassles for relocating, a resourceful alumni network with graduate students, faculty mentors, and industry collaborators,  Purdue's affiliation with pharmaceutical companies and health institutions can open a window of opportunity for future research grants or internships and the fact that Purdue is one of the best institutions in the states for research makes this program extremely valuable for my career and learning journey.  

I am particularly interested in predictive modeling of patient outcomes, ML model training on medical images, and NLP model development for patient-physician communication. SURF will enable me to enhance my technical capabilities on actual datasets and learn through algorithm design, data analysis with Python, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, and inter-disciplinary research collaboration with medical researchers and data scientists.  

SURF is more than just a research opportunity: it’s a direct path toward the career I envision, using AI to solve real-world problems in healthcare.

I am an AAE sophomore at Purdue, currently looking at either Astrodynamics and Space Applications or Propulsion as my specialization in the future. My passion for space was solidified in high school. I was a member of the astronomy club, and one night we got the perfect conditions for observing the planets. I looked through the Newtonian telescope and saw a crystal clear image of Saturn, the air was so still that I could almost see every division in the rings and the details of the atmosphere. Since then, my mind has been set on the dream of contributing to space exploration.

As of now, I’ve identified two areas of interest to me: improving propulsion efficiency beyond current chemical rocketry limits, and the design of complex trajectories and transfer windows for deep-space missions. Chemical rocketry appears to have plateaued in terms of efficiency, which presents a major limitation for long-duration and deep-space exploration. I am interested in contributing to research that addresses these limitations. In addition, the way mission designers plan gravity assists for deep-space probes such as the Voyager missions and New Horizons particularly fascinates me, and I would be interested in research related to trajectory optimization and mission design. These two areas are just a preliminary target, however, as one of the main reasons I’m joining SURF is also to refine my career interests. With further exploration and involvement in the aerospace field, like the SURF research opportunity, I’m sure that I would discover more topics of interest.

	The SURF program is particularly attractive to me because it offers hands-on, mentored research experience in an environment similar to graduate-level research while being accessible to undergraduate students. I hope to gain research experience through the SURF, as I plan to pursue at least a master's degree in Aerospace Engineering after Purdue. Working closely with a professor and fellow researchers would allow me to learn how research is conducted on a day-to-day basis while also building academic connections. These connections can open up opportunities both at Purdue, like continuing the research under the professor, and help with my career network in the future. In the long term, I aim to make an impactful career in the aerospace field to contribute to space exploration. Graduate school can better prepare me for an impactful career, and SURF can prepare me to be a stronger applicant for graduate school.

	While SURF would be my first experience in a professional research environment, I have gained relevant experience during my three semesters at Purdue. I have been a member of PSP Hybrids since my first semester and have completed two projects during this time. The first was a gas K-bottle stand, and the second was the design of a quick disconnect system for our newest rocket, Spectre. Through these projects, I gained hands-on experience with aluminum rail assembly, load cells, fittings and plumbing, 3D printing assembly, and 3D modeling. Continuing that, I have finished the NX 3D modeling course of MFET 163, which I took early specifically to be able to contribute to club projects, and I am now confident with NX CAD modeling.

	For specific aero courses, I have finished AAE 204, which mainly covers mechanics of materials and structures. While the workload was heavy, I learned quite a lot through this class, specifically through the 2 projects that we had to do by ourselves. The first one was a Truss design for a rocket recovery system, like the chopsticks for SpaceX. While this one mainly consisted of traditional hand calculations, I did learn some useful report-writing skills and performing trade studies. The second project was more interesting and complex. It, too, involved a truss design but now for an aircraft wing (like the Boeing Truss-braced wing). However, it also involved a criterion for weight and geometry optimization. Since hand calculations are suboptimal for trying out different geometries, I developed a MATLAB program that progressively solved for the truss internal forces and needed member sizes and weights for an arbitrary geometry. While the math by hand is relatively simple conceptually, there were difficulties with writing the solver, specifically with solving for variables and computational performance. I used the symbolic math toolbox and parallel computing add-on in order to solve these issues, features that were not covered in my previous MATLAB course, so I worked through the MATLAB documentation and other online resources in order to implement them.  With this, it was simple to run each wing geometry through the program to see which is optimal. The final geometry was as much as 3x lighter than an unoptimized geometry (250kg vs 750kg). While the time constraint, being less than a week, limited further refinement of the script, I am proud of both the results and the problem-solving process. This project closely resembled an open-ended research/design problem, requiring independent learning, iteration, and optimization with respect to criteria.

	In addition, another course I’d like to highlight is AAE 251, where we learned introductory aerodynamics, orbits, and aircraft design. My team worked on the aircraft project, where we designed a piston-prop racer aircraft from the ground up. I focused on the technical aspects of design through the semester, with calculations like the range, parasitic air drag, and engine power requirements. I also handled the final modeling of our designed aircraft, during which I had to learn new tools like draft along mesh and importing photos for sketching to model the complex geometry of the fuselage, mainly through online resources. I also approached the instructors many times to confirm the specific requirements for the project. We presented our aircraft in a video themed like a mock guest lecture, with the filming being directed by me, and it was noted by the instructor as “one of the best” he’s seen. (Also as “one of the most entertaining, likely because we plugged in some visual gags related to the topic at hand) Although I initially hoped to work on the rocket project, the aircraft project ultimately proved to be a valuable experience and produced results that exceeded both me and my team’s expectations.

	To summarize, I hope to gain research experience that would help me both in graduate school and in industry through SURF. I have been interested in space since junior high, and have consistently tried to explore the field through club work and coursework. I have a foundation in theoretical knowledge through coursework and gained hands-on experience and mechanical intuition through club participation. I have maintained strong academic performance at Purdue and am excited and prepared to contribute to a SURF research project.

My interest in electromagnetics started with experiences in flight simulation, where I had to learn the operation of, and therefore some of the engineering behind, pulse-Doppler radar. The idea of using time-of-flight calculations and purely electronic beamsteering to locate objects in the sky captivated me and gave me a glimpse into the power of electromagnetic wave theory. Additionally, learning about electricity and magnetism in my high school AP Physics course allowed me to appreciate how fundamental and fascinating electrodynamics is. My more recent fascination with optical-wavelength electromagnetics has been due to recent developments in related technologies. Additionally, I’ve come to appreciate the applications of photonics in computation. As the increase of computational power by scaling down transistors in traditional silicon chips slows down, other computing paradigms such as photonic computing are promising for the future of high-speed computation. Photonic computation allows for light-speed data transfer, significantly reduced heat dissipation, and lower susceptibility to electromagnetic interference. Photonics is also used in photonic quantum computing, which is an application of the devices I am doing research on currently. In general, I am interested in the broad applications of infrared-optical photonic engineering, as I believe it has a bright future in many different fields.

Be it through making new discoveries in an academic position or making use of these discoveries through a position in industry, my ultimate goal in life is to be able to make a dent in this world. The Purdue SURF program will act as a strong step toward achieving a PhD, and will get my foot in the door for applying to Purdue’s graduate program. This will grant me valuable insight regarding the state of the cutting edge of my area of interest. To explore my fascination with applied electromagnetics, I’ve participated in internship and research experiences. statement_of_purpose:
“What do you think the difference is between research and class work?” The question made me pause and my research mentor, Professor Peter Moeck turned to face me as we both came to a stop in the hallway. Seeing the thoughts bumping together but unable to form a complete answer in my eyes, he prompted me again, “just compare them.” I responded that, to me, research revealed what learning can truly be outside the classroom. I discovered how fulfilling it was to dedicate myself to a subject purely driven by passion. Research presented the unique thrill of acquiring and applying new knowledge immediately. 

That conversation happened midway through my first research experience under Professor Peter Moeck in Portland State University's Nanocrystallography Group—at a moment when I was beginning to understand the answer myself. There, I wrote a piece of scientific software, titled Histropy that can be used to differentiate between symmetries and pseudosymmetries in noisy 2D periodic images using crystallographic image processing techniques. Applying linear algebra and group theory concepts from my coursework to real-world problems and studying the information-theory-based classifications of crystallographic images, I discovered how much knowledge could be discovered about the crystal depicted in a photo simply from the distribution of pixel values. This work culminated in a paper on the Histropy program I developed, which was published on arXiv. This experience sparked my interest in condensed matter physics and the desire to pursue a career in research. 

That interest in condensed matter led me to pursue an REU at Purdue University last summer, where I worked in Professor Tiancong Zhu's lab on expanding Twistronics to wafer scale 2D films. The transition from computational crystallography to experimental 2D materials felt natural since both involved understanding the effect of structure on properties. I began by learning scotch tape exfoliation for graphene and hBN. While going through all my exfoliations under the optical microscope, I was keeping track of metrics, like the flake dimensions, on paper and then one by one moving them to a slideshow and spreadsheet. Noticing this massive inefficiency, I used the google service API and coded an interface in python that allowed me and my labmates to enter the information in one place as we used the microscope and have the slideshow and spreadsheet be created simultaneously, making it easier to track and view exfoliated flakes. 

My initial project involved characterizing materials with a Scanning Tunneling Microscope, but delays to the instrument’s arrival meant that plan wouldn’t work. Faced with the need to pivot, Professor Zhu presented me with two options: construct heterostructure stacks without characterizing them, or build a machine to peel MBE films from their substrates. I realized these two projects addressed complementary limitations in 2D materials research. Heterostructures built from exfoliated flakes are constrained by the small size of those flakes, while Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) can produce high-quality thin films at larger scales but makes those films difficult to manipulate since they're firmly attached to their growth substrate. Rather than choose one approach, I decided to pursue both—learning to build heterostructures from small flakes while simultaneously developing tools to work with wafer-scale films. I was willing to put in extra hours to make this possible because I wanted to use my limited time for broad exploration while still delivering tangible results.

With that dual focus in mind, I learned to stack graphene and hBN heterostructures as well as “Magic Angle” Twisted Bilayer Graphene (MATBG) under the supervision of my labmates. At the same time, I modeled the MBE film machine in Solidworks but my initial designs suffered from overcomplicated mechanisms. It took several iterations for me to be able to effectively alter a design based on feedback about limitations of the overall design rather than issues with specific elements. Upon reaching an effective design, I built the final machine with a combination of machined and 3D printed parts, and wrote software to allow for programmatic control. We were able to show that the machine created a very small angle when peeling the tape back, which is what we were looking for. At the end of this work, I gave a talk on the results of my work and its potential uses. I am continuing my work with the lab, this time on a project aimed at automating the process of identifying exfoliated flakes under an optical microscope. This experience gave me certainty about my path: I wanted to pursue research in experimental condensed matter physics.

My long-term goal is to pursue a Ph.D. in physics and conduct research in experimental/computational condensed matter physics and my previous work narrowed that research focus to 2D materials. Right now, the question I’m most interested in within that field is: “How does increasing the scale of constructed 2D heterostructures impact the observed properties as compared with their microscopic counterparts?” For example, one thing I want to study is how the observed superconductivity of twisted bilayer graphene changes at scale (this is exactly why my REU project focused on developing methods to create these larger samples). Purdue’s advanced facilities and instruments would give me essential experience with the scale and type of work that defines graduate-level experimental physics.

My REU experience allowed me to briefly work on several different things and right now I believe I would gain the most from diving deep into a specific project. SURF offers me the opportunity to do just that. The collaborative, curiosity-driven environment of Professor Zhu’s lab was exactly the kind of research culture where I knew I could thrive and the opportunity to return to that environment is something I find very enticing about SURF. The two projects I am most interested in, 'Epitaxial growth of wafer scale semiconductor thin films' and 'Fabrication of atomic clean 2D heterostructures,' directly address the limitations of my REU experience and since I no longer have that initial learning curve to overcome, I can now contribute meaningfully to these projects. Last summer I built a machine for MBE film work but never actually grew films myself; now I want to master that growth process and put my machine to use. Similarly, I fabricated simple stacks with supervision but never mastered the ability to produce high-quality heterostructures—a skill these projects would allow me to develop. Additionally, I really appreciate the program’s focus on building technical communication skills, such as creating and presenting scientific posters, as it is an area where I'm looking to grow.

Thank you for considering my application! I am eager to contribute to innovative research and take a significant step toward my goal of becoming a physicist and conducting impactful research in the future.

I’m a junior at Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology, majoring in Computer Science. My main interest is natural language processing and agent systems, especially in how models make decisions over multiple steps and how to make that behavior more reliable when tasks involve constraints or tool use. I love this area because it’s one of the few places where “it works” and “it works consistently” are two very different things, and the gap between them is usually where the research idea comes from.

My early research experiences have prepared me well for this role. Last summer was my first time working full-time in a research environment, and the first couple of weeks were rough. People used terms like “agent” and  “RAG”  as if everyone already knew them. I didn’t, and my instinct was to stay quiet until I caught up. What changed was that I stopped trying to hide it. I started asking my PhD mentor questions early instead of waiting until I “should” understand. We met frequently, and I had to show what I tried, what failed, and what we should plan to test next. In our check-ins, I walked him through concrete examples, what the agent saw, which tool it chose, and the exact step where things went off track. Therefore, once I started using papers to answer a specific question from our check-ins, reading papers went from intimidating to something I actually enjoyed.

Through the Summer Research Opportunities Program at Notre Dame’s DM2 Lab, I helped develop OpenTools, a collaborative multi-agent reasoning framework. In this project, I implemented a retrieval-augmented module for tool selection and built validation infrastructure so we could track whether individual tools were actually reliable. I also structured tool metadata to improve tool retrieval and expanded our tools library, making the agent’s decision-making more efficient and accurate. These improvements significantly boosted the system’s performance. More importantly, what I valued most wasn’t just the result; it was the workflow because the process taught me how to tackle complex problems in a methodical way. Working under Dr.  Jiang’s and my mentor’s guidance taught me how to push a system forward by iterating carefully: test, find the failure case, fix one part, and measure again.

In addition to my work with multi-agent systems, I explored applying machine learning to a different domain, like chemistry. I worked on an open-source Data Chemist Handbook that applies machine learning techniques to predict chemical reactions. I built and trained models to predict reaction outcomes and yields, achieving better accuracy on challenging reaction datasets compared to baseline models. I tested multiple model families, decision trees, feedforward networks, sequence-based models (RNNs), and graph-based models (GNNs), to understand trade-offs in representation, training stability, and implementation cost. Early on, when results were poor, I couldn’t tell if the issue was the model, the preprocessing, or the training setup. So I rewrote parts of the pipeline to change one factor at a time and track what actually moved the metric. Most iterations were small (learning rate, number of layers). That loop, reading the signal from loss/metrics, changing one thing, rerunning, taught me more about training behavior and architecture trade-offs than any single class. It also pushed me to explain ideas clearly; this handbook is now used for a summer program at Notre Dame for high school students, so I had to write in a way that’s accurate but still approachable.

Looking ahead, I plan to pursue graduate study in AI, focusing on reasoning models and agent systems. I grew up in Nepal, where boys were pushed toward big career goals while girls were often steered toward narrower options. My interest in computer science started when I watched my cousin build a working mobile app and technology suddenly felt reachable. Choosing this path was not simple when my father initially opposed it because of cultural expectations. After months of conversations, I earned his support, and I learned something that still guides me: talent cannot matter if people are discouraged before they even start.

After moving to the United States, that belief became personal. Three months after arriving, I was in an accident and later diagnosed with MODY 5 diabetes and atrophic kidney disease. Managing appointments, insurance, and daily care largely on my own showed me how easily people fall through gaps in monitoring and coordination. I had a smartphone full of sensors and apps, yet very little designed to warn me early or reduce risk at the moment it mattered. That experience changed how I define “useful” technology. In high-stakes settings, average performance isn’t reassuring if the failures happen in exactly the situations people face most.

Since then, my focus has narrowed to a few questions I can’t ignore: How can computer vision systems stay dependable when conditions change in ways the training set did not capture? How can we tell when a model is drifting or failing under distribution shift? When confidence is low, how can a system respond in a safer way instead of producing a quiet error?

To prepare for this work, I looked for projects where models break under messy conditions and where progress depends on understanding why. During a research experience with Stanford University, I built a convolutional neural network-based object detection pipeline to identify and measure crystals in lab images, reaching 90 percent detection accuracy in our evaluation and helping reduce the risk of damage to expensive detectors. The most meaningful part of the project was what happened after the first “good” result. Performance dropped on images with glare and uneven illumination, the kind of variation that is easy to miss until deployment. I treated these failures as the core problem. I grouped errors by lighting conditions and crystal size, then tested contrast-limited histogram equalization alongside targeted augmentation. To avoid improving only the easiest cases, I created a separate “hard” evaluation subset so we could track whether changes helped where reliability mattered most. That process reshaped how I judge ML systems: I don’t trust a single headline number until I have seen where the model breaks, what causes it, and whether the fix improves the hardest cases.

I continued building that mindset through other work. At Howard University, I analyzed student survey data to support improvements to the CS curriculum, which strengthened my ability to turn noisy data into clear findings. I also built a pedestrian alert prototype that detects walking patterns and warns users as they approach intersections while distracted. Testing made a safety lesson concrete: sensitivity alone does not make a tool helpful. Too many false alarms train users to ignore warnings, while missed detections create risk. I tuned thresholds to balance false positives and false negatives across varied user behavior, and I saw how “reliability” includes human response, not just model scores. 

Outside of projects, I mentor students adjusting to a new academic system as Vice President of the Howard University Nepalese Student Association and help organize programs that support women in tech through the Society of Women Engineers. Fortunately, he accepted me and let me join his research group in quantum optimal control. Here, I have learnt fundamental knowledge about superconducting quantum computing and the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gates (DRAG) method for quantum control, and we are working on the project that apply the DRAG method to build single qutrit gate for the transmon qubit.

At the summer of 2024, I had the opportunity to extend my study in the superconducting system by joining the research group of Prof. Qiming Shao at my home university and participating in the project of EDA for superconducting quantum computing. In the project, we studied quantization methods of superconducting circuits, and used Qiskit Metal to design and analyze some simple superconducting circuits. In addition, since the spring of 2025, I have started researching about another physical system of quantum information, which is nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond, under the supervision of Prof. Yang Sen at my home university. I have focused on studying the use of NV centers in sensing applications, as well as alternative color centers in diamond besides the NV, such as group IV color centers.

I also took a course in data science for neural engineering, in which I learnt about both neural engineering and machine learning, and developed a neural network model in python to guess the activity of rats from the neural data for my final project. Thus, I also have experience in python programming and machine learning that can be useful for my SURF project. 
This year, the SURF program at Purdue University offers several projects that are related to quantum science and technology. Among them, I found the projects in trapping cold neutral atoms on nanophotonics circuits hosted by Prof. Chen-Lung Hung is especially interesting, because it will introduce me to a new physical platform for quantum information processing that I have never had the chance to do research on before. Besides, the project on studying quantum properties of 2D materials and fabrication of atomic clean 2D heterostructures  hosted by Prof. Yihan Zeng and Prof. Tiancong Zhu also attracts me as they offer the opportunity to participate in fabrication and characterization of materials, which provides useful skills for my research interest and quantum properties that will be studied here can also harness scientific breakthroughs in quantum information science technology.

How can we make their decision-making process transparent and trustworthy?

For instance, the solutions from The Data Mine team mostly came from discussions with agricultural scientists. We needed to understand what they really needed for the final result so we did not go off track, rather than just talking to AI engineers.

I am fascinated by the transition of the hexagonal crystal lattice of Ice Ih as it absorbs latent heat from my surroundings. As I bite down, I am not just cooling off but also testing the fracture mechanics of a polycrystalline solid. The way the ice shatters depends entirely on its structural integrity. Based on personal preference, I design my perfect ice cubes from the rapid-frozen system (mainly household refrigerator) to have the formation of air bubbles or cloudy style ice design with a porous, softer matrix in the middle. This internal architecture allows for easier deformation than the rigid, transparent lattice of slow-frozen ice.

This daily ritual served as my earliest introduction to the relationship between microstructure and macroscopic properties. I began to see the world through the lens of phase diagrams and thermal conductivity, realizing that the same principles governing the "crunch" of an ice cube – the nucleation of voids and the propagation of cracks – are fundamental to polymer science. Whether it is enhancing the mechanical/chemical properties of a thin film or combining the use of porous materials, the ability to manipulate internal structure to achieve a specific mechanical response is what drives my passion for material science research.

During my undergraduate studies, I have actively engaged in Professor Wei Chen lab at my home institution – Mount Holyoke College. My research focuses on how polymer-substrate interactions dictate film stability and dewetting behavior, specifically polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) thin films on hydrophobic substrates. During a nine-week intensive in Summer 2025, I did the examination with PVP films on silane-modified surfaces, including the use of N-(2-aminoethyl)-3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (AEAPTES), Octyldimethylchlorosilane (C8), and N,N-Dimethyltrimethylsilylamine (TMS–NMe2). Also, I got used to running organic synthesis reactions to produce different structures of metal-organic frameworks, monomers purifying, and crystallization of materials.

The mentorship and rigorous environment of SURF will help me refine my research questions and prepare me for the challenges of graduate-level inquiry.

As I explored academic paths that would align with my interests, Pharmaceutical Science emerged as a great fit due to it being a combination of both molecular mechanisms and therapeutic applications. I am particularly motivated to apply the knowledge to the development of innovative cancer treatments, especially immunotherapy, where the body’s own immune system is enhanced to combat tumor cells.

The SURF program offers an immersive 11-week research experience that would significantly foster my growth as a future researcher. Through SURF, I would have access to expert mentorship from faculty and graduate students who specialize in cancer research, allowing me to expand my scientific knowledge and laboratory skill set. I am specifically interested in Professor Matosevic’s project that focuses on advancing immunotherapies targeting cancer and neurological disorders using immunoengineering. In addition, the program’s professional development seminars would expose me to the processes and various aspects of academic research, and the SURF symposium is a great platform where I can practice presenting my own findings and receive constructive feedback. Finally, the interdisciplinary academic environment in SURF is perfect for me to build meaningful connections with experts and peers in the field of cancer biology and pharmaceutical science. 

The research experience gained through SURF, specifically through Matosevic Lab’s project, would directly support my goal of pursuing a research career in developing innovative cancer therapies. Under the guidance of the mentors, I hope to acquire laboratory techniques, including gene-editing, tumor organoid system development, cell culture, and assays, as well as enhance my data analytical and visualization skills. In addition, I look forward to learning about the systematic process of how great research questions are formulated and how experiments are strategically designed to answer them. Given the opportunity to present at the SURF symposium, I can strengthen my ability to effectively communicate complex scientific findings. Together, all of the skills mentioned above are foundational preparations for my academic journey in the future, especially for my PhD application.

Although my prior research experience was not directly focused on immunotherapy in cancer, I have been actively expanding my biological and pharmaceutical foundation through the relevant coursework and hands-on lab experience. I am currently an undergraduate research assistant in Professor Qingfei Zheng’s chemical biology lab, where I shadow a graduate mentor on a project developing chemical probe to study cancer-related post-translation modifications. I have gained experience in setting up organic synthesis reactions, analyzing and purifying products using tools such as LC-MS, HPLC and NMR, and improving experimental workflow. Additionally, past and current coursework in immunology, biochemistry, microbiology, organic chemistry, and human anatomy and physiology have provided me with crucial biological and chemical foundations that are necessary to understand more complex disease and treatment mechanisms in cancer. I actively explored these different areas through my coursework, research experience, lab publications and conversations with my research PI and graduate mentors. The process of constant exploration and reflection clarified my interest in cancer, especially immunotherapy as it integrates both my interest in immunology and therapeutic development. With a clear academic path in mind, I am motivated and prepared to conduct in-depth research contributing to next-generation immunotherapies.

I am writing to express my strong interest in Purdue SURF Program. I am a third-year student at the University of South Florida studying physics and mathematics, and I plan to pursue a PhD in physics with interests in both theory and experiment.

I am drawn to physics because it forces me to think carefully about how abstract ideas meet the real world. While theory can be so elegant, my experience in research often drills in me the fact that physical systems rarely behave as cleanly as equations suggest. Learning how to navigate the gap between what should happen and what actually does has become my main motivation for pursuing physics.

My research experience so far has focused on magnetic nanoparticles for biosensing in Dr. Phan’s lab. Working in an experimental setting taught me how sensitive measurements can be to noise, material imperfections, and experimental limitations. Over time, this work made me increasingly curious about the physics underlying magnetic order itself. Topics such as magnetism, phase transitions, and symmetry currently excite me most, because they offer a deeper framework for understanding why materials behave the way they do. These are still discrete pieces of ideas in my mind, but what excites me most is that I know they must be very connected; I just can’t prove it yet. That is why I’m trying to dig in this direction.

One challenge that im starting to feel the weight now is limited access to coursework in condensed matter, solid-state physics, and computational physics at my home institution. A computational physics course I was especially excited about was canceled this semester due to low enrollment. As a result, most of my exposure has come through experimental work. This has motivated me to seek research-based learning opportunities like Purdue SURF, where close mentorship and immersion in active research can help me develop a more balanced understanding.

Purdue SURF appeals to me because its research opportunities closely align with these interests. I am particularly interested in Prof. Chen-Lung Hung’s work because trapping atoms on nanophotonic circuits provides a controllable system where I can explore ideas like magnetism, phase transitions, and symmetry in a quantum many-body setting. Working with him would give me a chance to see how the theory I’m interested in plays out in real experiments.

I am also drawn to synthesizing characterizing 2D materials, such as the work of Prof. Yihang Zeng and Prof. Tiancong Zhu. One of the things I am most excited to try is growing 2D samples. I have only seen 0D synthesis up close when our PhD student guided me to make iron oxide nanoparticles by thermal decomposition, and even that required so much control over temperature, timing, and atmosphere that it made me curious about how much more delicate 2D fabrication must be, where every atomic layer and interface determines the final properties.
By the start of the program, I will have completed coursework in quantum mechanics, electricity and magnetism, statistical physics, and several upper-level math courses, which will help me appreciate the theoretical side of the projects. Working in Dr. Phan’s lab has taught me how to handle delicate samples, operate complex equipment, and build intuition from noisy real-world data. I am also comfortable coding in Python and MATLAB, which I have used for data analysis and visualization. Utilizing these skills, I will contribute meaningfully to the research while learning as much as I can from my mentors. 

I plan to pursue a PhD in physics, and I see Purdue SURF as an important step toward that goal. Recently, when I attended the Conference on Magnetism and Magnetic Materials, I realized how much progress in the field relies on collaboration when people from different countries share techniques and approach the same problems with completely different scientific “instincts.” Thus, I want to experience a different academic culture, gain a clearer sense of what daily research looks like in a strong physics department, and test my interests through sustained, hands-on work. More broadly, I hope this experience will help me grow into a physicist who is comfortable working at the boundary between theory and experiment. 

Thank you very much for your consideration. I would be delighted to provide any additional information or answer questions.

statement_of_purpose:
My passion for computer science (CS) stems from the potential of the field to unlock value in various disciplines, especially with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML). I was first exposed to this breadth through a research project that applied ML to electroencephalography (EEG) data, where we explored the possibility of interpreting inner speech (internalized verbal communication) from neural signals. Although the project was specifically rooted in neuroscience, it highlighted the interdisciplinary nature of CS, as computational methods can be adapted to fundamentally different types of problems.
This experience reshaped how I view CS. I now see it as a way to engage with problems that lack clear formulations, rather than as a discipline focused solely on conventional software development. Therefore, I am eager to learn more about how ideas from AI and ML can impact various domains.

This is one of the main reasons I want to join SURF. The program offers a variety of projects that could not only enhance my CS skills but would also allow me to explore further interdisciplinary applications of AI/ML with real-world relevance, such as the project “Gradual Verification: Assuring Programs Incrementally.” A major reason for this is that it applies ML and large language models to a domain—program verification—that I have not previously worked in, yet is critical for building reliable software systems. Beyond the research itself, SURF’s seminars, collaborative environment, and close interaction with faculty and graduate students are especially valuable to me. I hope to build meaningful professional relationships through the program and to continue working in a research lab beyond the summer, whether on the same project or on related work. 
Whether in academia or in industry, my long-term career goals involve being a researcher with a specific focus on AI/ML. Because these methods are applicable across many domains, I see SURF as an ideal opportunity to broaden my exposure to interdisciplinary research while developing both my technical and soft skills. Thus, SURF promises to be instrumental in preparing me for such a career path.

I have explored my interest in AI/ML through a combination of interdisciplinary research projects and experiences mentored by Purdue faculty.
During my junior and senior years of high school, I worked on an interdisciplinary project focused on developing a computational model to advance brain–computer interface applications. We used EEG data from subjects who imagined one of four movement directions (left, right, up, or down) per trial (specifically, this imagination is called “inner speech”) to train an ML model to predict the intended direction. My role involved surveying prior research to identify effective classification and feature extraction techniques, then implementing these approaches on our dataset. Through this work, I gained experience building end-to-end ML pipelines in Python and working with signal processing (e.g., Discrete Fourier Transform) and modeling techniques (e.g., Support Vector Machines).
In addition to technical skills, this project significantly strengthened my ability to communicate research. The parent organization the project was under would host symposiums at the end of every term, so I got many opportunities to practice communicating our highly technical work with an audience who came from many different disciplines, not just STEM. Additionally, our project was selected to be presented at the International Brain Research Organization’s 2023 World Congress Conference, so I also had a chance to engage in highly technical discussions with other faculty and graduate students who had spent much of their time in the same field. This variety of experiences taught me how to communicate complex ideas to audiences with diverse backgrounds, a skill that has remained central to my research involvement.
More recently, I joined the Automated Music Transcription (AMT) sub-team of the AI for Musicians Lab at Purdue. Here, we have been working on performing a literature review of how accurate past deep learning architectures are in transcribing various types of music (e.g., music of different genres, combinations of instruments, etc.). Since these past transcription models are “black boxes,” we are interested in seeing if there is any connection between the complexity of a music piece and how well deep learning architectures can transcribe the song. My contributions have included conducting an extensive literature review on methods for quantifying musical complexity and implementing these techniques computationally (with technologies such as Python, Java, etc.). Since this analysis has not been previously explored in the context of automated transcription, our team developed a novel methodology to establish the potential presence of this connection. Hence, this experience has strengthened my skills in both literature review and methodology design. Additionally, the project has also improved my technical writing skills, as our work is currently being prepared for a journal submission.
Finally, a project which is not necessarily “research” but has still greatly benefited me is the Human-in-the-Loop Chatbot for Coursework Assistance project advised by Professor Bruno Ribeiro. The goal of this project is to support instructional staff by generating AI-assisted draft responses to student questions that the staff can review and refine, therefore cutting response times. To accomplish this, I have been building a retrieval augmented generation system and refining the system with technologies such as cross-encoders. Additionally, we have created API endpoints using technologies such as Uvicorn and FastAPI to interface with our frontend. We have also made a custom evaluation framework to benchmark different embedding and generation model combinations. While this project is more applied in nature, it has provided valuable insight into how AI systems are designed, evaluated, and deployed responsibly in an educational setting.
Together, these experiences demonstrate my sustained commitment to research and my readiness to engage in exciting research through SURF. Building up to this summer, I am also excited to engage in new research initiatives as well. This semester, as a part of Purdue’s Discovery Undergraduate Interdisciplinary Research Internship program, I will be working with Professor Romila Pradhan. Our project will focus on evaluating the applicability of an existing source-free machine unlearning algorithm to tabular data, which is of great interest because of the privacy concerns present when users no longer want their data to be used when training these ML models. I am looking forward to exploring this novel field of unlearning, and I hope to come away with a better understanding of ML.

For the AMT project, when we initially started looking into how to quantify music complexity, we did not have a clear research direction. As it was the first semester in the lab for all of us in the complexity sub-team, none of us had prior experience reviewing academic literature in music research. As a result, our early weekly updates consisted of disconnected findings that lacked a clear connection to the overarching goals of the project. Thus, after recognizing this issue, we sought guidance from our undergraduate team lead due to their prior experience in the field. Together, we established a set of concrete criteria to guide our literature review, such as whether a study measured the complexity of entire musical pieces and whether its methods were reproducible. This allowed us to better focus our efforts more effectively. By clearly communicating our obstacles with our peers and mentor, we were able to get back on track and start producing preliminary results.

statement_of_purpose:
The year Covid broke out was also when Simulation-based inference started to bloom. As a Computer Science major minoring in Biology, I observed a critical gap: It is not enough to assist from viral mRNA sequencing to precise vaccination. We must also infer evolutionary processes to predict future mutations. I am intrigued by the problem of how viruses mutate under the selection pressure of non-therapeutic measures. This kind of computational forecasting became invaluable in 2021 when coronavirus’s mRNA – a highly unstable form of genetic materials – evolved into a more severely destructive Delta variant. For instance, the transition to Delta variants may have a strong relation to the selection for asymptomatic Covid strains in the regions where non-therapeutic measures were applied, such as strict physical quarantines. I am determined to develop a simulation model to programmatically mimic the intensity of non-therapeutic measures and how viral mRNA mutations would progress given those situations. Understanding that pattern will unlock a vision towards more precise immunology and vaccine designs.
I aspire to enter a PhD program in Computational Biology, emphasizing public health, and tackling the huge viral genome data and agent-based simulations with high-performance computing (HPC). While many programs offer summer research, Purdue SURF stands out thanks to its world-class infrastructure, such as the Rosen Center for Advanced Computing (RCAC). Accessing RCAC’s HPC resources will provide me with the cutting-edge technology for me to accomplish my virology and immunology simulation goals. I am specifically drawn to the work of Dr. Xiaoping Bao, whose research into hPSC-derived CAR-T and NK cells addresses the critical bottleneck of scalability in immunotherapy. My background in genomic sequence analysis and agent-based simulation uniquely positions me to contribute to the development of robust, chemically-defined platforms for immune cell production. While my long-term career aspirations are rooted in viral evolution and pathogen-immunity modeling, exemplified by the work of Dr. Pienaar, the experience of engineering and characterizing genetically-enhanced immune cells in the Bao lab will provide the foundational biological knowledge I need to design more precise vaccines and oncology.
Participating in the SURF program will serve as a critical bridge between my undergraduate studies and the heightened demands for PhD in Computational Biology. Beyond the technical aspects of simulations, I am eager to gain scientific literacy and critical analysis. In the era of high-throughput data, possessing the ability to thoroughly evaluate the validity of research articles, including statistical pitfalls such as p-hacking, is indispensable. The SURF program will provide me with a formal environment to hone this discernment. Furthermore, I hope to gain institutional knowledge and mentorship connections by collaborating with Purdue’s faculty and graduate students. Learning how they structure their complex research timelines as well as manage their research agendas will get me ready to lead my own research as a PhD student.
However, my dream could not proceed without challenges. Coming from a pure technical background, supplementing myself with biological knowledge becomes vital to practice bioinformatics. I recognized that a simulation is only as good as the biological logic behind it. I started working diligently through Campbell Biology to force me to think hard about the current high throughput informatic problems in Biology and hence take initiatives. After the two Biology classes I took in college for my minor, I was proud to get a Biology department’s Leading-edge Award for the best student in the department despite my non-Biology major. This experience taught me that I can quickly master new domains through initiative and rigorous study, a trait I consider vital to interdisciplinary research.
During my sophomore year, I was invited to a project simulating ecological and evolutionary processes using parallel computing. Wondering the effectiveness of parallel computing, I tried translating my CUDA program simulating the evolutionary pattern of the Moth species over 100 years to a standard sequential program with pure C++; and the simulation time jumped from 5 minutes to several hours. That helped me realize how powerful parallel computing is to manage complex high-throughput biological data using numerous parallel cores, especially in agent-based simulations. 
Additionally, captivated by numerous bioinformatics posts on social media, I explored human genomics using Variant-Call Format (VCF) data from the 1000 human genomes project. I conducted a principal component analysis with Bioconductor to reduce high-dimensional genomes into their linear representations, facilitating easier interpretation of human evolution into diverse ethnicities. Achieving that opens my vision towards solving high-dimensional viral genome architectures, accelerating effective viral strain evolution generalization. I believe that these sequence analysis skills, combining with my simulation knowledge, will make me competent for precise immunology and vaccination research.

statement_of_purpose:
When my parents grew tired of their TV shows, they would put on space documentaries to pass to time. As a seven year old, I fell in love with the mysteries of the universe and soon began seeking them out in everything I learned. From the space chapters in the children’s encyclopedias to winning medals in the Science Olympiad Astronomy event, finally culminating in an astrophysics research project completed in my junior and senior year of high school. 
After years and years of this passion, I was suddenly at a crossroad: the research project bored me. I spent hours writing code to analyze spectroscopies taken from satellites, writing a research paper, and even getting it published. However, I craved something tangible, a result I could create and hold in my hands, not just limited to the code on my screen. So I began to think deeper about my research question and why it existed to begin with. The spectroscopies gathered had to be cleaned extensively, then further analyzed to determine chemical compositions. Though there is no complete way to rid of external noise in the data, I wondered about how to reduce it, how to increase the strength of satellite instruments, and how to design systems and structures that would survive the space environment. To answer my questions, I enrolled myself in a CubeSat development class, practicing assembly, wiring, and power conservation, culminating in a practice flight with the satellite mounted on a zipline. It was at this moment I knew I wanted to be an aerospace engineer. 
	Within entering college, I knew I wanted to pursue research again, except with an engineering perspective. Thus, I joined the VIP learning community, entering into the project: Laser-Assisted Processing. During this time, I wrote two papers. The first was a summary of recent developments in laser-based manufacturing. The second was about recent developments in AI integration and optimization in laser-based manufacturing machines. Though I felt this was an insightful project, improving manufacturing machines was not what I wanted to focus on in my career. So after I finished my first year in VIP, I chose to take a break and focus my energy on academic clubs instead.
Currently, I have been involved in the Purdue Space Program, since my freshman year. Specifically I joined the subteam Liquids – Test Stand, where we have designed a Test Stand for testing the club's rocket engines. I was responsible for materials choice and procurement. This included completing a trade study on aluminum, choosing the necessary type, and then acting as head of communication for the powder coating needed for the metal. Currently, I help manage the team Confluence, and complete in-person assembly of the Test Stand. 
At the beginning of my sophomore year, I became the Structures Lead for the National Defense Society Pulsejet Technical Team. As the project has just begun, I am currently learning ANSYS and designing preliminary models in NX, later to be simulated through ANSYS FEA. Secondarily, I oversee data organization and onboarding/teaching of our younger members to ensure the team runs smoothly and no one is left behind. Finally, I have decided to rejoin VIP through the team BoilerBird, where we are to design a launch platform for a flapping-wing UAV. I am currently working on the early sketches and concepts of the product, soon to go over reviews where one of the ideas/concepts is chosen.
While these projects taught me technical skills in assembly and materials, they sparked deeper questions about the future of flight and space travel. Rockets always felt too easy, their shape permanently determined in the Space Race. Satellites had variety, differences in their structure as per their purpose. Planes, particularly fighter jets, had that similar type of variety, in all different shapes and sizes. Some built for speed, others built for dog fights, and others built for stealth. I have found myself wondering about the option of an adaptable wing that can change airfoils midair to preserve speed or maneuverability. And, in particular, how to ensure the internal components of the wing reinforce its strength, ensuring that in battle, the plane will be strong. 
However, I recognize that solving these complex problems requires more than just my current technical skills. It requires a level of research maturity that I first began to develop while navigating early academic challenges. One of the biggest issues I faced completing my high school research project was finding the correct papers to read. In my passion, I wanted to know everything about this topic so I began by reading literature reviews. They were long and lengthy, throwing so much information at me from the basic physics to the complexities of the particles within the Medium. I kept digging through different papers to understand the concepts in the literature review, writing down tons and tons of facts that, in the end, were irrelevant to what I wanted to do.   
At this point, I felt overwhelmed and discouraged, so I turned to my research advisor. He told me that trying to learn everything, sometimes leads to learning nothing, that choosing three immediately relevant papers to my research question would help me learn far more than fifty partially relevant ones. He recommended one paper as a start. It made some assumptions about my knowledge but most importantly, it clearly showed the steps to find the Medium. Rather than reading the paper behind every single citation at the bottom, I only read the ones behind the assumptions. From there, I could expand out and properly understand the literature review, but at this point, I knew only to reference it if necessary. In conclusion, the goal of research is to specialize, to find the correct process and steps. 
As a researcher in SURF, I will be sure to do the same. In my future, I expect to complete my bachelor’s and enter the workforce for a few years. After finding my footing in industry, I hope to return to university and get a PhD in aerospace engineering. At the current moment, I plan on specializing in structures and materials within my bachelor’s degree. I expect to pursue a similar path during my PhD. One of my prospective projects includes the development of a material or type of structural wall mounted on a space station/satellite that successfully limits radiation exposure in deep space. If not, referencing my previous research question, the development of an internal wing structure that maintains its strength while the airfoil changes and adapts as per conditions.
I want to join SURF because of the support it offers to its participants. A lot of other universities push independence, creating a gap between student researchers and their advisors. But if there is anything I have learned doing research, it is that a guiding hand makes the process significantly less stressful and simple, especially as undergraduate students. I hope to use the resources to ensure that I am fully prepared for my PhD. From the professional workshops where I can network with fellow students to the symposium where I can sharpen my public speaking, culminating in a final research paper that I can possibly get published, fully readying me for a PhD.

I have always been passionate about mathematics, biology, and physiology, which initially led me to consider medical school. I especially hold an immense amount of respect for my mother, who has dedicated her career to nursing and consistently demonstrated compassion and care for her patients, often going above and beyond her formal responsibilities. 

After shadowing an anesthesiologist, I came to realize that my interests do not lie in direct patient care like my mother. Instead, I discovered biomedical engineering as a pathway to continually improve individuals’ most fundamental asset for a successful life: their body and its function. Engineering embodies what motivates me the most, requiring critical thinking, holistic problem-solving, and the integration of diverse perspectives.

This injury, along with earlier musculoskeletal injuries that continue to affect him, has deeply motivated my interest in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering/biomaterials. This early exposure motivated me to pursue Chemical Engineering, with the long-term goal of developing sustainable technologies to mitigate environmental challenges in my hometown.

In my freshman year, I was introduced to the research of Dr. Dang Bao Trong, whose work focuses on converting biomass waste into activated carbon for wastewater treatment. I was genuinely impressed by the substantial impact of the research, as it addresses biomass waste management and transforms them into porous material for environmental remediation. What impressed me the most was its dual impact: addressing biomass waste management while simultaneously transforming waste into a valuable material for environmental remediation. Motivated by this approach, I decided to join his research group and gained hands-on training in laboratory techniques, materials preparation, and data analysis. 

My current research studies on the sorption behavior of tetracycline on activated carbon derived from algae, corncob, and seafood shell waste. In this project, I was responsible for preparing carbon materials and conducting both batch adsorption as well as continuous adsorption experiments under varying pH and concentration conditions. Furthermore, I have independently studied scientific literature on functional materials and catalysts for environmental remediation and energy-related applications, which strengthened my ability to critically evaluate research papers and identify emerging research questions at the intersection of materials engineering and environmental sustainability.

During the early stages of the project, I encountered inconsistent adsorption data, which forced me to critically re-examine my experimental design. By implementing stricter control of key parameters such as pH and contact time, I was able to improve data reproducibility and adsorption trends interpretation.  Another challenge I encountered in my research training was connecting theoretical knowledge to effective experimental design, which motivated me to adopt experimental skills that go beyond standard coursework. To address this gap, I proactively sought mentorship from my advisor and senior lab members, asking detailed questions about experimental planning, characterization techniques, and data analysis. These experiences significantly strengthened my confidence in experimental work and reinforced my desire to pursue summer research training to further develop experimental design skills and independent research thinking.

I aspire to pursue an academic career as a professor conducting research at the intersection of materials engineering, electrochemistry, and environmental applications to address pollution challenges. My previous research has focused on porous carbon materials for pollutant sorption, where performance is governed by surface functional groups and interactions between materials and contaminants. However, the amorphous nature of activated carbons often limits the ability to selectively isolate the effects of specific surface features on interfacial behavior. In contrast, MXenes offer a well-defined two-dimensional framework with tunable surface terminations, providing an opportunity to investigate surface and interfacial mechanisms within a structurally well-controlled materials system.

I am particularly interested in learning how the Anasori group designs and synthesizes novel MXenes and investigates how transition metal ordering and surface chemistry influence electronic structure and interfacial properties. statement_of_purpose:
When applying to university, I was unsure of what I wanted to pursue. I was never drawn to any particular subject, including computer science, the major I applied to every school with. In hindsight, choosing computer science was naive. In high school, I enjoyed competing in Codebusters, a Science Olympiad event where teams of three raced to decode as many ciphers as possible. Years later, I realize now it wasn’t because I had a burning passion for cryptography, but more so because I loved the camaraderie of competing and working with my teammates. However, years later, I am still a computer science major. The classes I took at Purdue provided a sort of vindication, and I don’t regret choosing to study computer science one bit.

I owe a lot to Lara Du and her teaching in MA351 (Linear Algebra I), my first proof-based math class. It was this class that opened my eyes and helped grow a love for mathematics and computer science. I remember basically the whole class crammed into a small room in the math building every time the homework was close to being due. The homework was challenging because the problems were not a rehash of whatever was presented on the chalkboard during lecture, but they required applying what you already knew to prove and uncover new, untaught facts. For me, solving these types of problems was more fulfilling because it made me feel like I was the one proving these theorems for the first time. To me, computer science is more than teaching me what happens when I connect to my local coffee shop WiFi, how Google autocompletes its search queries, or how a .c file is turned into assembly code. For me, the classes at Purdue have shown that computer science, at its core, is teaching me how to problem-solve and think critically.

One class that reaffirms this belief is CS381 (Analysis of Algorithms). At the end of the class, we learned about reductions, which led to a brief introduction into complexity theory. Although it’s the most well-known open-ended question in computer science, whether P=NP has always intrigued me. To briefly explain, P is the set of problems that can be solved in polynomial time, while NP is the set of problems that can be verified in polynomial time. The class NP-complete contains the hardest problems in NP, meaning any NP problem can be reduced to an NP-complete problem. Why this problem is so fascinating to me is that all it takes is proving just a single NP-complete problem has a polynomial time solution for P=NP to be true, and there are currently thousands of known NP-complete problems. Even more fascinating is that a slight modification to an NP-complete problem can result in a polynomial-time solution. For example, take the independent set problem: given a graph and an integer k, is there an independent set of size at least k? If you knew the graph was a tree, this could be solved in polynomial time using dynamic programming. So to me, it seems that if P truly did equal NP, we would have proved it already, but on the flip side, no one has proved P doesn’t equal NP, which also takes just one problem: showing any NP problem does not have a poly-time solution. So, it seems to me that P=NP is a deceptively easy problem, but since it has eluded researchers for decades, it shows that there is a lot more that I need to learn, and there are different levels of understanding. Furthermore, the fact that something so abstract as complexity theory has real-world consequences is also captivating. In CS426 (Computer Security), I learned about RSA and how it relies on factoring being a hard problem to be computationally unbreakable. However, if P=NP, it would break RSA, which is foundational to many security practices widely used today.

As I mentioned earlier, there’s something deeply satisfying about coming up with the solutions to problems on homework and exams by yourself. What would be even more satisfying is finding solutions to problems that no one else has solved before and pushing the boundaries of what is known. Combine this with the oxymoronic feeling that the more I learn, the less I know; it is one of my future career goals to obtain a PhD in computer science or a computer-science-adjacent field. Yet, one thing I learned from high school is that I have trouble pinpointing where my desires truly lie. For me, SURF is a prime opportunity to test if my heart is where my mind is. Lastly, because SURF takes place at Purdue, I’m already familiar with the environment, so I don’t have to waste time acclimating and can get to work right away.

A common theme throughout my journey in computer science is dispelling my own perceived misconceptions. I remember in high school, I thought computer science was just developing software and making cool applications. I was completely oblivious to the theoretical side. Last summer, I self-studied evolutionary optimization algorithms with a PhD student in China. I read through select chapters of Evolutionary Optimization Algorithms, did the exercises, and programmed some of the algorithms. Before that, I never really had any interest in machine learning. However, through reading the book, I developed an interest, especially after reading the theoretical sections and learning topics outside of my coursework, such as finite state machines. In addition, I thought it was quite creative that some algorithms drew their inspiration from biology, which is a completely different subject. As a result, last semester I joined the Data Mine to work with Bayer on a machine learning project. The goal of this project was to evaluate various machine learning methods for predicting crop yield. Last semester, we reviewed the existing literature, conducted exploratory data analysis, wrangled public datasets, and trained and evaluated models, such as gradient-boosted decision trees and convolutional neural networks. 

Looking back, I felt so apathetic to learning in high school and kind of dreaded college because of that. Yet, my time at Purdue, through the classes I’ve taken, the people I’ve met, and the experiences I’ve had completely changed my mindset. I remember despising low-level programming because to me, it felt like the opposite of theory. It was the malloc project in CS252 (Systems Programming) that opened my eyes. Since malloc is such a widely used function, I expected it to be quite complicated, but in fact, it was quite simple: just a collection of doubly linked lists with metadata. I guess there’s something about the ingenuity and creativity of how people approach and solve problems that I admire. In a sense, I want to imitate that. Getting the opportunity to attend SURF would let me chase this intangible.

“Necessity is the mother of wisdom” - that is how I came to fall in love with the field of Operations Research and Machine Learning. During my first year as a Computer Science major, I was tasked with building a Neural Architecture Search system to automatically discover deep learning models that are versatile across multiple image processing tasks. However, due to limited computing resources, I was forced to optimize the system as much as possible simply to make it work. Coupled with stories of how major scientific discoveries were motivated by the constraints that scientists faced - such as how the DeepSeek team invented new architectures and training methods to overcome limited computing resources - I became passionate about studying optimization algorithms and how they can make computation in various Machine Learning and Operations Research applications more scalable.

By the end of my second year, this interest became more concrete when I was fortunate to be selected as a summer undergraduate researcher in the Georgia Tech REU program under the guidance of Prof. Siva Theja Maguluri. During the program, I studied the almost sure convergence of stochastic approximation (SA), a fundamental iterative framework for finding fixed points of noisy operators, with broad applications in reinforcement learning and control. Our focus was on understanding how step-size choices should depend on the tail behavior of the noise: assuming only that the noise has a finite p-th moment for some p>1, what are the appropriate step sizes to ensure almost sure convergence? It was previously shown for p = 2 that non-summable but square-summable step sizes are required, which suggests that picking the right step size is crucial to obtain almost sure convergence. While classical results largely focus on the finite-variance case p=2, many modern machine learning systems exhibit heavy-tailed noise (1<p<2), where these guarantees no longer apply; at the same time, when stronger moment assumptions hold (p>2), practitioners are naturally motivated to use larger step sizes to accelerate convergence. Although the analytical tools for SA are well developed, state-of-the-art methods could only recover partial and often suboptimal results for this problem, and typically addressed either the regime 1<p<2 or p>2 under additional, more restrictive assumptions. Rather than pursuing an ad hoc approach tailored to a specific regime, I focused on the Lyapunov drift framework, whose central idea is to construct a potential function and derive a one-step drift analysis. This one-step drift will then be used to obtain finite-time bounds and, in our case, almost sure convergence via the Supermartingale Convergence Theorem. However, after many attempts, I realized that existing constructions of Lyapunov drift, while intuitive, could only yield suboptimal results under stringent assumptions, with limited practical implications. This realization proved to be an enlightening moment, prompting me to ask whether the weaknesses of other methods could instead be addressed through a more flexible use of the Lyapunov drift framework, rather than applying it head-on. The outcome was a projection-based iteration technique that combines Lyapunov drift with the upcrossing interval method, rooted in stopping -time analysis from stochastic process theory. This development was exciting for both my advisor and me, as it opened a new analytical perspective that bridges several existing approaches and provides a unified method capable of addressing a broader class of problems, such as finite time bounds for reinforcement learning algorithms or high probability convergence of stochastic algorithms. As a first step, our work on almost sure convergence using this method has been accepted by NeurIPS MLxOR workshop and is currently under submission to ACM SIGMETRICS. For me personally, this experience solidified my research goals: to develop algorithms, methods, and analytical frameworks that are broadly applicable across interdisciplinary domains.
