Moreover, Purdue’s support for international students is especially meaningful to applicants like myself. I am particularly interested in projects proposed by Prof. Vishrant Tripathi, Prof. Reem Khir, and Prof. Yan Gu, whose projects are closely aligned with my past experience and current interest in Optimization, Applied Probability, Reinforcement Learning, Computer Vision, and Optimal Transport.  I am also open and eager to work with other professors, especially those working on Machine Learning and Deep Learning. For these reasons, Purdue’s Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowships (SURF) program represents an ideal opportunity for me to further pursue state-of-the-art research.
Looking ahead, my long-term goal is to pursue a Ph.D in Operations Research or Machine Learning and build a research career at the intersection of Optimization, Applied Probability stochastic systems, and Large-scale Machine Learning. I see SURF as a critical step toward this goal, as it would allow me to engage deeply in theory-driven research while learning from a rigorous and collaborative research environment. More importantly, I value the opportunity to grow as an independent researcher, learn how to ask sharper questions, refine assumptions, and connect theory with practice. I am confident that the mentorship, resources, and academic culture at Purdue would help me mature both technically and intellectually, and I would be grateful for the opportunity to contribute my dedication and curiosity to the SURF program.

statement_of_purpose:
I like to think that the reason why we evolved to stand on our feet is to get closer to the stars. We are a species bound by the earth’s gravity, by our limited lifespan, and by how much we can see with our naked eyes. I am drawn to physics from the wish to push against those boundaries and see beyond the dust clouds. This path has brought me from observing the cosmos to building the materials and tools to make it possible.

That wish led me to join Dr. Kendall Hall's astronomy research at Chico State in June 2024. Our project aimed to determine the best hydrogen tracer for molecular clouds, which is crucial for modeling stellar and galaxy evolution. However, since molecular hydrogen emission is hard to detect in cold diffuse regions, other gases are required to trace it. I helped reveal Perseus's structure by aligning emission maps and validating tracer relationships - turning invisible infrared signals into a map of star-forming regions. Analysis results indicate that hydroxyl associates with hydrogen better than carbon monoxide, but hydroxyl and hydrogen do not quantitatively correlate in diffuse regions. Like carbon monoxide's limitations in detecting CO-dark gas, hydroxyl has its own blind spots, and understanding when to use each tracer is crucial to mapping stellar nurseries.

Dissatisfied with only seeing the universe through a computer screen, I joined the Rocketry Club at Chico State. Like any other team trying to make a rocket fly, we faced complications beyond what some naive dreamers anticipate, from wiring issues and power management to spatial constraints and funding limits. Technical problems felt within my control: I rewired a microSD module to ensure proper SPI communication and designed a compact PCB to save space and reduce wiring-related power loss. But funding was a different issue, because not every experiment could go in the payload if we could not afford the parts. Just like my body is bound by gravity, my dream is bound by money.

At the AAS 245 conference, Dr. Shouleh Nikzad's talk on building ultraviolet detectors for space missions further showed me how finance influences this dream. Silicon's bandgap makes it terrible for ultraviolet spectroscopy. However, her team was constrained by existing silicon infrastructure and funding, so building detectors from other materials would cost more. To overcome this constraint, they created a Si CMOS imaging array on a 2D material capable of detecting UV light. Her team’s work on delta-doping showed me that a key limitation of UV spectroscopy lies in the materials used to build our telescopes. That redefined my interests: constraints are parameters that shape my designs, and I want to engineer the materials that overcome those limits.

If silicon can be modified to detect UV when it "shouldn’t," then maybe we can keep expanding what is possible. This draws me to materials science: the thrill of defying conventional expectations to build better tools. This thrill brought me to Dr. Hanjong Paik and Dr. Thirumalai Venkatesan's research on thin film deposition and characterization, where I characterized barium hexaferrite (BaM) thin film grown on yttrium orthoaluminate (YAO). Traditionally, high-quality thin films require matching film-substrate symmetry, limiting the interfaces we can study. Our project aimed to explore the mismatched growth of hexagonal BaM on orthorhombic YAO. The strain on YAO's pseudocubic surface creates a six-fold oxygen layer matching BaM's basal plane. I analyzed whether this strain-induced growth results in high-quality epitaxy. I performed XRD and XRR to evaluate the sample’s thickness and roughness. I also performed superconducting magnetometry to measure the hysteresis behavior of the film. My measurements supported our hypothesis, showing film quality comparable to bulk materials and those grown on hexagonal substrates, despite symmetry-mismatching.

Just as no single tracer can reveal Perseus's whole structure, no single characterization technique can reveal everything about a sample. At Purdue SURF, I want to expand my toolkit with Raman spectroscopy, photoluminescence, atomic force microscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy to bridge nanoscopic features with macro-scale magnetic properties of materials. Under Dr. Beechem, I want to investigate if the oxygen vacancy that causes ferroelectric fatigue can be mitigated using the same interfacial engineering I work on at OU. Learning from Dr. Zhu, I want to utilize MBE to grow materials that I currently only characterize. Dr. Li’s focus on 3D-integrated CMOS systems would show me how materials innovations can be applied to fully functional computing systems. My characterization experience allows me to make meaningful contributions to each project while learning the fabrication and integration skills I need. SURF would prepare me for graduate school and ultimately a research career in materials engineering, with a goal of overcoming today's constraints - from atomic interfaces to fully integrated systems.

I know my time is finite, but the materials I help build will outlast me. Someone else will use those tools to see the wonders I cannot. In this brief existence, I get to be one of the people who help expand what is possible, building energy-efficient infrastructures that allow humanity to bypass current physical and financial constraints.

statement_of_purpose:
Introduction: I am a highly inquisitive Computer Science and Mathematics junior at DePauw University. Much of my research focuses on the reliability, evaluation, and interpretability of learning-based and generative models, particularly large language models (LLMs) and transformers. In addition, I’m also interested in models that operate on structured sequential data or physical measurements such as audio, vision, and geometric representations. At the Purdue Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) program, I hope to work on projects that integrate modern deep learning with real-world sensing, structure-aware generation, and rigorous evaluation.
Academic Preparation: Despite language barriers, I have structured my coursework to support advanced study in artificial intelligence and machine learning, while developing the theoretical rigor to engage with proof-based research since my first year. I also spent a semester at the Budapest Semesters in Mathematics, studying theory-intensive courses with respected Hungarian mathematicians. This experience improved my ability to read dense mathematical texts and translate assumptions into experiments.
Research Experience: My first scholarly work was with Professor Mamunur Rashid on a question I kept running into in machine learning: when can we trust a model’s predictions and decisions? This becomes especially hard when data are limited, the assumed data distribution is slightly wrong, or evaluation metrics hide important failure cases [1, 2]. In simulation settings where we can generate realistic outcomes but cannot write down a usable likelihood, I explored ABC–MCMC and synthetic likelihood to create training data for tree-based models used in transportation forecasting [3]. I subsequently extended this line of thinking with Professor Sarkar by studying finite-sample decision and ranking rules, showing how the “best” strategy can change with the loss function and sample size, and how often empirical rankings can be misleading [5, 8]. Together, these projects taught me that what looks best under one metric can fail under another, so I learn to frame model performance as a function of objective, data regime, and evaluation design.
As LLMs are increasingly used as general-purpose problem solvers, reliability becomes less about whether the final answer is correct and more about whether the reasoning is sound [4]. I saw this gap clearly as a math tutor, noticing that students often obtained correct answers from LLMs, but the intermediate steps were inconsistent or simply wrong. This motivated my research with Professors Sutthirut Charoephon and Brian Howard to evaluate LLM reasoning in undergraduate computational mathematics [7]. We built CUMath, a benchmark of 2,100 course problems paired with step-by-step solutions, enabling evaluation of both final outcomes and reasoning trajectories. I designed an LLM-as-a-grader pipeline that combines answer accuracy with step-level reasoning scores and automated rubric-based grading, and we found that even strong models frequently misuse symbolic techniques and follow shortcut patterns, producing convincing solutions that break under stepwise scrutiny.
During a semester in Budapest, I extended my work on reasoning reliability while working with a mechanistic interpretability research group. We trained small transformer models to solve a structured game task in generalized tic-tac-toe: given a board state, the model predicts whether it contains a winning state. I then used mechanistic interpretability to understand how the model reaches its decision. We found that the task can be solved with an embedding dimension of just two, and that even minimal models represent the board’s structure geometrically. Attention mainly routes and combines a few learned directions rather than constructing new features. My contributions included implementing constrained model variants that solved a structured tic-tac-toe task with 100% accuracy, analyzing the embedding and attention structure, and designing experiments that linked internal geometry to empirical performance. 
In light of limited research resources at my home institution, I have pursued independent projects in model control and assessment beyond campus. statement_of_purpose:
Early in my undergraduate studies, I realized that coursework alone would not satisfy my intellectual goals. While problem sets and lab exercises were essential for building foundational knowledge, they gave me limited opportunities for the kind of collaborative, open-ended inquiry that I found most meaningful. I was drawn to research environments where problems were not predefined and solutions were not already known. In these environments, I could engage with faculty as a collaborator thinking through unresolved questions rather than simply as a student seeking answers. I wanted to contribute to new knowledge, discuss ideas with mentors, and work on problems with real-world applications. This motivation led me to pursue research experiences beyond the classroom from the beginning of my studies.
My earliest research efforts focused on nanoscale photonic systems. I was motivated by a desire to work with structures where physical behavior is strongly shaped by geometry and scale. I began with finite-difference time-domain simulations of nanoscale waveguide gratings, investigating resonant field enhancement and validating my simulation results against theoretical predictions. This work showed me how small changes in structure can produce significant changes in device behavior. I later explored quantum-scale modeling through simulations of cavity quantum electrodynamics systems, studying atom–photon entanglement and the effects of coupling strength and decoherence. These projects allowed me to engage with photonics and quantum systems as open research problems rather than predefined exercises, which reinforced my interest in nanoscale phenomena and their role in emerging technologies.
These computational experiences motivated me to seek experimental validation and hands-on work with photonics instrumentation. I joined the Translational Optics Imaging and Spectroscopy Lab, where photonics is central to the lab's research. There, I worked on redesigning a diffuse correlation spectroscopy data acquisition system, developing an FPGA-based architecture for real-time signal processing. This work required me to translate photonics theory into practical hardware, manage real-time constraints, and validate system performance using experimental data. Through this experience, I learned about the challenges of building reliable research instruments and how system-level design decisions affect experimental outcomes. Working closely with faculty and graduate students also emphasized the collaborative nature of research and confirmed my desire to pursue it as a long-term career.
My experimental work revealed a broader computational challenge in the biomedical optics community. In my Biomedical Optics course, I implemented a Monte Carlo photon transport simulator in MATLAB that processed tissue simulations at only 770 photons per second. Recognizing this as a fundamental bottleneck—clinical simulations require billions of photons—I pursued independent work to redesign the system for GPU acceleration. I designed a CUDA-based architecture from scratch that implemented complete photon physics, including multiple scattering, Fresnel reflection, and time-resolved propagation. Rather than focusing only on speed, I prioritized physical completeness and efficient memory management. The resulting system processes 5.1 million photons per second—a 6,600-fold speedup—while producing full time-resolved outputs and spatial absorption data. More importantly, inverse fitting of optical properties improved from ~10% error with the CPU baseline to <5% error with the GPU version, demonstrating that the architectural redesign enhanced both performance and accuracy. After completing this work, I presented it to my course professor, and we are currently exploring how to implement this GPU approach into his ongoing Monte Carlo simulation research. This experience reinforced an important lesson in that computational tools developed with real performance constraints in mind can transition from coursework to active research applications. The broader relevance of this work is evident as similar GPU-based approaches are now being adopted by leading biomedical optics research groups, suggesting that computational innovation is increasingly important for experimental progress in the field. Through this project, I independently learned CUDA programming, Python integration, and GPU optimization techniques, strengthening my ability to connect physical modeling with high-performance computing architecture.
My experiences in nanophotonics simulation, quantum modeling, experimental photonics instrumentation, and high-performance computing have shaped my current research interests. I am particularly interested in questions at the intersection of nanoelectronics and photonics, where structural design at small length scales plays a key role in system behavior. As traditional electronic scaling slows, challenges in interconnect bandwidth, energy efficiency, and integration are becoming more important. Optical–electronic integration, including approaches like silicon photonics and quantum-confined structures, offers promising ways to address these challenges. I am particularly interested in heterostructure integration—for example, how photonic and electronic components with different thermal, mechanical, and fabrication requirements can be designed and integrated on a single platform, or how quantum dot structures might enable new capabilities at the intersection of optics and electronics. My interests span electrical engineering, photonics, and materials science, fields that I see as increasingly connected as we develop next-generation electronic and photonic systems.
The SURF program at Purdue represents an ideal environment for the next stage of my development as a researcher. SURF's emphasis on mentored, hypothesis-driven research aligns closely with my goal of pursuing a PhD. It offers structured exposure to the rigor, independence, and collaborative problem-solving required for doctoral study. While my independent projects and research experiences have given me valuable technical skills, SURF offers something different from what I have experienced before: immersion in a large-scale research program with dedicated mentorship, peer collaboration, and access to advanced research facilities. I am particularly drawn to the opportunity to engage in sustained research over a full summer, with the expectation of producing outcomes that contribute meaningfully to an active research effort.
Purdue's strengths in microelectronics, nanotechnology, and heterogeneous integration make it especially well-suited to my research interests. Facilities like the Birck Nanotechnology Center and Purdue's interdisciplinary research culture provide an environment where device physics, fabrication, and system-level integration come together. Even without a specific faculty mentor identified at this stage, I am confident that Purdue's breadth in nanoscale device and photonics research would allow me to find an excellent match for my interests in optical–electronic integration or quantum-scale devices.
My long-term goal is to pursue a PhD focused on nanoscale electronic and photonic systems, with the aim of contributing to academic research or industrial research laboratories. I am motivated by fundamental questions about physical limits and emerging phenomena, but I am also interested in translating these insights into technologies with real-world impact. Participation in SURF would play an important role in preparing me for this path by strengthening my ability to formulate research questions, design experiments, and communicate results in an academic context. I want to develop hands-on experience with nanofabrication processes, advanced characterization techniques, and collaborative research within larger research groups, which would complement my current strengths in computation and instrumentation. Additionally, the professional connections I make with faculty mentors and fellow researchers during SURF would be valuable as I navigate PhD applications and identify programs that align with my research interests.
A challenge I face, which is common in early-stage interdisciplinary exploration, is developing sufficient depth within a broad range of interests. My experiences across computational photonics, quantum modeling, experimental instrumentation, and hardware systems have been valuable for building versatile skills, but I recognize that doctoral research requires deeper specialization. To address this, I have actively sought guidance from my research mentors about focusing my efforts and have used each project to explore different aspects of nanoscale systems. I view SURF as an opportunity to refine my research direction through sustained work on a focused project under dedicated mentorship. This will help me identify which specific questions within nanoscale integration I am best suited to pursue long-term.
In summary, my pursuit of research has been driven by a desire for open-ended inquiry, collaboration, and meaningful contribution beyond coursework. Through independent computational projects and experimental photonics research, I have developed a strong foundation for addressing nanoscale engineering challenges. The SURF program at Purdue represents a natural and necessary next step in this path, offering the mentorship, resources, and research environment I need to prepare for doctoral-level work. I am ready to contribute my computational modeling skills, FPGA-based instrumentation experience, and systems-level thinking to a SURF research project, while embracing the mentorship and collaborative environment that will prepare me for the challenges of doctoral research and a career in advancing nanoscale technologies.

When asked by competitive programmers, it’s quickly solving puzzles and efficiently applying your thought process. Discovering how all the devices I grew up with actually work was like uncovering the architecture of a city I had lived in all my life, the hell that our scientific pioneers endured to create what governs how the digital world works today. Now, we have the paradigm shift that quantum computers alludes to, the revolutionization machine learning has on most if not all, disciples. Nothing is more powerful than having another mind, especially one that will only ever be improving beyond the human scope of things. This topic gets even more philosophical as you question what a mind is in the first place. All these intersections make computer science not a field but a domain. One where saying it has infinite potential is meaningless when we haven’t even begun to realize it fully. I have a curiosity to sate and an endless universe to dine on. Also, I want to change the world. A very simple thing to say, nigh impossible to do. Yet, when you put so much on your plate, you’ll find a way to eat it. Through coursework in data structures and algorithms and computer architecture (where I entirely built a compiler for a simple version of C), I’ve come to understand how it all comes together. How simple gates are used to manipulate information, and what it truly means to be efficient on a digital scale where you can have millions upon millions of data. This understanding was further enhanced through linear algebra, revealing the mathematical foundations underpinning my fixations, quantum computing and machine learning. What captivated me about quantum computing is how novel the way information is conveyed through qubits, bits that are, well... quantum. After participating in a quantum computing school, I gained exciting insight into how this information can enhance our approach to complex computational problems. A less research-oriented but still thrilling endeavor I’ve been partaking in is, simply put, solving problems. More specifically, the art of competitive programming, where you solve interesting, sometimes silly, problems that put my understanding of algorithms and data structures to good use while keeping my mind sharp and fresh. Beyond individual pursuits, I’ve also had experience applying computer science through impactful projects like an internship with a non-profit with the aim of global free education and founding an initiative named Saudi Bits to curate Arabic resources on computer science. Being in a team with others, whether in the workforce or as their leader, is an inspiring experience in and of itself. Seeing your love for something reflected in others and acting on it is a huge motivator.

The most significant obstacle I’ve faced was the leap from high school to college, especially when that leap took me from one country to another. The first year here was challenging. I was genuinely lost. All this talk about dining on the universe would go down the drain, and these ambitious goals were overtly imaginative. Over time, I came to a realization that much of this was in my head. Meditation became the simplest yet most effective method for overcoming the obstacles that plagued me. Sitting down and just thinking, just like a computer listening to its instructions and then processing the information. With time (and the correct instructions and data), there will be a tangible and brilliant output. For me, this was more of the bridge between the problem and its solution. For example, I need more clarification on the subject, so instead of trying to do everything on my own, I’ve concluded that taking the time to think and asking for help is much better than wallowing in my self-anxiety (this a very simple and, now silly, example, but the core idea is simply that acting like a student by taking the time to think to learn rather than think you already know what to do to solve a problem). But, then you slowly realize you can only do so much until the architecture itself is limiting progress. From there, I read up on literature and tried out different architectures to find something I could understand and implement for my model. 

I know I will be immersed in a similarly transformative environment at SURF. I will be on the frontier with like-minded individuals with the expertise and knowledge to back it up and allow me the room to thrive. Seeing the investments that Purdue has been putting into machine learning and quantum computing is exciting. I’ve been given a lot of knowledge here at Purdue, and I’m more than willing to give back by finding what’s beyond our realm of knowledge. Here is where I put my foot in the door to fully realize my dreams and develop the skills to start up the quantum computing research center I’ve always been itching at. I am eager to develop the skills and connections needed to make a lasting impact. Talking with others about SURF, I see there’s more to research skills than just knowing how to write a paper correctly or do a literature review. These are still very important, but I know I’ll be given more, mainly because I know that to achieve what I want, I must make an equivalent effort to get the result. By refining my ability to think, how to present to groups of varying levels, building ideas from the ground up, and tackling challenges collaboratively. My interest in machine learning centers on understanding why models fail when conditions change. Working with hyperspectral imaging, I saw models achieve strong accuracy but collapse under domain shifts, revealing that correlation based learning breaks when data distributions shift. This drove me to explore how structural inductive biases like graph topology, spectral grouping, causal constraints and enable robust generalization under sparse, multimodal, or physically constrained conditions. This research direction aligns with Purdue's strengths in graph neural networks, robust machine learning, and computational imaging, making SURF the ideal environment to advance these ideas toward a PhD in machine learning.
I have been working with Dr. Vishwas Rathi at NIT Kurukshetra and Dr. Puneet Goyal at IIT Ropar(Purdue alumnus) on hyperspectral imaging where I kept seeing models with 98% accuracy suddenly dropped to 75% when spectral bands failed and it bothered me because standard methods treat each band independently. I developed a method to exploit the natural correlation structure between spectral bands by learning to group them and process groups as units. When the bands fail, it maintains accuracy while the baselines collapse because the group structure creates inherent redundancy and the learned groups align with actual physical spectral regions without supervision.
Also with Andreas Zeigler (ETH alumnus), I'm working on event based GNNs. We're developing strictly past dependent graph construction like at each timestamp, topology only includes events that already occurred, enforcing causality by design. This forces reasoning with genuine causal structure rather than bidirectional correlations.
In parallel, through ongoing collaborative investigation with Andreas Roth from TU Dortmund, I am exploring how graph topology and spectral structure act as implicit regularizers that stabilize GNN representations against rank collapse, particularly under scale and depth variations.
In 3D medical imaging, I developed RefineFormer3D, which integrates anatomical priors to identify critical regions like organ boundaries and pathological structures, allocating attention where it matters. UltraLiteFormer3D pushes this further for deployment scenarios like surgical guidance, using adaptive separable convolutions with spatially adaptive token pruning to achieve extreme efficiency. Both are currently under review for publication in IEEE journals.
Beyond academic research, I contribute to PyTorch Lightning and OpenCV. Working on production grade code has taught me the engineering discipline needed for systems that actually work at scale.

Being far from ML research hubs meant no local mentors to debug with, so I built international collaborations through cold emails to Andreas Zeigler at ETH and Dr. Roth at TU Dortmund. This taught me to communicate research through code and visualizations, which translated directly to contributing to PyTorch Lightning where everything happens on GitHub. The first time I encountered ChatGPT, I was struck by both its power and its fragility. It felt uncanny to interact with a system that could mimic understanding so fluently, yet it quickly became clear that something fundamental was missing. Despite their impressive performance, modern AI systems remain constrained by architectures that optimize pattern matching rather than genuine reasoning, abstraction, or conceptual understanding. These limitations convinced me that artificial general intelligence cannot emerge from incremental refinements alone.

I want to dedicate my life to understanding why intelligence arises and how it can be recreated. In particular, I am fascinated by the relationship between the brain’s physical structure and the emergence of consciousness, abstraction, and logical reasoning. I aim to study the inner workings of the mind and to translate those principles into new computational models that move beyond today’s paradigms.

My goal is to work at the intersection of computer science, neuroscience, and mathematics to develop fundamentally new architectures for intelligence. Rather than improving existing systems at the margins, I want to help redefine how intelligence itself is modeled and implemented. This pursuit matters deeply to me because true artificial general intelligence (AGI) has the potential not only to transform every sector of society, but also to advance humanity’s understanding of its own mind.

I wish to attend SURF at Purdue over any other program because it uniquely aligns with my long-term goal of developing artificial general intelligence. My aspirations are interdisciplinary, and it is rare to find a program that brings together the fields necessary to pursue them. SURF’s emphasis on diverse, cross-disciplinary research projects are exactly what I am looking for in my career. 

Beyond the research itself, I am drawn to SURF because of the people it brings together. I hope to meet like-minded students from a wide range of backgrounds and build collaborations with peers I may work alongside for decades to come. I am also eager to learn from leading professors in artificial intelligence and related fields, gaining insight into how experienced researchers approach foundational questions in intelligence. I have enjoyed working with many Purdue professors, and I am blown away by their patience and passion for the subject. Ultimately, I want to work within an institution that understands the profound influence of AI, and Purdue’s commitment to advancing this field makes SURF an ideal environment for my growth.

Extremely passionate about AGI, I have accepted many labs that are related to AI. I am a part of Coral Lab, where I worked on a project with physics-informed neural networks adapted to complex path finding and a project involving reinforcement learning to solve shortest path by learning a latent mapping of space to high dimension. I also worked on a project on semantic mapping and navigation, a method that imitates how humans navigate and remember their surroundings. These projects gave me crucial knowledge about neural network optimization and how the human mind remembers and thinks, and I believe it is instrumental to AGI. 

I also worked on an interesting problem at the AutoIC Lab where I developed an algorithm inspired by the human brain’s intuition to quickly check the accessibility of a floorplan for wheelchair users. With traditional algorithms, this problem was either impossible or took an astronomical amount of time (billions of years) for a solution, but with an algorithm inspired by human intuition, it took 2 seconds. This taught me more about how the human brain visually perceives, and how it logically reasons, and showed me that algorithms imitating the human brain can be powerful. 

Finally, at the PurSec Lab, I developed a dynamic benchmark for evaluating AI security agents based on their ability to act responsibly when faced with malicious prompts. Many of these scenarios required advanced reasoning capabilities, including spatial awareness, chain of thought, and the ability to interpret social cues. Designing these challenges shows how far current systems still are from robust general intelligence. I believe this work is crucial to the pursuit of AGI because meaningful benchmarks are essential for measuring progress. Through conversations with professors, graduate mentors, and peers, I came to understand that negative results are not a reflection of ability but a fundamental part of the research process. I also became more deliberate about seeking guidance when I felt stuck, which helped me move forward more efficiently and reduced unnecessary isolation. I also kept telling myself to enjoy the process, and once I was immersed in doing the research instead of constantly looking at the result, I found myself loving it more. 

By developing healthier habits and a more disciplined mindset, I transformed this obstacle into a source of growth. I am now better equipped to handle uncertainty, persist through setbacks, and maintain motivation. These skills are essential for rigorous research and higher education.

This experience sparked a new interest by offering a fresh perspective on chemistry and its applications. As a track athlete, I found biochemistry particularly engaging because it explains the chemical processes underlying biological phenomena. For example, I pursued a private research project on lactic acid due to its relevance to my daily athletic training. Contrary to the common notion from what I previously knew, believing that lactic acid is detrimental to runner performance, it is actually an essential energy source in the body. The performance loss and muscle “burn” experienced during intense exercise results from the associated drop in pH when pyruvate is converted to lactic acid, which temporarily inhibits enzyme activity. Understanding this direct connection between biochemical processes and real-world athletic experiences deepened my interest in studying biochemistry and its practical applications. Additionally, I question if there are ways to help prevent the pH drop, hence reducing muscle fatigue as a runner. I hope to research this more in my career as a chemist.

One major obstacle I recently encountered involved analyzing data that appeared to contradict previously established findings. In my study of ruthenium based ethenolysis catalysis, I found in multiple publications that electron donating functional groups on the catalyst top ligand were beneficial in preventing catalyst decomposition, a trend I was also confirming in my own research. To further explore this relationship, I modified the catalyst with electron withdrawing functional groups to validate the trend. Unexpectedly, these modified catalysts performed equally well, and in certain cases, better than the original catalysts with electron donating groups. This result appeared to contradict work published more than twenty years ago by Robert H. Grubbs. I returned to the foundational literature and independently explored more recent publications focusing on electron withdrawing functional groups in all types of catalytic structures and behaviors. I also sought guidance from my principal investigator to gain insight into these unanticipated results. Together, we decided to computationally model the electron orbitals of both catalyst variants and analyze their respective individual energy states, both the HOMO and LUMO orbitals. This approach allowed us to formulate an explanation for the apparent contradiction. Differences in electronic properties altered the behaviors of different types of chemical bonds, with electron donating groups primarily influencing sigma bonds and electron withdrawing groups affecting pi bonds. This experience demonstrates how I approach obstacles from multiple perspectives to arrive at a solution. In addition to conducting independent literature research, I actively seek insight from individuals with greater expertise, including my principal investigator and additional physical chemistry faculty outside my research group.

statement_of_purpose:
During my freshman year at SSN College of Engineering, I encountered a research competition that would fundamentally redirect my understanding of what computer science could accomplish. The task, a part of the CLEF CheckThat! Lab competition asked a deceptively complex question: can we teach machines to evaluate whether a tweet is worth fact checking?

This wasn't about keyword matching or simple classification. It required modeling credibility, intent, and information quality. The messy, fascinating dimensions of human communication that traditional algorithms struggle with. Working under Dr. D. Thenmozhi's guidance, I built a multi model pipeline testing BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT, alongside classical approaches like SVM and Random Forest. My system achieved F1-scores of 0.77 for English, 0.61 for Arabic, and 0.57 for Dutch tweets. But the metrics weren't what captivated me, it was the failure cases. Why did the model miss sarcasm? Why did it struggle with code switched tweets mixing multiple languages? Why did performance degrade so sharply across languages?

These questions led me deeper. In my next project with the ILSUM competition, I developed a system to detect factual incorrectness in cross lingual summaries across English, Hindi, and Gujarati. I categorized errors into four types: Misrepresentation, Quantity Errors, False Attribution, and Fabrication and discovered that different languages required fundamentally different modeling approaches. A BERT model that excelled at detecting fabrications in English completely failed at identifying quantity errors in Hindi. This wasn't a bug, it revealed something profound about how linguistic structure shapes meaning.

What keeps me in this field is a realization that emerged from these competitions: language isn't a sequence of tokens rather it's a network of dependencies. Words don't exist in isolation; they form syntactic relationships, semantic clusters, and discourse level structures that determine meaning. At IIT Madras, working with Dr. Rajendran C on aspect-based sentiment analysis of employee reviews, I used LDA topic modeling and BERT to analyze 1,000+ reviews from logistics companies. But I found myself constantly thinking beyond the task: How do we model the relationships between aspects? How do sentiment networks shift when employees discuss "work culture" versus "career growth"? How do we capture the morphosyntactic structures that make certain phrases credible versus suspect?

These questions sit squarely at the intersection of NLP, network science, and robust machine learning, precisely where your SURF projects reside.

I've done internships. At Sure Streak, I configured AWS infrastructure, trained YOLO models, and built Python libraries for standardizing object detection outputs. At MaitiLabs, I facilitated 100+ networking connections for sustainability focused partnerships. These experiences taught me production workflows and stakeholder management, but not intellectual ownership. They answered "how" questions, not "why" questions.

SURF is fundamentally different. It treats undergraduates as researchers, not code executors. Three aspects of SURF align uniquely with my goals:
-> First, publication oriented mentorship. Both my CheckThat! and ILSUM projects were selected for paper submission, but I had minimal guidance on how to structure research narratives, position contributions within existing literature, or communicate negative results. SURF's emphasis on scholarly writing, from hypothesis formulation through manuscript preparation provides exactly this training. I want to learn how to ask questions that advance fields, not just complete tasks.

-> Second, access to faculty working at the exact intersection of my interests. Dr. Arielle Borovsky's work on building morphosyntactic networks for precision assessment and intervention combines everything I'm passionate about: NLP, network science, and real-world impact in language disorders. Her research on semantic network structures for learning interventions addresses the exact questions I've been circling: how do we model language as interconnected systems rather than linear sequences, and how do we leverage these structures for measurable clinical or educational outcomes? 

Similarly, Dr. David Inouye's work on robust machine learning directly addresses my biggest frustration from competition work: models that perform well in controlled settings but collapse under distribution shift, noisy data, or adversarial conditions. His research on causality and robustness would teach me to build systems that work reliably when it matters.

-> Third, depth over breadth. Ten weeks of sustained inquiry allows for meaningful iteration and failure, the kind that produces real learning. Unlike summer internships where timelines demand working solutions, SURF offers space to explore dead ends, reformulate hypotheses, and produce work worthy of contributing to the research community. My best learning came from understanding why my Arabic tweet classifier failed, not from the 0.61 F1-score I eventually achieved.

My goal is to pursue a MS in computer science focusing on robust NLP systems that work reliably in high stakes domains like clinical language assessment, educational technology, or misinformation detection where model failures have real consequences for real people. SURF would provide two critical stepping stones:

1. Research methodology: Moving beyond competition metrics to principled experimental design, evaluation under distribution shift, and interpretation with appropriate epistemic humility. My current work tests many models and reports F1-scores, but I lack training in why certain architectures fail, how to design controlled ablations, or how to measure robustness systematically.

2. Theoretical depth: My coursework in AI Foundations, Data Science, Design and Analysis of Algorithms, and supplemental NPTEL courses in Affective Computing and Privacy/Security in Social Media gave me implementation skills. But I need exposure to theory driven ML research, understanding generalization bounds, learning dynamics, and the mathematical foundations that explain when and why methods work.

My exploration has been structured around 4 pillars:
1. Coursework foundation: I've completed core CS courses including Data Structures, Object-Oriented Programming, Operating Systems, Database Management Systems, and crucially, Foundations of Data Science and Foundations of Artificial Intelligence. My coursework in Discrete Mathematics and Probability and Statistics provided the mathematical grounding for ML theory. To supplement this, I completed NPTEL courses in Affective Computing (relevant to emotion detection in text) and Privacy and Security in Online Social Media (relevant to misinformation research).

2. Competition driven research: Beyond tweet worthiness and cross-lingual summarization, I've systematically explored different NLP tasks. Each competition taught specific lessons: CLEF CheckThat! taught me about multilingual model degradation; ILSUM taught me about error categorization and language-specific preprocessing; the IIT Madras project taught me about aspect extraction and topic modeling. Together, these experiences exposed me to BERT architectures, classical ML pipelines (SVM, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, XGBoost), and the practical challenges of noisy real world data.

3. Independent technical projects: During my first year, I built a course registration system in C that implemented the Gale-Shapley stable matching algorithm to assign students to courses based on preferences and capacity constraints. This project taught me about constraint optimization and algorithmic thinking beyond ML. As part of my AI Foundations coursework, I developed a digital implementation of the board game Splendor in Python, where I designed an intelligent agent that makes strategic decisions using game specific heuristics. This taught me about state space search, decision making under uncertainty, and heuristic evaluation functions in adversarial settings. At Sure Streak, I developed a Python library that standardized outputs from different YOLO based object detection models, reducing evaluation overhead through unified prediction formats teaching me about API design and production ML systems.

4. Self-directed learning: I actively read recent NLP and robustness papers, particularly work on graph neural networks for linguistic structure, adversarial robustness in language models, and uncertainty quantification. I'm especially interested in recent work on semantic networks for clinical populations and morphosyntactic dependency parsing directly relevant to Dr. Borovsky's research.

The hardest challenge I've faced isn't technical, it's conceptual. Competition work taught me to optimize metrics; research requires formulating meaningful questions.
Early in my ILSUM project, I had a functional error detection system achieving >0.6 F1-scores across languages. But when I tried to write up the work, I realized I had no compelling research narrative. I could report that BERT outperformed SVM, but I couldn't explain why Quantity Errors required different models than Fabrications, or why Hindi preprocessing needed different strategies than English. I had results without insight.

I addressed this through three approaches:
1. Faculty mentorship: I met regularly with Dr. Thenmozhi to discuss not just what worked, but why certain approaches succeeded or failed. She taught me to think in terms of linguistic hypotheses. For example, Misrepresentation errors might require understanding semantic similarity while Fabrication errors might require entity recognition. This reframed my model choices from arbitrary experimentation to hypothesis driven testing.

2. Literature deep-dives: Instead of surveying NLP papers broadly, I picked specific subfields like aspect-based sentiment analysis, cross-lingual transfer learning, robustness under distribution shift and read deeply until I could identify gaps. For instance, reading papers on ABSA made me realize that most work treats aspects independently, ignoring the network structure of how sentiment toward "management" influences sentiment toward "work-life balance."

3. Iterative refinement through failure: My first attempt at the employee review project tried to analyze all aspects simultaneously and got overwhelmed. I learned to decompose problems, first validate review authenticity (improving data integrity by 3%), then extract aspects using LDA, then apply BERT for sentiment, then analyze relationships. Breaking research into manageable, testable components became crucial.

This process taught me essential research skills: learning unfamiliar concepts independently (I taught myself LDA topic modeling through documentation and papers), tolerating ambiguity when problems don't have clear solutions, and persisting through technical dead ends (my Arabic classifier failed for three weeks before I realized the preprocessing pipeline was stripping critical morphological markers).

Through SURF, I specifically hope to develop:
-> Experimental rigor: Learning to design controlled ablations, measure model robustness systematically, and interpret results with appropriate uncertainty rather than chasing leaderboard metrics
-> Network-based NLP methods: Hands-on experience building morphosyntactic networks and semantic dependency graphs, particularly in Dr. Borovsky's lab working on language disorder assessment
-> Robust learning paradigms: Understanding how to build models that maintain performance under distribution shift, noisy annotations, and adversarial conditions. The practical challenges I faced in every competition but never formally studied

Growing up, I couldn't choose between my interests- science, art, badminton, Carnatic music- they all fascinated me equally. When India's education system demanded I pick either medicine or engineering, the decision was made easier by my father's unfulfilled dream of cracking IIT. I prepared intensely, setting aside my extracurriculars, working towards a goal that at least spared me from forcefully narrowing my curiosity to just one field.

In 2023, during my entrance exams, my grandfather passed away from colon cancer. We couldn't afford chemotherapy. In those final days, watching helplessly, something shifted in me. For the first time, I felt a pull towards something larger than just academic achievement- I wanted my work to matter, to actually help people. The thought "I should have pursued medicine" haunted me, but it was too late; the exams were done.

I entered IIT Madras in Naval Architecture, then transferred to Metallurgical and Materials Engineering- a change that felt random at first. But once I began exploring the courses, I realized why I ended up here. Materials science sits at the intersection of everything: physics, chemistry, mechanics, and even biology. It doesn't force you to choose one narrow path. More importantly, I discovered that research in this field creates tangible impact- from the devices we use to solutions for global issues.

What captivate me are the fundamental questions: How do superconductors work at the atomic level? What makes materials invisible or capable of camouflaging? How do we engineer materials with properties that don't exist in nature? The fact that materials scientists investigate the tiniest scales is extraordinary. Every material breakthrough has benefited humanity in some way.

That experience with my grandfather taught me something crucial: I don't need to be a doctor to make a difference in people's lives. Research is my way of contributing—working hands-on to solve meaningful problems. 

A PhD is how I plan to pursue research that creates meaningful impact- spending dedicated years in the lab, fully immersed in understanding a problem at its deepest level. Purdue has been at the top of my list for graduate studies. When I learned that Neil Armstrong graduated from Purdue, it genuinely gave me goosebumps- not just because of the achievement itself, but because it represents the kind of environment that pushes boundaries and produces people who do amazing things. Purdue's global ranking in the top 50 for materials science confirms that this is where magic happens.

But before committing to a PhD, I need to truly understand what that path entails. SURF offers exactly what I'm looking for: the chance to work intensively on research, experience the reality of graduate-level work, and connect with faculty who could potentially become my PhD mentors. I've always believed that good mentorship leads to great results, and this internship would let me identify professors whose work aligns with my goals and whose guidance could shape my trajectory. An alumnus from my department did his SURF internship at Purdue and went on to complete his PhD at Cambridge- his journey showed me how transformative this experience could be.

What excites me most about a research internship abroad is the exposure it provides- collaborating with researchers from different backgrounds and gaining perspectives that simply cannot be replicated in a classroom. The research topics I've selected align with my interests while offering opportunities where I can genuinely contribute. While I haven't yet narrowed down my specific domain within materials science, my career goal remains clear: to conduct research that helps people in tangible ways.

My journey in materials research began in the classroom but quickly extended far beyond it. My coursework (CGPA: 9.15/10) gave me the theoretical foundation, but hands-on research revealed what truly drives me. Under Dr. Ranjit Bauri (a professor in IIT Madras), I worked on improving lithium-ion battery efficiency using silicon extracted from discarded solar panels- turning waste into a solution for energy storage. Currently, I'm collaborating with Prof. Tiju Thomas on developing an aluminum-copper nanoparticle-based plasmonic rooftop coating for nighttime radiative cooling as an alternative to air conditioning, specifically targeting vulnerable populations in Southern India. We are in the process of building experimental models at both lab scale and a larger house-like prototype. This project embodies what I realized after my grandfather's death: research can directly improve lives, even without being in medicine.

Recently, I was one of two students—and the only woman—nominated by my department and sponsored by the Tata Group to represent IIT Madras at the International Conference on Advanced Materials & Critical Minerals for Energy Transition at IIT Hyderabad. Interacting with scholars from Japan's National Institute for Materials Science, Kyoto University, and other leading institutions reinforced my commitment to materials research with real-world applications.

Beyond the lab, I've tried to ensure research remains connected to people. As a member of the Effective Altruism group (Oxford, UK chapter at IIT Madras), I engaged with peers on global challenges and meaningful solutions. As a 2024 UN Millennium Fellow, I worked to improve technical skills among underprivileged children- an experience that reminded me why impact matters more than just publications.

A challenge I've been facing, has been figuring out my specific direction within materials science. The field is vast, and I haven't narrowed down to one subdomain yet. Instead of seeing this as a weakness, I've approached it as an opportunity- taking diverse courses like nanomaterials and FEM in the upcoming semester, and exploring different research areas including batteries and computational methods. SURF would be crucial in this regard: experiencing intensive research in a specific area will help me identify what truly resonates with me before committing to a PhD.

SURF at Purdue would be the next critical step in testing whether a PhD is truly my path while building the skills, knowledge, and mentorship connections I'll need to pursue it, and I strongly look forward to this opportunity.

My interest began through the Shell Eco-marathon, where I was pushed into motor controller development. Instead of starting from a clean and functional design, I began by analyzing old nonfunctional controller boards, tracing failures, studying datasheets, and learning why making a motor spin is easy, but making a motor spin efficiently, reliably, and safely is far more difficult. That experience pulled me into the intersection of embedded systems and power electronics, where hardware, firmware, and control theory must operate together as a single system. I realized that combining Electrical and Computer Engineering was necessary to work effectively in this space.

A key moment for me was learning PWM-based commutation from scratch. Early on, trapezoidal waveforms made intuitive sense, but sinusoidal PWM felt impossible because I could not visualize how discrete switching could create smooth phase voltages. I kept rebuilding the concept from fundamentals, understanding how duty-cycle modulation shapes the average voltage and how increasing switching resolution approximates analog behavior. Over time, the idea became clear. Sinusoidal behavior is not analog magic; it is structured switching and timing. That realization changed how I approach engineering problems. That shift began moving me from guessing toward reasoning from first principles, and showed me how much deeper there still was to go. Since then, I have been motivated by deeper questions centered on efficiency and robustness in real systems. How can switching losses and thermal stress be reduced while maintaining control performance? How can field-oriented control remain efficient and stable under parameter variation, noisy sensors, and imperfect models? How can data-driven methods improve energy systems, especially lithium-ion battery state-of-health prediction, so that energy storage and conversion can be optimized together rather than treated as separate problems?

I am applying to SURF because I want to move from project-based learning to structured, mentored research. In particular, the opportunity to work directly within a Purdue research group and contribute to ongoing work, rather than run a standalone project, is what makes SURF distinct from other programs I considered. Many students build systems, but fewer learn how to turn technical curiosity into a defensible research process involving literature review, hypothesis formation, experimental design, validation, iteration, and communication of results. SURF is especially meaningful to me as an international student because it provides a rigorous and legitimate pathway into immersive research, which is otherwise difficult to access through informal opportunities. Its emphasis on faculty mentorship, integration into active research groups, and the expectation of producing research-quality outcomes aligns directly with the training I need to prepare for graduate study and a research-driven career.
My long-term goal is to pursue graduate studies and become a research-driven engineer in embedded systems, power electronics, and intelligent energy systems. I want to work in environments where performance matters and improvements must be measurable, whether that involves motor control efficiency, inverter reliability, or battery diagnostics that enable better energy management. SURF would accelerate that path by strengthening the skills that graduate programs and R&D roles demand. These include the ability to ask precise questions, build reproducible methods, analyze results rigorously, and communicate findings clearly through technical writing and presentations. I also hope to build relationships with mentors and researchers whose work can shape my direction and help me grow into the kind of contributor who produces useful and publishable research.

I have already taken consistent steps to explore and commit to this field. In Shell Eco-marathon, I worked on motor controller development using designs such as Duke University’s EasyController 3 as a learning reference while developing my own understanding of PWM commutation and system constraints. Our first competition involved significant challenges, but we placed 15th out of 22 teams and achieved approximately 74 miles per kilowatt-hour. Since then, I have expanded from simply making systems function to improving efficiency and deepening technical understanding. I am currently involved in faculty-guided research focused on motor control and computation, and I am developing a stronger foundation in field-oriented control and VESC-based workflows to understand tuning, stability, and performance tradeoffs. In parallel, I am working on battery state-of-health research, beginning with baseline models such as linear regression and progressing toward neural network approaches for lithium-ion life prediction. To strengthen my research capability, I pursued advanced machine learning coursework with faculty permission alongside its prerequisites. Outside the university, I completed an internship at Flo Labs where I worked on an ESP32-S3 wearable assistant called CAIPO, contributing to embedded development and system integration, including storage and PCB-level work. I also led a robotics-focused research effort that required rapid learning, coordination, and technical decision-making. Prompt 1:
Briefly describe to us what instances or experiences have led you to pursue your current field of study, and why you continue to pursue it. Answer 1:
I remember a time when I was a young kid where I didn’t really know what I wanted to do when I grew up. A lot of my friends at the time wanted to be doctors, lawyers, or even just simply the trash man, yet I didn’t really have anything in mind. At the time, I didn’t feel like I was “into” something. However, this all changed when I was around ten years old and went to Cedar Point with my family one summer. At the time, I was a bit of a “daredevil” kid. I always wanted to go on the fastest rides or be at the edge of the tallest buildings. However, at an amusement park, I was always significantly limited by the Achilles heel of any adrenaline junkie: my height. Despite this, I managed to still satisfy my want for thrills as a kid. After some time, I found that I had this fascination with roller coasters: how they worked, what they were made from, how they were maintained, etc. So, at home, I started building them out of K’nex. K’nex is a plastic building system, kind of like LEGO, but different in that you only have connecting rods and connectors to create various structures. I quickly accumulated thousands of these parts and began building my own roller coasters from scratch because the ones with instruction manuals were far too basic for me. I started recreating roller coasters from real-life and coming up with some of my own. This included traditional chain lift roller coasters, as well as launching roller coasters (which were much harder) where I used resistance bands inside a “cable guide” in the middle of the track. These systems I made were inspired from real-world methods of lifting and launching roller coaster trains. In doing this, I learned a plethora of engineering concepts that I wasn’t going to be formally exposed to in school for a while. Important concepts such as mechanical energy, friction on axles (which killed me as a kid because it meant that my track layouts were far shorter than I wanted), gear ratios, tension, and pulleys. One thing I remember very distinctly was the first time I learned about tension wheels when designing a chain lift. When a roller coaster train, which is very heavy, is loaded onto a moving chain drive system the tension in the chain is no longer uniform. This meant that when I built my models, the chain would usually snap since the train was either too heavy or the lift-hill was too tall since I had areas of high stress. However, I discovered that if you add a tension wheel to the gear system, which for me was a gear that chain could pass over with just rubber bands attached to the sides, then the tension in the chain would remain uniform and account for the weight of the train entering and exiting the lift at all times. Not only was this an easy solution, but this really got me interested in math, engineering, and physics. While I am now interested in so many more things than I was when I was young, I’ll still never forget what got me into this field in the first place.

In high school, I took all the engineering, math, and physics courses offered, while they were great for basic understanding, I was left wanting to learn more. So, I applied to Purdue and luckily got in! I am currently a sophomore majoring in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mathematics which are both so exciting to me in different ways. For ME, I have really taken an interest in rigid-body-dynamics and thermodynamics. I am currently a part of PURPL (Purdue Undergraduate Research Propulsion Lab) where I am on the sub team TTP (Torch Training Program). In this club, we are designing and manufacturing our own torch igniter which could theoretically be used on future PURPL rocket engines. One big takeaway from this project for me is how designing for manufacturing, as well as other processes specific to the product, is so important. Having a great theoretical design is good, but if it cannot be made a reality, there is a lot of room for improvement. For applied math, I am so fascinated by partial differential equations, particularly with application to engineering problems (such as fluid mechanics), but just by their mystery. We can write these seemingly simple expressions describing macro and even microscopic behavior, yet there is so much more than what meets the eye. One thing that comes to mind is the infamous Navier Stoke’s equations. From a mathematical perspective, we still have a lot of work to do, however, from the engineering perspective they are hard to work with but useful. I find it interesting that better mathematical tools will allow for a more complete understanding of their behavior. Another topic that I have been interested recently is chaos theory: I find it so interesting that so many of the everyday interactions we have (like weather modeling) are so insanely complicated. This reveals that we fundamentally lack many of the tools needed to develop better models for these phenomena. I think it would be super interesting to learn how we can develop advanced mathematical tools to help us with these questions. Next year, when I’m a junior, I want to take MA 520: Boundary Value Problems Of Differential Equations to learn more about the current methods to derive and solve PDEs, which can partially answer that question for me. 
Another thing I’ve been thinking about lately that is related to Navier Stokes that I could delve deeper into, is that perhaps there exists some other fundamental quantity that may allow us to analyze complex dynamics in an easier fashion. Like the role the Action plays in physics or entropy in thermodynamics. I feel like there must be something that we are missing, but I obviously can’t quite tell what it is because all the theory is perfectly sound. Perhaps this is just a thought, but something does feel off related to the topic in my opinion.

I, as I’m sure many others, have encountered challenges during a research project. I mentioned how I was part of PSP (Purdue Space Program) Astrodynamics earlier, and while it truly was a great experience, it was a bit of a struggle for me at the start. The main issue was that I didn’t know anything about orbital mechanics before joining the team, but the main coordinator of the Astrodynamics, Paulo Ramirez, really got me interested in the fundamental mathematics governing the paths we wished to find, and I just couldn’t pass it up. Mathematical relationships such as Kepler’s Equation to find the true anomaly, which requires solving a transcendental equation, or Lambert’s Problem, which is a version of the two-body problem, allowing for us to determine the Keplerian orbit itself, really interested me. At the time, my knowledge of material in this field was practically zero and I also had very little experience with MATLAB, the IDE we would be using to write the code for this specific problem. Despite this, I did have one thing that was the saving grace: curiosity. Either way, I had my work cut out for me. The first thing that helped a lot were these mini lectures that Paulo or other PSP team members would give for us to understand some of the basics, but they moved very quickly, frankly because they needed to. Since Paulo was a graduate student, he had other obligations to attend to so he couldn’t be at every meeting, but I remember myself and a few other peers in the team asking what other resources we could use to learn some of the basics. He ended up sending us this folder with a bunch of resources from 500-level courses, which as a freshman at the time was overwhelming, but extremely helpful. So, we got to work and started reading through these documents. As we learned more about orbital mechanics, it was time for me to gain some MATLAB skills. One course that I took was ENGR 16200, which was instrumental for me to learn how to program in MATLAB since that course requires its students to be proficient in it. I also spent time after class asking my instructor what other topics I could learn in MATLAB that wasn’t already being taught in lecture. He recommended that given the complexity of the project, that I learn how to numerically solve differential equations, a skill that would prove very useful for this project and others. While I knew how to solve a lot of differential equations by hand, I didn’t know exactly how that transferred to the programming world, especially with the various numerical methods that have been developed. So, I asked Paulo to help me and he did considerably. He taught me about particular methods within MATLAB, such as ode45 which was a perfect fit for our particular problem. After some time spent refining my newly developed skills, I finally felt like a contributing member to the team. While I definitely did not write all of the code myself or understand concepts the first time when they were taught to me, I learned about how to ask for help which is one of the most valuable things I’ve ever learned to be honest. I realized that while it may seem easy to try and learn everything on your own and sort of pretend to others, it is so much better just to bite the bullet and ask for help. It is okay not to know something, that is why you are here in the first place! For me, PSP was a humbling experience, but it made me grow so much and I’m so happy that I was a part of it.
